m.1.4.13: have been established by me in the world in many ways, likewise through your grace. Yet even for me, who am thus, a teacher in every respect,
m.1.4.14: the supremely wondrous knowledge that is the means to liberation does not arise. I perform austerity for the sake of liberation; I do not know the reason for that failure.
m.1.4.15: Thus entreated by the sage Vyāsa, the blessed and capable Kumāra, O best of brahmins, declared the definite cause of liberation:
m.1.4.16: Hearing, praising, and the still greater reflection on Śambhu — this triad is declared the means, and it is approved by the Veda.
m.1.4.17: Long ago I too, perplexed and bewildered about other means, performed austerities on the immovable mountain Mandara.
m.1.4.18: Then, by Śiva's command, the blessed Nandikeśvara arrived — that compassionate lord, witness of all, chief of the gaṇas.
m.1.4.19: He affectionately told me the supreme means to liberation: hearing, praising and reflecting on Śambhu, approved by the Veda.
m.1.4.20: This triad, the means to liberation, was told to me by Śiva. O brahmin, practise the triad beginning with hearing — so he said again and again.
m.1.4.21: Having thus spoken to Vyāsa, the son of Brahmā, with his attendants, then went in his own aerial car to his supremely splendid abode.
m.1.4.22: Thus the excellent ancient account has been told in brief. The sages said: O Sūta, you have declared the triad beginning with hearing as the means to liberation.
m.1.4.23: A person incapable of the triad beginning with hearing — by doing what is he liberated? By what action, by what cause, may liberation come even without effort?
m.1.4.iti: Thus ends the fourth adhyāya, in the Sādhyasādhana-khaṇḍa of the first saṃhitā, the Vidyeśvara-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.1.5.1: Sūta said: One who is unable to practise the triad beginning with hearing (śravaṇa, kīrtana, manana) should install Śaṅkara's liṅga and image, worship them daily, and so cross the ocean of worldly existence.
m.1.5.2: He should indeed bring materials according to his means, without holding back, offer them for the sake of the liṅga and image, and worship continually.
m.1.5.3: A pavilion, a gateway tower, a sacred bathing place, a monastery, a sacred precinct, and likewise a festival; cloth, fragrance, garlands, incense and lamps, with devotion;
m.1.5.4: food offerings of various kinds with cakes and relishes; an umbrella, a banner, a fan and a chowrie with all their accessories —
m.1.5.5: all this he should provide for the liṅga and image, as in the services rendered to a king; likewise circumambulation, prostration and japa according to his capacity.
m.1.5.6: He should daily perform the rites from invocation to dismissal with deep devotion. Worshipping the god in this way in Śaṅkara's liṅga and image,
m.1.5.7: he attains perfection through Śiva's grace even without hearing and the rest. Great persons of old were liberated merely by worshipping the liṅga and image.
m.1.5.8: The sages said: Everywhere the hosts of deities are worshipped only in images; how is it that Śiva is everywhere worshipped in both the liṅga and the image?
m.1.5.9: Sūta said: Ah, lords of sages, this question is holy and most wondrous! The one to answer it is Mahādeva; there is no other being anywhere.
m.1.5.10: I shall tell in order what was spoken by Śiva, as heard from my teacher's mouth. Śiva alone, being of the nature of Brahman, is proclaimed as partless (niṣkala).
m.1.5.11: Likewise, because he has form, he is with parts (sakala); therefore he is both with and without parts. Because he is partless, the formless liṅga belongs to him;
m.1.5.12: and likewise, because he has parts, the image with form is appropriate to him. Being of a form both with and without parts, the Supreme is designated by the word Brahman.
m.1.5.13: So he is constantly worshipped by people in both the liṅga and the image. Since others than he are not Brahman, partlessness never belongs to them.
m.1.5.14: Therefore those lords of the gods are not worshipped in the partless liṅga; and likewise the other hosts of deities, because they are not Brahman and are individual souls (jīva),
m.1.5.15: are worshipped quietly only in images, since they possess only the form with parts. Individual-soul-hood belongs to those other than Śaṅkara, and Brahman-hood to Śaṅkara —
m.1.5.16: this is established as the essence of Vedānta, being revealed in the meaning of the praṇava (Om). Just so, long ago, Nandikeśvara was asked on Mount Mandara
m.1.5.17: by the wise sage Sanatkumāra, son of Brahmā. Sanatkumāra said: For all those devoted to gods other than Śiva, everywhere,
m.1.5.18: only an image for worship has been heard of and seen many times; but in the worship of Śiva alone both liṅga and image are seen.
m.1.5.19: Therefore, O auspicious one, tell me that truth, which gives right understanding. Nandikeśvara said: This question is unsurpassed, a secret, marked by the nature of Brahman;
m.1.5.20: I shall tell you, O sinless one, endowed with devotion, what was spoken by Śiva. Because Śiva is of the form of Brahman and is partless, the partless
m.1.5.21: liṅga is approved in all the Vedas for his worship alone. And because he alone also has parts, so he is both with and without parts;
m.1.5.22: and likewise the image with parts is accepted by the world for worship. As for those other than Śiva, because they are individual souls and in every way have parts,
m.1.5.23: only the image is approved for their worship in the Vedic determination. Indeed, when the gods manifest themselves, their form is only one with parts;
m.1.5.24: but in Śiva's manifestation both liṅga and image are indeed seen. Sanatkumāra said: O illustrious one, you have explained the use of liṅga and image,
m.1.5.25: distinguishing, in truth, that of Śiva and that of the others. Hence that supreme liṅga, arising before images and the rest —
m.1.5.26: O lord of yogins, I wish to hear the account of the manifestation of the liṅga. Nandikeśvara said: Listen, child; out of affection for you I shall tell it as it truly is.
m.1.5.27: Long ago, in a former kalpa, when the great age renowned in the worlds had arrived, the two great-souled ones, Brahmā and Viṣṇu, fought with each other.
m.1.5.28: To dispel their pride, the Supreme Lord revealed his own nature between them in the form of a partless pillar.
m.1.5.29: Then, since the pillar bore the mark of his liṅga, Śiva, out of desire for the welfare of the worlds, showed from the pillar his own partless liṅga.
m.1.5.30: From that time on in the worlds, the partless liṅga of the Lord, and likewise the image with parts, were ordained for Śiva alone.
m.1.5.31: For gods other than Śiva only an image was ordained. The image of each of those gods is auspicious and grants its respective enjoyments; but Śiva's worship as liṅga and image is auspicious and grants both enjoyment and liberation.
m.1.5.iti: Thus ends the fifth adhyāya, named The glory of Śiva's liṅga, in the first saṃhitā, the Vidyeśvara-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.1.6.1: Nandīśvara said: Long ago, once, O lord of yogins, Viṣṇu, whose couch is the serpent, lay asleep in supreme splendour, surrounded by his own attendants.
m.1.6.2: Brahmā, foremost among the knowers of Brahman, having come there by chance, asked the lotus-eyed one, who was lying there, all-beautiful:
m.1.6.3: Who are you, lying there like an ordinary man, arrogantly, even after seeing me? Get up, child, look at me—your lord, who has come here.
m.1.6.4: For the deluded, hostile one who, seeing a venerable elder who has arrived, behaves arrogantly, an expiation is prescribed.
m.1.6.5: Hearing these words, Viṣṇu, angry yet outwardly behaving calmly, said: Welcome to you, good health to you, child. Stay; come here and take a seat.
m.1.6.6: Why does your face look as if agitated, with eyes askew? Brahmā said: Child Viṣṇu, know me as the one of great dignity, who has come through the course of time,
m.1.6.7: the grandfather of the world and your protector too, little child. Viṣṇu said: This world rests in me, child; yet you, like a thief, think it yours.
m.1.6.8: You are a son born from the lotus of my navel; you speak in vain. Nandikeśvara said: As the two deluded unborn ones were speaking thus there,
m.1.6.9: I alone am supreme, not you; I am the lord, I am the lord — each wishing to kill the other, they made ready for battle.
m.1.6.10: The two heroic immortals, whose mounts were the swan and the king of birds Garuḍa, fought; and likewise the followers of Brahmā and of Viṣṇu then fought one another.
m.1.6.11: Meanwhile all the classes of gods, travelling in aerial cars, assembled, eager to see that most wondrous battle,
m.1.6.12: showering flowers and watching freely from the sky. There the one whose mount is Suparṇa Viṣṇu, enraged, at Brahmā's chest
m.1.6.13: released unbearable arrows and many weapons of various kinds. Then Vidhi Brahmā, enraged, released at Viṣṇu's chest unbearable
m.1.6.14: arrows resembling fire, and weapons in great numbers. Then, clearly seeing that wonder taking place in the battle between the two,
m.1.6.15: the hosts of gods, greatly agitated, praised it. Then Viṣṇu, exceedingly enraged, breathing hard, worn down by distress,
m.1.6.16: the wise one fitted the Māheśvara missile against Brahmā. Then Brahmā, greatly enraged, making the whole universe tremble,
m.1.6.17: fitted the terrible Pāśupata missile against Viṣṇu's chest. Then it rose up in the sky, like ten thousand suns,
m.1.6.18: thousand-mouthed, extremely fierce, frightful like a violent storm—this pair of missiles of Brahmā and Viṣṇu there was terrifying.
m.1.6.19: Thus the battle between Brahmā and Viṣṇu took place. Then all the hosts of gods, dejected and greatly agitated, spoke to one another, dear one, as brāhmaṇas do when the king is in turmoil.
m.1.6.20: To him from whom creation, preservation, destruction, concealment and grace proceed—to that Brahman, the trident-bearer, we bow.
m.1.6.21: He without whose grace even the destruction of a blade of grass here is impossible for others, anywhere, of their own will.
m.1.6.22: Thus, seized by fear, the gods, searching for Śiva's abode, went to the peak of Kailāsa, where the moon-crested one dwells.
m.1.6.23: Seeing thus that abode of the Supreme Lord, the immortals rejoiced; they bowed to it, shaped like the Praṇava Om, and entered that dwelling.
m.1.6.24: There, in the midst of the assembly, in the pavilion, upon a jewelled seat, they beheld the foremost of gods shining together with Umā,
m.1.6.25: with his left foot placed over the other, his lotus-hand resting upon it, attended on all sides by his own gaṇas, marked with every auspicious sign,
m.1.6.26: being fanned by skilled women of intense devotion, ever praised by the Vedas—the Lord, bestowing grace.
m.1.6.27: Seeing the Lord thus, the immortals, their eyes wet with tears of joy, together with the great gaṇas, prostrated like a staff from afar, dear one.
m.1.6.28: Seeing those gods, the Lord summoned them near through his gaṇas. Then the god, crest-jewel of the gods, gladdening the gods, spoke words deep, sweet and auspicious.
m.1.6.iti: Thus ends the sixth adhyāya, named The journey of the gods to Kailāsa, in the first saṃhitā, the Vidyeśvara-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.1.7.1: Īśvara said: Dear children, is all well with you? Under my command, are the world and the race of gods continuing in their own duties, or not?
m.1.7.2: O gods, the battle of Brahmā and Viṣṇu was already known to me; yet because of your distress it has been told to me again and again.
m.1.7.3: Thus, O Kumāra, with smiling, sweet speech, he, the husband of Ambā, gladdened that host of gods.
m.1.7.4: Then the overlord of Hari and Brahmā, intending to go to the battlefield, commanded a hundred chiefs of the gaṇas right there in the assembly.
m.1.7.5: Then there arose music of many kinds for the departure of the supreme Lord, and the lords of the gaṇas stood equipped, with various vehicles and ornaments.
m.1.7.6: The Lord, husband of Ambikā, mounted the auspicious chariot shaped like the praṇava (Om), complete from beginning to end, adorned with five circles. All the gods, Indra and the others, followed him along with his sons and gaṇas.
m.1.7.7: Honoured with multitudes of bright banners, fans, chowries, showers of flowers, songs and dances, and with bands of musical instruments, Paśupati, together with the supreme Goddess, went with his army to the battlefield of those two.
m.1.7.8: Having observed their battle, he stationed himself, hidden, in the sky, the sound of the instruments ended and the din of the great hosts stilled.
m.1.7.9: Then the two heroes Brahmā and Acyuta, desiring to kill each other, fought with the Māheśvara weapon and likewise with the Pāśupata.
m.1.7.10: Then, by the flames of the weapons of Brahmā and Viṣṇu, the three worlds were burnt. The Lord too, having seen that untimely dissolution, grew intensely...
m.1.7.11: ...he, the partless one, took on a terrifying form like a great pillar of fire in the ground between them.
m.1.7.12: And those two weapons, flaming and capable of destroying the worlds, fell down in a single instant when the great fire appeared.
m.1.7.13: Having seen that wondrous, strange, auspicious sight that quelled the weapons, they said to one another, what is this of wondrous form?
m.1.7.14: What is this pillar, beyond the senses and in the form of fire, that has arisen? Its top and its bottom must indeed be our goal to discover.
m.1.7.15: Thus resolved, the two heroes, proud of their valour, joined together and, intent on it, quickly set out to investigate it.
m.1.7.16: If we two stay together, the single task cannot be accomplished there. Having said this, Viṣṇu, in the body of a boar, went towards its base.
m.1.7.17: Likewise Brahmā, in the body of a swan, went to see its end. Hari, having pierced through the realm of Pātāla and gone very far,
m.1.7.18: did not see the base of that pillar of fiery splendour. Exhausted, that boar-Hari returned to the former battlefield.
m.1.7.19: Then, dear child, Vidhi, your father, travelling through the sky, saw a wondrous ketakī flower that had fallen somewhat,
m.1.7.20: exceedingly fragrant and unwithered, though it had been falling for many years. And having observed the doings of those two, the blessed Supreme Lord
m.1.7.21: laughed in jest; from the shaking his head moved, and from it the excellent ketaka fell, in order to show favour to those two.
m.1.7.22: Brahmā asked: Why are you falling, O lord of flowers? King of flowers, by whom were you held? The flower replied: I have been falling for a long time from the middle of the pillar of the primeval, immeasurable one.
m.1.7.23: I do not see its end; therefore give up hope of seeing the end. Brahmā said: I have come here in the form of a swan for the sake of reaching its end.
m.1.7.24: From now on, friend, you must today do what I desire: together with me you must say this in the presence of Viṣṇu:
m.1.7.25: The end of the pillar was seen by the Creator; I am the witness to that, O Acyuta. Having said this, he bowed to the ketaka there again and again. Even untruth is approved in a time of distress — such is the precept.
m.1.7.26: Seeing Acyuta there, long wearied and with his joy gone, he danced for joy; and then that Vidhi, having taken up false, unmanly speech, spoke to Acyuta as though it were the truth:
m.1.7.27: The top of this pillar has been seen, O Hari; and this ketaka here is surely the witness to it. Then the ketaka falsely said there, in his presence, it is so, confirming the Creator's words.
m.1.7.28: And Hari, thinking it to be true, himself paid homage to Vidhi, and worshipped that Vidhi with the sixteen offerings.
m.1.7.29: To punish the deceitful Vidhi, the Lord there emerged with a form from the fiery liṅga. Then Viṣṇu, rising up at the sight of the Master, with trembling hands clasped his feet and said:
m.1.7.30: Regarding you, whose body has neither beginning nor end, great inquiry born of desire, pursued with a deluded mind, does not save one here. So be gracious, O mine of compassion; forgive our fault and let it be wiped away — it was brought about by you yourself in play.
m.1.7.31: Īśvara said: Child Hari, I am pleased, since you, though desiring lordship, spoke truthful words. Therefore among people you shall have equality with me, and honour too has been obtained by you.
m.1.7.32: From now on, for you as a separate self, there shall be establishment of sacred sites, festivals, and worship.
m.1.7.33: Thus long ago the God, greatly pleased by his truthfulness, granted Hari supreme equality with himself, while the host of gods looked on.
m.1.7.iti: Thus ends the seventh adhyāya, named The appearance of the pillar of fire, in the first saṃhitā, the Vidyeśvara-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.1.8.1: Nandīśvara said: Then Mahādeva created, from between his brows, a certain wondrous being called Bhairava, with the intent of destroying Brahmā's pride.
m.1.8.2: Then, there in the courtyard, having bowed to his lord Śiva, he said: What task shall I do here? Command me quickly, O Lord.
m.1.8.3: Śiva said: Child, this Vidhi Brahmā here, who is in person the primal deity of the worlds — surely worship him, the supreme one, swiftly with a sharp sword.
m.1.8.4: He, seizing with one hand the hair of that fifth head — arrogant and speaking falsehood — cut off the head and was ready to kill him, brandishing the sword conspicuously in his hands.
m.1.8.5: Your father, his ornaments, garments, garland, upper cloth and mass of clean hair all fallen away, trembling like a plantain tree in the wind or like a creeper, fell at Bhairava's lotus feet.
m.1.8.6: Meanwhile, dear one, the compassionate Acyuta, wishing to see Vidhi safe, bathed the tender feet of our lord with tears and, with joined palms, spoke in sweet faltering syllables, as a child to his own father.
m.1.8.7: Acyuta said: O Lord, since it was you who formerly, with care, gave him this five-faced mark, therefore forgive him; he deserves grace today — show favour to this Vidhi.
m.1.8.8: Thus entreated by Acyuta, the Lord, pleased, in the courtyard thronged by the hosts of gods, then restrained Bhairava from punishing Brahmā.
m.1.8.9: Then the god said to the cheat Vidhi, whose fifth head was gone: O Brahmā, craving worship, you assumed lordship by deceit.
m.1.8.10: Therefore may there be no honour for you in the world — no shrines, festivals and the like. Brahmā said: Master, be gracious today, O one of great glory; I regard the sparing of my remaining heads as a boon.
m.1.8.11: Salutation to you, the Blessed One, the kinsman of all, source of the universe, forbearing of faults, Śambhu, whose bow is a mountain.
m.1.8.12: Īśvara said: Without fear of a ruler this whole world will perish. Therefore you, child, strike down those deserving punishment and bear the burden of the world.
m.1.8.13: I grant you a boon in this; accept it, rare and supreme: in śrauta and domestic rites and in sacrifices you shall be the presiding priest.
m.1.8.14: Without you a sacrifice, even complete with its subsidiary parts and fees, is fruitless. Then the god spoke to the cheat Ketaka, the false witness:
m.1.8.15: O Ketaka, you are wicked. Deceiver, go far from here. From now on let there be no love of mine for your flower in worship.
m.1.8.16: When the god had said this, all the classes of gods then drove Ketaka away from his side to elsewhere.
m.1.8.17: The ketaka flower said: Salutation to you, Lord. By your command my birth has become fruitless. Let it be made fruitful, father; let my sin be forgiven.
m.1.8.18: Remembrance of you destroys sin committed knowingly or unknowingly. Now that I have seen such a one as you, how could the fault of falsehood remain in me?
m.1.8.19: Thus praised by Ketaka in the assembly hall, the Lord said: It is not proper for me to wear you; I, the Lord, am truthful of speech.
m.1.8.20: My own devotees will wear you; thereby your birth will be fruitful. And you shall be above me in the form of a canopy.
m.1.8.21: Having thus shown grace to Ketaka, Vidhi and Mādhava, the Lord shone in the midst of the assembly, praised by all the gods.
m.1.8.iti: Thus ends the eighth adhyāya, named Śiva's grace, in the first saṃhitā, the Vidyeśvara-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.1.9.1: Nandīśvara said: Meanwhile the two, Vidhi (Brahmā) and Mādhava (Viṣṇu), bowed to the Lord and stood silent with palms joined in reverence, one on his right and one on his left.
m.1.9.2: There, having seated the god together with his family on an excellent seat, the two worshipped the worshipful one with holy articles of the puruṣa kind.
m.1.9.3: A pauruṣa article and a prākṛta article should be understood as long-lasting and short-lasting respectively. With necklaces, anklets, armlets, crowns and jewelled earrings,
m.1.9.4: with sacred threads, upper garments, garlands, silk cloths, wreaths and rings; with flowers, betel, camphor, and unguents of sandal and aguru,
m.1.9.5: with incense, lamps, white umbrellas, fans, banners and chowries, and with other divine offerings whose splendour is beyond speech and mind,
m.1.9.6: with things fit for the Lord and unattainable by bound souls (paśu), the two worshipped the Lord (Pati). Whatever most excellent article was fit for the Lord, O Hitadhvaja,
m.1.9.7: all those articles the Lord, delighted, wishing to establish a tradition, gave away there to the members of the assembly, separately and in due order.
m.1.9.8: A great clamour arose there: Let this article be taken. There itself Śaṅkara, earlier worshipped by Brahmā and Viṣṇu,
m.1.9.9: pleased, the increaser of devotion smilingly spoke to the two, who were bowing humbly. The Lord said: I am pleased with you today, dear children, by your worship on this great day.
m.1.9.10: Therefore this day will become supremely holy. This lunar day, famed as Śivarātri, is dear to me.
m.1.9.11: Whoever performs worship of my liṅga and my image at this time, that man would, as it were, perform the work of the world—maintenance, creation and the rest.
m.1.9.12: On Śivarātri, fasting day and night, with senses subdued, one should worship according to rule and according to one's strength, without deceit.
m.1.9.13: The fruit that comes from worshipping me continuously for one year—that fruit one obtains at once by worshipping me on Śivarātri.
m.1.9.14: This is the time for the growth of my dharma, like the moon's time for the ocean; in it should be held my festival of installation and the like, a home of auspiciousness.
m.1.9.15: Moreover, the time when I formerly manifested myself in the form of a pillar—that time, O children, is in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa under the asterism Ārdrā.
m.1.9.16: Whoever, on Ārdrā in Mārgaśīrṣa, sees me as the companion of Umā, or even my image or liṅga, is dearer to me than even Guha.
m.1.9.17: On that auspicious day the fruit from mere sight is ample; if there is worship, the fruit is greater still, beyond the reach of words.
m.1.9.18: Since on this battlefield I expanded in the body of a liṅga, like a liṅga, therefore this shall be the place of the liṅga.
m.1.9.19: This pillar without beginning or end will become small in size, for the worlds to see it and to worship it, O dear sons.
m.1.9.20: This liṅga brings enjoyment and is the sole means to worldly enjoyment and liberation; through seeing, touching and meditating on it, creatures are released from birth.
m.1.9.21: Since this liṅga rose up resembling a mountain of fire, it will gain fame as Aruṇācala.
m.1.9.22: Here there will be many great holy places, and here too creatures will obtain liberation by residing and by dying.
m.1.9.23: There will be auspicious events such as chariot festivals and habitations of people all around. Whatever is given, offered in fire, or recited here will become ten-million-fold.
m.1.9.24: This sacred field is greater than all my other sacred fields. Here embodied beings attain liberation by mere remembrance.
m.1.9.25: Therefore this sacred field is greater, exceedingly beautiful, full of every auspiciousness, auspicious, and the bestower of liberation on all.
m.1.9.26: By worshipping here me alone, the Lord who abides in the liṅga, within the liṅga, one attains sālokya (same world), sāmīpya (proximity), sārūpya (same form), sārṣṭi (equal power),
m.1.9.27: and sāyujya (union)—these five are held to be the fruits of ritual action and the rest. All of you will swiftly obtain your every desire.
m.1.9.28: Nandikeśvara said: Having thus blessed the humble Vidhi and Mādhava, the Lord—the armies of the two which had earlier struck each other down in battle—
m.1.9.29: those he fully revived by a stream of nectar, his own power. And to remove their delusion and enmity he spoke to the two:
m.1.9.30: I have two forms, with parts (sakala) and without parts (niṣkala). No one else has them; therefore all others are not Lord.
m.1.9.31: First in the form of a pillar, and afterwards in embodied form, O children: the partless is declared to be Brahman-hood, and the form with parts likewise Lordship.
m.1.9.32: Both are established in me alone, not in anyone other than me. Therefore Lordship belongs nowhere to others, not even to you two.
m.1.9.33: Through ignorance of this, your most astonishing pride of lordship arose; to dispel it I thus rose up here on the battlefield.
m.1.9.34: Abandon your own pride and fix your mind on me, the Lord. By my grace every object in the worlds becomes manifest.
m.1.9.35: In that, the teacher's word is what reveals, or is the authority, again and again. Out of affection for you I declare this hidden truth of Brahman.
m.1.9.36: I alone am the supreme Brahman; my nature is both with parts and without parts. Because of being Brahman I am also Īśvara; my functions are grace and the rest.
m.1.9.37: Because of vastness (bṛhattva) and expanding (bṛṃhaṇatva) I am Brahman, O Brahmā and Keśava; likewise, because of sameness and all-pervasiveness I am the Self (Ātman), O children.
m.1.9.38: All others are not the Self; they are only individual souls (jīva), without doubt. And the fivefold work of the world, beginning with grace and ending with creation,
m.1.9.39: is always mine, by virtue of my Lordship, and not anyone else's. In the beginning, the partless liṅga rose up so that my Brahman-hood might be understood.
m.1.9.40: Then, to make clearly manifest to you the Lordship that was unknown to you, I at once became embodied (sakala), the Lord in person.
m.1.9.41: Therefore my lordship (Īśa-hood) should quickly be understood as my embodied (sakala) aspect, while this formless (niṣkala) pillar makes known my Brahman-nature.
m.1.9.42: Because it possesses the characteristics of a liṅga (mark), this shall be my liṅga. Therefore, dear sons, this should be worshipped by you two here constantly.
m.1.9.43: This is ever of my very nature and the means of my presence. It is always to be greatly worshipped, because there is no difference between the liṅga and the one it signifies (the liṅgin).
m.1.9.44: Wherever and by whomever such a liṅga of mine is installed, there I myself am installed, though I am in truth beyond installation, O dear children.
m.1.9.45: Equality with me is declared to be the fruit of installing one liṅga; when a second liṅga is installed, the fruit is indeed oneness with me.
m.1.9.46: The liṅga is to be installed as the principal object of worship, while the image (bera) is secondary. Where there is no liṅga, that place is not a sacred site, even if it has images on all sides.
m.1.9.iti: Thus ends the ninth adhyāya, named The naming of Śiva as Maheśvara, in the first saṃhitā, the Vidyeśvara-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.1.10.1: Brahmā and Viṣṇu said: O Lord, tell us the defining nature of the five tasks beginning with creation. Śiva said: Out of compassion I shall explain to you both the secret teaching about my tasks.
m.1.10.2: Creation, maintenance, dissolution, concealment and grace — these five alone are my eternally established tasks concerning the world, O Aja (Brahmā) and Acyuta (Viṣṇu).
m.1.10.3: Creation is the setting in motion of saṃsāra; its establishment is considered maintenance. Dissolution is its crushing; concealment is its removal.
m.1.10.4: Liberation from it is grace. Thus indeed my task is fivefold. Another carries this task silently, like the figure on a gateway tower.
m.1.10.5: The four tasks beginning with creation are the unfolding of saṃsāra; the fifth is indeed the cause of liberation, and it is ever firmly established in me.
m.1.10.6: This is seen by my people in the five elements: creation in earth, maintenance in water, and likewise dissolution in fire,
m.1.10.7: concealment in wind, and similarly grace here in space. Everything is produced by earth; everything grows by waters;
m.1.10.8: everything is consumed by fire and carried away by wind; everything is graced by space. Thus indeed should it be understood by the wise.
m.1.10.9: To carry out these five tasks I have a set of five faces: four faces in the four directions and a fifth face in their middle.
m.1.10.10: O sons, you two obtained through austerity these two tasks called creation and maintenance — a very dear good fortune — from me, who was pleased.
m.1.10.11: Likewise the other pair of tasks was obtained by Rudra and Maheśa; but the supreme one called grace cannot be obtained by anyone at all.
m.1.10.12: All that former deed has been forgotten by you two through time; such a deed has not been forgotten by Rudra and Maheśa.
m.1.10.13: Therefore, for that reason, I have granted them equality with me in form, attire, task, vehicle, seat, weapons and the like.
m.1.10.14: O dear ones, through lack of meditation on me this delusion has come upon you two. When there is knowledge of me, there would not be such pride, even having a form like Maheśa's.
m.1.10.15: Therefore, for the attainment of knowledge of me, from now on repeat my mantra named Oṃkāra, which breaks pride.
m.1.10.16: I have taught you my own mantra, the greatly auspicious Oṃkāra. The Oṃkāra arose first from my mouth, revealing me.
m.1.10.17: This is the signifier, I am the signified; this mantra is indeed of my very nature. Its constant remembrance would be constant remembrance of me.
m.1.10.18: First the syllable a arose from the northern face, u from the western face, m from the southern face, and likewise the bindu from the eastern face,
m.1.10.19: and the nāda from the middle face. Thus it unfolded fivefold; then, becoming unified again in the same way, it became the single syllable Om.
m.1.10.20: Everything consisting of name and form — the two groups of Veda (words) and beings — is pervaded by this mantra; and it reveals Śiva and Śakti.
m.1.10.21: From this was born the five-syllabled mantra, which reveals all — in the order of a and the rest, its syllables beginning with na in due sequence.
m.1.10.22: From this five-syllabled mantra arose the mātṛkās (the letters of the alphabet) in five divisions; from that, from the head and the four faces, arose the three-footed Gāyatrī.
m.1.10.23: From that the whole Veda was born, and from that indeed crores of mantras. By each particular mantra comes its particular accomplishment; from this Oṃkāra comes every accomplishment.
m.1.10.24: By this root of mantras both enjoyment and liberation are accomplished. All the other auspicious royal mantras directly grant enjoyment.
m.1.10.25: Nandīśvara said: Then there the Guru, together with Ambikā, having arranged a screen for the two of them, and gently placing his lotus-hand on their heads as they sat facing north, imparted the supreme mantra.
m.1.10.26: The mantra having been uttered three times, each received the mantra along with the explanation of yantra and tantra; and the two disciples offered themselves as the teacher's fee.
m.1.10.27: With joined hands, standing near him, the two of them spoke to him, the best of gods, the Guru of the world.
m.1.10.28: Brahmā and Acyuta said: Salutation to the one whose form is without parts; salutation to the one whose radiance is without parts; salutation to the Lord of all; salutation to you, the Self of all.
m.1.10.29: Salutation to the one signified by the Praṇava; salutation to the one whose emblem is the Praṇava; salutation to the maker of creation and the rest; salutation to you, the five-faced one.
m.1.10.30: Salutation to you, whose nature is the five Brahmans, who perform the five tasks; to you, the Self, Brahman, whose power consists of endless qualities;
m.1.10.31: salutation to Śambhu, the Guru, whose form is both with parts and without parts. Having thus praised the Guru with verses, Brahmā and Viṣṇu bowed down.
m.1.10.32: Īśvara said: O dear children, the whole truth has been told and shown to you both. Repeat the Praṇava mantra, taught by the Goddess, which is of my very nature.
m.1.10.33: Knowledge becomes firmly established, and all good fortune becomes everlasting. Repetition of it on the fourteenth lunar day when the asterism is Ārdrā becomes inexhaustible in merit.
m.1.10.34: On the Mahārdrā, determined by the sun's course, a single repetition becomes a crore-fold. The last part of Mṛgaśīrṣa and likewise the first part of Punarvasu
m.1.10.35: should always be known as equal to Ārdrā for worship, fire-offering, libations and the like. The viewing of the deity is best at dawn, in the early-morning and saṅgava (forenoon) periods.
m.1.10.36: Likewise the fourteenth lunar day to be adopted should be one that extends through midnight; one extending through the evening twilight (pradoṣa), joined with the following day, is also commended.
m.1.10.37: The liṅga and the image are equal for me; yet for worshippers the liṅga is superior. Therefore those seeking liberation should worship the liṅga as higher even than the image.
m.1.10.38: The liṅga should be installed with the Oṃkāra mantra, and the image with the five-syllabled mantra, with good materials, by oneself or even by others.
m.1.10.39: One should worship with the ritual offerings; then my abode becomes easy to attain. Having thus instructed the two disciples, Śiva vanished right there.
m.1.10.iti: Thus ends the tenth adhyāya, named The teaching of Oṃkāra, in the first saṃhitā, the Vidyeśvara-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.1.11.1: The sages said: How should the liṅga be installed, and what are its characteristics? And how, at what place and time, and by whom, should it be worshipped?
m.1.11.2: Sūta said: For your sake I shall explain; let it be understood attentively. At a favourable, auspicious time, at a holy sacred place or on a riverbank,
m.1.11.3: a liṅga should be set up as one wishes, where there may be daily worship, made of earth, of water-born substance, or of fiery metal, according to one's liking.
m.1.11.4: A liṅga endowed with the marks prescribed in the ritual manuals obtains the fruit of worship; one endowed with all the marks gives the fruit of worship immediately.
m.1.11.5: For a movable liṅga a small one is preferred; for a fixed one, a large one indeed. One should install a liṅga fashioned for Śiva, with the proper marks and with a pedestal.
m.1.11.6: The liṅga pedestal—circular, square, or else triangular—narrow in the middle like the leg of a bedstead (khaṭvāṅga), yields great fruit.
m.1.11.7: First, the liṅga is made from clay, stone and the like, or made of metals and the like. For a fixed liṅga, the pedestal made of the same material as the liṅga is preferred.
m.1.11.8: In a movable liṅga, liṅga and pedestal are one piece, except for the bāṇa-liṅga. The best measure of a liṅga is twelve finger-breadths of the maker.
m.1.11.9: If it is smaller, the fruit will be small; larger is not faulty at all. For a movable one too, likewise, it should be one finger-breadth of the maker less.
m.1.11.10: First a temple (vimāna) adorned with hosts of deities should be built by craftsmanship; there, in a sanctum that is beautiful, firm, and gleaming like a mirror,
m.1.11.11: adorned with the nine gems, with doors in the cardinal directions and a principal door—the nine gems being sapphire, ruby, cat's-eye, dark-blue stone, emerald,
m.1.11.12: pearl, coral, gomeda and diamond—these are the nine gems. In the centre is placed the liṅga; one should deposit precious substances along with the Vedic rites.
m.1.11.13: Having worshipped the liṅga with the mantras beginning with Sadyojāta in the five places in due order, and having offered oblations of ghee in many ways into the fire to me together with my retinue,
m.1.11.14: having honoured the guru and the preceptor with wealth, and kinsmen with desired things, one should give riches to supplicants, both inanimate and animate gifts.
m.1.11.15: Having carefully satisfied every living being, stationary and moving, in a pit filled with gold and filled with the nine gems,
m.1.11.16: having uttered the Brahma mantras beginning with Sadyojāta, having meditated on the supreme auspicious god, and having pronounced the great mantra Om resounding with nāda,
m.1.11.17: having installed the liṅga there, one should join the liṅga to the pedestal; having set the liṅga with its pedestal, one should fix it with permanent cement.
m.1.11.18: In the same way a supremely auspicious image (vera) should be installed right there, with the five-syllable mantra; and likewise an image for festivals outside.
m.1.11.19: One should receive the image from gurus, or one worshipped by holy men. Thus worship of the liṅga and of the image grants the abode of Śiva.
m.1.11.20: Again, the liṅga is said to be of two kinds, stationary and moving. They call trees, shrubs and the like the stationary liṅga;
m.1.11.21: they call worms, insects and the like the moving liṅga. Tending the stationary and satisfying the moving—
m.1.11.22: with delight in the well-being of each, the wise know this as worship of Śiva. The whole pedestal is of the nature of the Mother (Ambā), and the Śiva-liṅga is of the nature of consciousness.
m.1.11.23: Just as Śaṅkara abides holding the goddess Umā on his lap, so this liṅga abides constantly, holding the pedestal.
m.1.11.24: Having thus installed the great liṅga, one should worship it with the services; there should be daily worship according to one's ability, and likewise the setting up of banners and the like.
m.1.11.25: In this way one should install the liṅga, which directly grants the abode of Śiva. Or else a movable liṅga, with the sixteen services,
m.1.11.26: one should worship according to rule; it gradually grants the abode of Śiva. The services are: invocation, seat, arghya-water and foot-water likewise,
m.1.11.27: sipping water as part of that, bath preceded by anointing with oil, garment, fragrance, flowers, incense, lamp, food-offering,
m.1.11.28: waving of lights, betel, obeisance and dismissal. Or else, having performed the services from arghya up to the food-offering according to rule,
m.1.11.29: or else one should always perform, according to ability, ablution, food-offering, obeisance and libation; it gradually grants the abode of Śiva.
m.1.11.30: Or else, at a liṅga installed by men, by sages, by gods, or self-manifested, or at a newly installed liṅga, with services in whatever way one can,
m.1.11.31: when articles of worship are given, one obtains some fruit; with circumambulations and obeisances, it gradually grants the abode of Śiva.
m.1.11.32: Or merely seeing the liṅga as a regular observance grants Śiva's state. With clay, flour, cow-dung, flowers, karavīra, or fruits,
m.1.11.33: with jaggery, fresh butter, sacred ash, or grains, as one likes—having carefully made a liṅga, one should then worship it accordingly.
m.1.11.34: Some likewise prefer worship on the thumb and the like. In the rites of the liṅga there is never any prohibition anywhere.
m.1.11.35: For Śiva everywhere gives fruit in proportion to the effort. Or else the gift of a liṅga, or even the price of a liṅga,
m.1.11.36: given with faith to a devotee of Śiva, grants the abode of Śiva. Or else one should daily repeat the praṇava ten thousand times,
m.1.11.37: or a thousand times at the two twilights; this should be known as granting the abode of Śiva. At the time of japa, the praṇava ending in m purifies the mind.
m.1.11.38: In meditative absorption mental repetition is prescribed; whispered repetition is for all times. This they know as the even praṇava, joined with bindu and nāda.
m.1.11.39: Or one should daily repeat the five-syllable mantra ten thousand times with reverence, or a thousand times at the two twilights; this should be known as granting the abode of Śiva.
m.1.11.40: For brāhmaṇas, the mantra joined with the praṇava at the beginning is preferred. And to obtain the fruit, the mantra should be received from a guru together with initiation.
m.1.11.41: For the pot-bath (kumbha-snāna), mantra initiation and also mātṛkā-nyāsa, a brāhmaṇa guru who is wise and whose self is purified by truth is preferred.
m.1.11.42: For the twice-born the mantra is recited with namaḥ first; for others, ending with namaḥ. For women too, some prefer it ending with namaḥ, according to rule.
m.1.11.43: For brāhmaṇa women, some prefer this with namaḥ first. Having performed japa of five crores, one becomes equal to Sadāśiva.
m.1.11.44: By one, two, three or four crores one reaches the abode of Brahmā and the others. Or one should repeat a lakh for each syllable, separately for each syllable.
m.1.11.45: Or else, a lakh per syllable should be known as granting Śiva's abode. A thousand thousands of repetitions over a thousand days—
m.1.11.46: —by such japa of the mantra, together with daily feeding of brāhmaṇas, comes the attainment of what one desires. A thousand and eight Gāyatrīs, in the morning indeed,
m.1.11.47: a brāhmaṇa should repeat daily—the Gāyatrī which in due course grants Śiva's abode. Keeping to discipline, he should also repeat Vedic mantras and hymns (sūktas).
m.1.11.48: The ten-syllabled mantra is to be repeated one time, or a hundred less one, or more than that; ten thousand, a thousand, or a hundred less one may be the count.
m.1.11.49: Recitation of the entire Veda (veda-pārāyaṇa) too should be known as granting Śiva's abode. Other, more numerous mantras one should repeat at a lakh per syllable.
m.1.11.50: Likewise monosyllabic mantras one should repeat at a crore per syllable. Beyond that one should also repeat a thousand more with devotion.
m.1.11.51: Thus one should act according to one's capacity; in due course one attains Śiva's abode. Daily, one single mantra that one likes, until death,
m.1.11.52: one should repeat Om a thousand times; by Śiva's command it yields all that is desired. Also making flower gardens and the like, and likewise sweeping and the like—
m.1.11.53: having done these for Śiva, for the sake of Śiva's service, one attains Śiva's abode. Likewise one should always dwell in a Śiva-kṣetra with devotion.
m.1.11.54: Such residence grants enjoyment and liberation to all, the dull and the not-dull alike. Therefore the wise should dwell in a Śiva-kṣetra until death.
m.1.11.55: In a kṣetra whose liṅga was installed by humans, they know the area for a hundred cubits from the liṅga to be holy; in a kṣetra installed by sages, the area of a thousand aratnis is holy.
m.1.11.56: For a liṅga installed by the gods, likewise, it should be known by the measure of a thousand aratnis; in a self-manifested (svayambhū) kṣetra, the area of a thousand bow-lengths is holy.
m.1.11.57: A tank, a well and the like, and ponds situated in a holy kṣetra should be known as Śiva-Gaṅgā, according to Śiva's word.
m.1.11.58: Having bathed there, likewise having given gifts and done japa, one goes to Śiva. Taking refuge in a Śiva-kṣetra, one should likewise dwell there until death.
m.1.11.59: The second-day rite, the tenth-day rite, the monthly rite, or the sapiṇḍīkaraṇa, or the annual rite in a Śiva-kṣetra, or even offering a piṇḍa in the kṣetra—
m.1.11.60: thereby one is freed from all sins and at once attains Śiva's abode. Or one may dwell there for seven nights, or five nights,
m.1.11.61: or three nights, or one night; in due course one attains Śiva's abode. In the world, a man obtains fruit in accordance with his own varṇa through his own proper conduct.
m.1.11.62: Through elevation of varṇa and through devotion, a man obtains an excess of that fruit. Everything done with desire yields its fruit at once.
m.1.11.63: Everything done without desire directly grants Śiva's abode. Morning, midday and evening—the day is divided into three, one after another in order.
m.1.11.64: The morning should be known as suited to prescribed rites, the midday to desire-oriented rites, and the evening should be known as for pacificatory rites; at night too, likewise indeed.
m.1.11.65: The time called niśītha is declared to be the two middle watches of the night. Śiva-worship at that time especially grants the attainment of what is desired.
m.1.11.66: Knowing thus, a man who acts accordingly becomes a sharer of the fruit as stated. Especially in the Kali age, attainment of fruit comes through action—
m.1.11.67: —through any action that has been stated, according to the differences of eligibility. If one is of good conduct and fearful of sin, one obtains the respective fruit.
m.1.11.68: The sages said: Now tell us briefly about the holy kṣetras, resorting to which all women and men may attain the supreme state.
m.1.11.69: O Sūta, best among excellent yogins, tell us likewise the traditions (āgamas) of the Śiva-kṣetras. Sūta said: Listen with faith to the account of all the kṣetras and their traditions.
m.1.11.iti: Thus ends the eleventh adhyāya, named The worship of Śiva's liṅga and other matters, in the first saṃhitā, the Vidyeśvara-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.1.12.1: Sūta said: Listen, O wise sages, to the account of Śiva's sacred regions, which grant liberation. After that I shall tell their traditions, indeed only for the protection of the world.
m.1.12.2: The earth, extending over fifty crores of yojanas, with its mountains, woods and forests, stands by Śiva's command, bearing the world.
m.1.12.3: Here and there are Śiva's sacred places; for the liberation of those who dwell in those various places, the Lord God out of compassion fashioned the sacred region.
m.1.12.4: Some arose through being taken up by the sages, and some through being taken up by the gods; others again are self-manifested, indeed only for the protection of the world.
m.1.12.5: At a holy ford or sacred region one should always perform bathing, giving, recitation and the like; otherwise a man may incur disease, poverty, dumbness and so on.
m.1.12.6: Now, if a man meets death in this land of Bhārata, by having dwelt in a self-manifested sacred place he will attain human birth again.
m.1.12.7: Sin committed in a sacred region becomes firmly fixed, O brahmins; so while dwelling in a holy region one should not commit even the slightest sin.
m.1.12.8: By whatever means possible a man should dwell in a holy region. On the banks of the hundred streams of the Sindhu there are sacred regions in great number.
m.1.12.9: The river Sarasvatī is declared holy and likewise sixty-mouthed; a wise man should dwell on its various banks, and in due course he will attain the state of Brahmā.
m.1.12.10: The Gaṅgā, born of the Himālaya mountain, is a holy river with a hundred mouths; on its banks too are many holy regions, Kāśī and others.
m.1.12.11: There the bank is especially praised in the month of Makara, when Jupiter is in Makara. The Śoṇabhadra, ten-mouthed and holy, grants desired fruits.
m.1.12.12: By bathing and fasting there one attains the realm of Vināyaka. The Narmadā, too, is a holy great river with twenty-four mouths.
m.1.12.13: By bathing in it and dwelling by it one attains the realm of Viṣṇu. The Tamasā has twelve mouths; the river Revā has ten mouths.
m.1.12.14: The Godāvarī is supremely holy, destroying the sin of killing a brahmin or a cow; it is declared twenty-one-mouthed and grants the world of Rudra.
m.1.12.15: The Kṛṣṇaveṇī is a holy river that brings about the destruction of all sins; it is declared eighteen-mouthed and grants the world of Viṣṇu.
m.1.12.16: The Tuṅgabhadrā, ten-mouthed, grants the world of Brahmā; the holy Suvarṇamukharī is likewise declared nine-mouthed.
m.1.12.17: Right there those fallen from Brahmā's world are born well. The Sarasvatī, the Pampā, the Kanyā and the auspicious Śvetanadī—
m.1.12.18: —by dwelling on the banks of these one attains the world of Indra. The great river called Kāverī, born of the Sahya mountain, is supremely holy.
m.1.12.19: It is declared twenty-seven-mouthed, granting all desires; its banks bestow heaven and grant the states of Brahmā and Viṣṇu.
m.1.12.20: The Śaiva places there grant Śiva's world and likewise the desired fruits. One should bathe at Naimiṣa and Badarī when Jupiter and the Sun are in Meṣa (Aries).
m.1.12.21: One should know that this grants Brahmā's world, and likewise worship and so on there. Likewise bathing in the river Sindhu when Jupiter is in Siṃha and the Sun in Karkaṭa—
m.1.12.22: —and drinking the water of Kedāra and bathing there, they know to bestow knowledge. One should bathe in the Godāvarī in the month of Siṃha, when Jupiter is in Siṃha;
m.1.12.23: that it grants Śiva's world was thus declared by Śiva of old. One should bathe in the Yamunā and Śoṇa when Jupiter and the Sun have entered Kanyā (Virgo);
m.1.12.24: they know it to grant great enjoyments in the world of Dharma and the world of the elephants. Likewise one should bathe in the Kāverī when the Sun and Jupiter are in Tulā (Libra);
m.1.12.25: by the greatness of Viṣṇu's word they know it to grant all desires. When the month of Vṛścika (Scorpio) has arrived, with the Sun and Jupiter in Vṛścika,
m.1.12.26: by bathing in the river Narmadā one attains Viṣṇu's world. Bathing in the Suvarṇamukharī when Jupiter and the Sun are in Dhanus (Sagittarius)—
m.1.12.27: grants Śiva's world, according to Brahmā's word. Likewise in the month of Makara one should bathe in the Jāhnavī (Gaṅgā) when Jupiter is in Makara;
m.1.12.28: it grants Śiva's world, according to Brahmā's word; having enjoyed the pleasures in the realms of Brahmā and Viṣṇu, at their end one attains knowledge.
m.1.12.29: In the Gaṅgā in the month of Māgha, when the Sun has entered Kumbha (Aquarius), a śrāddha, or an offering of rice-balls, or else water mixed with sesame—
m.1.12.30: they know to uplift ten million generations of the family of the ancestors of both lineages. They praise bathing in the Kṛṣṇaveṇī when Jupiter and the Sun are in Mīna (Pisces).
m.1.12.31: Bathing at each such holy ford in its proper month grants the state of Indra. A wise man should dwell resorting to the Gaṅgā or the Sahya-born Kāverī;
m.1.12.32: thereby the destruction of sins committed at that time certainly comes about. There are many sacred regions which grant Rudra's world.
m.1.12.33: The Tāmraparṇī and Vegavatī bestow the fruit of Brahmā's world; on their banks there are indeed sacred regions that grant heaven.
m.1.12.34: Between them there are abundant sacred regions bestowing merit; a wise man dwelling in each of them would obtain the corresponding fruit.
m.1.12.35: With good conduct, right livelihood and constant devout contemplation, the compassionate wise man should dwell there; otherwise he will not obtain that fruit.
m.1.12.36: Merit done in a holy region attains manifold increase; sin done in a holy region, even if minute, becomes great.
m.1.12.37: If the sin was committed at that time for the sake of livelihood, it will be destroyed by merit. They declare that merit grants prosperity; merit of body, likewise of speech,
m.1.12.38: and likewise of mind, destroys sin of the same kind, O brahmins. But mental sin is like an adamantine coating, following one from kalpa to kalpa.
m.1.12.39: It perishes only through meditation; otherwise it is not destroyed. Verbal sin perishes by abundant recitation, bodily sin by mortifying the body,
m.1.12.40: and sin committed through wealth perishes through giving, not otherwise even in millions of kalpas. Sometimes merit too is destroyed by sin that has grown beyond it.
m.1.12.41: Of merit and sin there are a seed-portion, a growth-portion and an enjoyment-portion. The seed-portion is destroyed by knowledge; the growth-portion is destroyed in the manner already stated.
m.1.12.42: But the enjoyment-portion is destroyed only by experiencing it, not otherwise, not even by millions of meritorious acts. When the sprouting of the seed has been destroyed, the remainder serves only for being experienced.
m.1.12.43: By the worship of the gods, by gifts to brahmins, and by intense austerity, in the course of time the experience of karmic fruit becomes bearable for men. Therefore one who desires happiness should dwell in the sacred place without committing sin at all.
m.1.12.iti: Thus ends the twelfth adhyāya, named Śiva's sacred regions, in the first saṃhitā, the Vidyeśvara-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.1.13.1: The sages said: Quickly make us hear about right conduct, by which a wise man may win the worlds. Tell us also about the practices made up of dharma and adharma, which likewise give heaven and hell.
m.1.13.2: Sūta said: A learned man endowed with right conduct is called by name a Brāhmaṇa; one endowed with Vedic practice is a Vipra; one who has only one of these is a Dvija.
m.1.13.3: One of little conduct and little Vedic learning, who serves a king, is a Kṣatriya -brāhmaṇa; one with some conduct who engages in agriculture and trade is likewise a Vaiśya -brāhmaṇa.
m.1.13.4: One who himself ploughs is called a Śūdra-brāhmaṇa; one who is envious and injures others is called a Caṇḍāla-dvija.
m.1.13.5: Among Kṣatriyas, the protector of the earth is a king; the others are regarded as Kṣatriyas. One who trades in grain and the like is a Vaiśya; the other is called a merchant.
m.1.13.6: One who serves Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas is called a Śūdra; a ploughman should be known as a Vṛṣala, and the others as Dasyus.
m.1.13.7: Everyone, at dawn, facing east, should reflect on the duties, beginning with those toward the gods, and on wealth, its troubles, income and expenditure.
m.1.13.8: Long life, enmity, death, sin, fortune, disease, nourishment and strength — these are the results of the direction faced on rising in the morning.
m.1.13.9: The last watch of the night should be known as Uṣā; half a watch at the junction is called Sandhi. Rising at that time, the twice-born should void excrement and urine.
m.1.13.10: Then, going far from the house, outside, covered with a cloth, he should sit facing north; if there is an obstacle, facing another direction,
m.1.13.11: not facing water, fire, Brāhmaṇas and the like, or the gods; covering the genital with the left hand and the mouth with the other hand.
m.1.13.12: Having voided the excrement and risen, he should not look at that excrement. He should perform cleansing outside the water, with water drawn out from it.
m.1.13.13: Or else, without entering the tīrthas of the gods, ancestors and sages, he should cleanse the anus with earth seven, five or three times.
m.1.13.14: For the genital, an amount of earth the size of a karkoṭa fruit is prescribed; for the anus, a handful. Then, rising, he should do the cleansing of feet and hands and eight mouth-rinsings.
m.1.13.15: Tooth-cleaning is declared to be done outside the water with any leaf or twig, avoiding the forefinger.
m.1.13.16: Having saluted the water-deities, he should bathe with mantra. If unable to immerse fully, entering water neck-deep or else waist-deep,
m.1.13.17: or entering knee-deep water, he should perform the mantra-bath. There the wise man should offer libations to the gods and others with the water of the tīrtha.
m.1.13.18: Taking a washed cloth, he should wear it with five tucks; and an upper garment too must be worn in all rites.
m.1.13.19: When bathing at a tīrtha such as a river, one should not wash the bathing cloth there; but at a tank, well, house and the like, the wise man should take it away after bathing and wash it.
m.1.13.20: On stone, wood or the like, or in water, or on the ground, having washed the cloth one should wring it for the satisfaction of the ancestors, O twice-born ones.
m.1.13.21: He should apply the tripuṇḍra with ash, with the mantra taught in the Jābāla Upaniṣad. If it is done otherwise, and the ash falls into water, then he goes to hell.
m.1.13.22: With the mantra āpo hi ṣṭhā he should sprinkle the head to remove sin; with the mantra yasya the feet. This is called the sandhi-sprinkling.
m.1.13.23: Sprinkling on the heart, head and feet; on the head, heart and feet; and on the heart, feet and head — this the wise know as the mantra-bath.
m.1.13.24: In case of a slight impure contact, of ill health, of danger from the king or the realm, and when one must travel with no other option, one should perform the mantra-bath.
m.1.13.25: Having sipped water with the Sūrya-anuvāka in the morning and with the Agni-anuvāka in the evening, and likewise at midday, he should again perform the sprinkling.
m.1.13.26: At the end of reciting the Gāyatrī mantra, he should cast water upward three times toward the east; and at midday, one arghya to the Sun, along with the mantra, O twice-born ones.
m.1.13.27: When evening has come, he should offer it on the ground, facing west; in the morning he should offer it lifting the water up, and at midday likewise with the fingers.
m.1.13.28: Through the gap between the fingers he should look at the sun as it hangs in the sky; then, having turned around himself clockwise, he should perform pure ācamana.
m.1.13.29: The sandhyā performed in the evening before the proper muhūrta is futile. Only the right time is called time, as opposed to the wrong time. When the day has passed without it, expiation is in due order:
m.1.13.30: If a day of the daily rite has lapsed, he should recite the Gāyatrī a hundred times in order; if it has lapsed beyond ten days, he should practise the Gāyatrī a hundred thousand times.
m.1.13.31: If the daily rite has lapsed for a month, he must undergo the upanayana again. Īśa, Gaurī, Guha, Viṣṇu, Brahmā, Candra and Yama —
m.1.13.32: such gods he should satisfy with libations for the accomplishment of his aims. Then, having made the offering to Brahman, he should perform pure ācamana.
m.1.13.33: To the south of the tīrtha, in an approved hermitage or a hall for mantras, or there in a temple, or at home in a fixed place, the wise man —
m.1.13.34: having saluted all the gods, steady in mind and steady in posture, should first practise the praṇava and then practise the Gāyatrī.
m.1.13.35: Understanding that it has as its subject the oneness of the individual self and Brahman, he should practise the praṇava. Its meaning is: The creator of the three worlds, the sustainer Acyuta,
m.1.13.36: and likewise the destroyer Rudra, the self-luminous, we worship. May he direct the organs of knowledge and action, the functions of the mind, and the intellects
m.1.13.37: ever impel them towards dharma, which grants enjoyment and liberation, and towards knowledge. Meditating thus on this meaning with his intellect, one certainly attains Brahman.
m.1.13.38: Or he may simply recite it daily, for the fulfilment of his brāhmaṇa-hood. The foremost of brāhmaṇas should practise it a thousand times daily in the morning.
m.1.13.39: For others, according to their ability. At midday he should recite it a hundred times; in the evening twenty times should be known as the rule, together with eight more (śikhāṣṭaka).
m.1.13.40: Beginning with the mūlādhāra, he should contemplate likewise those situated in the twelve stations: Vidyeśa, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Īśa, the individual self and the Supreme Lord —
m.1.13.41: With the understanding that it is Brahman, and with the meditation I am he (so'ham), realising identity with it, one should do japa. One should contemplate those very mantras at the brahmarandhra and other centres, and also outside the body.
m.1.13.42: Beginning from the mahat-tattva, the bodies are a thousand; by each single round of japa, passing beyond one of them gradually,
m.1.13.43: one should unite the individual soul with the Supreme; this is declared to be the essence of japa. The body is counted as a hundred and twenty, together with an eightfold śikhā;
m.1.13.44: such indeed is the japa of mantras; they understand japa according to the initial order. One should know that a thousand repetitions bestow Brahmā's state; a hundred, they know, bestow Indra's.
m.1.13.45: The other lesser number serves for self-protection; by it one is born in brahmin families. Having worshipped the Sun, one should do thus daily.
m.1.13.46: One endowed with twelve lakhs of Gāyatrī japa is declared a complete brahmin. One who lacks even a lakh of Gāyatrī should not be employed in Vedic rites.
m.1.13.47: Up to seventy years one should keep the observance; afterwards one should take up renunciation. The renunciant should do japa of the praṇava twelve thousand times in the morning.
m.1.13.48: If a day lapses, one should make it up day by day by doing japa thus in due order; if a month or more has gradually lapsed, it is made up by japa of a lakh and a half.
m.1.13.49: If the lapse extends beyond this, one should perform the praiṣa, the rite of renunciation, again. Doing so, the fault is pacified; otherwise one goes to Raurava hell.
m.1.13.50: Then one who has desires should strive for dharma and wealth, not the other the desireless. A brahmin should be desirous of liberation and should always practise knowledge of Brahman.
m.1.13.51: From dharma comes wealth, from wealth enjoyment, and from enjoyment arises dispassion. Through enjoyment of wealth earned by dharma, dispassion is born.
m.1.13.52: Through enjoyment of wealth gained in the contrary way, only attachment arises. Dharma is said to be twofold, by way of the pair: substance and body.
m.1.13.53: Dharma of substance takes the form of sacrifice and the like; bathing at tīrthas and the like is bodily. By dharma one obtains wealth; by austerity, a divine form.
m.1.13.54: The desireless one attains purity, and through purity knowledge, without doubt. In the Kṛta and following ages austerity is praised; in the Kali age, the dharma of substance.
m.1.13.55: In Kṛta, knowledge is attained through meditation; in Tretā, likewise through austerity; in Dvāpara, knowledge through sacrifice; in Kali, through worship of images.
m.1.13.56: Whatever the merit or sin, such indeed is the fruit; there is diminution, increase, loss and so on according to the difference of substance, body and limb.
m.1.13.57: Adharma has the nature of harm; dharma has the nature of happiness. From adharma one obtains sorrow; from dharma one indeed thrives in happiness.
m.1.13.58: One should know that sorrow comes from bad conduct and happiness from good conduct. Therefore one should acquire dharma for the accomplishment of enjoyment and liberation.
m.1.13.59: To a brahmin with a family of four persons one should give a livelihood for a hundred years; that bestows Brahmaloka.
m.1.13.60: A thousand cāndrāyaṇa fasts, they know, bestow Brahmaloka. A kṣatriya should establish the livelihood of a thousand families;
m.1.13.61: one should know that this bestows Indra's world; ten thousand families bestow Brahmaloka. Whatever deity a man places foremost when he makes a gift,
m.1.13.62: he attains that very deity's world — so the knowers of the Veda know. One who lacks wealth should likewise always acquire merit through austerities.
m.1.13.63: Through tīrthas and austerity one enjoys imperishable happiness that is to be gained. Now I shall speak of acquiring wealth justly; listen attentively.
m.1.13.64: From his own work, from receiving gifts and from officiating at sacrifices — by pure means, without servility and without excessive hardship — a brahmin should earn wealth.
m.1.13.65: A kṣatriya should earn by the might of his arms, a vaiśya by agriculture and cattle-keeping. By giving away wealth justly earned one attains success.
m.1.13.66: Through the attainment of knowledge comes the attainment of liberation for all, by the guru's grace. From liberation comes realisation of one's true nature; one enjoys supreme bliss.
m.1.13.67: All this arises for men from the company of the good, O brahmins. All wealth, grain and the like should be given by the householder.
m.1.13.68: Whatever goods, fruit or grain appear in whatever season — all that should be given to brahmins by one who desires his own welfare.
m.1.13.69: Water should always be given, and food for allaying hunger and illness. Field, grain, uncooked food and cooked food — thus food is fourfold.
m.1.13.70: For as long as one who has eaten that food thrives in hearing sacred teaching, half the merit earned during that time belongs to the giver, without doubt.
m.1.13.71: The receiver, for what he has received, should purge his sin by giving and likewise by austerity; otherwise he goes to Raurava.
m.1.13.72: One should divide one's wealth into three: for dharma, for growth and for one's own enjoyment. One should perform the obligatory, occasional and desire-motivated rites from the dharma portion.
m.1.13.73: The practitioner should increase his wealth by means of the growth portion; with the enjoyment portion he should enjoy what is wholesome, moderate and pure.
m.1.13.74: Of what is earned by agriculture, a tenth should be given for the purification of sin; with the remainder one should perform dharma and the rest; otherwise one goes to Raurava,
m.1.13.75: or he becomes sinful-minded, or the crop will go to ruin. In moneylending and trade, the wise should give a sixth part.
m.1.13.76: From a pure acceptance of gifts, the best of brahmins should give a fourth part; from wealth that comes unexpectedly, the best of brahmins should give half.
m.1.13.77: In an improper acceptance of gifts, one should cast that entire bad gift into the ocean. Gifts should be made after inviting the recipients, for the prosperity of one's own enjoyment.
m.1.13.78: Whatever is asked for should always be given, according to one's own capacity. If a thing asked for is not given, one becomes a debtor in another birth.
m.1.13.79: The wise man should not proclaim the faults of others; likewise, O brahmin, he should not out of hatred repeat what he has heard or seen.
m.1.13.80: The wise man should not say what provokes anger in the heart of any creature. At the two twilights one should perform the fire-rite for the attainment of prosperity.
m.1.13.81: Or, if unable to do so twice, one should worship the Sun and Fire once a day according to rule, offering rice grains, other grain, ghee, fruit, roots, or other oblation material likewise.
m.1.13.82: Likewise one should perform the sthālīpāka pot-cooked offering properly and according to rule; or, in the absence of oblation material, one should perform just the principal homa.
m.1.13.83: This is called the constant kindling (nityasandhāna); the wise know it as the perpetual fire. Or else one may do mere japa, or just salutation to the Sun.
m.1.13.84: Thus should those who seek the Self act, and also he who seeks wealth, according to rule. Those always devoted to the Brahmayajña Vedic study, likewise devoted to the worship of the gods,
m.1.13.85: always intent on fire-worship, and likewise devoted to the worship of the guru, and those who satisfy brāhmaṇas — all are sharers in heaven.
m.1.13.iti: Thus ends the thirteenth adhyāya, named Right conduct, in the first saṃhitā, the Vidyeśvara-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.1.14.1: The sages said: O lord, tell us in due order about the fire-sacrifice, the sacrifice to the gods, the Brahma-sacrifice, the worship of the guru, and the satisfaction of Brahman.
m.1.14.2: Sūta said: Whatever substance one offers into the fire is called the fire-sacrifice. For those in the stage of celibate studentship it is simply the laying of fuel-sticks on the fire.
m.1.14.3: In the fuel-stick fire are performed vows and the like, and special worship and so on; thus it is for those of the first stage of life, O brahmins, until they take up the aupāsana domestic fire.
m.1.14.4: For forest-dwellers and renunciants who have deposited the fires within themselves, O brahmins, the eating of wholesome, measured and pure food at the proper time is their oblation.
m.1.14.5: Beginning from the kindling of the aupāsana fire, the fire well guarded in a fire-pit or in a vessel—that is called perpetual (ajasra).
m.1.14.6: When, through compulsion of the king or of fate, out of fear of abandoning the fire, one firmly places the fire in oneself or in the kindling-stick, it is said to be deposited (samāropita).
m.1.14.7: The evening oblation to Agni, O brahmins, should be known as bringing prosperity; likewise the morning oblation to Sūrya should be known as bestowing long life.
m.1.14.8: This is called the fire-sacrifice, since by day the sun enters the fire. That which one offers into the fire with all the gods, Indra and the rest, in view—
m.1.14.9: —that one should know as the sacrifice to the gods, namely, rites such as the sthālīpāka; likewise the tonsure and similar rites should be known as established in the ordinary fire.
m.1.14.10: A twice-born should perform the Brahma-sacrifice repeatedly for the satisfaction of the gods. What is called the Brahma-sacrifice is the study of the Veda.
m.1.14.11: It is done after the daily rites up to evening; after that it is not prescribed. Now hear with faith and reverence the worship of the gods without fire.
m.1.14.12: At the first creation Mahādeva, the omniscient Lord, the mine of compassion, devised the days of the week for the benefit of all the worlds.
m.1.14.13: The physician of worldly existence, the omniscient one, the medicine of all medicines, the Lord first made his own day, which grants health.
m.1.14.14: Then he made the day of his own Māyā, which brings prosperity. After that, for those whose birth is beset by misfortune, the day of Kumāra—
m.1.14.15: —the Lord devised a day for overcoming sloth and evil. Likewise, desiring the welfare of the worlds, the day of Viṣṇu the protector—
m.1.14.16: —the Lord devised a day for nourishment and for protection. Then the life-giving day of the very maker of life-spans—
m.1.14.17: —of Brahmā Parameṣṭhin, the creator of the three worlds, the Lord devised a day for securing the longevity of the world.
m.1.14.18: In the beginning, merit and sin having been devised for the growth of the three worlds, then the days of their two agents, Indra and Yama—
m.1.14.19: —granting enjoyment and removing death for the worlds, were devised. Then Āditya and the others, his own forms, indicators of pleasure and pain—
m.1.14.20: —having first fashioned them as lords of the days, established in the circle of luminaries; worship of them on their respective days grants their respective fruits.
m.1.14.21: Health, prosperity, the cure of diseases, nourishment, long life, enjoyment and the warding off of death, in that order—
m.1.14.22: —they declare to be the fruits of the days in sequence, preceded by the gods' pleasure. Śiva is the giver of the fruit of the worship of the other gods as well.
m.1.14.23: For the pleasure of the gods worship is devised in five ways: the repetition of their respective mantras, fire-offering, gift, and austerity,
m.1.14.24: and worship on a prepared altar-ground, in an image, in fire, or in the person of a brahmin, with the sixteen services.
m.1.14.25: Each later one is superior to the earlier; in the absence of the earlier, the later may be used. For diseases of the eyes and head, and for the cure of leprosy,
m.1.14.26: one should worship Āditya and then feed brahmins, for a day, a month, a year, or even three years.
m.1.14.27: If the karma already begun (prārabdha) is strong, then by this, disease, old age and the like would be destroyed. They know japa and the rest addressed to one's chosen deity as the fruit of the days and so on.
m.1.14.28: On Sunday especially one should make offering for the pacification of sins; worship of Āditya, of the gods and of brahmins bestows special benefit.
m.1.14.29: On Monday the wise man should worship Lakṣmī and the others for wealth, and should feed brahmins together with their wives with food prepared with ghee.
m.1.14.30: On Tuesday one should worship Kālī and the others for the alleviation of disease, and feed brahmins with food of black gram, green gram and pigeon pea.
m.1.14.31: On Wednesday likewise the wise man should worship Viṣṇu with curd-rice; thereby the nourishment of sons, friends, wife and others always comes about.
m.1.14.32: One desiring long life should, on Thursday, for attaining nourishment, worship the gods with a sacred thread, cloth, and milk with ghee—so should the wise man do.
m.1.14.33: For enjoyments, on Friday one should worship the gods with a collected mind, and give food endowed with the six flavours for the satisfaction of brahmins.
m.1.14.34: Likewise, for the satisfaction of women, auspicious garments and the like should be given. On Saturday, which removes untimely death, the wise man should worship Rudra and the others,
m.1.14.35: with sesame oblations and gifts, and should feed brahmins with sesame food. Worshipping the gods in this way one would obtain fruits such as health.
m.1.14.36: In the daily worship of the gods and in special worship too, in bathing, giving, japa, fire-offering, and in the satisfying of brahmins,
m.1.14.37: at conjunctions of lunar days and constellations, in the worship of the respective deities, on Sunday and the other days, the omniscient Lord of the world—
m.1.14.38: —in the form of each deity, grants to all the fruits such as health, according to place and time, and likewise according to the recipient,
m.1.14.39: according to the materials and the faith, and likewise according to the people; in graded measure the god bestows health and the rest.
m.1.14.40: At the start of auspicious events and at the end of inauspicious ones, and on birth-star days, the householder should worship at home the planets Āditya and the rest for abundance of health and the like.
m.1.14.41: Therefore the worship of the gods, which grants all desired fruits, performed with Vedic mantras for brāhmaṇas, and in the Tantric manner for others,
m.1.14.42: should always be performed by men according to their capacity, on all seven days of the week, by men desiring auspicious fruits.
m.1.14.43: A poor man should worship the gods through austerity, a wealthy one through wealth. And again he performs such dharma with faith,
m.1.14.44: and again, having enjoyed various pleasures, he is born on earth. Shade trees, reservoirs of water, installation of brāhmaṇas, accumulation of merit —
m.1.14.45: all this a wealthy man should always do for the attainment of enjoyment. And in time, through the ripening of merit, the attainment of knowledge arises.
m.1.14.46: O twice-born ones, the man who hears or recites this chapter, and also one who helps others to hear it, would obtain the fruit of worshipping the gods.
m.1.14.iti: Thus ends the fourteenth adhyāya, named The fire-sacrifice and other rites, in the first saṃhitā, the Vidyeśvara-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.1.15.1: The sages said: O Sūta, foremost among knowers of all matters, tell us in due order about place and the rest. Sūta said: In rites such as worship of the gods, a clean house gives the standard (equal) result.
m.1.15.2: Ten times that is a cowshed; ten times that, the bank of a water-body; ten times that, the foot of a bilva, tulasī or aśvattha tree.
m.1.15.3: Then one should know a temple as ten times greater; ten times that, the bank of a holy place; ten times that, the bank of a river; ten times that, of a sacred river.
m.1.15.4: The holy bank of the seven Gaṅgā-rivers would be ten times that. Gaṅgā, Godāvarī, Kāverī, Tāmraparṇikā,
m.1.15.5: Sindhu, Sarayū and Revā — these are proclaimed the seven Gaṅgās. Then the seashore is ten times that, and a mountain peak ten times that.
m.1.15.6: But the place where the mind delights should be known as superior to all. In the Kṛta age, sacrifice, gifts and the like are to be known as yielding full fruit.
m.1.15.7: In the Tretā age three quarters, and in the Dvāpara half, is always declared; in Kali one quarter is to be known, and in its latter half, that quarter reduced by a quarter.
m.1.15.8: For one of pure self, a pure day is meritorious and gives the standard result, so they know. Ten times that, O wise ones, is to be known at the sun's transit into a sign.
m.1.15.9: At the equinox ten times that; at the solstice ten times that is declared; ten times that at the transit into Capricorn (Mṛga); and ten times that at a lunar eclipse.
m.1.15.10: And beyond that, at a solar eclipse, the supreme time, they know the result to be full. Because the sun, whose form is the world, is joined with poison, that time causes disease.
m.1.15.11: Therefore, to pacify that poison, one should perform bathing, gifts and japa. Because it is the time for pacifying poison, that time is declared to bestow merit.
m.1.15.12: On the day of one's birth-star and at the end of a vow, they know the time to be equal to a solar eclipse. And the time of association with great souls they know as equal to an eclipse of ten million suns.
m.1.15.13: Those steadfast in austerity, those steadfast in knowledge, yogins and renunciants — these indeed are worthy recipients of worship and a cause of the destruction of sin.
m.1.15.14: Or a brāhmaṇa who has completed twenty-four lakh japa of the Gāyatrī becomes a worthy recipient, granting enjoyment of the complete fruit.
m.1.15.15: It protects from falling — thus the word pātra is used in scripture. Because it protects the giver from sin, it is called pātra.
m.1.15.16: She protects the one who chants her from a fall; therefore she is called Gāyatrī. Just as one without wealth in this world does not give wealth to another,
m.1.15.17: while one who is wealthy here in the world gives wealth to another — so one who is himself pure, of purified self, is able to save men.
m.1.15.18: One purified by Gāyatrī japa is called a pure brāhmaṇa. Therefore in giving, japa, fire-offering, worship and in every rite,
m.1.15.19: the brāhmaṇa deserves the status of recipient, so that the gift may be made and the giver protected. For food, the worthy recipient is the hungry person, whether woman or man.
m.1.15.20: Having invited an excellent, well-composed brāhmaṇa at the proper time, giving for his sake words or wealth that is truly enlightening and fulfils desires —
m.1.15.21: and giving to one who desires it — they know such giving to yield the full fruit. What is given after being asked, they know to yield half the fruit.
m.1.15.22: What is given to a servant, they know to yield a quarter of the fruit. O best of the twice-born, to a vipra who is so by birth alone and of wretched livelihood,
m.1.15.23: wealth given yields enjoyment for ten years on the earthly world; given to a vipra versed in the Veda, ten years in heaven.
m.1.15.24: Given to one devoted to Gāyatrī japa, ten years in Satyaloka; what is given to a vipra devoted to Viṣṇu, they know to bestow Vaikuṇṭha.
m.1.15.25: What is given to a vipra devoted to Śiva, they know to bestow Kailāsa. For the enjoyment of those respective worlds, giving is recommended to all.
m.1.15.26: A man who gives tenfold food to a vipra on Sunday enjoys health for ten years in his next birth.
m.1.15.27: Great respect, invitation, oil-anointing, service of the feet, clothing, worship with fragrances and the like, food with ghee-cakes and choice juices,
m.1.15.28: dishes of six flavours, betel, followed by a fee (dakṣiṇā), salutation and accompanying the guest on departure — this is the ten-part gift of good food.
