m.1.15.29: A man who gives tenfold food to ten vipras on Sunday likewise enjoys health for a hundred years.
m.1.15.30: On Monday and the other days, the fruit of food-giving is to be known as according to the quality of each day, in the earthly world in the next birth.
m.1.15.31: On all seven days too, having given tenfold food to ten vipras, one enjoys health and the like for a hundred years.
m.1.15.32: Thus a man who gives to a hundred vipras on Sunday enjoys health for a thousand years in the world of Śarva (Śiva).
m.1.15.33: Likewise, having given to a thousand, one enjoys it for ten thousand years. Thus it should be understood by the wise for Monday and the other days.
m.1.15.34: Having given food on Sunday to thousands whose minds are purified by the Gāyatrī, one enjoys health and the like in Satyaloka.
m.1.15.35: Likewise, having given to ten thousand, one enjoys it in Viṣṇu's world; having given food to lakhs, one enjoys it in Rudra's world.
m.1.15.36: Men seeking learning should give to boys, regarding them as Brahmā; men desiring sons should give to youths, regarding them as Viṣṇu.
m.1.15.37: Men seeking knowledge should give to the aged, regarding them as Rudra; the best of men desiring intelligence should give to young girls, regarding them as Bhāratī (Sarasvatī).
m.1.15.38: The best of men desiring enjoyments should give to young women, regarding them as Lakṣmī; those seeking the Self should give to old women, regarding them as Pārvatī.
m.1.15.39: What is earned by gleaning ears of grain (śila) or scattered grains (uñcha), or as a teacher's fee, they call pure wealth; they know it yields the full fruit.
m.1.15.40: What is given out of honest acceptance of gifts is called middling wealth; what is obtained through agriculture and trade is called inferior wealth.
m.1.15.41: For kṣatriyas and vaiśyas, wealth earned through valour and through trade respectively is said to be the best wealth; for śūdras, it is wealth earned through wage-labour.
m.1.15.42: For women who seek dharma, proper wealth is that received from the father and likewise from the husband. The twelve gifts, beginning with the cow, should be given in order in the months beginning with Caitra,
m.1.15.43: or, all together at an auspicious time, one should give them for the flourishing of what one desires: cow, land, sesame, gold, ghee, cloth, grain and jaggery,
m.1.15.44: silver, salt, pumpkin, and a maiden — these are the twelve. From the gift of a cow, through the cow-products given and through the beneficial cow-dung,
m.1.15.45: there is removal of sins connected with wealth, grain and the like; and of sins connected with water, oil and the like, removal by cow's urine.
m.1.15.46: and of the three kinds of sin, bodily and the rest, by milk, curd and ghee; and likewise their nourishment by these should be understood by the wise.
m.1.15.47: The gift of land, O brahmins, is for a firm foundation here and in the hereafter; the gift of sesame is for strength, and they know it always as conquering death.
m.1.15.48: Gold increases the digestive fire and gives virility; ghee one should know as nourishing; cloth they know as granting long life.
m.1.15.49: Grain is for abundance of food; jaggery bestows sweet food; silver is for the increase of semen; and salt is for the six tastes.
m.1.15.50: All given together are for every kind of prosperity; the pumpkin they know as nourishing. These bestow the attainment of all enjoyments here and hereafter, O brahmins.
m.1.15.51: The gift of a maiden is declared to bestow enjoyment for as long as life lasts. The fruit of trees such as jackfruit, mango and wood-apple,
m.1.15.52: and the fruit of plants such as the plantain, and likewise that produced from shrubs; and likewise the produce of māṣa beans and the like and of mudga beans, and vegetables and so on,
m.1.15.53: and likewise the vegetable condiments, pepper, mustard and the like — whatever fruit is ripe in whatever season, that should be given by the wise.
m.1.15.54: Satisfaction of the senses, beginning with the ear, should always be given by the wise; for the ten enjoyments beginning with sound, it brings contentment to the deities of the directions and the rest.
m.1.15.55: The conviction that actions bear fruit, formed by taking up the Veda and śāstra and understanding them oneself from the guru's mouth, is called āstikya (faith).
m.1.15.56: A conviction arising from fear of relatives or of the king is also faith (śraddhā), but it is inferior. In the absence of all means, a poor man should worship by speech or by bodily action.
m.1.15.57: One should know verbal worship as mantra, hymns, japa and the like; pilgrimage to sacred places, vows and the like they know as bodily worship.
m.1.15.58: By whatever means, whether little or much, what is done with the intention of offering it to the deity becomes a source of enjoyment.
m.1.15.59: Both the practice of austerity and charity should always be performed. A dwelling should be given, befitting one's own class and adorned with good qualities,
m.1.15.60: it is given by the wise for the abundant satisfaction of the gods and bestows all enjoyments. The wise one obtains an excellent birth here and hereafter and constant enjoyment; but having done it with the intention of offering it to Īśvara, he obtains the fruit of liberation.
m.1.15.61: The man who reads this chapter, or who always listens to it — in him arise a mind set on dharma and the attainment of knowledge.
m.1.15.iti: Thus ends the fifteenth adhyāya, named Place, time, recipient and other matters, in the first saṃhitā, the Vidyeśvara-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.1.16.1: The sages said: O best of the virtuous, tell us the procedure for worshipping an earthen image, the procedure of worship by which every desired thing is obtained.
m.1.16.2: Sūta said: You have asked very well. This worship always bestows every aim and at once allays sorrow. Listen; I shall tell you.
m.1.16.3: O brahmins, it removes untimely death and destroys even death at its appointed time; it at once grants wife, sons and the like, wealth and grain.
m.1.16.4: Since food such as rice, clothing and the like—everything—arises from the earth, therefore worship of an image of clay and the like grants what is desired on earth.
m.1.16.5: Both men and women certainly have eligibility for this. One should bring clay from beneath the water of a river, a pond or a well.
m.1.16.6: Having purified it with fragrant powder and had it ground in a good pavilion, one should make the image by hand, well prepared with milk.
m.1.16.7: Having made it complete with major and minor limbs, furnished with weapons and seated on a lotus seat, one should worship it with reverence.
m.1.16.8: The twice-born should always worship the images of Vighneśa, Āditya, Viṣṇu, Ambā and Śiva—and, of Śiva, the Śivaliṅga.
m.1.16.9: He should perform it with the sixteen services to attain its fruit. He should sprinkle water with a flower and perform the ablution with mantras.
m.1.16.10: The food-offering should be of śāli rice only, all of it measured in kuḍavas. For worship at home a kuḍava is to be known as the measure; for a liṅga set up by men a prastha is prescribed.
m.1.16.11: For a divinely installed liṅga three prasthas are proper; for a self-manifest one, five prasthas. Thus one should know that full fruit results; two or three times that amount is more fruitful.
m.1.16.12: By a thousand such worships the twice-born truly attains Satyaloka. A vessel twelve aṅgulas in length, and twice that, and more than that,
m.1.16.13: with a thickness of one aṅgula and a height of three times five aṅgulas—such a vessel made of iron or wood is called śiva by the wise.
m.1.16.14: An eighth part of that is a prastha; that is held to be four kuḍavas. Ten prasthas, a hundred prasthas and a thousand prasthas—
m.1.16.15: —of water, oil and the like, and of fragrances, in measure as is fitting, for liṅgas installed by men, by sages and self-manifest, is called the great worship.
m.1.16.16: From ablution comes self-purification; from fragrance merit is gained; from the food-offering, long life and satisfaction; from incense, wealth is gained.
m.1.16.17: From the lamp one gains knowledge; from betel one obtains enjoyment. Therefore one should carefully perform the six beginning with bathing.
m.1.16.18: Prostration and japa—both grant all desires; they should always be performed at the end of worship by men seeking enjoyment and liberation.
m.1.16.19: Having first worshipped mentally, a man should always perform each rite. By the worship of the gods one attains the world of each respective god.
m.1.16.20: And in the intermediate worlds within those, enjoyments are obtained as one wishes. I shall tell the particulars of these; listen with faith, O brahmins.
m.1.16.21: By proper worship of Vighneśa one gains one's desires in Bhūrloka. On a Friday, on the fourth lunar day of the bright fortnight in Śrāvaṇa and Bhādrapada,
m.1.16.22: under the asterism Bhiṣak (Śatabhiṣaj), and in the month when the sun is in Dhanus, one should duly worship Vighneśa. One should complete a hundred or a thousand worships over as many days.
m.1.16.23: Done daily with faith in the deity and the fire, it grants sons and desired things to men, quells all sins and destroys the respective misfortunes.
m.1.16.24: They know that worship of Śiva and the others on the weekdays grants self-purification; the weekday is the basis of tithis, nakṣatras and yogas, and fulfils all desires.
m.1.16.25: Likewise, because it has no increase or decrease, they know it to be of the nature of the full Brahman. The weekday runs from sunrise to sunrise for rites such as Vedic ones.
m.1.16.26: Worship of the gods on tithis and the like grants full enjoyment to men. For the ancestors, the former part of the tithi, joined with night, is commended.
m.1.16.27: For the gods, the latter part, joined with daytime, is commended. The tithi prevailing at sunrise is to be accepted, if that tithi extends to midday.
m.1.16.28: Likewise, in rites for the gods, auspicious tithis, asterisms and the like are to be adopted. Having carefully considered the weekdays and so on, one should perform worship, japa and the rest.
m.1.16.29: Pūr is born by this — such is the construal of the meaning of pūjā in the Vedas: pūr, the accomplishment of the fruit of enjoyment, arises through that act.
m.1.16.30: Likewise it produces mental dispositions and knowledge through bringing about desired enjoyments and aims. Thus indeed is the meaning of the word pūjā well known in the world and in the Veda.
m.1.16.31: Regular and occasional rites bear fruit in course of time; an optional rite, when well performed, at once. Performed daily, monthly, fortnightly and yearly, in due order,
m.1.16.32: there is attainment of the fruit of each respective rite and a corresponding destruction of sin, in order. Worship of Mahāgaṇapati on the fourth day of the dark fortnight
m.1.16.33: destroys the sins of a fortnight and grants a fortnight's fruit of enjoyment. Worship done on the fourth day in Caitra grants the fruit of a month.
m.1.16.34: Worship performed in Bhādrapada when the sun is in Siṃha should be known to grant a year's enjoyment. On a Sunday in Śrāvaṇa, on the seventh day, on a day of the Hasta asterism,
m.1.16.35: and on the seventh day of the bright fortnight of Māgha, one should perform the worship of Āditya. In Jyeṣṭha and Bhādrapada, on a Wednesday, on the twelfth day, under the Śravaṇa asterism,
m.1.16.36: worship of Śrī Viṣṇu performed then they know to bring desired prosperity. Worship of Viṣṇu in Śrāvaṇa grants desired things and health.
m.1.16.37: Whatever fruit comes from giving the twelve objects beginning with cows, together with their accessories, that fruit one obtains by gratifying Viṣṇu on the twelfth day.
m.1.16.38: On the twelfth day one should worship twelve brahmins with the sixteen services, addressing them by the twelve names of Viṣṇu; thus one obtains his favour.
m.1.16.39: In the same way, for all the gods, worship of twelve brahmins with the respective twelve names of each god brings about the favour of that god.
m.1.16.40: One desiring prosperity should worship Ambā, the giver of the fruit of all enjoyments, in the month of Karkaṭa, on a Monday, on the ninth day, under the Mṛgaśīrṣa asterism.
m.1.16.41: The ninth day of the bright fortnight of Āśvayuja grants the fruit of all desired things. On a Sunday, on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, especially,
m.1.16.42: and under the asterism Ārdrā and the great Ārdrā, the worship of Śiva is especially excellent. On the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of Māgha it grants the fruit of all desired things;
m.1.16.43: it bestows long life, removes death and brings every attainment to men. In the month of Jyeṣṭha under the great Ārdrā, and also on the fourteenth day,
m.1.16.44: or under Ārdrā in Mārgaśīrṣa, having worshipped Śiva in his respective forms with the sixteen services, one obtains indeed the sight of his feet.
m.1.16.45: The worship of Śiva should be known as granting enjoyment and liberation to men. The worship of the gods of the weekdays and the rest is especially excellent in Kārtika.
m.1.16.46: When the month of Kārtika has arrived, the wise man should worship all the gods, with gifts, austerity, fire-offerings, recitation and observances,
m.1.16.47: and with the sixteen services, through images, brāhmaṇas and mantras, and by feeding brāhmaṇas; thus one who is free of desire becomes a remover of afflictions.
m.1.16.48: Worship of the gods in Kārtika grants all enjoyments; it also removes diseases, and there is destruction of evil spirits and seizing planets.
m.1.16.49: On the Sundays of Kārtika, through men's worship of the Sun and by gifts of oil and cotton, leprosy and the like are destroyed.
m.1.16.50: By gifts of myrobalan and pepper, of cloth, milk and the like, and by installing an image of Brahmā, consumption is destroyed.
m.1.16.51: And by gifts of lamps and mustard, epilepsy is destroyed. On the Mondays of the month of Kṛttikā, men's worship of Śiva
m.1.16.52: allays great poverty and brings all prosperity, especially with gifts of houses, fields and the like, and of household utensils and so on.
m.1.16.53: On the Tuesdays of Kṛttikā, by men's worship of Skanda and by gifts of lamps, bells and the like, mastery of speech soon arises.
m.1.16.54: On the Wednesdays of Kṛttikā, men's worship of Viṣṇu and the gift of curd-rice bring good offspring.
m.1.16.55: On the Thursdays of Kṛttikā, by worshipping Brahmā with riches and by gifts of honey, gold and ghee, men's enjoyments increase.
m.1.16.56: On the Fridays of Kṛttikā, by worship of the elephant-faced Gaṇeśa and by gifts of perfume, flowers and food, men's objects of enjoyment increase.
m.1.16.57: A barren woman obtains a fine son by gifts of gold, silver and the like. On the Saturdays of Kṛttikā, the salutation of the guardians of the quarters,
m.1.16.58: the worship of the elephants of the quarters, of the Nāgas and of the guardians of the bridges, and of Tryambaka Rudra and of Viṣṇu the remover of sin,
m.1.16.59: and likewise of Brahmā, and of Dhanvantari and the two Aśvins, bestows knowledge, removes disease and untimely death, and gives immediate relief from illness,
m.1.16.60: together with gifts of salt, iron and oil, and of black gram and the like; with gifts of the three pungents, fruits and perfumes, and of water and the like;
m.1.16.61: giving liquids by the prastha and solids by the pala measure, one attains heaven. In the month of Dhanus, worship at dawn
m.1.16.62: of Śiva and all the others in due order is enjoined for every attainment. An offering of śāli rice prepared as sacrificial food is declared commendable.
m.1.16.63: An offering of various foods is especially excellent in the month of Dhanus. For one who gives food in Mārgaśīrṣa, every desired fruit comes about.
m.1.16.64: Destruction of sin, fulfilment of wishes, health and dharma, thorough knowledge of the Veda and good practice,
m.1.16.65: great enjoyments here and hereafter, eternal union (yoga) at the end, and the attainment of Vedāntic knowledge — these the giver of food in Mārgaśīrṣa obtains.
m.1.16.66: In Mārgaśīrṣa, at dawn, or else for three days, one who desires enjoyment should worship the gods; he should not be one who neglects the Dhanus month.
m.1.16.67: The Dhanus-month worship is prescribed up to the saṅgava period of the morning. In the Dhanus month, fasting for the whole month and with senses controlled,
m.1.16.68: a brāhmaṇa should recite the Gāyatrī, mother of the Vedas, until midday; afterwards he should recite the five-syllable and other mantras until bedtime.
m.1.16.69: Having gained knowledge, the brāhmaṇa attains liberation at the end of the body. For other men and women, by bathing three times a day and by recitation
m.1.16.70: of the five-syllable mantra always, pure knowledge is attained. By always reciting the chosen mantras one obtains the destruction of great sins.
m.1.16.71: In the month of Dhanus especially, one should perform the great food-offering: with a bhāra of śāli rice grains and a prastha of pepper,
m.1.16.72: everything twelvefold in count, with a kuḍava of honey and ghee, with green gram amounting to a droṇa, and with twelve side-dishes,
m.1.16.73: with cakes cooked in ghee, sweet balls, śālikā and the like — twelve of each — and with curd and milk to the amount of twelve prasthas,
m.1.16.74: and coconuts and other fruits likewise by count; furnished with twelve areca nuts and with thirty-six betel leaves,
m.1.16.75: together with powdered camphor and khura and the five fragrant substances, and accompanied by betel — this is the definition of the great food-offering.
m.1.16.76: This great food-offering, after first being offered to the deity, should be distributed to his devotees in the order of the varṇas.
m.1.16.77: Thus by an offering of cooked rice one becomes a ruler of a realm on earth; by giving the great food-offering a man attains heaven.
m.1.16.78: By giving a thousand great food-offerings, O best of the twice-born, one attains Satyaloka and a full life-span in that world.
m.1.16.79: By giving thirty thousand great food-offerings, one reaches the world above that and does not again partake of birth.
m.1.16.80: Thirty-six thousand is declared the lifetime offering; a gift of offerings to that extent is called the great complete (mahāpūrṇa).
m.1.16.81: The food-offering of the Mahāpūrṇa (great full measure) is held to be the birth-offering (janma-naivedya). By giving the birth-offering there is no rebirth.
m.1.16.82: In the month of Ūrja (Kārttika), on a holy day that coincides with a saṅkrānti, a vyatīpāta, one's birth-star, the full moon and the like, one should perform the birth-offering.
m.1.16.83: On one's yearly birthday one should perform the excellent birth-offering, and also in other months on the day when the birth-star coincides with the full moon.
m.1.16.84: At such a conjunction, or else gradually, one should perform it up to a thousand times. By giving the birth-offering one obtains the fruit of offering up one's very birth.
m.1.16.85: Pleased by the offering of one's birth, Śiva indeed grants union with himself (sāyujya). This birth-offering should be given to Śiva alone.
m.1.16.86: In the form of yoni and liṅga, Śiva is the one who determines birth. Therefore, for the cessation of birth, the birth-worship is to be offered to Śiva.
m.1.16.87: The whole world, moving and unmoving, consists of bindu and nāda. Bindu is Śakti, nāda is Śiva; the world consists of Śiva and Śakti.
m.1.16.88: This bindu has nāda as its support; this world has bindu as its support. Bindu and nāda stand firmly as the support of the world.
m.1.16.89: Everything joined with bindu and nāda becomes sakalīkaraṇa (the making-whole). From this sakalīkaraṇa the world undoubtedly attains birth.
m.1.16.90: The liṅga, consisting of bindu and nāda, is called the cause of the world. Bindu is the Goddess, nāda is Śiva; their union is called the Śivaliṅga.
m.1.16.91: Therefore, for the cessation of birth, one should worship the Śivaliṅga. The Goddess in the form of bindu is the mother; Śiva in the form of nāda is the father.
m.1.16.92: When the parents are worshipped there is supreme bliss indeed. To obtain supreme bliss one should worship the Śivaliṅga.
m.1.16.93: That Goddess is the mother of the worlds, that Śiva is the father of the world. For one who constantly serves the parents, their compassion grows ever greater.
m.1.16.94: Out of compassion Śiva grants the worshipper inner sovereignty. Therefore, O best of sages, to gain inner bliss—
m.1.16.95: —one should worship the Śivaliṅga as the form of father and mother. Bharga is said to be of the form of Puruṣa, and Bhargā is said to be Prakṛti.
m.1.16.96: The womb whose inner abode is unmanifest is called Puruṣa; the womb whose inner abode is clearly manifest is called Prakṛti.
m.1.16.97: Puruṣa is the primal womb, since he, possessing the womb, is the begetter. What is joined from Puruṣa into Prakṛti is called the first birth.
m.1.16.98: Its emergence into manifestation from Prakṛti is called the second birth. The creature obtains birth—a birth bound to death—from Puruṣa.
m.1.16.99: That which is necessarily brought into being from another through māyā is called birth. Because it decays from the time of birth, it is known as jīva.
m.1.16.100: It is born and stretched out (bound) by fetters—this is the very meaning of the word jīva. For the removal of the fetters of birth, one should worship the birth-liṅga.
m.1.16.101: From the sense bha, that is, it goes to growth, Prakṛti is called bhaga. Because of the enjoyment, by the natural senses, of natural objects such as the subtle element of sound—
m.1.16.102: —'this belongs to bhaga, hence bhoga (enjoyment)': this is the meaning of the word chiefly heard in scripture. The principal bhaga is Prakṛti; Śiva is called Bhagavān.
m.1.16.103: Bhagavān is the giver of enjoyment; there is no other bestower of enjoyment. Being the lord of bhaga, Bhagavān is called Bharga by the wise.
m.1.16.104: The liṅga accompanied by the bhaga, the bhaga united with the liṅga—for enjoyment here and hereafter, and for everlasting enjoyment—
m.1.16.105: —one should worship the Śivaliṅga, Bhagavān Mahādeva. The Sun is the progenitor of the world; its sign arises from procreation.
m.1.16.106: A man should worship, in the liṅga, the bearer of the liṅga who is the maker of procreation. The sign which conveys the meaning of the liṅga is called liṅga.
m.1.16.107: It is called liṅga because it makes known the meaning, namely Puruṣa, Śiva. And the union of the emblems of Śiva and Śakti is called the liṅga.
m.1.16.108: Śiva being pleased by the worship of his own emblem, the effect of the emblem does not proceed. The effect of the emblem is birth and the like; thus birth and what follows cease.
m.1.16.109: With natural and personal offerings, arising from outer and inner means, and with the sixteen upacāras, one should worship the Śivaliṅga.
m.1.16.110: Thus worship on Sunday ends birth. On Sunday one should worship the great liṅga with the praṇava alone.
m.1.16.111: On Sunday ablution with the five cow-products is especially recommended. Cow-dung, cow-urine, milk, curd and ghee form the pañcagavya.
m.1.16.112: Ablution with milk and the rest also separately, with honey and with sugarcane juice; and one should make a food-offering of cooked rice with cow's milk, with the praṇava alone.
m.1.16.113: The praṇava is the sound-liṅga; the nāda-liṅga is that of the Self-born; the bindu-liṅga is the yantra; the syllable m is the installed liṅga.
m.1.16.114: The letter u is the movable liṅga; the letter a is the embodied form of the guru. Through constant worship of the six liṅgas one is liberated while living—there is no doubt.
m.1.16.115: Worship of Śiva with devotion brings men release from birth. By wearing rudrākṣa one gains a quarter, by wearing sacred ash a half,
m.1.16.116: three quarters by repeating the mantra, and through worship one becomes full of devotion. Having worshipped the Śivaliṅga and the devotee, a man attains liberation.
m.1.16.117: Whoever reads this chapter or listens to it attentively—his devotion to Śiva grows very firm, O brahmins.
m.1.16.iti: Thus ends the sixteenth adhyāya, named The method of worship of the earthen liṅga and other matters, in the first saṃhitā, the Vidyeśvara-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.1.17.1: The sages said: O great sage, O lord, tell us in due order the greatness of the Praṇava, of the sixfold liṅga, and the worship due to a devotee of Śiva.
m.1.17.2: Sūta said: This question has been well put by you who are rich in austerity. Mahādeva knows its answer, and no one else.
m.1.17.3: Even so, I shall explain it, solely through the grace of Śiva. May Śiva grant abundant protection to us and to you.
m.1.17.4: Pra refers to the great ocean of saṃsāra born of Prakṛti; nava means a new boat to cross it — thus the wise understand the Praṇava.
m.1.17.5: Pra is the phenomenal world (prapañca); na — for you it does not exist: so they understand the Praṇava. Because it leads you eminently (prakarṣeṇa) to liberation, they understand it as Praṇava.
m.1.17.6: For yogins who repeat their own mantra and who worship, having brought about the destruction of all karma, it bestows a divine knowledge that is new.
m.1.17.7: That knower alone, free from māyā, they call new; the Praṇava makes the great soul eminently new, of pure nature.
m.1.17.8: Because it makes him new, the wise know it as Praṇava. The Praṇava is said to be twofold, by the distinction of subtle and gross.
m.1.17.9: One should know the subtle as the single-syllabled Om; the gross they know as the five-syllabled mantra. The subtle has its five letters unmanifest; the other has its letters clearly manifest.
m.1.17.10: The subtle Praṇava, the essence of all, is for the one liberated while living, for whom it is truly beneficial; he should practise contemplation of its meaning through the mantra until the dissolution of his body.
m.1.17.11: When his body falls away, he certainly attains the complete Śiva. But one who merely repeats the mantra certainly attains yoga.
m.1.17.12: One who repeats it thirty-six crore times will certainly attain yoga. The subtle Praṇava too should be known as twofold, by the distinction of short and long.
m.1.17.13: The letter A, the letter U, and after that the letter M, joined with bindu and nāda, endowed with sound, time and kalā —
m.1.17.14: — this is the long Praṇava, which abides only in the hearts of yogins. The M, embodying the three principles, is called the short Praṇava.
m.1.17.15: Śiva, Śakti and their union — the M has this threefold nature. Thus the short Praṇava is to be repeated by those who seek the destruction of all sins.
m.1.17.16: Earth, wind, fire (kanaka), water and sky, and likewise sound and the rest — these are ten; those bound by desire for these ten are called the pravṛtta (worldly-active).
m.1.17.17: The short Praṇava is for the pravṛtta, the long for the nivṛtta (renouncers). At the beginning of the vyāhṛtis and of mantras, it is used as desired, endowed with sound and kalā.
m.1.17.18: It should be employed at the beginning of the Veda and in the worship at the two twilights. Having done nine crore repetitions, a man becomes thoroughly purified.
m.1.17.19: Again, with nine crore more, he gains mastery over earth; and again with nine crore, he gains mastery over the waters.
m.1.17.20: Again with nine crore he gains mastery over fire; again with nine crore he gains mastery over wind; and with nine crore repetitions he attains mastery over ether.
m.1.17.21: Mastery over smell and the other sense-objects in due order, each with nine crore repetitions; and again over ego (ahaṅkāra) with nine crore repetitions.
m.1.17.22: By repeating the mantra a thousand times daily, a man becomes ever pure. Beyond that, O twice-born, the repetition serves for one's own perfection.
m.1.17.23: Thus, again, having repeated the Praṇava one hundred and eight crore times, one awakened by it attains pure yoga.
m.1.17.24: United with pure yoga, he is liberated while living, without doubt — always repeating, always meditating on Śiva in the form of the Praṇava.
m.1.17.25: Established in samādhi, the great yogin is Śiva himself, without doubt. Having placed (nyāsa) the ṛṣi, metre, deity and the rest on the body, one should then repeat the mantra.
m.1.17.26: Having placed the Praṇava together with the mātṛkā letters on the body, one becomes a ṛṣi; one obtains the entire fruit of nyāsa, such as that of the ten mātṛs, the six paths and the rest.
m.1.17.27: For the worldly-engaged and those of mixed disposition, the gross Praṇava is prescribed. Śiva-yogins are of three kinds, engaged respectively in ritual action, austerity and repetition.
m.1.17.28: One who is engaged in ritual worship with wealth and other resources, with the limbs such as the hands, and with salutations and the like, is called a kriyā-yogin.
m.1.17.29: One who is engaged in worship, eats moderately, has conquered the outer senses, and is free from harming others and the like, is called a tapo-yogin.
m.1.17.30: One endowed with these, always pure, free from all desires and the like, always devoted to repetition and tranquil — him they know as a japa-yogin.
m.1.17.31: By worshipping Śiva-yogins with the sixteen offerings (upacāras), a man becomes pure and attains liberation in the order of sālokya and the rest.
m.1.17.32: Now I shall describe japa-yoga; listen, O twice-born, as I speak. Japa is declared the means for one who practises austerity, for by repeating the mantra he purifies himself.
m.1.17.33: The name of Śiva in the dative, preceded by namaḥ, comprising five principles — that, O twice-born, is Śiva's five-syllabled mantra, the form of the gross Praṇava.
m.1.17.34: By repetition of the five-syllabled mantra alone a man obtains every perfection. One should always repeat the five-syllabled mantra joined at the beginning with the Praṇava.
m.1.17.35: Having received the teacher's instruction, dwelling in a comfortable abode on good ground, beginning in the bright fortnight and continuing until the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, O twice-born —
m.1.17.36: Māgha and Bhādrapada are especially distinguished, the very best of all times. Eating moderately once a day, restrained in speech, with senses controlled,
m.1.17.37: he should daily render service to his own parents, to the king and to the ancestors. By a thousand repetitions alone he becomes pure; otherwise he remains a debtor.
m.1.17.38: He should repeat the five-syllabled mantra five lakh times, meditating on Śiva — seated in the lotus posture, the giver of welfare, adorned with the Gaṅgā and the crescent moon,
m.1.17.39: resplendent with Śakti seated on his left thigh and with the great gaṇas, the god holding the deer and the axe, his hands showing the gestures granting boons and fearlessness,
m.1.17.40: meditating on Sadāśiva, the ever-gracious, having first worshipped him mentally, in the heart or in the orb of the sun.
m.1.17.41: Facing east and performing pure rites, one should repeat the five-syllabled vidyā. In the morning of the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, after completing the daily rites,
m.1.17.42: in a pleasant, clean place, self-controlled and pure in mind, one should repeat the five-syllabled mantra twelve thousand times.
m.1.17.43: He should invite excellent Śaiva brāhmaṇas together with their wives, and choose one cultured, eminent guru as the embodiment of Śiva with Ambā (Sāmba),
m.1.17.44: and five excellent twice-born devotees of Śiva representing Īśāna, Tatpuruṣa, Aghora, Vāmadeva and Sadyojāta.
m.1.17.45: Having procured the materials of worship, he should begin the worship of Śiva; and having performed Śiva's worship according to rule, he should begin the homa.
m.1.17.46: Having performed the preliminaries up to the mukha rite according to his own sūtra, he should perform the homa—eleven, or one hundred and one, or one thousand and one oblations.
m.1.17.47: He should offer them himself, with ghee from a tawny cow only; or the wise man may have Śiva's devotees offer one hundred and eight.
m.1.17.48: At the end of the homa the sacrificial fee should be given, and likewise a pair of cows to the guru, regarding those brāhmaṇas as the forms of Īśāna and the rest, and the guru as Sāmba (Śiva with Ambā).
m.1.17.49: He should bathe his own head with the water that has sprinkled their feet; he at once obtains the fruit of bathing in thirty-six crores of holy places.
m.1.17.50: He should give them, with devotion, food of ten ingredients; and honour the guru's wife with the thought of her as Parā (the Supreme Goddess), and the others' wives in the order of Īśāna and the rest,
m.1.17.51: having worshipped them with sweet rice-pudding, as lavishly as his means allow, beginning with rudrākṣas and garments, along with vaṭakas and cakes,
m.1.17.52: Then, having made the bali offering, he should hold an abundant feeding. Then, having prayed to the Lord of the gods, he should thus conclude the japa.
m.1.17.53: Having performed the puraścaraṇa in this way, a man becomes a master of the mantra. Further, by five lakhs of repetitions all his sins are destroyed.
m.1.17.54: Beginning from Atala up to Satyaloka in succession, by each five lakhs of japa one attains the lordship of each of those worlds.
m.1.17.55: If he dies midway, at the end of his enjoyment he is born on earth as a repeater of that mantra. Again, by five lakhs he attains nearness (sāmīpya) to Brahmā.
m.1.17.56: Again, by five lakhs he attains the lordship of sameness of form (sārūpya). Altogether, by a hundred lakhs he becomes directly equal to Brahmā.
m.1.17.57: Having thus attained union (sāyujya) with the effected (kārya) Brahmā, he enjoys pleasures as he wishes, as that Brahmā, until the dissolution.
m.1.17.58: Again, when another kalpa has begun, he is born as a son of Brahmā; and again, shining through austerity, he will gradually be liberated.
m.1.17.59: The worlds were created in succession from the effected elements beginning with earth: from Pātāla up to Satya are the fourteen worlds of Brahmā.
m.1.17.60: Above Satya, up to Kṣamā, are the fourteen worlds of Viṣṇu. In the Kṣamā world, in Vaikuṇṭha, the excellent city, the effected (kārya) Viṣṇu
m.1.17.61: presides there, enjoying great delights with the effected Lakṣmī and providing protection. Above that are situated twenty-eight worlds ending with Śuci.
m.1.17.62: In the Śuci world, in Kailāsa, dwells Rudra, the destroyer of beings. Above that are fifty-six worlds ending with Ahiṃsā.
m.1.17.63: Occupying the Ahiṃsā world, in the city of Jñāna-Kailāsa, the effected Lord (Kāryeśvara) presides, having brought about the concealment of all.
m.1.17.64: At its end is the wheel of time (Kālacakra); beyond that is what transcends time. There Kāla, called Cakreśvara, is presided over by Śiva.
m.1.17.65: Mounted on Dharma in the form of a buffalo, he yokes all with time. Untruth, impurity, violence and mercilessness—
m.1.17.66: this buffalo has the four feet of untruth and the rest; it is complete in all parts, assumes forms at will, has the splendour of unbelief, evil company, and always the sound of what is outside the Veda,
m.1.17.67: attached to anger, black in colour, bearing the form of a great buffalo. Up to that point the Lord is called Maheśvara; the concealment extends only that far.
m.1.17.68: Below that is the enjoyment of karma; above it, the enjoyment of knowledge. Below that is the māyā of karma; above it, the māyā of knowledge.
m.1.17.69: Mā is Lakṣmī, the enjoyment of karma; that which goes (yā) to it is therefore called māyā. Mā is Lakṣmī, the enjoyment of knowledge; that which goes to it is called māyā.
m.1.17.70: Above that is eternal enjoyment; below it, they know, all is perishable. Below that is concealment; above it there is no concealment.
m.1.17.71: Below that is bondage by the noose; above it there is no bondage at all. Below that revolve those who follow desire-motivated actions.
m.1.17.72: Above that is declared the enjoyment of desireless action. Below that revolve those devoted to the worship of the bindu.
m.1.17.73: Desireless worshippers of the liṅga go above it. Below that revolve worshippers of gods and asuras other than Śiva.
m.1.17.74: Those who are devoted solely to Śiva go beyond it. Below that is the class of individual souls (jīvas); above it are those of the supreme class.
m.1.17.75: Below that are the worldly ones; those who go above it are indeed the liberated. Below that revolve worshippers using material (prākṛta) substances.
m.1.17.76: Those who worship with substances of the Puruṣa (spiritual) go above it. Below that is the liṅga of Śakti; above it, the liṅga of Śiva.
m.1.17.77: Below that the liṅga is covered; above it, it is formless. Below that the liṅga is fashioned; above it, it is not fashioned.
m.1.17.78: Below that is the external liṅga; above it, the inner one. Below that are the worlds of Śakti, one hundred and twelve in number.
m.1.17.79: Below that is the form of bindu; beyond it, the form of nāda. Below that is the world of karma; above it, the world of knowledge.
m.1.17.80: Above that is namaskāra (obeisance), the destroyer of pride and egoism; for from there a man does not return to birth and concealment.
m.1.17.81: Thus indeed is the meaning of the word knowledge (jñāna), because it removes concealment. Those who worship only the material (ādhibhautika) revolve in saṃsāra below that.
m.1.17.82: Only the worshippers of the spiritual (ādhyātmika) go beyond that. That much indeed is the altar-portion in the liṅga which is the self of the great world.
m.1.17.83: The eightfold bond beginning with prakṛti is also known as established there. In this way all such things, worldly and Vedic, should be understood.
m.1.17.84: Those who are endowed with dharma beginning with truth, and those who are devoted to the worship of Śiva, cross the wheel of time mounted on the buffalo of adharma.
m.1.17.85: Above that is Dharma as the bull, bearing the form of brahmacarya, endowed with the feet of truth and the rest, standing in front of Śivaloka.
m.1.17.86: The bull has forbearance as its horns, tranquillity as its ears; it is adorned with the sound of the Vedas, has faith (āstikya) as its eyes, and breath, the guru, intellect and mind as its other faculties.
m.1.17.87: The bulls beginning with action (kriyā) should always be known to stand in the causal worlds and the rest. The One beyond time presides over that Dharma, the bull of action.
m.1.17.88: The lifespan of each of Brahmā, Viṣṇu and Maheśa is called one day. Above that there is no day, no night, no birth, death and the like.
m.1.17.89: Again, likewise the worlds of the causal Brahmā, ending with the causal Satya-loka, are always fashioned above that from the elements beginning with smell.
m.1.17.90: These fourteen worlds exist, having the nature of subtle smell. Again, fourteen worlds of the causal Viṣṇu exist.
m.1.17.91: Again, the worlds of the causal Rudra are held to be twenty-eight; and again, those of the causal Īśa, lying above that, are fifty-six.
m.1.17.92: Beyond that is the world called Brahmacarya-loka, approved by Śiva. There, in the Jñāna-Kailāsa endowed with five enclosures,
m.1.17.93: there indeed is the primal liṅga, endowed with five maṇḍalas, possessed of the kalās of the five Brahmans, and united with the Primal Śakti.
m.1.17.94: This is declared to be the abode of Śiva, the Supreme Self. There itself dwells the Supreme Lord, united with the Supreme Śakti,
m.1.17.95: Creation, maintenance, dissolution, concealment and grace — he is expert in these five acts, his form being being-consciousness-bliss.
m.1.17.96: He whose dharma is ever meditation, who is ever intent on grace, seated in the posture of samādhi, delighting in his own Self, shines there.
m.1.17.97: The vision of him is to be attained gradually through ritual action, meditation and the like. By performing the daily and other rites, the mind becomes inclined toward Śiva's rites.
m.1.17.98: Through Śiva's rites beginning with kriyā one should accomplish knowledge of Śiva. All who have attained his vision are surely liberated; there is no doubt.
m.1.17.99: Liberation is indeed nothing but delighting in one's own Self, in the form of the Self. One well-established in the dharmas of rite, austerity, japa, knowledge and meditation,
m.1.17.100: having gained the vision of Śiva, attains indeed the state of delighting in his own Self. Just as the sun with its own rays removes impurity,
m.1.17.101: so Śambhu, skilled in compassion, removes ignorance. When ignorance ceases, knowledge of Śiva arises.
m.1.17.102: Through knowledge of Śiva one attains one's own true nature, delight in the Self. When delight in the Self is perfected, a man has accomplished all that is to be done.
m.1.17.103: And again, by a hundred lakhs of japa one would attain the position of Brahmā; and again, by a hundred lakhs one would attain the position of Viṣṇu.
m.1.17.104: And again, by a hundred lakhs one would attain the position of Rudra; and again, by a hundred lakhs one would attain the position of Lordship (aiśvarya).
m.1.17.105: And again, well-concentrated, by japa of just this kind one would attain the wheel of time which forms the beginning of Śivaloka and the rest.
m.1.17.106: The wheel of time is a fivefold wheel, each one successively higher. Creation and delusion form Brahmā's wheel; enjoyment and delusion form Viṣṇu's.
m.1.17.107: Anger and delusion form Rudra's wheel; wandering they know as Īśvara's; knowledge and delusion form Śiva's wheel. The wise know these as the five wheels.
m.1.17.108: And again, by ten crores of japa one attains the position of the causal Brahmā; and again, by ten crores one would attain the lordship of that position.
m.1.17.109: Thus, having successively obtained the position of the mighty Viṣṇu and the others, and having successively obtained the lordship of that position of the great-souled one,
m.1.17.110: having untiringly repeated the mantra a hundred and five crores of times, one attains Śivaloka, outside the fifth enclosure.
m.1.17.111: There is a rājasa pavilion, the excellent abode of Nandin; and right there the bull in the form of austerity is seen.
m.1.17.112: That place of Sadyojāta is the excellent fifth enclosure; and the place of Vāmadeva, further, is the fourth enclosure.
m.1.17.113: Next, the abode of Aghora is the excellent third enclosure; the auspicious second enclosure belongs to Tatpuruṣa, Śiva with Ambā (Sāmba).
m.1.17.114: Then the first enclosure belongs to the supreme Īśāna. Then the place of the dharma of meditation is the fifth pavilion.
m.1.17.115: There is the abode of Balinātha, bestowing the full nectar. Next is the fourth pavilion, containing the image of Candraśekhara.
m.1.17.116: The place of Somaskanda is the excellent third pavilion. The faithful call the second pavilion the dance-pavilion.
m.1.17.117: The first pavilion there is the beautiful place of Mūlamāyā. Beyond that is the sanctum, the supremely auspicious place of the liṅga.
m.1.17.118: Beyond Nandin's abode, people do not know Śiva's glory. Nandīśvara, standing outside, worships the five-syllabled mantra.
m.1.17.119: Thus this knowledge was received by me through the succession of gurus and again from Nandīśa. Beyond that is self-knowable, experienced only through Śiva.
m.1.17.120: Only by Śiva's grace directly can the glory of Śivaloka be known by all, and not otherwise — so say the faithful.
m.1.17.121: Thus, stage by stage, Brāhmaṇas who have conquered their senses become liberated. I shall also describe the procedure for others; listen attentively to me as I speak.
m.1.17.122: Through the guru's instruction, the five-syllabled mantra ending in namaḥ is to be repeated by Brāhmaṇas; one should repeat it five lakh times for long life — this is the rule.
m.1.17.123: To remove womanhood, a woman should again repeat it five lakh times; having become a man through the mantra, the wise one gradually becomes liberated.
m.1.17.124: A Kṣatriya, by five lakh repetitions, will remove his Kṣatriya-hood; and again by five lakh, the Kṣatriya becomes a Brāhmaṇa.
m.1.17.125: Through repetition comes perfection in the mantra, and the man gradually becomes liberated. A Vaiśya, by five lakh repetitions, will remove his Vaiśya-hood;
m.1.17.126: again by five lakh he is called a mantra-Kṣatriya; and again by five lakh he will remove Kṣatriya-hood;
m.1.17.127: and again by five lakh he is called a mantra-Brāhmaṇa. And a Śūdra, through the mantra ending in namaḥ, by twenty-five lakh repetitions,
m.1.17.128: attaining the status of a mantra-Brāhmaṇa, afterwards becomes a purified twice-born. Whether woman or man, Brāhmaṇa or anyone else,
m.1.17.129: one in distress should always repeat the mantra either ending with namaḥ or with namaḥ placed first. In this matter, for women, the guru, having reasoned it out likewise, should show the procedure in due order.
m.1.17.130: At the completion of five lakh repetitions, the practitioner, solely for Śiva's pleasure, should perform a great ablution and food-offering and should worship the devotees.
m.1.17.131: By the worship of Śiva's devotee, Śiva becomes more pleased. There is no difference between Śiva and Śiva's devotee; he is indeed Śiva.
m.1.17.132: By holding the mantra which is Śiva's own form, he is indeed Śiva himself. Toward Śiva present in the body of Śiva's devotee one should be wholly devoted.
m.1.17.133: Śiva's devotees know all rites, the whole of Vedic ritual. To whatever extent the Śiva mantra has been repeated progressively by someone,
m.1.17.134: to that extent is Śiva's presence in that body; there is no doubt. Likewise, the form of a woman devoted to Śiva becomes the emblem (liṅga) of the Goddess.
m.1.17.135: As much as she repeats the mantra of the Goddess, so much is the Goddess's presence in her. The wise one, himself partaking of the form of sound, should worship Śiva fully.
m.1.17.136: And having himself become Śiva, he should worship the supreme Śakti. Having depicted Śakti, the image and the liṅga, he should worship them without deceit.
m.1.17.137: Regarding the Śiva-liṅga as Śiva and himself as having the form of Śakti; or regarding the Śakti-liṅga as the Goddess and himself as having the form of Śiva;
m.1.17.138: regarding the Śiva-liṅga as having the form of nāda, and Śakti as having the form of bindu, together with Śakti — liṅgas mutually united in the relation of subordinate and principal —
m.1.17.139: he should worship Śiva and Śakti; through meditation on the root mantra he is Śiva. Śiva's devotees, who embody the Śiva mantra and bear Śiva's form,
m.1.17.140: he should worship with the sixteen services; he will obtain what he desires. The learned one who, by service and the like, gives a Śiva devotee bearing the liṅga
m.1.17.141: joy — the learned one who produces such joy, Śiva becomes more pleased with him. Śiva's devotees together with their wives, the worshipper with his own wife should always
m.1.17.142: worship with food and the like — five, or ten, or a hundred. One who is without deceit in wealth, body, mantra and contemplation,
m.1.17.143: worshipping them as embodiments of Śiva and Śakti, is not born again on earth. Below the navel is Brahmā's portion; up to the throat is Viṣṇu's portion;
m.1.17.144: the face is the liṅga — thus is the body of Śiva's devotee declared. For the dead, whether they received cremation and other rites or the dead lacking cremation and other rites,
m.1.17.145: on their behalf one should worship Śiva himself, the primal Father; having also performed worship of the primal Mother, one should worship Śiva's devotees.
m.1.17.146: The deceased, reaching the world of the ancestors, gradually becomes liberated. One devoted to austerity excels ten devoted to rites;
m.1.17.147: one devoted to japa excels hundreds devoted to austerity; a knower of Śiva excels thousands devoted to japa;
m.1.17.148: among lakhs of knowers of Śiva, one devoted to meditation excels; one established in samādhi excels crores of those devoted to meditation.
m.1.17.149: Because of their successively higher excellence, in worshipping them the fruit is successively higher, of the nature of excellence, and hard to comprehend even for the wise.
m.1.17.150: Therefore, what man knows the greatness of Śiva's devotee? The worship of Śiva and Śakti and the worship of Śiva's devotee —
m.1.17.151: the man who performs these with devotion becomes Śiva and prospers in auspiciousness. Whoever reads this chapter, full of meaning and in accord with the Veda,
m.1.17.152: that Brāhmaṇa becomes a knower of Śiva and rejoices together with Śiva. O lords of sages, one who knows its special significance should make Śiva's devotees hear it;
m.1.17.153: for him there would be the attainment of Śiva's favour, through Śiva's compassion, O wise ones.
m.1.17.iti: Thus ends the seventeenth adhyāya, named The greatness of the praṇava and of the five-syllabled mantra, in the first saṃhitā, the Vidyeśvara-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.1.18.1: The sages said: O best knower of all meanings, tell us the nature of bondage and liberation. Sūta said: I shall describe bondage, liberation, and likewise the means to it; listen attentively.
m.1.18.2: The jīva bound by the eightfold bond beginning with prakṛti is called bound; freed from the eightfold bond beginning with prakṛti, he is called liberated.
m.1.18.3: Bringing prakṛti and the rest under control is in itself called liberation. The bound soul, once freed, is called the liberated soul.
m.1.18.4: Prakṛti first, then buddhi, ahaṅkāra consisting of the guṇas, and the five tanmātras — this they know as the group of eight beginning with prakṛti.
m.1.18.5: The body is born of the eight beginning with prakṛti; action is said to be born of the body; and again the body is born of action — thus birth and action occur again and again.
m.1.18.6: The body should be known as threefold: gross, subtle and causal. The gross is said to provide activity; the subtle provides the enjoyment of the senses.
m.1.18.7: The causal body is for the experience of the self, in accordance with the jīva's karma. Through actions of merit and sin the jīva reaps the fruit, happiness and sorrow.
m.1.18.8: Therefore, bound by the rope of karma, the jīva is ever whirled again and again like a wheel by the three bodies and karma.
m.1.18.9: To stop the whirling of the wheel, one should praise the maker of the wheel. The great wheel begins with prakṛti; Śiva is beyond prakṛti.
m.1.18.10: Maheśa is the maker of the wheel, since he is beyond prakṛti. Just as the basin round a jīvā plant drinks in water and gives it out,
m.1.18.11: so Śiva, having brought prakṛti and the rest under control, presides over them. Because all is brought under his control, therefore he is known as Śiva. Śiva alone is omniscient, perfectly full and free of desire.
m.1.18.12: Omniscience, contentment, beginningless awareness, independence, ever-undiminished power and infinite power belong to Maheśvara — this the Veda knows as his mental sovereignty.
m.1.18.13: Therefore by Śiva's grace prakṛti and the rest come under control. To obtain Śiva's grace, one should worship Śiva alone.
m.1.18.14: How can there be worship of him who is desireless and full? Action done with Śiva as its aim produces grace.
m.1.18.15: One should worship, with Śiva in view, in the liṅga, in an image, or in a devotee; one should worship with body, mind, speech and wealth too.
m.1.18.16: Through worship, Maheśa, Śiva supreme beyond prakṛti, truly bestows grace, especially on the worshipper.
m.1.18.17: By Śiva's grace, karma and the rest gradually come under one's own control. When everything, from karma up to prakṛti, comes under control,
m.1.18.18: then he is called liberated and shines, delighting in his own Self. When, by the grace of the Supreme Lord, the karma-body is under control,
m.1.18.19: then dwelling in Śiva's world is called sālokya. And when the tanmātras have come under control, one attains nearness (sāmīpya) to Sāmba, Śiva with Ambā.
m.1.18.20: Then comes union with Śiva, with his weapons and the like and his activities and so on. And on gaining great grace, the intellect too comes under control.
m.1.18.21: The intellect is an effect of prakṛti; that state is called sārṣṭi. Again, by great grace, prakṛti will come under control.
m.1.18.22: Then Śiva's mental sovereignty will be his without effort. Having gained Śiva's sovereignty beginning with omniscience, he shines in his own Self.
m.1.18.23: Those devoted to the Vedas and Āgamas call that sāyujya. Thus, step by step, liberation comes of itself through worship in the liṅga and the like.
m.1.18.24: Therefore, for Śiva's grace, one should worship Śiva with rites and the like: rites for Śiva, austerity for Śiva, constant japa of Śiva's mantra,
m.1.18.25: knowledge of Śiva and meditation on Śiva — one should practise these, each higher than the last. Until sleep, until death, one should pass the time in thought of Śiva.
m.1.18.26: He who worships Śiva with the Sadyojāta and other mantras and with flowers will attain Śiva. The sages said: O you of good vows, tell us the procedure of Śiva-worship in the liṅga and the like.
m.1.18.27: Sūta said: I shall tell the order of the liṅgas; listen properly, O twice-born. The first liṅga is the praṇava itself, which fulfils all desires.
m.1.18.28: The subtle form is the subtle praṇava, and the subtle form is partless (niṣkala). The gross liṅga is with parts (sakala); it is called the five-syllabled mantra.
m.1.18.29: Worship of these two is called austerity; both directly grant liberation. And there are very many liṅgas arising from puruṣa and prakṛti.
m.1.18.30: Śiva knows how to describe them in detail, and no one else. I shall declare to you the known liṅgas that are modifications of earth.
m.1.18.31: The Svayambhū liṅga is first, the Bindu liṅga second, then the Pratiṣṭhita and the Cara, and the Guru liṅga is the fifth.
m.1.18.32: Pleased by the austerity of gods and sages, for the sake of his presence there, Śarva, lying within the earth as a seed in the form of nāda,
m.1.18.33: breaking through the ground like the sprout of a plant, becomes manifest. Because it is born self-existent, they know it as Svayambhū.
m.1.18.34: By worship of that liṅga, knowledge increases of its own accord. On gold, silver and the like, or on the earth, or on a prepared ground,
m.1.18.35: a liṅga drawn with one's own hand, bearing the pure praṇava mantra — having drawn such a yantra-liṅga, one should perform installation and invocation.
m.1.18.36: The liṅga consisting of bindu and nāda, whether fixed or movable — this is made of mental contemplation and is seen by Śiva; there is no doubt.
m.1.18.37: Wherever Śambhu is trusted in, there he grants the fruit to that person. In a yantra drawn with one's own hand, or in a natural, fixed object and the like,
m.1.18.38: having invoked Śambhu, one should worship him with the sixteen services. One attains sovereignty oneself, and knowledge arises through practice.
m.1.18.39: That liṅga which was made by gods and sages, for their own spiritual accomplishment, with mantra and by their own hand, in a pure maṇḍala, …
m.1.18.40: A liṅga installed with pure devotion is excellent. They call that liṅga pauruṣa, and it is said to be pauruṣa-installed.
m.1.18.41: By constant worship of that liṅga one would obtain pauruṣa lordship. Liṅgas installed by great brāhmaṇas and by kings of great wealth as well…
m.1.18.42: A liṅga fashioned by a craftsman and installed with mantra—that installed liṅga is prākṛta, granting enjoyment of prākṛta lordship.
m.1.18.43: That which is powerful and lasting is called pauruṣa; that which is weak and transient is called prākṛta.
m.1.18.44: The genital organ, the navel, the tongue, the tip of the nose and the crown-tuft, in order—located in the three worlds of the body beginning with the hips—constitute the spiritual (ādhyātmika), moving liṅga.
m.1.18.45: A mountain is declared pauruṣa; the surface of the earth they know as prākṛta. Trees and the like are to be known as pauruṣa; shrubs and the like they know as prākṛta.
m.1.18.46: Ṣāṣṭika rice is to be known as prākṛta; śāli rice and wheat as pauruṣa. One should know as pauruṣa the lordship that bestows the eight siddhis beginning with aṇimā.
m.1.18.47: Objects such as good wives and wealth the faithful call prākṛta. First among the moving liṅgas is declared the rasaliṅga (mercury liṅga).
m.1.18.48: The rasaliṅga would grant all desires to brāhmaṇas; the auspicious bāṇaliṅga grants great kingship to kṣatriyas.
m.1.18.49: The golden liṅga for vaiśyas grants mastery of great wealth; the auspicious stone liṅga for śūdras brings great purification.
m.1.18.50: The crystal liṅga and the bāṇaliṅga grant all wishes to everyone. In the absence of one's own, using another's is not forbidden in worship.
m.1.18.51: For women the earthen liṅga is prescribed, especially for those whose husbands are living; for widows engaged in worldly life the crystal one is declared.
m.1.18.52: For widows who have renounced, the rasaliṅga is preferred. Whether in childhood, youth or old age, O you of good vows,
m.1.18.53: a liṅga of pure crystal grants women all enjoyments. For those engaged in worldly life, worship of the pedestal grants all desires on earth.
m.1.18.54: The one engaged in worldly life should perform all worship with a vessel; after the ablution he should make the food offering with cooked śāli rice.
m.1.18.55: At the end of worship he should place the liṅga in caskets in a separate room. Renunciants who worship the liṅga on the hand should offer their own food.
m.1.18.56: For renunciants the supreme subtle liṅga alone is preferred. One should worship with sacred ash and offer sacred ash.
m.1.18.57: Having performed the worship, one should always bear that liṅga on the head. Sacred ash is declared to be threefold, by worldly, Vedic and Śiva fires.
m.1.18.58: Ash produced from worldly fire one should use for purifying substances—things made of clay, wood and metal, and grains likewise,
m.1.18.59: of substances such as sesame, and of cloth and the like likewise, and also of stale things—purification by ash is prescribed.
m.1.18.60: For things defiled by dogs and the like, too, purification by ash is prescribed. One should apply ash with water or without water, as is fitting.
m.1.18.61: Likewise, ash produced from Vedic fire one should wear at the conclusion of those rites. Produced by mantra and ritual action, the rite in the fire takes the form of ash.
m.1.18.62: By wearing that ash, the rite becomes placed upon one's own self. With the Aghora mantra, the mantra of the self, one should burn bilva wood.
m.1.18.63: That is called Śiva-fire; what is burnt by it is ash born of Śiva-fire. First the dung of a tawny cow, or simply cow-dung alone,
m.1.18.64: or śamī, aśvattha and palāśa, or vaṭa, āragvadha and bilva wood—one should burn them with Śiva-fire; that pure ash is indeed śivāgnija.
m.1.18.65: Or one should burn the wood in a fire of darbha grass, chanting the Śiva mantra; having sifted it well through cloth, one should deposit it in a new pot.
m.1.18.66: It is to be collected for radiance; it is esteemed and also worshipped. Such is the meaning of the word bhasma; Śiva did so in the beginning.
m.1.18.67: Just as a king in his realm takes the essence, which is the tax, and as men, having burnt crops and the like, enjoy the essence,
m.1.18.68: and just as the digestive fire, having burnt many and various foods, nourishes its own body with the finer essence drawn from the essence,
m.1.18.69: so too that Śiva, the Supreme Lord, though the maker of the universe, having burnt the universe over which he presides, took its essence.
m.1.18.70: Having burnt the universe, Śiva placed that ash upon himself; under the pretext of smearing ash, he took the essence of the world.
m.1.18.71: He placed his jewel in his own body: he adorned his hair with the essence of ether, his face with the essence of air,
m.1.18.72: his heart with the essence of fire, his waist with the essence of water, his knee with the essence of earth—and likewise all his limbs.
m.1.18.73: The tripuṇḍra, the essence of Brahmā, Viṣṇu and the Rudras, Maheśvara wears likewise in the form of a tilaka on his forehead.
m.1.18.74: Through the growth of this ash he regards all this as himself. The entire essence of the universe has been brought under control by him alone.
m.1.18.75: Therefore there is no other who can control him; he is known as Śiva. Just as the slayer of all beasts is the beast-slayer the lion,
m.1.18.76: and there is no beast that slays him, he is therefore called siṃha (lion). Śam is eternal happiness and bliss; the letter i is held to be the Puruṣa;
m.1.18.77: the letter va is Śakti, the nectar; their union is called Śiva. Therefore, having thus made one's own self Śiva, one should worship Śiva.
m.1.18.78: Therefore one should first smear the body with ash and then wear the tripuṇḍra. At the time of worship it should be with water; for purification, without water.
m.1.18.79: Whether by day or by night, whether woman or man, one should, for worship, wear ash mixed with water in the form of the tripuṇḍra.
m.1.18.80: Whoever wears the tripuṇḍra of ash mixed with water and then performs worship, to him alone is the fruit of Śiva-worship, complete in all its parts, surely assured.
m.1.18.81: Having worn ash with Śiva's mantra, one becomes a member of the highest āśrama. He is called a Śivāśramī, because Śiva alone is supreme for him.
m.1.18.82: For one wholly devoted to the vow of Śiva there is no impurity from death nor impurity from birth. On the front of the forehead he should wear white ash, or a tilaka with clay.
m.1.18.83: Applied by one's own hand or by the guru's hand, this is the mark of Śiva's devotee. He restrains the guṇas — this is declared to be the analysis of the word guru.
m.1.18.84: He checks and removes the guṇas, rajas and the rest, together with their modifications. The supreme Śiva, who is beyond the guṇas, has taken on the form of the guru.
m.1.18.85: Because, having first removed the triad of guṇas, he awakens the disciple to Śiva, he is called the guru of trusting disciples.
m.1.18.86: Therefore, the wise know, the guru's body is the guru-liṅga, and worship of the guru-liṅga is service to the guru.
m.1.18.87: Service (śuśrūṣā) carries out what has been heard, with body, mind and speech: whatever was told earlier by the guru, whether possible or impossible,
m.1.18.88: the pure-souled one does it, even at the cost of his life and wealth. Therefore one who is fit to be instructed is called a disciple (śiṣya).
m.1.18.89: The good disciple, having given to the guru everything meant for his own body and the like, and having first offered him the first portion of cooked food, should eat with the guru's permission.
m.1.18.90: A disciple is called a son because of his constant discipleship. Having poured the semen of the mantra from the liṅga of the tongue into the womb of the ear,
m.1.18.91: the son so born is a mantra-son; he should worship the guru as his father. The begetting father plunges the son into saṃsāra,
m.1.18.92: but the guru, the father who awakens, carries him across saṃsāra. Knowing the difference between the two, one should worship the guru as father.
m.1.18.93: One should honour the guru also by bodily service and with wealth and the like earned by oneself. Since the limbs of the guru, from the feet up to the hair, are liṅgas,
m.1.18.94: one should worship them fully with offerings in the form of wealth such as sandals, with clasping of the feet and the like, with bathing, ablution and food-offerings, and with meals.
m.1.18.95: Worship of the guru is itself worship of Śiva, the supreme Self. Service to the guru, whatever it may be, all of it brings about purification of the self.
m.1.18.96: The guru's leftover is Śiva's leftover; water and things made of food and the like left by him are to be accepted and eaten by disciples who are Śiva's devotees, O brāhmaṇas.
m.1.18.97: Everything done without the guru's permission is like theft. One should diligently take as guru one who has special knowledge, superior even to an ordinary guru.
m.1.18.98: Release from ignorance is what is to be achieved, and it is the one with special knowledge who releases. At the beginning, the removal of obstacles should be done for the completion of a rite.
m.1.18.99: A rite performed without obstacles and complete in its parts becomes fruitful. Therefore at the start of all rites the wise should worship the Lord of Obstacles (Vighneśa).
m.1.18.100: For the removal of all afflictions the wise should worship all the gods. Fever and the like, tumours and diseases are considered the ādhyātmika (bodily) affliction.
m.1.18.101: On the appearance of piśācas, jackals and the like, likewise at the rising up of anthills and the like, and at the sudden falling of creatures such as lizards,
m.1.18.102: and at the sight in the house of a tortoise, a snake, a strange woman or a wicked person, and in cases of unusual births among trees, women, cows and the like,
m.1.18.103: future sorrow comes; therefore these are considered bhautika (from beings). The falling of impure things and of thunderbolts, and likewise a great plague,
m.1.18.104: epidemic fever, cholera, cattle-plague and smallpox, transits of planets into one's birth-star and planetary conjunctions in one's own rāśi,
m.1.18.105: and seeing bad dreams and the like, are considered ādhidaivika. When, through contact with a corpse, a cāṇḍāla or an outcaste, such a one has entered the inner house,
m.1.18.106: when something of this kind has arisen, a sign of future sorrow, the wise person should perform a pacificatory sacrifice (śānti-yajña) to appease that fault.
m.1.18.107: In a temple, or a cowshed, or a sacred shrine, or the courtyard of a house, on a raised altar-place two cubits in size and well adorned,
m.1.18.108: having placed rice grain amounting to one bhāra and spread it around, having drawn a lotus in the middle and likewise drawn lotuses in the directions,
m.1.18.109: having placed in the middle a great pot wound with thread and fumigated with fresh guggulu, he should likewise set pots in the directions too,
m.1.18.110: and likewise pitchers with stalked mango leaves, kūrca-bundles and the like in the eight directions; he should fill them with water purified by mantra and mixed with the five substances.
m.1.18.111: He should put in the nine gems, sapphire and the rest, in order. The wise one should engage an ācārya who knows the rite, along with his wife.
m.1.18.112: He should place in the pots golden images of Viṣṇu and of Indra and the others; in the central pot, covered with its lid, he should invoke and worship Viṣṇu.
m.1.18.113: In the east and the other directions he should worship Indra and the others in order, with their respective mantras, using each one's name in the dative ending with namaḥ, in due sequence.
m.1.18.114: He should have all the rites such as invocation performed by the ācārya himself. Together with the ācārya and the ṛtvij priests he should recite their mantras a hundred times.
m.1.18.115: At the end of the recitation he should perform a homa on the western side of the pot: ten million, a hundred thousand, a thousand, or a hundred and eight oblations, O wise ones.
m.1.18.116: He should perform it for one day, or nine days, or for a maṇḍala period, as is suitable, in accordance with time and place.
m.1.18.117: A homa with śamī wood is for pacification, and with palāśa for livelihood. He should offer oblations with substances—fuel-sticks, cooked food and ghee—with the deity's name or with the mantra.
m.1.18.118: Whatever substance was used at the beginning, he should continue it to the end of the rite. At the end, having had the puṇyāha recited, on the final day he should sprinkle all with the waters.
m.1.18.119: Afterwards he should feed brāhmaṇas, as many as the number of oblations. The ācārya and the ṛtvij priests should eat only sacrificial food, O wise ones.
m.1.18.120: Having worshipped the planets beginning with the Sun, at the very end of all the oblations one should give the officiating priests their fee, the nine gems, in due order.
m.1.18.121: Then one should perform the ten gifts, and after that the abundant gift; one should give wealth to children, to initiated students, to householders, to forest-dwellers,
m.1.18.122: to maidens, to married women, and after that to widows. All the ritual implements one should present to the preceptor.
m.1.18.123: Yama is held to be the lord of the sufferings caused by portents and plagues; therefore, to please Yama, one should have the gift of Kāla given.
m.1.18.124: One should make it with a hundred niṣkas, or else with ten niṣkas; one should fashion Kāla in human form, holding a noose and a goad.
m.1.18.125: One should make the gift of that golden image together with a fee. Then one should make a gift of sesame for securing a full span of life.
m.1.18.126: And for the removal of disease one should make the gift of ghee in which one has looked at one's reflection. One should feed a thousand brāhmaṇas, or, if poor, just a hundred.
m.1.18.127: A poor man lacking wealth should do as much as he can. For the pacification of spirits and the like, one should perform a great worship of Bhairava.
m.1.18.128: At the end one should have the great ablution and food-offering made to Śiva; afterwards one should feed brāhmaṇas in the form of a lavish feast.
m.1.18.129: By a sacrifice performed in this way one obtains pacification of faults. One should perform this pacificatory sacrifice every year in the month of Phālguna.
m.1.18.130: In case of an ill-omened sight and the like, one should perform it promptly, within a month. When a great sin or the like has befallen, one should perform the worship of Bhairava.
m.1.18.131: When a grave disease arises, one should again make the resolve and perform the rite. But a poor man lacking everything should then make a gift of lamps.
m.1.18.132: One unable even to do that should bathe and give whatever gift he can, and should bow to the Sun with a mantra a hundred and eight times.
m.1.18.133: The wise man may have the prostrations done a thousand, ten thousand, a hundred thousand or ten million times. By the sacrifice consisting of salutation all the deities become pleased.
m.1.18.134: Contemplating thus: My intellect is offered into your own nature; it takes no delight in what is not filled by you. And the sense of I that was in us is abandoned once you are seen.
m.1.18.135: I bow down with my own body; O Lord, you are great. My own nature is not void; now I am your servant.
m.1.18.136: One should, as is fitting, perform salutation as a sacrifice of one's own self. Then, having offered food to Śiva here, one should bring betel.
m.1.18.137: One should oneself circumambulate Śiva a hundred and eight times; a thousand, ten thousand, a hundred thousand or ten million times one may have done by another.
m.1.18.138: Through circumambulation of Śiva every sin perishes in an instant. Disease is the root of suffering, and sin is the root of disease.
m.1.18.139: It is declared that sins are dispelled only by dharma. Dharma performed with Śiva as its aim is able to remove sin.
m.1.18.140: Circumambulation is declared to be foremost among the rites of Śiva. Circumambulation is, through action, a form of japa — it is the praṇava itself.
m.1.18.141: Birth and death, the pair of opposites, is called the wheel of māyā. That wheel of Śiva's māyā is said to be the offering-pedestal (balipīṭha).
m.1.18.142: Starting from the offering-pedestal and moving clockwise, step after step, one should come back to the offering-pedestal.
m.1.18.143: Then one should make a prostration; this is called circumambulation. Going forth from the pedestal is birth attained; the bow is the offering of the self.
m.1.18.144: Thus the pair, birth and death, is offered to Śiva's māyā. One who has offered the pair to Śiva's māyā does not again become a partaker of individual selfhood.
m.1.18.145: As long as he has a body and is subject to action, that soul is called bound. Mastery over the three bodies is called liberation by the wise.
m.1.18.146: Śiva, the supreme cause, is indeed the driver of the wheel of māyā; and Śiva wipes away the pair that has been offered to Śiva's māyā.
m.1.18.147: The pair fashioned by Śiva one should offer back to him alone. Know, O wise ones, that circumambulation and prostration are exceedingly dear to Śiva.
m.1.18.148: Circumambulations and prostrations to Śiva, the supreme Self, and worship done with the sixteen services, bestow their fruit.
m.1.18.149: There is no sin on earth that cannot be destroyed by circumambulation; therefore one should destroy all sin by circumambulation alone.
m.1.18.150: Devoted to Śiva's worship, observing silence, endowed with truthfulness and other virtues, one should practise each of ritual action, austerity, japa, knowledge and meditation in turn.
m.1.18.151: Lordly power, a divine body, knowledge, destruction of ignorance, and nearness to Śiva — this is the fruit of ritual action and the rest.
m.1.18.152: By performance one attains the fruit, through the removal of darkness and the wiping away of birth, the fruits arising as though produced by the knowing intellect.
m.1.18.153: The devotee of Śiva should perform ritual action and the rest as is fitting, according to place, time, bodily capacity and wealth.
m.1.18.154: The wise man should live in a holy place of Śiva on good wealth justly earned, a livelihood free from harm to living beings and the like, and without excessive toil.
m.1.18.155: Water and food over which the five-syllable mantra has been recited they know to be wholesome. Or, they say, for a poor man alms-food becomes the giver of knowledge.
m.1.18.156: For a devotee of Śiva, alms-food increases devotion to Śiva. The alms-food of a Śiva-yogin they call Śambhu's sacrificial feast (śambhusattra).
m.1.18.157: By whatever means, wherever on earth, eating only pure food and always silent, one should not reveal the secret.
m.1.18.158: But to devotees one should reveal only the greatness of Śiva. The secret of Śiva's mantra Śiva knows, no other.
m.1.18.159: A devotee of Śiva should always dwell taking refuge in the Śiva-liṅga. By taking refuge in the liṅga of Sthāṇu alone, O brāhmaṇas, one becomes Sthāṇu.
m.1.18.160: By the worship of a movable liṅga one certainly becomes liberated, in due course. Thus everything has been told in brief: the supreme goal and the means to attain it.
m.1.18.161: This is what was formerly taught by Vyāsa and what I heard long ago. May there be good fortune for you and for us; may that devotion to Śiva be firm.
m.1.18.162: The man who always reads this chapter, or who listens to it, obtains knowledge of Śiva by Śiva's grace, O wise ones.
m.1.18.iti: Thus ends the eighteenth adhyāya, named The greatness of Śiva's liṅga, in the Sādhyasādhana-khaṇḍa of the first saṃhitā, the Vidyeśvara-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.1.19.1: The sages said: O Sūta, O Sūta, may you live long. You are blessed and devoted to Śiva. The glory of the liṅga, which bestows good fruit, has been well described by you.
m.1.19.2: Now tell us again that account in which the glory of the earthen liṅga of Maheśa, supreme above all, was narrated by Vyāsa.
m.1.19.3: Sūta said: Listen, all you sages, every one of you, with true devotion and reverence: the glory of Śiva's earthen liṅga is being declared by me.
m.1.19.4: Among these liṅgas that have been mentioned, the earthen liṅga is the best. O brahmins, through its worship many have attained spiritual success.
m.1.19.5: Hari, Brahmā, the sages and likewise the Prajāpatis, having duly worshipped the earthen liṅga, obtained all they desired, O twice-born ones.
m.1.19.6: Gods, asuras and humans, Gandharvas, serpents and Rākṣasas, and many others too, having worshipped it, attained the highest success.
m.1.19.7: In the Kṛta age the liṅga made of gems is best, in the Tretā one made of gold, in the Dvāpara one of mercury is best, but in the Kali age the earthen one.
m.1.19.8: Among all the eight forms of Śiva, the earthen form is indeed the finest. O brahmins, worshipped with undivided devotion it is itself austerity; hence its fruit is great.
m.1.19.9: Just as among all gods Maheśvara is the eldest and the best, so among all liṅgas the earthen one is said to be the best.
m.1.19.10: Just as among all rivers the celestial river Gaṅgā is the eldest and best, so among all liṅgas the earthen one is said to be the best.
m.1.19.11: Just as among all mantras the Praṇava is regarded as great, so this earthen liṅga is the best, indeed the one to be adored and worshipped.
m.1.19.12: Just as among all classes the brahmin is said to be the best, so among all liṅgas the earthen one is said to be the best.
m.1.19.13: Just as among all cities Kāśī is regarded as the very best, so among all liṅgas the earthen one is said to be the best.
m.1.19.14: Just as among all vows the Śivarātri vow is supreme, so among all liṅgas the earthen one is said to be the best.
m.1.19.15: Just as among all goddesses Śiva's Śakti is regarded as supreme, so among all liṅgas the earthen one is said to be the best.
m.1.19.16: Whoever, having made an earthen liṅga, worships another god—that worship becomes futile; his bathing, giving and the rest are futile.
m.1.19.17: Worship of the earthen liṅga is meritorious, auspicious and life-prolonging; it grants contentment, nourishment and prosperity, and should be performed by the best of practitioners.
m.1.19.18: Endowed with devotion and faith, one should worship the earthen liṅga, which grants the fulfilment of all desires and aims, with whatever offerings are available.
m.1.19.19: Whoever makes an earthen liṅga with an auspicious pedestal and worships it becomes wealthy and prosperous in this very life, and at the end is born as Rudra.
m.1.19.20: Hear the meritorious fruit of one who, having made an earthen liṅga, worships it with bilva at the three junctions of the day for as long as ten times eleven days.
m.1.19.21: In this very body of his he is honoured in Rudra's world; by being seen and even touched he destroys the sins of all mortals.
m.1.19.22: He is liberated while living, truly a knower, Śiva himself—there is no doubt. By merely seeing him both enjoyment and liberation arise.
m.1.19.23: Whoever worships Śiva daily throughout his whole life, having made an earthen liṅga, goes to Śiva's abode.
m.1.19.24: He dwells with Mṛḍa in Śiva's world for countless years; if he has desires, he returns again and becomes a great king in Bhārata.
m.1.19.25: One who, free of desire, worships the excellent earthen liṅga daily remains forever in Śiva's world and attains union (sāyujya) with him.
m.1.19.26: If a brahmin does not worship the earthen Śiva-liṅga, he goes to a terrible, most dreadful hell where beings are impaled on stakes.
m.1.19.27: One should have a beautiful liṅga made by whatever method; for the earthen one, one need not consider the rule of the five measuring-lines (pañcasūtra).
m.1.19.28: It must indeed be made undivided; one should not make it in separate parts. One who makes it in parts certainly does not obtain the fruit of worship.
m.1.19.29: A liṅga made of gems, of gold, of mercury, likewise of crystal, of earth, or of topaz—one should have it made undivided.
m.1.19.30: An undivided liṅga is regarded as movable, a two-part one as immovable; this distinction of divided and undivided is prescribed with regard to the movable and the immovable.
