m.2.3.6.26: Then it was a most auspicious time: the constellations, planets and stars were calm, the sky became clear, and there was brightness in all directions.
m.2.3.6.27: The earth, with its forests, villages and oceans, was full of auspiciousness; in lakes, rivers and wells lotuses bloomed.
m.2.3.6.28: Various breezes pleasant to the touch blew, O lord of sages; all the good rejoiced, and sorrow quickly befell the wicked.
m.2.3.6.29: The immortals came into the sky and beat kettledrums; a shower of flowers fell there, and the best of the Gandharvas sang.
m.2.3.6.30: The Vidyādhara women and likewise the Apsarases danced in the sky; then there was a great festival of the gods and others in the heavens.
m.2.3.6.31: At that moment the Goddess, the primal Śakti, Śivā, who had been Satī, appeared before Menā in her own form.
m.2.3.6.32: In the spring season, in the month of Madhu, on the ninth day, under the Mṛga asterism, at midnight she was born, like Gaṅgā from the orb of the moon.
m.2.3.6.33: At that time Śivā, in that very form of hers, came forth from Menakā's womb and was born, like Lakṣmī from the ocean.
m.2.3.6.34: Then, when she was born, Bhava became pleased; a favourable wind blew, deep, fragrant and auspicious.
m.2.3.6.35: There was a shower of flowers, preceded by a shower of rain; the sacred fires blazed up serenely, and the clouds then thundered.
m.2.3.6.36: As she was being born, every kind of wealth came about there in Himavat's city, and all sorrow perished.
m.2.3.6.37: At that moment all the gods, Viṣṇu and the rest, came there joyfully and with love, and beheld the Mother of the World.
m.2.3.6.38: They praised her — Śivā, the Mother, Kālikā, beloved of Śiva, of divine form, the Great Māyā, dweller in Śiva's world.
m.2.3.6.39: The gods said: O Mother of the World, Great Goddess, bestower of all attainments, you indeed accomplish the gods' task; therefore we ever bow to you.
m.2.3.6.40: In every way bring about the welfare of the gods, O you who love your devotees. You have fulfilled Menā's heart's desire; fulfil Hara's too.
m.2.3.6.41: Brahmā said: Having thus praised Śivā and bowed deeply to her, the gods led by Viṣṇu went, delighted, each to his own abode, extolling her supreme state.
m.2.3.6.42: O Nārada, seeing the goddess thus born, dark in complexion, with the lustre of a blue lotus petal, Menakā was filled with joy.
m.2.3.6.43: Then, beholding her divine form, the beloved of the mountain gained understanding; recognising her as the supreme Goddess, she praised her, exceedingly delighted.
m.2.3.6.44: Menā said: O Mother of the world, O Great Goddess, you have shown great compassion, in that you have appeared before me in radiance, O Ambikā.
m.2.3.6.45: You are the first of all powers, the mother of the three worlds, O Śivā; ever beloved of Śiva, O Goddess, supreme, praised by all the gods.
m.2.3.6.46: Be gracious, O Great Goddess; abide in my meditation. Instead of this form, take before my eyes a form like that of a daughter.
m.2.3.6.47: Brahmā said: Hearing these words of Menā, the mountain's wife, the goddess Śivā, well pleased, replied to the mountain's beloved.
m.2.3.6.48: The Goddess said: O Menā, formerly you, devoted, served me well; greatly pleased by your devotion, I came near you to grant a boon.
m.2.3.6.49: Hearing my words bidding you ask a boon, you chose this boon: Become my daughter, O Great Goddess, and accomplish the welfare of the gods.
m.2.3.6.50: Having thus granted you the boon, I went with respect to my own abode; when the time came, I became your daughter, O beloved of the mountain.
m.2.3.6.51: I have assumed this divine form today so that you may remember me; otherwise, through the mortal condition, you would have ignorance regarding me.
m.2.3.6.52: You two, thinking of me again and again, either as a daughter or as divine, and bearing affection for me, will attain my supreme state.
m.2.3.6.53: I shall accomplish the gods' task, performing a wondrous play on earth; I shall become Śambhu's wife and shall deliver the virtuous.
m.2.3.6.54: Brahmā said: Having said this, Śivā Ambikā fell silent, and by her own māyā, while the mother looked on with love, she at once took on the body of an infant daughter.
m.2.3.6.iti: Thus ends the sixth adhyāya, named The description of the birth of Pārvatī, in the third khaṇḍa, the Pārvatī-khaṇḍa, of the second saṃhitā, the Rudra-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.2.3.7.1: Brahmā said: Then, in front of Menā, she of great radiance, having become her daughter, began to cry there, adopting the way of the world.
m.2.3.7.2: Around the lying-in bed, by her excellent, widely spreading brilliance, the midnight lamps at once became dimmed in their light, O sage.
m.2.3.7.3: Hearing that charming crying, all the women of the household rejoiced and came there in haste, full of affection.
m.2.3.7.4: Then an attendant of the inner apartments quickly announced to the mountain-king the birth of Pārvatī, which was joyful, auspicious, and would accomplish the gods' purpose.
m.2.3.7.5: For that attendant of the inner apartments who swiftly brought the good news of a daughter's birth, there was nothing that king of mountains would not give, not even his white royal parasol.
m.2.3.7.6: The mountain went there joyfully with his family priest and excellent brāhmaṇas, and saw that daughter shining with beautiful radiance.
m.2.3.7.7: Seeing such a girl, dark like the petal of a blue lotus, radiant and most lovely, the lord of mountains rejoiced greatly.
m.2.3.7.8: And all rejoiced there—the citizens, men and women. Then there was a great festival, and musical instruments sounded abundantly.
m.2.3.7.9: There was auspicious singing; courtesans danced. And having performed the birth rite (jātakarma), he gave gifts to the twice-born.
m.2.3.7.10: Then, coming to the gate, Himācala, glad at heart, held a very great festival and gave wealth to mendicants.
m.2.3.7.11: Then, at an auspicious moment, Himavān together with the sages gave his daughter joy-bestowing names, beginning with Kālī.
m.2.3.7.12: Then he gladly and respectfully gave many gifts to the brāhmaṇas, and had various festivities held, accompanied by song.
m.2.3.7.13: Having thus held abundant festivities, and gazing at Kālī again and again, the mountain, together with his wife, found delight, though he already had many sons.
m.2.3.7.14: There, in the house of the king of mountains, the goddess Śivā grew, like the Gaṅgā in the rainy season, or like moonlight in autumn.
m.2.3.7.15: Thus that goddess Kālikā, lovely-limbed and beautiful to behold, took on day by day a growing charm, like a digit of the moon's disc.
m.2.3.7.16: Her kinsfolk called her, who was dear to her relatives and endowed with the virtue of good conduct, by the name Pārvatī, befitting her family.
m.2.3.7.17: Kālikā, forbidden by her mother from practising austerity with the words u mā (O, don't), the fair-faced one later came to be known in the world as Umā, O sage.
m.2.3.7.18: The gaze of the mountain, though he had sons, found no satiety in that child named Pārvatī, endowed with every good fortune.
m.2.3.7.19: For though spring has endless flowers, the swarm of bees has a special attachment to the mango tree, the fragrant sahakāra, O lord of sages.
m.2.3.7.20: By her the mountain Himālaya became both purified and adorned, just as a wise man is by refined speech.
m.2.3.7.21: As the lamp of a house shines by its flame of great radiance, as the celestial path by the three-pathed Gaṅgā, so the mountain shone by the mountain-born girl.
m.2.3.7.22: In childhood, amid her friends, she played again and again with balls, dolls, and sand-altars on the banks of the Gaṅgā.
m.2.3.7.23: Then, when the time for instruction came, O sage, the goddess Śivā studied the sciences with great delight and a controlled mind under a good teacher.
m.2.3.7.24: The knowledge of her former birth came to her, as in autumn the row of swans comes to the heavenly river, and as at night their own luminosity comes to the great herbs.
m.2.3.7.25: Thus some part of Śivā's play has been well described. I shall tell another episode of her play; listen with love, O sage.
m.2.3.7.iti: Thus ends the seventh adhyāya, named The description of the childhood play of Pārvatī, in the third khaṇḍa, the Pārvatī-khaṇḍa, of the second saṃhitā, the Rudra-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.2.3.8.1: Brahmā said: Once you, a knower of Śiva and the best among those who know Śiva's divine play, went with affection to the house of Himācala, impelled by Śiva.
m.2.3.8.2: O sage Nārada, on seeing you, the lord of mountains bowed and worshipped you; and calling his own daughter, he made her fall at your feet.
m.2.3.8.3: O lord of sages, bowing to you again, the snowy mountain, with joined palms and head deeply bowed, considering himself fortunate, spoke to you.
m.2.3.8.4: Himavān said: O sage Nārada, wise one, best of Brahmā's sons, O lord, you are all-knowing, compassionate, and devoted to helping others.
m.2.3.8.5: Tell me my daughter's horoscope, with the good and bad qualities arising from it. Whose beloved will my fortunate daughter become?
m.2.3.8.6: Brahmā said: Thus addressed by Himādri, the lord of mountains, O best of sages, you examined Kālikā's hand and especially all her limbs.
m.2.3.8.7: Dear son, you, Nārada—playful, skilled in speech, wise, knowing the whole matter, and pleased at heart—spoke to the mountain.
m.2.3.8.8: Nārada said: O Menā, O king of mountains, this daughter of yours has grown like the first digit of the moon, endowed with all auspicious marks.
m.2.3.8.9: She will give the utmost happiness to her husband and increase the fame of her parents; a great chaste woman, she will always bring great joy to all women.
m.2.3.8.10: O mountain, all the marks on your daughter's hand are auspicious; but there is one unusual line—hear its result truly.
m.2.3.8.11: Her husband, it seems, will be like this: a yogin, naked, without qualities, free of desire, without mother or father, without pride, and of inauspicious attire.
m.2.3.8.12: Brahmā said: Hearing your words and taking them to be true, the couple, Menā and Himācala, both became distressed.
m.2.3.8.13: But Śivā, the Mother of the world, hearing such words of yours and recognising Śiva from those marks, rejoiced greatly in her heart, O sage.
m.2.3.8.14: Reflecting that Nārada's words cannot be false, Śivā then conceived in her heart a deep love for Śiva's pair of feet.
m.2.3.8.15: Then the mountain, grieved at heart, said to you, Nārada: O sage, what remedy should I adopt? Great sorrow has arisen.
m.2.3.8.16: Hearing that, O sage, you, the maker of great wonders and skilled in speech, spoke, delighting Himācala with auspicious words.
m.2.3.8.17: Nārada said: O mountain, listen with affection to my words: they are true, not false. The lines of the hand are Brahmā's writing; they certainly never prove false.
m.2.3.8.18: O mountain, her husband will be such—there is no doubt. Hear with pleasure the remedy for it, by following which you will attain happiness.
m.2.3.8.19: Such a bridegroom is Śambhu, the Lord who assumes forms in play; in him all the ill marks are equal to good qualities.
m.2.3.8.20: In a mighty lord a defect does not cause sorrow; it causes great sorrow only in one who is not a lord. The sun, fire and the Gaṅgā should be known as examples of this.
m.2.3.8.21: Therefore, with discernment, give your daughter Śivā to Śiva. Śiva is the lord of all, worthy of service, changeless, the imperishable Lord.
m.2.3.8.22: That Śiva, quick to be gracious, will undoubtedly accept her; he is attained especially through austerity, if Śivā performs austerity.
m.2.3.8.23: For that Śiva, the lord of all, is fully capable in every way; he can shatter even the thunderbolt, has Brahmā under his control, and bestows happiness.
m.2.3.8.24: Brahmā said: Having said this, dear son, you—playful sage and knower of Brahman—again spoke to the king of mountains, delighting him with auspicious words.
m.2.3.8.25: She will become the beloved of Śambhu, ever agreeable to Hara, a great chaste woman of good vows, increasing her parents' happiness.
m.2.3.8.26: Through austerity she will bring Śambhu's mind under her control, and he too will marry no other woman except her.
m.2.3.8.27: Love like that of these two has never been anyone's, nor will be, nor exists now.
m.2.3.8.28: Through these two, O best of mountains, the tasks of the gods that must be done, and whatever ones had died, will be revived again and again.
m.2.3.8.29: Through this daughter of yours, O mountain, Hara will become Ardhanārīśvara; and joyfully the two will be united once again.
m.2.3.8.30: This daughter of yours, having pleased Maheśa, the lord of all, by the power of austerity, will take half of Hara's body.
m.2.3.8.31: Having pleased Hara by austerity, this daughter of yours will become golden-fair, gleaming like gold, fairest like lightning.
m.2.3.8.32: This maiden will win fame by the name Gaurī, and will be worshipped by all the hosts of gods, as well as by Hari, Brahmā and others.
m.2.3.8.33: O best of mountains, you should not give her to anyone else here. And this secret of the gods must never be revealed.
m.2.3.8.34: Brahmā said: Hearing these words of yours, O divine sage Nārada, Himavān, skilled in speech, spoke to you, O sage.
m.2.3.8.35: Himavān said: O wise sage Nārada, I make a certain request; listen to it with affection, and so bring me joy.
m.2.3.8.36: It is heard that Mahādeva has renounced all attachment, is self-controlled, and constantly practises austerity, beyond the reach even of the gods.
m.2.3.8.37: O divine sage, how will he, established on the path of meditation, divert his mind fixed on the supreme Brahman? About this I have great doubt.
m.2.3.8.38: He contemplates his own form called Sadāśiva—the imperishable supreme Brahman, like the flame of a lamp, changeless, beyond the unborn Brahmā,
m.2.3.8.39: which is both without and with qualities, undifferentiated and free of activity. Hence he sees it everywhere and does not look at anything external.
m.2.3.8.40: So it is constantly heard about him, O sage, from the mouths of the Kinnaras who come here with great affection. Is that surely a false report?
m.2.3.8.41: In particular, it is heard that Hara himself, in person and by name, made a vow in the past. Hear it as I relate it.
m.2.3.8.42: O Dākṣāyaṇī, O beloved Satī, apart from you I will not choose another; I will not take anyone as a wife. I tell you this truly.
m.2.3.8.43: Thus a vow was made by him with Satī long ago. Now that she is dead, how will he himself take another?
m.2.3.8.44: Brahmā said: Having said this, the mountain fell silent in front of you. Hearing that, O divine sage, you then spoke in accordance with the real truth.
m.2.3.8.45: Nārada said: you need not worry, O king of mountains, O wise one. This daughter of yours, Kālī, was indeed born formerly as Dakṣa's daughter.
m.2.3.8.46: Her name was Satī, ever bestowing all auspiciousness. That Satī, being Dakṣa's daughter, became the beloved of Rudra.
m.2.3.8.47: Then, at her father's sacrifice, having met with disrespect, and seeing that of Śaṅkara too, Satī, on seeing it, became enraged and gave up her body.
m.2.3.8.48: That very one, Ambikā Śivā, has been born again in your house. This Pārvatī will become Hara's wife; there is no doubt.
m.2.3.8.49: All this, O sage, you told the mountain in detail — Pārvatī's former form and her story, which increases delight.
m.2.3.8.50: Having heard from the sage's mouth that entire former history of Kālī, the mountain, together with his sons and wife, was then freed of doubt.
m.2.3.8.51: Then Kālī, having heard the account from Nārada's mouth, lowered her face in shyness, her face broadened with a smile.
m.2.3.8.52: Having heard her story, the mountain touched her with his hand, and kissing her on the head again and again, seated her beside his own seat.
m.2.3.8.53: Then, O sage, seeing her again seated there, you spoke, delighting the king of mountains and Menakā together with their sons.
m.2.3.8.54: But what need would she have of a throne, O king of mountains? Hence her seat will always be on Śambhu's lap.
m.2.3.8.55: Having obtained the seat on Hara's lap, your daughter will remain there forever, where no one's sight or mind can reach.
m.2.3.8.56: Brahmā said: Having spoken these noble words to the lord of mountains, O Nārada, you went joyfully to heaven at that very moment. The lord of mountains too, his heart filled with lovely delight, went to his own home, rich in every prosperity.
m.2.3.8.iti: Thus ends the eighth adhyāya, named The description of the dialogue of Nārada and Himālaya, in the third khaṇḍa, the Pārvatī-khaṇḍa, of the second saṃhitā, the Rudra-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.2.3.9.1: Nārada said: O Vidhi, dear father, best of Śiva's devotees, O wise one, out of compassion you have narrated a wondrous story, and my delight has grown all the more.
m.2.3.9.2: O Vidhi, after I, of divine vision, had gone to my own abode, what happened then, dear father? Kindly tell me that now.
m.2.3.9.3: Brahmā said: O sage, after you had gone to heaven and some time had passed, Menā one day approached the mountain Himālaya and bowed to him.
m.2.3.9.4: Standing there humbly, the mountain's beloved, that virtuous lady whose daughter was dear to her as life, spoke to her own lord, the king of mountains.
m.2.3.9.5: Menā said: Owing to a woman's nature, I have not properly understood the sage's words. Arrange the marriage of our daughter with a handsome bridegroom.
m.2.3.9.6: Then that wedding would in every way bring unprecedented happiness; and the bridegroom of Girijā should have good marks and be born of a good family.
m.2.3.9.7: My daughter is dear to me as life; act so that the beloved girl may be happy and delighted on obtaining a worthy husband. Salutation to you.
m.2.3.9.8: Brahmā said: Having said this, Menā, her face wet with tears, then fell at her husband's feet. Raising her up, the mountain, foremost of the wise, spoke fittingly.
m.2.3.9.9: Himavān said: Listen, O goddess Menakā; I speak what is true, in reality. Give up your confusion: the sage's words are never false.
m.2.3.9.10: If you have affection for your daughter, instruct her respectfully that she should perform austerity for Śaṅkara with devotion and a steady mind.
m.2.3.9.11: If Śiva, pleased, takes Kālī's hand, O Menakā, everything will be auspicious and the inauspiciousness spoken of by Nārada will vanish.
m.2.3.9.12: All inauspicious things are ever auspicious in Śiva. Therefore quickly instruct our daughter in austerity for attaining Śiva.
m.2.3.9.13: Brahmā said: Hearing the mountain's words, Menā became very pleased and went near her daughter to instruct her to take up austerity.
m.2.3.9.14: But seeing her daughter's very delicate body, Menakā was pained, and both her eyes quickly filled with tears.
m.2.3.9.15: The mountain's beloved could not instruct her daughter in that; Pārvatī quickly understood her mother's intention.
m.2.3.9.16: Then that goddess Kālikā, the all-knowing supreme ruler, at once spoke to her mother, comforting her again and again.
m.2.3.9.17: Pārvatī said: Mother, O very wise one, listen: last night, at the hour of Brahmā (before dawn), I saw a dream. I shall tell it; be kind and hear it.
m.2.3.9.18: A brahmin ascetic, compassionate, lovingly instructed me, mother, to perform intense austerity for Śiva.
m.2.3.9.19: Brahmā said: Hearing that, Menakā quickly called her husband there and told him in full the dream her daughter had seen.
m.2.3.9.20: Then, hearing the daughter's dream from Menakā, the lord of mountains, greatly pleased, spoke, addressing his beloved with these words.
m.2.3.9.21: Himavān said: O beloved, at the end of the latter part of the night I too saw a dream. Listen to it with great delight; I shall tell it with due respect.
m.2.3.9.22: A supreme ascetic, bearing the bodily marks of the bridegroom described by Nārada, came gladly to the outskirts of our city to perform austerity.
m.2.3.9.23: Very pleased, I went there taking my daughter. I recognised him as Śambhu, the lord, the bridegroom spoken of by Nārada.
m.2.3.9.24: Having instructed my daughter to serve that ascetic, I requested him to accept her service; but at that time he did not agree to it.
m.2.3.9.25: A very great debate arose, in keeping with Sāṅkhya and Vedānta. Then, by his permission, my daughter remained there.
m.2.3.9.26: Holding that desire in her heart, she served him with devotion. This is the dream I saw, which I have told you, O fair-faced one.
m.2.3.9.27: Therefore, O Menā, beloved, its outcome should be watched for some time. This alone is fitting here; know this from me for certain.
m.2.3.9.28: Brahmā said: Having said this, O lord of sages, the king of mountains and Menakā remained, with pure minds, watching for its outcome.
m.2.3.9.29: When a few days had thus passed, the supreme lord, refuge of the good, the creator, greatly agitated by separation from Satī, was wandering everywhere.
m.2.3.9.30: The lord came there gladly, accompanied by a few attendants (gaṇas), to perform austerity, his mind distraught by separation from his beloved Satī.
m.2.3.9.31: He performed his own austerity there; Pārvatī, devoted to serving him, together with her two friends, was constantly engaged then to please him.
m.2.3.9.32: Though pierced with arrows by Smara (Kāma), sent by the gods to infatuate him, Lord Śambhu did not undergo any change.
m.2.3.9.33: Burning Smara right there with his fiery eye, and recalling my words, he, angry with me, then vanished.
m.2.3.9.34: Then after some time, having destroyed Girijā's pride and being propitiated by her intense austerity, Maheśvara became pleased.
m.2.3.9.35: Following worldly custom, Rudra, propitiated by Viṣṇu, married Kālī; from that came great auspiciousness.
m.2.3.9.36: Thus, dear son, I have told you in brief this supreme, divine story of the all-pervading Śaṅkara. What more do you wish to hear?
m.2.3.9.iti: Thus ends the ninth adhyāya, named The description of Śiva's deeds in brief, preceded by the description of a dream, in the third khaṇḍa, the Pārvatī-khaṇḍa, of the second saṃhitā, the Rudra-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.2.3.10.1: Nārada said: O disciple of Viṣṇu, O most fortunate one, O Vidhi (Brahmā), best of Śiva's devotees, O lord, you should kindly tell me in detail this sport (līlā) of Śiva.
m.2.3.10.2: What deeds did Śambhu, afflicted by separation from Satī, perform? And when did he go to the excellent plateau of Himavat to perform austerities?
m.2.3.10.3: How did the dispute between Śivā and Śiva arise, and how did the destruction of Kāma take place? How did Pārvatī, having performed austerities, attain Śiva, Śambhu?
m.2.3.10.4: O Brahman, you should tell me all that, and also any other supreme, auspicious, good deeds of Śiva that bring great bliss.
m.2.3.10.5: Sūta said: Hearing this question of Nārada, Vidhi, the foremost of the lords of the worlds, remembering the lotus feet of Śiva, spoke with great delight.
m.2.3.10.6: Brahmā said: O divine sage, foremost among Śiva's devotees, listen with reverence to his glory, which is purifying, auspicious, excellent, and increases devotion.
m.2.3.10.7: Having come to his own mountain, Śambhu, distressed by separation from his beloved, remembered in his heart his dear goddess Satī, dearer to him than life.
m.2.3.10.8: Addressing the Gaṇas and grieving for her, he described with great love her qualities that increased affection, displaying the way of worldly people.
m.2.3.10.9: Then, abandoning the good path of householder life, he became sky-clad (naked); and he, skilled in divine sport, again wandered through all the worlds.
m.2.3.10.10: Grieved by separation from Satī, he found no sight of her anywhere; and Śaṅkara, who brings welfare to his devotees, came back to the mountain.
m.2.3.10.11: Concentrating his mind with effort, he entered meditative absorption (samādhi), the destroyer of sorrow, and beheld his own imperishable true form.
m.2.3.10.12: Thus Sthāṇu remained for a very long time, the three guṇas dissolved—changeless, the supreme Brahman, lord of Māyā, the Lord himself.
m.2.3.10.13: Then, when countless years had passed, he gave up samādhi; what happened then quickly, that episode I shall tell you.
m.2.3.10.14: A drop born of exertion (sweat) fell from the Lord's forehead onto the earth; there it quickly became a child.
m.2.3.10.15: O sage, he was four-armed, reddish in hue, of charming form, with unearthly radiance, splendid, brilliant, and unbearable to others.
m.2.3.10.16: That child cried there before the supreme Lord, who was engaged in worldly conduct, just like an ordinary son.
m.2.3.10.17: Then the Earth, reflecting with her good intellect and fearing Śaṅkara, assumed the form of a fair woman and appeared right there.
m.2.3.10.18: Quickly lifting that excellent child, she placed him on her lap and lovingly suckled him with her breast milk, the milk that welled up in her.
m.2.3.10.19: She kissed his face with affection and, smiling, played with the child—herself truly a mother, devoted to the welfare of the supreme Lord.
m.2.3.10.20: Seeing that deed, Śambhu Hara—playful, the skilled agent of creation, the indweller—knowing her to be the Earth, laughed and then spoke.
m.2.3.10.21: Blessed are you, O Earth; lovingly nurture this excellent son of mine, born upon you from the sweat of me, the greatly radiant one.
m.2.3.10.22: O Earth, though this child, who will do what is dear to you, is born of my sweat, he shall be famed by your name and ever be free from the three afflictions.
m.2.3.10.23: This child will indeed be virtuous and a giver of land to you; he will also be a giver of joy to me. Take him as you wish.
m.2.3.10.24: Brahmā said: Having said this, Rudra—his mind somewhat freed from the grief of separation, following worldly custom, changeless, dear to the good—fell silent.
m.2.3.10.25: And the Earth, having received Śiva's command, quickly went with the son to her own abode and attained supreme happiness.
m.2.3.10.26: That child, obtaining the name Bhauma and quickly becoming a youth, served Lord Śaṅkara for a long time in Kāśī.
m.2.3.10.27: By the grace of Viśveśvara, the Earth-born one attained the status of a planet and quickly went to an excellent divine world beyond the world of Śukra.
m.2.3.10.28: Thus has been told Śambhu's deed connected with separation from Satī. Now, O sage, listen with reverence to Śambhu's practice of austerity.
m.2.3.10.iti: Thus ends the tenth adhyāya, named The description of the birth of Bhauma and of Śiva's sport, in the third khaṇḍa, the Pārvatī-khaṇḍa, of the second saṃhitā, the Rudra-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.2.3.11.1: Brahmā said: When that daughter of the mountain, the Śakti worshipped by the worlds, Satī reborn, was growing up and had become eight years old in Himālaya's house,
m.2.3.11.2: Giriśa, who was distressed by separation from Satī, learned of her birth and, holding that wondrous one within his heart, rejoiced exceedingly, O Nārada.
m.2.3.11.3: Meanwhile Śambhu, adopting worldly conduct, wished to perform penance in order to concentrate his mind properly.
m.2.3.11.4: Taking with him some excellent and tranquil gaṇas, Nandin and others, he went to Gaṅgāvatāra, the excellent plateau of Himavat.
m.2.3.11.5: where, long ago, the Gaṅgā, flowing from Brahmā's city, fell down — the supreme purifier, for the destruction of all masses of sin, O sage.
m.2.3.11.6: Staying there, the self-controlled Hara began his penance; untiring, he meditated one-pointedly on his own Self,
m.2.3.11.7: which is consciousness, arising from knowledge, eternal, of the form of light, free from affliction, pervading the universe, consciousness and bliss, devoid of duality, without support.
m.2.3.11.8: While Hara was engrossed in meditation, some Pramathas too became intent on meditation, as did other gaṇas such as Nandin and Bhṛṅgin.
m.2.3.11.9: Then some gaṇas served Śambhu, the supreme Self; remaining silent, they made no sound at all; and some became door-keepers.
m.2.3.11.10: Meanwhile the snowy mountain Himavat, having heard of Śaṅkara's arrival at Oṣadhiprastha, went there respectfully.
m.2.3.11.11: The lord of mountains, with his attendants, bowed to the lord Rudra, worshipped him, and, greatly pleased, praised him with joined palms.
m.2.3.11.12: Himavān said: O God of gods, Mahādeva, Kapardin, Śaṅkara, O Lord, by you alone, the lord of the world, the three worlds are protected.
m.2.3.11.13: Obeisance to you, O Lord of the gods of gods, who bear the form of a yogin; obeisance to you who are without attributes, who have attributes, who sport in the world.
m.2.3.11.14: O Śambhu, obeisance to you, dweller on Kailāsa, who roam through all worlds, the supreme lord, who take forms in play, the trident-bearer.
m.2.3.11.15: Obeisance to you, the receptacle of perfect qualities, free from modification; to the desireless, the one beyond striving, the steadfast, the supreme Self.
m.2.3.11.16: Obeisance to you whose enjoyment is not external, O lover of people; O master of the three guṇas, Lord of Māyā, obeisance to Brahman, the supreme Self.
m.2.3.11.17: To you who are served by Viṣṇu, Brahmā and others, who have the form of Viṣṇu and Brahmā, the sole bestower on Viṣṇu and Brahmā — O lover of devotees, obeisance be to you.
m.2.3.11.18: O you who delight in penance, O abode of penance, obeisance to you, giver of the fruit of good penance, fond of penance, tranquil, having the form of Brahman.
m.2.3.11.19: Obeisance be to you who engage in worldly dealings and follow the customs of the world, who have attributes, the supreme lord, the supreme Self.
m.2.3.11.20: Your sport, O Maheśāna, is unknowable and gives happiness to the good. You are by nature subject to your devotees; controlled by devotees, you perform actions.
m.2.3.11.21: Through the rising of my good fortune you have come here, O Lord. You have made me one who has a protector; you are rightly described as kind to the lowly.
m.2.3.11.22: Today my birth is fruitful, my life is fruitful; today everything of mine is fruitful, since you have come here.
m.2.3.11.23: Knowing me to be your steadfast servant, give me your command, O Maheśvara, and I shall serve you with great love, with mind fixed on nothing else.
m.2.3.11.24: Brahmā said: Having heard these words of the lord of mountains, Maheśvara opened his eyes slightly and saw the mountain with his attendants.
m.2.3.11.25: Seeing that king of mountains thus with his attendants, the bull-bannered lord of the world, abiding in meditative yoga, spoke as if smiling.
m.2.3.11.26: Maheśvara said: I have come in secret to perform penance on your ridge. Arrange it so that no one comes near.
m.2.3.11.27: You are great-souled, an abode of penance, and the constant refuge of sages, of gods, of rākṣasas and of other great beings;
m.2.3.11.28: always the dwelling of the twice-born and others, ever purified by the Gaṅgā, benefactor of all, the overlord and master of mountains.
m.2.3.11.29: Relying on you, well pleased and self-controlled, O king of mountains, I shall practise penance here at the place of the Gaṅgā's descent.
m.2.3.11.30: O protector of mountains, best of mountains, make every effort now by which my penance here may be free of obstacles.
m.2.3.11.31: This alone is the highest service to me, O best of mountains. Go to your home with true affection and accomplish this with care.
m.2.3.11.32: Brahmā said: Having said this, the lord of the worlds, the creator, fell silent. Then the king of mountains affectionately said this to Śambhu.
m.2.3.11.33: Himavān said: You have been worshipped by me, O lord of the world, O supreme Lord, with a welcome. What shall I request of you, who today dwell in my realm?
m.2.3.11.34: Indeed, even by great penance you are not attained by the gods who strive with effort, O Maheśāna; yet that very you has come here of your own accord.
m.2.3.11.35: There is no one superior to me, no one more meritorious than me, since your Honour has come onto my ridge for penance.
m.2.3.11.36: I consider myself greater than the lord of the gods, O supreme Lord, for by coming here with your attendants you have made me a recipient of your grace.
m.2.3.11.37: Perform your supreme penance free of obstacles, O lord of the gods, as you are independent. I shall render service accordingly; I am ever your servant, O Lord.
m.2.3.11.38: Brahmā said: Having said this, that king of mountains quickly returned to his own house and respectfully related the whole account to his beloved.
m.2.3.11.39: Summoning all his attendants who were being led there and his own followers, O Nārada, the lord of mountains spoke to them truthfully.
m.2.3.11.40: Himavān said: From today onward, by my command, let no one go to Gaṅgāvatāraṇa, my plateau. This I declare truly.
m.2.3.11.41: If any person goes there, I shall punish that great scoundrel severely; this I have declared truly.
m.2.3.11.42: O sage, having quickly restrained all his attendants in this way, the mountain Himavat made a careful effort; listen to it, I shall tell you.
m.2.3.11.iti: Thus ends the eleventh adhyāya, named The description of the meeting of Śiva and the mountain, in the third khaṇḍa, the Pārvatī-khaṇḍa, of the second saṃhitā, the Rudra-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.2.3.12.1: Brahmā said: Then the lord of the mountains, delighted, took a collection of fine flowers and fruits and, accompanied by his daughter, went into the presence of Hara.
m.2.3.12.2: Having gone and bowed to the Lord of the three worlds, who was intent on meditation, he offered to him wholeheartedly his wondrous daughter Kālī.
m.2.3.12.3: Placing all the fruits, flowers and other things before him, and putting his daughter in front, the king of mountains said this to Śambhu.
m.2.3.12.4: Himavān said: O Lord, my daughter, eager to serve you, the moon-crested one, has been brought here out of her desire to worship you.
m.2.3.12.5: Let her, together with her two friends, serve you, Śaṅkara, constantly. Permit her, O Lord, if you have favour towards me.
m.2.3.12.6: Brahmā said: Then Śaṅkara looked at her, who had just reached early youth, whose lustre was like the petals of a blooming blue lotus, and whose face resembled the full moon;
m.2.3.12.7: who shone with an auspicious attire, the abode of every grace; whose neck was like a conch, whose eyes were large, and who was radiant with a pair of lovely ears;
m.2.3.12.8: charming with her two arms, long and slender to their ends like lotus-stalks; bearing breasts like lotus buds, full, plump and firm;
m.2.3.12.9: bearing them, slender-waisted, beautified by the three folds at her middle, and resplendent with two feet like land-lotuses;
m.2.3.12.10: able, merely by being seen, to dislodge even the minds of sages bound fast in the cage of meditation; the crest-jewel of all womankind.
m.2.3.12.11: Having seen her thus, dear one, captivating even to meditators, one who in her very form augments the power of tantras and mantras, assuming forms at will,
m.2.3.12.12: the great yogin quickly closed his eyes and meditated on his own supreme form, the highest reality, beyond the three guṇas, imperishable.
m.2.3.12.13: Seeing then the all-pervading Lord of all, engaged in austerity with eyes closed, with matted locks, adorned with the digit of the moon, knowable through Vedānta, seated on the supreme seat,
m.2.3.12.14: Himācala bowed again with his head; he, though of undaunted spirit, fell into doubt. Then the lord of mountains, foremost among those skilled in speech, addressed words to the sole friend of the world.
m.2.3.12.15: Himavān said: O God of gods, Mahādeva, mine of compassion, Śaṅkara, open your eyes, O all-pervading one, and look at me who have come to you for refuge.
m.2.3.12.16: O Śiva, Śarva, Maheśāna, O Lord who brings joy to the world, I bow to you, Mahādeva, who removes all calamities.
m.2.3.12.17: O Lord of gods, the Vedas and the scriptures do not know you completely. Your greatness ever transcends the path of speech and mind.
m.2.3.12.18: Through the exclusion of what is not you, all of Śruti ever describes you hesitantly, with awe; what then is to be said of others?
m.2.3.12.19: Many devotees know you, having obtained your grace through devotion. For devotees who have taken refuge in you there is no delusion or the like anywhere.
m.2.3.12.20: Now, out of kindness to me, hear the request of me, your own servant. By your command, O God, dear one, I relate it out of my humility.
m.2.3.12.21: I am fortunate, Mahādeva, by your grace, Śaṅkara. Regarding me as your own servant, O Lord, show kindness; salutations to you.
m.2.3.12.22: And every day I shall come to see you, O Lord, together with this daughter; O master, please grant your permission.
m.2.3.12.23: Brahmā said: Hearing these words of his, Maheśvara opened his eyes; abandoning meditation and reflecting, the God of gods spoke these words.
m.2.3.12.24: Maheśvara said: You may come daily to see me, O mountain, but leave the maiden at home; otherwise there is no seeing me.
m.2.3.12.25: Brahmā said: Hearing such words of Maheśa, the mountain, father of Śivā, bowing his neck, replied thus to Giriśa.
m.2.3.12.26: Himavān said: Why should I not come together with her? Let that be told. Is she unfit for service? I do not know the reason for this.
m.2.3.12.27: Brahmā said: Then Śambhu, whose banner bears the bull, laughing, spoke to the mountain, showing especially the worldly conduct appropriate for unworthy yogins.
m.2.3.12.28: Śambhu said: This maiden, with fine hips, slender, moon-faced and beautiful, must not be brought near me; I forbid it again and again.
m.2.3.12.29: Woman is held by the learned, masters of the Veda, to be a form of Māyā; a young woman especially is an obstacle to ascetics.
m.2.3.12.30: I am an ascetic and a yogin, ever untouched by Māyā. What need have I of a young woman, O bearer of the earth?
m.2.3.12.31: You should not speak thus again, O refuge of the best ascetics, since you are skilled in Vedic dharma, foremost among the wise, and learned.
m.2.3.12.32: O mountain, from association with her sensual desire quickly arises; detachment perishes, and thereby true austerity falls away.
m.2.3.12.33: Therefore, O mountain, an ascetic should not keep company with women, for that company is the root of great sensual attachment and the destroyer of knowledge and detachment.
m.2.3.12.34: Brahmā said: Having said this and much more to that lord of mountains, Maheśvara, the great yogin, the Lord, foremost among great yogins, fell silent.
m.2.3.12.35: Hearing these words of Śambhu—untroubled, free of desire and harsh—Kālī's father was startled, O celestial sage, and, somewhat perturbed by them, remained silent.
m.2.3.12.36: Hearing the words spoken by the ascetic, and perceiving the lord of mountains thus startled, Bhavānī then bowed to Śiva and spoke clear words.
m.2.3.12.iti: Thus ends the twelfth adhyāya, named The description of the dialogue of Śiva and Himācala, in the third khaṇḍa, the Pārvatī-khaṇḍa, of the second saṃhitā, the Rudra-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.2.3.13.1: Bhavānī said: O yogin, hear from me, O all-pervading lord, O one skilled among the wise, the answer to what you, an ascetic, said to the king of mountains.
m.2.3.13.2: O Śambhu, you perform extensive austerity because you are endowed with the power of austerity. This resolve to practise austerity has arisen in you, the great-souled one, through that power.
m.2.3.13.3: That power should be known as Prakṛti, the source of all actions whatsoever. By her everything is created, preserved and destroyed.
m.2.3.13.4: Who are you, and who is subtle Prakṛti? O Lord, let that be reflected upon. And without Prakṛti, how could Maheśvara exist in the form of the liṅga?
m.2.3.13.5: It is through Prakṛti that you are ever worthy of worship, of homage and of meditation by living beings. Having reflected on this in your heart, let all that be stated.
m.2.3.13.6: Brahmā said: Having heard those words of Pārvatī, Maheśa, intent on bestowing great favour, laughed heartily and, with a pleased mind, spoke these words.
m.2.3.13.7: Maheśvara said: By supreme austerity alone I destroy Prakṛti. In truth I, Śambhu, remain free from Prakṛti.
m.2.3.13.8: Therefore the virtuous should never embrace Prakṛti; they should remain free from change and removed from worldly conduct.
m.2.3.13.9: Brahmā said: Thus addressed by Śambhu, dear one, in the manner of worldly usage, Kālī smiled inwardly and spoke sweet words.
m.2.3.13.10: Kālī said: O yogin, Śaṅkara, Lord, the words you have spoken — how are they not Prakṛti? How then are you beyond her?
m.2.3.13.11: Having considered this, you should state it truly, exactly as it is. All this is continuously bound by Prakṛti.
m.2.3.13.12: Therefore you should not speak, nor do anything at all. Know with your mind that all speaking and all making belong to Prakṛti.
m.2.3.13.13: What you hear, what you eat, what you see, what you do — all that is the effect of Prakṛti. False talk is meaningless.
m.2.3.13.14: If you are beyond Prakṛti, then why, O Śambhu, O Lord, are you now performing austerity on this mountain Himavat?
m.2.3.13.15: You have been swallowed by Prakṛti; you do not know your own self, O Hara. If you know your own self, O Lord, why do you perform austerity?
m.2.3.13.16: O yogin, what is the use of my arguing with you in words? Where there is direct perception, the wise do not regard inference as a means of proof.
m.2.3.13.17: As long as things fall within the range of the senses of embodied beings, so long should the wise regard all of it, with their intellect, as belonging to Prakṛti.
m.2.3.13.18: What is the use of saying much, O lord of yogins? Hear my supreme word: I am she Prakṛti and you are Puruṣa. This is true, true; there is no doubt.
m.2.3.13.19: It is by my grace that you are regarded as possessing qualities and form. Without me you are inactive and cannot do anything at all.
m.2.3.13.20: You are always dependent on another, though self-controlled, performing various actions. How then are you changeless, and how are you not tainted by me?
m.2.3.13.21: If your statement that you are beyond Prakṛti is true, then, O Śaṅkara, you need not fear being near me.
m.2.3.13.22: Brahmā said: Having heard her words, expressed according to the Sāṃkhya doctrine, Śiva, who is established in the Vedānta view, spoke to Śivā.
m.2.3.13.23: Śrī Śiva said: If you speak thus, O Girijā, holding to Sāṃkhya, then render me daily service that is not forbidden, O sweet-spoken one.
m.2.3.13.24: If I am Brahman, untainted by Māyā, the Supreme Lord, knowable through Vedānta, the master of Māyā, what will you do then?
m.2.3.13.25: Brahmā said: Having spoken thus to Girijā, the Lord, who delights his devotees and bestows grace on them, addressed the mountain.
m.2.3.13.26: Śrī Śiva said: Right here, O mountain, on your excellent and most lovely plateau, I, by supreme austerity, move upon the earth, clearly beholding the blissful nature that is the state of the highest truth.
m.2.3.13.27: O lord of mountains, you should grant me permission to perform austerity; without permission no austerity can be performed.
m.2.3.13.28: Brahmā said: Hearing these words of the trident-bearing god of gods, Himavat bowed to Śambhu and spoke these words.
m.2.3.13.29: Himavān said: The whole world, with gods, demons and humans, is indeed yours. What can I, being insignificant, say to you, O Mahādeva?
m.2.3.13.30: Brahmā said: Thus addressed by Himavat, Śaṅkara, the benefactor of the worlds, smiled and respectfully said to the king of mountains: Go.
m.2.3.13.31: Permitted by Śaṅkara, Himavat went to his own home; and together with Girijā he remained coming daily for darśana of the Lord.
m.2.3.13.32: Even without her father, that Kālī, intent on devotion, went daily with her two friends to Śaṅkara's presence to serve him.
m.2.3.13.33: No gaṇa, Nandīśvara or any other, stopped her, dear one, by Maheśa's command, each being pure and obedient to his order.
m.2.3.13.34: This dialogue between Śiva and Śivā, voicing the Sāṃkhya and Vedānta views, who are truly non-different, has been narrated; on careful reflection it is ever auspicious and gives happiness.
m.2.3.13.35: At the word of the king of mountains, Śaṅkara, who is beyond the senses, accepted his daughter close by his side, also out of regard for him.
m.2.3.13.36: The lord of beings said these words to Kālī with her two friends: Let her serve me daily and go home; let her stay here without fear.
m.2.3.13.37: Having spoken thus, Hara — the changeless great yogin, the Lord who performs many sports — accepted that goddess for his service.
m.2.3.13.38: This indeed is the great steadfastness of the steadfast and of true ascetics: that even on encountering circumstances full of obstacles, they are not overcome by those obstacles.
m.2.3.13.39: Then the king of mountains, having returned to his city with his attendants, rejoiced greatly in his mind together with his beloved, O lord of sages.
m.2.3.13.40: And Hara, through the yoga of meditation, with an undisturbed mind, remained intent on reverently contemplating the Supreme Self.
m.2.3.13.41: Kālī, accompanied by her two friends, served the moon-crested Mahādeva every day, keeping to her coming and going.
m.2.3.13.42: Having washed Śambhu's feet, she drank the water from his feet, and with a cloth purified by fire she wiped his body.
m.2.3.13.43: Having duly worshipped Hara with the sixteen offerings and bowed to him again and again, she would daily go back to her father's house.
m.2.3.13.44: O best of sages, while Śivā thus served Śaṅkara, who was intent on meditation, a long time passed.
m.2.3.13.45: Sometimes Kālī, together with her two friends, sang in Śaṅkara's hermitage a beautiful song, well set to rhythm, that heightens love.
m.2.3.13.46: Sometimes she herself brought kuśa grass, flowers and fuel-sticks, and then stayed there, cleaning the place with her two friends.
m.2.3.13.47: Sometimes, staying restrained in the dwelling of the moon-bearer, she, full of longing, gazed intently at the moon-crested one and was filled with wonder.
m.2.3.13.48: Then the Lord of beings, with the ardour of his austerity, having seen her standing nearby free of attachment, reflected: She abides in a body made of the elements.
m.2.3.13.49: Giriśa did not take as wife Kālī, who stood near him, a treasury of great beauty, enchanting even to sages.
m.2.3.13.50: Mahādeva, again seeing her thus with controlled senses and ever devoted to serving him, compassionately reflected.
m.2.3.13.51: Only when this Kālī performs the vow of austerity will I accept her, free of the seed of pride.
m.2.3.13.52: Brahmā said: Having thus reflected, the Lord of beings quickly took to meditation; the Lord, great master of yogins and performer of great sport, became absorbed.
m.2.3.13.53: Then, O sage, in the heart of Śiva, the Supreme Self absorbed in meditation, no other thought whatever remained.
m.2.3.13.54: But Kālī served Śambhu day after day with true devotion, constantly contemplating the form of that great one.
m.2.3.13.55: Hara, intent on meditation, daily saw Kālī standing steadily; having forgotten his former thought, though seeing her, he did not see her.
m.2.3.13.56: Meanwhile the gods headed by Śakra, and those sages, at Brahmā's command respectfully sent Smara there,
m.2.3.13.57: so as to bring about through him, by means of desire, the union of Kālī with Rudra, for they were oppressed by Tāraka, the asura of great might.
m.2.3.13.58: Going there, Smara employed all his own means; Hara was not disturbed in the least, and he reduced him to ashes.
m.2.3.13.59: Pārvatī too, O sage, became free of pride at his direction; then, having performed great austerity, the virtuous one obtained Śiva as husband.
m.2.3.13.60: Pārvatī and the Supreme Lord both became very joyful, and, devoted to helping others, they accomplished the task of the gods.
m.2.3.13.iti: Thus ends the thirteenth adhyāya, named The description of the dialogue of Pārvatī and the Supreme Lord, in the third khaṇḍa, the Pārvatī-khaṇḍa, of the second saṃhitā, the Rudra-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.2.3.14.1: Nārada said: O disciple of Viṣṇu, great devotee of Śiva, O Vidhi (Brahmā), you have told well this supreme account of Śivā and of Śiva.
m.2.3.14.2: O Brahman, who is the asura Tāraka, by whom the gods were oppressed? Whose son was he? Tell me, and tell his story, which is connected with Śiva.
m.2.3.14.3: And how did Śaṅkara, the self-controlled one, reduce Smara to ashes? Tell that too with great kindness — that wondrous deed of the Lord.
m.2.3.14.4: How did Śivā perform extremely fierce penance for the sake of happiness? How did the primordial Śakti, supreme beyond the world, obtain Śambhu as her husband?
m.2.3.14.5: O greatly wise one, tell all this completely and in detail to me, your own son, who has faith and whose soul is devoted to Śiva.
m.2.3.14.6: Brahmā said: O best of sons, greatly wise, divine sage of praiseworthy vows: remembering Śaṅkara, I shall tell it; hear that whole account.
m.2.3.14.7: First, O Nārada, hear well the origin of Tāraka himself, for whose slaying a great effort was made by the gods who took refuge in Śiva.
m.2.3.14.8: My son is Marīci; Kaśyapa is his son. He had thirteen wives, who were daughters of Dakṣa.
m.2.3.14.9: Diti was the eldest of his wives; she bore two sons: Hiraṇyakaśipu the elder, and then Hiraṇyākṣa the younger.
m.2.3.14.10: Those two daityas, who caused great misery, were slain by Viṣṇu in the forms of Man-lion and Boar; then the gods, freed from fear, attained happiness.
m.2.3.14.11: Diti was grief-stricken; she went to Kaśyapa for refuge. Serving him again with devotion, that woman of good vows conceived an embryo.
m.2.3.14.12: Learning of it, the great Indra too, very energetic, having found an opening, entered there and cut her embryo again and again with his thunderbolt.
m.2.3.14.13: By the power of her vow, that embryo did not die. As she slept, by the working of fate, it became seven times seven sons.
m.2.3.14.14: Those sons all became gods, known by name as the Maruts. Then, made his own by Indra, king of the gods, they went to heaven.
m.2.3.14.15: Again Diti, remorseful over her own deed, resorted to her husband and, by supreme service, made that sage well pleased.
m.2.3.14.16: Kaśyapa said: Perform penance, having become pure, for ten thousand years of Brahmā. If that is accomplished first, then you will have a son.
m.2.3.14.17: O sage, that penance was completed thus by Diti with faith. Then, receiving an embryo from her husband, she bore such a son.
m.2.3.14.18: That son of Diti was named Vajrāṅga, equal to the immortals, a hero whose body matched his name (adamantine), very valiant and mighty from his very birth.
m.2.3.14.19: At his mother's command, that son at once seized the lord of the gods by force and inflicted various punishments on the gods as well.
m.2.3.14.20: Diti attained great joy seeing the wretched plight of Śakra and the others; and the immortals, Śakra and the rest, met with sorrow on account of their own deeds.
m.2.3.14.21: Then I, ever devoted to the welfare of the gods, quickly came there with Kaśyapa and, with conciliatory words, had the gods released from him.
m.2.3.14.22: Having released the gods, that Vajrāṅga — a devotee of Śiva, very pure-souled, unperturbed and serene-minded — then spoke respectfully.
m.2.3.14.23: Vajrāṅga said: Indra is wicked, a killer of my mother's offspring, a pursuer of his own interest. He has received his reward today; let him now rule his own kingdom.
m.2.3.14.24: O Brahman, all this I did under the compulsion of my mother's command; I have no desire to enjoy any world at all.
m.2.3.14.25: O Vidhi, best of knowers of the Vedas, tell me the essence of truth, by which I may be ever happy, unperturbed and serene-minded.
m.2.3.14.26: Hearing that, O sage, I said: The sāttvic disposition is called the essence of truth. And with affection I created an excellent woman.
m.2.3.14.27: Having given her, named Varāṅgī, to that son of Diti, I went, well pleased, to my own abode; and Kaśyapa, his father, too went.
m.2.3.14.28: Then that daitya Vajrāṅga, adopting the sāttvic disposition and abandoning the demonic one, free of enmity, attained happiness.
m.2.3.14.29: But in Varāṅgī's heart the sāttvic disposition did not arise. Full of desire, that virtuous woman served her husband with faith in various ways.
m.2.3.14.30: Then, from her service, the great lord Vajrāṅga, her husband, soon became pleased, and he then spoke these words.
m.2.3.14.31: Vajrāṅga said: What do you wish, beloved? Tell me — what is in your mind? Hearing that, she bowed to her husband and told him her heart's desire.
m.2.3.14.32: Varāṅgī said: If you are pleased, O good husband, give me a son of great might, a conqueror of the three worlds, who will bring distress to Hari.
m.2.3.14.33: Brahmā said: Hearing these words of his beloved, he became astonished and troubled. That wise one, sāttvic and free of enmity, spoke within his heart:
m.2.3.14.34: My beloved desires hostility with the gods, but it does not please me. What shall I do? Where shall I go? How may my pledge not be destroyed?
m.2.3.14.35: If my beloved's desire is fulfilled, the three worlds, and the gods and sages as well, will again be greatly afflicted.
m.2.3.14.36: If my beloved's desire is not fulfilled, then hell will be my lot. Either way there is loss of dharma — so he had heard from tradition.
m.2.3.14.37: Thus, O sage, Vajrāṅga wavered in this dilemma of dharma, and there he weighed with his intellect the strength and weakness of the two alternatives.
m.2.3.14.38: By Śiva's will, O sage, that wise one accepted the woman's words, and the king of daityas said to his beloved, so be it.
m.2.3.14.39: For that purpose he, with senses controlled, performed another intense and difficult penance for many years, directing it with great devotion to me.
m.2.3.14.40: Seeing that great penance, I went to grant him a boon, and with a well-pleased mind I said to him: Ask for a boon.
m.2.3.14.41: Then Vajrāṅga, seeing me, the lord, pleased and standing in the sky, bowed down deeply, praised me much, and chose a boon that was dear to his beloved and for her benefit.
m.2.3.14.42: Vajrāṅga said: O lord, grant my own wife a son who will bring her great benefit — mighty in strength, of great valour, highly capable, and a treasure-house of austerity.
m.2.3.14.43: Brahmā said: Having heard his words, O sage, I said, so be it. Having granted that, I went to my own abode, troubled in mind, remembering Śiva.
m.2.3.14.iti: Thus ends the fourteenth adhyāya, named The description of the birth and austerity of Vajrāṅga, in the account of the birth of Tāraka, in the third khaṇḍa, the Pārvatī-khaṇḍa, of the second saṃhitā, the Rudra-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.2.3.15.1: Brahmā said: Then Varāṅgī, with devotion, conceived an embryo from him, as arranged before; and it grew within her womb over many years with great radiance.
m.2.3.15.2: Then, when the time was complete, Varāṅgī gave birth to a son of huge body and great valour, blazing so as to light up the ten directions.
m.2.3.15.3: At that very moment, as that son of Varāṅgī—the bringer of grief to the gods—was being born, great portents arose, causes of sorrow.
m.2.3.15.4: In heaven, on earth and in the mid-air they appeared, terrifying to all the worlds, heralds of calamity; dear son, I shall tell you of those three kinds.
m.2.3.15.5: Thunderbolts fell along with meteors, with great, terrifying crashes; and fierce comets, bringers of misery, rose up.
m.2.3.15.6: The earth with its mountains shook; all the directions blazed; all the rivers, and the oceans especially, were agitated.
m.2.3.15.7: A wind harsh to the touch blew, uttering dreadful howls, uprooting great trees—an army of whirlwinds with dust for its banner.
m.2.3.15.8: Again and again halos appeared around the sun and moon, together with Rāhu, O best of brahmins—heralds of great terror, robbers of happiness.
m.2.3.15.9: Then, at that time, from the caves of the mountains arose rumblings, omens of fear, like the rattling of chariots.
m.2.3.15.10: Inauspicious she-jackals, vomiting fire from their mouths, howled hideously within the villages, amid the cries of jackals and owls.
m.2.3.15.11: Here and there dogs, raising their necks, let out various cries, now like singing, now like weeping.
m.2.3.15.12: Then, dear son, asses, frenzied and wild with braying, ran about hither and thither in herds, striking the earth with their hooves.
m.2.3.15.13: Birds, their minds terrified by the asses' braying, flew up from their nests, and screeching, with agitated hearts, found rest nowhere.
m.2.3.15.14: Overwhelmed by fear, the animals in pen and forest discharged dung and urine; they wandered about as though beaten and found no rest.
m.2.3.15.15: The cows, terrified, with tearful eyes and stricken with fear, yielded blood when milked; and the clouds there became frightening, raining pus.
m.2.3.15.16: There the images of the gods wept, as though about to fly up; trees fell without wind; and a war of the planets took place in the sky.
m.2.3.15.17: These and many other portents arose, O best of sages; the ignorant people there thought it was the dissolution of the universe.
m.2.3.15.18: Then the Prajāpati Kaśyapa, after due reflection, gave that mighty asura the name Tāraka.
m.2.3.15.19: That great hero, his innate manliness swiftly becoming manifest, grew with a body harder than stone, like the lord of mountains.
m.2.3.15.20: Then that high-minded daitya Tāraka, of great strength and prowess, asked his mother's permission to perform penance.
m.2.3.15.21: Having obtained permission, that great master of illusion, who deludes even the illusionists, set his mind on penance in order to conquer all the gods.
m.2.3.15.22: Going to the forest of Madhu, obedient to his elder's command, he performed according to rule an extremely severe penance directed to Vidhi (Brahmā).
m.2.3.15.23: With arms raised, standing on one foot, gazing at the sun with his eyes, firm of mind and firm of vow, he performed penance for a hundred years.
m.2.3.15.24: Touching the ground with his big toe, and in the same state, that resolute lord Tāraka, king of asuras, performed penance for another hundred years.
m.2.3.15.25: For a hundred years he consumed only water, for a hundred years lived on air, for a hundred years stood in water, and for a hundred more practised austerity on the bare ground.
m.2.3.15.26: Likewise for a hundred years in fire, for a hundred years head downwards, and for a hundred years standing on the ground on the palm of his hand.
m.2.3.15.27: For a hundred years, O sage, hanging by his feet from the branch of a tree, head downwards, he drank the smoke of a pure fire.
m.2.3.15.28: Thus that king of daityas, aiming at his desire, performed according to rule an excellent penance of the hardest kind, unbearable even to those who merely hear of it.
m.2.3.15.29: As he performed penance there in this way, a great radiance issued from his head, spreading everywhere and causing great calamity, O sage.
m.2.3.15.30: By it those worlds of the gods were almost burnt up, and all the divine sages, O sage, fell into distress on every side.
m.2.3.15.31: Then Indra, lord of the gods, was seized with great fear: Someone is performing penance now; surely he will assail my position.
m.2.3.15.32: This mighty one will destroy the universe untimely. Fallen into such doubt, they could reach no certainty.
m.2.3.15.33: Then all those gods and sages, after consulting well among themselves, frightened and dejected, went to my world and approached me.
m.2.3.15.34: Bowing to me and praising me well, all of them, troubled in mind, with joined palms, reported to me everything that had happened.
m.2.3.15.35: Having fully ascertained the whole cause of it with clear understanding, I went to grant a boon to where that asura was performing penance.
m.2.3.15.36: I spoke to him these words, O sage: Ask for a boon. You have performed intense penance; there is nothing that cannot be given to you.
m.2.3.15.37: Hearing these words of mine, the great asura Tāraka bowed to me, praised me well, and chose an exceedingly terrible boon.
m.2.3.15.38: Tāraka said: When you, the giver of boons, are pleased, what could be impossible for me? Therefore I ask a boon of you; hear it from me, O Grandsire.
m.2.3.15.39: If you are pleased, O lord of the gods, if a boon is to be given to me, then, showing mercy towards me, grant me two boons.
m.2.3.15.40: In this entire world created by you, O great lord, let there surely be no man at all as strong as I am.
m.2.3.15.41: When a son born of Śiva's seed, having become commander of the army, hurls a weapon at me, then alone may my death occur.
m.2.3.15.42: Thus addressed then by that demon, O lord of sages, I granted such a boon and quickly went to my own world.
m.2.3.15.43: That demon too, having obtained the excellent boon desired in his mind, became exceedingly delighted and went to the city called Śoṇita.
m.2.3.15.44: Then that great demon, together with the asuras, was consecrated to the kingship of the three worlds by Śukra, preceptor of the demons, at my command.
m.2.3.15.45: Thereafter that great demon became the ruler of the three worlds; he enforced his own command, oppressing all beings, moving and unmoving.
m.2.3.15.46: That Tāraka ruled the three worlds according to rule, and protected the subjects while oppressing the gods and others.
m.2.3.15.47: Then that demon Tāraka took the jewels of Indra and the other guardians of the worlds, which they gave of their own accord out of fear of him.
m.2.3.15.48: Out of fear of him Indra surrendered Airāvata to him; Kubera then gave the nine treasures.
m.2.3.15.49: By Varuṇa white horses were given, by the sages likewise the wish-granting cow; and by Indra the divine Uccaiḥśravas was surrendered to him out of fear.
m.2.3.15.50: Wherever that demon saw any excellent thing, he seized it by force; the three worlds became bereft of their essence.
m.2.3.15.51: And likewise the oceans gave him jewels out of fear, O sage. The earth yielded crops without ploughing, and all subjects had their desires fulfilled.
m.2.3.15.52: The sun shone in such a way that it caused him no discomfort; the moon was visible with full radiance, and the wind was favourable in every way.
m.2.3.15.53: Whatever wealth belonged to the gods, to the ancestors and to others, all of it was seized by that wicked demon.
m.2.3.15.54: Having subdued the three worlds, he himself became Indra. He was the unrivalled lord, and, self-controlled, he exercised a wondrous rule.
m.2.3.15.55: Having expelled all the gods, he then installed the demons in their places; he himself set the divine beings to their own tasks.
m.2.3.15.56: Then all the gods, led by Śakra, afflicted by him, helpless and greatly distressed, came to me for refuge, O sage.
m.2.3.15.iti: Thus ends the fifteenth adhyāya, named The description of the austerity and reign of the asura Tāraka, in the third khaṇḍa, the Pārvatī-khaṇḍa, of the second saṃhitā, the Rudra-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.2.3.16.1: Brahmā said: Then all those gods, oppressed by Tāraka, bowed deeply to the lord of creatures Brahmā and praised him with supreme devotion.
m.2.3.16.2: Having heard the gods' praise, true and heart-touching, I became exceedingly pleased and replied to the dwellers of heaven.
m.2.3.16.3: Welcome. Are your own offices free of obstacles, O gods? For what purpose have you all come here? Tell me.
m.2.3.16.4: Hearing these words of mine, all those dwellers of heaven, humbled and wretched, oppressed by Tāraka, bowed and spoke to me.
m.2.3.16.5: The gods said: O Lord of the worlds, the demon Tāraka, made arrogant by your boon, has driven us out by force and himself seized our places by violence.
m.2.3.16.6: Is the misery that has befallen us not known to you? Destroy that misery quickly; we have come to you for refuge.
m.2.3.16.7: Day and night he torments us wherever we stay; even as we flee, wherever we go we see Tāraka.
m.2.3.16.8: And by the misery that has arisen for us from Tāraka, O Lord of all, all of us, dear father, are oppressed and utterly distraught.
m.2.3.16.9: Agni, Yama, Varuṇa, Nirṛti and Vāyu, and the other guardians of the quarters too — all are under his control.
m.2.3.16.10: All of them, behaving like humans, together with all their retinues, serve that great demon; never are they independent.
m.2.3.16.11: Thus afflicted by him, the gods are always under his sway; all are devoted to doing his will, living as his dependents.
m.2.3.16.12: All the women there were, and the hosts of Apsarases as well — that mighty demon Tāraka has seized them all.
m.2.3.16.13: Sacrifices are not performed, ascetics do not practise austerities; nothing such as charity and righteous duty goes on in the worlds.
m.2.3.16.14: His general is Krauñca, a greatly sinful Dānava; he has gone to the nether world and torments its creatures ceaselessly.
m.2.3.16.15: By that sinful, pitiless Tāraka this entire triad of worlds of ours has been seized by force, O creator of the universe.
m.2.3.16.16: We shall go to whatever place you assign. Though we dwelt at ease, we have been driven from it by that enemy of the gods, O Lord of the worlds.
m.2.3.16.17: You alone are our refuge, ruler, sustainer and protector. All of us are burnt in the fire called Tāraka and are utterly distressed.
m.2.3.16.18: By him all our fierce means have been rendered powerless, as potent medicines fail in a sannipāta disorder.
m.2.3.16.19: Hari's discus Sudarśana, in which lay our hope of victory, became blunted on his neck, as if a flower had been offered there.
m.2.3.16.20: Brahmā said: Having heard these words of the gods, O sage, I replied to all the gods with words suited to the occasion.
m.2.3.16.21: Brahmā said: It is by my own word that the demon named Tāraka has grown powerful; it is not proper that he be slain by me, O dwellers of heaven.
m.2.3.16.22: Hence his slaying by me is not fitting, since he attained growth through me; even a poison tree, once one has reared it oneself, it is improper to cut down oneself.
m.2.3.16.23: Śaṅkara is able to accomplish your whole task; but even when urged, he cannot himself counter him directly.
m.2.3.16.24: Tāraka will come to ruin by his own sin. I shall give you counsel so that you may make the arrangements.
m.2.3.16.25: Tāraka cannot be slain by me, nor by Hari, nor by Hara, nor by anyone else or by the gods, because of my boon — this is spoken in truth.
m.2.3.16.26: If there were a son born of Śiva's seed, O gods, he alone, and no other, would be the slayer of the demon named Tāraka.
m.2.3.16.27: Carry out the means I tell you, O best of gods; by the grace of Mahādeva it will surely succeed.
m.2.3.16.28: Satī, daughter of Dakṣa, who formerly gave up her body, has been born from Menakā's womb; that story is known to you.
m.2.3.16.29: Giriśa will certainly take her hand in marriage; even so, O dwellers of heaven, you should work out a means for it.
m.2.3.16.30: Act with great effort so that Śiva's seed may be made to fall into that Pārvatī, born of Menakā.
m.2.3.16.31: She alone is able to make that Śambhu, whose seed is held upward, release his seed; no other woman whatever can do so, even by force.
m.2.3.16.32: That daughter of the king of mountains, now in the full bloom of youth, constantly serves Hara as he performs austerities on the Himālaya.
m.2.3.16.33: At the word of Himavat, her own father, and by her own insistence, Kālī the auspicious one, together with two friends, serves the Supreme Lord who is absorbed in meditation.
m.2.3.16.34: Though she, the most beautiful woman in the three worlds, worships him right before him, Maheśa, intent on meditation, does not waver even in mind.
m.2.3.16.35: Act with effort, O gods, so that before long the moon-crested one may desire Kālī as his wife.
m.2.3.16.36: Now I shall go to the demon's abode and restrain that Tāraka from his wicked obstinacy. Go to your own places, O immortals.
m.2.3.16.37: Having said this to the gods, I quickly approached the demon named Tāraka, greeted him very cordially, and spoke thus:
m.2.3.16.38: Brahmā said: You are ruling this heaven of ours, the very essence of splendour, as your kingdom; yet you desire more than that for which you performed great austerity.
m.2.3.16.39: The boon I gave was a lesser one; sovereignty over heaven was not granted by me. Therefore, leaving heaven, rule a kingdom on earth.
m.2.3.16.40: All the deeds befitting the gods will take place right there for you, O best of Asuras; there need be no hesitation about this.
m.2.3.16.41: Having spoken thus and having admonished that asura, I, the lord of all beings, remembered Śivā together with Śiva and vanished from there.
m.2.3.16.42: Tāraka too, abandoning heaven, then went to the earth; staying in the city called Śoṇita, he ruled over the entire kingdom.
m.2.3.16.43: All the gods too, having heard those words of mine, bowed low to me and went gladly to Śakra's abode, well composed, together with Śakra.
m.2.3.16.44: Having gone there, met, and deliberated among themselves, all those gods affectionately spoke these words to Maghavan.
m.2.3.16.45: The gods said: O Maghavan, you must carry out all that Brahmā has said, so that Śambhu's longing for Śivā may arise through Kāma.
m.2.3.16.46: Brahmā said: Having thus reported the whole account to the lord of the gods, those gods went joyfully from there, each to his own place.
m.2.3.16.iti: Thus ends the sixteenth adhyāya, named The description of the consoling of the gods, in the third khaṇḍa, the Pārvatī-khaṇḍa, of the second saṃhitā, the Rudra-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.2.3.17.1: Brahmā said: When those gods had gone, Śakra, sorely afflicted by the wicked demon Tāraka, called Smara (Kāma) to mind.
m.2.3.17.2: At that very moment Kāma came, together with Vasanta, the lover of Rati, proud, accompanied by Rati, the lord who conquers the three worlds.
m.2.3.17.3: Then, having bowed and standing before him, Smara, high-spirited, dear one, with joined palms spoke to Śakra.
m.2.3.17.4: Kāma said: What task has arisen for you? For what reason have I been remembered? Tell it, O lord of the gods; I have come to accomplish it.
m.2.3.17.5: Brahmā said: Hearing those words of Kandarpa, the lord of the gods spoke with affection, praising him, saying, well said, well said.
m.2.3.17.6: Śakra said: Your undertaking is good, since you are ready to accomplish the task that has come upon me. You are blessed, O Makaradhvaja.
m.2.3.17.7: Hear my words on the matter at hand; I will tell you before you. Whatever task is mine is also yours, not otherwise.
m.2.3.17.8: I do have many friends, and very great ones; but, O Smara, a true friend equal to you is nowhere at all.
m.2.3.17.9: For my victory, dear one, a pair has been made: the excellent thunderbolt and you. The thunderbolt may prove fruitless, but you never.
m.2.3.17.10: Who indeed is dearer than the one from whom benefit arises? Therefore you, the best of friends, should accomplish my task.
m.2.3.17.11: A sorrow has arisen for me, born of time and otherwise incurable; no one at all can remove it except you.
m.2.3.17.12: The test of a giver comes in famine, of a hero in battle, of a friend in time of calamity, and of women and of a family in times of helplessness.
m.2.3.17.13: The test of humility is in conduct; of the truthful, when a crisis has come; and likewise of true affection, behind one's back, dear one. This truth has been declared, not otherwise.
m.2.3.17.14: Now that a calamity has come upon me which no one else can avert, today your test will take place, O best of friends.
m.2.3.17.15: This task, bringing happiness, is not mine alone; rather it is the task of all the gods and others—there is no doubt.
m.2.3.17.16: Brahmā said: Hearing these words of Maghavan, Makaradhvaja, smiling sweetly, spoke words deep with affection.
m.2.3.17.17: Kāma said: Why do you speak like this? I give you no answer in words. In the world a true helper is seen in deeds, not spoken of; mere talk is artificial.
m.2.3.17.18: He who talks much in a crisis—what task will he accomplish? Even so, great king, I will speak; listen, O lord.
m.2.3.17.19: Whoever performs fierce austerity to drag you from your position, that enemy of yours I will bring down completely, O friend.
m.2.3.17.20: In an instant, with the sidelong glance of a lovely woman, I will make gods, sages, Dānavas and the rest fall; men do not even count for me.
m.2.3.17.21: Let the thunderbolt and the many other weapons stay far away; what task will they accomplish for you when I, your friend, am at hand?
m.2.3.17.22: I could make even Brahmā or Hari fall, no doubt; others do not count at all. I could bring down even Hara.
m.2.3.17.23: My arrows are only five, soft, and made of flowers; my bow, curved in three places, is made of flowers; its string is formed of bees.
m.2.3.17.24: My strength is my dear beloved Rati; Vasanta is known as my minister. I possess fivefold strength, O god, and my friend is the moon, the treasury of nectar.
m.2.3.17.25: My commander is Śṛṅgāra (erotic sentiment), and amorous gestures and moods are my soldiers. All of them are soft, O Śakra, and I too am of that kind.
m.2.3.17.26: A wise man should employ for a task whoever can accomplish it. Whatever task is suited to me—assign all of it to me.
m.2.3.17.27: Brahmā said: Hearing these words of his, Śakra was delighted, and, bowing with his speech, addressed Kāma, the bringer of joy to lovers.
m.2.3.17.28: Śakra said: The task that I have conceived in my mind, dear Manobhava, you are able to accomplish; it cannot come about through anyone else.
m.2.3.17.29: Listen, Kāma, best of friends; I will tell you truly the purpose for which the longing for you arose in me today, O Manobhava.
m.2.3.17.30: The great demon named Tāraka, having obtained a wondrous boon from Brahmā, has become invincible and a cause of suffering to all.
m.2.3.17.31: By him the world is oppressed and dharma has been destroyed in many ways; all the gods are distressed, and likewise all the sages.
m.2.3.17.32: All the gods fought with him according to their strength, but earlier all their weapons proved futile there.
m.2.3.17.33: The noose of the lord of waters (Varuṇa) was broken; and Hari's discus Sudarśana, hurled by Viṣṇu at his neck, was blunted.
m.2.3.17.34: The lord of creatures (Brahmā) has declared that this wicked one's death will come from a boy born of the seed of Śambhu, the great lord of yogins.
m.2.3.17.35: This task must be carried out well by you with great effort; then, O best of friends, supreme happiness will come to us gods.
m.2.3.17.36: Therefore, remembering in your heart the duty of friendship, you should now accomplish what I too have planned, which brings happiness to all the worlds.
m.2.3.17.37: That Śambhu has undertaken supreme austerity on the king of mountains; that lord, the independent Supreme Lord, is not moved even by desire.
m.2.3.17.38: I have heard that near him, for the sake of the gods, Pārvatī, with her companions, remains serving him, as commanded by her father.
m.2.3.17.39: You must surely act, O Māra, so that in that self-controlled Śiva an intense attraction for her arises.
m.2.3.17.40: Having done this, you will have succeeded; all suffering will perish, and your glory in the world will be lasting—not otherwise.
m.2.3.17.41: Brahmā said: Thus addressed, Kāma, his lotus-face blossoming with joy, lovingly said to the lord of the gods: I will do it; there is no doubt.
m.2.3.17.42: Having spoken these words to him, Kāma, deluded by Śiva's māyā, promptly accepted that command of Indra, saying, so be it, Om.
m.2.3.17.43: Greatly pleased, together with his wife and accompanied by Vasanta, he went to the place where the lord of yogins himself was performing supreme austerity.
m.2.3.17.iti: Thus ends the seventeenth adhyāya, named The description of the dialogue of Śakra and Kāma, in the third khaṇḍa, the Pārvatī-khaṇḍa, of the second saṃhitā, the Rudra-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.2.3.18.1: Brahmā said: Having gone there, the proud Smara, deluded by Śiva's māyā, that enchanter, stood there, first of all spreading forth the nature of Madhu the spring.
m.2.3.18.2: And the nature of spring spread everywhere in Maheśa's place of austerity, on the Oṣadhiprastha, O lord of sages.
m.2.3.18.3: And the forests of trees there became especially full of blossoms through its power, O great sage, O lord of sages.
m.2.3.18.4: The blossoms of the mango trees in the groves of aśoka shone, fragrant and greatly kindling love.
m.2.3.18.5: And the white lotus blossoms, swarmed over by bees, became especially productive of the onset of passion.
m.2.3.18.6: The sweet warbling of the cuckoos, which strongly kindles desire, was exceedingly delightful, charming and most pleasing.
m.2.3.18.7: Likewise, O sage, there arose the various hums of the bees, charming to all and also kindling desire.
m.2.3.18.8: The clear radiance of the moon, spread all around, became like a go-between for amorous men and women.
m.2.3.18.9: At that time the light of the season served to urge on lovers sulking in pride; and a pleasant breeze blew, O good one, yet unwelcome to one separated from the beloved.
m.2.3.18.10: Thus the spread of spring, causing possession by passion, then became exceedingly hard to bear there for the sages dwelling in the forest.
m.2.3.18.11: Then, O sage, even in insentient beings there arose attachment to desire; what need is there to tell the tale of sentient creatures?
m.2.3.18.12: Thus that Madhu, kindling desire in all living beings, displayed his own power, which was most hard to bear.
m.2.3.18.13: Seeing then, dear one, what Madhu had produced out of season, Hara, the Lord who had taken a body through his own play, considered it a great wonder.
m.2.3.18.14: Then that performer of divine play, Hara, the master of the self-controlled, the Lord who removes sorrow, practised there austerity that was supremely difficult.
m.2.3.18.15: When spring had spread there, Kāma, accompanied by Rati, drew the mango-blossom arrow and stood at his left side.
m.2.3.18.16: He spread his power, deluding all people. Who indeed, seeing Kāma then united with Rati, would not be deluded?
m.2.3.18.17: When the two had thus begun their love-sport, Śṛṅgāra (the erotic sentiment) too, with his attendants, endowed with amorous gestures and moods, entered there into Hara's presence.
m.2.3.18.18: Madana, who moves within the mind, dwelt there visible outside; he did not then see in Śambhu any weak spot through which he could enter.
m.2.3.18.19: And when Smara found no opening in that best of yogins, Mahādeva, he became confounded by great fear.
m.2.3.18.20: Who indeed is able to approach Śaṅkara, absorbed in meditation, possessing a forehead-eye like a fire with blazing flames?
m.2.3.18.21: Meanwhile, Śivā, accompanied by her two friends, went there for the worship of Śiva, carrying flowers of many kinds.
m.2.3.18.22: Whatever great beauty is described by people on earth, all that, and more, is certainly present in that Pārvatī.
m.2.3.18.23: When she wore the lovely flowers of the season, how could that beauty of hers be described even in hundreds of years?
m.2.3.18.24: When that daughter of the mountain came near Śiva, at that very moment Śaṅkara, leaving his meditation, remained so for an instant.
m.2.3.18.25: Finding that opening, Madana first, with the arrow Harṣaṇa, excited the Moon-crested One standing nearby.
m.2.3.18.26: Then, O sage, Pārvatī, endowed with amorous moods and feelings, went to Hara, in aid of Kāma, together with Spring.
