m.2.3.18.27: At that very moment, drawing that bow, Smara, well composed, swiftly released the flower-arrow at the Trident-bearer, to arouse his liking.
m.2.3.18.28: Just as she came constantly every day, so now she came to Śiva; having bowed to him and performed his worship, she stood before him.
m.2.3.18.29: That Pārvatī was seen there by the Lord Giriśa as she then, from a woman's nature and with great bashfulness, revealed her limbs.
m.2.3.18.30: Recalling well the boon given to her formerly by Vidhi Brahmā, Lord Śiva too described her limbs with delight, O sage.
m.2.3.18.31: Śiva said: Is this a face, or the moon? Are these eyes, or blue lotuses? And these two eyebrows are the bows of the great-souled Kandarpa.
m.2.3.18.32: Is this a lower lip, or a bimba fruit? Is this a nose, or a parrot's beak? Is this a voice, or the cooing of a cuckoo? Is this a waist, or an altar?
m.2.3.18.33: How can her gait be described? How can her form be described again and again? And how can her flowers be described, and likewise again her garments?
m.2.3.18.34: Whatever lovely grace there is in creation has been fashioned in one place in her. All her limbs are charming in every way; there is no doubt.
m.2.3.18.35: Ah, most blessed is this Pārvatī of wondrous form! There is no woman in the three worlds so beautiful as to equal her.
m.2.3.18.36: She is a treasure of great loveliness, bearing wondrous limbs, an enchantress even of sages, increasing great joy.
m.2.3.18.37: Brahmā said: Having thus described her limbs again and again, Hara, under the influence of the boon given by Vidhi, then fell silent.
m.2.3.18.38: When Śaṅkara moved his hand toward the edge of her garment, she, out of a woman's nature, abashed, went some distance away.
m.2.3.18.39: Revealing her own limbs and glancing again and again with lovely looks, Śivā, from great joy, broke into a sweet smile, O sage.
m.2.3.18.40: Seeing such behaviour then, Śambhu became infatuated, and Maheśvara, of great divine play, spoke these words.
m.2.3.18.41: By merely seeing her, great bliss arises in abundance. If I were to embrace her, what joy would there be then?
m.2.3.18.42: Having reflected thus for just a moment and then having honoured Girijā, that great yogin, awakened to himself and wholly dispassionate, spoke as follows.
m.2.3.18.43: What has happened, what strange conduct? Have I fallen into delusion? Even though I am the master and the Lord, today I have been disturbed by Kāma.
m.2.3.18.44: If I, the Lord, should indeed desire to touch another's body, then what will any other petty, powerless being not do?
m.2.3.18.45: Having thus attained dispassion, the Supreme Lord, the Self of all, checked that sitting of Pārvatī's upon the couch. How could he fall here?
m.2.3.18.iti: Thus ends the eighteenth adhyāya, named The description of the disturbance caused by Kāma, in the third khaṇḍa, the Pārvatī-khaṇḍa, of the second saṃhitā, the Rudra-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.2.3.19.1: Nārada said: O Brahmā, O Creator, O greatly fortunate one, what happened after that? Graciously tell me that sin-destroying story.
m.2.3.19.2: Brahmā said: Listen, dear child, to that story of what happened after that. Out of affection for you I shall narrate Śiva's joy-bringing sport.
m.2.3.19.3: Seeing the disturbance of his composure, the great yogin Maheśvara, greatly astonished, then reflected thus in his mind.
m.2.3.19.4: Śiva said: Why have obstacles arisen while I am performing supreme austerity? What evil-doer here has made my mind agitated?
m.2.3.19.5: I have indeed lovingly made an improper description concerning another's woman. A violation of dharma has occurred here; the boundary of the Veda has been transgressed.
m.2.3.19.6: Brahmā said: Having reflected thus, the great yogin, the Supreme Lord, the refuge of the good, then, suspicious, looked around in all directions.
m.2.3.19.7: He saw Kāma standing on his left side with his arrow drawn, eager to shoot his own arrow, proud and deluded in mind.
m.2.3.19.8: Seeing Kāma in that state, O Nārada, a tumult of anger arose instantly in Girīśa, the Supreme Self.
m.2.3.19.9: Kāma, standing in the sky and holding that bow with its arrow, discharged at Śaṅkara, O sage, his irresistible, unfailing missile.
m.2.3.19.10: But that unfailing missile became futile against the Supreme Self; it then subsided before that enraged Supreme Lord.
m.2.3.19.11: When his own missile had become futile against Śiva, Manmatha was quickly seized by fear, and standing before him, seeing the lord Mṛtyuñjaya, he trembled.
m.2.3.19.12: His effort being fruitless, that Smara, overwhelmed with fear, O tiger among sages, called to mind all the gods headed by Śakra.
m.2.3.19.13: Being intently remembered by Kāma, O lord of sages, all those gods headed by Śakra came, bowed to Śambhu, and praised him.
m.2.3.19.14: While the gods were offering praise, from the third eye of the greatly enraged Hara there then issued forth a great fire,
m.2.3.19.15: From that eye situated in the middle of the forehead, that swiftly arisen fire blazed with upward flames, shining, with a radiance like the fire of dissolution.
m.2.3.19.16: Swiftly flying up into the sky and dropping onto the surface of the earth, whirling round and round about itself, it fell all over the earth.
m.2.3.19.17: O good one, it reduced Madana to ashes even while the gods were still crying, forgive, forgive.
m.2.3.19.18: When that heroic Smara was slain, the gods fell into grief; overwhelmed, they wept, crying loudly: What has happened?
m.2.3.19.19: Then the daughter of the king of mountains, pale of limb and distraught in mind, went to her own house taking her companions with her.
m.2.3.19.20: Then Rati there became unconscious for a moment; through the grief born of her husband's death she fell as if dead.
m.2.3.19.21: When consciousness returned, Rati, utterly distraught, lamented there, uttering various words.
m.2.3.19.22: Rati said: What shall I do? Where shall I go? What have the gods done here? Having summoned my proud lord, they had him destroyed.
m.2.3.19.23: Alas, alas, my protector Smara, my lord, dear as life, giver of joy! What is this that has happened here? Alas, alas, beloved, beloved!
m.2.3.19.24: Brahmā said: Lamenting thus and uttering many words, she then beat her hands and feet and tore at her hair.
m.2.3.19.25: Hearing her lament then, all the forest creatures there became sorrowful, O Nārada, and even the immobile beings.
m.2.3.19.26: Meanwhile, all the gods there headed by Śakra, remembering Maheśvara, consoled Rati and spoke to her.
m.2.3.19.27: The gods said: Take some of the ashes and guard them carefully; give up fear. That Lord will revive him, and you will regain your beloved.
m.2.3.19.28: No one is the giver of happiness, nor anyone the giver of sorrow; everyone experiences what he himself has done. You blame the gods in vain.
m.2.3.19.29: Brahmā said: Having thus consoled Rati, all the gods approached Śiva and, having fully propitiated Śiva with devotion, spoke these words.
m.2.3.19.30: The gods said: O Blessed One, O Lord, O Maheśāna, affectionate to those who seek refuge, be merciful and listen to this auspicious speech of ours.
m.2.3.19.31: O Śaṅkara, consider well and kindly the deed of Kāma. What Kāma did here was not for his own sake, O Maheśvara.
m.2.3.19.32: O all-pervading one, that deed was caused to be done by all of us gods oppressed by the wicked Tāraka. O Lord, Śaṅkara, know it not to be otherwise.
m.2.3.19.33: O god, Rati, all alone and grief-stricken, is lamenting. O Giriśa, O giver of all, console her.
m.2.3.19.34: O Śaṅkara, if you have slain that Smara, then with this anger you intend to destroy everyone, along with the gods.
m.2.3.19.35: Seeing the grief of that Rati, the gods are almost ruined. Therefore you must remove Rati's sorrow.
m.2.3.19.36: Brahmā said: Having heard their words, the Blessed Śiva was pleased and spoke these words to all the gods.
m.2.3.19.37: Śiva said: O gods and all sages, listen attentively to my words. What has happened through my anger will remain so; it cannot be otherwise.
m.2.3.19.38: The mighty Kāma, Rati's husband, shall remain bodiless (anaṅga) only until Kṛṣṇa, the husband of Rukmiṇī, descends upon the earth.
m.2.3.19.39: When, dwelling in Dvārakā, he begets sons, then Kṛṣṇa will beget Kāma in Rukmiṇī.
m.2.3.19.40: He will be named Pradyumna; there is no doubt. And as soon as that son is born, Śambara will carry him off.
m.2.3.19.41: Śambara, the foremost of the Dānavas, having carried him off and thrown him into the ocean, and deluded, believing him dead without reason, will go to his own city.
m.2.3.19.42: Meanwhile, O Rati, you should stay in his city as you please; right there you will obtain your own husband, reborn as Pradyumna.
m.2.3.19.43: There Kāma, named Pradyumna, having met her and slain Śambara in battle, will be happy with his own beloved, O gods.
m.2.3.19.44: And taking whatever wealth was his (Śambara's), he will go back to the city together with her, O gods; my word is true.
m.2.3.19.45: Brahmā said: Having heard these words of Śambhu, the gods, somewhat relieved at heart, bowed to him and, with folded hands and bodies bent low, spoke.
m.2.3.19.46: The gods said: O God of gods, Mahādeva, ocean of compassion, Lord, quickly revive Kāma; save Rati's life, O Hara.
m.2.3.19.47: Brahmā said: Hearing these words of the immortals, the Supreme Lord, pleased, the ocean of compassion, the Lord of all, spoke again.
m.2.3.19.48: Śiva said: O gods, I am well pleased, and I shall revive him in due course. That Kāma, having become my attendant (gaṇa), will roam about forever.
m.2.3.19.49: This account must not be told before anyone, O gods. Go to your own abodes; I shall destroy your sorrow in every way.
m.2.3.19.50: Brahmā said: Having said this, Rudra vanished then while the gods were praising him. All the gods became well pleased, their amazement gone.
m.2.3.19.51: Then, abiding by Rudra's word, they consoled her, told her his message, and went each to his own abode, O sage.
m.2.3.19.52: Kāma's wife then went to the city indicated to her, awaiting the time appointed by Rudra, O lord of sages.
m.2.3.19.iti: Thus ends the nineteenth adhyāya, named The description of the destruction of Kāma, in the third khaṇḍa, the Pārvatī-khaṇḍa, of the second saṃhitā, the Rudra-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.2.3.20.1: Nārada said: O Creator, where did that flame of fire that arose from Hara's eye go? Tell me that story of the moon-crested Śiva.
m.2.3.20.2: Brahmā said: When the fire of Śambhu's third eye had swiftly reduced Kāma to ashes, it then blazed on all sides, without purpose.
m.2.3.20.3: A great cry of distress arose in the three worlds with their moving and unmoving beings. All the gods and sages, dear son, quickly came to me for refuge.
m.2.3.20.4: Agitated, they all bowed down deeply, praised me well, joined their hands, and with faces lowered reported that distress to me.
m.2.3.20.5: Hearing that, I remembered Śiva, reflected carefully on its cause, and went there with a humble mind for the protection of the three worlds.
m.2.3.20.6: That fire, eager to burn everything, blazing intensely with garlands of flames, was quickly checked by me through the great power obtained by Śambhu's grace.
m.2.3.20.7: Then, O sage, I drew away that fire made of wrath, eager to burn the three worlds, giving it the form of the submarine mare-fire with a gentle flaming mouth.
m.2.3.20.8: Taking that fire in the body of the mare-fire, by Śiva's will I, the lord of the worlds, went to the ocean for the welfare of the people.
m.2.3.20.9: Seeing me arrive, O sage, the Ocean, assuming a human form, came into my presence with joined palms.
m.2.3.20.10: Then the Ocean bowed deeply to me and praised me according to rule, and with great affection he spoke to me, the grandfather of all the worlds.
m.2.3.20.11: The Ocean said: For what purpose have you come here, O Brahmā, lord of all? Instruct me about that kindly, regarding me as your own servant.
m.2.3.20.12: Then, having heard the Ocean's words spoken with affection, I remembered Śaṅkara and spoke, bringing about the welfare of the world.
m.2.3.20.13: Brahmā said: Listen, dear one, highly intelligent one, bringer of welfare to all worlds. O Ocean, impelled in my heart by Śiva's will, I speak with affection.
m.2.3.20.14: This is the wrath of Maheśa, a mighty power in the form of the mare-fire. Having quickly burnt Kāma, it then became eager to burn everything.
m.2.3.20.15: By Śaṅkara's will I was quickly entreated by the afflicted gods; coming there swiftly, dear one, I checked that fire.
m.2.3.20.16: It assumed the form of the mare-fire; taking it, I have come here. O abode of waters, I, the merciful one, direct you:
m.2.3.20.17: This wrath of Maheśa, which has taken the form of the mare-fire with a flaming mouth, must be held by you until the dissolution of beings.
m.2.3.20.18: When I come here and dwell here, O lord of rivers, then this wondrous wrath of Śaṅkara should be released by you.
m.2.3.20.19: Your water will always be its food. It must be held with care so that it does not come out.
m.2.3.20.20: Thus addressed by me, the Ocean then firmly agreed to take in the fierce mare-fire, which could not be held by anyone else.
m.2.3.20.21: Then that fire in the body of the mare-fire entered the ocean, burning its floods of water, blazing with garlands of flames.
m.2.3.20.22: Then, with a contented mind, I went to my own abode, O sage; and the Ocean, of divine form, bowed to me and disappeared.
m.2.3.20.23: The whole world regained its well-being, freed from the fear arising from that; the gods and the sages became happy, O great sage.
m.2.3.20.iti: Thus ends the twentieth adhyāya, named The description of the story of the submarine fire, in the third khaṇḍa, the Pārvatī-khaṇḍa, of the second saṃhitā, the Rudra-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.2.3.21.1: Nārada said: O Vidhi, dear father, greatly wise one, disciple of Viṣṇu, maker of the three worlds: this wondrous story of the great-souled Śaṅkara has been told by you.
m.2.3.21.2: When Smara had been reduced to ashes by the fire of Śambhu's third eye, and when that fire had entered the ocean, tell me what happened after that.
m.2.3.21.3: What did the goddess Pārvatī, daughter of the mountain, do then? Where did she go with her two friends? Tell me that now, O treasure of compassion.
m.2.3.21.4: Brahmā said: Listen, dear son, greatly wise one, with reverence to the deeds of the moon-crested one, the bestower of great grace, my own Lord.
m.2.3.21.5: When the fire born from Śambhu's eye burned Madana, a great and wondrous sound arose, by which the sky was filled.
m.2.3.21.6: Frightened by that great sound, and having seen Kāma burned, she went, distraught, to her own home together with her two friends.
m.2.3.21.7: At that sound Himavat, together with his household, was astonished and deeply distressed, remembering his daughter who had gone there.
m.2.3.21.8: The lord of mountains fell into grief on seeing his daughter so agitated; the lord of mountains approached her as she wept from separation from Śambhu.
m.2.3.21.9: Having approached, wiping her two eyes with his hand, he said, do not fear, Śivā; do not weep, and then took hold of her.
m.2.3.21.10: Himavat, lord of mountains, quickly placed his daughter on his lap and then brought her to his own abode, consoling her in her great distress.
m.2.3.21.11: When Hara, having burned Smara, had vanished, Śivā, through separation from him, became extremely distressed and found comfort nowhere.
m.2.3.21.12: Then, having gone to her father's house and met her mother, Śivā, the daughter of the mountain, felt as though she had been born again.
m.2.3.21.13: She reproached her own beauty and then said, alas, I am ruined! Even when counselled by her friends, the daughter of the mountain-king would not be consoled.
m.2.3.21.14: Whether sleeping or drinking, bathing or walking, or standing among her friends, Śivā found no happiness at all.
m.2.3.21.15: Fie on my beauty, and likewise on my birth and my deeds! So she kept saying, constantly remembering Hara's actions.
m.2.3.21.16: Thus Pārvatī, her mind tormented by separation from Śambhu, found no happiness whatever, and kept saying, Śiva, Śiva.
m.2.3.21.17: Dwelling in her father's house, her mind fixed on the bearer of Pināka, Śivā grieved, dear son, and swooned again and again.
m.2.3.21.18: Then the king of mountains, and Menakā too, and all their sons headed by Maināka, steadfast in spirit, consoled her; yet she did not forget Hara.
m.2.3.21.19: Then, O wise divine sage, you, sent by Indra the slayer of Bala, came of your own free will to the tableland of Himavat.
m.2.3.21.20: Then you were honoured by that great-souled mountain, and, seated on an excellent seat, you asked him about his welfare.
m.2.3.21.21: Then the lord of mountains related from the beginning his daughter's story, including her service to Hara and the burning of Kāma by Hara.
m.2.3.21.22: Having heard this, O sage, you said to that lord of mountains: Worship Śiva. Then, taking leave of him, you rose, remembering Śiva in your mind.
m.2.3.21.23: Leaving him, you went quickly to that Kālī in private, O sage—you, the benefactor of the world, wise and dear to Śiva.
m.2.3.21.24: Approaching Kālī and addressing her, intent on her welfare, you, the best of all the wise, spoke true words with respect.
m.2.3.21.25: Nārada said: Listen, Kālī, to my words; devoted to compassion, I speak the truth—what is wholly beneficial to you, free of fault, and grants good desires.
m.2.3.21.26: Because Mahādeva was served by you here without austerity, while you were proud, he who shows grace to the humble destroyed that pride.
m.2.3.21.27: And that Lord of yours, Maheśvara the great yogin, being dispassionate, burned Smara and left you, O Śivā—though he is loving to his devotees.
m.2.3.21.28: Therefore, devoted to good austerity, worship the Lord for a long time. When you are refined by austerity, Rudra will make you his consort.
m.2.3.21.29: And you too will never abandon Śaṅkara Śambhu; O goddess, you will not obstinately accept any husband other than Śiva.
m.2.3.21.30: Brahmā said: Having heard these words of yours, O sage, that daughter of the mountain, Kālī, breathing a little more freely, joyfully spoke to you with folded hands.
m.2.3.21.31: Śivā said: O all-knowing one, benefactor of the worlds, O lord, O sage, give me a mantra for the worship of Rudra.
m.2.3.21.32: No rite of anyone succeeds without a true guru; I heard this eternal scriptural teaching long ago, and it is true.
m.2.3.21.33: Brahmā said: Having heard these words of Pārvatī, you, best of sages, imparted to her according to rule the five-syllabled mantra of Śambhu.
m.2.3.21.34: And, O sage, arousing faith in her, you told her of the power of that king of mantras, which surpasses all.
m.2.3.21.35: Nārada said: Listen, O goddess, to the supremely wondrous power of this mantra, by the mere hearing of which Śaṅkara is greatly pleased.
m.2.3.21.36: This mantra is the overlord of all mantras and fulfils desires; it bestows enjoyment and liberation and is exceedingly dear to Śaṅkara.
m.2.3.21.37: O fortunate one, when this is repeated according to rule, Śiva, thus worshipped, will surely and swiftly appear before you without delay.
m.2.3.21.38: Meditating on his form and abiding in observances, repeat the five-syllabled mantra, O Śivā; Śiva will quickly be pleased.
m.2.3.21.39: Thus perform austerity, O virtuous one; Maheśvara is to be won by austerity. Through austerity alone is the fruit obtained by all, never in any other way.
m.2.3.21.40: Brahmā said: Having spoken thus to Kālī, O Nārada, you, dear to Śiva, wandering at will and devoted to the welfare of the gods, went to heaven.
m.2.3.21.41: Then Pārvatī, having heard your words, O Nārada, was greatly delighted, and then received the five-syllabled mantra, the most excellent of all.
m.2.3.21.iti: Thus ends the twenty-first adhyāya, named The instruction of Nārada, in the third khaṇḍa, the Pārvatī-khaṇḍa, of the second saṃhitā, the Rudra-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.2.3.22.1: Brahmā said: O divine sage, when you had gone, Pārvatī, glad at heart, judged that Hara could be won through penance, and she set her mind on penance.
m.2.3.22.2: Then, taking along her two friends, Jayā and Vijayā, she asked leave of her mother and her father through the two friends.
m.2.3.22.3: First, going to her father Himavat, lord of mountains, and bowing low, she, full of humility, asked him.
m.2.3.22.4: The two friends said: O Himavat, let your daughter's words be heard, which are now being told: she herself wishes to bring fulfilment to her body and likewise to her beauty,
m.2.3.22.5: and indeed to this family of yours—she wishes to make them fruitful. He is to be won through penance; otherwise he would not come within sight.
m.2.3.22.6: Therefore, O best of mountains, permission should now be given by you, respectfully, for Girijā to go to the forest and perform penance.
m.2.3.22.7: Brahmā said: Thus questioned then by the two friends on Pārvatī's behalf, O best of sages, the king of mountains, after careful thought, said this:
m.2.3.22.8: Himavān said: It pleases me greatly; let it also please Menā. If this is how it is to be, what could be better than this?
m.2.3.22.9: It will surely be the fulfilment of my family; there is no doubt. If it pleases her mother too, what could be more auspicious than that?
m.2.3.22.10: Brahmā said: Having heard these words spoken by the father, the two friends, permitted by him, then went with her to the mother.
m.2.3.22.11: Going to Pārvatī's mother, O Nārada, they bowed low, joined their palms, and respectfully spoke these words:
m.2.3.22.12: The two friends said: Mother, O goddess, salutation to you; hear your daughter's words, and having heard them with full grace, you ought to fulfil them here.
m.2.3.22.13: Your daughter, wishing to perform supreme penance for Śiva's sake, having obtained her father's permission, now asks you as well.
m.2.3.22.14: She wishes to make her own form fruitful, O devoted wife; if your permission is granted, then she will perform penance accordingly.
m.2.3.22.15: Brahmā said: Having said this, the two friends then fell silent, O lord of sages. Menā, dejected at heart, did not accept their words.
m.2.3.22.16: Then Pārvatī herself, humble in spirit, with joined palms and remembering Śiva's lotus feet, spoke to her mother.
m.2.3.22.17: Pārvatī said: Mother, tomorrow morning I shall go to perform penance in order to attain Maheśvara. Permit me today to go to the penance-grove for penance.
m.2.3.22.18: Brahmā said: Hearing her daughter's words, Menā was struck with grief; then, distraught, she called her daughter to her and spoke.
m.2.3.22.19: Menā said: O Śivā, my daughter, if you are pained and longing to perform penance as before, practise penance at home today; do not go outside, Pārvatī.
m.2.3.22.20: Where are you going to perform penance? The gods are in my house, and all the sacred fords and various holy places too.
m.2.3.22.21: Do not be obstinate, daughter; you must not go outside anywhere. What did you achieve before by penance? What more will you achieve now?
m.2.3.22.22: Your body is tender, my child, but penance is hard and great. Therefore you should do your penance here; do not go outside.
m.2.3.22.23: It has never been heard that women go to a penance-grove in pursuit of a desire. So, daughter, do not set out to go for penance.
m.2.3.22.24: Brahmā said: Thus the daughter was dissuaded by her mother in many ways. Yet she said: I declare there is no happiness at all without worshipping Maheśvara.
m.2.3.22.25: Because she was forbidden by Menā with the words u mā (O, do not) from going to the forest for penance, Śivā then received the name Umā.
m.2.3.22.26: Then, knowing Śivā to be distressed, Menā, beloved of the Mountain, gave Pārvatī her consent for penance, O sage.
m.2.3.22.27: Having received her mother's permission, O best of sages, Pārvatī of fine vows, remembering Śaṅkara, then felt happiness in her heart.
m.2.3.22.28: Then Śivā joyfully bowed to her mother and father and, with her two friends, remembering Śiva, set out to perform penance.
m.2.3.22.29: Casting off her many favourite garments of various kinds, she quickly put on bark garments, having tied on a fine girdle of muñja grass.
m.2.3.22.30: Laying aside her necklace, she likewise wore an excellent deerskin, and went for penance there, towards Gaṅgāvataraṇa.
m.2.3.22.31: That plateau of Himavat, where Manobhava (Kāma) was burnt by Śambhu while he was meditating, is named Gaṅgāvataraṇa.
m.2.3.22.32: Then, O dear one, coming there, Kālī—Pārvatī, the Mother of the world—saw that plateau of the snow-mountain empty of Hara.
m.2.3.22.33: Where Śambhu had formerly stayed and performed arduous penance, there she stood for a moment and became afflicted by separation.
m.2.3.22.34: There Śivā, the mountain's daughter, weeping and crying, alas, Hara, lamented, deeply pained by grief and filled with anxiety and sorrow.
m.2.3.22.35: Then after a long while Pārvatī, daughter of Himavat, steadied her bewilderment through fortitude and was consecrated there for the observance of vows.
m.2.3.22.36: She performed penance there at the most excellent Śṛṅgitīrtha; because of her penance there, that place came to be called Gaurīśikhara.
m.2.3.22.37: There, O sage, Śivā planted beautiful, sacred trees, fruit-bearing, as a test of her penance.
m.2.3.22.38: Then the beautiful one purified the ground, built an altar, and so began a penance hard even for sages.
m.2.3.22.39: Quickly restraining all the senses together with the mind, she performed supreme penance there, in that place close at hand.
m.2.3.22.40: In summer, having kindled a fire blazing all around her day and night, she stood in its midst, continually reciting the mantra.
m.2.3.22.41: And in the rainy season, sitting firmly and constantly on the bare ground and on the surface of a rock, she was drenched by the torrents of water.
m.2.3.22.42: In the cold season she stood constantly in the midst of water, wholly intent on devotion; fasting, she performed penance there amid the snows and through the nights.
m.2.3.22.43: Thus performing penance, devoted to the recitation of the five-syllabled mantra, Śivā meditated there on Śiva, the giver of the fruits of all desires.
m.2.3.22.44: Joyfully watering, with her friends, the auspicious trees she herself had planted, she offered hospitality there every day whenever she had leisure.
m.2.3.22.45: Wind, and cold rain of many kinds, and heat too though hard to bear, were all endured by her, steady of mind.
m.2.3.22.46: The various hardships that came upon her there she did not reckon; fixing her mind on Śiva alone, she remained steadfast, O sage.
m.2.3.22.47: Performing penance first by eating fruits and then by eating leaves, the goddess gradually passed countless years.
m.2.3.22.48: Then Śivā, the daughter of Himavat, giving up even leaves, became wholly without food, the goddess absorbed in the practice of penance.
m.2.3.22.49: Because the daughter of Himavat gave up leaves as food, Śivā was therefore called by the gods by the name Aparṇā.
m.2.3.22.50: Pārvatī stood on one foot, remembering Śiva, and reciting the five-syllabled mantra she performed great penance.
m.2.3.22.51: Clad in rags and bark garments, wearing a mass of matted locks, absorbed in contemplation of Śiva, she surpassed the sages by her penance.
m.2.3.22.52: As Kālī thus practised penance, meditating on Maheśvara, three thousand years passed in the penance-grove.
m.2.3.22.53: Then, having stayed for a moment at the place where Hara had performed penance for sixty thousand years, Śivā reflected:
m.2.3.22.54: O Mahādeva, do you not know me now, abiding in my vows, that I, devoted to penance for so long, have not been sought out by you?
m.2.3.22.55: In the world and in the Veda, Giriśa is ever sung of by the sages: that Śaṅkara is indeed all-knowing, the Self of all, all-seeing,
m.2.3.22.56: the god who bestows all prosperity, who brings about all states of being, who ever grants the wishes of his devotees and removes all afflictions.
m.2.3.22.57: If, having renounced all desires, I am devoted to the bull-bannered one, then may that Śaṅkara be gracious to me here.
m.2.3.22.58: If the five-syllabled mantra taught in the Nārada Tantra has been recited by me daily with true devotion and according to rule, may Śaṅkara be gracious.
m.2.3.22.59: If, through devotion to Śiva, the Lord of all, I am utterly unwavering as has been prescribed, may Śaṅkara be gracious.
m.2.3.22.60: Thus reflecting constantly, she performed penance for a very long time, face bowed down, unwavering, wearing matted locks and bark garments.
m.2.3.22.61: Such penance was performed by her as is difficult even for sages; recalling it, the people there were struck with the highest wonder.
m.2.3.22.62: They all came together to see that penance; considering themselves blessed, they spoke thus in agreement:
m.2.3.22.63: Going to those who are advanced in dharma is declared the highest good even for the great. There is no measure for penance; dharma is always to be honoured by the wise.
m.2.3.22.64: Having heard of and seen her penance, what penance is it that others perform? Greater penance than this has never been in the world, nor will be.
m.2.3.22.65: Speaking thus, all of them, having highly praised Śivā's penance, went joyfully to their own abodes, even those who were hardened in body.
m.2.3.22.66: Now hear, O great sage, another great and most wondrous effect of the penance of Pārvatī, the Mother of the world.
m.2.3.22.67: Those creatures which came to her hermitage, though hostile by nature, then became free of enmity through its power.
m.2.3.22.68: Lions and cows, ever subject to faults such as passion, did not harm one another there, by her greatness.
m.2.3.22.69: Moreover, O best of sages, others too, such as cats and mice, enemies by nature, never behaved with hostility there.
m.2.3.22.70: There the trees bore fruit, and there were grasses of many kinds and colourful flowers, O best of sages.
m.2.3.22.71: And that whole forest then became comparable to Kailāsa; it became the very embodiment of the fulfilment of her penance.
m.2.3.22.iti: Thus ends the twenty-second adhyāya, named The description of the austerity of Pārvatī, in the third khaṇḍa, the Pārvatī-khaṇḍa, of the second saṃhitā, the Rudra-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.2.3.23.1: Brahmā said: O lord of sages, while Pārvatī was thus performing austerities to attain Śiva, a long time passed, but Hara did not appear.
m.2.3.23.2: Then Himālaya, together with his wife, his sons and his ministers, came and spoke to Pārvatī, the supreme goddess, who had made her firm resolve.
m.2.3.23.3: Himavān said: Do not torment yourself with this austerity, O greatly fortunate Pārvatī. Rudra is not to be seen, child; he is detached from worldly attachment, there is no doubt about this.
m.2.3.23.4: You are slender, with delicate limbs, and you will become overcome by this austerity, no doubt; I tell you the truth, the truth.
m.2.3.23.5: Therefore rise and come to your own home, O fair one. What have you to do with that Rudra, by whom Smara was burnt long ago?
m.2.3.23.6: Hence, because he is free from any passion, Hara will not come to take you, excellent as you are, O queen of the gods; how will you win him by entreaty?
m.2.3.23.7: Just as the moon standing in the sky cannot be seized, so too, O sinless one, know Śambhu here to be beyond reach.
m.2.3.23.8: Brahmā said: In the same way the virtuous maiden was addressed by Menā, likewise by the Sahya mountain, by Meru, by Mandara, and likewise by Maināka.
m.2.3.23.9: So too the unperturbed Girijā was addressed in the same manner by other mountains such as Krauñca, who put forward various arguments.
m.2.3.23.10: When the slender maiden, steadfast in austerity, had been thus addressed by all, she of pure smile spoke to Himavat, laughing.
m.2.3.23.11: Pārvatī said: Father, mother, I told you before—have you forgotten it? Even now, hear my vow, O my kinsmen.
m.2.3.23.12: That Mahādeva is indeed detached, he by whom Smara was burnt in wrath; yet I will please that Śaṅkara, who is loving to his devotees, through austerity.
m.2.3.23.13: All of you, go happily each to your own abode. He will surely be pleased; there need be no deliberation about this.
m.2.3.23.14: He by whom Madana was burnt, by whom the forest of the mountain was burnt—him I shall bring right here by austerity alone.
m.2.3.23.15: By the great power of austerity Sadāśiva is easily won; know this, O fortunate ones—I tell you the truth, the truth.
m.2.3.23.16: Having thus addressed Menakā, her father Himālaya the kinsman of Maināka, together with Mandara, Girijā—Śivā, the sweet-spoken daughter of the king of mountains—quickly fell silent.
m.2.3.23.17: Thus addressed by Śivā, those wise mountains, led by the lord of the golden mountain, went back the way they had come, greatly astonished, praising Girijā again and again.
m.2.3.23.18: When they had all gone, she, surrounded by her friends and firmly resolved on the supreme goal, performed austerity even more intensely.
m.2.3.23.19: By that great austerity, O best of sages, all that moves and does not move—the three worlds with gods, asuras and humans—became heated.
m.2.3.23.20: Then all the gods and asuras, yakṣas, kinnaras and cāraṇas, siddhas and sādhyas, sages, vidyādharas and great serpents,
m.2.3.23.21: together with the Prajāpatis, the guhyakas and others too, fell into ever greater distress, and they did not know its cause.
m.2.3.23.22: All of them, led by Śakra, gathering together in agitation and having consulted their preceptor, with all their limbs scorched, went to me, Vidhi, on Sumeru for refuge.
m.2.3.23.23: Having gone there, agitated and with their splendour lost, they quickly bowed, and all of them, praising me, spoke to me with one voice.
m.2.3.23.24: The gods said: This whole world, moving and unmoving, created by you, is intensely heated—for what reason? The cause is not known, O lord.
m.2.3.23.25: So tell us the cause, O Brahmā; you should find it out for us, O lord. For the gods whose bodies are burnt, there is no protector other than you.
m.2.3.23.26: Brahmā said: Hearing their words, I remembered Śiva in my heart and, reflecting on everything in my mind, realised that it was the result of Girijā's austerity,
m.2.3.23.27: and knowing that the universe was being burnt, I went quickly, respectfully, with all of them, to the Ocean of Milk to tell this to Hari.
m.2.3.23.28: Having gone there and seen Hari resplendent on his comfortable seat, I bowed deeply, praised him well, and spoke with folded hands, together with the gods.
m.2.3.23.29: Save us, save us, O Mahāviṣṇu. We have come to you for refuge, scorched by the fierce and supreme austerity of Pārvatī, who is engaged in penance.
m.2.3.23.30: Hearing these words of us dwellers of heaven, beginning with me, the lord of Ramā, seated on Śeṣa, spoke to us.
m.2.3.23.31: Viṣṇu said: The whole cause, Pārvatī's austerity, is now known to me. Together with you, I go today to the Supreme Lord.
m.2.3.23.32: We shall entreat that Mahādeva to accept Girijā, for the purpose of taking her hand in marriage now, O immortals, for the welfare of the worlds.
m.2.3.23.33: The god of gods, the bearer of Pināka, will go there to give a boon to Śivā; and as he wishes, so we shall now do there.
m.2.3.23.34: Therefore we shall go where Rudra, the great lord, supremely auspicious, now dwells engaged in fierce austerity.
m.2.3.23.35: Brahmā said: Hearing those words of Viṣṇu, all the gods and the others, greatly afraid of the angry one who wished to burn and who causes dissolution, spoke vehemently:
m.2.3.23.36: The gods said: None of us will go to Virūpākṣa, the great lord, who is most terrifying, angry, and blazing like the fire of final destruction.
m.2.3.23.37: Just as he once burnt Madana, who was hard to overcome, so too, filled with anger, he will burn us—there is no doubt.
m.2.3.23.38: Brahmā said: Hearing those words of Śakra and the others, O sage, Hari, the lord of Ramā, consoling all those gods, spoke.
m.2.3.23.39: Hari said: O gods, all of you, listen to my words with goodwill and attention. That lord, the destroyer of the gods' fear, will not burn you.
m.2.3.23.40: Therefore, wise ones, you should go with me to the refuge of that good lord, regarding Śambhu as the bestower of welfare.
m.2.3.23.41: We go for refuge to that Śiva, the ancient Person, the supreme Lord, whose form is most worthy of choice, the supreme ancient one, who is devoted to austerity, whose form is the Supreme Self, higher than the highest.
m.2.3.23.42: Brahmā said: Thus addressed then by the mighty Viṣṇu, all the gods went with him, wishing to see the bearer of the Pināka bow.
m.2.3.23.43: First, since it lay on their way, all of them, Viṣṇu and the others, full of curiosity, went to the hermitage of the mountain's daughter to see her austerity.
m.2.3.23.44: Having seen Pārvatī's excellent austerity, and being then enveloped by her radiance, they bowed to her, the sustainer of the world, whose form was radiance and who was established in austerity.
m.2.3.23.45: Praising the austerity of her who was perfection (siddhi) embodied, the gods then went to the place where the bull-bannered Śiva was.
m.2.3.23.46: Having gone there, the gods then sent you, O sage, and stood watching from afar, fearing Hara who had reduced Kāma to ashes.
m.2.3.23.47: O Nārada, you, ever fearless and a devotee of Śiva in particular, then went to Śiva's abode and saw the Lord pleased.
m.2.3.23.48: Returning, you then carefully summoned those gods and led Viṣṇu and the others to Śaṅkara's abode, O sage.
m.2.3.23.49: Then Viṣṇu and all the others, having gone there, saw Lord Śiva seated at ease, gracious, affectionate to his devotees.
m.2.3.23.50: They saw Śambhu seated in the yoga posture with the yoga-band, surrounded by his Gaṇas, bearing the form of austerity, embodying the Supreme Lord.
m.2.3.23.51: Then Viṣṇu, I Brahmā, and the others—gods, Siddhas and chief sages—bowed and praised him with hymns drawn from the Vedas and Upaniṣads.
m.2.3.23.iti: Thus ends the twenty-third adhyāya, named The description of the consoling of Pārvatī and of the gods' sight of Śiva, in the third khaṇḍa, the Pārvatī-khaṇḍa, of the second saṃhitā, the Rudra-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.2.3.24.1: The gods said: Obeisance to Rudra, the god, and to the one who put an end to Madana; to the one worthy of praise, to the one of abundant radiance, to the three-eyed one, obeisance, obeisance.
m.2.3.24.2: Obeisance again and again to Śipiviṣṭa, to the terrible one, to the one of terrible eyes. Obeisance to Mahādeva, the lord, the master of heaven.
m.2.3.24.3: You are the protector of all the worlds, the father and the mother; you are the Lord. You are Śambhu, Īśa, Śaṅkara; you are especially compassionate.
m.2.3.24.4: You are the creator of all the worlds; you ought to protect us, O lord. Without you, who is able to destroy our sorrow, O Maheśvara?
m.2.3.24.5: Brahmā said: Having heard these words of the gods, Nandikeśvara, filled with supreme compassion, began to petition Śambhu.
m.2.3.24.6: Nandīśvara said: The hosts of gods headed by Viṣṇu and the assemblies of sages and Siddhas are especially eager just to see you, O best of gods. Seeking the fulfilment of their purpose, being harassed by the chief Asuras, they have fallen utterly into the deepest state of defeat.
m.2.3.24.7: Therefore, O lord of all, the sages and gods must indeed be protected by you. You are especially called the friend of the distressed and the one affectionate to devotees.
m.2.3.24.8: Brahmā said: Thus earnestly petitioned by the compassionate Nandin, Śambhu slowly withdrew from meditation, opening his eyes.
m.2.3.24.9: Then the Lord Śambhu, supremely wise, the Supreme Self, having withdrawn from samādhi, spoke to all the gods.
m.2.3.24.10: Śambhu said: Why have you come to my presence, O lords of gods, all of you headed by Hari and Brahmā? Tell me that reason quickly.
m.2.3.24.11: Brahmā said: Hearing these words of Śambhu, all the gods, filled with joy, looked at Viṣṇu's face so that he would make the petition.
m.2.3.24.12: Then Viṣṇu, the great devotee, the benefactor of the gods, spoke this most important task of the gods, as had been told to him by me.
m.2.3.24.13: O Śambhu, Tāraka has inflicted on the gods a most extraordinary distress, worse than the worst; all the gods have come to make this known.
m.2.3.24.14: O Śambhu, the demon Tāraka will be slain only by your own begotten son; my words are not otherwise.
m.2.3.24.15: Considering this, O Mahādeva, show mercy; obeisance to you. O master, rescue the gods from the distress caused by Tāraka.
m.2.3.24.16: Therefore, O god Śambhu, Girijā must be taken by you with your right hand. Through the very rite of taking her hand, make your own that noble one, given by the lord of mountains.
m.2.3.24.17: Hearing those words of Viṣṇu, Śiva, devoted to yoga, was pleased and spoke, showing all of them the good path.
m.2.3.24.18: Śiva said: When the goddess Girijā, beautiful in every way, is accepted by me, then all the lords of gods, the munis and the ṛṣis, then—
m.2.3.24.19: —will become full of desire and will not be capable on the supreme path. Through the marriage, that Durgā will bring Smara back to life.
m.2.3.24.20: Madana was burnt by me for the accomplishment of everyone's purpose, at Brahmā's word, O Viṣṇu; there should be no doubt about this.
m.2.3.24.21: Having thus reflected in your mind on the determination of what should and should not be done, you who are wise, O lord of gods, should not, together with all these, press me insistently.
m.2.3.24.22: With Kāma burnt by me, O Viṣṇu, a great task of the gods has been accomplished. Let all remain free of desire together with me—this is certain.
m.2.3.24.23: Just as I do, so you, all the gods, will effortlessly perform extremely difficult austerity, endowed with supreme self-control.
m.2.3.24.24: O gods, through that samādhi, without Madana, may you be endowed with supreme bliss and free from all perturbation.
m.2.3.24.25: O Vidhi, O Hari, O Mahendra, O sages and gods, let all that former event caused by Smara, which has been forgotten, be reflected upon.
m.2.3.24.26: O gods, by that very Madana, the great bowman, the meditation of all was forcibly destroyed in the past, O immortals.
m.2.3.24.27: Desire leads only to hell; from it anger arises. From anger comes delusion, and through delusion austerity is lost.
m.2.3.24.28: Desire and anger must be abandoned by you, the best of gods. And my word must be heeded by all of you, never otherwise.
m.2.3.24.29: Brahmā said: Having thus made them hear, the blessed Mahādeva, whose banner bears the bull, instructed the gods, Vidhi and Viṣṇu, and likewise the sages.
m.2.3.24.30: Śambhu became silent, resorting once more to meditation, and remained as before like a motionless pillar, surrounded by his gaṇas.
m.2.3.24.31: Śambhu contemplated his own Self by the Self within the Self alone—stainless, beyond appearance, changeless, free from affliction,
m.2.3.24.32: higher than the highest, eternal, free of possessiveness, unrestricted, beyond words, attributeless, attainable through knowledge, transcending the transcendent.
m.2.3.24.33: Thus contemplating his supreme nature, established in meditation, the creator of manifold beings became immersed in supreme bliss.
m.2.3.24.34: Seeing the lord of all established in meditation, all the heaven-dwellers, headed by Hari and Śakra, bowing down, spoke to Nandin.
m.2.3.24.35: The gods said: What shall we do now? Śambhu, detached, is established in meditation. You are Śaṅkara's friend, all-knowing, a pure servant.
m.2.3.24.36: By what means may Giriśa become pleased, O lord of gaṇas? Tell us that means; we have come to you for refuge.
m.2.3.24.37: Brahmā said: Thus petitioned then by the gods headed by Hari, O sage, Nandin, the gaṇa dear to Śambhu, replied to those gods.
m.2.3.24.38: Nandīśvara said: O Hari, O Vidhi, O Śakra, O immortals and sages, listen to my words, which will bring about Śiva's satisfaction.
m.2.3.24.39: If you are indeed insistent today on Śiva's taking a wife, then all of you, in utter humility, offer fine praise with reverence.
m.2.3.24.40: Mahādeva is won over by devotion, O gods, not by ordinary means. Through true devotion the Supreme Lord does even what ought not to be done.
m.2.3.24.41: So act, all you gods headed by Brahmā and Viṣṇu; otherwise go back by the way you came, without delay.
m.2.3.24.42: Brahmā said: Having heard his words, O sage, the gods headed by Viṣṇu, thinking, so be it, praised Śaṅkara with great delight.
m.2.3.24.43: O God of gods, Mahādeva, ocean of compassion, Lord, lift us out of great distress; protect us who have come to you for refuge.
m.2.3.24.44: Brahmā said: Thus, with very piteous words, the gods praised Śaṅkara; all of them wept aloud, their minds overwhelmed by love.
m.2.3.24.45: Hari, together with me, made an earnest petition with very humble words, remembering Śambhu in his mind, filled with supreme devotion.
m.2.3.24.46: Thus intensely praised by the gods, by Hari and by me, Śambhu, the Great Lord, out of affection for his devotees, came out of meditation.
m.2.3.24.47: Hara, very gracious at heart, gladdening Hari and the others, looking upon them with a compassionate glance, Śaṅkara, loving to his devotees, spoke.
m.2.3.24.48: Śaṅkara said: O Hari, O Vidhi, O gods headed by Śakra, all of you together — for what purpose have you come? Tell the truth before me.
m.2.3.24.49: Hari said: You are omniscient, O Maheśāna, the inner controller, lord of all. Do you not know what lies in our minds? Still, at your command, I shall speak.
m.2.3.24.50: Manifold suffering has arisen for all of us from the asura Tāraka, O Mṛḍa; it is for that reason that you have been propitiated by the gods.
m.2.3.24.51: That Śivā has been born from the mountain Himālaya for your sake. His death can come only from a son born of you in her, and not otherwise.
m.2.3.24.52: Since such a boon was given to that demon by Brahmā, he cannot die at anyone else's hands, and he oppresses the whole world.
m.2.3.24.53: At Nārada's instruction she is performing severe penance; by its fiery energy the entire three worlds, with all moving and unmoving beings, are pervaded.
m.2.3.24.54: Go, O Supreme Lord, to grant the boon to Śivā; destroy the gods' suffering, O master, and bring us happiness.
m.2.3.24.55: In the hearts of the gods and in mine there is great eagerness to behold your marriage, O Śaṅkara; therefore do what is fitting.
m.2.3.24.56: The occasion for the boon you granted to Rati has now swiftly arrived, O higher than the highest; make your promise fruitful.
m.2.3.24.57: Brahmā said: Having said this and bowed to him, Viṣṇu, the gods and the great sages, having praised him with various hymns, all stood before him.
m.2.3.24.58: Then Śaṅkara, who is subject to his devotees and guardian of the bounds of the Veda, having heard the gods' words, laughed and replied at once.
m.2.3.24.59: Śaṅkara said: O Hari, O Vidhi, O gods, all of you listen attentively. I shall speak what is fitting, in detail and with discernment.
m.2.3.24.60: Entering into marriage is surely not a fitting course for men; marriage, known as a great fetter, is a firm bondage.
m.2.3.24.61: There are many evil attachments in the world, and among them attachment to women is the greatest. One may be released from all bonds, but one is not freed from attachment to women.
m.2.3.24.62: Even one firmly bound with fetters of iron and wood is set free; but one tightly bound by the fetters of women and the like is never set free.
m.2.3.24.63: Sense-objects, which cause great bondage, keep on increasing; for one whose mind is overpowered by sense-objects, liberation is hard to attain even in a dream.
m.2.3.24.64: If a wise man desires happiness, he should duly renounce sense-objects. They call sense-objects poison-like, for by sense-objects one is destroyed.
m.2.3.24.65: A person falls in an instant merely through conversation with a sensualist. The teachers call sense-enjoyment an indravāruṇī (bitter colocynth) coated with sugar.
m.2.3.24.66: Although I know all this, and all knowledge in particular, nevertheless I shall make your request fruitful.
m.2.3.24.67: I am indeed dependent on my devotees; under their sway I do every deed. I am famed in the three worlds as one who does even what is not fitting.
m.2.3.24.68: The vow of Sudakṣiṇa, king and lord of Kāmarūpa, who had fallen into bondage, was made fruitful by me.
m.2.3.24.69: In the matter of Gautama's affliction I acted as Tryambaka, the bringer of happiness, and in particular I pronounced a curse on the wicked ones who had caused him that trouble.
m.2.3.24.70: Bearing the disposition of love for my devotees, I drank the poison for the sake of the gods; O gods, the gods' distress has always been removed by me with effort.
m.2.3.24.71: For my devotees' sake I have endured hardship many times with great effort; becoming Gṛhapati, I removed the sorrow of the sage Viśvānara.
m.2.3.24.72: What need of saying much, O Hari, O Vidhi? I speak the truth: you all truly know that this is my vow.
m.2.3.24.73: Whenever and wherever misfortune befalls my devotees, then I always remove it swiftly, at that very moment, completely.
m.2.3.24.74: I know the suffering that has arisen for all of you from Tāraka; I shall remove that suffering caused by the asura — truly, truly I say.
m.2.3.24.75: Although I have no desire whatever to marry, I shall marry Girijā for the purpose of begetting a son.
m.2.3.24.76: Go to your own homes, all you gods, free from fear. I shall accomplish your task; there is no need for any doubt in this.
m.2.3.24.77: Brahmā said: Having said this, Hara observed silence and became absorbed in samādhi; and all the gods headed by Viṣṇu went to their own abodes, O sage.
m.2.3.24.iti: Thus ends the twenty-fourth adhyāya, named The acceptance of marriage with Pārvatī, in the third khaṇḍa, the Pārvatī-khaṇḍa, of the second saṃhitā, the Rudra-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.2.3.25.1: Nārada said: When those gods, Brahmā, Viṣṇu and the rest, and all the sages had gone away gladly, what happened after that?
m.2.3.25.2: What did Śambhu do, dear father? After how long, and in what way, did he come to grant the boon? Tell me that and bring me joy.
m.2.3.25.3: Brahmā said: When those gods, Brahmā and the others, had gone to their own abodes, Bhava became absorbed in samādhi in order to test her penance thoroughly.
m.2.3.25.4: Making his own Self the object by the Self, he contemplated within his own Self that which is higher than the highest, self-abiding, free of māyā and unconstrained.
m.2.3.25.5: He, the blessed Lord bearing the bull-banner, who is himself that reality, whose ways are unknown, the source of all, is Hara, the supreme Lord.
m.2.3.25.6: Brahmā said: Then indeed, dear son, Girijā performed supreme penance; by that penance even Rudra came to great amazement.
m.2.3.25.7: He was stirred from his samādhi, being subject to his devotee, and not for any other reason. Hara, the creator, called to mind the seven sages, Vasiṣṭha and the rest.
m.2.3.25.8: All seven sages came at once, merely upon being remembered, all with cheerful faces, greatly extolling their good fortune.
m.2.3.25.9: Bowing to that great Lord, full of joy, they praised him with faltering voices, hands joined and necks bent low.
m.2.3.25.10: The seven sages said: O God of gods, Mahādeva, ocean of compassion, O Lord, we have become truly blessed, since you have now remembered us.
m.2.3.25.11: For what purpose have we been called to mind, O Lord? Give us that command. O master, show us grace befitting your own servants; salutation to you.
m.2.3.25.12: Brahmā said: Hearing this request of the sages, the treasury of compassion, his lotus-eyes blooming, spoke smiling with affection.
m.2.3.25.13: Maheśvara said: O seven sages, dear ones, listen promptly to my words. You are doers of my welfare, skilled in all knowledge.
m.2.3.25.14: Pārvatī Girijā, the queen of the gods, is now performing penance with a resolute mind on the mountain called Gaurīśikhara.
m.2.3.25.15: Wishing to obtain me as husband, she, attended by her friends, O brahmins, has abandoned all other desires and reached a supreme resolve.
m.2.3.25.16: Go there at my command, O best of sages, and test the firmness of her loving heart.
m.2.3.25.17: Your speech should be wholly full of deceit. Have no hesitation, O ones of good vows, since it is by my command.
m.2.3.25.18: Brahmā said: Thus commanded, those sages went swiftly to where the radiant Mother of the world, the mountain's daughter, was shining.
m.2.3.25.19: There they saw Śivā, like a second, embodied perfection of penance itself, of supreme brilliance, shining with great splendour.
m.2.3.25.20: Bowing to her in their hearts, those seven sages of good vows, humbly inclined and specially honoured by her, spoke these words.
m.2.3.25.21: The sages said: Listen, O goddess, daughter of the mountain: why is this penance being performed? Which god do you desire, and what is the fruit? Tell us that now.
m.2.3.25.22: Brahmā said: Thus addressed by the brahmins, the goddess Śivā, daughter of the lord of mountains, replied truthfully before them, though the matter was a deep secret.
m.2.3.25.23: Pārvatī said: O lords of sages, listen with an affectionate heart to my words. I shall tell you my own resolve, which I have pondered with my own mind.
m.2.3.25.24: You will laugh at me on hearing words about something impossible. O brahmins, I feel shy about describing it; but what can I do?
m.2.3.25.25: This mind of mine is very firm, yet beyond control, doing others' bidding; it wishes to build a great, towering wall upon water.
m.2.3.25.26: Having received the instruction of the divine sage, I perform very firm penance, cherishing the wish that Rudra may become my husband.
m.2.3.25.27: The bird of my mind, though wingless, insists on flying up into the sky. May Lord Śaṅkara, treasury of compassion, fulfil that hope.
m.2.3.25.28: Brahmā said: Hearing her words, those sages laughed, and, honouring Girijā affectionately, spoke false words full of deceit.
m.2.3.25.29: The sages said: O daughter of the mountain, though you are very wise, you have not understood the conduct of that divine sage, cruel-minded and falsely proud of his learning.
m.2.3.25.30: Nārada is a deceitful talker who churns up others' minds; by listening to his words harm comes in every way.
m.2.3.25.31: In this regard, listen with a good mind to a fine story; as we instruct you step by step with affection, take it to heart.
m.2.3.25.32: Dakṣa, the son of Brahmā, at his father's command begot ten thousand sons on his own wife and set those dear sons to penance.
m.2.3.25.33: Those sons went to Nārāyaṇa-saras in the western direction, having vowed themselves to penance; Nārada went there too.
m.2.3.25.34: There the sage Nārada made them hear a deceptive teaching, and by his direction all of them did not return to their father's house.
m.2.3.25.35: Hearing that, Dakṣa was enraged; his mind consoled by his father, he then begot sons numbering a thousand and engaged them likewise.
m.2.3.25.36: Those sons too went there for penance at their father's command; and Nārada went there again, to give his own teaching.
m.2.3.25.37: He gave them that same teaching; they went the way of their brothers, did not return to their father's house, and became devoted to the mendicant's life.
m.2.3.25.38: Such is Nārada's famous good conduct, O daughter of the mountain. Hear another deed of his, which makes men turn away from the world.
m.2.3.25.39: There was a Vidyādhara named Citraketu; formerly Nārada, having given him his own kind of teaching, made his house empty.
m.2.3.25.40: Having given his teachings to Prahlāda, this splitter of others' minds also brought great grief to Hiraṇyakaśipu.
m.2.3.25.41: Whoever is made by that sage Nārada to hear his own lore, so pleasing to the ear, quickly leaves his home and, as a rule, wanders about begging.
m.2.3.25.42: Nārada is indeed dark of mind, though always bright of body. We know him especially well, since we are his companions.
m.2.3.25.43: People describe the heron as a saint, as though it never eats fish at all; but a companion knows the character of his companions.
m.2.3.25.44: Having received his instruction, you too, though esteemed by the wise, have become foolish for nothing and are performing austerity that is hard to do.
m.2.3.25.45: He for whose sake, O girl, you perform such vast austerity is indifferent, unchanging, the enemy of Madana — there is no doubt.
m.2.3.25.46: He bears an inauspicious body, is shameless, homeless, without lineage, ill-dressed, keeps company with ghosts, spirits and the like, is naked, and carries a trident.
m.2.3.25.47: That rogue, having destroyed your discernment by his own māyā, deluded you with clever reasoning and made you perform austerity.
m.2.3.25.48: Having obtained such a husband, what happiness will there be? Consider this yourself, O goddess, O daughter of the mountain.
m.2.3.25.49: First, having married with good intent the virtuous Satī, Dakṣa's daughter, the fool did not keep up the marriage for even a few days.
m.2.3.25.50: Likewise, that lord himself, laying blame on her, abandoned her, and meditating on his own partless, sorrowless nature, he rejoiced, content.
m.2.3.25.51: He is solitary, supremely at rest, unattached and non-dual; how, O goddess, will a woman's life with him be sustained?
m.2.3.25.52: Even now, accepting our counsel, come home and give up this wrong resolve, O fortunate one, and there will be well-being for you.
m.2.3.25.53: The husband worthy of you is Viṣṇu, the lord endowed with every good quality, dweller in Vaikuṇṭha, lord of Lakṣmī, skilled in many kinds of play.
m.2.3.25.54: We will arrange your marriage with him, which will give every happiness. So give up such obstinacy and be happy, O Pārvatī.
m.2.3.25.55: Brahmā said: Hearing such words, Pārvatī, the Mother of the world, laughed and spoke again to the sages learned in knowledge.
m.2.3.25.56: Pārvatī said: What you have said from your own knowledge is true, O lords of sages; but my resolve is not given up, O twice-born.
m.2.3.25.57: Because my body is born of a mountain, hardness is natural to it. Considering this wisely, you ought not to dissuade me.
m.2.3.25.58: I shall never abandon the wholesome words of the divine sage; the knowers of the Veda know that the words of gurus are wholesome.
m.2.3.25.59: Those whose conviction is firm that the gurus' words are true have supreme happiness here and hereafter, and never unhappiness anywhere.
m.2.3.25.60: Those in whose heart there is no conviction that the gurus' words are true have sorrow both here and hereafter, and never happiness.
m.2.3.25.61: In no way should the gurus' words be abandoned, O twice-born. Whether I come to dwell in a home or it remains empty, my resolve is always a source of joy to me.
m.2.3.25.62: The words you have so well spoken, O best of sages, are otherwise in truth; I shall describe the discernment of it briefly.
m.2.3.25.63: Viṣṇu is indeed proclaimed the abode of qualities and one given to play; Sadāśiva is declared to be beyond qualities. The reason for this is now told.
m.2.3.25.64: Śiva is the changeless Brahman; he has assumed a form for the sake of his devotees, and he does not wish to display worldly lordship.
m.2.3.25.65: Therefore Śambhu, who is supreme bliss, takes on, in the form of an avadhūta, the way of life most dear to the paramahaṃsas.
m.2.3.25.66: A liking for ornaments and the like belongs to those smeared with māyā, not to Brahman. That lord is beyond qualities, unborn, free of māyā, of imperceptible course, the cosmic being (virāṭ).
m.2.3.25.67: Śambhu does not bestow grace on the basis of dharma, caste and the like, O twice-born. Only by my guru's grace do I know Śiva as he truly is.
m.2.3.25.68: If that Śiva will not marry me, O brahmins, I shall remain unmarried forever. Truly, truly I say this.
m.2.3.25.69: Even if the sun should rise in the western quarter, if Meru should move, if fire should turn cold, if a lotus should bloom on a rock on a mountain peak — my resolve will not waver. This truth I declare.
m.2.3.25.70: Brahmā said: Having said this and quickly bowed to those sages, the daughter of the mountain fell silent, remembering Śiva with an unwavering mind.
m.2.3.25.71: The sages too, thus recognising Girijā's firm resolve, uttered words of victory there and gave her an excellent blessing.
m.2.3.25.72: Then, bowing to that goddess, the sages who had tested her, glad at heart, went swiftly to Śiva's abode, O sage.
m.2.3.25.73: Having gone there, bowed to Śiva and reported that whole account, they received his leave and went respectfully to heaven.
m.2.3.25.iti: Thus ends the twenty-fifth adhyāya, named The description of the test made by the seven sages, in the third khaṇḍa, the Pārvatī-khaṇḍa, of the second saṃhitā, the Rudra-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.2.3.26.1: Brahmā said: When those sages had gone to their own world, Śaṅkara himself, the Lord and creator, wished to test the Devī's penance.
m.2.3.26.2: On the pretext of a test, Śambhu, pleased at heart, wishing to see her, assumed the form of a matted-haired ascetic and went to Pārvatī's forest.
m.2.3.26.3: Very aged, bearing the body of a brahmin, blazing with his own splendour, delighted in mind, he became one carrying a staff and an umbrella.
m.2.3.26.4: There he saw the Devī seated on a raised altar, surrounded by her friends, pure, like an auspicious digit of the moon.
m.2.3.26.5: Having beheld that Devī, Śambhu, in the form of a celibate student, the one affectionate to his devotees, then went near her with love.
m.2.3.26.6: Seeing that brahmin arrived then, wondrous in his radiance, the Devī Śivā worshipped him with all the offerings of worship.
m.2.3.26.7: The brahmin, well honoured with due rites and worshipped with supreme joy, Pārvatī respectfully and lovingly asked about his welfare.
m.2.3.26.8: Pārvatī said: Who are you, in the form of a celibate student, and from where have you come? You illumine this forest. Tell me, O best of the knowers of the Veda.
m.2.3.26.9: The brahmin said: I am one who goes wherever he wishes, an old man in a brahmin's body, wise, an ascetic, a giver of happiness to others and a benefactor—there is no doubt.
m.2.3.26.10: Who are you? Whose daughter are you? For what purpose do you practise, in this lonely forest, a penance hard to sustain even for eminent sages?
m.2.3.26.11: You are neither a child nor old; you shine as a beautiful young woman. How is it that you practise severe penance in the forest without a husband?
m.2.3.26.12: Are you, good lady, an ascetic woman, the companion of some ascetic? Does that ascetic not support you, O Devī, and has he gone elsewhere?
m.2.3.26.13: Tell me, in whose family were you born? Who is your father, what is your name? You are the very form of great good fortune; your fondness for penance is pointless.
m.2.3.26.14: Are you the mother of the Vedas Gāyatrī, or Lakṣmī, or the lovely Sarasvatī? Which among these are you? I cannot guess.
m.2.3.26.15: Pārvatī said: I am not the mother of the Vedas, O brahmin, nor Lakṣmī, nor Sarasvatī. I am the daughter of Himācala, now named Pārvatī.
m.2.3.26.16: Formerly, in another birth, I was born as Dakṣa's daughter named Satī; I abandoned my body through yoga because my husband was reviled by my father.
m.2.3.26.17: In this birth Śiva too was attained through the power of destiny, but having burnt Manmatha to ashes he abandoned me and went away.
m.2.3.26.18: When Śaṅkara had departed, distressed by grief I came from my father's house for penance, O brahmin, firmly resolved, to the bank of the Gaṅgā.
m.2.3.26.19: Having performed severe penance for a very long time and not having obtained the beloved of my life, I was about to enter the fire; seeing you, I stopped for a moment.
m.2.3.26.20: Go now; I enter the fire, since I have not been accepted by Śiva. Wherever I take birth, I shall choose Śiva as my bridegroom.
m.2.3.26.21: Brahmā said: Having said this, Pārvatī entered the fire before him, though she was forbidden again and again by the brahmin in front of her.
m.2.3.26.22: As Pārvatī entered the fire, through her power the fire at that very instant became like sandal paste.
m.2.3.26.23: After staying within it for a moment, as the fair-bodied one was rising up toward heaven, Śiva in the brahmin's form, laughing, suddenly questioned her again.
m.2.3.26.24: The brahmin said: Ah, what is this penance of yours, good lady? Nothing at all is understood: your body was not burnt by the fire, nor has your wish been attained.
m.2.3.26.25: Therefore, O Devī, tell me truly and fully your heart's wish, before me, the best of brahmins, the giver of all joy.
m.2.3.26.26: Let it be declared by you, O Devī, properly and wholeheartedly. Friendship has arisen between us; so nothing should be concealed by you.
m.2.3.26.27: What boon do you desire, O Devī? This above all I wish to ask. For in you alone, O Devī, all fulfilment is seen.
m.2.3.26.28: And if the penance is for some other aim, it would remain mere penance; it is as if, having taken a jewel in the hand, one has thrown it away and gathered glass.
m.2.3.26.29: How have you made such beauty of yours worthless? Abandoning many garments, you have put on hides and the like.
m.2.3.26.30: Tell me truly the whole reason for this penance, so that hearing it I, the best of brahmins, may attain joy.
m.2.3.26.31: Brahmā said: Thus questioned by him, Ambikā, firm in her vows, urged her friend, and through her mouth alone had everything told.
m.2.3.26.32: Urged there by Pārvatī, her friend named Vijayā, dear as life and knowing her firm vow, spoke to the matted-haired ascetic.
m.2.3.26.33: The friend said: Listen, O good man; I shall tell you Pārvatī's excellent story and the whole reason for her penance, if you wish to hear it.
m.2.3.26.34: This friend of mine is the daughter of the king of mountains, Himālaya; she is well known by the name Pārvatī, and her mother is Menakā.
m.2.3.26.35: She has not been married by anyone, and she desires no one other than Śiva. For three thousand years she has been engaged in the practice of penance.
m.2.3.26.36: For that purpose this friend of mine has undertaken such penance. I shall tell you the reason for it here; listen, O good man, best of brahmins.
m.2.3.26.37: Passing over the gods headed by Indra, as well as Hari and Brahmā, Pārvatī wishes to obtain the Pināka-bearer as her husband.
m.2.3.26.38: This friend of mine formerly planted trees; on all of them fruits, flowers and the like have appeared, O brahmin.
m.2.3.26.39: To make her beauty fruitful, to adorn her father's family, and aiming at Maheśāna, also for the sake of favour to Kāma—
m.2.3.26.40: —my friend, on Nārada's instruction, performs terrible penance. How could her heart's wish fail to bear fruit, O ascetic?
m.2.3.26.41: O best of the twice-born, what you asked my friend about, the wish in her heart, I have told you out of affection. What else do you wish to hear?
m.2.3.26.42: Brahmā said: O sage, having heard these words of Vijayā spoken truthfully, that matted-haired ascetic, Rudra, laughing, spoke these words.
m.2.3.26.43: The matted-haired ascetic said: This was told by her friend; in that a jest is suspected. If it is true, then let the goddess speak with her own mouth.
m.2.3.26.44: Brahmā said: When this had been said then by that matted-haired twice-born, the goddess Pārvatī spoke to that brahmin with her own mouth.
m.2.3.26.iti: Thus ends the twenty-sixth adhyāya, named The dialogue of Śivā and the ascetic with matted hair, in the third khaṇḍa, the Pārvatī-khaṇḍa, of the second saṃhitā, the Rudra-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.2.3.27.1: Pārvatī said: Listen, O best of brāhmaṇas, O matted-haired one, to my whole story. What my friend told you today is true; it is exactly so and not otherwise.
m.2.3.27.2: In mind, in word and directly in deed I have chosen Śaṅkara as my husband. I speak the truth, not falsehood.
m.2.3.27.3: I know it is a thing hard to obtain; how could it be gained by me? Even so, out of my mind's longing, I am practising austerity today.
m.2.3.27.4: Brahmā said: Having spoken these words to him, Girijā then remained silent. Hearing Pārvatī's words, the brāhmaṇa spoke there.
m.2.3.27.5: The brahmin said: Until now I had a great desire to know: what thing does the goddess long for, that she performs such very great austerity?
m.2.3.27.6: Now that I have learned it all, O goddess, hearing it from your lotus-mouth, I shall go from this place. Do as you wish.
m.2.3.27.7: If you do not tell me, our friendship would be fruitless. As the matter is, so it will turn out; it should be told freely.
m.2.3.27.8: Brahmā said: Having spoken these words, just as he wished to leave, the goddess Pārvatī bowed and spoke to that brāhmaṇa.
m.2.3.27.9: Pārvatī said: Why will you go, O chief of brāhmaṇas? Stay, and tell me what is beneficial. When she had said this, the staff-bearer stayed and spoke.
m.2.3.27.10: The brahmin said: If, O goddess, wishing to listen, you keep me here out of devotion, I shall tell you the whole truth, by which you will gain understanding.
m.2.3.27.11: I know Mahādeva thoroughly, through the tradition of my teacher. I shall tell you exactly as it is; listen attentively.
m.2.3.27.12: Mahādeva has the bull on his banner, is smeared with ash, wears matted locks, is clad in a tiger-skin garment and wrapped in an elephant's hide.
m.2.3.27.13: He carries a skull, is coiled about all his limbs with masses of serpents, is smeared with poison, eats what is not to be eaten, has odd eyes and is very terrifying.
m.2.3.27.14: His birth is unknown; he is ever without home and pleasures; he is sky-clad, ten-armed, and always accompanied by ghosts and spirits.
m.2.3.27.15: For what reason do you desire him as husband? Where has your good sense gone, O goddess? Think it over and tell me now.
m.2.3.27.16: I have heard before of his dreadful vow. Listen, I shall tell it to you now, if you have a taste for hearing it.
m.2.3.27.17: Long ago, by fate, the chaste Satī, Dakṣa's daughter, chose the bull-rider as husband; the outcome of her union with him is well known.
m.2.3.27.18: Satī was shunned by Dakṣa as the wife of the skull-bearer, and Śambhu too was excluded from receiving a share at the sacrifice.
m.2.3.27.19: Through that very insult Satī, greatly agitated with anger, gave up her dear life there, and Śaṅkara was abandoned by her.
m.2.3.27.20: You are a jewel among women; your father is king of all mountains. Why do you seek such a husband with fierce austerity?
m.2.3.27.21: Giving away a gold coin, you wish to take glass; abandoning bright sandal-paste, you wish to smear yourself with mud.
m.2.3.27.22: Forsaking the sun's brilliance, you want the glow of a firefly; giving up fine silk, you want here a garment of hide.
m.2.3.27.23: Abandoning life at home, you seek life in the forest; casting away the finest treasure, O queen of gods, you want iron.
m.2.3.27.24: Leaving aside Indra and the other world-guardians, you are devoted to Śiva. This is not well done; it appears now contrary to custom in the worlds.
m.2.3.27.25: Where are you, with eyes like lotus petals, and where is he, the three-eyed one? You have a face like the moon, while Śiva is said to be five-faced.
m.2.3.27.26: On your head is a divine braid, shining like a she-serpent; Śiva's, they say, is the well-known mass of matted locks.
m.2.3.27.27: Sandal-paste is on your limbs, and pyre-ash on Śiva's. Where is your fine silk, and where Śaṅkara's elephant hide?
m.2.3.27.28: Where are your divine ornaments, and where Śaṅkara's serpents? Where all the attendant deities around you, and where he who delights in offerings to ghosts?
m.2.3.27.29: Where the playing of the mṛdaṅga, and where that ḍamaru of his? Where the array of kettledrums, and where the inauspicious sound of the horn?
m.2.3.27.30: Where the sound made by the ḍhakkā drum, and where the inauspicious throat-noise? Your excellent beauty and Śiva's are not a fit match.
m.2.3.27.31: If he had wealth, how would he be naked? His vehicle is a bull; he has no possessions at all.
m.2.3.27.32: Of the qualities declared in bridegrooms that bring women happiness, not even one is found in Virūpākṣa.
m.2.3.27.33: Even Kāma, dear to you, was burnt by that Hara; and then his disregard for you was seen, when he left you and went elsewhere.
m.2.3.27.34: No lineage of his is to be seen, nor likewise learning or knowledge; his companions are goblins, and poison is seen in his throat.
m.2.3.27.35: He is always alone, and above all detached. So is it really fitting for you to join your mind to Hara alone?
m.2.3.27.36: Where is your necklace, and where his garland of skulls? Where your divine cosmetic, and where the pyre-ash on his body?
m.2.3.27.37: Everything, form and the rest, is at odds between you and Hara, O goddess. This does not please me; do as you wish.
m.2.3.27.38: Whatever is worthless, all that you yourself are seeking. Turn your mind away from it; if not, do as you wish.
m.2.3.27.39: Brahmā said: Hearing such words of that brāhmaṇa, Pārvatī, with an angry mind, spoke to the twice-born who was bent on reviling Śiva.
m.2.3.27.iti: Thus ends the twenty-seventh adhyāya, named The description of the deceiving words of the brahmacārin, in the third khaṇḍa, the Pārvatī-khaṇḍa, of the second saṃhitā, the Rudra-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.2.3.28.1: Pārvatī said: This much I had indeed understood: that this one who came was someone else. Now everything is understood. You, above all, are not to be slain.
m.2.3.28.2: What you have said, O lord, is understood: it is false and nothing else. Had it truly been spoken by you, you would not say what is self-contradictory.
m.2.3.28.3: At times Maheśvara is seen wearing such a guise—the supreme Brahman who, in his own play, has taken on a body by his own will.
m.2.3.28.4: Intent on deceiving me in the form of a brahmacārin, you came and, with crooked reasoning, spoke words full of trickery.
m.2.3.28.5: But I know Śaṅkara's true nature very particularly; therefore, having reflected well, I shall speak of the truth of Śiva as is fitting.
m.2.3.28.6: In reality he is Brahman without attributes; he has attributes only for a purpose. How could there be a birth-lineage for him, who is attributeless yet the very self of the attributes?
m.2.3.28.7: That Sadāśiva is the very ground of all branches of knowledge; what need has he, the complete supreme Self, of learning?
m.2.3.28.8: Long ago, at the beginning of the kalpa, the Vedas were given to Viṣṇu by that Śambhu in the form of his breath. Who is so great a lord as to equal him?
m.2.3.28.9: How then can there be a measure of age for him who is the origin of all? Prakṛti was born from him; what other source could there be of his power?
m.2.3.28.10: Those who always worship with love that Śaṅkara, lord of Śakti—to such a one Śambhu grants the threefold power, ever imperishable.
m.2.3.28.11: By worshipping him alone the soul, free of fear, conquers death; hence his name Mṛtyuñjaya is famed in the three worlds.
m.2.3.28.12: By his favour alone Viṣṇu attains Viṣṇu-hood, Brahmā Brahmā-hood, and the gods their godhood.
m.2.3.28.13: When the king of the gods first goes to have sight of Śiva, he meets Bhūta and the others, the doorkeepers of Śiva, who are devoted to him;
m.2.3.28.14: his crown is struck by their staffs and battered all over. What need has he of many partisans? He himself is the great lord.
m.2.3.28.15: What would not come about here through service to him whose form is auspiciousness? What does that god lack, that Sadāśiva should desire me?
m.2.3.28.16: Even one who has been poor for seven births—if he serves Śaṅkara, by that service of his, prosperity (Lakṣmī) in the world becomes unfailing for him.
m.2.3.28.17: Before him the eight siddhis constantly dance to please him, ever with downcast faces; how then could any good be hard to obtain from him?
m.2.3.28.18: Even if auspicious things here do not attend upon Śaṅkara, still auspiciousness arises merely by remembering him.
m.2.3.28.19: He by the power of whose worship all desires are fulfilled in every way—how could there be any change in him, who is ever changeless?
m.2.3.28.20: In whose mouth the auspicious name Śiva is constantly present—by the mere sight of him others are always purified.
m.2.3.28.21: If the ash from the funeral pyre were impure, as you have said, how is it that, clinging always to his body, it is borne by the gods on their heads?
m.2.3.28.22: The god who is creator, sustainer and destroyer of the worlds, possessed of attributes, and also attributeless, called Śiva—how could he be known?
m.2.3.28.23: The attributeless form of Brahman, of Śiva the supreme Self—how could those like you, who are turned away from it, know it?
m.2.3.28.24: Those of evil conduct and sinful, who have strayed outside the Vedas, do not at all know the truth of Śiva whose form is beyond attributes.
m.2.3.28.25: The man who here reviles Śiva without knowing the truth—the merit he has gathered since birth is turned to ash.
m.2.3.28.26: Since you have here reviled Hara of boundless splendour, and I have worshipped you, I therefore incur sin.
m.2.3.28.27: On seeing a hater of Śiva, one should bathe with one's clothes on; on seeing a hater of Śiva, one should perform expiation.
m.2.3.28.28: O you wicked one, you said: I know Śaṅkara. But certainly the eternal Śiva has not been known by you.
m.2.3.28.29: Whatever Rudra may be like, or however many forms he may have, he is ever most dear to me—changeless, beloved of the good.
m.2.3.28.30: Not even Viṣṇu or Brahmā is in any way equal to that great-souled one; how then the other gods and the rest, who are always subject to time?
m.2.3.28.31: Having considered this truly with my own sound understanding, I have come to the forest for Śiva's sake and perform great austerity.
m.2.3.28.32: My longing is indeed to attain him alone—the supreme lord, lord of all, loving to his devotees, bestower of grace on the lowly.
m.2.3.28.33: Brahmā said: Having spoken thus, O sage, Girijā, daughter of the lord of mountains, fell silent and meditated on Śiva with an unwavering mind.
m.2.3.28.34: Hearing the goddess's words, that brahmin brahmacārin was just beginning to speak again,
m.2.3.28.35: when Girijā, her mind wholly attached to Śiva and averse to the reviling of Śiva, quickly said to her friend Vijayā:
m.2.3.28.36: Girijā said: Friend, this vilest of brahmins must be stopped with effort; he intends to speak again and will revile Śiva.
m.2.3.28.37: Sin falls not only on the one who reviles Śiva; whoever listens to that reviling also becomes a sharer in sin here.
m.2.3.28.38: A reviler of Śiva is by all means to be slain by Śiva's servants; if he is a brahmin, he is to be shunned, and one should quickly leave that place.
m.2.3.28.39: This wicked one will revile Śiva again. If, being a brahmin, he cannot be slain, he must be shunned and not looked upon at all.
m.2.3.28.40: Leaving this place this very day, we shall go elsewhere without delay, so that there may be no further conversation with this ignorant one.
m.2.3.28.41: Brahmā said: Having said this, O sage, the moment Umā lifted her foot to leave, at that very moment Śiva himself, in person, took hold of his beloved.
