m.2.5.14.36: Then there was a great festival at their wedding; the male and female rivers and all the asuras attained happiness, O sage.
m.2.5.14.37: The Ocean was exceedingly happy on seeing his son with a wife, and gave gifts according to rule to the twice-born and to others too.
m.2.5.14.38: The Daityas who had earlier been defeated by the gods and dwelt in Pātāla came to the earth, fearless, taking refuge in him.
m.2.5.14.39: Then those asuras headed by Kālanemi, having given the daughter to that son of the Ocean, became exceedingly joyful, relying on him for the conquest of the gods.
m.2.5.14.40: And that hero too, the child of the ocean, named Jalandhara, the mightiest hero among the heroic asuras, having obtained an exceedingly beautiful wife, and being self-controlled, ruled the kingdom through the power of Kavi Śukra.
m.2.5.14.iti: Thus ends the fourteenth adhyāya, named The description of the birth and marriage of Jalandhara, in the account of the slaying of Jalandhara, in the fifth khaṇḍa, the Yuddha-khaṇḍa, of the second saṃhitā, the Rudra-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.2.5.15.1: Sanatkumāra said: Once the son of the ocean, the lord of Vṛndā, noble-minded and heroic, was seated with his wife, accompanied by all the Asuras.
m.2.5.15.2: Then Bhārgava Śukra, very pleased and radiant, came there, like a mass of splendour in bodily form, illuminating all the directions.
m.2.5.15.3: Seeing their preceptor coming, all those Asuras quickly bowed with joyful minds; the son of the ocean too bowed respectfully.
m.2.5.15.4: Having given them words of blessing, Bhārgava, the treasure of splendour, sat on a beautiful seat; they too remained seated as before.
m.2.5.15.5: Then the heroic son of the ocean, Jalandhara, whose excellent command was never thwarted, seeing his own assembly with affection, became delighted.
m.2.5.15.6: Seeing Rāhu present there with his head severed, that king of the Daityas, the son of the ocean, quickly asked Bhārgava this:
m.2.5.15.7: Jalandhara said: By whom was this beheading of Rāhu done, O lord? Tell me the whole event exactly and truly, O preceptor.
m.2.5.15.8: Sanatkumāra said: Hearing these words of the son of the ocean, Bhārgava, remembering the lotus-feet of Śiva, replied truthfully.
m.2.5.15.9: Śukra said: O Jalandhara, great hero, helper of all the Asuras, listen: I shall tell you the whole story exactly.
m.2.5.15.10: Formerly there was the heroic and mighty Bali, son of Virocana and great-grandson of Hiraṇyakaśipu, O best of the knowers of dharma.
m.2.5.15.11: Defeated by him, the gods together with Vāsava Indra went for refuge to the lord of Ramā Viṣṇu, and, seeking their own ends, related their plight.
m.2.5.15.12: Then, at his command, the gods, skilled in deceitful deeds, made a truce with the Asuras to accomplish their own purpose, dear one.
m.2.5.15.13: Then, for the sake of nectar, all those gods, with Viṣṇu as their helper, zealously churned the ocean together with the Asuras.
m.2.5.15.14: Then the enemies of the Daityas carried off the jewels; the gods took them with effort and also drank the nectar by deceit.
m.2.5.15.15: Then, with Viṣṇu's help, those gods with Śakra, strengthened by drinking the nectar, defeated the Asuras.
m.2.5.15.16: In the assembly of the gods, Hari, always partial to Hari Indra, cut off the head of Rāhu as he was drinking the nectar.
m.2.5.15.17: Sanatkumāra said: Thus Kavi Śukra narrated to him the beheading of Rāhu and the churning of the ocean for nectar caused by the gods,
m.2.5.15.18: and the seizure of the jewels, the defeat of the Daityas, and the drinking of nectar by the gods — all this in detail.
m.2.5.15.19: Hearing that — the churning of his own father — the mighty great hero, the child of the ocean, then became furious, his eyes red with anger.
m.2.5.15.20: Then, summoning his excellent messenger named Ghasmara, he told him the whole story that the self-possessed preceptor had related.
m.2.5.15.21: Then, honouring him greatly with affection and granting him safety, he sent that skilful messenger of his to the presence of Śakra.
m.2.5.15.22: The wise Ghasmara, messenger of the ocean's child, went swiftly to Triviṣṭapa heaven, filled with all the gods.
m.2.5.15.23: Having gone there and quickly reached the hall Sudharmā, that messenger, holding his head high out of pride, spoke these words to the lord of the gods.
m.2.5.15.24: Ghasmara said: Jalandhara, son of the ocean, lord of all the Daitya folk, very valorous, a great hero, himself has Kavi Śukra as his helper.
m.2.5.15.25: I am the messenger of that hero, named Ghasmara, yet not a devourer; sent by that hero, I have come here into your presence.
m.2.5.15.26: Jalandhara, of lofty intellect, whose command is unobstructed everywhere, who has conquered all the enemies of the Daityas — hear what he has said.
m.2.5.15.27: Jalandhara said: Why was my father, the ocean, churned by you with a mountain? And all my father's jewels carried off, O vilest of gods?
m.2.5.15.28: What you did was not proper; give them back to me quickly today. Reflecting thus, come to me for refuge together with the gods.
m.2.5.15.29: Otherwise, O vilest of gods, great danger will befall you, and the destruction of your kingdom too — this I tell you truly.
m.2.5.15.30: Sanatkumāra said: Hearing these words of the messenger, Indra, lord of the thirty gods, astonished, filled with fear and anger, recalling the past, spoke to him.
m.2.5.15.31: Because the mountains, terrified out of fear of me, were given shelter in his own belly, and other Daityas, my enemies, were also protected by him in the past —
m.2.5.15.32: therefore I indeed took away all his collection of jewels. No one hostile to me remains at ease — I speak the truth.
m.2.5.15.33: Likewise, formerly the Daitya Śaṅkha, a son of the ocean, hating me, became deluded in mind, having abandoned the company of the good.
m.2.5.15.34: That evil-minded, most sinful one, a tormentor of the community of the good, was slain within the ocean by my younger brother Hari.
m.2.5.15.35: So go quickly, messenger, and tell this son of the ocean truly the whole reason for the churning of the ocean.
m.2.5.15.36: Sanatkumāra said: Thus dismissed by Indra, the very intelligent messenger named Ghasmara then went swiftly to where the hero Jalandhara was.
m.2.5.15.37: Then the king of the Daityas was told by that wise messenger all these words spoken by Śakra.
m.2.5.15.38: Hearing that, the Daitya, his lip trembling with rage, swiftly made preparations, desiring to conquer all the gods.
m.2.5.15.39: Then, at the war-preparation of the lord of Asuras, the sons of Diti arrived from all directions and likewise from Pātāla, by crores upon crores.
m.2.5.15.40: Then the mighty great hero, the son of the ocean, set out with Śumbha, Niśumbha and others, and with crores of army commanders.
m.2.5.15.41: Surrounded by his whole army, he at once reached Triviṣṭapa heaven. The ocean-born one blew his conch, and the warriors roared on every side.
m.2.5.15.42: Having gone to heaven, the Daitya stationed himself in the garden Nandana, surrounding it with his whole army and roaring like a lion.
m.2.5.15.43: Seeing that great host of troops standing and besieging the city, the gods, clad in armour, sallied out of Amarāvatī to fight.
m.2.5.15.44: Then battle broke out between the armies of the gods and the Dānavas, with pestles, iron clubs, arrows, maces, axes and spears.
m.2.5.15.45: The two armies rushed at each other and struck one another; in a moment both armies were drenched in floods of blood.
m.2.5.15.46: With elephants, horses, chariots and foot-soldiers fallen and falling, the ground in battle shone as if covered with banks of twilight clouds.
m.2.5.15.47: There in the battle Bhārgava Śukra revived those Daityas who had died, by means of the lore that revives the dead, with drops of water charged with mantras.
m.2.5.15.48: Likewise, in that battle Aṅgiras (Bṛhaspati) revived the gods again and again, bringing divine herbs from Mount Droṇa.
m.2.5.15.49: Seeing them thus risen up again in the battle, Jalandhara, overcome by anger, spoke these words to Bhārgava.
m.2.5.15.50: Jalandhara said: The gods were slain by me in battle—how do they rise again? The reviving lore is known to be with you alone and nowhere else.
m.2.5.15.51: Sanatkumāra said: Hearing these words of the son of the Ocean, Bhārgava—the preceptor Śukra—replied to Jalandhara with a pleased mind.
m.2.5.15.52: Śukra said: Bringing divine herbs from Mount Droṇa, this Aṅgiras revives the gods, dear son; know my word to be true.
m.2.5.15.53: If you desire victory, dear son, hear my auspicious counsel: then quickly carry that Droṇa with your two arms and cast it into the ocean.
m.2.5.15.54: Sanatkumāra said: Thus addressed by the preceptor Bhārgava, that lord of the Daityas went swiftly to where that king of mountains stood.
m.2.5.15.55: Then the Daitya forcefully lifted that Droṇa with his two arms and swiftly hurled it into the ocean—no wonder in one born of Hara's energy.
m.2.5.15.56: The great hero, son of the Ocean, came back to the great battle and, exerting great might, struck down the gods with various weapons.
m.2.5.15.57: Then, seeing the gods slain, the preceptor, honoured by the gods, went to Mount Droṇa; but there he did not see that lord of mountains.
m.2.5.15.58: Knowing that Droṇa had been carried off by the Daitya, Dhiṣaṇa—Jīva Bṛhaspati—overwhelmed with fear and troubled in mind, came and spoke to the gods.
m.2.5.15.59: The guru said: Flee, all you gods. The great mountain Droṇa is gone; surely it has been destroyed by the Daitya, the son of the Ocean.
m.2.5.15.60: This great Daitya Jalandhara cannot be conquered, for he is born of a portion of Rudra, the crusher of all the immortals.
m.2.5.15.61: I know his power and how he himself came into being, O gods; remember fully the deed of Śakra, who insulted Śiva.
m.2.5.15.62: Sanatkumāra said: Hearing those words spoken by the preceptor of the gods, the gods, overwhelmed with fear, gave up hope of victory.
m.2.5.15.63: Being smitten severely on all sides by that king of the Daityas, the gods together with Vāsava Indra abandoned their courage and fled in the ten directions.
m.2.5.15.64: Seeing the gods put to flight, the Daitya, son of the Ocean, entered Amarāvatī amid the sounds of conches, kettledrums and cries of victory.
m.2.5.15.65: When the Daitya had entered the city, the gods headed by Śakra, tormented by the Daitya, reached a cave of the golden mountain Meru and dwelt there.
m.2.5.15.66: At that very time, O sage, the Asura duly installed Śumbha and other leading Daityas, each separately, in all the offices of Indra and the other gods, and himself went to the cave of the golden mountain.
m.2.5.15.iti: Thus ends the fifteenth adhyāya, named The description of the battle between the gods and Jalandhara, in the account of the slaying of Jalandhara, in the fifth khaṇḍa, the Yuddha-khaṇḍa, of the second saṃhitā, the Rudra-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.2.5.16.1: Sanatkumāra said: Seeing the demon approaching once more, the gods together with Indra all trembled with fear and fled away together in haste.
m.2.5.16.2: They all went to Vaikuṇṭha, placing Prajāpati (Brahmā) at their head; and all those gods, together with the Prajāpatis, bowed and praised Viṣṇu.
m.2.5.16.3: The gods said: O Hṛṣīkeśa, mighty-armed one, O Lord, slayer of Madhu, salutation to you, lord of the god of gods, destroyer of all demons.
m.2.5.16.4: Salutation to you, O Viṣṇu, in the form of a fish, who brought back the Vedas, who sported in the ocean of dissolution with the good king Satyavrata.
m.2.5.16.5: Salutation to you in the form of a tortoise, who bore Mount Mandara for the gods as they strenuously exerted themselves in churning the ocean.
m.2.5.16.6: Salutation to you, O blessed Lord, who are the sacrifice itself in the form of a boar; salutation to you who bear on your head the earth, the support of beings.
m.2.5.16.7: Salutation to you, Vāmana, Viṣṇu called Upendra, who in the guise of a brahmin outwitted Bali, lord of the demons, O all-pervading one.
m.2.5.16.8: Salutation to you, Paraśurāma, who rid the earth of kṣatriyas, who did good to your mother, wrathful, the foe of the wicked.
m.2.5.16.9: Salutation to you, Rāma, delight of the world, the ideal man of propriety, who swiftly ended Rāvaṇa, husband of Sītā.
m.2.5.16.10: Salutation to you, Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Self, hidden in knowledge, who delights in sporting with Rādhā and performs many divine plays.
m.2.5.16.11: Salutation to you of hidden body, who censured the Vedas, the teacher of yoga, the Jaina, the one in Buddha's form, O lord of Mā (Lakṣmī).
m.2.5.16.12: Salutation to you in the form of Kalki, destroyer of the barbarians, whose form is infinite power, and establisher of true dharma.
m.2.5.16.13: Salutation to you in the form of Kapila, the great soul, who taught Sāṅkhya-yoga to Devahūti, to the teacher of Sāṅkhya, O Lord.
m.2.5.16.14: Salutation to the Paramahaṃsa who imparts the supreme knowledge, to the Ordainer whose form is knowledge, by whom the self becomes serene.
m.2.5.16.15: Salutation to Vedavyāsa, who divided the Vedas and composed the Purāṇas for the welfare of all the worlds.
m.2.5.16.16: Thus, salutation to you, O Lord, who through bodies such as the fish are intent on the work of your devotees, the maker of creation, preservation and destruction, who are Brahman.
m.2.5.16.17: Salutation to you, Hari, remover of the distress of your servants, giver of happiness, the auspicious one, clad in yellow, who ride on Tārkṣya (Garuḍa). Salutation, salutation to the sole agent of all actions, the refuge of all.
m.2.5.16.18: O thunderbolt that shatters the sorrows and other ills of the immortals tormented by demons, salutation to you who lie on the couch of Śeṣa, whose eyes are the sun and moon.
m.2.5.16.19: O ocean of compassion, lord of Ramā, protect us who have come to you for refuge. All the gods have been driven out of heaven by Jalandhara.
m.2.5.16.20: The sun has been driven from his place, and likewise the moon and fire; the king of serpents has been driven from Pātāla, and Dharmarāja (Yama) has been expelled.
m.2.5.16.21: Those gods wander about like mortals and no longer shine. We have come to you for refuge; let his slaying be considered.
m.2.5.16.22: Sanatkumāra said: Hearing these piteous words of the gods, Madhusūdana, the ocean of compassion, spoke in a voice resounding like thunder.
m.2.5.16.23: Viṣṇu said: Give up fear, O gods. I shall go to battle; I shall display my prowess against the demon Jalandhara.
m.2.5.16.24: Having said this, the foe of demons, loving to his devotees, rose up at once, troubled in mind, and out of compassion swiftly mounted Garuḍa.
m.2.5.16.25: Seeing her beloved departing with the gods, Lakṣmī, born of the ocean, with joined palms and tearful eyes, spoke these words.
m.2.5.16.26: Lakṣmī said: O lord, if I am your beloved and always devoted to you, then how can my brother be slain by you in battle, O treasure of compassion?
m.2.5.16.27: Viṣṇu said: I shall display my prowess against the demon Jalandhara; praised by them, I shall go in haste to battle.
m.2.5.16.28: Because he is born of a portion of Rudra, because of Brahmā's word, and out of love for you, this Jalandhara is not to be slain by me.
m.2.5.16.29: Sanatkumāra said: Having said this, Viṣṇu, mounted on Garuḍa and bearing conch, discus, mace and sword, swiftly went to fight together with the gods headed by Śakra.
m.2.5.16.30: He quickly reached the very place where the demon Jalandhara was, roaring like a lion, with the gods blazing with Viṣṇu's splendour.
m.2.5.16.31: Then, battered by the wind from the swift wings of Aruṇa's younger brother (Garuḍa), the demons, whirled about by the gale, spun in the sky like clouds.
m.2.5.16.32: Then Jalandhara, seeing the demons afflicted by the gale, raised his voice in anger and quickly advanced against Viṣṇu.
m.2.5.16.33: Meanwhile the gods, exultant, strengthened by Hari's splendour and endowed with great might, joined battle.
m.2.5.16.34: Seeing the army of the gods arrayed and ready for battle, Jalandhara commanded the demons, who were exceedingly fierce in combat.
m.2.5.16.35: Jalandhara said: Ho, ho, best of demons, wage a fierce battle today against the immortals led by Śakra, who seem mighty now but are ever cowardly.
m.2.5.16.36: The Mauryas numbering a hundred thousand, the Dhaumras numbering a hundred, the Asuras numbering ten million, and likewise the Kālakeyas,
m.2.5.16.37: and of the Kālakas, Daurhṛdas and Kaṅkas by the hundred thousand—these and others too, joined with their own forces, let them march out at my command.
m.2.5.16.38: March out, all of you, equipped, accompanied by great armies, furnished with various weapons and missiles, fearless and free of doubt.
m.2.5.16.39: Ho, ho, Śumbha and Niśumbha, you two of very great valour, destroy in an instant the paltry gods, cowardly in battle.
m.2.5.16.40: Sanatkumāra said: Thus commanded by Jalandhara, those Daityas, skilled in warfare—all those Asuras, accompanied by their fourfold army—fought.
m.2.5.16.41: With maces and sharp arrows, with tridents, paṭṭiśas and lances, and some with axes and spears, they struck one another.
m.2.5.16.42: There, those mighty ones struck with various other weapons. Likewise the gods, great heroes endowed with the strength of Hṛṣīkeśa, fought, hurling sharp arrows and roaring like lions.
m.2.5.16.43: Some with very sharp arrows, some with pestles and lances, some with axes and spears—they struck one another.
m.2.5.16.44: Thus a great battle took place between the gods and the Daityas, exceedingly fierce, indeed causing fear to the sages and the Siddhas.
m.2.5.16.iti: Thus ends the sixteenth adhyāya, named The description of the gods' battle, in the account of the slaying of Jalandhara, in the fifth khaṇḍa, the Yuddha-khaṇḍa, of the second saṃhitā, the Rudra-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.2.5.17.1: Sanatkumāra said: Then the mighty Daityas struck down all the gods, whose minds were distraught with fear, with spears, axes and paṭṭiśa blades.
m.2.5.17.2: Their bodies pierced by the weapons of the Daityas, all the gods together with Vāsava Indra, their minds distraught with fear, fled from the battle.
m.2.5.17.3: Then, seeing the gods intent on flight, Hṛṣīkeśa, Viṣṇu, mounted on Garuḍa, quickly came forward to fight.
m.2.5.17.4: Flashing on all sides with radiance from the discus Sudarśana, his lotus-hand finely adorned by it, he who grants fearlessness to his devotees shone forth.
m.2.5.17.5: Bearing the conch, sword, mace and the bow Śārṅga, filled with anger, wielding fierce weapons, the great hero, skilled in every kind of warfare, came on.
m.2.5.17.6: Twanging the bow named Śārṅga, he roared; by that mighty sound of his, O sage, the three worlds were filled.
m.2.5.17.7: And with the arrows issuing from Śārṅga, Lord Viṣṇu, seething with rage, cut off the heads of the sons of Diti by the crore.
m.2.5.17.8: Then, battered by the wind of the swift wings of Aruṇa's younger brother Garuḍa, the Daityas, whirled about by the gale, wheeled in the sky like clouds.
m.2.5.17.9: Then Jalandhara, the great Daitya who terrified the hosts of gods, seeing the Daityas battered by the gale, grew exceedingly angry.
m.2.5.17.10: Seeing him crushing the Daityas, the hero, his lip quivering, rushed forward with speed to fight with Hari.
m.2.5.17.11: That lord of the Daityas let out a great roar that terrified gods and asuras; ears were split from hearing it.
m.2.5.17.12: Then, filled by the dreadful, mighty roar of the Daitya Jalandhara, the whole world trembled.
m.2.5.17.13: Then a great battle arose between Viṣṇu and the lord of the Daityas, who with their arrows made the sky as if it had no space left.
m.2.5.17.14: And by that fearsome battle between the two of them, O sage, great amazement arose among the gods, asuras, sages and Siddhas alike.
m.2.5.17.15: With floods of arrows Viṣṇu cut down the Daitya's banner, parasol, bow and arrows, and struck him in the heart with a single arrow.
m.2.5.17.16: Then the Daitya, leaping up swiftly, mace in hand, struck Garuḍa on the head and felled him to the ground.
m.2.5.17.17: Filled with anger, his lip quivering, the Daitya struck Viṣṇu in the heart with a sharp spear blazing with light.
m.2.5.17.18: Viṣṇu, the slayer of Daityas, as if laughing, cut the mace with his sword, and twanging Śārṅga, pierced him with sharp arrows.
m.2.5.17.19: Viṣṇu, the slayer of the gods' foes, overcome with wrath, swiftly struck the Daitya Jalandhara with a terrifying, exceedingly sharp arrow.
m.2.5.17.20: Seeing that arrow of his approaching, the mighty Daitya cut it with an arrow and quickly struck Viṣṇu in the heart.
m.2.5.17.21: Keśava too, the hero, cut that mighty arrow shot by the asura into pieces the size of sesame seeds and roared.
m.2.5.17.22: Trembling with anger, he again fitted an arrow to the bow; then the mighty one Jalandhara cut that shaft with an arrow.
m.2.5.17.23: Vāsudeva, in anger, again fitted an arrow to his bow for the destruction of the gods' enemy, and roared like a lion.
m.2.5.17.24: Then Jalandhara, the mighty lord of the Daityas, biting his lip in fury, cut Viṣṇu's bow called Śārṅga with an arrow of his own.
m.2.5.17.25: And again, with very sharp arrows, the great hero of fierce valour, the terror of the gods, struck Madhusūdana.
m.2.5.17.26: Lord Keśava, protector of the worlds, his bow cut, hurled his supreme mace for the destruction of Jalandhara.
m.2.5.17.27: That mace, hurled by Hari, resembling a blazing fire and unfailing in its course, swiftly struck his body.
m.2.5.17.28: Struck by it, the great Daitya Jalandhara, drunk with pride, did not move in the least, as though hit by a garland of flowers.
m.2.5.17.29: Then the wrathful Jalandhara, terror of the gods, frenzied in battle, hurled at Hari a trident that looked like fire.
m.2.5.17.30: Then Viṣṇu, remembering the lotus-feet of Śiva, forcefully and quickly cut that trident with his sword named Nandaka.
m.2.5.17.31: When the trident was cut, the lord of the Daityas suddenly leapt up, came quickly, and struck Viṣṇu in the chest with his firm fist.
m.2.5.17.32: That great hero Viṣṇu too, disregarding the pain of it, struck Jalandhara in the chest with his firm fist.
m.2.5.17.33: Then the two mighty ones fought hand to hand, with arms, fists and knees, making the earth resound.
m.2.5.17.34: Having thus fought for a very long time with that asura, he Viṣṇu was astonished, O best of sages, and felt weariness in his heart.
m.2.5.17.35: Then the Lord, the master of māyā, foremost of those who know illusion, being pleased, spoke to the king of Daityas in a voice deep as a thundercloud.
m.2.5.17.36: Viṣṇu said: O, O best among the foremost Daityas, frenzied in battle, you are blessed, since you, a great lord, are not afraid of these great and excellent weapons.
m.2.5.17.37: By these very fierce weapons many Daityas have been slain; arrogant heroes in great battles, their bodies cut apart, have gone to death.
m.2.5.17.38: I am pleased with your fighting, O great Daitya; you are great. No hero equal to you has been seen in the three worlds with their moving and unmoving beings.
m.2.5.17.39: Choose a boon, O lord of Daityas; I am pleased by your valour. I will give you even what should not be given—whatever is in your mind.
m.2.5.17.40: Sanatkumāra said: Hearing these words of Viṣṇu, Hari, the master of illusion, the greatly intelligent king of the Daityas, Jalandhara, replied.
m.2.5.17.41: Jalandhara said: If you are pleased, O gracious one, grant me this boon: dwell in my house together with my sister and with me, along with your attendants.
m.2.5.17.42: Sanatkumāra said: Having heard those words of the great demon, the lord of the gods, the blessed Hari, with a dejected mind, said, so be it.
m.2.5.17.43: Then that Viṣṇu, having come to the city named Jalandhara together with Ramā, dwelt there along with all the hosts of gods.
m.2.5.17.44: Then the demon Jalandhara, having reached his own abode, lived there with his sister and with Viṣṇu, his mind overflowing with joy.
m.2.5.17.45: Then Jalandhara, having installed the Dānavas in the offices of the gods, returned joyfully to the surface of the earth.
m.2.5.17.46: Whatever jewels had been amassed among the gods, Gandharvas and Siddhas, the son of the Ocean brought them under his own control and remained there.
m.2.5.17.47: Having installed the very mighty demon Niśumbha in the realm of Pātāla, the powerful one brought Śeṣa and the others up to the earth.
m.2.5.17.48: Making the hosts of gods, Gandharvas and Siddhas, and serpents, Rākṣasas and humans citizens in his own city, he ruled the three worlds.
m.2.5.17.49: Thus Jalandhara, having made the gods subject to his will, protected his subjects righteously, like his own sons.
m.2.5.17.50: While he ruled the kingdom righteously, no one was seen who was sick, nor sorrowful, nor emaciated, nor wretched.
m.2.5.17.iti: Thus ends the seventeenth adhyāya, named The description of the battle between Viṣṇu and Jalandhara, in the account of Jalandhara, in the fifth khaṇḍa, the Yuddha-khaṇḍa, of the second saṃhitā, the Rudra-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.2.5.18.1: Sanatkumāra said: While that great Asura was thus ruling the earth righteously, the gods became miserable, O lord of sages, because they had lost their lordship.
m.2.5.18.2: All those distressed gods went in their minds for refuge to Śiva, to Śaṅkara, the god of gods, the lord of all, the master.
m.2.5.18.3: To end their own sorrow they praised with pleasing words the blessed Maheśvara, the giver of all, who is loving toward his devotees.
m.2.5.18.4: That Mahādeva, who grants all desires to his devotees, summoned Nārada and sent him forth, wishing to accomplish the gods' task.
m.2.5.18.5: Then the divine sage Nārada, wise, a devotee of Śambhu and the refuge of the good, went by Śiva's command to the gods in the city of the Daitya.
m.2.5.18.6: All those agitated gods, led by Vāsava, seeing the sage Nārada coming, quickly rose up.
m.2.5.18.7: Bowing, those gods headed by Śakra, with eager faces, lovingly offered a seat to the sage Nārada.
m.2.5.18.8: Having bowed deeply to that excellent sage, comfortably seated on the seat, the dejected gods led by Vāsava again addressed the lord of sages.
m.2.5.18.9: The gods said: O best among excellent sages, O mine of compassion, hear our sorrow; having heard it, destroy it quickly, for you are able, being dear to Śaṅkara.
m.2.5.18.10: We gods have been utterly routed by the Daitya Jalandhara from our own places and from our lordship; we are distressed and bewildered.
m.2.5.18.11: The hot-rayed Sun and likewise the Moon have been expelled from their own places, as have Fire, the King of Dharma, and the other guardians of the worlds.
m.2.5.18.12: All the gods have been sorely oppressed by that exceedingly mighty one; we have met with great sorrow and have come to you for refuge.
m.2.5.18.13: In battle that mighty one, the great Daitya Jalandhara, crusher of all the immortals, brought Hṛṣīkeśa under his control.
m.2.5.18.14: Subject to him and bound by a boon, Hari has dwelt in his house—that Viṣṇu, together with Lakṣmī, who is the accomplisher of all our aims.
m.2.5.18.15: O great-minded one, make an effort for Jalandhara's destruction. You have come to us by the power of destiny, you who always accomplish every aim.
m.2.5.18.16: Sanatkumāra said: Having heard these words of the immortals, Nārada, tiger among sages and mine of compassion, comforted them and spoke.
m.2.5.18.17: Nārada said: I know, O gods, that you have been defeated by the king of the Daityas, have met with sorrow, are oppressed, and have indeed been expelled from your places.
m.2.5.18.18: With my own power I will accomplish your aim; of this there is no doubt. I am favourable to you here, since you, O immortals, have met with sorrow.
m.2.5.18.19: Sanatkumāra said: Having spoken thus and comforted all the gods, the best of sages went to Jalandhara's assembly to see the beloved of the Dānavas.
m.2.5.18.20: Then, seeing the best of sages arrive, the Daitya Jalandhara rose and with supreme devotion gave him an excellent, foremost seat.
m.2.5.18.21: Having duly honoured him, the lord of the Dānavas, greatly amazed, then laughed heartily and spoke these words to the best of sages.
m.2.5.18.22: Jalandhara said: From where have you come, O Brahmin? And what have you seen anywhere? Command me, O sage, regarding the purpose for which you have come here.
m.2.5.18.23: Sanatkumāra said: Having heard these words of the lord of the Daityas, the great sage Nārada, pleased at heart, replied to Jalandhara.
m.2.5.18.24: Nārada said: O Jalandhara, lord of all Dānavas and Daityas, O great-minded one, you are blessed, O lord of all worlds; you alone are the enjoyer of jewels.
m.2.5.18.25: Hear the reason for my coming, O best of Daitya lords; I will tell you all of it—the purpose for which I have come here.
m.2.5.18.26: O lord of the Daityas, I went by chance to the peak of Kailāsa, a great forest of wish-fulfilling trees extending ten thousand yojanas,
m.2.5.18.27: filled with hundreds of wish-granting cows, brilliantly lit by wish-fulfilling gems, made wholly of gold, divine, and everywhere adorned with wonders.
m.2.5.18.28: There I saw Śaṅkara seated with Umā—beautiful in every limb, fair-complexioned, three-eyed, moon-crested.
m.2.5.18.29: Seeing that great marvel, a question then arose in me: could such prosperity exist anywhere else in the three worlds or not?
m.2.5.18.30: At that moment, O lord of the Daityas, I remembered your prosperity too; wishing to behold it, I have come here into your presence.
m.2.5.18.31: Sanatkumāra said: Hearing this from Nārada, that Daitya lord Jalandhara respectfully showed him his entire prosperity.
m.2.5.18.32: Having seen it, the wise Nārada, a skilled accomplisher of the gods' task, spoke to that Daitya lord Jalandhara, prompted by the Lord.
m.2.5.18.33: Nārada said: Indeed, O excellent hero, you now possess complete and splendid prosperity. You are the lord of the three worlds—so what wonder is possible here?
m.2.5.18.34: Gems, heaps of jewels, riches such as elephants—these shine in your house here today, and whatever precious things there are, those too.
m.2.5.18.35: You have brought the jewel among elephants, Śakra's Airāvata, and likewise, O great hero, the jewel among horses, the Sun's steed Uccaiḥśravas.
m.2.5.18.36: You have brought the wish-fulfilling tree and the treasures of Dhanada (Kubera), and you have brought the swan-yoked aerial chariot of Vedhas (Brahmā).
m.2.5.18.37: Thus, O lord of the Daityas, whatever excellent jewels exist in heaven, on earth and in the netherworld, all of them shine in your house on every side.
m.2.5.18.38: Seeing this prosperity of yours, complete and manifold, splendidly adorned with elephants, horses and the like, I am pleased, O great hero.
m.2.5.18.39: But, O Jalandhara, the supreme jewel of a wife is not in your house. You ought especially to bring that jewel among women.
m.2.5.18.40: O Jalandhara, in whose house all fine jewels exist, if there is no jewel of a wife, those do not shine—they are surely in vain.
m.2.5.18.41: Sanatkumāra said: Having heard these words of the great-souled Nārada, the king of the Daityas, his mind agitated by desire, spoke.
m.2.5.18.42: Jalandhara said: O Nārada, O divine sage, salutations to you, O great lord. Tell me now where that finest jewel of a wife is to be found.
m.2.5.18.43: If that jewel exists anywhere at all in the universe, I shall bring it from there, O Brahmin — truly, truly, there is no doubt.
m.2.5.18.44: Nārada said: On Kailāsa, which is exceedingly delightful and filled with every kind of riches, there dwells Śambhu, bearing the form of a yogin, sky-clad.
m.2.5.18.45: His wife is truly most lovely, marked with all auspicious marks, beautiful in every limb, enchanting, named Pārvatī.
m.2.5.18.46: Such a form, unmatched by any other, has never been seen anywhere — full of wonder, utterly marvellous, bewitching even to accomplished yogins, most lovely to behold, and bestowing supreme prosperity.
m.2.5.18.47: I reckon in my own mind today, O hero Jalandhara, that in the three worlds there is no one more prosperous than Śiva, who is endowed with this jewel of a wife.
m.2.5.18.48: Immersed in the ocean of her loveliness, the four-faced Brahmā once lost his composure — to which woman can she be compared?
m.2.5.18.49: By her, through her own playful charm, even the foe of Madana, though free of passion and wholly self-dependent, was brought under her control.
m.2.5.18.50: Such prosperity as belongs to him who enjoys that jewel among women is not yours, O lord of the Daityas, even though you are master of all jewels.
m.2.5.18.51: Sanatkumāra said: Having said this, the divine sage Nārada, renowned throughout the worlds, departed through the sky, intent on rendering service to the gods.
m.2.5.18.iti: Thus ends the eighteenth adhyāya, named The dialogue of the divine sage and Jalandhara, in the account of the slaying of Jalandhara, in the fifth khaṇḍa, the Yuddha-khaṇḍa, of the second saṃhitā, the Rudra-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.2.5.19.1: Vyāsa said: O all-knowing Sanatkumāra, when Nārada had gone to heaven, what did that king of the Daityas do? Tell me that in full detail.
m.2.5.19.2: Sanatkumāra said: When Nārada had taken leave of the Daitya and gone to heaven, the king of the Daityas, from hearing of her beauty, became tormented by the fever of love.
m.2.5.19.3: Then the Daitya Jalandhara, under the sway of Time, his reason destroyed and deluded, summoned his messenger, the son of Siṃhikā Rāhu.
m.2.5.19.4: Seeing him arrive, Jalandhara, son of the Ocean, his mind overpowered by desire, addressed him properly and spoke.
m.2.5.19.5: Jalandhara said: O best among excellent messengers, accomplisher of every task, O greatly wise son of Siṃhikā, go to Mount Kailāsa.
m.2.5.19.6: There lives a yogin called Śambhu, an ascetic wearing matted locks, his whole body adorned with ash, dispassionate, with senses subdued.
m.2.5.19.7: Having gone there, O messenger, you must speak thus, with a fearless heart, to that dispassionate yogin Śaṅkara who wears matted locks:
m.2.5.19.8: O yogin, ocean of compassion, what use is a jewel of a wife to you, a forest-dweller attended by bhūtas, pretas, piśācas and the like?
m.2.5.19.9: In a world of which I am lord, O yogin, such a state of affairs is not fitting. Therefore give your own jewel of a wife to me, the enjoyer of jewels.
m.2.5.19.10: Whatever fine jewels exist in the three worlds, they are mine. Know that the whole world, moving and unmoving, is under my control.
m.2.5.19.11: Indra's jewel of an elephant, and the supreme jewel Uccaiḥśravas, were seized suddenly by force, as was the Pārijāta tree.
m.2.5.19.12: The aerial chariot yoked with swans, a jewel, greatly divine, excellent and wondrous, belonging to Brahmā, stands in my courtyard.
m.2.5.19.13: The divine jewel-treasures, Mahāpadma and the rest, of the giver of wealth Kubera, and Varuṇa's umbrella that streams gold, are in my house.
m.2.5.19.14: The great filamented garland of ever-unfading lotuses that belonged to my father is now mine alone, and so too is the noose of the lord of waters Varuṇa.
m.2.5.19.15: Death's excellent spear, which causes the departure of life, was taken by me by force. Agni gave me two divine garments purified by fire.
m.2.5.19.16: Thus, O lord of yogins, all jewels shine in my possession. Therefore you too, O wearer of matted locks, give me your jewel of a wife.
m.2.5.19.17: Sanatkumāra said: Having heard his words, Rāhu, admitted by Nandin, went to the assembly hall of Ugra Śiva, his eyes wide with wonder.
m.2.5.19.18: Having gone there, he saw Śiva himself, the God of gods, the great Lord, who dispels darkness by his own splendour, resplendent with a coating of ash,
m.2.5.19.19: shining with the honours of a great king, most wondrous, beautiful in every limb, Hara adorned with divine ornaments.
m.2.5.19.20: His body overwhelmed by that splendour, the messenger named Rāhu, falling from his pride, bowed to him and drew near to Śambhu.
m.2.5.19.21: Then the son of Siṃhikā, seated before him and eager to speak, prompted by a sign, addressed these words to the Three-eyed One.
m.2.5.19.22: Rāhu said: I am the messenger of the lord of the three worlds, who is ever served by Daityas and serpents; sent by him, I have come here into your presence.
m.2.5.19.23: Jalandhara, son of the Ocean, lord of all the Daitya folk, has become ruler of the three worlds and supreme commander of all.
m.2.5.19.24: That mighty king of the Daityas, like Death to the gods, has said something addressed to you, the yogin; hear it.
m.2.5.19.25: O bull-bannered one, hear the command of that lord, the master of the Daityas, of great divine power, lord of all jewels.
m.2.5.19.26: How can the lovely daughter of Himavat be the wife of you, who always dwell in cremation grounds, wear a garland of bones and go naked?
m.2.5.19.27: I am the overlord of jewels, and she is called a jewel among women; therefore she is fit for me alone, not for you who live on alms.
m.2.5.19.28: The three worlds are under my control; I enjoy the shares of the sacrifices. Whatever jewels there are in these three worlds are in my palace.
m.2.5.19.29: We are enjoyers of jewels, whereas you are surely a naked yogin. Give me your jewel of a wife; subjects should bring happiness to their king.
m.2.5.19.30: Sanatkumāra said: As Rāhu was speaking thus, from between the brows of the trident-bearer there arose a fierce being with a roar like a violent thunderbolt.
m.2.5.19.31: He had a lion's face with a darting tongue, fiery blazing eyes; huge, with hair standing on end and a gaunt body, he was like a second Nṛsiṃha.
m.2.5.19.32: With a huge body, mighty arms and legs like palm trees, terrifying, that being rushed swiftly and with force at Rāhu.
m.2.5.19.33: Seeing him coming to devour him, Rāhu, stricken with fear, ran outside at great speed; but he caught hold of him.
m.2.5.19.34: Rāhu said: O God of gods, great Lord, protect me who have come to you for refuge. You are the Lord, ever to be worshipped by gods and demons, possessed of supreme sovereignty.
m.2.5.19.35: O Mahādeva, O Īśāna, this most terrifying being, your servant, has come to devour me, a Brāhmaṇa.
m.2.5.19.36: Protect me from him, O Lord of gods, you who are tender to those who seek refuge, so that he does not devour me. Salutations to you again and again.
m.2.5.19.37: Sanatkumāra said: Hearing then the words of the Brāhmaṇa, O sage, Mahādeva, the Lord who loves the wretched and helpless, spoke to that gaṇa of his.
m.2.5.19.38: Mahādeva said: Spare this Brāhmaṇa messenger named Rāhu, a lord in his own right, who has sought refuge; those who seek refuge are to be protected, not punished, O best of gaṇas.
m.2.5.19.39: Sanatkumāra said: Thus addressed by the compassionate Lord of Girijā, the gaṇa, having heard the word Brāhmaṇa, at once released Rāhu.
m.2.5.19.40: Then that being, having released Rāhu in the sky, came near to Śiva and addressed Mahādeva in a plaintive voice.
m.2.5.19.41: The being said: O God of gods, Mahādeva, mine of compassion, Śaṅkara, you who are tender toward those who come for refuge, you have made me give up my food.
m.2.5.19.42: Hunger torments me, O Lord, and I am utterly emaciated with hunger. What is to be my food, O Lord of gods? Command me that, O master.
m.2.5.19.43: Sanatkumāra said: Hearing these words of that being, the great Lord, of wondrous ways, playful, and the doer of good to his own, replied.
m.2.5.19.44: Maheśvara said: If your hunger is very great, if hunger torments you, then quickly eat the flesh of your own hands and feet.
m.2.5.19.45: Sanatkumāra said: Thus commanded by Śiva, that being ate his own flesh from the hands and feet, until only the head remained.
m.2.5.19.46: Seeing that only the head was left, Sadāśiva, greatly pleased and amazed, spoke to that being of terrible deeds.
m.2.5.19.47: Śiva said: O great Gaṇa, you are blessed, a keeper of my command. I am exceedingly pleased with you for this deed, O best of the good.
m.2.5.19.48: Named Kīrtimukha, be always my door-keeper, a great Gaṇa, a great hero, causing fear to all the wicked.
m.2.5.19.49: You are dear to me; in my worship you shall always be worshipped by my people. Those who do not worship you are by no means doers of what pleases me.
m.2.5.19.50: Sanatkumāra said: Having thus received the boon from Śambhu, that being rejoiced. From that time on, Kīrtimukha has stood at the door of the Lord of gods.
m.2.5.19.51: That Gaṇa is to be worshipped especially in the worship of Śiva. Those here who do not worship him first, their worship would be in vain.
m.2.5.19.iti: Thus ends the nineteenth adhyāya, named The dialogue of the messenger, in the account of the slaying of Jalandhara, in the fifth khaṇḍa, the Yuddha-khaṇḍa, of the second saṃhitā, the Rudra-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.2.5.20.1: Vyāsa said: O Sanatkumāra, all-knowing one, you have let me hear a wonderful story, in which the purifying sport (līlā) of the great lord Śaṅkara is told.
m.2.5.20.2: Now, O great sage, showing kindness towards me, tell me with great affection: where did Rāhu go after he was released by the Puruṣa?
m.2.5.20.3: Sūta said: Hearing these words of Vyāsa of boundless intellect, the great sage, son of Brahmā, replied with a pleased heart.
m.2.5.20.4: Sanatkumāra said: Rāhu, who had been released by him, fell in that Barbara region; therefore he became a Barbara — thus he gained renown on earth.
m.2.5.20.5: Then, regarding himself as born again, humbled and with his pride gone, he slowly went to the city of Jalandhara.
m.2.5.20.6: Approaching Jalandhara, the lord of the Daityas, he related to him in detail, O Vyāsa, everything that Īśa had done.
m.2.5.20.7: Hearing that, Jalandhara, the mighty son of the Ocean, best of Daitya chiefs, had his body agitated with rage.
m.2.5.20.8: Then the best of Daityas, his mind overpowered by anger, ordered the mobilisation of all the Daitya armies.
m.2.5.20.9: Jalandhara said: Let all the Daityas headed by Kālanemi march forth, and likewise the heroes led by Śumbha and Niśumbha, together with their forces.
m.2.5.20.10: Let crores born of heroic families go, and those of the Kambu clan, the Daurhṛdas, the Kālakas, the Kālakeyas, the Mauryas and likewise the Dhaumras.
m.2.5.20.11: Having commanded thus, the valourous lord of the Asuras, son of the Ocean, quickly marched out, surrounded by crores of Daityas.
m.2.5.20.12: Then in front of him appeared Śukra, and Rāhu with severed head; and his crown, slipping through the force of his movement, fell to the ground.
m.2.5.20.13: The sky appeared filled with clouds as in the rainy season; many ill omens arose, foretelling the great sleep of death.
m.2.5.20.14: Seeing his preparations thus, the gods together with Vāsava went unseen to Kailāsa, the abode of Śaṅkara.
m.2.5.20.15: Going there and seeing Śiva, all the gods with Vāsava bowed deeply, and with shoulders bent and palms joined they praised him.
m.2.5.20.16: The gods said: O God of gods, Mahādeva, mine of compassion, Śaṅkara, salutation be to you, O great lord; protect us who have come to you for refuge.
m.2.5.20.17: O lord, we are terribly distressed by the dreadful calamity caused by Jalandhara; together with the king of gods we have been expelled from our places and dwell on the earth.
m.2.5.20.18: How is it, master, that you do not know of this calamity of the gods, O lord? Therefore, to protect us, slay the son of the Ocean.
m.2.5.20.19: Garuḍa-bannered Viṣṇu, whom you formerly appointed for our protection, O master, is today unable to protect us.
m.2.5.20.20: Subject to him, he lives in his house together with Ramā; and we gods too stay there, subject to his commands.
m.2.5.20.21: Unnoticed, we have come here into your presence, O Śambhu. That mighty son of the Ocean is coming to make war with you.
m.2.5.20.22: Therefore, master, all-knowing one, you should slay that Jalandhara in battle without delay; protect us who have sought refuge.
m.2.5.20.23: Sanatkumāra said: Having said this, all the gods with Vāsava bowed to the lord and stood humbly, gazing at the feet of Maheśa.
m.2.5.20.24: Hearing these words of the gods, the Bull-bannered one laughed, quickly summoned Viṣṇu, and spoke these words.
m.2.5.20.25: Īśvara said: O Hṛṣīkeśa, great Viṣṇu, the gods have come here to me for refuge, greatly distressed and oppressed by Jalandhara.
m.2.5.20.26: O Viṣṇu, how is it that Jalandhara was not slain by you in battle? And you have even gone to his house, abandoning your own Vaikuṇṭha.
m.2.5.20.27: For you were appointed by me, the independent sporting one, for the protection of the good and for the restraint of the wicked.
m.2.5.20.28: Sanatkumāra said: Hearing these words of Maheśa, Hari, the Garuḍa-bannered, humble in spirit, bowing with joined palms, replied.
m.2.5.20.29: Viṣṇu said: Because he was born from a portion of you, and because he is the brother of Śrī, I did not slay him in battle; you slay this Dānava.
m.2.5.20.30: He is of great strength, a great hero, invincible to all the gods and to others as well, O lord of gods; I tell you this truly.
m.2.5.20.31: I fought with him for a long time, together with the gods, but my means did not prevail against that bull among Dānavas.
m.2.5.20.32: Pleased by his valour, I said, ask for a boon. Hearing my words, he chose an excellent boon:
m.2.5.20.33: Live in my house with the gods, together with my sister and me, subject to me, O great Viṣṇu. Thus I went to his house.
m.2.5.20.34: Sanatkumāra said: Hearing these words of Viṣṇu, Śaṅkara, the great lord, compassionate and loving to his devotees, laughed and, well pleased, spoke.
m.2.5.20.35: Maheśvara said: O Viṣṇu, best of gods, listen attentively to my words: I shall slay the great Daitya Jalandhara, there is no doubt.
m.2.5.20.36: Go to your own abode without fear; let the gods too surely go, fearless and free of doubt, considering the lord of the Asuras as already slain.
m.2.5.20.37: Sanatkumāra said: Hearing these words of Maheśa, the lord of Ramā, his doubt removed, quickly went with the gods to his own abode.
m.2.5.20.38: Meanwhile, O Vyāsa, that mighty lord of the Daityas, of great prowess, went to the foot of the mountain together with the armed Asuras.
m.2.5.20.39: Then, besieging Kailāsa with a vast army, the great one stood there like Death, roaring like a lion.
m.2.5.20.40: Then, hearing the tumult arising from the roars of the Daityas, the great lord Maheśāna, of mighty sport, destroyer of the wicked, became exceedingly angry.
m.2.5.20.41: Having taken count of them, Mahādeva Hara, of great might and fond of sport, commanded his own very powerful gaṇas, Nandin and the rest.
m.2.5.20.42: By Śiva's command all the gaṇas, headed by Nandin, the elephant-faced one and the Commander Kārttikeya, armed themselves for battle, filled with great haste.
m.2.5.20.43: All the gaṇas, frenzied with wrath, descended from Kailāsa, great heroes leaping and raising battle cries, eager indeed for the fight.
m.2.5.20.44: Then on the foothills of Kailāsa there arose a terrible battle between the lords of the pramathas and the daityas, thronged with weapons and missiles.
m.2.5.20.45: With masses of kettledrums, mṛdaṅgas and conches, with sounds that thrilled the heroes, and with the noise of elephants, horses and chariots, the earth resounded and trembled.
m.2.5.20.46: With masses of spears, javelins and arrows, with clubs, nooses and paṭṭiśa-axes, the sky, filled with them, shone as if strewn with pearls.
m.2.5.20.47: The earth shone with slain elephants, horses and foot-soldiers, just as of old it was thickly covered with the great mountains struck down by the thunderbolt.
m.2.5.20.48: With masses of daityas slain by the pramathas, and likewise of gaṇas slain by the daityas, the earth then became impassable, thick with a mire of fat, blood and flesh.
m.2.5.20.49: Bhārgava Śukra revived the masses of daityas slain by the pramathas, again and again in the battle, by the power of the Mṛtasañjīvanī lore.
m.2.5.20.50: Seeing those daityas stirring again, all the gaṇas, stricken with fear, reported to the God of gods all that Śukra was doing.
m.2.5.20.51: Hearing that, Lord Rudra became violently angry; he became terrifying and exceedingly fierce, setting the directions ablaze.
m.2.5.20.52: Then from Rudra's mouth there arose a Kṛtyā, exceedingly dreadful, with legs like palm trees, a mouth like a cavern, and breasts that crushed the trees.
m.2.5.20.53: She swiftly reached the battlefield, O best of sages; that very terrible one roamed about, devouring the great asuras.
m.2.5.20.54: Then, fearless, she went quickly into the very midst of the battle, where Bhārgava stood surrounded by the foremost lords of the daityas.
m.2.5.20.55: Pervading the sky with her own radiance and filling the earth too, O sage, she held Bhārgava in her yoni and, vanishing, went off into the sky.
m.2.5.20.56: Seeing Bhārgava seized, the troops of the daitya army, though frenzied for war, withdrew from the battle with faces downcast.
m.2.5.20.57: Then the army of the daityas, stricken with fear of the gaṇas, broke apart, like a heap of grass scattered by the force of the wind.
m.2.5.20.58: Seeing the daitya army broken through fear of the gaṇas, the commanders Niśumbha and Śumbha, and Kālanemi, utterly unable to bear it, grew furious.
m.2.5.20.59: Those three mighty ones held back the army of the gaṇas, releasing showers of arrows like clouds in the rainy season.
m.2.5.20.60: Then those masses of daitya arrows, like swarms of locusts, blotted out the sky and all the directions, and made the gaṇa army tremble.
m.2.5.20.61: The gaṇas, pierced by hundreds of arrows and pouring streams of blood, looked like kiṃśuka trees in spring, and were aware of nothing at all.
m.2.5.20.62: Then, seeing their own force routed, Nandin, Lambodara and Kārttikeya, unable to bear it and full of haste, forcibly held back the foremost daityas.
m.2.5.20.iti: Thus ends the twentieth adhyāya, named The description of the general battle between the gaṇas and the Asuras, in the account of the slaying of Jalandhara, in the fifth khaṇḍa, the Yuddha-khaṇḍa, of the second saṃhitā, the Rudra-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.2.5.21.1: Sanatkumāra said: Seeing those lords of the gaṇas, Nandī, the elephant-faced one and the six-faced one, the Dānavas rushed at them in indignation for single combat.
m.2.5.21.2: Kālanemi rushed at Nandī, Śumbha likewise at Lambodara, and Niśumbha, wary, rushed at the six-faced god.
m.2.5.21.3: Niśumbha forcefully pierced Kārttikeya's peacock in the breast with five arrows, and it fell down in a swoon.
m.2.5.21.4: Then the wielder of the spear, enraged, with five arrows pierced his horses and his charioteer on the chariot.
m.2.5.21.5: With another sharp arrow the hero, battle-mad, swiftly struck Niśumbha, enemy of the gods, and roared.
m.2.5.21.6: The asura named Niśumbha too, a great and exceedingly mighty hero, struck that roaring Kārttikeya in battle with his own arrow.
m.2.5.21.7: Then, just as Kārttikeya seized his spear in anger, Niśumbha swiftly felled him with his own spear.
m.2.5.21.8: Thus, O Vyāsa, a great battle took place right there between Kārttikeya and Niśumbha, both roaring heroic cries.
m.2.5.21.9: Then Nandīśvara pierced Kālanemi with arrows, and with seven more cut down his horses, banner, chariot and charioteer.
m.2.5.21.10: Kālanemi, greatly enraged, cut Nandī's bow with very sharp arrows released from his own bow.
m.2.5.21.11: Then the hero Nandīśvara, driving back that great asura Kālanemi, struck him hard in the chest with his trident.
m.2.5.21.12: He, his heart pierced by the trident, his horses and charioteer slain, tore off a mountain peak and struck Nandī with it.
m.2.5.21.13: Then Śumbha and Gaṇeśa, riding chariot and mouse respectively, fighting, pierced each other with volleys of arrows.
m.2.5.21.14: Gaṇeśa then pierced Śumbha in the breast with an arrow, and with three arrows knocked his charioteer to the ground.
m.2.5.21.15: Then Śumbha too, furious, pierced the lord of the gaṇas with a shower of arrows and the mouse with three, and roared with a voice like a thundercloud.
m.2.5.21.16: The mouse, its body pierced by arrows, staggered in severe pain; and Lambodara, fallen, indeed became a foot-soldier.
m.2.5.21.17: Then Lambodara struck Śumbha in the breast with his axe and felled him to the ground, and he remounted the mouse.
m.2.5.21.18: The elephant-faced lord was again ready for battle; the two demons, laughing, struck the great elephant-faced one in anger with a goad.
m.2.5.21.19: Kālanemi and Niśumbha, both together, in anger swiftly struck Lambodara at once with arrows like venomous serpents.
m.2.5.21.20: Seeing him being harassed, the mighty Vīrabhadra rushed forward swiftly, accompanied by ten million bhūtas.
m.2.5.21.21: Kūṣmāṇḍas, Bhairavas, Vetālas, hosts of Yoginīs, Piśācas, bands of Ḍākinīs and gaṇas too went along together.
m.2.5.21.22: Then, resounding with shrill kila-kila cries, lion-roars with rumbling, and with ḍamarus, the earth trembled.
m.2.5.21.23: Then the bhūtas, rushing forward, devoured the Dānavas; leaping up they felled them, and danced on the battlefield.
m.2.5.21.24: Meanwhile, O Vyāsa, those two, Nandī and Guha, having regained consciousness, rose up and roared mightily in battle.
m.2.5.21.25: Nandī and Kārttikeya, coming together in haste, struck down the Daityas in battle with ceaseless streams of arrows.
m.2.5.21.26: With its Daityas cut, pierced, slain, felled and devoured, that army became distraught, with downcast faces.
m.2.5.21.27: Thus Nandī, Kārttikeya, the valiant Vikaṭa, Vīrabhadra and other gaṇas roared mightily in the battle.
m.2.5.21.28: Niśumbha and Śumbha, those two generals of the son of the Ocean, the great Daitya Kālanemi, and other asuras were defeated.
m.2.5.21.29: Then, seeing his army routed, the mighty son of the Ocean advanced against the gaṇas in a chariot with lofty banners.
m.2.5.21.30: Then even the defeated Daityas became greatly elated; ready for battle, O Vyāsa, they roared loudly.
m.2.5.21.31: All the gaṇas of Rudra too, flushed with victory, roared, O sage: Nandī, Kārttika, the elephant-faced one, Vīrabhadra and others.
m.2.5.21.32: The clamour of elephants, horses and chariots, the sound of conches and kettledrums, and lion-roars arose in both armies.
m.2.5.21.33: By Jalandhara's volleys of arrows, like sheets of mist, the space between heaven and earth became covered.
m.2.5.21.34: Having pierced Śailādi with five, Gaṇeśa with five arrows and Vīrabhadra with twenty, he roared with a voice like a thundercloud.
m.2.5.21.35: Then Kārttikeya, the great hero, son of Rudra, swiftly pierced the Daitya Jalandhara with his spear and roared.
m.2.5.21.36: That Daitya, his eyes rolling, his body pierced by the spear, fell to the ground; but the mighty one quickly rose up.
m.2.5.21.37: Then Jalandhara, chief of the Daityas, his mind seized by fury, struck Kārttikeya on the chest with his mace.
m.2.5.21.38: Showing the mace's power to be effective, owing to the boon granted by Brahmā, O Vyāsa, the son of Śaṅkara quickly fell to the ground.
m.2.5.21.39: Likewise Nandī, struck by the mace, fell to the ground; that great hero and slayer of foes was somewhat confused in mind.
m.2.5.21.40: Then the lord of the gaṇas, enraged and exceedingly strong, remembering the lotus feet of Śiva, came up and cut the Daitya's mace with his axe.
m.2.5.21.41: Vīrabhadra pierced the Dānava in the heart with three arrows, and with seven he cut down his horses, banner, bow and parasol.
m.2.5.21.42: Then the lord of the Daityas, greatly enraged, raised a dreadful spear, struck down the leader of the Gaṇas, and mounted another chariot.
m.2.5.21.43: Then that mighty lord of the Daityas, full of fury, rushed forward swiftly, disregarding that Vīrabhadra in his heart.
m.2.5.21.44: He quickly struck that Vīrabhadra with a sharp serpent-like arrow, and the great hero Jalandhara, king of the Daityas, roared.
m.2.5.21.45: Vīrabhadra too, enraged, cut that arrow with a sharp-edged shaft and pierced him with a great arrow.
m.2.5.21.46: Then those two, resplendent like the sun, the foremost of the best heroes, fought each other for a long time with various weapons and missiles.
m.2.5.21.47: Then Vīrabhadra felled his horses with arrows, and swiftly cut the bow and banner of the chariot-warrior.
m.2.5.21.48: Then that king of the Daityas, wielding an iron club, leapt down, and the mighty one quickly reached the side of Vīrabhadra.
m.2.5.21.49: The mighty hero, son of the Ocean, struck Vīrabhadra on the head with a very huge iron club and roared.
m.2.5.21.50: His head split by the very huge club, Vīrabhadra, lord of the Gaṇas, fell to the ground and shed much blood.
m.2.5.21.51: Seeing Vīrabhadra fallen, Rudra's Gaṇas, out of fear, left the battle and fled, crying out to Maheśvara.
m.2.5.21.52: Then, hearing the uproar of the Gaṇas, the moon-crested Śiva asked the heroes, the best of the Gaṇas, standing at his side.
m.2.5.21.53: Śaṅkara said: Why has this great uproar arisen among my Gaṇas? Let it be looked into, O great heroes; peace must surely be made by me.
m.2.5.21.54: While the lord of the gods was thus respectfully questioning the Gaṇas, those excellent Gaṇas arrived before the Lord.
m.2.5.21.55: Seeing them distressed, Lord Rudra asked about their welfare, and the Gaṇas recounted in detail what had happened, just as it was.
m.2.5.21.56: Hearing that, the blessed Lord Rudra, performer of great divine play, granted them freedom from fear, increasing their great enthusiasm.
m.2.5.21.iti: Thus ends the twenty-first adhyāya, named The description of the special battle, in the account of Jalandhara, in the fifth khaṇḍa, the Yuddha-khaṇḍa, of the second saṃhitā, the Rudra-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.2.5.22.1: Sanatkumāra said: Then Rudra, the great Lord, assuming a fierce form and mounted on his bull, advanced into the battle with his heroic gaṇas, as if laughing.
m.2.5.22.2: Seeing Rudra coming, the fierce gaṇas who had earlier been defeated turned back again to the battle with lion-roars.
m.2.5.22.3: And those other gaṇas of Śaṅkara too, raising heroic shouts, joyful and armed, struck down the daityas with showers of arrows.
m.2.5.22.4: All the daityas, seeing the terrifying Rudra, fled out of fear of him, as sins flee on seeing a devotee of Śaṅkara.
m.2.5.22.5: Then Jalandhara, seeing the daityas turning back from the battle, rushed at the Lord of Caṇḍī, discharging arrows by the thousands.
m.2.5.22.6: And thousands of daitya chiefs, led by Niśumbha and Śumbha, swiftly charged at Śiva, biting their lips in fury.
m.2.5.22.7: Likewise the hero Kālanemi, Khaḍgaromā, Balāhaka, Ghasmara, Pracaṇḍa and others too went against Śiva.
m.2.5.22.8: They quickly covered Rudra's gaṇas with arrows, and all those heroes headed by Śumbha hacked at their limbs, O sage.
m.2.5.22.9: Hara, seeing the army of gaṇas shrouded in a darkness of arrows, cut through that net of arrows and covered the sky with his own arrows.
m.2.5.22.10: Then he tormented the daityas with gales of arrows, and with floods of fierce arrow-nets felled them to the ground.
m.2.5.22.11: Likewise with his axe he severed Khaḍgaromā's head from his body, and with his khaṭvāṅga he split Balāhaka's head in two.
m.2.5.22.12: Having bound the daitya Ghasmara with his noose, he struck him down on the ground; and he cut down the great hero Pracaṇḍa with his trident.
m.2.5.22.13: Some were killed by the bull, some were felled by arrows; the asuras could not stand their ground, like elephants harassed by a lion.
m.2.5.22.14: Then the great daitya Jalandhara, his mind seized by anger, reproached the daityas in battle; and, steadfast, he spoke laughingly to Śumbha and the others.
m.2.5.22.15: Jalandhara said: What use are you, mere refuse cast out by your mothers, running away and being struck from behind? The slaying of the frightened is neither praiseworthy nor does it grant heaven to those who think themselves heroes.
m.2.5.22.16: If you have faith in battle, or any strength in your hearts, O petty ones, stand before me just for a moment—unless you crave vulgar comforts.
m.2.5.22.17: Death in battle is excellent, granting the fruit of all desires; above all it bestows fame, and it is declared to grant liberation as well.
m.2.5.22.18: The renunciant of supreme knowledge, and he who is slain in battle facing the foe, pierce the orb of the sun and go to the supreme abode.
m.2.5.22.19: The wise should never, anywhere, fear death, since it cannot be averted even by all possible means.
m.2.5.22.20: O heroes, for those who are born, death is born together with the body. Whether today or at the end of a hundred years, death is certain for living beings.
m.2.5.22.21: Therefore, casting off the fear of death, fight joyfully in battle; in every way there is supreme bliss both here and hereafter, without doubt.
m.2.5.22.22: Sanatkumāra said: Having said this, he exhorted his warriors repeatedly; but they did not take courage, and out of fear fled swiftly from the battle.
m.2.5.22.23: Then, seeing that army of his intent on flight, the mighty hero Jalandhara, son of the Ocean, became extremely angry.
m.2.5.22.24: Then Jalandhara, his mind seized by wrath, with a voice like a fierce thunderbolt, angrily challenged Rudra to battle.
m.2.5.22.25: Jalandhara said: Fight with me today. What is gained by slaying these? Whatever strength you have, show it, O wearer of matted locks.
m.2.5.22.26: Sanatkumāra said: Having said this, the great daitya Jalandhara struck the bull-bannered Śambhu, whose deeds are effortless, with seventy arrows.
m.2.5.22.27: Mahādeva, as if laughing, swiftly cut down those arrows of Jalandhara before they reached him, with his own sharp arrows.
m.2.5.22.28: Then with seven arrows he cut down the horses, banner, parasol and bow of the daitya Jalandhara; that was no wonder for Hara, O sage.
m.2.5.22.29: His bow cut and chariotless, the asura, son of the Ocean, enraged and swift, raised his mace and rushed at Śiva.
m.2.5.22.30: And the Lord Maheśvara, of great playfulness, at once swiftly split with his arrows into two the mace hurled by him, O son of Parāśara.
m.2.5.22.31: Even so, the great asura, greatly enraged, raised his fist and charged at that Rudra with great speed, wishing to kill him.
m.2.5.22.32: Just then that Jalandhara was quickly driven back a krośa's distance by floods of arrows from the Lord, the doer of effortless deeds.
m.2.5.22.33: Then the daitya Jalandhara, judging Rudra superior in strength, created a wondrous Gāndharva illusion to bewilder Rudra.
m.2.5.22.34: Through the power of his illusion, many troops of gandharvas and apsarases appeared, in order to bewilder Rudra.
m.2.5.22.35: Then the troops of gandharvas and apsarases sang and danced, while others played cymbals, flutes and mṛdaṅga drums.
m.2.5.22.36: Seeing that great marvel, Rudra together with his gaṇas was bewildered; he did not even notice the weapons falling from his hands.
m.2.5.22.37: Seeing Rudra wholly absorbed, the daitya Jalandhara, driven by lust, quickly went to where Gaurī was staying.
m.2.5.22.38: Having stationed the mighty Śumbha and Niśumbha in the battle, he became one with ten staff-like arms, five faces, three eyes and matted locks,
m.2.5.22.39: mounted on a great bull, in every way resembling Rudra—thus did Jalandhara become through his asura illusion, O Vyāsa.
m.2.5.22.40: Then Bhava's beloved, seeing Rudra approaching, came forward from the midst of her companions and came within his range of sight.
m.2.5.22.41: The moment the lord of the Dānavas beheld Pārvatī of lovely limbs, at that very moment he released his semen and then became numb in his limbs.
m.2.5.22.42: Then Gaurī, recognising the Dānava, overwhelmed with fear, vanished and swiftly went to the northern Mānasa lake.
m.2.5.22.43: Then the Daitya, no longer seeing her, who had vanished in an instant like a streak of lightning, went back swiftly to fight where the god Maheśvara was.
m.2.5.22.44: Pārvatī too then remembered the great Viṣṇu in her mind; at once she saw that god seated near her.
m.2.5.22.45: Seeing that Viṣṇu bowing with joined palms, Pārvatī, the Mother of the world, beloved of Śiva, spoke with a gracious mind.
m.2.5.22.46: Pārvatī said: O Viṣṇu, the Daitya Jalandhara has done a most astonishing thing. Is that conduct of the evil-minded one not known to you?
m.2.5.22.47: Hearing those words of the Mother of the world, the Garuḍa-bannered one, bowing to Śivā with joined palms and bent neck, replied.
m.2.5.22.48: The Lord said: By your grace, O Goddess, that event is known to me. Whatever you command me, O Mother, I shall do with your permission.
m.2.5.22.49: Sanatkumāra said: Hearing those words of Viṣṇu, Pārvatī spoke again, the Mother of the world, instructing Hṛṣīkeśa well in the policy of dharma.
m.2.5.22.50: Pārvatī said: The path has been shown by him alone; understand it in just the same way. By my command, violate the dharma of wifely chastity of his wife.
m.2.5.22.51: Otherwise that great Daitya cannot be slain, O lord of Ramā; there is no other dharma on the face of the earth equal to wifely chastity.
m.2.5.22.52: Sanatkumāra said: Hearing this command and receiving it on his head, Hari quickly went again to Jalandhara's city to practise deceit.
m.2.5.22.iti: Thus ends the twenty-second adhyāya, named The description of Jalandhara's battle, in the account of the slaying of Jalandhara, in the fifth khaṇḍa, the Yuddha-khaṇḍa, of the second saṃhitā, the Rudra-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.2.5.23.1: Vyāsa said: O Sanatkumāra, all-knowing one, best of speakers, tell me: what did Hari do there, and how did she abandon her dharma?
m.2.5.23.2: Sanatkumāra said: Viṣṇu, having gone to Jālandhara, the city of the demon, set his mind on breaking the wifely chastity of Vṛndā.
m.2.5.23.3: He, the best of illusionists, caused Vṛndā to see a dream, while he himself, in a wondrous form, stayed in the garden of her city.
m.2.5.23.4: Then, at night, the goddess Vṛndā, his wife of good vows, through the power of Hari's māyā, saw a bad dream.
m.2.5.23.5: Within the dream, through Viṣṇu's māyā, she saw her husband mounted on a buffalo, smeared with oil, naked,
m.2.5.23.6: adorned with ornaments of black flowers, attended by hosts of flesh-eaters, gone to the southern direction, shaven-headed, and enveloped in darkness then;
m.2.5.23.7: and her own city suddenly sunk in the ocean together with herself — such and many other bad dreams she saw at the end of the night.
m.2.5.23.8: Then, waking up, the young woman, pondering that dream of hers, saw the risen sun again and again as full of holes and lustreless.
m.2.5.23.9: Knowing this to be an ill omen, weeping and overwhelmed with fear, she found no comfort anywhere — on the gate-towers, the turrets, or the grounds.
m.2.5.23.10: Then, accompanied by two friends, she went to the city garden; though she went there too, the young woman found happiness nowhere.
m.2.5.23.11: Then that wife of Jalandhara, her mind dejected and agitated, went from forest to forest, not then knowing even herself.
m.2.5.23.12: Wandering, the young woman then saw two extremely terrifying rākṣasas with lion faces, gleaming with teeth.
m.2.5.23.13: Seeing those two, extremely distraught and intent on fleeing, she then saw a calm ascetic with his disciple, observing silence.
m.2.5.23.14: Then, out of fear, placing her creeper-like arms around his neck, she said: O sage, protect me; I have come for refuge.
m.2.5.23.15: The sage, seeing her distraught and pursued by the rākṣasas, quickly turned those two dreadful ones away with a mere huṃ sound.
m.2.5.23.16: Seeing those two, terrified by fear of that huṃ, turn and go away, the wife of the demon-lord became greatly amazed in her heart, O sage.
m.2.5.23.17: Then Vṛndā, freed from fear, with joined palms, prostrating like a staff on the ground before that lord of sages, spoke these words.
m.2.5.23.18: Vṛndā said: O lord of sages, ocean of compassion, remover of others' suffering, I have been protected by you from this dreadful danger arising from the wicked ones.
m.2.5.23.19: You are capable in every way and all-knowing too, O treasury of compassion. I wish to submit something; kindly listen to it.
m.2.5.23.20: Jalandhara, my husband, has gone to fight Rudra, O lord. How is he faring there in battle? Tell me that, O you of good vows.
m.2.5.23.21: Sanatkumāra said: The sage, hearing her words, maintaining a deceitful silence, skilled in contrivance, to accomplish his own purpose, looked upward as if in compassion.
m.2.5.23.22: Meanwhile two monkey-chiefs arrived, bowed to him and stood before him; then, directed by a sign of his creeper-like eyebrow, they went into the sky.
m.2.5.23.23: Having taken half a moment, they came back and again stood before him; with them were his Jalandhara's head, trunk and two hands, O lord of sages.
m.2.5.23.24: Seeing the head, trunk and two hands of the Ocean's son, she fell unconscious to the ground, grieved by her husband's calamity.
m.2.5.23.25: Vṛndā said: O lord, you who formerly delighted me with pleasant conversations — how is it that you do not speak today to me, your beloved, who am blameless?
m.2.5.23.26: He by whom the gods along with the Gandharvas, together with Viṣṇu, were conquered — how has that conqueror of the three worlds been slain today by an ascetic?
m.2.5.23.27: You, not knowing the true nature of Rudra, did not accept my word, O best of demons, when I said that Śiva is the supreme Brahman.
m.2.5.23.28: Hence you were truly understood by me through the power of my service to you; but you, proud and under the sway of bad company, did not understand at all.
m.2.5.23.29: Having spoken thus in many ways, his beloved, firm in her own dharma, lamented in diverse ways with a burning heart.
m.2.5.23.30: Then, taking courage and heaving sighs of grief, she bowed deeply with joined palms and spoke to that best of sages.
m.2.5.23.31: O treasury of compassion, best of sages, devoted to helping others, O good one, showing compassion to me, revive this lord of mine.
m.2.5.23.32: Since you are, in my view, able to bring him back to life, therefore revive this lord of my life, O lord of sages.
m.2.5.23.33: Sanatkumāra said: Having said this, the demon's wife, devoted to wifely fidelity, fell at his feet, heaving sighs of grief.
m.2.5.23.34: The sage said: This one, slain by Rudra in battle, cannot be revived; those slain by Rudra in battle never live again.
m.2.5.23.35: Nevertheless, filled with compassion, I shall revive him, knowing the eternal dharma that those who come for refuge must be protected.
m.2.5.23.36: Sanatkumāra said: Having said this and revived her husband, O sage, that sage — Viṣṇu, the best of all illusionists — then vanished.
m.2.5.23.37: Quickly revived by him, the son of the Ocean rose up and, embracing Vṛndā, kissed her face with a delighted mind.
m.2.5.23.38: Then Vṛndā too, seeing her husband, delighted in mind, cast off all her grief and considered it all in her heart as a dream.
m.2.5.23.39: Then, with a joyful heart and with desire arisen in her, she sported with him for many days, staying in the middle of that forest.
m.2.5.23.40: Once, at the end of their lovemaking, having seen that it was indeed Viṣṇu himself, Vṛndā, filled with anger, rebuked him and spoke these words.
m.2.5.23.41: Vṛndā said: Fie on such conduct, O Hari, of one who goes to the wives of others! I have come to know you fully: you are the deceiver who appeared before my eyes as an ascetic.
m.2.5.23.42: Sanatkumāra said: Having said this, she, devoted to wifely fidelity, fell into a rage and, displaying her own power, cursed Keśava, O Vyāsa.
m.2.5.23.43: O you vilest of the vile, enemy of the Daityas, corrupter of another's dharma, take, O rogue, this curse given by me, fiercer than every poison.
m.2.5.23.44: Those two whom you, by your illusion, presented to me as your own attendants, those very two, becoming Rākṣasas, will carry off your wife.
m.2.5.23.45: And you too, tormented by grief for your wife, shall wander in the forest with monkeys as your helpers, together with this lord of serpents who has become your disciple.
m.2.5.23.46: Having said this, Vṛndā then entered the fire, even though she was being held back by Viṣṇu, whose mind was attached to her.
m.2.5.23.47: At that moment, O sage, all the gods headed by Brahmā arrived in the sky together with their wives, eager to witness her blessed destiny.
m.2.5.23.48: Then that supreme, great radiance of the wife of the Daitya lord swiftly went to the realm beyond the worlds, while all the gods looked on.
m.2.5.23.49: That radiance of Vṛndā became merged in the body of Śivā; and cries of victory, victory arose among the ranks of immortals stationed in the sky.
m.2.5.23.50: Thus Vṛndā, the great queen, the excellent daughter of Kālanemi, attained supreme liberation, O sage, through the power of her wifely fidelity.
m.2.5.23.51: Then Hari, remembering her again and again, smeared with the dust of the ashes of Vṛndā's pyre, remained right there; though consoled by the hosts of gods and Siddhas, he found no peace.
m.2.5.23.iti: Thus ends the twenty-third adhyāya, named The description of the breaking of Vṛndā's wifely chastity and her giving up of her body, in the account of the slaying of Jalandhara, in the fifth khaṇḍa, the Yuddha-khaṇḍa, of the second saṃhitā, the Rudra-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.2.5.24.1: Vyāsa said: O best son of Vidhi (Brahmā), O wise one, you have narrated this wondrous story. And then what happened in the battle? How was the demon slain? Tell me.
m.2.5.24.2: Sanatkumāra said: When the lord of demons had come back to the battle and the Gandharva illusion had vanished, Vṛṣadhvaja (Śiva), not seeing Girijā there, regained his awareness.
m.2.5.24.3: Seeing that the illusion had disappeared, Śaṅkara, the Destroyer, understood; and adopting worldly behaviour, he became exceedingly angry.
m.2.5.24.4: Then Śiva, astonished in mind, went again in wrath to fight Jalandhara. And that demon too, seeing Śiva come back, covered him in the battle with floods of arrows.
m.2.5.24.5: The Lord Hara swiftly cut down with his own excellent arrows that fierce net of arrows hurled by the exceedingly mighty Jalandhara; there is nothing wonderful in this for the destroyer of the three worlds.
m.2.5.24.6: Then Jalandhara, seeing Rudra of wondrous valour, created Gaurī by illusion, as if to delude the Three-eyed One.
m.2.5.24.7: Śiva saw Pārvatī placed upon a chariot, bound and weeping, being beaten by the demons Niśumbha and Śumbha.
m.2.5.24.8: Seeing Gaurī in such a state, Śiva too, displaying worldly behaviour, became distressed in mind like an ordinary person.
m.2.5.24.9: He, skilled in manifold sports, stood silent with face downcast, limbs slack, dejected in spirit, forgetting his own prowess.
m.2.5.24.10: Then Jalandhara swiftly pierced that Rudra with three arrows, sunk in up to the feathers, in the head, the chest and the belly.
m.2.5.24.11: Then the Lord Rudra, of great sport, grasping the truth in an instant, assumed a terrible form, exceedingly fearsome with garlands of flames.
m.2.5.24.12: Seeing his exceedingly terrible form, the great asuras could not stand before him; they fled to the ten directions.
m.2.5.24.13: Even Niśumbha and Śumbha, who were famed as the best of heroes, were not at all able to stand in the battle, O lord of sages.
m.2.5.24.14: And the illusion created by Jalandhara vanished that very moment; a great cry of dismay arose on every side of the battlefield.
m.2.5.24.15: Then Rudra, filled with anger, seeing those two, Śumbha and Niśumbha, fleeing, reproached them and pronounced a curse upon them.
m.2.5.24.16: Rudra said: You two are wicked, utterly vile, offenders against me, inflicters of punishment on Pārvatī, and have turned your backs on this battle.
m.2.5.24.17: One who has turned his back is not to be slain—hence you two are not to be slain by me. Having escaped from my battle, you shall be slain by Gaurī.
m.2.5.24.18: As the Lord of Gaurī spoke thus, Jalandhara, son of the Ocean, resembling a blazing fire, became exceedingly enraged at Rudra.
m.2.5.24.19: In the battle he rained sharp arrows on Rudra with great force, and the surface of the earth became covered in a darkness of arrows.
m.2.5.24.20: While Rudra swiftly cut down his volleys of arrows, the mighty demon quickly struck the bull with an iron club.
m.2.5.24.21: By that blow the bull turned back from the battlefield; though pulled by Rudra, it would not stay on the field of battle.
m.2.5.24.22: Then the great Rudra displayed to everyone in the world his own utterly unbearable splendour—this is true, O lord of sages.
m.2.5.24.23: Then the Lord Rudra, supremely enraged, bearing a terrible body, suddenly became dreadful like the fire of dissolution.
m.2.5.24.24: Seeing the demon standing before him like a peak of Meru, and though he had heard of the demon's invulnerability to others, he became ready to slay him.
m.2.5.24.25: Upholding Brahmā's word, the Lord, protector of the worlds, extending grace in his heart, set his mind on slaying him.
m.2.5.24.26: Becoming supremely angry, the Trident-bearer playfully, with his big toe, quickly made in the great waters a terrible and wondrous discus.
m.2.5.24.27: Having made the sharp discus in the waters of the ocean, the blessed Lord, enemy of the cities—slayer of Dakṣa's sacrifice, of Andhaka, of Antaka and of the three cities, bringer of the end of the three worlds—remembering that the three worlds had been afflicted by this demon, spoke, laughing.
m.2.5.24.28: Mahārudra said: O Jalandhara, a discus has been fashioned with my foot in the great waters. If you are strong enough to lift it out, stay and fight—otherwise not.
m.2.5.24.29: Sanatkumāra said: Hearing those words of his, he, his eyes blazing with anger, looking at Śaṅkara as if to burn him with his eyes, spoke.
m.2.5.24.30: Jalandhara said: Having lifted up the line you drew, and having slain you together with your Gaṇas, O Śaṅkara, and having slain the worlds along with the gods, I shall take my own share, as Garuḍa took his.
m.2.5.24.31: I am able to slay all that moves and does not move, along with Vāsava (Indra). O Maheśvara, who in the three worlds is not pierceable by my arrows?
m.2.5.24.32: Even in my childhood the blessed Brahmā, the mightiest, together with the sages and the foremost gods, was overcome by me in my place through austerity alone.
m.2.5.24.33: By me the whole triple world with its moving and unmoving beings was burned in a moment by austerity. What, O Rudra—has even the Lord Brahmā been conquered by you?
m.2.5.24.34: Indra, Agni, Yama, the Lord of Wealth (Kubera), Vāyu, the Lord of Waters (Varuṇa) and others could not withstand me, just as serpents cannot bear the scent of the lord of birds.
m.2.5.24.35: O Śaṅkara, no vehicle worthy of me was found in heaven or on earth; reaching all the mountains, I assailed the lords of the Gaṇas.
m.2.5.24.36: The glorious Mandara, king of mountains, Nīla, and the most beautiful Meru were crushed by my staff-like arm to rid me of an itch.
m.2.5.24.37: The Gaṅgā was held back by my two arms on the Himālaya mountain for sport; and by my servants victory was won over my enemies, the heaven-dwellers.
m.2.5.24.38: Seizing the mare (Vaḍavā) with my hand, I bound her mouth; at that very instant everything then became a single ocean.
m.2.5.24.39: Airāvata and the other elephants were flung onto the waters of the ocean, and the blessed Indra with his chariot was flung a hundred yojanas.
