m.2.5.36.25: Their arms, thighs, hands, waists, pairs of ears and feet were severed; their banners, arrows, swords, armour and fine ornaments were shattered.
m.2.5.36.26: The earth shone, strewn with heads whose crowns had been knocked off, along with earrings, and with thighs shapely like elephant-trunks, destroyed in the fury.
m.2.5.36.27: —and with mighty arms severed, still bearing ornaments and weapons, and with other limbs, suddenly strewn as if with clusters swarming with bees.
m.2.5.36.28: In the battle, warriors, seeing with the eyes of their own severed heads their headless trunks running about, leapt up there with strong arms raising weapons.
m.2.5.36.29: Leaping about vigourously, the heroes of great strength and valour fought one another there with various weapons and missiles.
m.2.5.36.30: Some, having slain warriors in battle with golden-tipped arrows, roared heroic roars like rain-laden clouds.
m.2.5.36.31: One hero covered another hero, together with his chariot and charioteer, on all sides with a mass of arrows, as a cloud covers the sun in the rainy season.
m.2.5.36.32: Engaging one another, the duelists fought, challenging, pressing forward, and striking each other at the vital points.
m.2.5.36.33: Everywhere in the great battle bands of heroes were seen, with various arms, banners and weapons, raising lion-like roars.
m.2.5.36.34: The great heroes, thrilled with delight, each blew their loud-sounding conches and leapt about there.
m.2.5.36.35: Thus for a very long time there raged between the gods and the Dānavas a great, fierce, terrible battle that delighted the heroes.
m.2.5.36.36: This is the sport (līlā) of the great Lord Śaṅkara, the Supreme Self, by which everything, including gods, asuras and humans, is bewildered.
m.2.5.36.iti: Thus ends the thirty-sixth adhyāya, named The description of the battle between the two sides, in the slaying of Śaṅkhacūḍa, in the fifth khaṇḍa, the Yuddha-khaṇḍa, of the second saṃhitā, the Rudra-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.2.5.37.1: Sanatkumāra said: Then all the hosts of gods, defeated by the Dānavas, fled in fear, their bodies wounded by weapons and missiles.
m.2.5.37.2: Turning back, they went for refuge to Śaṅkara, lord of the universe, and said in a trembling voice, save us, save us, O Lord of all.
m.2.5.37.3: Seeing the defeat of the gods and the others, and hearing their fearful words, Śaṅkara became greatly enraged.
m.2.5.37.4: Looking on them with a glance of compassion, he granted the gods freedom from fear, and by his power he increased the strength of his own Gaṇas.
m.2.5.37.5: Then, commanded by Śiva, Skanda, the great hero and son of Hara, fought fearlessly in battle against the hosts of the Dānavas.
m.2.5.37.6: Growing angry and raising a warrior's cry, the god who was the slayer of Tāraka slew a hundred akṣauhiṇīs in battle.
m.2.5.37.7: Lotus-eyed Kālī made their blood flow; cutting off their heads, she suddenly devoured them.
m.2.5.37.8: She drank the blood of those Dānavas on every side, and fought a varied battle, terrifying to gods and Dānavas alike.
m.2.5.37.9: Likewise in battle, seizing with one hand ten million of the Dānavas' lordly elephants, she playfully tossed them into her mouth.
m.2.5.37.10: A thousand headless trunks danced wildly on the battlefield; a great uproar arose, terrifying to the cowardly.
m.2.5.37.11: Again Skanda, flaring into fierce anger, let loose a rain of arrows, and in an instant felled the Asura leaders by the crore.
m.2.5.37.12: Then all the Dānavas who had escaped death, their bodies wounded by Skanda's net of arrows, fled in fear.
m.2.5.37.13: Vṛṣaparvan, Vipracitti, Daṇḍa and Vikampana—all of them fought with Skanda one after another.
m.2.5.37.14: Mahāmārī too fought and did not turn away; and they the demons were wounded in their limbs, sorely afflicted by Skanda's spear.
m.2.5.37.15: Then, O sage, victory went to Mahāmārī and Skanda; drums resounded in heaven and a shower of flowers fell.
m.2.5.37.16: Seeing Skanda's fight—most fierce and wondrous, destructive of the Dānavas like a cosmic dissolution—
m.2.5.37.17: and the havoc wrought by Mahāmārī that was causing their destruction, he Śaṅkhacūḍa suddenly grew exceedingly angry and then armed himself in person.
m.2.5.37.18: Mounting an excellent aerial chariot, furnished with many kinds of weapons and missiles, safe against all warriors, and adorned with many gems,
m.2.5.37.19: Śaṅkhacūḍa went forth amid his chariots with great heroes; drawing his bow to his ear, he released a shower of arrows.
m.2.5.37.20: That rain of his arrows was irresistible and terrifying, and a most dreadful darkness fell upon the field of slaughter.
m.2.5.37.21: All the gods fled, as did the others, Nandīśvara and the rest; Kārttikeya alone stood at the forefront of the battle.
m.2.5.37.22: The king Śaṅkhacūḍa sent down an irresistible, terrifying shower of mountains, serpents, elephants and trees.
m.2.5.37.23: Struck by that shower, Skanda, the son of Śiva, was like the sun covered by dense mist.
m.2.5.37.24: He Śaṅkhacūḍa worked his own magic of many kinds, taught by Maya; none of the gods or Gaṇas could comprehend it, O best of sages.
m.2.5.37.25: At that very moment Śaṅkhacūḍa, master of great magic and of great strength, cut his Skanda's bow with a single divine arrow.
m.2.5.37.26: He shattered his divine chariot, cut down the chariot's guards, and with a divine missile he battered the peacock.
m.2.5.37.27: He hurled a deadly spear, radiant as the sun, at his chest; by that blow he Skanda suddenly fainted for a moment.
m.2.5.37.28: Regaining consciousness, Kārtika, slayer of enemy heroes, mounted his own mount, made of the finest gems.
m.2.5.37.29: Remembering the feet of Maheśa together with Ambikā, the six-faced one took up his weapons and missiles and waged a fierce battle.
m.2.5.37.30: The son of Śiva in his wrath cut down all the serpents, mountains, trees and rocks with a divine missile.
m.2.5.37.31: He warded off the fire with a Pārjanya (rain) arrow, and with ease cut down Śaṅkhacūḍa's chariot and bow,
m.2.5.37.32: his armor, all his steeds, and his crown gleaming with its diadem; he raised a warrior's cry and roared again and again.
m.2.5.37.33: He hurled a spear radiant as the sun at the chest of the lord of the Dānavas; by that blow he Śaṅkhacūḍa fell into a very long swoon.
m.2.5.37.34: Shaking off that pain within a mere moment, the mighty one regained consciousness, rose up, and roared like a lion.
m.2.5.37.35: He in turn struck the mighty Kārtikeya with a spear; he Kārtikeya fell to the ground, honouring the unfailing power of the spear granted by Brahmā.
m.2.5.37.36: Kālī took him in her lap and carried him into Śiva's presence; and Śiva, by his knowledge, revived him with ease.
m.2.5.37.37: He gave him boundless strength; the valiant son of Śiva rose up and resolved to go there, to the battle, again.
m.2.5.37.38: Meanwhile the heroic and mighty Vīrabhadra fought in battle with the powerful Śaṅkhacūḍa.
m.2.5.37.39: Whatever missiles the Dānava rained down in battle, the hero cut each of them to pieces with ease with his own arrows.
m.2.5.37.40: The lord of the Dānavas released divine missiles by the hundred; the valiant Vīrabhadra cut them down and struck him with arrows.
m.2.5.37.41: Then the valiant Śaṅkhacūḍa became exceedingly furious and struck him on the chest with a spear; he trembled and fell to the ground.
m.2.5.37.42: Regaining consciousness in a moment, the lord of the gaṇas, Vīrabhadra, foremost among the gaṇas, rose up and took up his bow once more.
m.2.5.37.43: Meanwhile Kālī went to the battle again, at Kārttikeya's wish, to devour the Dānavas and to protect her own side.
m.2.5.37.44: And the heroes followed her—Nandīśvara and the others—as well as all the gods, Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Rākṣasas and serpents.
m.2.5.37.45: There were wine-vessels in abundance and hundreds of bearers of musical instruments. Once again all the heroes on both sides stood ready for battle.
m.2.5.37.iti: Thus ends the thirty-seventh adhyāya, named The description of the battle with Śaṅkhacūḍa and his army, in the slaying of Śaṅkhacūḍa, in the fifth khaṇḍa, the Yuddha-khaṇḍa, of the second saṃhitā, the Rudra-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.2.5.38.1: Sanatkumāra said: She went to the battle and let out a lion's roar, and at that roar of the Goddess the Dānavas fainted.
m.2.5.38.2: Again and again she gave out a dreadful, boisterous laugh; then she drank honey-wine and danced at the forefront of the battle.
m.2.5.38.3: Ugradaṃṣṭrā, Ugradaṇḍā and Koṭavī drank wine, and the other goddesses there in the battle danced and drank wine.
m.2.5.38.4: Then a great uproar arose in the army of the Gaṇas and gods; all the hosts of gods and the rest rejoiced, roaring loudly.
m.2.5.38.5: Seeing Kālī, Śaṅkhacūḍa quickly came to the battle; the Dānavas were struck with fear, and the king gave them reassurance.
m.2.5.38.6: Kālī hurled fire resembling the flames of the fire of cosmic dissolution; the king swiftly destroyed it with ease by a Vaiṣṇava weapon.
m.2.5.38.7: The Goddess swiftly hurled the Nārāyaṇa missile at him; seeing the Dānava hostile, that weapon grew in power.
m.2.5.38.8: Seeing it, resembling the flames of the fire of dissolution, Śaṅkhacūḍa fell flat on the ground like a staff and bowed again and again.
m.2.5.38.9: Seeing the Dānava humbled, that weapon withdrew. Then the Goddess hurled the Brahmā missile, accompanied by mantras.
m.2.5.38.10: Seeing it blazing, the lord of the Dānavas bowed and stood on the ground, and warded it off with a Brahmā missile.
m.2.5.38.11: Then the enraged lord of the Dānavas, drawing his bow swiftly, hurled divine missiles at the Goddess, accompanied by mantras.
m.2.5.38.12: Opening wide her mouth, she devoured them in the battle and roared with loud laughter; the Dānavas were seized with fear.
m.2.5.38.13: He hurled at Kālī a spear a hundred yojanas long; the Goddess cut it into a hundred pieces with a network of divine missiles.
m.2.5.38.14: He then hurled the Vaiṣṇava missile at Caṇḍikā, and Kālī warded it off with the Māheśvara missile.
m.2.5.38.15: Thus the battle between them went on for a very long time, and all the gods and the Dānavas too became spectators.
m.2.5.38.16: Then the great Goddess Kālī, enraged and like Death in battle, angrily took up the Pāśupata arrow, consecrated with mantras.
m.2.5.38.17: Before it was released, a bodiless voice arose to forbid it: O Goddess, do not in anger hurl this missile at Śaṅkhacūḍa.
m.2.5.38.18: O Caṇḍikā, there is no death for the hero Śaṅkhacūḍa even from the unfailing Pāśupata; consider some other means.
m.2.5.38.19: Hearing this, Bhadrakālī did not hurl that missile; out of hunger she playfully devoured ten million Dānavas.
m.2.5.38.20: The terrifying one rushed to devour Śaṅkhacūḍa, but the Dānava held her back with the divine Raudra missile.
m.2.5.38.21: Then the enraged lord of the Dānavas quickly hurled a sword, like the summer sun, sharp-edged and exceedingly terrifying.
m.2.5.38.22: Seeing it coming, blazing, Kālī in anger opened her mouth and devoured it while he looked on.
m.2.5.38.23: The lord of the Dānavas cut down her other divine missiles; even before they reached him he broke them into a hundred pieces.
m.2.5.38.24: Again the great Goddess rushed at him to devour him, but that glorious lord of all siddhis made himself invisible.
m.2.5.38.25: Not seeing the Dānava, Kālī with a swift blow of her fist smashed his chariot and, it is said, slew his charioteer.
m.2.5.38.26: Then the illusion-wielding Śaṅkhacūḍa, quickly reappearing, swiftly hurled at Bhadrakālī a discus resembling the flames of the fire of dissolution.
m.2.5.38.27: The Goddess then playfully caught that discus with her left hand and, in anger, quickly devoured it with her own mouth.
m.2.5.38.28: With great fury the Goddess swiftly struck him with her fist; the lord of the Dānavas reeled and fainted for a moment.
m.2.5.38.29: Regaining consciousness in a moment, the mighty one rose up; but regarding her as his mother, he did not engage in hand-to-hand combat with her.
m.2.5.38.30: The Goddess seized the Dānava, whirled him round again and again, and with great fury flung him swiftly upward.
m.2.5.38.31: The mighty Śaṅkhacūḍa flew up with speed, and having fallen down, rose again and bowed to Bhadrakālī.
m.2.5.38.32: Cheerful in mind and not bewildered even in that great battle, he mounted a most charming aerial chariot built of the finest jewels.
m.2.5.38.33: Kālikā, out of hunger, drank the blood of the Dānavas. Meanwhile a bodiless voice arose there:
m.2.5.38.34: A hundred thousand arrogant Dānava chiefs now remain in the battle, together with those roaring ones; so you, O Īśvarī, devour them.
m.2.5.38.35: Do not set your mind on killing the lord of the Dānavas in battle; O Goddess, be certain that this Śaṅkhacūḍa cannot be slain by you.
m.2.5.38.36: Hearing these words issuing from the sky, the Goddess, having eaten the flesh of many Dānavas and drunk their blood as well,
m.2.5.38.37: having eaten and drunk, Bhadrakālī came into the presence of Śaṅkara and related the course of the battle in due order, from beginning to end.
m.2.5.38.iti: Thus ends the thirty-eighth adhyāya, named The description of Kālī's battle, in the slaying of Śaṅkhacūḍa, in the fifth khaṇḍa, the Yuddha-khaṇḍa, of the second saṃhitā, the Rudra-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.2.5.39.1: Vyāsa said: Having heard what Kālī said, what did Īśāna do, and what did he say? Tell me the truth, O greatly wise one; my curiosity is intense.
m.2.5.39.2: Sanatkumāra said: Having heard the words spoken by Kālī, Śaṅkara, the supreme Lord, Śambhu who performs great sports, laughed and reassured her.
m.2.5.39.3: Having heard the voice from the sky, Śaṅkara, expert in the knowledge of reality, went himself into battle together with his gaṇas.
m.2.5.39.4: Mounted on the great bull, accompanied by Vīrabhadra and others, attended by the Bhairavas and Kṣetrapālas who were equal to himself,
m.2.5.39.5: Maheśa reached the battlefield and, having assumed a heroic form, Rudra shone there exceedingly, like Death (Antaka) embodied.
m.2.5.39.6: Śaṅkhacūḍa, on seeing Śiva, descended from his aerial chariot and bowed with supreme devotion, touching his head to the ground, prostrate like a staff.
m.2.5.39.7: Having bowed to him by yogic power, he mounted the aerial chariot; swiftly he armed himself and seized his bow together with arrows.
m.2.5.39.8: The battle between Śiva and the Dānava lasted a hundred years; that shower of arrows was then as fierce as the rain of two clouds pouring down.
m.2.5.39.9: Śaṅkhacūḍa, the great hero, hurled terrible arrows; Śaṅkara cut them down playfully with his own volleys of arrows.
m.2.5.39.10: And in anger Mahārudra, the odd-eyed one, the punisher of the wicked and refuge of the good, struck his limbs with floods of weapons.
m.2.5.39.11: The swift Dānava, taking a sharp sword and a shield, struck on the head the bull, Śiva's excellent mount.
m.2.5.39.12: When his mount was struck, Rudra playfully and swiftly cut, with a razor-edged arrow, his sword and also his brilliantly shining shield.
m.2.5.39.13: When his shield was cut, that Asura then hurled a spear; Hara split it in two with his own arrow as it came at him.
m.2.5.39.14: Swollen with rage, the Dānava Śaṅkhacūḍa hurled a discus; Hara suddenly pulverized that too with a blow of his fist.
m.2.5.39.15: Whirling a mace with force, he hurled it at Hara; it too, struck suddenly by Śambhu, was shattered and reduced to ashes.
m.2.5.39.16: Then the lord of the Dānavas, Śaṅkhacūḍa, seizing an axe in his hand and overcome with fury, rushed swiftly at Hara.
m.2.5.39.17: Striking him with floods of his own arrows, Śaṅkara playfully and quickly felled that axe-wielding Asura to the ground.
m.2.5.39.18: Then, regaining consciousness in a moment, he mounted his fine chariot and, bearing divine weapons and arrows, shone forth, pervading the whole sky.
m.2.5.39.19: Seeing him approach, Hara intently sounded his ḍamaru and also made the unbearable twang of his bowstring.
m.2.5.39.20: The Lord filled the quarters with the blast of his horn, and Giriśa himself roared, terrifying the Asuras then.
m.2.5.39.21: The lord of bulls, with mighty bellows that made elephants abandon their great pride, suddenly filled the sky, the earth and the eight directions.
m.2.5.39.22: Mahākāla, leaping up, struck the earth and the sky with his two hands; by that resounding, all earlier sounds were drowned out.
m.2.5.39.23: The Kṣetrapāla let out an ominous, booming laugh, and Bhairava too made a great roar in that great battle.
m.2.5.39.24: A great, terrifying uproar arose in the midst of the battle, and then heroic shouts rang out on all sides among the gaṇas.
m.2.5.39.25: All the Dānavas trembled at those harsh, fear-inspiring sounds; hearing them, the mighty lord of the Dānavas became exceedingly enraged.
m.2.5.39.26: When Hara cried, stand, stand, O wicked one, the gods and the gaṇas at once shouted, victory, victory!
m.2.5.39.27: Then the very valourous son of Dambha came forward and hurled at Rudra a spear exceedingly terrible with garlands of flame.
m.2.5.39.28: As it came on, blazing like a mass of fire, the Kṣetrapāla swiftly advanced and repelled it in the battle with a great meteor issuing from his mouth.
m.2.5.39.29: Again a great battle began between Śiva and the Dānava; the earth and heaven shook, together with mountains, oceans and lakes.
m.2.5.39.30: Śambhu then cut the arrows released by Dambha's son, and he cut the arrows sent by him, with fierce arrows, by thousands and by hundreds.
m.2.5.39.31: Then Śambhu, greatly enraged, struck him with his trident; unable to bear that blow, he quickly fell to the ground unconscious.
m.2.5.39.32: Then in a moment that Asura regained consciousness and, taking up his bow, struck Rudra and all those gaṇas with arrows.
m.2.5.39.33: Assuming ten thousand arms, the valourous Śaṅkhacūḍa suddenly covered Śaṅkara with ten thousand discuses.
m.2.5.39.34: Then Rudra, lord of Durgā and destroyer of the distress of the afflicted, enraged, quickly cut those discuses with his excellent arrows.
m.2.5.39.35: Then the Dānava, suddenly seizing a mace, surrounded by a great army, rushed with speed to kill Hara.
m.2.5.39.36: As he charged, Hara, the remover of the pride of the wicked, greatly enraged, swiftly cut his mace with a sharp-edged sword.
m.2.5.39.37: When his mace was cut, the Dānava became exceedingly enraged; the mighty one seized a blazing spike unbearable to others.
m.2.5.39.38: As the handsome lord of the Dānavas came on, lance in hand, Hara swiftly pierced him in the heart with his own trident.
m.2.5.39.39: From Śaṅkhacūḍa's heart, split by the trident, there emerged another mighty person, who said, stand, stand.
m.2.5.39.40: As he was emerging, Hara then, laughing loudly, quickly cut off his fearsome head with the sword, and he fell to the ground.
m.2.5.39.41: Then Kālī, opening her mouth wide in anger, fiercely devoured those many asuras, whose necks were crushed by her fangs.
m.2.5.39.42: The Kṣetrapāla, agitated with rage, devoured many other daityas. Some perished cut down by the Bhairava weapon, and others likewise perished pierced.
m.2.5.39.43: Vīrabhadra in anger destroyed many other warriors; Nandīśvara slew many others, the oppressors of the immortals.
m.2.5.39.44: In this way many heroic gaṇas, then arming themselves in fury, destroyed many daityas and asuras, the oppressors of the gods.
m.2.5.39.45: Thus a very great part of his army perished there, and many other warriors fled, distressed with fear.
m.2.5.39.iti: Thus ends the thirty-ninth adhyāya, named The description of the slaying of Śaṅkhacūḍa's army, in the fifth khaṇḍa, the Yuddha-khaṇḍa, of the second saṃhitā, the Rudra-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.2.5.40.1: Sanatkumāra said: Then, seeing his own army slain, its chief and greater part, and likewise his heroes who were dear to him as life, the Dānava became extremely angry.
m.2.5.40.2: He spoke these words to Śambhu: I stand in the battle; you too stand firm. What does it matter that these of mine have been slain today? Fight with me face to face.
m.2.5.40.3: Having said this, O sage, that lord of the Dānavas, armed for battle, made up his mind and went straight towards Śaṅkara.
m.2.5.40.4: The Dānava hurled divine missiles at the great Rudra and released a shower of arrows, as a cloud releases a shower of rain.
m.2.5.40.5: He produced many kinds of illusions, invisible and terrifying to behold, which could not be fathomed even by all the hosts of gods, even the best of them.
m.2.5.40.6: Seeing that illusion, Śaṅkara there playfully discharged the Māheśvara missile, most divine, the destroyer of all illusions.
m.2.5.40.7: By its brilliance his illusions were then quickly destroyed, and those very divine missiles also became powerless.
m.2.5.40.8: Then in the battle the mighty Great Lord, to kill him, suddenly seized his trident, irresistible even to the most powerful.
m.2.5.40.9: At that very moment, to restrain it, a bodiless voice arose: Do not hurl the trident now; hear our request, O Śaṅkara.
m.2.5.40.10: You are surely capable in every way of destroying the whole cosmic egg in an instant; what then, O Lord, of a single Dānava, Śaṅkhacūḍa, now?
m.2.5.40.11: Even so, the bounds set by the Veda should not be destroyed by you, the Master. Hear it, O Mahādeva, and make it fruitful in truth.
m.2.5.40.12: As long as the supreme, most formidable armour of Hari is on his hand body, and as long as the chastity of his chaste wife remains,
m.2.5.40.13: so long there is no old age or death for this Śaṅkhacūḍa, O Śaṅkara. Make true, O Lord, this word of Brahmā.
m.2.5.40.14: Hearing the heavenly voice, Hara then said, so be it. Viṣṇu came by Hara's wish, and Hara, the refuge of the good, instructed him.
m.2.5.40.15: In the guise of an old brāhmaṇa, Viṣṇu, the best of illusionists, went near Śaṅkhacūḍa and then spoke to him.
m.2.5.40.16: The old brahmin said: Give alms, O lord of the Dānavas, to me who have now come to you.
m.2.5.40.17: I will not state it openly now to you, who are kind to the needy; I will tell you afterwards, and you will then make your promise true.
m.2.5.40.18: The great king, with a cheerful face and eyes, said, Om, yes. Then, with clever deceit, the brāhmaṇa said, I am a person who seeks the armour.
m.2.5.40.19: Hearing that, that lord of the Dānavas, devoted to brāhmaṇas, truthful in speech and mighty, gave that divine armour, dear to him as life, to the brāhmaṇa.
m.2.5.40.20: Thus by deceit Hari took the armour from him, and in the form of Śaṅkhacūḍa went to Tulasī.
m.2.5.40.21: Having gone there, Hari, the Lord skilled in illusion, quickly deposited his seed in her womb for the sake of the gods' purpose.
m.2.5.40.22: Meanwhile, as Hari conveyed his word to Śambhu, the Lord seized the blazing trident to slay Śaṅkhacūḍa.
m.2.5.40.23: That trident of Śaṅkara, the Supreme Self, named Vijaya, shone forth, illuminating all the directions, heaven and earth.
m.2.5.40.24: It was like ten million midday suns and the flames of the fire of dissolution; irresistible, unassailable, never failing, the slayer of enemies;
m.2.5.40.25: a most fierce circle of radiance, the chief of all weapons and missiles, unbearable and terrifying to all gods and asuras;
m.2.5.40.26: capable of playfully destroying the whole universe, it stood there supreme, blazing, as if all splendour had gathered in one place;
m.2.5.40.27: a thousand bows in length and a hundred cubits in breadth; of the nature of the individual soul and Brahman, eternal in form and uncreated.
m.2.5.40.28: Whirling in the sky, that trident, by Śiva's command, fell upon Śaṅkhacūḍa in an instant and swiftly reduced him to ashes.
m.2.5.40.29: Then the trident of the Great Lord, its task accomplished, swift as thought, quickly returned through the sky to Śaṅkara, O brāhmaṇa.
m.2.5.40.30: Kettledrums sounded in heaven, Gandharvas and Kinnaras sang, sages and gods offered praise, and the hosts of Apsarases danced.
m.2.5.40.31: A shower of flowers fell continuously upon Śiva; Hari, Brahmā, Indra and the others, and likewise the sages, praised him.
m.2.5.40.32: Then Śaṅkhacūḍa, lord of the Dānavas, by Śiva's grace was freed from the curse and regained his former form.
m.2.5.40.33: From the bones of Śaṅkhacūḍa arose the species of conches; and conch-water is held sacred for all, except for Śaṅkara.
m.2.5.40.34: Especially to Hari and Lakṣmī conch-water is very dear, and also to those connected with him, but not to Hara, O great sage.
m.2.5.40.35: Having thus slain him, Śaṅkara, greatly delighted, mounted on his bull and surrounded by Umā, Skanda and the Gaṇas, went to Śivaloka.
m.2.5.40.36: Hari went to Vaikuṇṭha; Kṛṣṇa became at ease; the gods, filled with supreme bliss, reached their own domains.
m.2.5.40.37: The world attained great well-being; everything became free of obstacles and happy; the sky became clear, and the whole earth most auspicious.
m.2.5.40.38: Thus has been told the story of the Great Lord, which brings joy, removes all sorrow, bestows prosperity and fulfils all desires;
m.2.5.40.39: blessed, bringing fame and long life, warding off all obstacles, granting enjoyment and liberation, and yielding the fruit of all desires.
m.2.5.40.40: The wise man who constantly listens to this story of the moon-crested Śiva, or causes it to be heard, or reads it, or causes it to be read —
m.2.5.40.41: Here in this world one would obtain wealth, grain, sons and happiness; there is no doubt. One attains all desires, and above all, devotion to Śiva.
m.2.5.40.42: This incomparable narrative destroys all calamities, generates supreme knowledge, and increases devotion to Śiva.
m.2.5.40.43: By hearing it, a brāhmaṇa becomes endowed with the radiance of sacred knowledge, a kṣatriya becomes victorious, one born a vaiśya becomes rich in wealth, and a śūdra attains excellence.
m.2.5.40.iti: Thus ends the fortieth adhyāya, named The account of the slaying of Śaṅkhacūḍa, in the fifth khaṇḍa, the Yuddha-khaṇḍa, of the second saṃhitā, the Rudra-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.2.5.41.1: Vyāsa said: And by what means did the Lord Nārāyaṇa deposit his seed in the womb of Tulasī? Please tell me that.
m.2.5.41.2: Sanatkumāra said: Nārāyaṇa, the accomplisher of the gods' tasks and the refuge of the good, in the form of Śaṅkhacūḍa sported with his Śaṅkhacūḍa's wife.
m.2.5.41.3: Hear that very delightful account of Viṣṇu, Hari, the executor of Śiva's command and the mother (nourisher) of the worlds.
m.2.5.41.4: In the midst of battle, having heard the voice from the sky and been urged by the god Śambhu, Hari, having taken the supreme armour of Śaṅkhacūḍa,
m.2.5.41.5: Hari, first in the guise of a brahmin, swiftly by his own māyā went in the form of Śaṅkhacūḍa to Tulasī's house.
m.2.5.41.6: He had the kettledrum sounded near Tulasī's door, and right there, with a cry of victory, he made the beautiful lady aware of his arrival.
m.2.5.41.7: Hearing that, the virtuous lady, filled with supreme joy, looked at the royal road through the window with great eagerness.
m.2.5.41.8: Having given wealth to brahmins, she had auspicious rites performed; knowing her own husband had come, she quickly adorned herself.
m.2.5.41.9: Getting down from the chariot, Viṣṇu—that master of māyā, doer of the gods' work, in the form of Śaṅkhacūḍa—went to the goddess's dwelling.
m.2.5.41.10: Seeing him, her beloved, arrived before her, she, full of joy, washed his feet, bowed, and wept.
m.2.5.41.11: She seated the auspicious one on a lovely jewelled throne and gave him betel perfumed with camphor and other fragrances.
m.2.5.41.12: Today my birth and life have become fruitful, as I see again at home the lord of my life who had gone to battle.
m.2.5.41.13: Having said this, she looked at him joyfully with sidelong glances and a smile, and asked her beloved in a sweet voice about the events of the battle.
m.2.5.41.14: Tulasī said: He is the destroyer of countless universes, the foremost of gods, the Lord, whose command the gods Viṣṇu, Brahmā and others always obey.
m.2.5.41.15: He is the progenitor of the three gods, whose self is the three guṇas yet who is beyond the guṇas; by the wish of his devotees he takes on qualities, and sets Hari and Brahmā to work.
m.2.5.41.16: At Kubera's request Hara assumed a form with qualities; he dwells on Kailāsa, is lord of the gaṇas, the supreme Brahman, the refuge of the good.
m.2.5.41.17: By a mere moment of whose time crores of universes are dissolved, and in a mere instant many Viṣṇus, Brahmās and others have passed away—
m.2.5.41.18: with him you went to wage battle, my lord. How did the war go with him, the ally of the gods?
m.2.5.41.19: You have come here safe, having conquered that Supreme Lord. How did your victory come about? Tell me just that.
m.2.5.41.20: Hearing Tulasī's words thus, the lord of Ramā, bearing the form of Śaṅkhacūḍa, laughed and spoke nectar-like words to her.
m.2.5.41.21: The Lord said: When I, fond of battle, went to the battlefield, a great uproar arose and a mighty battle began.
m.2.5.41.22: A battle took place between the gods and the Dānavas, both eager for victory; there the Daityas were defeated by the immortals, proud of their strength.
m.2.5.41.23: Then I fought there with the gods, fierce in strength, and those gods, defeated, went to Śaṅkara for refuge.
m.2.5.41.24: Rudra too came to the battle to help them, and I, proud of my strength, fought with him for a long time.
m.2.5.41.25: Our battle, beloved, went on for a full year, and all the Asuras perished, O loving one.
m.2.5.41.26: Brahmā himself brought about friendship between us two, and by Brahmā's command the gods were given back their offices.
m.2.5.41.27: I have come to my own home, and Śiva has gone to Śivaloka. Complete well-being has been attained and the trouble is gone.
m.2.5.41.28: Sanatkumāra said: Having said this, the lord of the worlds went to bed, and there the lord of Ramā joyfully made love with that lady.
m.2.5.41.29: The chaste lady, because of a difference in the pleasure, the union and the embrace, suspected everything and said, who are you?
m.2.5.41.30: Tulasī said: Who are you? Tell me quickly. I have been enjoyed by you through deceit; my chastity has been destroyed—now I shall curse you.
m.2.5.41.31: Sanatkumāra said: Hearing Tulasī's words, Hari, out of fear of the curse, playfully assumed his own most charming form, O brahmin.
m.2.5.41.32: Seeing that form and recognising Viṣṇu by his marks, Tulasī, enraged at the loss of her wifely fidelity, spoke to him.
m.2.5.41.33: Tulasī said: O Viṣṇu, you have no compassion; your mind is like stone. By the violation of my wifely dharma my husband has surely been slain.
m.2.5.41.34: Since you are like stone, pitiless and wicked, therefore by my curse become now a stone in form.
m.2.5.41.35: Those who call you an ocean of compassion are deluded, no doubt. How was your devotee slain without any offence, for another's sake?
m.2.5.41.36: Sanatkumāra said: Having said this, Tulasī, the chaste beloved of Śaṅkhacūḍa, stricken with grief, wept bitterly and lamented again and again.
m.2.5.41.37: Then, seeing her weeping, Viṣṇu the Supreme Lord called to mind the god Śaṅkara, by whom the world is bewildered.
m.2.5.41.38: Then Śaṅkara, affectionate to his devotees, appeared; he was bowed to and humbly praised by Hari.
m.2.5.41.39: Seeing Hari overwhelmed with grief and his Śaṅkhacūḍa's beloved lamenting, Śiva consoled him and her with sound counsel, she being tender toward the afflicted.
m.2.5.41.40: Śaṅkara said: Do not weep, Tulasī, for a person reaps the fruit of his own actions. In this world, an ocean of karma, there is no one who gives happiness or sorrow to another.
m.2.5.41.41: Listen, free from sorrow, to what is now at hand; Hari too listens with a glad mind. What brings happiness to you both, that I declare for the sake of your happiness.
m.2.5.41.42: O good lady, penance was performed by you; this is the fruit of that very penance. How could it be otherwise? So it has come to pass in you.
m.2.5.41.43: Abandoning this body and assuming a divine body, delight forever with Hari; become equal to Ramā (Lakṣmī).
m.2.5.41.44: This body of yours, cast off, shall become a river here; in Bhārata, holy in form, it will be renowned as the Gaṇḍakī.
m.2.5.41.45: After some time, O great goddess, by my boon, Tulasī will become the chief means in the worship of the gods.
m.2.5.41.46: In heaven, in the mortal world and in the netherworld, abide near Hari. Become the Tulasī plant, O beautiful one, the best among flowers.
m.2.5.41.47: You, the presiding goddess of the plant, divine in form in Vaikuṇṭha, will forever sport in private together with Hari.
m.2.5.41.48: As the presiding goddess of the river, who bestows great merit in Bhārata, you will become the wife of the Salt Ocean, a portion of Hari.
m.2.5.41.49: And Hari, in the form of a rock, will take up his abode near the bank of the Gaṇḍakī in Bhārata, because of your curse.
m.2.5.41.50: There crores of fearsome insects with sharp teeth, boring into it, will make in its hollow its characteristic discus-mark.
m.2.5.41.51: That indeed is the Śālagrāma stone, extremely meritorious owing to that boring; according to the varieties of discus-marks it will be named Lakṣmīnārāyaṇa and so on.
m.2.5.41.52: The union of Viṣṇu's Śālagrāma stone with you, Tulasī, which is ever of matching form, greatly increases merit.
m.2.5.41.53: Whoever separates a Tulasī leaf from the Śālagrāma, O good lady, will in another birth suffer separation from his wife.
m.2.5.41.54: Whoever, setting aside the conch, separates a Tulasī leaf from it, he too will be without a wife and diseased for seven births.
m.2.5.41.55: The Śālagrāma, the Tulasī and the conch — the man of great wisdom who keeps them together in one place becomes dear to Śrī Hari.
m.2.5.41.56: You were the beloved of Śaṅkhacūḍa for the span of one manvantara; your separation from the conch is only a cause of grief to you.
m.2.5.41.57: Sanatkumāra said: Having spoken thus, Śaṅkara then declared there the greatness of the Śālagrāma stone and of Tulasī, which bestows much merit.
m.2.5.41.58: Then, having vanished after gladdening Hari and her, Śambhu — ever the giver of bliss to the good — went to his own abode.
m.2.5.41.59: Having heard these words of Śambhu, Tulasī became pleased; and abandoning that body, she assumed a divine form.
m.2.5.41.60: The Lord of Kamalā (Viṣṇu) went with her to Vaikuṇṭha, and at once the river Gaṇḍakī came into being, born from her body.
m.2.5.41.61: Acyuta too became a rock on its bank, bestowing merit on men; and there insects make holes of many kinds, O sage.
m.2.5.41.62: The stones that fall into the water there are extremely meritorious; those that stay on land are to be known as tawny (piṅgalā) and indeed lead to affliction.
m.2.5.41.63: Thus all has been told in accordance with your question: the merit-giving story of Śambhu, which grants men all their desires.
m.2.5.41.64: This holy narrative, blended with the greatness of Viṣṇu and granting enjoyment and liberation, has been narrated. What more do you wish to hear?
m.2.5.41.iti: Thus ends the forty-first adhyāya, named The description of Tulasī's curse, in the account of the slaying of Śaṅkhacūḍa, in the fifth khaṇḍa, the Yuddha-khaṇḍa, of the second saṃhitā, the Rudra-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.2.5.42.1: Nārada said: Having heard of the slaying of Śaṅkhacūḍa, the deed of the moon-crested Śiva, I am not yet satisfied hearing from you, just as a person is never sated having drunk nectar.
m.2.5.42.2: O Brahmā, tell me the deed of that great-souled Maheśa, who, resorting to māyā, performs noble sport that gives joy to his devotees.
m.2.5.42.3: Brahmā said: Having heard of the slaying of Śaṅkhacūḍa, Vyāsa, son of Satyavatī, asked about this very matter the son of Brahmā, the lord of sages.
m.2.5.42.4: Sanatkumāra, having highly praised the deed of Maheśa, which is the abode of auspiciousness, spoke to Vyāsa, son of Satyavatī.
m.2.5.42.5: Sanatkumāra said: Listen, O Vyāsa, to the auspicious deed of Maheśa: how Andhaka attained the leadership of the gaṇas of Śambhu, the Supreme Self,
m.2.5.42.6: having first fought a supreme battle with him, O lord of sages, and having propitiated that Maheśāna again and again through a pure (sāttvic) disposition.
m.2.5.42.7: Hear the wondrous greatness of Śambhu, protector of those who seek refuge, loving towards true devotees, who sports in many kinds of play.
m.2.5.42.8: Having heard this greatness of the bull-bannered one, the sage, son of Gandhavatī, bowing with devotion, spoke words of great import to that son of Brahmā, the chief of sages.
m.2.5.42.9: Vyāsa said: Who indeed is Andhaka, O Lord, O master of sages? In whose mighty lineage on earth was that great-souled, strong and foremost one born? Of what nature is Andhaka, and whose son?
m.2.5.42.10: Tell me all this today with its secrets, O son of Brahmā, out of your grace. For I have learned some of it well from Skanda, the son of Maheśa, of boundless understanding.
m.2.5.42.11: How did he attain the leadership of the gaṇas of Śambhu of supreme splendour? Exceedingly blessed indeed is that Andhaka who became a lord of gaṇas.
m.2.5.42.12: Brahmā said: Having heard this speech of Vyāsa, that son of Brahmā then narrated the deeds of Maheśvara, which bring supreme fortune, to the father of Śuka, who was eager to hear them.
m.2.5.42.13: Sanatkumāra said: Formerly that emperor of the immortals, bestower of grace on devotees, accompanied by the mountain's daughter and the gaṇas, desiring to sport, came from Kailāsa, his own mountain, to Kāśī.
m.2.5.42.14: Having made his capital there, he performed many deeds that gave happiness to the people; and having made the hero named Bhairava its protector, he sported together with the mountain-born Pārvatī.
m.2.5.42.15: Once he went to the mountain named Mandara, owing to the excellent power of the boon granted to it. There too, accompanied by Śivā, he sported abundantly with the chief heroes of various gaṇas.
m.2.5.42.16: Then, on the eastern side of the Mandara mountain, Pārvatī, staying there, playfully and in jest closed the eyes of the matted-haired one of fierce valour.
m.2.5.42.17: With her lotus-hands bearing the lustre of coral, gold and lotus, she closed his eyes. When Hara's eyes were closed, in an instant a very great darkness arose.
m.2.5.42.18: Through contact with Maheśvara's touch, the moisture of passion dripped from her hands; and on Śambhu's forehead, heated in a moment by the fire of his eye, a large drop of water issued forth.
m.2.5.42.19: Then it became an embryo and a being: with a dreadful face, terrifying, given to wrath, ungrateful, blind, misshapen, matted-haired, black, non-human, deformed, and thickly haired.
m.2.5.42.20: Singing, laughing, weeping, dancing, licking its lips, with a deep and dreadful roar — when that one of wondrous appearance was born, Bhava said to Gaurī with a smile:
m.2.5.42.21: Śrī Maheśa said: Having closed my eyes, you yourself did the deed; why then, beloved, do you fear this one? Gaurī, having heard these words from Hara, laughing, released his eyes.
m.2.5.42.22: When light had returned, the one of dreadful form, born from darkness, was still eyeless. Seeing that being of such a kind, Gaurī questioned Maheśa, the Supreme Person.
m.2.5.42.23: Gaurī said: Who is this misshapen one, O Lord, born before us, dreadful and terrifying? Tell me the truth: for what reason, or by whom, was he created, and whose son is he?
m.2.5.42.24: Sanatkumāra said: Hearing these words of his beloved, Hara the sportive, maker of creation, smiling slightly, spoke about the blind form to the playful mother of the three worlds.
m.2.5.42.25: Maheśa said: Listen, Ambikā, doer of wondrous deeds: this one of wondrous, fierce valour has been born. When my eyes were closed by you, he was born of my sweat; his name is Andhaka.
m.2.5.42.26: You are his maker; he should be protected by you, together with your friends, with compassion, from the gaṇas, as befits. Regarding him as one with you, O noble lady, you should act with understanding.
m.2.5.42.27: Sanatkumāra said: Then Gaurī, having heard her husband's words, out of compassion, together with her friends, protected him by many and various means, as if he were her own son.
m.2.5.42.28: Then, at that time in the cool season, Hiraṇyanetra, desirous of a son, having seen the line of sons of his own elder brother, and urged by his wife, set out.
m.2.5.42.29: Resorting to the forest, the asura born of Kaśyapa then performed penance for a son, motionless like a log, having conquered the fault of anger, in order to behold Maheśvara.
m.2.5.42.30: Well pleased by his penance, the Pināka-bearer went to grant a boon, O best of the twice-born. Reaching that place, Maheśa, the bull-bannered, spoke to the foremost of the daityas.
m.2.5.42.31: Maheśa said: O lord of daityas, do not bring ruin on your senses. For what purpose have you undertaken this vow? Tell me your desire; I, Bhava, am the giver of boons. Whatever you wish, I will give it all.
m.2.5.42.32: Sanatkumāra said: Hearing Maheśa's gracious words, the daitya Kanakākṣa, exceedingly pleased, with joined palms and bowed head, having bowed to Girīśa and praised him in various ways, spoke:
m.2.5.42.33: Hiraṇyākṣa said: O moon-browed one, I have no son of great valour, befitting the race of the daityas. For that purpose I have undertaken this vow; grant me such a son of great valour, O lord of the gods.
m.2.5.42.34: Since my brother has five sons of boundless valour, headed by Prahlāda, while I here have none, I am without a line; who will seek to possess this kingdom of mine?
m.2.5.42.35: He who, having seized another's kingdom by his own strength, enjoys it, or enjoys his own kingdom, known to be his father's — he is called a son here and hereafter; through him that father too becomes one who has a son.
m.2.5.42.36: The upward course to heaven of those who have sons is declared by the wise, the best of the upholders of dharma. All beings strive thus for that very purpose; hence even beasts proceed so by their own nature.
m.2.5.42.37: For one without offspring there are no higher worlds; for that reason people seek sons from the gods; always worshipping the lotus-feet of the gods, they pray thus for even a single son.
m.2.5.42.38: Sanatkumāra said: Having heard these words of his, the compassionate Bhava, pleased with the daitya king, said to him: O lord of daityas, no son born of your own seed exists for you; but I shall give you a son.
m.2.5.42.39: My own son, named Andhaka, equal to you in valour and unconquered — choose him as your son; casting off all sorrow, accept that son yourself.
m.2.5.42.40: Having spoken thus, the great-souled Hara, pleased, accompanied by Gaurī, the lord of the bhūtas and other beings, the fierce enemy of Tripura, gave a son to Hiraṇyanetra.
m.2.5.42.41: Then that great-souled Daitya, having received the son from Hara, circumambulated him in due order, worshipped Rudra with many hymns, and, satisfied, went to his own kingdom.
m.2.5.42.42: Then, having obtained the son from Giriśa, the Daitya of fierce valour, after conquering all the gods without exception, carried this earth to Rasātala, his own realm.
m.2.5.42.43: Then Viṣṇu of infinite might, propitiated by the gods, sages and Siddhas, assumed the supreme boar form, all-pervading, made of sacrifice and terrifying.
m.2.5.42.44: Splitting the earth with various blows of his snout and entering the depths of Pātāla, he crushed the Daityas by hundreds with his snout and with his foremost, unbroken tusks,
m.2.5.42.45: and churning up the armies of the night-roamers with kicks shining like thunderbolts, afterwards he of wondrous fierce splendour, with the Sudarśana discus equal to ten million suns,
m.2.5.42.46: cut off the blazing head of Hiraṇyanetra and burnt up the wicked Daityas. Then, delighted, he there consecrated that Andhaka as king of the lords of the Diti-born.
m.2.5.42.47: Then the great-souled one, delighted, lifting up the earth from the depths of Pātāla with the tip of his tusk and bringing it to its own place, sustained the land and restored its former portion.
m.2.5.42.48: Praised by all the gods and the delighted sages, and by that Lotus-born Brahmā, Hari of fierce body, in the form of a boar, the accomplisher of the good task, went to his own world.
m.2.5.42.49: When Hiraṇyanetra, lord of the asuras, had thus been swiftly slain by the god in boar form, all the gods, all the sages and the other living beings became happy.
m.2.5.42.iti: Thus ends the forty-second adhyāya, named The slaying of Hiraṇyākṣa, in the fifth khaṇḍa, the Yuddha-khaṇḍa, of the second saṃhitā, the Rudra-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.2.5.43.1: Vyāsa said: O Sanatkumāra, all-knowing one, when that enemy of the gods had been slain, what did his elder brother, the great asura, do then?
m.2.5.43.2: O lord of sages, I have a curiosity here to hear this. Out of compassion, let me hear it, O son of Brahmā; salutation be to you.
m.2.5.43.3: Brahmā said: Having heard these words of Vyāsa, that lord of sages, Sanatkumāra, spoke, remembering the lotus-feet of Śiva.
m.2.5.43.4: Sanatkumāra said: When his brother had thus been slain by Hari in the form of a boar, O Vyāsa, Hiraṇyakaśipu burned with anger and grief.
m.2.5.43.5: Then he commanded the heroic asuras, who loved slaughter, to carry out a slaughter of the people; for he delighted in enmity toward Hari.
m.2.5.43.6: Then those asuras, fond of slaughter, receiving their master's command on their heads, wrought slaughter among the subjects of the gods.
m.2.5.43.7: Then, when the world was harassed by those evil-minded asuras, the gods abandoned heaven and wandered on earth unnoticed.
m.2.5.43.8: Hiraṇyakaśipu, grieving, performed the hand-offered water libations and other rites for his departed brother, and consoled his wives and others.
m.2.5.43.9: Then that king of daitya kings wished to make himself invincible, free from old age and death, without rival, and sole ruler.
m.2.5.43.10: He performed an extremely severe austerity in a valley of Mandara, with arms raised, gaze fixed on the sky, resting on the earth only by his big toes.
m.2.5.43.11: While he was performing austerity, all the gods, endowed with strength, conquered all the daityas and regained their own places.
m.2.5.43.12: From his head arose a smoky fire born of austerity; spreading in every direction, it scorched the worlds across, above and below.
m.2.5.43.13: Scorched by it, the gods left heaven and went to Brahmaloka; with faces distorted by his austerity, they reported to the Creator.
m.2.5.43.14: Then, informed by those gods, O Vyāsa, the self-born Creator, surrounded by Bhṛgu, Dakṣa and others, went to the hermitage of the lord of the daityas.
m.2.5.43.15: Then he, who had scorched all the worlds, saw the lotus-born Brahmā who had arrived. Wishing to grant a boon, the Creator, the Grandfather, said to him: Choose a boon. Hearing the sweet speech of the Creator, he of undeluded intellect spoke these words thus.
m.2.5.43.16: Hiraṇyakaśipu said: O Lord, lord of creatures, Grandfather, O god, may I never have fear of death from the strikes of weapons, missiles, nooses, thunderbolts, dry trees, great mountains, water, fire or enemies,
m.2.5.43.17: from gods, daityas, sages, siddhas, or beings created by you — why many words? — in heaven or on earth, by day or by night, neither from above nor from below, O lord of creatures.
m.2.5.43.18: Sanatkumāra said: Hearing such words of his, the lotus-born Brahmā, full of compassion, mentally bowing to Viṣṇu, said to him: O lord of daityas, I am pleased; obtain everything.
m.2.5.43.19: Enough of your austerity, performed for ninety-six thousand years; your desires are fulfilled. Arise, rule the kingdom of the dānavas. Hearing these words, he became cheerful.
m.2.5.43.20: Consecrated to kingship by the great-grandfather, he set his mind on destroying the three worlds. Intoxicated with power, he abolished all dharmas and conquered all the gods in battle.
m.2.5.43.21: Then, out of fear, all the gods led by Indra, oppressed by the best of daityas, having received the Grandfather's instruction, went to the ocean of milk where Hari reclines.
m.2.5.43.22: They worshipped Viṣṇu intensely, praising him with words, regarding him as the giver of happiness; then each of them related all their own sorrow to the gracious lord.
m.2.5.43.23: Having heard all their sorrow, the lord of Ramā, pleased, granted them boons. Upendra, rising from that couch, with various words befitting himself,
m.2.5.43.24: having consoled all the gods and sages, he whose splendour equals fire said: I will forcibly slay the daitya, O lords of the gods; go, contented, to your own abodes.
m.2.5.43.25: Hearing the words of Ramā's lord, all those lords of the gods, Śakra and the rest, greatly pleased, went to their own abodes, considering the younger brother of Hiraṇyanetra as already slain, O lord of sages.
m.2.5.43.26: Assuming a form with matted mane, terrifying, with tusks for weapons, sharp claws and a fine nose, part lion and part man, with gaping mouth, resembling ten million suns, most dreadful,
m.2.5.43.27: with power equal to the fire at the end of the age, pervading the universe — why many words? — when the sun had set, that lord, the great soul, went forth and reached the city of the asuras.
m.2.5.43.28: Having fought with the mighty daityas, and having slain and seized those hosts of daityas, Nṛsiṃha of wondrous valour roamed there and crushed those asuras one after another.
m.2.5.43.29: He of incomparable might was seen by the daityas, and all of them likewise set upon him. Seeing that all-pervading lion, Prahlāda by name, son of the lord of Diti's sons, said to the king: This king of beasts pervades the universe; why has he come?
m.2.5.43.30: Prahlāda said: This is the Lord, the Infinite, who in the mere form of a man-lion has entered within your city. Turn back from battle and go for refuge; I see the dreadful form of the lion,
m.2.5.43.31: than whom there is no equal warrior even in the three worlds. Rule your kingdom bowing to the king of beasts. Hearing his son's words, the wicked one said to him: Are you afraid here, son?
m.2.5.43.32: Having spoken thus to his son, that king, overlord of Diti's sons, said to the bull-like daityas, the best of heroes: You heroes, seize this lion with the hideous frowning gaze.
m.2.5.43.33: At his command those best of daityas, wishing to seize him, rushed into the king of beasts; in a moment they were burnt, like moths eager to enter a fire out of longing for its form.
m.2.5.43.34: Even though the daityas had been burnt, the king of daityas fought with the lord of beasts using all weapons and likewise all missiles — spears, lances, nooses, goads, fire and the like.
m.2.5.43.35: While those two, weapons in hand, were fighting, a day of Brahmā passed, O Vyāsa — the two great heroes roaring at each other with heroic cries, their minds full of anger.
m.2.5.43.36: Then that daitya, suddenly creating many arms holding weapons, and eyeing the Nṛsiṃha form, rushed at the king of beasts, who was fighting, suddenly from all sides.
m.2.5.43.37: Then, having waged a fierce and most unbearable battle with all weapons and all missiles, the great chief of daityas, when these were exhausted, approached Nṛsiṃha holding a trident.
m.2.5.43.38: Then he was seized by the lord of beasts with many arms hard as mountains; placing him on his knee, between his arms, with claw-tips that pierce the vital points of dānavas,
m.2.5.43.39: and tearing out with the weapon of his claws the lotus of the heart, mixed with blood, the daitya departed from life in a moment. Then he was cast aside like a log, all his limbs crushed again and again.
m.2.5.43.40: When that enemy of the gods had been slain, Viṣṇu of wondrous valour, well pleased, addressed Prahlāda, who had bowed to him, consecrated him in the kingship, and then departed to his unfathomable abode.
m.2.5.43.41: Then all the lords of the gods, Brahmā and the others, overjoyed, bowed in that direction, O brahmin, to Viṣṇu, the adorable Lord who had accomplished his own task, and went to their own abodes.
m.2.5.43.42: Thus, in the course of the narrative, have been described the birth of Andhaka from Rudra, the death of Hiraṇyanetra at the hands of the Boar, the destruction of his brother by Nṛsiṃha, and Prahlāda's attainment of the kingship.
m.2.5.43.43: Now hear from me, O best of brahmins, of Andhaka's might obtained from the creator of the world, of his battle with Hara, and afterwards of his attaining the lordship of the gaṇas of Giriśa.
m.2.5.43.iti: Thus ends the forty-third adhyāya, named The description of the attainment of the lordship of the gaṇas, the birth of Andhaka, and the slaying of Hiraṇyanetra and Hiraṇyakaśipu, in the fifth khaṇḍa, the Yuddha-khaṇḍa, of the second saṃhitā, the Rudra-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.2.5.44.1: Sanatkumāra said: Then once, while Hiraṇyākṣa's son was at play together with those brothers of his, he was made to hear these words from them, who were jesting and blind with intoxication: O blind one, what business have you with the kingdom now?
m.2.5.44.2: Hiraṇyanetra was indeed a fool, who obtained you—quarrelsome, eyeless, deformed and ugly—by propitiating Giriśa with fierce austerities.
m.2.5.44.3: So you are surely no sharer in the kingdom; can even one born of another obtain the kingdom? Let this be considered by you yourself; it is we who are truly its sharers.
m.2.5.44.4: Sanatkumāra said: Having heard those words of theirs and reflected on them with his intellect, he, dejected, pacified them himself with various words and went at night to a deserted forest.
m.2.5.44.5: There he performed austerity for ten thousand years and repeated the prayer to be muttered, standing on one foot, without food, with arms raised in his vow—an austerity which could not be performed even by gods and demons.
m.2.5.44.6: Kindling a fire, he offered into it, for a whole year, the flesh of his limbs along with blood, cutting it from his body with a sharp weapon and offering it each day with mantras.
m.2.5.44.7: Then he was a corpse with only sinews and bones left, and all his blood was exhausted. When there was no flesh left on him, he wished to cast his very body into the fire.
m.2.5.44.8: Then he was seen by all the dwellers of heaven, who were greatly astonished and filled with fear. Thereupon the Creator, praised with hymns by the immortals, was very quickly propitiated.
m.2.5.44.9: Then the Grandsire, restraining him, said to him: Choose a boon now. Whatever you desire to obtain, even what is very hard to get in all the world, O Dānava, take it.
m.2.5.44.10: Hearing the words of the lotus-born one, the Daitya, humble and bowing, said: May those cruel ones by whom my kingdom was snatched away—Prahrāda and the others—become my servants.
m.2.5.44.11: Likewise, may I, the blind one, have divine sight; may Indra and the others pay me tribute. And may there be no death for me from gods, Daityas, Gandharvas, Yakṣas, serpents or humans,
m.2.5.44.12: or from Nārāyaṇa, the foe of the lords of Diti's sons, or from any being, or from Śarva who pervades all. Hearing those very dreadful words of his, the lotus-born one, greatly apprehensive, said to him:
m.2.5.44.13: Brahmā said: O lord of Daityas, all this shall come to pass; but accept also some cause of your death. For there is none, born or yet to be born, who has not entered the mouth of Death.
m.2.5.44.14: Let good men like you renounce the wish for an excessively long life. Hearing these conciliatory words from the Grandsire, the Daitya spoke again.
m.2.5.44.15: Andhaka said: Among the women who exist in the three times—the best, the middling and the lowest—there is one, a very jewel among them, who is ever like a mother even to me;
m.2.5.44.16: a woman unapproachable by body, speech and even mind, and hard to obtain in the world of men. If I desire her, may destruction come to me from my Daitya-lordship, O blessed Self-born one.
m.2.5.44.17: Hearing those words, the lotus-born one, greatly astonished, remembered the lotus feet of Śaṅkara; and quickly receiving Śambhu's command, he then spoke to Andhaka.
m.2.5.44.18: Brahmā said: O Daitya, the boons you long for—all of it shall be as your words desire. Rise, O lord of Daityas, obtain your wish, and ever wage war with heroes.
m.2.5.44.19: O lord of sages, hearing these words of the Ordainer, the son of Hāṭakanetra, reduced to sinews and bones, quickly bowed with devotion to that god, the lord of the worlds, and said to him:
m.2.5.44.20: Andhaka said: How, O lord, can I enter the enemy's forces and fight with this body? Make this frame of mere sinews and bones full of flesh; touch me now with your holy hand.
m.2.5.44.21: Sanatkumāra said: Hearing his words, the lotus-born one touched his body with his hand and went to his own abode together with the lords of the gods, being worshipped by hosts of sages and Siddhas.
m.2.5.44.22: As soon as he was touched, that king of Daityas became full-bodied and strong; with eyes come into being he became handsome, and, delighted, he thus entered his own city.
m.2.5.44.23: Then the Dānava lords headed by Prahlāda, yielding the whole kingdom to him and knowing that he had come having obtained a boon, became his obedient servants.
m.2.5.44.24: Then Andhaka, accompanied by his army and with his band of servants, went to conquer heaven; having vanquished all the gods in battle, he made the wielder of the thunderbolt pay him tribute.
m.2.5.44.25: He conquered in battles the Nāgas, the Suparṇas, the foremost Rākṣasas, Gandharvas, Yakṣas and humans as well, the lords of mountains and the trees, and all quadrupeds, lions and the rest.
m.2.5.44.26: He brought these three worlds, moving and unmoving, under his control, subjecting them to himself. Then, going to many thousands of agreeable and beautiful women—
m.2.5.44.27: the lovely damsels in Rasātala, on earth and in heaven—he, united with them, sported on other delightful mountains and riverbanks.
m.2.5.44.28: Sporting in their midst with great delight, that lord of Dānavas drank, for his enjoyment, divine and choice human drinks left over after they had drunk.
m.2.5.44.29: Obtaining other divine things full of flavour—fruits and fragrant flowers—vehicles with fine mounts, and excellent mansions built by Maya,
m.2.5.44.30: beautified with flowers, offerings, incense, food and unguents, and wondrous to behold—thus ten thousands of years passed here for Andhaka as he sported.
m.2.5.44.31: That foolish Andhaka, chief of Daityas, his mind blinded by pride and having taken to evil company, never knew anything good for the hereafter that would bring happiness to himself.
m.2.5.44.32: Then, intoxicated, overpowering all the chief sons with sophistical arguments, that mighty one roamed about with the Daityas, destroying all Vedic dharmas.
m.2.5.44.33: Overcome by the pride of wealth, he respected neither the Vedas nor the brāhmaṇas, nor the immortals nor his elders. Thus, under the sway of fate, his life-span doomed, he took his pleasure, spending his years in days of self-indulgence.
m.2.5.44.34: Then once, when many crores of years had passed on this earth, he, delighted, went with his army to Mount Mandara.
m.2.5.44.35: Seeing its golden splendour there, he, maddened with pride, roamed about with his armies; and having reached that king of mountains for sport, he, out of delusion, resolved to dwell there.
m.2.5.44.36: Having built there a splendid, strong city, the lord of Daityas stayed joyfully by his power; and again, step by step, he settled a most wondrous city on the slope of Mount Mandara.
m.2.5.44.37: Duryodhana, and the two named Vaidhasa and Hasti, were ministers of that best of Dānavas. Once, on a fair spot of the mountain, all three of them saw a beautiful woman.
m.2.5.44.38: Those swift chiefs of the Daityas, out of joy, quickly approached the great lord of Daityas, Andhaka, foremost of heroes, and all of them told him with great delight what they had seen.
m.2.5.44.39: The ministers said: O lord of Daityas, here in a cave we saw a certain sage with eyes closed in meditation, handsome, his crest marked by the crescent moon, with the hide of a great elephant tied round his waist;
m.2.5.44.40: his whole body encircled by the coils of great serpents, adorned with a garland of skulls, with matted hair; he holds a trident, bears arrows and quiver, has a mighty bow, and a rosary of beads displayed.
m.2.5.44.41: He bears a sword, a trident and a staff, has matted locks, is four-armed and of a very fair form. He is smeared with ash, shines with splendid radiance, is the foremost of ascetics, and his whole attire is wondrous.
m.2.5.44.42: Not far from him a man was also seen — monkey-like, terrible-faced and frightful, holding every weapon, rough-handed, standing on guard; and there was an old white bull.
m.2.5.44.43: And beside that seated ascetic a certain woman was seen — young, charming, of exquisite form, auspicious, a very jewel on earth.
m.2.5.44.44: Clad in coral, pearls, gems, gold, jewels and garments, beautifully embraced by garlands — whoever has seen her truly has eyes; what purpose is there here in seeing anything else?
m.2.5.44.45: That divine woman, worthy of a great lord, is the beloved wife of a meritorious sage. O lord of Daityas, enjoyer of fine jewels, having her properly brought here, she is fit to be seen by you.
m.2.5.44.46: Sanatkumāra said: Having heard these words of theirs, that Daitya, overcome by lust, all his limbs reeling, at once dispatched Duryodhana and the others to the sage's presence.
m.2.5.44.47: Having approached that immeasurable sage of great vows, those foremost ministers of his, skilled in sound royal policy, bowed to him, O lord of sages, and spoke the Daitya's command.
m.2.5.44.48: The ministers said: The great-souled son of Hiraṇyanetra, overlord of the Daityas, named Andhaka, lord of the three worlds, by the command of the Creator, is staying here today, delighting in pleasure.
m.2.5.44.49: We are indeed his ministers, his personal heroes, and have come near you. Sent by him, O ascetic, listen attentively to what he has said to you.
m.2.5.44.50: Whose son are you? Why are you sitting here at ease, O wise best of sages? Whose is this young, beautiful woman? This auspicious one should be given to the lord of Daityas, O chief of sages.
m.2.5.44.51: How does this body of yours, smeared with ash, deformed, adorned with a garland of skulls, go with quivers, fine bows, arrows, swords, bhuśuṇḍis, tridents, thunderbolts and javelins?
m.2.5.44.52: Where is the most holy Jāhnavī on the crest of your matted locks, and where this moon — or a fragment of corpse-bone? Where the long-mouthed serpent with poisonous fire, and where union with a full-breasted woman?
m.2.5.44.53: Riding an old bull is not commendable, and such an appearance does not befit one who is forbearing. Where is this dharma of twilight salutation, and where this kind of eating? This is contrary to the world.
m.2.5.44.54: Give the woman to me peacefully. What austerity are you practising with a woman, O deluded one? This is improper and unbecoming in you, since I am the lord of jewels in the three worlds.
m.2.5.44.55: As told by me today, cast off your weapons; afterwards practise only pure austerity. If you transgress my irresistible command, you will lose this entire body.
m.2.5.44.56: Considering Andhaka wicked, the supreme Maheśvara, adopting a worldly manner, having heard the whole speech of the messengers, spoke thus to the Daitya with a smile.
m.2.5.44.57: Śiva said: If I am Rudra, what is that to you from me? Why do you speak falsely like this? Hear my power, O lord of Daityas: it is not proper for you to speak words in this way.
m.2.5.44.58: I do not remember my own father anywhere, nor my mother — I, most ignorant and deformed. Within the cave I practise this terrible Pāśupata vow, practised by no other.
m.2.5.44.59: This rootlessness is well known in me; all this that I have is very hard to give up. This young, beautiful woman is my wife — all-enduring, the very accomplishment of the all-pervading one.
m.2.5.44.60: Now, whatever pleases you, take that indeed, O Rākṣasa. Having said this much, Śambhu in ascetic's guise fell silent before them.
m.2.5.44.61: Sanatkumāra said: Having heard this profound speech, those Dānavas bowed to him with their heads and then went to the son of the foremost Daitya, who had vowed the destruction of the three worlds.
m.2.5.44.62: Undaunted in spirit, they all bowed there to the infatuated king, the lord of Daityas, and, beginning with cries of victory, told him what Rudra had said with a smile.
m.2.5.44.63: The ministers said: A night-roamer of fickle valour and courage — where is such a Dānava, wretched and devoid of strength, cruel, ungrateful and ever sinful? Where is a Dānava who fears the son of the Sun (Yama)?
m.2.5.44.64: O king, you, lord of all Daityas, have been addressed with a laugh by that ascetic sage — surely a hero of great might, who by his own understanding regards the three worlds as a straw.
m.2.5.44.65: He said: Where am I, and where are dreadful weapons, and where battle that terrifies even Death? Where is the warrior resembling a monkey-face, a night-roamer with limbs worn out by old age?
m.2.5.44.66: Where is this one of fair form, and where the unfortunate one? Where is your strength, and where mere plants? If you are capable, strive to make war — then come and do something.
m.2.5.44.67: Here is a weapon like the thunderbolt, terrible, destroying those like you. Where is your body, soft as a lotus? Having considered thus, do what pleases you.
m.2.5.44.68: These and similar words, sir, were spoken by the ascetic, O lord of Dānavas. Battle with him here is not proper for you — so he told you, O king, smiling indeed.
m.2.5.44.69: If you understand through the many utterances we have spoken, seemingly empty of substance, well; otherwise you will later remember this speech of the sage, the ascetic endowed with austerities.
m.2.5.44.70: Sanatkumāra said: Then, having heard their words — true and beneficial, yet crooked and very sharp — that dull-witted one blazed with rage like fire sprinkled with ghee.
m.2.5.44.71: Seizing a sword, intoxicated by the boon, rushing like a fierce wind, pierced by Smara's arrows, he whose fate had turned adverse made ready to go there.
m.2.5.44.iti: Thus ends the forty-fourth adhyāya, named The dialogue of the messenger, in the account of Andhaka's attainment of the rank of lord of the gaṇas, in the fifth khaṇḍa, the Yuddha-khaṇḍa, of the second saṃhitā, the Rudra-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.2.5.45.1: Sanatkumāra said: Then he set out, moving like a rutting lord of elephants, having drunk liquor, his eyes rolling. He was mighty, accompanied by a large army, a fierce hero marching with excellent warriors.
m.2.5.45.2: Then the demon, pierced by the arrows of Smara (Kāma), saw the cave whose path was blocked by Vīraka, just as an insect called a moth, seeing an oil-fed wick-lamp, rushes towards it.
m.2.5.45.3: Thus, showing himself quickly again and again, though harassed by Vīraka, that deluded Andhaka, lord of the great demons, had his body thoroughly scorched by the fire of lust.
m.2.5.45.4: Though harassed by terrors of stones, trees, thunderbolts, water, fire, serpents, weapons and missiles, he could not be driven back again; and he was asked, who are you that have come here?
m.2.5.45.5: Hearing those words, he declared his intent to him, and then fought with Vīraka for a while, a wondrous and immeasurable fight; in battle the demon was defeated by the greater hero.
m.2.5.45.6: Then, abandoning the forefront of battle, his throat parched with hunger and thirsty, he went away; his fine sword shattered and himself exhausted, he fled, his pride gone.
m.2.5.45.7: Then the chief sons of Diti, led by Prahlāda, did battle with Vīraka; their minds driven by the goad of shame, they became very fierce, with many hundreds of weapons.
m.2.5.45.8: There Virocana fought, and Bali, and thousand-armed Bāṇa, Bhaji, Kujambha and Śambara, and the valiant ones beginning with Vṛtra.
m.2.5.45.9: Fighting, they were defeated on all sides and cut in two by the gaṇa Vīraka. When many Dānavas had been slain, the hosts of Siddhas proclaimed, he is victorious!
m.2.5.45.10: On that terrifying field, a mire of blood, where bheruṇḍa creatures were dancing about, amid fat, marrow, flesh and pus, crowded with throngs of flesh-eaters—
m.2.5.45.11: When the Daityas had been routed, the Lord Pinākin, having consoled Dākṣāyaṇī well, said to her: Beloved, the very dreadful great Pāśupata vow which was formerly performed by me—
m.2.5.45.12: Śiva said: Therefore that strength of mine has been lost, since the immortal falls through association with mortals. O Devī, through constant attachment to you day and night, a grip that destroys merit has arisen.
m.2.5.45.13: To produce again that divine, supremely wondrous power, going to an excellent and more dreadful place, I shall therefore practise a still more terrible vow. O beautiful one, be wholly fearless and free from sorrow.
m.2.5.45.14: Sanatkumāra said: Having spoken these words, the great-souled one, raising a sound, slowly set about it; going there, blazing fiercely with the vow, he went to a most holy and very dreadful forest.
m.2.5.45.15: —a vow such as could not be practised by gods or demons, lasting a full thousand years. Pārvatī, staying on Mount Mandara, awaiting Bhava's return—
m.2.5.45.16: —devoted to her husband, endowed with good conduct and virtues, alone and ever frightened, was overcome with grief inside the cave, guarded by her son Vīraka.
m.2.5.45.17: Then that demon, intoxicated by the boons granted to him, his composure shattered by the arrows born of Māra, came again to that cave together with those leading warriors.
m.2.5.45.18: There the enraged one, with his troops, giving up food, drink and sleep, fought a most wondrous battle with Vīraka, night and day, for five hundred and five days.
m.2.5.45.19: With swords, spears and bhindipālas, with maces and bhuśuṇḍīs, with great shafts, arrows, fierce crescent-headed arrows, span-long darts and blazing tortoise-headed missiles,
m.2.5.45.20: with the finest iron arrows, sharp tridents, axes, lances and hammers, swords, iron balls, mountains and trees, and divine chariot-weapons, assailed by the hosts of Daityas—
m.2.5.45.21: Lustreless, his body pierced, he fell; the entrance of the cave was entirely covered by those weapons hurled by the Daityas' arms, and afterwards he lay unconscious at the cave's mouth.
m.2.5.45.22: Vīraka was covered by all the Daityas with nets of missiles for a moment, and it was impossible to uncover him. Seeing the very dreadful sons of Diti, the Devī—
m.2.5.45.23: —out of fear, the Devī, together with her companions, called to mind the Grandsire and Viṣṇu; staying inside the cave, she also caused the entire army of my best of heroes to be called to mind.
m.2.5.45.24: As soon as she remembered them, Brahmā and Lord Viṣṇu, bearing female forms, together with all the Indras and their troops, assuming female forms, arrived.
m.2.5.45.25: Having become women, they then entered the interior of the cave of the daughter of the king of mountains, along with the hosts of great sages of great power, the Siddhas, Nāgas and Guhyakas.
m.2.5.45.26: Because entry of men into the inner apartments of those seated on royal thrones is forbidden, they therefore displayed thousands, indeed countless numbers, of shapely women—
m.2.5.45.27: —showing divine and greatly wondrous forms to Gaurī in the cave, the delighted women, together with the noble Vīraka, entered the inner cave of the mountain-king's daughter, the maiden of the king of mountains.
m.2.5.45.28: By the many thousands and hundreds of women, kettledrums bestowing victory in battle resounded with a roar like the clouds at the end of an aeon, and fine conches were blown by the shapely women.
m.2.5.45.29: Casting off his swoon, Vīraka, of wondrous and fierce valour, standing in front, seized the weapons of the great chariot-warriors and with those very weapons slew the sons of Diti.
m.2.5.45.30: Then Brāhmī, staff in hand, opposed them; Gaurī too, her mind seized by anger; and Nārāyaṇī, bearing conch, mace, fine discus and bow, her staff-like arms full—
m.2.5.45.31: —went forth; another went forth with plough and staff in hand, with sky-like locks, gold-coloured; then Baiḍaujasī (Aindrī), thunderbolt in hand, of fierce speed, teeming with thousands of streams,
m.2.5.45.32: thousand-eyed, steadfast in battle, very hard to conquer, unassailable by hundreds of Daityas; the power of Vaiśvānara (Agni), with a fierce face; and the fierce Yāmyā, her hand raised with a staff.
m.2.5.45.33: Nairṛtī, with a dreadful bow, her hand raised with a very sharp sword, came forward; Toyālikā (Vāruṇī), noose in hand, went forth eager for battle.
m.2.5.45.34: And the goddess born of the fierce wind, her body gaunt as hunger, goad in hand; and she who sprang from Dhanada (Kubera), taking in her hand a mace like the fire at the end of an aeon—
m.2.5.45.35: —Yakṣeśvarī, sharp-faced, misshapen, with claws for weapons, terrifying even to serpents: these and other goddesses by the hundreds went forth to the crowded battlefield.
m.2.5.45.36: Seeing that endless army, the goddesses turned pale, greatly astonished, agitated and startled with fear, dejected at heart.
m.2.5.45.37: Composing their minds, all those wives of the gods, headed by the Śakti of Brahmā, with the full approval of the daughter of the mountain-lord, made Vīraka the commander, a hero of very dreadful valour.
m.2.5.45.38: The chief sons of Diti, resolving in their minds on either retreat or their own death, waged a great, unprecedented battle; others, emboldened by their boons, fought with the women.
m.2.5.45.39: Then Gaurī, together with her companions, fought a most wondrous battle there, having made Vīraka, of dreadful valour and wondrous skill of mind, commander in the battle.
m.2.5.45.40: The king, son of Hiraṇyanetra, skilled in action, quickly formed a great battle-array, very dreadful, named Gila (the Swallower), having taken Viṣṇu into account and observed Yāmyā.
m.2.5.45.41: When, through the performance of the rite, his face had been made terrible, the Lord Kṛttivāsas (clad in a hide) came, angry, spread with a radiance like that of a thousand fearsome suns at the end of a kalpa.
m.2.5.45.42: Then, when a mere thousand years had passed, seeing Maheśvara arrived, the women, greatly delighted, fought an exceedingly great battle together with Vīraka.
m.2.5.45.43: Gaurī bowed with her head to Giriśa and, displaying the very great valour of her husband, joyful Gaurī joined in the fighting. Then Hara, the daughter of the king of mountains…
m.2.5.45.44: …taking her by the neck, entered the cave; the thousands of women were dismissed. Gaurī too, having honoured them with hundreds of marks of respect, Śiva stationed Vīraka alone at the mouth of the cave.
m.2.5.45.45: Then the lord of the asuras, skilled in policy, not seeing Gaurī and Giriśa, quickly sent his own messenger named Vidhasa into Śiva's presence.
m.2.5.45.46: He, whose limbs had been battered in that battle by the various blows hurled by the hosts of gods, entered, bowed his head to Śambhu, and spoke words proud and fierce.
m.2.5.45.47: The messenger said: Sent by him, I have entered the cave. This Andhaka has spoken this message to you: You have no business at all with a woman; release the young, beautiful woman.
m.2.5.45.48: You are, for the most part, an ascetic; so keep to that. I put up with the lovely one being inside with you, thinking, a sage is not to be opposed. But you are no sage, O ascetic—you are an enemy.
m.2.5.45.49: You are an exceedingly great foe of the daityas. Fight with me at once; having crushed you, O roguish ascetic, I shall lead you to Yama's abode, which is like the depths of Pātāla.
m.2.5.45.50: Sanatkumāra said: Hearing these words from the messenger's mouth, the skull-garlanded one—the great three-eyed one, refuge of the good, destroyer of the pride of the wicked—blazing with vexation, spoke to him in anger.
m.2.5.45.51: Śiva said: Your speech is plain and very fierce; the truth has been spoken. Go quickly. Make war on me by force, if indeed you are capable through strength.
m.2.5.45.52: For one who is powerless on earth, what use are wives or very charming riches? Let the daityas, drunk with strength, come; having considered thus, I have done this.
m.2.5.45.53: For the powerless, whence even the sustenance of the body? Let them do whatever is ordained for them; and whatever is to be done by me, that I shall do—there is no doubt about this.
m.2.5.45.54: Sanatkumāra said: Having heard these words from Hara, Vighasa too went out, delighted; then, roaring and uttering huṃ sounds, he proceeded to the presence of the lord of the daityas.
m.2.5.45.iti: Thus ends the forty-fifth adhyāya, named The description of the start of the battle and the dialogue of the messenger, in the fifth khaṇḍa, the Yuddha-khaṇḍa, of the second saṃhitā, the Rudra-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.2.5.46.1: Sanatkumāra said: And that king of the Daityas, who understood his intention, quickly took up a mace and, with his army, then put in front the one named Gila, exceedingly fierce and impenetrable even by the foremost gods.
m.2.5.46.2: Reaching the mouth of Maheśvara's cave, he broke it open with weapons blazing like thunderbolts. Then some showered weapons on Vīraka himself, and others likewise on the Mountain's Daughter.
m.2.5.46.3: Some broke the beautiful gate; they destroyed flowers and leaves, fruits, roots and the pleasant water, and even tore up the garden paths.
m.2.5.46.4: Some, delighted, churned up the shining peaks of the mountain. Then Hara, the trident-bearer, angered, remembered his own army, summoning it.
m.2.5.46.5: He summoned other most fearsome beings too, and the gods with their armies, headed by Viṣṇu. As soon as called, the attendants came with their armies, with chariots, elephants, horses, bulls and cows,
m.2.5.46.6: with camels, donkeys, excellent birds and lions—all those gods with hosts of Bhūtas—with tigers, deer, boars and cranes, with fishes and with dolphins foremost,
m.2.5.46.7: and with other hosts of creatures of many kinds, with broken-fanged ones, with burst-open cremation grounds, with serpents, hundreds of Pretas and Piśācas, with divine aerial cars and with lotus-ponds,
m.2.5.46.8: with rivers and streams and with mountains as mounts—having assembled, with joined palms they bowed to Kapardin and stood there with undaunted spirit, having made Vīraka the commander.
m.2.5.46.9: Then the Pināka-bearer sent forth to battle the gods, whose mounts had rested, with Vīraka as chief, steadfast in battle and victorious; and they, dispatched by Maheśvara,
m.2.5.46.10: all waged a battle like the end of an age, without bounds, ever dreadful, against Gila and the army of the Daitya lord; but in the fight the gods were swallowed in his fury.
m.2.5.46.11: At that moment all who were fighting, headed by Brahmā, Indra, Viṣṇu, the Sun and the Moon, were swallowed by that Vighasa; when the army had been swallowed, only Vīraka remained.
m.2.5.46.12: Leaving the battlefront, entering that cave and bowing his head to Śarva, the valiant Vīraka, best of speakers, stricken with grief, then told the Enemy of Smara what had happened.
