m.2.5.46.13: O Lord, your army has today been swallowed by the Daitya Vighasa; swallowed is Viṣṇu, teacher of the three worlds, crusher of Daityas; swallowed are the Moon and the Sun, and Druhiṇa and Maghavan, the boon-givers; swallowed are they all—Yama, Varuṇa, Vāyu and Dhanada.
m.2.5.46.14: I alone remain, bowed before you; what should I do here? The Daitya lord, joyful at heart and accompanied by Daityas, is unconquerable.
m.2.5.46.15: Having come to you, the unconquerable, he is of fearsome mind and swift as the wind. The god Viṣṇu himself, out of devotion, tore Kanakakaśipu, son of Kaśyapa, with sharp nails; even so the Lord, obedient to the righteous, set forth—may he, with gaping mouth, blow away the filth of the three worlds.
m.2.5.46.16: He was cursed by Vasiṣṭha and the others, the seven sages, lords of the world: You shall again be thus for a very long time, together with the Daityas.
m.2.5.46.17: Then they were addressed by him with affectionate words beneficial to himself: When, O best of sages, will my release from this terrible state come? Whereupon the angry ones said: At the time of battle, after the swallowing by Vighasa, when your mouth is split by terrible arrows and by fists,
m.2.5.46.18: then in the forest called Badarī, in Hari's abode, a holy dwelling, restraining yourself and freed of sin, you will go to the Supreme. Then, because of their words, this swallower of Daityas, tormented by hunger, roams daily from battle, again delighted with joy.
m.2.5.46.19: And this terrible darkness covers the world despite the risen Sun and Moon. Likewise Śukra, your supreme enemy, exceedingly harmful, by the words of the hymn of the immortal-making lore, makes the Daityas slain by the gods again vigourous and joyful, freed of hundreds of wounds.
m.2.5.46.20: Better that I give up my life for you at the time of battle; you, chosen by me, are witness even for a moment in the doing of this task.
m.2.5.46.21: Sanatkumāra said: Hearing this from his good son, the Lord of the Pramathas, angered, meditated long, and the Lord of the three worlds first created an incomparable chant called Pragāyat-sāma, with a body shaped like the rays of the sun; then, by laughter (prahāsa), by that name, the darkness was destroyed by it.
m.2.5.46.22: When this world was lit up, the sage Vīraka again waged a great battle with the distorted-faced Daityas—he who was born of the eminent sage who had eaten stone-dust, and who formerly, having waged battle, had conquered even the city.
m.2.5.46.23: That great Rudra was at once swallowed outright by the Daitya. Then that Nandin, with sharp arrows, spear and sword, chief of warriors, great even among hundreds of eminent sages, abode of learning, endowed with calm, self-control and great fortitude—
m.2.5.46.24: Seeing this, the Lord Kapardin then mounted the excellent bull, eager for battle, facing the Daitya Vighasa, and muttering a divine mantra that makes the swallowed be disgorged, stood ready, having made ready his bow and arrows like thunderbolts.
m.2.5.46.25: Then the sage Vīraka came out from Vighasa's mouth, bringing all his own matchless forces; all were disgorged, with Viṣṇu—the Lotus-born, the Enemy of Bala, the Moon and the Sun; and that army, delighted, again waged a great battle.
m.2.5.46.26: When he had been defeated, and Śukra thereafter, by the power of his lore, again revived the Daityas slain in battle, then that preceptor of the Dānavas was bound and brought like a beast by the Gaṇas to the Lord of beings, and swallowed by him, the Enemy of Tripura.
m.2.5.46.27: When the one called Śukra had vanished, that whole abode of the gods' enemies was conquered, destroyed, broken and utterly shattered by the gods, and by vast hosts of Bhūtas relishing the devouring of Daitya corpses, with headless trunks dancing, hands raised holding sharp arrows and spears,
m.2.5.46.28: by frenzied Vetālas, by birds with very strong talons and beaks, by wolves of many kinds with mouths full of mouthfuls of corpse-flesh—when the battlefield was thus strewn, the descendant in the line of Kanakakaśipu, having fought long, was defeated by Hari, Hara and Mahendra.
m.2.5.46.29: When the Daityas had fled into Pātāla and likewise into the caves of mountains and oceans, and the army was depleted, the bull among Daityas, the mighty Andhaka—bringer of slaughter, crusher of the world, in the wrath of the gods—had his pride shattered by Hari with terrible blows of the mace.
m.2.5.46.30: He who never abandons battle, since he had obtained a boon—then, his body tormented by terrible blows from the Lord of the gods, he quickly defeated the gods with floods of weapons and missiles, trees, mountains and waters, roaring loudly and slowly challenging the Lord of the Pramathas.
m.2.5.46.31: He stood fighting with many kinds of weapons fallen on the battlefield; when all these were spent, he then assailed Girijā and Rudra, likewise with trees, serpents, masses of thunderbolts, showers of weapons, grotesque illusions and hundreds of deceitful Śambara-like contrivances.
m.2.5.46.32: To conquer the Lord of the mountain he devised yet another trick there—the hero of great might, equal to the Enemy of Tripura, intelligent, not to be slain by the gods, overpowered by the madness of mind born of hundreds of boons; but the Daitya at once had his body battered by abundant weapons and missiles.
m.2.5.46.33: From the oozing of his blood, the field became pervaded by hosts of Andhakas sprung on the ground, dreadful, distorted-faced, resembling himself; he was most fiercely pierced on the trident by the Lord of beings, the Enemy of Tripura, whose form was like the fire at the end of a kalpa.
m.2.5.46.34: When from the army slain by Paśupati another army arose, from the very hot drops issuing from his flesh and springing from his wounds, then the wise Viṣṇu, through yoga, having called on the Lord of the Pramathas, created a fierce, invincible female form with a distorted face.
m.2.5.46.35: a form dreadful and emaciated; and the Lord, angry, overspread with many creeper-like arms, came forth from the ear at the head of Śambhu's Gaṇas.
m.2.5.46.36: That goddess, standing on the battlefield, the earth adorned by her pair of feet, praised by all the gods, her mind then urged on by the Lord, tormented by hunger, drank up that army issuing from the Daitya and that blood, very hot, and the mire of gore at the battlefront, completely.
m.2.5.46.37: Then the lone Daitya, even with his blood dried up, fought Giriśa with terrible palm-blows like thunderbolts, with knees and feet, with nails like vajras, with mouth, arms and heads, remembering the eternal, unborn warrior's duty enjoined for his own clan.
m.2.5.46.38: Afterwards, subdued in battle, his heart pierced by the Lord of the Pramathas, impaled on the trident and held up in the sky like a post, his lower body dried up, his frame wasted by the sun's rays, his body drenched by clouds with downpours and winds,
m.2.5.46.39: shrivelled by the fierce-rayed sun, then broken into pieces like flakes of frost—even in that state the bull among Daityas did not give up his life. Then Śambhu, that ocean of supreme compassion, being pleased and praised by him, lovingly granted him the rank of a lord of Gaṇas.
m.2.5.46.40: Then, at the end of the battle, the lords of the worlds with their consorts, having duly worshipped the Lord of the Pramathas with hymns of many kinds—Hari, Brahmā and the others—praised him abundantly with supreme eulogies, their shoulders bowed, delighted and happy, crying out, victory, victory!
m.2.5.46.41: Hara, delighted, stayed with those gaṇas in a cave of the best of mountains. He dismissed with honour the hosts of gods, worshipped with offerings of many kinds. Then, having gained the joyful daughter of the best of mountains, and likewise the sinless son freed from the terrible devouring mouth, he issued his commands and engaged in play.
m.2.5.46.iti: Thus ends the forty-sixth adhyāya, named The description of the battle with Andhaka, in the account of the slaying of Andhaka, in the fifth khaṇḍa, the Yuddha-khaṇḍa, of the second saṃhitā, the Rudra-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.2.5.47.1: Vyāsa said: In that great battle, terrible and hair-raising, Śukra, the learned master of the Daityas, was swallowed by the enemy of Tripura Śiva.
m.2.5.47.2: This I have heard in brief; tell it again in detail. What did that great yogin do while he was in the belly of the Pināka-bearer?
m.2.5.47.3: How did the fire of Śambhu's belly—the burner at the end of the kalpa, Time itself—not burn that Śukra, though Bhārgava too was of blazing energy?
m.2.5.47.4: How did the wise one come out of the cage of Śambhu's belly? How, and for how long, did that Bhārgava worship him?
m.2.5.47.5: And how did he obtain that supreme lore which quells death? What is that supreme lore, dear one, by which death is warded off?
m.2.5.47.6: How did Andhaka, released from the trident, obtain the leadership of the Gaṇas of Śambhu, the god of gods, the sage who sports in play?
m.2.5.47.7: O greatly wise one, be gracious and narrate all this fully to me, who am listening, dear one—the nectar of Śiva's sport.
m.2.5.47.8: Brahmā said: Having heard these words of Vyāsa of boundless splendour, Sanatkumāra spoke, remembering the lotus-feet of Śiva.
m.2.5.47.9: Sanatkumāra said: Listen, O Vyāsa of great intellect, to the supreme nectar of Śiva's sport. You are blessed, you are foremost among Śaivas, and of yourself you give me joy.
m.2.5.47.10: While the battle was going on between those two, Śaṅkara and Andhaka, the lords of the impenetrable thunderbolt-array and of the mountain-array,
m.2.5.47.11: at first victory went to the mighty Daityas; then, O sage, through Śiva's power, victory came to the Pramathas.
m.2.5.47.12: Hearing that, the great Daitya Andhakāsura became dejected, and he became absorbed in thinking, how may I win?
m.2.5.47.13: Then the heroic Andhaka, of keen intellect, withdrew from the battle and quickly went alone into Śukra's presence.
m.2.5.47.14: Getting down from his chariot and bowing to his own guru Kāvya, he, most expert in policy, then reflected and spoke this with joined palms.
m.2.5.47.15: Andhaka said: O lord, relying on you we hold you in the regard due to a guru; we are never defeated but always victorious.
m.2.5.47.16: Through your power we have always regarded all the gods with their followers—even those headed by Hara and Upendra—as mere blades of grass.
m.2.5.47.17: By your grace the gods then fear us, as elephants fear lions and as serpents fear Garuḍas.
m.2.5.47.18: By your grace the Daityas and Dānavas, scattering the whole army of the Pramathas, entered the impenetrable thunderbolt-array.
m.2.5.47.19: Having you as our refuge, O Bhārgava, we always stand firm like cattle under their herdsman and move about fearlessly even in battle.
m.2.5.47.20: Protect, protect on all sides, O brahmin, coming forth, the asuras who have sought refuge in you, harassed by heroic enemies—and even the dead.
m.2.5.47.21: See my excellent troops, Huṇḍa and others, overrun by the foremost Pramathas of terrible valour, crushers of death itself, slain and fallen.
m.2.5.47.22: You who long ago, drinking the smoke of chaff for a thousand years, obtained the excellent lore—its time has now come.
m.2.5.47.23: Today, O Bhārgava, let all the Pramathas see that fruit of the lore of yours, as you mercifully revive all the asuras.
m.2.5.47.24: Sanatkumāra said: Hearing Andhaka's words thus, the steadfast Bhārgava then reflected with an anguished mind:
m.2.5.47.25: What should I do now? How may it go well for me? The procedure of reviving those slain in combat is wholly unfitting for me.
m.2.5.47.26: This lore was obtained from Śaṅkara; should I then employ it against his Gaṇas—to revive those crushed in battle by the heroic Pramathas, Śaṅkara's followers?
m.2.5.47.27: Yet the duty toward those who seek refuge is supreme above all. Having reflected thus with heart and intellect, Śukra then accepted his words.
m.2.5.47.28: Then, smiling slightly, Bhārgava, remembering Śiva's lotus-feet with a composed mind, spoke to the lord of the Dānavas.
m.2.5.47.29: Śukra said: What you have said, dear one, is all true indeed. I acquired this lore for the sake of the Dānavas.
m.2.5.47.30: Having drunk the unbearable smoke of chaff for a thousand years, I obtained this lore from the Lord; it ever brings happiness to kinsmen.
m.2.5.47.31: With this lore I shall raise up the Daityas crushed by the Pramathas in battle, as a cloud revives withered crops.
m.2.5.47.32: In this very moment you will see those Daityas of yours risen up, free of wounds, free of pain, healthy, as if risen again from sleep.
m.2.5.47.33: Sanatkumāra said: Having said this to Andhaka, the sage Śukra recited the lore, directing it at each Daitya one by one, reverently remembering the Lord of the lore.
m.2.5.47.34: By the mere recitation of the lore, all those heroic Daityas and Dānavas rose up at once, weapons in hand, as if from sleep,
m.2.5.47.35: as Vedas constantly practised come forth, or as clouds rise in their season, or as wealth given with faith to brahmins returns in a time of distress.
m.2.5.47.36: Seeing those great asuras, Huṇḍa and the others, revived, all the asuras roared like clouds full of water.
m.2.5.47.37: Of great strength and valour, fearless, they were again ready for battle with the Pramathas, roaring dreadful roars.
m.2.5.47.38: Seeing the Daityas and Dānavas revived by Śukra, all the Pramathas, Nandin and the others, fierce in battle, were then astonished.
m.2.5.47.39: This whole deed must be reported thus to Śaṅkara, lord of the gods—having considered, the wise ones spoke thus to one another.
m.2.5.47.40: While that wondrous sacrifice of battle of the lords of the Pramathas was going on thus, Śilāda's son Nandin, indignant at seeing Bhārgava's deed, went to Maheśa.
m.2.5.47.41: Having said, victory, Nandin spoke to the fierce source of victory (Śiva), who is bright like gold: O God, the battle-deed of the lords of the gaṇas, which is difficult even for the gods together with Indra—
m.2.5.47.42: that deed of ours Bhārgava (Śukra) has today made futile, O Lord, for he has revived those slain enemies, playfully reciting the vidyā that gives life to the dead, aiming it at each one.
m.2.5.47.43: The great demon-chiefs Tuhuṇḍa, Huṇḍa and the rest, Kumbha, Jambha, Vipāka, Pāka and others, having returned today from Yama's abode, roam about routing the Pramathas.
m.2.5.47.44: If he revives here again and again those excellent Daityas who have been struck down, how will victory be ours, O Maheśa? How indeed will there be peace for the lords of the gaṇas?
m.2.5.47.45: Sanatkumāra said: Thus addressed by Nandin, the lord of the Pramathas, the God who is Lord over the lords of the Pramathas, laughing, then spoke to Nandin, king of all the gaṇa-lords.
m.2.5.47.46: Śiva said: Nandin, go with the utmost speed, and from the midst of the sons of Diti seize that best of the chief Brahmins and bring him quickly here, as a hawk seizes a young quail.
m.2.5.47.47: Sanatkumāra said: Thus addressed by the bull-bannered Śiva, Nandin roared with a roar like a bull's or a lion's, and plunging into the army he went quickly to where the lamp of Bhṛgu's lineage was.
m.2.5.47.48: Though Kāvya (Śukra) was guarded by all the sons of Diti, holding nooses, swords, trees, stones and rocks in their hands, the mighty Nandin, throwing the Daityas into turmoil, carried him off, as a śarabha carries off an elephant.
m.2.5.47.49: The enemies of the gods followed him, seized by the mighty one, his garments slipping, his ornaments fallen, his hair loosened, as if meaning to free him, sending forth lion-like roars.
m.2.5.47.50: The Dānava chiefs poured upon Nandīśvara a fierce rain of thunderbolts, tridents, swords and axes, of raised staffs, discuses, stones and kampanas, like rain-clouds.
m.2.5.47.51: The sovereign of the gaṇas, having got hold of Bhārgava and burnt hundreds of weapons with the fire of his mouth, came to Bhava's side while the battle of asuras and gods raged on, having distressed the enemy side.
m.2.5.47.52: Here is that Śukra, O Lord — thus he quickly reported to Bhava. And the God of gods took Śukra like an offering presented by a pure devotee.
m.2.5.47.53: Saying nothing, the protector of beings threw the chief of sages (Śukra) into his mouth like a fruit. All those asuras raised a loud cry of lament, crying ha ha ha again and again.
m.2.5.47.iti: Thus ends the forty-seventh adhyāya, named The swallowing of Śukra, in the war with Andhaka, in the fifth khaṇḍa, the Yuddha-khaṇḍa, of the second saṃhitā, the Rudra-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.2.5.48.1: Vyāsa said: When Śukra had been swallowed by Rudra, what did the Dānavas do, those great heroes whose lord was Andhaka? Tell me the truth, O great sage.
m.2.5.48.2: Sanatkumāra said: When Kāvya had been swallowed by the Lord of Girijā, the Daityas became bereft of the hope of victory, like lordly elephants deprived of their trunks, and like bulls without horns,
m.2.5.48.3: like masses of bodies without heads, like twice-born men lacking Vedic study, like hosts of living beings without effort, and like efforts devoid of good fortune,
m.2.5.48.4: like women bereft of their husbands, like flocks of birds without wings, like life-spans devoid of merit, like Vedic learning devoid of observances,
m.2.5.48.5: as multitudes of rites become void of their fruits without the one power of divine glory, as kṣatriyas without valour, and just as the whole body of dharma without truth.
m.2.5.48.6: With Śukra carried off by Nandin and swallowed by the Poison-eater, the Daityas, though striving in the festival of battle, fell into despair.
m.2.5.48.7: Seeing them disheartened, Andhaka, of great steadfastness and valour, addressed the Daityas Huṇḍa, Huṇḍa and the others.
m.2.5.48.8: Andhaka said: We have been tricked by Nandin, who carried off Kavi by force. Surely today the life-breaths of all of us have been separated from our bodies.
m.2.5.48.9: Courage, vigour, recourse, fame, strength, splendour, valour — all has been taken from us at once, now that the one Bhārgava has been taken.
m.2.5.48.10: Shame on us, by whom the one revered by our race, the best of our race, our all-capable preceptor and protector, was not protected in his calamity!
m.2.5.48.11: Therefore, O heroes, without delay fight here with the enemies, those heroic Pramathas, remembering the lotus-feet of our preceptor.
m.2.5.48.12: Remembering the bliss-giving lotus-feet of our preceptor Kāvya, I shall slay all the Pramathas along with Nandin.
m.2.5.48.13: Today, having slain these helpless ones together with the gods and Vāsava, I shall free Bhārgava, as a yogin frees the soul from karma.
m.2.5.48.14: Or else that yogin, the master himself, the protector of what remains of us, may by his yoga come out of his body.
m.2.5.48.15: Sanatkumāra said: Hearing these words of Andhaka, the Dānavas, roaring like clouds, pitiless and resolved to die, spoke as they faced the Pramathas:
m.2.5.48.16: If our life-span still holds, the Pramathas can never overpower us by force; if our life-span is not to last, what is gained by going off and abandoning our master in battle?
m.2.5.48.17: Those men, rich in high honour, who go away from here abandoning their master, surely go to the abode Andhatāmisra.
m.2.5.48.18: Having greatly sullied their renown with the darkness of infamy, those routed on the battlefield would be happy neither here nor hereafter.
m.2.5.48.19: What use are gifts, what use austerities, what use bathing in sacred fords, if there is bathing in the holy ford of the battleground, which removes the impurity of rebirth?
m.2.5.48.20: Having thus resolved upon those words, the Daityas and Danujas churned the Pramathas in battle, sounding the war-drum.
m.2.5.48.21: There, with masses of arrows, swords and thunderbolts, with hard missiles made of stone, with bhuśuṇḍis and bhindipālas, with spears, javelins and axes,
m.2.5.48.22: with khaṭvāṅgas, paṭṭiśas, tridents, cudgels and maces, striking one another fiercely, they wrought a great slaughter.
m.2.5.48.23: There arose the sound of drawn bows, of falling arrows, of bhindipālas and bhuśuṇḍis, and of war-cries.
m.2.5.48.24: With the blare of war-instruments, the many trumpetings of elephants and the neighing of horses, there was a great uproar.
m.2.5.48.25: The space between heaven and earth was filled with the tremendous noise; the fearless and the fearful alike had their hair standing on end.
m.2.5.48.26: The armies, filled with the loud, distinct cries of elephants and horses, with banners and flags broken, with weapons spent,
m.2.5.48.27: variegated with gushing blood, bereft of horses, elephants and chariots, and thirsty — the armies on both sides swooned.
m.2.5.48.28: Then those heroic Pramathas, led by Nandin, struck down all the Asuras with their might and won victory, O sage.
m.2.5.48.29: Seeing his army being shattered here and there by the Pramathas, Andhaka himself mounted his chariot and rushed at the Gaṇas.
m.2.5.48.30: By those missiles hurled in torrents of arrows, the Pramathas perished like mountains under thunderbolt strikes, and vanished like clouds emptied of water.
m.2.5.48.31: Looking at each one, whether going or coming, far or near, Andhaka pierced him with arrows as numerous as his hairs.
m.2.5.48.32: Seeing the army being shattered by the mighty Andhaka, Skanda, Vināyaka, Nandin, Somanandin and others,
m.2.5.48.33: mighty, heroic Pramathas, Śaṅkara's own Gaṇas, of great strength, grew angry and waged a wondrous battle.
m.2.5.48.34: By Vināyaka, by Skanda, by Nandin, by Somanandin, by the heroic Naigameya, by the mighty Vaiśākha,
m.2.5.48.35: and by these and other fierce Gaṇas, who rained down streams of tridents, spears and floods of arrows, even Andhaka was made blind.
m.2.5.48.36: Then a tumult arose between the armies of the Pramathas and the Asuras. At that great sound, Śukra, who was within Śambhu's belly,
m.2.5.48.37: seeking an opening, wandered about homeless like the wind, and beheld within Rudra's body the seven worlds along with the Pātālas,
m.2.5.48.38: the wondrous realms of Brahmā, Nārāyaṇa and Indra, along with those of the Ādityas and Apsarases, and the battle of the Pramathas and Asuras.
m.2.5.48.39: Wandering all around in Bhava's belly for a hundred years, he found no opening in it, just as a wicked man finds no flaw in a pure one.
m.2.5.48.40: Then Bhārgava, through the Śāmbhava yoga, in the form of semen, having recited this excellent mantra, emerged from the cage of Śambhu's belly.
m.2.5.48.41: He came out by the path of the liṅga and then bowed to Śiva. Gaurī took him as a son, and he was thereby made free of obstacles by the Goddess.
m.2.5.48.42: Then, seeing Kāvya the Bhārgava, who had come out by the path of semen, Maheśāna, the treasure-house of compassion, laughed and said:
m.2.5.48.43: Maheśvara said: Since you have come forth like semen from my liṅga, O delight of Bhṛgu, by that deed you are Śukra; you are my son. Go now.
m.2.5.48.44: Sanatkumāra said: Thus addressed by the god, Śukra, whose radiance was like the sun's, bowed again to Śiva and, with joined palms, praised him.
m.2.5.48.45: Śukra said: You have endless feet and endless forms, endless heads; you are the Ender and Śiva; you have endless arms. How shall I, bowing with my head, praise one such as you, who are worthy of praise?
m.2.5.48.46: You are the eight-formed one, you are the one of endless forms; you are the giver of what is desired to all gods and asuras, and the crusher of the one with evil gaze. How shall I praise one such as you, who are worthy of praise?
m.2.5.48.47: Sanatkumāra said: Having thus praised Śiva, Śukra bowed again and, at Śiva's command, entered the army of the Dānavas, as the moon enters a garland of clouds.
m.2.5.48.48: Thus has been told the swallowing of Kavi by Śaṅkara in battle. Now hear also that mantra which was recited by Kavi in Śambhu's belly.
m.2.5.48.iti: Thus ends the forty-eighth adhyāya, named The swallowing of Śukra, in the fifth khaṇḍa, the Yuddha-khaṇḍa, of the second saṃhitā, the Rudra-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.2.5.49.0: Sanatkumāra said: Om, salutation to you: to the Lord of the gods, revered by gods and asuras; to the Great God of past and future; to him whose eyes are green and tawny; to Strength; to him whose form is intellect; to him clad in a tiger-skin garment; to Āraṇeya; to the source of the three worlds; to the Lord; to Hara; to him whose eyes are like Hari's; to him who brings the end of the ages; to Fire; to the lord of the gaṇas; to the guardian of the worlds; to the great-armed, the great-handed; to the trident-bearer; to him with great fangs; to Time; to Maheśvara; to the Imperishable; to him whose form is Time; to the blue-necked; to the great-bellied; to the chief of the gaṇas; to the Self of all; to the creator of all; to the all-pervading; to the slayer of Death; to Pāriyātra-Suvrata; to the celibate; to him who has reached the end of the Veda; to him who has reached the end of austerity; to Paśupati; to Vyaṅga; to him with the trident in hand; to him whose banner is the bull; to Hari; to the one with matted hair; to the one with the crest-lock; to the staff-bearer; to the greatly famed; to the lord of beings; to the cave-dweller; to him who has the lute, the drum and the cymbal; to the Immortal; to the one fair to behold; to him who shines like the rising sun; to the dweller in the cremation ground; to the Blessed One; to Umā's lord; to the subduer of foes; to him who struck out Bhaga's eyes; to the destroyer of Pūṣan's teeth; to the doer of fierce deeds; to him with the noose in hand; to the time of dissolution; to him with a meteor-like face; to him whose banner is fire; to the sage; to the blazing one; to the lord of the people; to the uplifter; to the begetter; to the Fourth; to the best in the worlds; to Vāmadeva; to him who is gracious in speech; to the mendicant on the left side; to him whose form is a mendicant; to the one with matted hair, himself matted-haired; to him who paralysed Śakra's arm; to the restrainer of the Vasus; to the sacrifice; to the maker of sacrifice; to Time; to the wise; to the maker of honey; to the moving one; to the lord of trees; to him worshipped in the Vājasaneya and in all the āśramas; to the sustainer of the world; to the maker of the world; to the Person; to the eternal; to the steadfast; to the overseer of dharma; to him of the three paths; to the producer of beings; to the three-eyed; to the many-formed; to him whose splendour equals ten thousand suns; to the God; to him who sounds all instruments; to him who frees from all afflictions; to the binder; to the bearer of all; to the highest dharma; to Puṣpadanta; to the undivided; to the Face; to the remover of all; to Hiraṇyaśravas; to the door-keeper; to the terrible one; to him of terrible valour: Om, salutation, salutation.
m.2.5.49.1: Having repeated this excellent mantra, Śukra came out of the cage of Śiva's belly by the path of the liṅga, like Śambhu's potent semen.
m.2.5.49.2: He was taken by Gaurī as a son; then he was made by the Lord of the universe ageless, immortal and glorious, like a second Śaṅkara.
m.2.5.49.3: When three thousand years had passed on earth, Śukra, the sage who was a treasury of the Vedas, was born again from Maheśvara.
m.2.5.49.4: He saw Andhaka on the trident, utterly dried up, the lord of the Dānavas, full of fortitude, an ascetic, meditating on the Supreme Lord —
m.2.5.49.5: meditating on Mahādeva, the odd-eyed, who wears the half-moon as his crest, the nectar, the eternal, the steadfast pillar, the blue-throated, the bearer of Pināka;
m.2.5.49.6: the bull-eyed, the greatly-to-be-known, the Person, the giver of all desires, the enemy of Kāma, the burner of Kāma, who takes forms at will, the one with braided hair;
m.2.5.49.7: the many-formed, Giriśa, the terrible, garlanded, wearing red garments, the yogin, the burner of Time, the destroyer of Tripura, the skull-bearer;
m.2.5.49.8: of hidden vows, of secret mantra, profound, reached through devotion, the support of the powers beginning with aṇimā, the giver of sovereignty over the three worlds;
m.2.5.49.9: the hero, the slayer of heroes, the fierce, the deformed, the stout, the skilful, the great eater of flesh, the frenzied, Bhairava, indeed Maheśvara;
m.2.5.49.10: who makes the three worlds flee, the eager one, the hunter, the destroyer of the sacrifice, accompanied by the son of the Kṛttikās, the frenzied, clad in a hide;
m.2.5.49.11: wearing an elephant-hide, agitated, adorned with serpents, the giver of support, the Vetāla, the fierce, worshipped by Śākinīs;
m.2.5.49.12: Aghora, the slayer of fierce Daityas, of terrible roar, the lord of trees, with ash-smeared limbs, matted-haired, pure, served by hundreds of Bheruṇḍa birds;
m.2.5.49.13: the lord of beings, the master of beings, abiding in the five elements, moving in the sky, wrathful, harsh, fierce, the lord of Caṇḍī, dear to Caṇḍikā;
m.2.5.49.14: the fierce, the lofty, the winged one, ever partaking of liquor, the one who licks the worlds, the very dreadful, Death, beyond the reach of death;
m.2.5.49.15: the death of Death, the great commander, dwelling in cremation grounds and forests, passion, dispassion, blind with passion, worshipped by hundreds who are free of passion;
m.2.5.49.16: sattva, rajas, tamas, dharma and adharma, the younger brother of Vāsava, truth and untruth, of the form of being and of non-being, without cause;
m.2.5.49.17: the Lord who is half woman, the sun, with the splendour of hundreds of crores of suns, the sacrifice, the lord of sacrifice, Rudra, Īśāna, the giver of boons, Śiva.
m.2.5.49.18: These are the hundred and eight forms of Śiva, the Supreme Self; meditating on them, the Dānava was freed from that great fear.
m.2.5.49.19: He was bathed by Kapardin with a divine shower of nectar; released by the pleased Lord, he was lowered from the tip of that trident.
m.2.5.49.20: Then that great Daitya, the asura Andhaka, was addressed by Maheśāna with conciliation; all this was done by the great-souled one.
m.2.5.49.21: Īśvara said: O lord of the Daityas, I am pleased with your restraint and observance, with your valour and your fortitude; choose a boon, O you of good vows.
m.2.5.49.22: I have been constantly worshipped by you, and you are cleansed of all sins; I am the giver of boons and you are worthy of a boon, O best among the great lords of Daityas.
m.2.5.49.23: Whatever fruit of merit is yours from sustaining your life through three thousand years, by that may you have bliss.
m.2.5.49.24: Sanatkumāra said: Hearing this, Andhaka, trembling, with joined palms, placing both knees on the ground, spoke to the Blessed Lord of Umā.
m.2.5.49.25: Andhaka said: O Lord, you who are higher than the highest — what you were called by me earlier on the battlefield, now I, wretched and lowly, address you with a voice faltering with joy.
m.2.5.49.26: Whatever deeds, condemned in the worlds, I did through delusion, not knowing you — all that, O Lord, do not keep in your mind.
m.2.5.49.27: And whatever wrong I did toward Pārvatī through the fault of lust, forgive it, O Mahādeva; I am pitiable and deeply afflicted.
m.2.5.49.28: Compassion should always be shown by you to one who is afflicted, especially to one who is pitiable, wretched and full of devotion.
m.2.5.49.29: Such am I, wretched and devoted, come to you for refuge; protection should be granted to me — here I have joined my palms.
m.2.5.49.30: May this Goddess, Mother of the world, be fully pleased with me; abandoning all anger, may she look upon me graciously.
m.2.5.49.31: Where is her anger, and where am I, a pitiable Daitya, O moon-crested one? I cannot endure it, O you with the half-moon as diadem, O Śambhu, O Maheśvara.
m.2.5.49.32: Where are you, supremely generous, and where am I, made helpless by faults such as lust and anger, and likewise by old age and death?
m.2.5.49.33: This son of yours, Vīraka, skilled in battle and very mighty — seeing me pitiable, may he not yield to anger.
m.2.5.49.34: May I always behold Pārvatī as my mother, with reverence due to an elder — she whose hue is like frost, a pearl necklace, the cool-rayed moon, the conch and the jasmine.
m.2.5.49.35: Ever devoted to you both, free from enmity with the gods, may I dwell together with the gaṇas, tranquil in spirit, contemplating yoga.
m.2.5.49.36: May I not again recall my hostile birth as a Dānava; by your grace, O Maheśāna, grant this supreme boon.
m.2.5.49.37: Sanatkumāra said: Having spoken these words, the lord of the Daityas fell silent, meditating on the three-eyed God and gazing at Pārvatī, his mother.
m.2.5.49.38: Then, looked upon by Rudra with a gracious eye, he remembered his former history and his wondrous birth.
m.2.5.49.39: When that history was remembered, his desire was fulfilled; bowing to his mother and father, he then became one who had accomplished his purpose.
m.2.5.49.40: Smelled on the head in affection by Pārvatī and by the wise Śaṅkara, he thus obtained what he desired from the pleased one who bears the crescent moon as his crest-ornament.
m.2.5.49.41: All this ancient account of Andhaka's attaining the chieftainship of the gaṇas through the grace of Mahādeva, which bestows supreme happiness, has been narrated to you.
m.2.5.49.42: And the Mṛtyuñjaya mantra, destroyer of death, has been told; it should be recited with diligence, for it grants the fruit of all desires.
m.2.5.49.iti: Thus ends the forty-ninth adhyāya, named The hosts of Andhaka regain life, in the fifth khaṇḍa, the Yuddha-khaṇḍa, of the second saṃhitā, the Rudra-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.2.5.50.1: Sanatkumāra said: Listen, O Vyāsa, to how the supreme knowledge (vidyā) that quells death was obtained by the sage Kāvya from Śiva, who is called Mṛtyuñjaya.
m.2.5.50.2: Long ago this descendant of Bhṛgu went to the city of Vārāṇasī and performed austerities for a long time, meditating on the Lord Viśveśvara.
m.2.5.50.3: Right there he installed a liṅga of Śambhu, the Supreme Self, and in front of it, O Vedavyāsa, he made a very lovely well.
m.2.5.50.4: With great effort he bathed the Lord of gods a hundred thousand times with the five nectars, each measuring a droṇa, and abundantly with fragrant bathing waters.
m.2.5.50.5: A thousand times, with great love, he anointed the Lord of gods with sandal paste and yakṣakardama, following fragrant unguent-rubbings.
m.2.5.50.6: With rājacampaka and dhattūra flowers, with karavīra and lotuses, with mālatī and karṇikāra, with kadamba, bakula and blue lotuses,
m.2.5.50.7: with mallikā and śatapatrī, with sindhuvāra along with kiṃśuka, with bandhūka flowers, punnāga, and nāgakeśara stamens,
m.2.5.50.8: with navamallī and cibilika, with kunda along with mucukunda, with mandāra and bilva leaves, with droṇa, marubaka and bṛka, with granthiparṇa and damanaka, and with lovely mango shoots,
m.2.5.50.9: with tulasī, devagandhārī, bṛhatpatrī and kuśa sprouts, with nandyāvarta and agastya, and with deodars together with śāla,
m.2.5.50.10: with kāñcanāra and kurabaka, with dūrvā sprouts and kuruṇṭaka — with each of these flowers and with other shoots as well,
m.2.5.50.11: and with leaves and thousand-petalled lotuses, lovely, of many kinds and auspicious — attentively and with great love he worshipped Śaṅkara.
m.2.5.50.12: With offerings of song and dance, praising him abundantly with hymns, with the thousand names and with other hymns, he extolled Śaṅkara.
m.2.5.50.13: Thus for five thousand years Śukra worshipped Maheśvara, the great Lord, by rites of many kinds.
m.2.5.50.14: When he did not see the god inclined in the least to grant a boon, he then took up another vow, terrible and extremely hard to endure.
m.2.5.50.15: Having thoroughly and repeatedly washed away, with the waters of contemplation, the great impurity called fickleness from his mind together with the senses,
m.2.5.50.16: and having made that jewel of a mind stainless and offered it to the Pināka-bearer, Kavi drank streams of smoke-particles for a thousand years.
m.2.5.50.17: Seeing Kāvya, firm of mind, performing such terrible austerity, Maheśvara became pleased with the Bhārgava.
m.2.5.50.18: Emerging from that liṅga, with splendour surpassing a thousand suns, Virūpākṣa, the very husband of Dākṣāyaṇī, spoke to him.
m.2.5.50.19: Maheśvara said: O treasure of austerity, O greatly fortunate one, son of Bhṛgu, great sage, by this austerity of yours I am ever and especially pleased.
m.2.5.50.20: Choose as a boon all that your mind desires, O Bhārgava. With love I shall grant all your wishes; there is nothing that cannot be given to you.
m.2.5.50.21: Sanatkumāra said: Hearing these words of Śambhu, an excellent offer bringing great joy, Kavi was delighted, immersed in an ocean of happiness.
m.2.5.50.22: His body covered with hair standing on end from the welling flood of bliss, the lotus-eyed brahmin joyfully bowed to Śambhu.
m.2.5.50.23: Delighted, with the corners of his eyes wide open, placing his folded hands on his head and saying, victory, victory, he praised the eight-bodied one.
m.2.5.50.24: Bhārgava said: Overpowering all darkness with these rays of yours, you bring to an end the cherished designs of the night-roamers. You blaze in the sky, O jewel of heaven, for the welfare of the three worlds, O Lord of the world — therefore obeisance to you.
m.2.5.50.25: In the world, beyond all measure, with boundless great splendours you shine on earth and in the sky, eye of all the worlds; you who have driven away all darkness, most excellent one, O cool-rayed moon, filled with floods of nectar — therefore obeisance to you.
m.2.5.50.26: You are ever the motion on the purifying path, and worthy of worship. Who lives here without you, O life of the worlds? By you, the wind — which when stilled destroys and when moving nourishes all creatures — they are gladdened; O all-pervading one, obeisance to you.
m.2.5.50.27: O sole purifier of the universe, protector of those who bow, O you whose unique power is fire, without you there is no immortal divine rite for the dead; how would the world breathe? O inner Self of the world, you are fire, granting peace at every step — obeisance to you.
m.2.5.50.28: O you in the form of water, Supreme Lord, purifier of the world — wondrously you are surely the maker of wondrous good conduct. This universe indeed becomes pure and stainless, O Lord of the universe, through bathing in water; hence I bow.
m.2.5.50.29: O you in the form of space, by giving room outside and within, this universe here expands, O Lord; from you, O compassionate one, it ever breathes, and by its nature it contracts into you — therefore I bow to you.
m.2.5.50.30: O you whose self is the earth, you bear the universe here, O all-pervading one. Who other than you, O Lord of the universe, is the foe of darkness? Such as you are, destroy my darkness, O serpent-adorned one, beyond all praise, higher than the highest — therefore I bow to you.
m.2.5.50.31: O you whose nature is the Self, this world in the form of the moving and unmoving is pervaded by these successions of your forms, O Hara. O you who dwell as the inner Self of all, whose form is in every form, I, your devotee, ever bow, O Supreme Self, O eight-formed one.
m.2.5.50.32: Thus, joined with these eight forms, O friend of the friendless, you indeed make all this, O you whose form benefits all people; this universe is spread out and widely extended by you, O guide of the prostrate, O supreme goal of the whole host of aims — therefore I bow.
m.2.5.50.33: Sanatkumāra said: Having thus praised Bharga with this octad on the eight forms, the Bhārgava bowed again and again, his head touching the ground.
m.2.5.50.34: Thus praised by the exceedingly radiant Bhārgava, Mahādeva lifted that prostrate brahmin from the ground, holding him with his two arms,
m.2.5.50.35: and spoke with great affection in a gentle voice deep as the rumble of clouds, lighting up the spaces between the directions with the radiance of his teeth.
m.2.5.50.36: Mahādeva said: O best of brahmins, Kavi, dear one, you are my pure devotee. By this extremely fierce austerity and by conduct befitting your lineage,
m.2.5.50.37: by the merit of installing the liṅga and by worshipping the liṅga, by the pure and unwavering offering of your mind,
m.2.5.50.38: and by your holy conduct in the great sacred field of Avimukta, I look upon you with compassion; there is nothing that cannot be given to you.
m.2.5.50.39: In this very body, having entered the cavern of my belly, you will attain birth as my son by way of my excellent organ.
m.2.5.50.40: Today I grant you a boon hard to obtain even for my attendants, which I have for the most part guarded even from Hari and Hiraṇyagarbha.
m.2.5.50.41: The pure lore of mine named Mṛtasañjīvanī, the reviver of the dead, was fashioned by me alone through great power of austerity.
m.2.5.50.42: Today I grant you that lore in the form of a mantra, O most pure one. You are worthy of that lore, O treasure of pure austerity.
m.2.5.50.43: Whoever it may be for whom you repeat this lore, the best among the lords of knowledge, with self-restraint, he will truly and surely come back to life.
m.2.5.50.44: Your splendour will surpass the sun and surpass fire, and in the sky you will be a blazing star. Be the foremost of the planets.
m.2.5.50.45: Moreover, women or men who undertake a journey facing you—through the fall of your gaze all their undertakings will come to ruin.
m.2.5.50.46: When you have risen, O one of good vows, marriages and the like, and all religious rites of people here, will bear fruit.
m.2.5.50.47: And all the lunar days, the Nandā tithis, will be auspicious through conjunction with you. Your devotees will be abundant in vigour (śukra) and have many offspring.
m.2.5.50.48: This liṅga established by you, called Śukreśa—those men who worship it will attain success.
m.2.5.50.49: Those who for a whole year, day after day, are devoted to the nakta vow, eating only at night, and who on your day, having performed all water rites at the Śukra well,
m.2.5.50.50: will worship Śukreśa—hear what their fruit is: those mortals will have unfailing seed, will have sons, and be of abundant virility,
m.2.5.50.51: they will be endowed with manliness and good fortune, no doubt. All those people will be possessed of learning and partakers of happiness.
m.2.5.50.52: Having thus granted the boons, the god merged into that liṅga there. Bhārgava too, his mind content, went to his own abode.
m.2.5.50.53: Thus I have told you, O Vyāsa, how the lore called Mṛtyuñjaya was obtained through the power of austerity. What else do you wish to hear?
m.2.5.50.iti: Thus ends the fiftieth adhyāya, named The obtaining of the Mṛtasañjīvinī lore, in the fifth khaṇḍa, the Yuddha-khaṇḍa, of the second saṃhitā, the Rudra-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.2.5.51.1: Vyāsa said: O Sanatkumāra, all-knowing one, out of your kindness and affection you have let me hear a wonderful and excellent story, full of Śambhu's grace.
m.2.5.51.2: Now I wish to hear the deeds of the moon-crested Śiva: how he lovingly granted the leadership of his Gaṇas to Bāṇāsura.
m.2.5.51.3: Sanatkumāra said: Listen attentively, O Vyāsa, to that story of Śambhu, the Supreme Self: how he lovingly granted the leadership of the Gaṇas to Bāṇāsura.
m.2.5.51.4: In this very story is the noble deed of Śaṅkara, the great Lord; and here too is the battle of Śambhu, who was showing favour to Bāṇa, with Kṛṣṇa.
m.2.5.51.5: Hear from me the fitting, supreme and most meritorious legend connected with Śiva's sport, which brings delight to the mind and the ears.
m.2.5.51.6: There was a sage of great intellect, Marīci, son of Brahmā, born of his mind, the eldest and best among all his sons, a Prajāpati.
m.2.5.51.7: His son was the great-souled Kaśyapa, best of sages, who greatly increased creation and was exceedingly devoted to his father and to Vidhi Brahmā as well.
m.2.5.51.8: O Vyāsa, that sage Kaśyapa had thirteen wives, daughters of Dakṣa, well-mannered and devoted to their husband.
m.2.5.51.9: Among them the eldest was Diti; the Daityas are known as her sons. From the other wives were born sons — the gods and others, together with the moving and unmoving beings.
m.2.5.51.10: The eldest, Diti, had two first-born sons of great strength: Hiraṇyakaśipu the elder, and after him his younger brother Hiraṇyākṣa.
m.2.5.51.11: Hiraṇyakaśipu had four sons, foremost among Daityas: Hrāda, Anuhrāda, Saṃhrāda and Prahrāda, in that order.
m.2.5.51.12: Among them Prahrāda was great, a devotee of Viṣṇu, master of his senses; none of the Daityas were able to destroy him.
m.2.5.51.13: His son was Virocana, the best of great givers, who gave his own head to Śakra when he came begging in the guise of a brahmin.
m.2.5.51.14: His son was Bali, a great giver, dear to Śiva, by whom the earth was given to Hari in the form of Vāmana.
m.2.5.51.15: His own son was Bāṇa, who became a devotee of Śiva: honoured, generous, wise, true to his word, a giver of thousands.
m.2.5.51.16: Long ago that lord of Asuras, dwelling in the city called Śoṇita, ruled a kingdom, having conquered by force the three worlds and their rulers.
m.2.5.51.17: By Śaṅkara's grace, the immortals became like servants to that Bāṇāsura, the devotee of Śiva.
m.2.5.51.18: In his kingdom, apart from the immortals, the subjects were not unhappy; the gods were distressed because of rivalry, being followers of another dharma.
m.2.5.51.19: Once that great Asura pleased Maheśvara with the Tāṇḍava dance, accompanied by music played with his thousand arms.
m.2.5.51.20: Delighted by that dance, Śaṅkara, loving to his devotees, became very gracious and looked at him with a compassionate glance.
m.2.5.51.21: The Lord, ruler of all worlds, the refuge, granter of devotees' wishes, invited that great Asura, son of Bali, to choose a boon.
m.2.5.51.22: Sanatkumāra said: That great Daitya Bāṇa, son of Bali, best of devotees and wise, bowed to Śaṅkara with devotion and praised the Supreme Lord.
m.2.5.51.23: Bāṇāsura said: O God of gods, Mahādeva, loving to those who seek refuge, O Maheśāna, O all-pervading one, if you are pleased with me,
m.2.5.51.24: be my protector always, staying near me as lord of my city; O Lord, be in every way a source of joy to me, together with your son and your Gaṇas.
m.2.5.51.25: Sanatkumāra said: That Bāṇa, son of Bali, deluded by Śiva's māyā, asked this of Maheśāna, the giver of liberation, who is surely hard to propitiate.
m.2.5.51.26: Śambhu, loving to his devotees, granted him those boons, and the Lord lovingly dwelt there accordingly, with his Gaṇas and his son.
m.2.5.51.27: Once, in Bāṇa's city, Hara sported together with gods and Asuras on the lovely bank of the river named Śoṇitaka.
m.2.5.51.28: The Gandharvas and Apsarases danced and laughed; the sages muttered prayers, bowed, worshipped him and praised him.
m.2.5.51.29: All the Pramathas leapt about, the seers offered oblations, hosts of Siddhas arrived and beheld Śaṅkara's delight.
m.2.5.51.30: False logicians perished, as did barbarians and enemies; the Mothers stood facing him, and terrors vanished.
m.2.5.51.31: The faults of worldly existence left those who were devoted to Rudra in true sincerity; when he was seen, all beings attained supreme joy.
m.2.5.51.32: Seeing the playful gestures of the women, the sages and Siddhas frolicked; and the seasons too displayed their full power there.
m.2.5.51.33: Gentle breezes blew, grey with flower pollen, and flocks of birds, greedy for nectar, sang in the trees.
m.2.5.51.34: And on trees bowed down under the weight of flowers, cuckoos kept calling sweetly, arousing love, in the forests and groves.
m.2.5.51.35: Then, during that playful sport, the one crested with the crescent moon, intoxicated and touched by unsubdued desire, spoke to Nandin.
m.2.5.51.36: Candraśekhara said: Bring my beloved Gaurī from Kailāsa, adorned; go quickly from this forest, tell her, and bring the fair one here.
m.2.5.51.37: Sanatkumāra said: He agreed, saying so be it, went there, and, as Śaṅkara's confidential messenger, bowing deeply with joined palms, spoke to Pārvatī.
m.2.5.51.38: Nandīśvara said: O Goddess, Maheśvara, God of gods, wishes to see you, his beloved, adorned in beauty; I have spoken at his command.
m.2.5.51.39: Sanatkumāra said: Then, O best of sages, at his words Gaurī, wholly devoted to her vow of fidelity to her husband, eagerly set about adorning herself.
m.2.5.51.40: I am coming. Go to the Lord and tell him so at my bidding. Then Nandin, swift as thought, came back to Rudra's side.
m.2.5.51.41: Then Rudra, intensely agitated by desire, again said to Nandin: Go once more, dear one, and quickly bring Pārvatī.
m.2.5.51.42: Saying very well, he went to her and said to the lovely-eyed Gaurī: Your husband wishes to see you, charming and fully adorned.
m.2.5.51.43: O Goddess, Śaṅkara is waiting eagerly to sport with you in many ways. Since your husband is thus sorely afflicted by desire, please go, O daughter of the mountain.
m.2.5.51.44: Meanwhile all the Apsarases consulted with one another: Having now conceived passion, he is at once eager for the sight of Pārvatī.
m.2.5.51.45: Whichever shapely woman this Pināka-bearer, the foe of Kāma, would choose, she surely becomes the queen of all divine women.
m.2.5.51.46: A glance cast in the form of Gaurī would make him sport with the hosts of love's arts; this desire overcomes even the foe of Kāma — so they eagerly said to one another.
m.2.5.51.47: Whatever woman other than Dākṣāyaṇī is able to touch him, let her go there without fear and enchant the lord of Pārvatī.
m.2.5.51.48: Then Citralekhā, the daughter of Kūṣmāṇḍa, spoke these words: I dare to touch Śaṅkara in the lovely form of Gaurī.
m.2.5.51.49: Citralekhā said: The Mohinī form that Keśava once assumed with the wish to delude — resorting, in truth, to that Vaiṣṇava yoga…
m.2.5.51.50: And then, having seen Urvaśī's transformation of form, Ghṛtācī took the form of Kālī, and Viśvācī the body of Caṇḍikā;
m.2.5.51.51: Rambhā took the form of Sāvitrī, Menakā likewise that of Gāyatrī, Sahajanyā the form of Jayā, and Puñjikasthalī that of Vijayā.
m.2.5.51.52: And other eminent Apsarases, not named here, endowed with their own arts, in turn assumed with effort the forms of the Mothers, also not named.
m.2.5.51.53: Then the daughter of Kumbhāṇḍa, having seen their forms and grasped the matter through the Vaiṣṇava yoga and her own yogic power, imitated them.
m.2.5.51.54: Ūṣā, daughter of Bāṇāsura, skilled in divine yoga, assumed the form of Pārvatī — divine, most wondrous and auspicious,
m.2.5.51.55: with feet like great red lotuses, of supreme radiance, endowed with divine marks, granting the objects desired by the heart.
m.2.5.51.56: Then Girijā, Śivā, the all-knowing inner controller of all, perceiving her intention of love-making, spoke.
m.2.5.51.57: Girijā said: Since you, friend Ūṣā, have assumed my very form out of desire, O proud one, when the time has come —
m.2.5.51.58: — in this month of Kārttika, after your season in Mādhava, on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight, in the dreadful onset of night, whoever —
m.2.5.51.59: the man who will enjoy you, while you, having fasted, lie asleep in the inner apartments — he has been appointed your husband by the gods; with him you will take delight.
m.2.5.51.60: For from childhood you have been a devotee of Viṣṇu, constantly and unwearied. So be it, she said in her mind, her face bashful.
m.2.5.51.61: Then the goddess Pārvatī, adorned with festive ornaments, came into Rudra's presence and sported with that Śambhu.
m.2.5.51.62: Then, at the end of the love-play, the blessed Rudra vanished from sight, together with his wife and his Gaṇas, and accompanied by the gods, O sage.
m.2.5.51.iti: Thus ends the fifty-first adhyāya, named The sport of Śiva and Śivā, in the account of the story of Ūṣā, in the fifth khaṇḍa, the Yuddha-khaṇḍa, of the second saṃhitā, the Rudra-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.2.5.52.1: Sanatkumāra said: Listen also to another episode of Śiva, the Supreme Self, one filled with his affection for devotees and bestowing supreme bliss.
m.2.5.52.2: Long ago an asura named Bāṇa, made arrogant through ill fate, performed the tāṇḍava dance and pleased Śaṅkara.
m.2.5.52.3: Knowing Śiva, the beloved of Pārvatī, to be pleased in mind, the asura Bāṇa, with bowed shoulders and joined palms, spoke.
m.2.5.52.4: Bāṇa said: O God of gods, Mahādeva, crest-jewel of all the gods, by your grace I am mighty. Hear my supreme request.
m.2.5.52.5: The thousand arms given by you have become a great burden to me; in the three worlds I find no opponent equal to me except you.
m.2.5.52.6: O God, what am I to do with this thousand of mountain-like arms without a battle, O bull-bannered one?
m.2.5.52.7: With my arms full of itching, eager to fight the elephants of the quarters, I went about pulverizing cities and mountains; and even they fled away in fear.
m.2.5.52.8: By me Yama was made a mere soldier, and great Agni a menial; Varuṇa too was made a cowherd, a tender of cows.
m.2.5.52.9: Kubera was made superintendent of elephants, and Nirṛti a maidservant; and Indra, conquered, was made a perpetual payer of tribute in the world.
m.2.5.52.10: Tell me of the coming of a battle in which these arms of mine will be shattered by weapons and missiles hurled by enemy hands.
m.2.5.52.11: Let them fall by an enemy's hand, or let them fell foes by the thousands. Fulfil this wish of mine, O Maheśvara.
m.2.5.52.12: Sanatkumāra said: Hearing that, Rudra, the remover of his devotees' afflictions, grew angry; filled with great wrath, he let out a most astonishing loud laugh and said:
m.2.5.52.13: Rudra said: Shame, shame on you, arrogant in every way, lowest of the whole Daitya race! Such speech is not fitting for a devotee, the son of Bali.
m.2.5.52.14: You will soon obtain a dreadful quelling of this pride of yours: a great battle, suddenly, with a mighty one equal to me.
m.2.5.52.15: There your mountain-like arms, cut down like firewood and made to fall like plantain stems by weapons and missiles, will drop to the ground.
m.2.5.52.16: This banner of yours, O wicked one, bearing a human head together with a peacock — when it falls,
m.2.5.52.17: — the banner set up in the armoury, without any danger caused by wind — then know in your mind that a most terrible battle has arrived.
m.2.5.52.18: Fixing this in mind, go forth to the dreadful battle with your whole army. For now, go to that dwelling of yours where it the banner stands; all is well for now.
m.2.5.52.19: And there, O evil-minded one, you will see those great portents of yours. Having said this, the remover of pride, affectionate to devotees, fell silent.
m.2.5.52.20: Sanatkumāra said: Hearing that, Bāṇa worshipped Rudra with divine bud-like folded palms, bowed to Mahādeva, and went to his own home.
m.2.5.52.21: Asked by Kumbhāṇḍa, he joyfully told him what had happened. The asura Bāṇa, ever eager, kept watching for that conjunction of events.
m.2.5.52.22: Then one day, by fate, the asura Bāṇa saw there that banner broken of its own accord, and, delighted, he set out for battle.
m.2.5.52.23: Summoning his army, accompanied by his eight divisions, he performed the sacrifice for war and looked upon the honey auspicious for battle;
m.2.5.52.24: and observing every auspicious sign in the quarters, the son of Bali — of great zeal, a great hero, a great chariot-warrior — set forth,
m.2.5.52.25: pondering in the lotus of his heart: Who will come, and from where — a warrior who loves battle and is master of many weapons and missiles?
m.2.5.52.26: Let him cut off my thousand arms like firewood; likewise I shall cut him into hundreds here with very sharp weapons.
m.2.5.52.27: Meanwhile the time arranged by Śaṅkara arrived, when Bāṇa's daughter, well-born, had performed auspicious rites.
m.2.5.52.28: Having worshipped Mādhava in the month of Mādhava (Vaiśākha) at deep night, she slept in the guarded inner apartments, and was made to experience union as a woman.
m.2.5.52.29: She was drawn by divine illusion by Kṛṣṇa's grandson (the son of Kṛṣṇa's son), who had been sent by Gaurī; and she wept like one without a protector.
m.2.5.52.30: He too, having enjoyed her by force, was carried back to Dvārakā within a moment by Pārvatī's companions through divine yoga.
m.2.5.52.31: Then she, ravished, rose up weeping and, telling her friends many words of grief, resolved on giving up her body.
m.2.5.52.32: O Vyāsa, she was reminded again by a friend of the fault of her own self; then, recalling that whole earlier account, she became composed.
m.2.5.52.33: Then Ūṣā, the daughter of Bāṇa, spoke in a sweet voice to Citralekhā, the daughter of Kumbhāṇḍa, O sage.
m.2.5.52.34: Ūṣā said: Friend, if this man was formerly ordained by Pārvatī as my husband, by what means may he, hidden from us, be rightfully obtained by me? Tell you me.
m.2.5.52.35: Or in what family was he born, by whom my heart has been stolen? Hearing these words of Uṣā, her friend then replied to her.
m.2.5.52.36: Citralekhā said: O lady, how shall I bring that man whom you saw in a dream, who is not known to me?
m.2.5.52.37: When she said this, the Daitya maiden, blinded by passion, became eager to die; and so on that first day she was protected by that friend.
m.2.5.52.38: Then the very wise Citralekhā, daughter of Kumbhāṇḍa, spoke again to Uṣā, the daughter of Bāṇa, O best of sages:
m.2.5.52.39: I will remove your distress: if he is to be found in the three worlds, I will bring the man who has stolen your heart. Point him out.
m.2.5.52.40: Sanatkumāra said: Having said this, she drew on a cloth panel gods, Daityas and Dānavas, as well as Gandharvas, Siddhas, Nāgas, Yakṣas and others.
m.2.5.52.41: Likewise she drew among them the men of the Vṛṣṇi clan: Śūra, Ānakadundubhi, Rāma and Kṛṣṇa, and Pradyumna, the best of men.
m.2.5.52.42: Seeing Aniruddha, the son of Pradyumna, drawn there, Ūṣā became bashful and cast her face down, her heart filled with joy.
m.2.5.52.43: Ūṣā said: That is the thief, the man whom I obtained in the night, friend, by whom the jewel of my heart was swiftly stolen.
m.2.5.52.44: By his mere touch I became so infatuated. I wish to know him; tell me everything, O lovely one.
m.2.5.52.45: In whose lineage was he born, and what is his name? Thus addressed, the yoginī told his name and his lineage.
m.2.5.52.46: Having heard everything about his family and the rest, O best of sages, Bāṇa's daughter, eager and full of longing, spoke.
m.2.5.52.47: Ūṣā said: Out of affection, friend, devise at once a means to obtain him, a means by which I may gain that beloved, dear as my life.
m.2.5.52.48: Without him, friend, I cannot bear to live even a single moment. Bring him here with earnest effort and make me happy, friend.
m.2.5.52.49: Sanatkumāra said: Thus addressed by that daughter of Bāṇa, the minister's daughter was astonished, O best of sages, and became absorbed in careful thought.
m.2.5.52.50: Then Citralekhā, swift as the mind, having spoken to her friend and having recognised him as Kṛṣṇa's grandson, set out to go to Dvārakā.
m.2.5.52.51: On the fourteenth of the dark half of Jyeṣṭha, when the third day had passed, within a muhūrta before dawn she reached the city of Dvārakā.
m.2.5.52.52: The divine yoginī went through the sky in a single instant; and then in the garden of the inner palace she saw Pradyumna's son,
m.2.5.52.53: sporting with the women and drinking Mādhavī wine, beautiful in every limb, dark-complexioned, sweetly smiling, in the fresh bloom of youth.
m.2.5.52.54: Then, by her tāmasa yogic power, she covered with a veil of darkness that descendant of Madhu, who had climbed onto his bed,
m.2.5.52.55: and then, taking that bed upon her head, within the blink of an eye she reached Śoṇitapura, where Bāṇa's daughter was.
m.2.5.52.56: There she, tormented by love, her mind maddened, was showing various emotions. Then, seeing him brought, she became afraid.
m.2.5.52.57: In that well-guarded inner apartment, at that new union, no sooner had they begun to make love than it was at once found out
m.2.5.52.58: by those stationed at the door of the inner apartments, cane staffs in hand, through signs and inferences — the maiden's misconduct being carried on.
m.2.5.52.59: And he too was seen by them there: a man of divine form, young, handsome, bold, and fond of battle.
m.2.5.52.60: Having seen him, those men, great heroes, guards of the maiden's inner apartments, reported everything to Bāṇa, the son of Bali.
m.2.5.52.61: The doorkeepers said: O lord, someone unknown, hidden in the inner apartments by force — who is he? — has violated your daughter, seizing her of his own accord.
m.2.5.52.62: O lord of the Dānavas, mighty-armed one, look, look at him here, and do whatever is proper; we are not at fault.
m.2.5.52.63: Sanatkumāra said: Hearing their words, the mighty lord of the Dānavas, having heard of his daughter's defilement, was astonished, O best of sages.
m.2.5.52.iti: Thus ends the fifty-second adhyāya, named The story of Ūṣā, in the fifth khaṇḍa, the Yuddha-khaṇḍa, of the second saṃhitā, the Rudra-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.2.5.53.1: Sanatkumāra said: Then Bāṇāsura, enraged, went there and saw him. His body had taken on a divine grace, and he was in the first bloom of youth.
m.2.5.53.2: Seeing him, Bāṇa, skilled in battle, his mind gripped by anger, was astonished. Then, as if laughing, he said: What is the reason for this?
m.2.5.53.3: Ah! A man rich in beauty, daring and steadfast! Who is this ill-fated fellow of deluded mind, whose last hour has come?
m.2.5.53.4: He has defiled the conduct of my family and my dear daughter. Kill him quickly in your fury with the most dreadful weapons.
m.2.5.53.5: Or else bind that wicked one, and then, O heroes, guard him with special care in a dreadful, grim prison for a long time.
m.2.5.53.6: I do not know who this fearless one is, or who this one of terrible valour is. Pondering thus, Śarāsura (Bāṇa), though of great intellect, fell into doubt.
m.2.5.53.7: Then the evil-minded Daitya ordered an army of ten thousand to advance steadily and slay that hero.
m.2.5.53.8: Commanded by him, those extremely fierce warriors swiftly surrounded the inner apartments on all sides, shouting, cut, pierce.
m.2.5.53.9: Then, seeing the enemy army, that Yādava roared and seized a matchless iron club that stood at the door of the inner apartments,
m.2.5.53.10: and came out of that building like Death with a thunderbolt in hand. With it he killed those servants and went back into the inner apartments.
m.2.5.53.11: In this way, O best of sages, his eyes red with fury and his strength increased by Śiva's energy, he slew ten thousand soldiers.
m.2.5.53.12: When a hundred thousand warriors had been slain, Bāṇāsura in his rage took Kumbhāṇḍa with him and challenged that warrior skilled in battle
m.2.5.53.13: — Aniruddha, son of Pradyumna, of great intellect, protected by Śiva's energy, his body blazing — to single combat in that great battle.
m.2.5.53.14: Then, with a sword he had taken in the fight, he destroyed ten thousand horses and the finest chariots of the lord of the Daityas.
m.2.5.53.15: Then, to kill him, Aniruddha seized a spear like the fire of Time at the dissolution, and with it he struck him.
m.2.5.53.16: Bāṇa was struck hard by that spear on the seat of his chariot, and at that very moment the hero vanished on the spot, together with his horses.
m.2.5.53.17: When he had become invisible, the unconquered son of Pradyumna looked around in all directions and stood motionless like a mountain.
m.2.5.53.18: Then that Dānava, a fighter by deceit, struck him again and again with thousands of various weapons while remaining unseen.
m.2.5.53.19: By trickery that mighty one bound him with serpent-nooses: Śarāsura, the son of Bali, a great hero and a devotee of Śiva.
m.2.5.53.20: Having bound him and put him inside a cage, he withdrew from the battle. Then Bāṇa, furious, spoke to the very mighty son of his charioteer.
m.2.5.53.21: Bāṇāsura said: O son of the charioteer, quickly cut off the head of this man, this wicked one who has forcibly defiled my pure and noble family.
m.2.5.53.22: Cut up all his limbs, sir, and give them to the Rākṣasas; then let the flesh-eaters, too, feast on his blood and flesh.
m.2.5.53.23: Or kill the sinner by throwing him into a bottomless well choked with grass. Why say more, O son of the charioteer? He must be killed by any means.
m.2.5.53.24: Sanatkumāra said: On hearing these words of his, the night-roamer Kumbhāṇḍa, righteous in mind and best among good counsellors, spoke to Bāṇa.
m.2.5.53.25: Kumbhāṇḍa said: This is not a fit deed to do, O lord; let it be reconsidered. My view is that if he is killed, you yourself would be destroyed.
m.2.5.53.26: This one, O lord, appears equal to Viṣṇu in valour, empowered by the splendid energy of the Moon-crested One (Śiva), your chosen deity.
m.2.5.53.27: Moreover, by the might of the Moon-browed One, this one has reached this state in battle, firmly grounded in his manly courage.
m.2.5.53.28: By Śiva's grace this mighty grandson of Kṛṣṇa regards us as mere straw, even though he has been forcibly bitten by serpents.
m.2.5.53.29: Sanatkumāra said: Having said this to Bāṇa, that Dānava, foremost among those who know statecraft, spoke these words to Aniruddha.
m.2.5.53.30: Kumbhāṇḍa said: Who are you, and whose son are you, O hero? Tell the truth in front of me. Or by whom were you brought here, you ill-behaved, lowest of men?
m.2.5.53.31: Praise the heroic lord of the Daityas and bow to him with joined palms, saying over and over the humble words, I am defeated.
m.2.5.53.32: If this is done, there may be release; otherwise, bondage and worse. Hearing his words, he (Aniruddha) gave a reply.
m.2.5.53.33: Aniruddha said: Hey, hey, you crony of the vile Daitya, living on morsels from his hand. O night-roamer, O ill-behaved one, you do not know the code of conduct toward an enemy.
m.2.5.53.34: My view is that for a hero, abject submission and flight are worse than death; they would go against his nature and be a thorn in his side.
m.2.5.53.35: For a Kṣatriya, death in battle facing the foe is always better. One who counts himself a hero should not stand on the ground with joined palms like a wretch.
m.2.5.53.36: Sanatkumāra said: He spoke many such heroic words to him. Hearing them, Bāṇa was astonished, and he also grew angry.
m.2.5.53.37: Then a voice from the sky spoke to calm Bāṇa, while all the heroes, Aniruddha and the minister were listening.
m.2.5.53.38: The heavenly voice said: O Bāṇa, great hero, you should not give way to anger. You are the son of Bali, O wise one, a devotee of Śiva; reflect on this.
m.2.5.53.39: Śiva is the lord of all, the witness of all actions, the supreme Lord. This whole world, moving and unmoving, depends on him.
m.2.5.53.40: He alone is always the creator, sustainer and destroyer of the worlds. He bears rajas, sattva and tamas, and his forms are Brahmā, Viṣṇu and Hara.
m.2.5.53.41: He is the Lord dwelling within all, the impeller, supreme beyond everything, changeless, imperishable, eternal, and though the master of Māyā, free of qualities.
m.2.5.53.42: By his will the strong is to be known as weak, O son of the excellent Bali. Knowing this in your mind, be at ease, O great-minded one.
m.2.5.53.43: The Blessed Lord, remover of pride, skilled in manifold sports, affectionate to his devotees, will now destroy your pride.
m.2.5.53.44: Sanatkumāra said: Having spoken thus, the voice from the sky fell silent, O great sage. Because of those words Bāṇāsura did not kill Aniruddha.
m.2.5.53.45: Instead, going to his own inner palace, he drank the finest liquor; and he forgot those words and, perverse-minded, indulged in pleasure.
m.2.5.53.46: Then Aniruddha, bound by serpent coils fierce with venom, his heart unsatisfied with his beloved, at that very moment remembered Durgā.
m.2.5.53.47: Aniruddha said: O Goddess, giver of refuge, I am bound and being burnt by serpents. Come, grant me protection, O giver of fame, O you of fierce wrath.
m.2.5.53.48: O devotee of Śiva, O great Goddess, maker of creation, preservation and dissolution, without you there is no other protector; therefore protect me, O Śivā.
m.2.5.53.49: Sanatkumāra said: Thus pleased by him, Kālī, lustrous like crushed collyrium, arrived there at the great midnight on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of Jyeṣṭha.
m.2.5.53.50: With heavy blows of her fists she shattered the cage, reducing to ashes those terrifying arrows that had taken the form of serpents.
m.2.5.53.51: Having freed Aniruddha and then brought him into the inner apartments, Durgā vanished right there.
m.2.5.53.52: Thus, by the grace of the Goddess, the power of Śiva, O lord of sages, Aniruddha was freed from distress, became happy and free of pain.
m.2.5.53.53: Then Aniruddha, son of Pradyumna, having gained victory through Śiva's power, rejoiced on obtaining his beloved, the daughter of Bāṇa.
m.2.5.53.54: Happy, he sported as before with his beloved; having drunk liquor, his eyes deep red, he then enjoyed himself with Bāṇa's daughter.
m.2.5.53.iti: Thus ends the fifty-third adhyāya, named The sport of Aniruddha and Ūṣā, in the story of Ūṣā, in the fifth khaṇḍa, the Yuddha-khaṇḍa, of the second saṃhitā, the Rudra-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.2.5.54.1: Vyāsa said: O best of sages, when Kṛṣṇa's grandson Aniruddha had been carried off by Kumbhāṇḍa's daughter, what did Kṛṣṇa do? Tell me that.
m.2.5.54.2: Sanatkumāra said: Then, after Aniruddha had gone, O best of sages, Kṛṣṇa heard the sound of his women weeping and became distressed.
m.2.5.54.3: And as his kinsmen and Hari, not seeing Aniruddha, kept grieving, the four months of the rainy season passed.
m.2.5.54.4: Hearing from Nārada that news, and the deeds of the captive, all the Vṛṣṇis, whose deity was Kṛṣṇa, were greatly distressed.
m.2.5.54.5: Kṛṣṇa, having heard that whole affair, at once summoned Tārkṣya (Garuḍa) and eagerly went to Śoṇitapura for battle.
m.2.5.54.6: Pradyumna and Yuyudhāna went, and Sāmba, then Sāraṇa, and Nanda, Upananda, Bhadra and others, followers of Rāma and Kṛṣṇa.
m.2.5.54.7: Joined with twelve akṣauhiṇīs, the bulls of the Sātvatas besieged Bāṇa's city on all sides, from every direction.
m.2.5.54.8: Seeing the city's gardens, ramparts, watchtowers and gateways being shattered, Bāṇa, filled with rage, sallied forth with an equal army.
m.2.5.54.9: For Bāṇa's sake, Lord Rudra, with his son, surrounded by the Pramathas, mounted the bull Nandin and came to fight.
m.2.5.54.10: There arose a most tumultuous, wondrous, hair-raising battle there between Kṛṣṇa and the others and those protectors of Bāṇa headed by Rudra.
m.2.5.54.11: There was combat between Kṛṣṇa and Śaṅkara, between Pradyumna and Guha, and of Balarāma with Kūṣmāṇḍa and Kūpakarṇa.
m.2.5.54.12: There was combat of Sāmba with Bāṇa's son, of Sātyaki with Bāṇa, of Garuḍa with Nandin, and of others with others.
m.2.5.54.13: Brahmā and the other lords of the gods, the sages, Siddhas and Cāraṇas, Gandharvas and Apsarases came in their vehicles and aerial cars to watch.
m.2.5.54.14: O chief of brahmins, a very fierce battle took place between those of the Yadu lineage and the Pramathas of various forms, down to the Revatīs.
m.2.5.54.15: Together with his brother Rāma and the wise Pradyumna, Kṛṣṇa waged an incomparable battle with the Pramathas.
m.2.5.54.16: There battle took place with Agni, with Yama and Varuṇa, with Vimukha, with the three-footed Fever, and with Guha.
m.2.5.54.17: Between the Vṛṣṇis and the Pramathas of various forms there arose an exceedingly fierce, dreadful, hair-raising battle.
m.2.5.54.18: It was with many terrifying apparitions, with Koṭarīs at every step, and with shameless, mighty women close by.
m.2.5.54.19: Śauri (Kṛṣṇa) put to flight Śaṅkara's followers—Bhūtas, Pramathas and Guhyakas—with sharp-tipped arrows shot from the Śārṅga bow.
m.2.5.54.20: Thus the heroes led by Pradyumna, for whom battle was a great festival, fought a most terrible battle, destroying the enemy army.
m.2.5.54.21: Seeing his own army being shattered, Rudra, extremely indignant, became greatly angry and roared a very fearsome roar.
m.2.5.54.22: Hearing that, Śaṅkara's Gaṇas roared and fought, crushing their opponents, strengthened by Śambhu's power.
m.2.5.54.23: Kṛṣṇa discharged various missiles from the Śārṅga against Pinākin; the trident-wielder, unperturbed, neutralized them with counter-weapons.
m.2.5.54.24: Against the Brahmāstra, the Brahmāstra; against the wind-missile, the mountain-missile; against the fire-missile, the rain-missile; and against Nārāyaṇa's missile, his own.
m.2.5.54.25: Kṛṣṇa's army, defeated by the opposing hero, fled; O Vyāsa, it could not stand in battle before the full, mighty splendour of Rudra.
m.2.5.54.26: When his army had been routed, the glorious Kṛṣṇa, scorcher of foes, released his own watery fever called Śītala, O sage.
m.2.5.54.27: With Kṛṣṇa's army routed, Kṛṣṇa's cold fever advanced upon Rudra, O sage, burning the ten directions.
m.2.5.54.28: Then Maheśvara, seeing it coming, released his own fever; and the two fevers, Māheśvara and Vaiṣṇava, fought each other.
m.2.5.54.29: Then the Vaiṣṇava fever, afflicted by the Māheśvara's might, crying out and finding no safety elsewhere, praised the bull-bannered Śiva.
m.2.5.54.30: Then Lord Hara, pleased at being praised by Viṣṇu's fever, kind to those who seek refuge, spoke to Viṣṇu's cold fever.
m.2.5.54.31: Maheśvara said: O cold fever, I am pleased; let your fear of my fever depart. Whoever remembers our dialogue will have no fear of fever.
m.2.5.54.32: Sanatkumāra said: Thus addressed, Nārāyaṇa's fever bowed to Rudra and departed. Seeing that event, Kṛṣṇa was amazed and filled with fear.
m.2.5.54.33: Then Skanda, harassed by Pradyumna's floods of arrows, enraged and fiercely indignant on behalf of the Daitya hosts, struck Pradyumna with his spear.
m.2.5.54.34: Struck there by Skanda's spear, Pradyumna, mighty though he was, shedding blood from his limbs, withdrew from the battle with effort.
m.2.5.54.35: Struck by Kumbhāṇḍa and Kūpakarṇa with various missiles, Balabhadra too fled; mighty as he was, he did not stand in battle.
m.2.5.54.36: Then Garuḍa, assuming a thousand bodies and drinking water from the great ocean, wrought destruction with whirlpools of cloud- and ocean-waters.
m.2.5.54.37: Then Maheśa's mount, the mighty bull, enraged, swiftly and with great force struck him (Garuḍa) with his two horns.
m.2.5.54.38: His limbs torn by the blows of the horns, Garuḍa, greatly astonished, quickly fled from the battle, abandoning Janārdana.
m.2.5.54.39: When things had turned out thus, the Lord, son of Devakī, greatly astonished by Rudra's power, quickly spoke to his charioteer.
m.2.5.54.40: Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: O charioteer, listen to my words: drive my chariot swiftly, so that I may stand near Mahādeva to speak to him.
m.2.5.54.41: Sanatkumāra said: Addressed thus by Hari, the charioteer Dāruka, foremost in his own skills, quickly drove that chariot toward Rudra.
m.2.5.54.42: Then Śrī Kṛṣṇa, bowing with joined palms, having taken refuge with devotion, addressed Śaṅkara, who is affectionate to his devotees.
m.2.5.54.43: Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: O God of gods, O Mahādeva, loving to those who come for refuge, I bow to you of infinite power, the Self of all, the Supreme Lord.
m.2.5.54.44: I bow to you, the cause of the origin, sustenance and dissolution of the universe, pure consciousness alone, the supreme Brahman-liṅga, peaceful, absolute, the Supreme Lord.
m.2.5.54.45: Time, destiny, karma, the individual soul, inherent nature, and matter; the field (body), the vital breath, the self, and the transformations—their aggregate—
m.2.5.54.46: —this continuous flow, like seed and sprout, is your māyā, O Lord of the world. Here I take refuge in you, the Supreme Lord, who holds it in check.
m.2.5.54.47: Through various forms assumed by yourself merely in sport, you, Lord of the worlds, surely sustain the gods and others, and by your very nature you slay those who go astray.
m.2.5.54.48: For you are Brahman, the supreme light, hidden in the Veda (the Brahman made of words), whom the wise see as the stainless Self, absolute like the sky.
m.2.5.54.49: You alone are the primeval Person, without a second, the fourth (turīya), the seer of the Self, the Lord; you are the cause and yet causeless, and you appear as endowed with transformations.
m.2.5.54.50: By your own māyā, for the manifestation of all the guṇas, O Blessed Lord, O Master, you are connected with everything and yet distinct from everything, O Maheśvara.
m.2.5.54.51: Just as the sun, though covered by cloud, illumines by its own light the shadow-forms too, O Lord, so indeed are you, the supreme Seer.
m.2.5.54.52: Though covered by the guṇa, you are not in the guṇa; self-luminous, you illumine the guṇas, O all-pervading one, O infinite one, O Giriśa, O Śaṅkara.
m.2.5.54.53: Those whose minds are deluded by your māyā, attached to sons, wives, houses and the like, rise up and sink down in the ocean of sin.
m.2.5.54.54: He who, having obtained this human world given by fate, with senses unconquered, does not honour your feet—he is to be pitied, a deceiver of himself.
m.2.5.54.55: By your command, O Lord, I have come to cut off Bāṇa's arms. This proud Bāṇa has been cursed by you yourself, the remover of pride.
m.2.5.54.56: Withdraw from the battle, O God, so that your curse may not be in vain. Give me your permission, O Lord, to cut off Bāṇa's arms.
m.2.5.54.57: Sanatkumāra said: Having heard these words of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, O lord of sages, Śambhu Maheśvara, pleased at heart by Kṛṣṇa's praise, replied.
m.2.5.54.58: Maheśvara said: You have spoken truly, dear one; the king of the Daityas was indeed cursed by me. By my command you have come to cut off Bāṇa's mace-like arms.
m.2.5.54.59: What can I do, O lord of Ramā? I am always subject to my devotees, O Hari. How, O hero, could Bāṇa's arms be cut while I look on?
m.2.5.54.60: Therefore, at my command, make me yawn with the yawning-weapon (jṛmbhaṇāstra). Then do your work as you wish, and be happy.
m.2.5.54.61: Sanatkumāra said: Thus addressed by Śaṅkara, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, greatly astonished, returned to his own place on the battlefield and rejoiced, O lord of sages.
m.2.5.54.62: Then Hari, skilled in many weapons, quickly fitting the yawning-weapon to his bow, released it at the Pināka-wielder, O Vyāsa.
m.2.5.54.63: Having stupefied Giriśa, who was made to yawn by the yawning-weapon, Śauri (Kṛṣṇa) struck down Bāṇa's army with swords, maces and spears.
m.2.5.54.iti: Thus ends the fifty-fourth adhyāya, named The battle of Bāṇāsura with Rudra, Kṛṣṇa and others, in the fifth khaṇḍa, the Yuddha-khaṇḍa, of the second saṃhitā, the Rudra-saṃhitā, of the Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.2.5.55.1: Vyāsa said: O Sanatkumāra, all-knowing son of Brahmā, salutations to you. Wonderful is this story, dear one, that you have narrated to me, O sage.
m.2.5.55.2: When Hara had been made to yawn in battle by Hari with the yawning weapon, and Bāṇa's army had been slain, what did Bāṇa do? Tell me that.
m.2.5.55.3: Sūta said: Having heard these words of Vyāsa of boundless splendour, the son of Brahmā, lord of sages, replied with a pleased heart.
m.2.5.55.4: Sanatkumāra said: Listen, O greatly wise Vyāsa, dear one, to the most wonderful story of Kṛṣṇa and Śaṅkara, who conform to worldly play.
m.2.5.55.5: When Rudra, together with his son and his attendants, had in sport fallen asleep, Bāṇa, the king of the Daityas, went out to fight with Kṛṣṇa.
