m.3.16.28: Then all the gods headed by Viṣṇu, thinking themselves heroes, exerted their prowess there and hurled their weapons.
m.3.16.29: Those weapons of the heaven-dwellers at once became futile there, through the power of Śiva, remover of their foolish pride.
m.3.16.30: Then there came a voice from the sky that dispelled the gods' astonishment: This Yakṣa, O gods, is Śaṅkara, remover of all pride.
m.3.16.31: He alone, the Supreme Lord, is creator, destroyer and sustainer. By his strength all beings are strong, not otherwise.
m.3.16.32: Deluded by the power of his māyā and through pride, even now they did not recognise their own Lord Śiva, the Lord whose body is consciousness.
m.3.16.33: Nandīśvara said: Hearing the heavenly voice, they understood, their pride gone; they bowed to Yakṣeśvara and praised that Lord.
m.3.16.34: The gods said: O God of gods, Mahādeva, remover of all pride, O Yakṣeśvara of great sport, your māyā is most wondrous, O Lord.
m.3.16.35: Deluded even now by the māyā of you who have taken the Yakṣa form, we spoke proudly before you, thinking ourselves separate from you.
m.3.16.36: Now, O Lord, knowledge has come by your grace alone: you alone are creator, destroyer and sustainer, none other, O Śaṅkara.
m.3.16.37: You alone are the initiator and withdrawer of all powers of all beings, the Lord of all, the Supreme Self, imperishable and non-dual.
m.3.16.38: In the form of Yakṣeśvara you have taken away the pride of all of us; we consider that a grace bestowed by you, the compassionate one.
m.3.16.39: Then that lord of Yakṣas, having favoured all the gods and enlightened them with various words, vanished right there.
m.3.16.40: Thus has been described Śambhu's incarnation named Yakṣeśvara, which brings happiness—giving joy to the good and, when pleased, granting fearlessness.
m.3.16.41: This stainless narrative removes all pride; it always grants deep peace to the virtuous and bestows worldly enjoyment and liberation upon men.
m.3.16.42: The wise man who listens to this with devotion, or causes it to be recited to others, obtains all his desires and thereafter attains the supreme goal.
m.3.16.iti: Thus ends the sixteenth adhyāya, named The incarnation as Yakṣeśvara, in the third saṃhitā, the Śatarudra-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.3.17.1: Now hear of the first ten incarnations of Giriśa, headed by Mahākāla, which are served with devotion through the section of scripture concerned with worship (upāsanā-kāṇḍa).
m.3.17.2: Among them the first is Mahākāla, granter of enjoyment and liberation to the good. His Śakti there is Mahākālī, who grants the fruits desired by devotees.
m.3.17.3: The second is named Tāra, and likewise his Śakti is Tārā. Both grant enjoyment and liberation and give happiness to their own servants.
m.3.17.4: The third is proclaimed to be Bhuvaneśa, called Bāla; there Śivā is Bhuvaneśī, called Bālā, giver of happiness to the good.
m.3.17.5: The fourth is Śrīvidyeśa, called Ṣoḍaśa, and Śivā is Śrīvidyā Ṣoḍaśī; he gives happiness to devotees and grants the fruits of enjoyment and liberation.
m.3.17.6: The fifth is known as Bhairava, ever fulfilling the desires of devotees; there Girijā is Bhairavī, fulfilling the desires of true worshippers.
m.3.17.7: Śiva named Chinnamastaka is proclaimed the sixth; and Girijā is Chinnamastakā, granting the desires of devotees.
m.3.17.8: The seventh is Śambhu as Dhūmavān, granting the fruits of all desires; there Śivā is Dhūmavatī, fulfilling the desires of true worshippers.
m.3.17.9: The eighth incarnation of Śiva, giver of happiness, is Bagalāmukha; his Śakti there is Mahānandā, renowned as Bagalāmukhī.
m.3.17.10: The ninth incarnation of Śiva is proclaimed to be Mātaṅga; there Śarvāṇī is Mātaṅgī, granting the fruits of all desires.
m.3.17.11: The tenth is Śambhu as Kamala, granting the fruits of enjoyment and liberation; there Girijā is Kamalā, protector of her own devotees.
m.3.17.12: These ten incarnations of Śiva are givers of happiness, and always grant enjoyment and liberation to good devotees.
m.3.17.13: These are indeed the ten incarnations of the great-souled Śaṅkara, constantly giving various kinds of happiness to those who serve them without deviation.
m.3.17.14: O sage, this greatness of the ten incarnations has been described; it should be known as granting all desires and as contained in the Tantra scriptures and others.
m.3.17.15: O sage, wondrous is the glory of these primal Śaktis; it should be known as granting all desires and as contained in the Tantra scriptures and others.
m.3.17.16: In rites such as slaying enemies, each respective Śakti is held supreme; she always punishes the wicked and increases the brahminical splendour.
m.3.17.17: Thus, O brahmin, I have told you of the ten auspicious incarnations of Maheśa together with their Śaktis, headed by Mahākāla.
m.3.17.18: Whoever, intent on devotion, recites this pure narrative on all Śaiva festival days becomes exceedingly dear to Śambhu.
m.3.17.19: A brahmin would become endowed with brahminical lustre, a kṣatriya victorious, a vaiśya a lord of wealth, and a śūdra would attain happiness.
m.3.17.20: Followers of Śaṅkara who abide in their own dharma and listen to this account would be especially happy, and may they become devotees of Śiva.
m.3.17.iti: Thus ends the seventeenth adhyāya, named The ten incarnations of Śiva, in the third saṃhitā, the Śatarudra-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.3.18.1: Nandīśvara said: Now listen to the eleven excellent incarnations of Śaṅkara, on hearing which one is not afflicted by the affliction that arises from untruth and the like.
m.3.18.2: Long ago all the gods, headed by Śakra, defeated by the Daityas, abandoned their own city Amarāvatī and fled in fear.
m.3.18.3: Oppressed by the Daityas, the gods went to Kaśyapa; joining their palms, with shoulders bowed, they prostrated before him in great distress.
m.3.18.4: Having praised him well and respectfully made their petition, all the gods reported everything to him: their own misery and their defeat.
m.3.18.5: Then, dear one, Kaśyapa, their father, whose mind was devoted to Śiva, hearing of the gods' misery, became sorrowful, though not excessively.
m.3.18.6: Then that sage, calm of mind, having comforted them and summoning his fortitude, went with great delight to Kāśī, the city of Viśveśvara, O sage.
m.3.18.7: Then, having bathed in the water of the Gaṅgā and performed the rite with reverence, he worshipped Viśveśvara, the Lord of all, the master, together with Ambā.
m.3.18.8: Having duly installed a Śiva-liṅga, he performed extensive austerity with great love, directed toward Śambhu, desiring the welfare of the gods.
m.3.18.9: A long time passed, O sage, while he practised austerity, steadfast, his mind attached to the lotus feet of Śiva.
m.3.18.10: Then Śambhu, friend of the afflicted and refuge of the virtuous, appeared to grant a boon to that seer whose mind was attached to his feet.
m.3.18.11: And Maheśvara, very pleased, affectionate to his devotees, said to Kaśyapa, the tiger among sages and his own devotee: Ask for a boon.
m.3.18.12: Having seen that Great Lord, Kaśyapa, the father of the gods, delighted and serene of mind, bowed with joined palms and praised him.
m.3.18.13: Kaśyapa said: O God of gods, Great Lord, affectionate to those who seek refuge, you are the Lord of all, the Supreme Self, reachable through meditation, non-dual and imperishable.
m.3.18.14: You, O Maheśvara, are the subduer of the mighty, the refuge of the virtuous, the friend of the afflicted, an ocean of compassion, whose mind is skilled in protecting devotees.
m.3.18.15: These gods are indeed yours, and especially your devotees. Today they have been defeated by the Daityas; protect them in their sorrow, O Lord.
m.3.18.16: Even the Lord of Ramā Viṣṇu is powerless; they the Daityas cause distress again and again. Therefore the gods have taken refuge in me, reporting that misery.
m.3.18.17: For that purpose, O Lord of the gods of gods, destroyer of the gods' sorrow, to fulfil that wish, I have undertaken steadfast austerity to win your favour.
m.3.18.18: I have taken refuge in you in every way, O Maheśvara. Fulfil my desire, O Master; destroy the sorrow of the gods.
m.3.18.19: And I am especially afflicted by the sorrows of my sons, O Lord of the gods. Make me happy, O Īśa; you are the helper of the heaven-dwellers.
m.3.18.20: O Lord, becoming my son — for the gods and Yakṣas have been defeated by the mighty Daityas — O Śambhu, be the giver of joy to the gods.
m.3.18.21: May you always be the helper of all the gods, O Great Lord, so that the affliction caused by the Daityas may not trouble the gods, O Lord.
m.3.18.22: Nandīśvara said: When he had spoken thus, Śaṅkara, the Lord of all, said, so be it, and the blessed Hara vanished right there as he looked on.
m.3.18.23: Kaśyapa too, greatly delighted, quickly went to his own abode and respectfully told the gods the whole account.
m.3.18.24: Then Śaṅkara, Śarva, to make his own word true, was born of Surabhī from Kaśyapa, assuming eleven forms.
m.3.18.25: Then there was a great festival; everything became full of auspiciousness (śivamaya). The gods were delighted, as was the sage Kaśyapa.
m.3.18.26: Kapālī, Piṅgala, Bhīma, Virūpākṣa, Vilohita, Śāstā, Ajapāt, Ahirbudhnya, Śambhu, Caṇḍa and likewise Bhava.
m.3.18.27: These eleven Rudras are known as the sons of Surabhī; they were born for the gods' purpose, are forms of Śiva, and are the abode of happiness.
m.3.18.28: Those heroic Rudras, sons of Kaśyapa, of great strength and valour, rendering help to the gods, slew the Daityas in battle.
m.3.18.29: By the grace of those Rudras, the gods, having conquered the Daityas and become fearless, all of them headed by Śakra, with minds at ease, ruled their own kingdom.
m.3.18.30: Even today those great Rudras, all of them forms of Śiva, shine forever in heaven for the protection of the gods.
m.3.18.31: Affectionate to their devotees, they made their dwelling in the city of Īśāna, in the north-east; skilled in various sports, they always delight there.
m.3.18.32: Their attendants, also Rudras, are declared to number in crores; they are stationed everywhere there, in the three worlds, according to their respective portions.
m.3.18.33: Thus, dear one, I have described to you the incarnations of Śaṅkara, the Rudras eleven in number, who bring happiness to all the worlds.
m.3.18.34: This pure narrative destroys all sins; it is blessed, brings fame and long life, and grants all desires.
m.3.18.35: Whoever, dear one, listens to this or recites it to others with a concentrated mind, enjoys every happiness here and thereafter attains liberation.
m.3.18.iti: Thus ends the eighteenth adhyāya, named The eleven incarnations, in the third saṃhitā, the Śatarudra-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.3.19.1: Nandīśvara said: Now hear with delight, O great sage, another deed of Śambhu: how Śaṅkara became Durvāsas for the sake of dharma.
m.3.19.2: There was a son of Brahmā, an exceedingly great ascetic, a knower of brahman, a master, the wise husband of Anasūyā, faithful in carrying out Brahmā's command.
m.3.19.3: At the clear instruction of Brahmā, he, together with his wife and desiring a son, went to the mountain named Tryakṣakula to perform austerity.
m.3.19.4: Restraining his breath according to rule on the bank of the river Nirvindhyā, the sage, free from the pairs of opposites, practised a very great austerity for a hundred years.
m.3.19.5: He had his mind fixed on this: Whoever is the one Lord, changeless, the great master — may he grant me an excellent son.
m.3.19.6: Much time passed while he performed true austerity; then from him arose a bright, immense flame.
m.3.19.7: By it all the worlds were almost burnt; the chief sages, and likewise all the gods and seers, Vāsava and the rest, were tormented.
m.3.19.8: Then all the gods led by Vāsava, and the sages, O sage, sorely tormented by that flame, quickly went to the abode of Brahmā.
m.3.19.9: Bowing to and praising Brahmā, the gods told him of their distress; and Brahmā, dear one, went swiftly with the gods to Viṣṇu's world.
m.3.19.10: Going there, Brahmā with the gods bowed to and praised the Lord of Ramā, and recounted to Viṣṇu that boundless distress of theirs, O sage.
m.3.19.11: And Viṣṇu, with Brahmā and the gods, went quickly to Rudra's abode; arriving there and bowing to Hara, he praised the Supreme Lord.
m.3.19.12: Having praised him at length, Viṣṇu reported to Śarva their distress, arisen from the flame of Atri's supreme austerity.
m.3.19.13: Then Brahmā, Viṣṇu and Maheśvara, gathered there, consulted with one another, O sage, about the welfare of the worlds.
m.3.19.14: Then those three gods, Brahmā and the others, foremost among bestowers of boons, quickly went to his hermitage to grant a boon to that seer.
m.3.19.15: Seeing them marked with their own emblems, Atri, best of sages, bowed and reverently praised them with pleasing words.
m.3.19.16: Then that brahmin, son of Brahmā, humble in spirit and astonished, with joined palms spoke to them, who were called Brahmā, Viṣṇu and Hara.
m.3.19.17: Atri said: O Brahmā, O Hari, O Rudra, you are held to be worthy of worship by the three worlds — the sources and lords, the agents of creation, preservation and dissolution.
m.3.19.18: Only one Lord was meditated upon by me, together with my wife, for the sake of a son — whoever is renowned as the Lord of the worlds.
m.3.19.19: Why have you three gods, foremost of boon-givers, come? Dispel this doubt of mine, and then grant the desired boon.
m.3.19.20: Hearing his words, the three gods replied: Just as your resolve was made, so has it come to pass, O lord of sages.
m.3.19.21: We three are equal lords of the world, foremost of boon-givers; therefore three sons born of our portions will be born to you.
m.3.19.22: All of them will be famed in the world, enhancing the glory of their parents. Having said this, the three gods joyfully went to their own abodes.
m.3.19.23: Having received the boon, the sage, giver of the bliss of brahman, then joyfully returned to his hermitage with Anasūyā, well pleased, O sage.
m.3.19.24: Then Brahmā, Hari and Śambhu, well pleased, descended into that woman in the form of sons, displaying various divine sports.
m.3.19.25: From a portion of Brahmā the Moon was born in Anasūyā from the lord of sages; it was he who later, cast into the ocean by the gods, emerged from the ocean.
m.3.19.26: From a portion of Viṣṇu, Datta was born to Atri in that woman, by whom the supreme path of renunciation was promoted, O sage.
m.3.19.27: From a portion of Śiva, O best of sages, was born to Atri in that woman Durvāsas, the tiger among sages, promulgator of excellent dharma.
m.3.19.28: And Rudra, having become Durvāsas, increaser of brahminical splendour, full of compassion, tested the dharma of many.
m.3.19.29: There was a king Ambarīṣa born in the Solar dynasty; he Durvāsas tested him — hear of that, O lord of sages.
m.3.19.30: That Ambarīṣa, best of kings, lord of the earth with its seven continents, kept a firm rule regarding the Ekādaśī vow.
m.3.19.31: The king was firmly resolved: Having kept the Ekādaśī vow, I shall break the fast on Dvādaśī.
m.3.19.32: Knowing of his observance, Durvāsas, best of sages, born of Śaṅkara's portion, went to him with many disciples.
m.3.19.33: Knowing that only a little of Dvādaśī remained for breaking the fast, just as he resolved to eat, he invited the sage who had arrived.
m.3.19.34: Then Durvāsas went with his disciples to bathe, and there the sage delayed long in order to test the king.
m.3.19.35: Then the king, seeing the obstacle to his dharma, sipped water as prescribed by scripture and waited there, longing for his return.
m.3.19.36: Meanwhile the sage Durvāsas arrived there; knowing the king had taken food, he assumed a wrathful form for the sake of the test.
m.3.19.37: He became furious with that king, in order to test his dharma; and the sage born of Śaṅkara's portion spoke fierce words.
m.3.19.38: Durvāsā said: Having invited me, O king, without feeding me you have drunk water, O wretch. I shall show you its fruit, for I am the wielder of the rod over the wicked.
m.3.19.39: Having said this, his eyes red with anger, he made ready to burn the king; at once the Lord's discus stationed there rose up to protect him.
m.3.19.40: That Sudarśana discus blazed fiercely to burn the sage, not knowing him to be a form of Śiva, being deluded by Śiva's māyā.
m.3.19.41: Meanwhile a bodiless voice from the sky spoke to Ambarīṣa, the great-souled one, devoted to brāhmaṇas and a Vaiṣṇava.
m.3.19.42: The heavenly voice said: This discus Sudarśana was bestowed on Hari by Śambhu. O king, now make it calm, blazing as it is against Durvāsas.
m.3.19.43: This Durvāsas is Śiva himself; it was he who gave the discus to Hari. Do not regard him, O best of kings, as an ordinary sage.
m.3.19.44: This lord of sages has come to test your dharma. Quickly go to him for refuge; otherwise destruction will follow.
m.3.19.45: Nandīśvara said: Having said this, O lord of sages, the voice from the sky fell silent. And Ambarīṣa too reverently praised him, that portion of Hara.
m.3.19.46: Ambarīṣa said: If there is merit from what I have given and sacrificed, or if my own dharma has been well performed, if our family holds brāhmaṇas as its deity, then may Hari's weapon be pacified.
m.3.19.47: If the Lord, devoted to me and affectionate to devotees, is pleased with us, may this weapon Sudarśana be pacified completely.
m.3.19.48: Nandīśvara said: As he was praising thus in front of Rudra, the Śaiva discus Sudarśana became wholly calm; and he, of clear understanding, knowing him to be a portion of Śiva,
m.3.19.49: then King Ambarīṣa bowed to that sage, recognising him as an incarnation of Śiva who had come to test him.
m.3.19.50: Then that sage, born of a portion of Śaṅkara, became very pleased; having eaten and granted him the boon he desired, he went to his own abode.
m.3.19.51: O sage, the deed of Durvāsas in testing Ambarīṣa has been told. Now hear another of his deeds, O lord of sages.
m.3.19.52: Again he tested Dāśarathi Rāma by means of the vow—the rule that had been made by Kāla in the guise of a sage, O sage.
m.3.19.53: At that very time that sage forcibly made Saumitri Lakṣmaṇa be sent in; and Rāma, bound by his pledge, at once abandoned his brother, O sage.
m.3.19.54: That story is well known in the world and has been told in many ways by sages; therefore I have not narrated it at length, since it is fully known to the wise.
m.3.19.55: Seeing his very firm adherence to the vow, the sage Durvāsas was highly pleased, and with a gladdened heart he granted him a boon.
m.3.19.56: He also tested the vow of Śrī Kṛṣṇa. Hear that, O best of sages; I shall tell you that story.
m.3.19.57: At Brahmā's request Viṣṇu became the son of Vasudeva, to remove the burden of the earth and to protect the good.
m.3.19.58: He who bore the name Kṛṣṇa slew the wicked, greatly sinful villains who harmed brāhmaṇas, and protected all the good people and brāhmaṇas.
m.3.19.59: That Kṛṣṇa, son of Vasudeva, showed exceeding devotion to brāhmaṇas; daily he fed many brāhmaṇas with delicious food.
m.3.19.60: Kṛṣṇa gained fame as being especially devoted to brāhmaṇas. Wishing to see him, that sage went to Kṛṣṇa's presence, O sage.
m.3.19.61: He himself had Kṛṣṇa, together with Rukmiṇī, harnessed to the chariot; having yoked them as the draught animal, he sat in it, and Kṛṣṇa, well pleased, drew him.
m.3.19.62: The sage got down from the chariot and, seeing that supreme steadfastness, became very pleased with him and gave him the boon of an adamantine body.
m.3.19.63: Once, while bathing in the celestial river, he became naked; the playful Durvāsas, best of sages, was embarrassed, O sage.
m.3.19.64: Knowing this, Draupadī, who was bathing there, respectfully covered his shame by giving a torn-off piece of the hem of her own garment.
m.3.19.65: The sage took that cloth, which had come near him with the current, covered his private parts with it, and became pleased with her.
m.3.19.66: He gave Draupadī the boon of the endless lengthening of her garment's hem; and through that boon Draupadī later made the Pāṇḍavas happy.
m.3.19.67: Two certain kings, Haṃsa and Ḍimbha, wicked men who had insulted him—that lord had them destroyed by giving a command to Hari.
m.3.19.68: He especially established brahminical splendour on earth, and also the path of renunciation (saṃnyāsa) according to the order of scriptural rules.
m.3.19.69: He uplifted many by imparting good instruction, and by bestowing knowledge he especially made many liberated.
m.3.19.70: Thus Durvāsas performed many wondrous deeds, which are blessed, bring fame and long life, and fulfil every wish of the one who hears them.
m.3.19.71: Whoever hears this account of Durvāsas with devotion and joy, or whoever causes others to hear it, is happy here and in the hereafter.
m.3.19.iti: Thus ends the nineteenth adhyāya, named The life of Durvāsas, in the third saṃhitā, the Śatarudra-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.3.20.1: Nandīśvara said: Hereafter, O sage, listen with affection to the story of Hanumān: how Hara quickly performed excellent sports in that form.
m.3.20.2: The Supreme Lord lovingly did great good for Rāma. O brahmin, hear that entire story, which brings every happiness.
m.3.20.3: Once Śambhu, the Lord who performs wondrous deeds, endowed with every virtue, beheld the Mohinī form of Viṣṇu.
m.3.20.4: Śambhu made himself agitated, as though struck by the arrows of Kāma; the Lord caused his semen to fall for the sake of Rāma's task.
m.3.20.5: Those seven sages, prompted by his mind, respectfully placed that semen on a leaf for the sake of Rāma's task.
m.3.20.6: Those great sages deposited Śambhu's semen into Añjanī, daughter of Gautama, through her ear, for the sake of Rāma's task.
m.3.20.7: Then in due time Śambhu was born from her, bearing the name Hanumān, in a monkey's body, of great strength and valour.
m.3.20.8: That Hanumān, lord of monkeys, mighty even as a child, at dawn quickly swallowed the sun's orb, thinking it a small fruit.
m.3.20.9: At the gods' entreaty he released it; and, the gods knowing him to be mighty and an incarnation of Śiva, he received boons given by the chief gods.
m.3.20.10: Then, greatly delighted, Hanumān went to his mother and respectfully told her all that had happened.
m.3.20.11: Then by her command that steadfast monkey, going daily into the Sun's presence, learned all knowledge from the Sun without effort.
m.3.20.12: By the Sun's command, having obtained his mother's permission, that best of monkeys, a portion of Rudra, went to Sugrīva, who was born of the Sun's portion.
m.3.20.13: Sugrīva, spurned by his elder brother Vālin, who enjoyed his wife, lived on Mount Ṛṣyamūka together with that Hanumān.
m.3.20.14: Then that wise, excellent monkey became the minister of Sukaṇṭha (Sugrīva); born of Hara's portion, he did Sugrīva good in every way.
m.3.20.15: He brought about a happy friendship between him and Rāma, who had come there with his brother, grieving, his wife having been abducted.
m.3.20.16: And Rāma slew Vālin, elephant among monkeys, the sinful enjoyer of his brother's wife, who fancied himself a hero.
m.3.20.17: Then, dear one, by Rāma's command the wise Hanumān, lord of monkeys, undertook the search for Sītā with many monkeys.
m.3.20.18: Learning that Sītā had been taken to Laṅkā, the lord of monkeys swiftly leapt across that ocean, uncrossable by others, and went there.
m.3.20.19: There he performed wondrous deeds full of valour, and lovingly gave Sītā the excellent token of his master.
m.3.20.20: That heroic leader of monkeys quickly removed Sītā's grief by telling her the news of Rāma, which saved her life.
m.3.20.21: Taking her token, he set out back toward Rāma; having wrecked Rāvaṇa's garden, he killed many rākṣasas.
m.3.20.22: At that very time, having slain Rāvaṇa's son along with many rākṣasas, he of great sport, fearless, created great havoc there.
m.3.20.23: When, O sage, he was set on fire by the mighty Rāvaṇa, who had wrapped him tightly in oil-soaked cloths,
m.3.20.24: then that monkey, born of Mahādeva's portion, leaping again and again, burned all of Laṅkā, making that very fire his pretext.
m.3.20.25: Having burned Laṅkā, sparing Vibhīṣaṇa's house, that heroic elephant among monkeys then dropped into the ocean.
m.3.20.26: Extinguishing his tail there, he reached its far shore; unwearied, he who was born of Giriśa's portion went to Rāma's presence.
m.3.20.27: Without delay the swift Hanumān, best of monkeys, came near Rāma and gave him Sītā's crest-jewel.
m.3.20.28: Then by his command the mighty hero, gathering many great mountains with the monkeys, had a bridge built over the ocean.
m.3.20.29: Then Rāma, going there and wishing to cross, installed a Śiva-liṅga and duly worshipped it, desiring victory.
m.3.20.30: By his boon he obtained the excellent gift of victory, then crossed the ocean, surrounded Laṅkā with the monkeys, and fought the rākṣasas.
m.3.20.31: Then the hero Hanumān slew the asuras and protected Rāma's army; and he revived Lakṣmaṇa, wounded by the Śakti weapon, with the sañjīvinī herb.
m.3.20.32: He made Lakṣmaṇa, together with Rāma, happy in every way; that lord, born of Mahādeva, protected the whole army.
m.3.20.33: Tirelessly he destroyed Rāvaṇa with his whole retinue; that monkey of mighty grip made the gods happy.
m.3.20.34: Having slain the one named Mahīrāvaṇa, he brought Rāma with Lakṣmaṇa back from that place to their own camp and protected them.
m.3.20.35: The bull among monkeys swiftly accomplished Rāma's task in every way; he subdued the asuras and performed various sports.
m.3.20.36: The lord of monkeys established devotion to Rāma on earth, himself becoming the foremost devotee, bestower of happiness on Sītā and Rāma.
m.3.20.37: He is the giver of life to Lakṣmaṇa, the remover of the pride of all the gods, the blessed incarnation of Rudra, the uplifter of devotees.
m.3.20.38: That Hanumān, the great hero, ever doing Rāma's work, is known in the world as Rāma's messenger, slayer of demons, loving toward devotees.
m.3.20.39: Thus, dear one, I have told you the excellent story of Hanumān, which is blessed, brings fame and long life, and grants the fruit of all desires.
m.3.20.40: Whoever hears this with devotion, or attentively causes it to be heard, enjoys all desires here and at the end attains supreme liberation.
m.3.20.iti: Thus ends the twentieth adhyāya, named The incarnation as Hanumān and his deeds, in the third saṃhitā, the Śatarudra-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.3.21.1: Nandīśvara said: Now, O sage, O son of the Self-born Brahmā, listen with delight to the supreme incarnation of the Lord Śaṅkara, which grants all desires to those who hear it.
m.3.21.2: Once, O tiger among sages, both Girijā and Śaṅkara, the supreme rulers, by their own will became desirous of sporting.
m.3.21.3: Making Bhairava the doorkeeper, they went inside, lovingly attended by various groups of companions, behaving in human fashion.
m.3.21.4: Having sported there for a long time, the two independent supreme lords, performers of various pastimes, became pleased, O sage.
m.3.21.5: Then the independent goddess Śivā, playfully assuming a frenzied form, came to the door in that form, having obtained the Lord's permission.
m.3.21.6: Then that Bhairava, looking at the goddess with the gaze one casts on a woman and infatuated by her form, forbade her to go out.
m.3.21.7: When she was gazed upon by Bhairava as a woman, O sage, the goddess Śivā became angry, and then Ambikā cursed him.
m.3.21.8: Śivā said: Since you look at me as a woman, O vilest of men, therefore, Bhairava, you shall become a human on earth.
m.3.21.9: Nandīśvara said: When Bhairava was thus cursed by Śivā, O sage, there was a great outcry of lamentation; he, through divine play, came to grief.
m.3.21.10: Then Śaṅkara, skilled in various ways of conciliation, quickly came to him, O lord of sages, and consoled Bhairava.
m.3.21.11: Then, because of that curse, Bhairava descended on earth, O sage, in a human womb, known by the name Vetāla, by Śaṅkara's will.
m.3.21.12: Out of affection for him, the all-pervading Śiva too descended on earth together with Śivā, engaged in noble play and adopting a worldly mode of life.
m.3.21.13: Śiva was named Maheśa and Girijā was Śāradā, O sage; the two, skilled in various pastimes, joyfully performed fine sport.
m.3.21.14: Thus, dear one, the excellent story of Maheśa has been told to you; it is blessed, bestows fame and long life, and grants the fruit of all desires.
m.3.21.15: Whoever hears this with devotion, or attentively causes it to be heard, enjoys all pleasures here and in the end attains liberation.
m.3.21.iti: Thus ends the twenty-first adhyāya, named The Maheśa incarnation, in the third saṃhitā, the Śatarudra-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.3.22.1: Nandīśvara said: Listen, O wise son of Brahmā, O lord of sages, to the excellent incarnation of Śiva named Vṛṣeśa, full of noble sport, which took away Hari's pride.
m.3.22.2: Long ago all the gods and demons, tormented by fear of old age and death, made a pact with each other and became eager to obtain the jewels.
m.3.22.3: Then all the gods and demons, O delight of the sage, set about churning the Ocean of Milk, the finest of oceans.
m.3.22.4: All the gods and demons, smiling brightly, wondered, O brahmin: By what means could this churning of it be done, for the accomplishment of our purpose?
m.3.22.5: Then a voice from the sky, its sound deep as a thundercloud, spoke to the gods and the demons by the Lord's command, reassuring them.
m.3.22.6: The heavenly voice said: O gods and demons, churn the Ocean of Milk; strength and wisdom will surely be yours, there is no doubt.
m.3.22.7: Make Mandara the churning rod and Vāsuki the rope; uniting together, all of you, churn with diligence.
m.3.22.8: Nandīśvara said: Having heard that voice from the sky, all the gods and demons then made effort to carry it out, O best of sages.
m.3.22.9: Having made a firm pact, they all went to Mandara, the finest of mountains, gold-hued, straight, and adorned with many splendours.
m.3.22.10: Having fully propitiated that lord of the mountain and being permitted by him, the gods and demons, wishing to carry it to the ocean of milk, uprooted it by force.
m.3.22.11: Having uprooted it with their arms, they all went toward the Ocean of Milk, O sage; but, their strength spent, they became unable to carry it there.
m.3.22.12: Slipping from their arms, that exceedingly heavy Mount Mandara suddenly fell at once right upon the gods and demons.
m.3.22.13: Thus, their effort shattered, the gods and demons were crushed; then, regaining consciousness, they praised the Lord of the world.
m.3.22.14: By his will they all rose up again, lifted that mountain, carried it, and cast it into the water at the northern shore of the Ocean of Milk.
m.3.22.15: Then the hosts of gods and demons, making Vāsuki the rope and desiring to obtain the jewels, churned the Ocean of Milk.
m.3.22.16: As the Ocean of Milk was being churned, Śrī, the great sovereign of the heavenly world, daughter of Bhṛgu and beloved of Hari, arose from the ocean.
m.3.22.17: Then arose Dhanvantari, the moon, the great tree Pārijāta, the horse Uccaiḥśravas, and likewise the elephant Airāvata;
m.3.22.18: wine (Surā), Hari's bow, the conch, then the wish-yielding cows, the jewel called Kaustubha, and also the nectar.
m.3.22.19: And as it was churned again, the great poison Kālakūṭa was born, blazing like the fire at the end of an age, bringing terror to gods and demons.
m.3.22.20: At the time the nectar was born, from the drops that spilled outside arose many beautiful women of wondrous appearance,
m.3.22.21: with faces like the full autumn moon, radiant as lightning, the sun and fire, adorned with necklaces, armlets, bracelets and divine gems.
m.3.22.22: Sprinkling the ten directions with the nectar-water of their loveliness, with long glances and arched brows, they drove the world to madness.
m.3.22.23: They were born by the crore from the nectar, issued forth as embodiments of desire. Then arose the nectar that wards off old age and death.
m.3.22.24: Keśava took Lakṣmī, the conch, the Kaustubha and the sword; the Sun respectfully took the divine horse Uccaiḥśravas.
m.3.22.25: Śacī's husband, the lord of the immortals, eagerly took the Pārijāta, best of trees, and Airāvata, lord of elephants.
m.3.22.26: Śaṅkara Śambhu, affectionate to his devotees, of his own will held the Kālakūṭa in his throat and bore the moon, for the protection of the gods.
m.3.22.27: The demons, deluded by the Lord's command, took the lovely woman named Surā, O Vyāsa; and all people took Dhanvantari.
m.3.22.28: All the sages, lords among sages, took the wish-granting cow; and those bewitching women remained as common to all.
m.3.22.29: For the sake of the nectar a great war broke out between the gods and demons, each seeking victory, their minds agitated against one another.
m.3.22.30: And the nectar was seized by force by the demons led by Bali, O Vyāsa, radiant like the fire and sun at the end of an age, having conquered the gods.
m.3.22.31: The gods, Śakra and the rest, all distressed by Śiva's māyā and harassed by the demons' might, sought refuge in Śaṅkara, dear son.
m.3.22.32: Then, by Śiva's command, that nectar was carefully taken back from the demons by the Lord of Ramā, through māyā, in the form of a woman, O sage.
m.3.22.33: Hari, best of masters of illusion, assuming a woman's form as Mohinī and deluding all the demons, made those gods drink it.
m.3.22.34: The chief demons went near her and said: Serve this nectar; let there be no discrimination here among the rows.
m.3.22.35: Having said this, all those Daityas and Dānavas, deluded by Śiva's māyā, gave the nectar to Viṣṇu, who wore a deceptive form.
m.3.22.36: Meanwhile, the chief Dānavas, seeing the women born from the nectar, led them away to their own places as they pleased.
m.3.22.37: Their cities were divine, a hundred times finer than heaven, well guarded by fearsome machines, and fashioned by the magic of Maya.
m.3.22.38: Having made all those cities secure, the demons, without having touched the women's breasts, went forth to battle, having indeed made a vow:
m.3.22.39: We shall not touch these women if we are defeated by the gods. Having said this, all those great heroic demons, eager for battle,
m.3.22.40: then roared lion-roars and blew their conches each separately, as though filling the sky and gratifying the clouds.
m.3.22.41: A terrifying battle took place between the gods and the asuras, known as the Devāsura war, unequalled and famous throughout the three worlds.
m.3.22.42: All the gods, protected by Viṣṇu, won victory; the daityas fled there, struck down by Viṣṇu together with the immortals.
m.3.22.43: The daityas, bewildered by the gods and by the great-souled Viṣṇu, those left over from the slaughter, entered Pātāla and its caverns.
m.3.22.44: Viṣṇu, the mighty one holding the discus in his hand, pursued them, going to the supreme Pātāla where they were staying as if utterly terrified.
m.3.22.45: Meanwhile Viṣṇu saw lovely women born from the nectar, with faces like the full moon, proud of their divine beauty.
m.3.22.46: Bewildered by the arrows of Kāma, he found delight right there, and he indeed took to sporting with those excellent women.
m.3.22.47: From them Viṣṇu begot sons of great valour, skilled in many kinds of warfare, making the whole earth tremble.
m.3.22.48: Then those sons of Hari, of great strength and valour, wrought great havoc, causing suffering in heaven and on earth.
m.3.22.49: Seeing the affliction of the worlds, the gods and sages then, bowing down to Brahmā, made a report about them to him.
m.3.22.50: Hearing that, Brahmā took them along and went to Mount Kailāsa; there, seeing the god Śiva, he bowed again and again.
m.3.22.51: With shoulders bowed and palms joined, he praised him with various hymns, saying: Victory, O god, O Mahādeva, O lord of all!
m.3.22.52: Brahmā said: O god of gods, O Mahādeva, O lord, protect all the worlds, afflicted by Viṣṇu's sons dwelling in Pātāla, who have become depraved.
m.3.22.53: O all-pervading one, Hari, his mind attached to the women born of the nectar, now stays in Pātāla and, being perverted, takes his pleasure there.
m.3.22.54: Nandīśvara said: Thus Śambhu was much praised by Brahmā together with the sages and gods, for the protection of the worlds and for bringing back Viṣṇu.
m.3.22.55: Then that blessed Śambhu, Maheśvara, ocean of compassion, understanding that affliction, took the form of a bull.
m.3.22.iti: Thus ends the twenty-second adhyāya, named The trouble caused by Viṣṇu and the bull incarnation, in the third saṃhitā, the Śatarudra-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.3.23.1: Nandīśvara said: Then the bearer of Pināka, roaring in the form of a bull, entered the cavern there, uttering terrifying roars.
m.3.23.2: At his roars the cities and towns fell down, and then a trembling seized all the inhabitants of the cities.
m.3.23.3: Then the Bull confronted the sons of Hari, who had raised their bows for battle, mighty in strength and valour, their minds deluded by Śiva's māyā.
m.3.23.4: Then those sons of Hari became enraged, O best of sages; the heroes, roaring loudly, rushed towards Śaṅkara.
m.3.23.5: Rudra, bearing the form of a bull, grew angry at those sons of Hari as they came on, and tore the sons of Viṣṇu apart with his hooves and horns.
m.3.23.6: All those sons of Hari, their limbs torn apart by Rudra, quickly perished, lifeless and senseless.
m.3.23.7: When those sons had been slain, Viṣṇu, the foremost of the mighty, came out, roared loudly, and went swiftly up to Hara.
m.3.23.8: Seeing Rudra, the Bull who had slain Viṣṇu's sons, moving about, Keśava struck him with arrows and with divine missiles.
m.3.23.9: Then Mahādeva, enraged, in the form of a bull, mighty in his fury, the dweller in the mountains, swallowed those missiles of Viṣṇu.
m.3.23.10: Then that Maheśvara in the form of a bull, flying into a great rage, bellowed most terribly, shaking the three worlds, O sage.
m.3.23.11: Then, leaping up with force, he tore with hooves and horns at Viṣṇu, Hari, who was agitated with anger, deluded, and did not recognise his own Lord.
m.3.23.12: Then Hari, deluded by māyā, unable to bear that blow, quickly became weakened in spirit and pained in his limbs.
m.3.23.13: Hari, his pride gone, bewildered and dazed, recognised the Supreme Lord sporting in the form of a bull.
m.3.23.14: Then, having realised that the Lord of Gaurī had come in the form of a bull, he spoke in a deep voice, with bowed shoulders and joined palms.
m.3.23.15: Hari said: O God of gods, Mahādeva, ocean of compassion, O Lord, O Maheśāna, deluded by your māyā, my mind was utterly confused.
m.3.23.16: I have fought a battle with you, the Lord, my own master, O Lord. Showing compassion to me, O master, may that offence indeed be forgiven.
m.3.23.17: Nandīśvara said: Hearing those words spoken by Hari in humility, O sage, the blessed Śaṅkara, loving to his devotees, spoke to the Lord of Ramā.
m.3.23.18: O Viṣṇu, O you of great intellect, how did you not recognise me? You fought a battle; how today has all your knowledge been forgotten?
m.3.23.19: Why do you not know yourself, whose valour depends on me? You should take no delight here; turn back from this wrongful conduct.
m.3.23.20: How can knowledge remain when one is subject to desire, attached to women and given to pleasure? This is not fitting for you, O Lord of gods; remember your role as the deliverer of the world.
m.3.23.21: Hearing those words of Śambhu, which bestow true understanding, with reverence, Viṣṇu, ashamed in his own mind, spoke to Maheśvara.
m.3.23.22: Viṣṇu said: My discus is here; taking it with care, I shall go to that world of mine, obeying your command.
m.3.23.23: Nandīśvara said: Hearing Viṣṇu's words, Hara, the great Lord in the form of a bull, the protector of dharma, replied again to Hari.
m.3.23.24: No delay should be made; you must go quickly from here. By my command, O Hari, go to your world; let the discus remain right here.
m.3.23.25: For the sake of maintaining the lineage and the Ādityas, and also on account of my word of auspicious grace, I therefore give you another discus, more terrible.
m.3.23.26: Having said this, Hara fashioned a divine, supreme discus, blazing like the fire of time, destroyer of all the wicked.
m.3.23.27: He gave the discus, shining like ten thousand fierce suns, to the great-souled Viṣṇu, protector of all the immortals and chief sages.
m.3.23.28: Having received that other discus, Sudarśana, of supreme brilliance, Viṣṇu, the foremost of the wise, spoke there to the gods.
m.3.23.29: You, the best of all the gods, listen attentively to my words; it should be done accordingly and quickly; then you will have well-being.
m.3.23.30: In Pātāla there are divine, excellent women endowed with youth; whoever wishes to enjoy great sport with them, let him do so.
m.3.23.31: Hearing those words from Keśava, the heroic beings of divine birth became eager to enter Pātāla together with Viṣṇu.
m.3.23.32: Then, perceiving their intention, the blessed Hara in anger pronounced a terrible curse upon the eight classes of divine beings.
m.3.23.33: Hara said: Except for a tranquil sage, or the Dānavas, or one born of my portion, whoever enters this place shall meet death in an instant.
m.3.23.34: Hearing these terrible words, which further the welfare of humankind, the gods, rebuffed by Rudra, returned to their own homes.
m.3.23.35: Thus the supreme Viṣṇu, who had become attached to women, was admonished by Śiva and went to the heavenly world, O Vyāsa; and the world regained its well-being.
m.3.23.36: And the blessed Śaṅkara as Vṛṣeśvara, loving to his devotees, having thus accomplished the gods' task, went to his own lord of mountains.
m.3.23.37: Thus has been described the Vṛṣeśvara incarnation of Śaṅkara — Śarva, remover of Viṣṇu's delusion, bringer of happiness to the three worlds.
m.3.23.38: This narrative is purifying, supremely removing the oppression of enemies; it leads to heaven, brings fame and long life, and grants enjoyment and liberation to the good.
m.3.23.39: Whoever listens to this with devotion, or attentively causes it to be heard, and whoever reads it or teaches it to wise men — he, having enjoyed all desires, attains liberation at the end.
m.3.23.iti: Thus ends the twenty-third adhyāya, named The incarnation of Śiva called Vṛṣeśvara, in the third saṃhitā, the Śatarudra-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.3.24.1: Nandīśvara said: O wise one, listen with great love to another incarnation of the great Lord, called Pippalāda. It is excellent and increases devotion.
m.3.24.2: The brāhmaṇa Dadhīci, best of sages, who was spoken of earlier, was a great Śaiva and very mighty, the son of Cyavana, born in the line of Bhṛgu.
m.3.24.3: In the battle with Kṣuva, he, with Maheśvara as his helper, defeated Viṣṇu together with the gods and then cursed him.
m.3.24.4: His wife, the highly fortunate Suvarcā by name, was a virtuous woman, supremely devoted to her husband. It was she who cursed the gods.
m.3.24.5: Therefore Mahādeva, who is skilled in many kinds of divine play, became manifest in her through him, radiant, under the name Pippalāda.
m.3.24.6: Sūta said: Hearing these wonderful words of Nandīśvara, Sanatkumāra, the foremost of sages, bowed his shoulders, joined his palms and spoke.
m.3.24.7: Sanatkumāra said: O Nandīśvara, greatly wise one, you bear the very form of Rudra himself. You are blessed, dear one, a true guru, for you have let me hear this wonderful story.
m.3.24.8: Long ago, dear son of Śilāda, I heard from Brahmā about Viṣṇu's defeat in the battle with Kṣuva, and about his curse as well.
m.3.24.9: Now I wish to hear about the curse that Suvarcā laid on the gods, and after that the auspicious story of Pippalāda.
m.3.24.10: Sūta said: Hearing these fine words of the son of Vidhi (Brahmā), the son of Śilāda, glad at heart, remembered Śiva's lotus feet and replied.
m.3.24.11: Nandīśvara said: Once, O lord of sages, all the gods, led by Vāsava (Indra), were defeated by the Daityas who were allies of the asura Vṛtra.
m.3.24.12: All the gods had deposited their own fine weapons in Dadhīca's hermitage, and so they were suddenly and swiftly defeated.
m.3.24.13: Then all the gods with Indra, and likewise the seers, as they were being slain, hurried to Brahmaloka and told of their calamity.
m.3.24.14: On hearing the gods' words, Brahmā, grandfather of the worlds, told them everything truly, including what Tvaṣṭṛ intended to do.
m.3.24.15: O gods, Tvaṣṭṛ produced him through austerity in order to kill you: Vṛtra by name, of great might, the mighty lord of all the Daityas.
m.3.24.16: So let an effort be made by which he may be killed. Listen, wise one, to the means for it; I tell it to you for the sake of dharma.
m.3.24.17: The great sage Dadhīci, an ascetic who has mastered his senses, long ago worshipped Śiva and obtained the boon that his bones would be as hard as the vajra.
m.3.24.18: Ask him for his bones; he will give them, no doubt. Make a staff-like vajra from them and slay Vṛtra, no doubt.
m.3.24.19: Nandīśvara said: Hearing Brahmā's words, Śakra, accompanied by his guru and the gods, came at once to Dadhīci's excellent hermitage.
m.3.24.20: Seeing the sage there with Suvarcā, Śakra, together with his guru and the gods, humbly bowed to him with reverence and joined palms.
m.3.24.21: Understanding their intention, the sage, best of the wise, sent his wife Suvarcā into the inner part of his hermitage.
m.3.24.22: Then the king of the gods, with the gods, intent on achieving his own purpose and following the science of statecraft, addressed the lord of sages.
m.3.24.23: Śakra said: All of us gods, and the seers too, have been harmed by Tvaṣṭṛ. We have come for refuge to you, the great Śaiva, the giver, who protects those who seek shelter.
m.3.24.24: O brāhmaṇa, give us your bones, which are made of great vajra. With your bone I will make my thunderbolt and kill the enemy of the gods.
m.3.24.25: Addressed thus by him, the sage, who delighted in helping others, meditated on Śiva, his own Lord, and gave up his body.
m.3.24.26: His bonds destroyed, the sage went at once to Brahmaloka. A rain of flowers fell there, and everyone was struck with wonder.
m.3.24.27: Then Śakra quickly summoned the cow Surabhi and had her lick the body clean. He directed Tvāṣṭra (Viśvakarman) to make weapons from those bones.
m.3.24.28: So commanded, Viśvakarman fashioned all the weapons from those bones, which were vajra-like and very hard through Śiva's power.
m.3.24.29: From the bones of his spine he made the vajra, an arrow and likewise the Brahmaśiras; from his other bones he made many other fine weapons.
m.3.24.30: O sage, Indra, strengthened by Śiva's power, raised that vajra and charged at Vṛtra in anger, as Rudra charged at Antaka (Death).
m.3.24.31: Then Śakra, fully armed, swiftly and with force cut off Vṛtra's head with that vajra, as one would a mountain peak.
m.3.24.32: Then, dear one, there was a great festival among the heaven-dwellers. The gods praised Śakra, and showers of flowers fell.
m.3.24.33: Thus, dear one, I have told you this story in passing. Now listen with great reverence as I tell of Śambhu's incarnation as Pippalāda.
m.3.24.34: Suvarcā, the devoted wife of the great-souled sage Dadhīca, went into her hermitage as he had commanded.
m.3.24.35: Having gone there, the ascetic woman, not seeing her husband, did all the household work as her husband had instructed,
m.3.24.36: and then came back there. O best of sages, seeing so much that was inauspicious, and those gods, Suvarcā was astonished.
m.3.24.37: Learning that all this was the doing of the gods, the virtuous Suvarcā, wife of the best of seers, became angry then; deeply enraged, she pronounced a curse on them.
m.3.24.38: She said: Ah! You gods are all most wicked, clever only at your own interests, foolish and greedy. Therefore, from this day on, by my word, may all of you, Indra included, become animals.
m.3.24.39: In this way the ascetic Suvarcā, the sage's beloved, laid a curse on all those gods, Śakra included.
m.3.24.40: Then that devoted, resolute wife wished to follow her husband to his world, and she built a funeral pyre with very pure firewood.
m.3.24.41: Then a voice from the sky, sent by Giriśa, comforting her and giving happiness, spoke to Suvarcā, the sage's beloved.
m.3.24.42: The heavenly voice said: Do not act rashly, O wise one; hear my supreme word. The sage's seed is in your womb; bring it forth with care.
m.3.24.43: After that, O lady, you may carry out the course you desire. A pregnant woman should not burn her body — this is Brahmā's injunction.
m.3.24.44: Nandīśvara said: Having said this, that heavenly voice fell silent, O lord of sages. Hearing it, the sage's wife was astonished for a moment.
m.3.24.45: That Suvarcā, the greatly chaste woman, longing for her husband's world, sat down and then tore open her belly with a stone.
m.3.24.46: From her womb came forth that embryo of the excellent sage, with a great divine body, radiant, illuminating the ten directions.
m.3.24.47: He was directly an incarnation of Rudra, born of the excellent energy of Dadhīci, manifested of himself, O dear one, capable of performing his own divine play.
m.3.24.48: Seeing that divine son of hers and his form, the sage's wife Suvarcā recognised in her mind that he was directly an incarnation of Rudra.
m.3.24.49: The greatly chaste woman was delighted; bowing at once, she praised him and installed that form in her heart, O lord of sages.
m.3.24.50: And the mother Suvarcā, of pure eyes, smiling, spoke with great affection to that son, longing for her husband's world.
m.3.24.51: Suvarcā said: O dear one, Supreme Lord, remain long near this aśvattha tree, O most fortunate one; may you be the giver of happiness to all.
m.3.24.52: Lovingly permit me now to go to my husband's world; staying there with my husband, I shall meditate on you, who bear the form of Rudra.
m.3.24.53: Nandīśvara said: Having thus spoken to her son, the chaste Suvarcā then followed her husband by means of supreme meditative absorption.
m.3.24.54: Thus that wife of Dadhīca, united with her husband, O sage, reached Śiva's world and joyfully served Śaṅkara.
m.3.24.55: Meanwhile the gods together with Indra, along with the sages, came there quickly, O dear one, delighted, as if they had been summoned.
m.3.24.56: Hari and Brahmā, with great joy, went with their own attendants to Śaṅkara, who had descended on earth in Suvarcā from Dadhīca.
m.3.24.57: Seeing there Rudra, who had descended and become the sage's son, all bowed and praised him with joined palms.
m.3.24.58: Then there was a great festival of the gods, O best of sages. Drums resounded there, and dancing women danced with joy.
m.3.24.59: The sons of the Gandharvas sang, and the Kinnaras, players of instruments, played; the immortals played music and showered flowers.
m.3.24.60: Having duly performed the sacraments for that resplendent son of Dadhīci, father of Pippalāda, all of them, Viṣṇu and the others, praised him again.
m.3.24.61: Brahmā, pleased in mind, gave him the name Pippalāda. Together with Hari and the gods he said: Be gracious, O Lord of the gods.
m.3.24.62: Having said this and taken leave of him, Brahmā, Viṣṇu and likewise the gods all went each to their own abode, having celebrated a great festival.
m.3.24.63: Then Rudra as Pippalāda, the great Lord, performed austerities at the root of the aśvattha tree for a very long time, desiring the welfare of the worlds.
m.3.24.64: Thus, while that Pippalāda, who conformed to the ways of the world, was performing intense austerities, a long time passed before him.
m.3.24.iti: Thus ends the twenty-fourth adhyāya, named The Pippalāda incarnation, in the third saṃhitā, the Śatarudra-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.3.25.1: Nandīśvara said: Then, having established order in the world, out of a wish to establish dharma, the Lord performed a great sport. Ah, listen to it, O good sage.
m.3.25.2: Once, while going to bathe in the Puṣpabhadrā river, the lord of sages saw Padmā, a young woman who was a portion of Śivā and exceedingly charming.
m.3.25.3: Desiring to obtain her, he—a wanderer through the worlds, discerning in the truth of the world—went to the residence of her father, King Anaraṇya.
m.3.25.4: The king of men, seeing him, bowed, and, overcome with fear, offered madhuparka and the rest and worshipped him with devotion.
m.3.25.5: Having accepted everything with affection, the sage asked for the maiden. The king fell silent, unable to say anything.
m.3.25.6: The sage said to the king: Give me the maiden with devotion; otherwise I shall reduce everything to ashes, together with you.
m.3.25.7: Then all the king's people were overwhelmed by the splendour of Pippalāda, the son of Dadhīci, the great sage.
m.3.25.8: Then the king, greatly frightened and lamenting again and again, gave the adorned maiden Padmā to the aged sage.
m.3.25.9: Having married Padmā, the king's daughter, a portion of Śivā, the sage Pippalāda took her and joyfully went to his own hermitage.
m.3.25.10: Having gone there, that best of sages, greatly decrepit with age, an ascetic not given to excessive passion, dwelt with that woman.
m.3.25.11: Then that daughter of Anaraṇya served the sage with devotion in deed, mind and speech, as Lakṣmī serves Nārāyaṇa.
m.3.25.12: Thus Pippalāda, the best of sages, a portion of Śiva, having become young through his own sport, delighted with that young woman.
m.3.25.13: Ten great-souled sons, excellent ascetics, were born, all equal to their father the sage, increasing Padmā's happiness.
m.3.25.14: Thus Pippalāda, the best of sages, the lord who performs many sports, is indeed a sportive incarnation of Śaṅkara, the great Lord.
m.3.25.15: It was he, the compassionate one, by whom a boon was lovingly granted to the people, having seen in the world the affliction caused by Śani, which none could ward off:
m.3.25.16: Up to sixteen years from birth, that affliction shall not befall men, nor likewise Śiva's devotees; this word of mine is indeed true.
m.3.25.17: If Śani, disregarding my word, should ever afflict those men, then he would be reduced to ashes—there is no doubt.
m.3.25.18: Thus, dear one, out of fear of that, Śanaiścara, the foremost of planets, though malignant, never causes affliction to them.
m.3.25.19: Thus, O good sage, the excellent story of Pippalāda, who became a man in sport, has been told to you; it grants the fruit of all desires.
m.3.25.20: Gādhi, Kauśika, and the great sage Pippalāda—these three, when remembered, destroy the affliction caused by Śanaiścara.
m.3.25.21: Whatever man on earth reads or hears, with true devotion, the story of Pippalāda together with the story of Padmā—
m.3.25.22: —whoever reads or hears this excellent story for the destruction of Śani's affliction would obtain all desires.
m.3.25.23: Blessed is that best of sages Dadhīci, wise, a great devotee of Śiva, dear to the good; his son is Maheśāna himself, named Pippalāda, self-possessed.
m.3.25.24: This narrative, dear one, is sinless, leads to heaven, removes the defects of malefic planets, grants all desires, and increases devotion to Śiva.
m.3.25.iti: Thus ends the twenty-fifth adhyāya, named The deeds of the Pippalāda incarnation, in the third saṃhitā, the Śatarudra-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.3.26.1: Nandīśvara said: Listen, dear one; I shall describe, O sage, the supremely blissful incarnation of Śiva, the Supreme Self, which is called Vaiśyanātha.
m.3.26.2: Long ago in Nandigrāma there lived a certain courtesan, renowned as Mahānandā, a devotee of Śiva and exceedingly beautiful.
m.3.26.3: She was endowed with great wealth, rich in fine riches, radiantly splendid, and full of the charm of adornment set off with many kinds of jewels.
m.3.26.4: She was skilled in all the arts of music and exceedingly captivating; queens and kings alike delighted in her singing.
m.3.26.5: That courtesan always joyfully worshipped Śaṅkara together with Ambā; she was devoted to repeating Śiva's name and wore ashes and rudrākṣa beads as ornaments.
m.3.26.6: Having worshipped Śiva every day and serving the Lord of the world, she danced with supreme devotion, singing Śiva's true glory.
m.3.26.7: Having adorned a monkey and also a cock with rudrākṣas, she would always make them dance with hand-claps and songs.
m.3.26.8: Seeing the two of them dancing, that courtesan, devoted to Śiva, would laugh aloud with affection, together with all her friends.
m.3.26.9: Decked with armlets and ear-ornaments made of rudrākṣas, the monkey, through her training, would dance before her like a child.
m.3.26.10: The cock, with a rudrākṣa tied to its crest, skilled in dancing, danced daily along with the monkey, bringing benefit to those who watched.
m.3.26.11: Thus, performing this entertainment with great care and always devoted to Śiva, that courtesan became filled with great bliss.
m.3.26.12: O best of sages, while that courtesan practised devotion to Śiva, a long time passed for her in supreme happiness.
m.3.26.13: One day Śiva himself, becoming a merchant, came to her house to test her disposition, auspicious and observing a vow.
m.3.26.14: His forehead shone with the tripuṇḍra, he wore rudrākṣa ornaments, was accomplished, devoted to repeating Śiva's name, had matted locks and bore the garb of a Śaiva.
m.3.26.15: Bearing a mass of ashes and on his forearm an excellent bracelet studded with great jewels, he, intent on a supreme sport, looked splendid.
m.3.26.16: When he arrived, the beautiful courtesan honoured the merchant well with great joy and respectfully seated him in her own place.
m.3.26.17: Seeing the excellent, most charming bracelet on his forearm, she conceived a longing for it and, greatly amazed, spoke to him.
m.3.26.18: Mahānandā said: This bracelet made of great jewels on your hand instantly steals my heart; it is fit to adorn a celestial woman.
m.3.26.19: Nandīśvara said: Seeing her thus longing for the hand-ornament rich with nine gems, the noble-minded merchant spoke with a smile.
m.3.26.20: The merchant lord said: If your heart longs for this excellent divine jewel, then take it yourself with pleasure; but what price will you give for it?
m.3.26.21: The courtesan said: We courtesans are women who act as we please, not devoted wives; the conduct fitting our class is free liaison—there is no doubt.
m.3.26.22: Since this hand-ornament captivates my whole mind, I shall be your wife for three days and nights.
m.3.26.23: The merchant said: So be it, if your word is true, O beloved of heroes; I give you the jewelled bracelet—be my wife for three nights.
m.3.26.24: In this transaction the moon and the sun are witnesses; saying the word true three times, touch my heart, O dear one.
m.3.26.25: The courtesan said: Becoming your wife for three days and nights, O lord, I shall live in shared dharma with you—this is true, true, without doubt.
m.3.26.26: Nandīśvara said: Having said this three times and made the moon and sun witnesses, Mahānandā gladly touched his heart.
m.3.26.27: Then the merchant, having given her the jewelled bracelet, placed a jewelled liṅga in her hand and said this:
m.3.26.28: The merchant lord said: This jewelled Śiva-liṅga is dear to me as my life; you must guard it, beloved, and keep it hidden with care.
m.3.26.29: Nandīśvara said: Saying, so be it, she took the jewelled liṅga, placed it in the middle of the dance pavilion, and entered the house.
m.3.26.30: United at night with that merchant who behaved as a lover, she slept happily on a couch adorned with soft bedding.
m.3.26.31: Then at midnight, O sage, by the will of the merchant-lord, a sound suddenly arose inside the dance pavilion.
m.3.26.32: A great blazing fire, aided by a strong wind, suddenly enveloped that very dance pavilion, dear one.
m.3.26.33: As the pavilion burned, the courtesan rose up hastily in alarm and freed the monkey there from its tether.
m.3.26.34: Freed from its bonds, the monkey, together with the cock, ran far away in fear, shaking off many sparks.
m.3.26.35: Seeing that liṅga burnt along with the pillar and broken to pieces, the courtesan and the merchant fell into boundless grief.
m.3.26.36: Seeing the liṅga, equal to his own self, burnt, the merchant-lord then, to learn her inner disposition, resolved upon death.
m.3.26.37: Sitting down in extreme sorrow, the merchant—Maheśāna of manifold sports, who had taken a human body in play—spoke to the grieving woman.
m.3.26.38: The merchant lord said: Now that the Śiva-liṅga, dear to me as life, is shattered and burnt, I tell you truly, without doubt—I cannot bear to live.
m.3.26.39: Good lady, have a pyre built for me quickly by your best servants; fixing my mind on Śiva, I shall enter the fire.
m.3.26.40: Even if Brahmā, Indra, Viṣṇu and the rest were to come together and stop me, still at this very moment, good lady, I shall enter the fire and give up my life.
m.3.26.41: Nandīśvara said: Knowing him to be so firmly resolved, she, deeply grieved, had her servants build a pyre outside her house.
m.3.26.42: Then that vaiśya, who was Śiva alone, steadfast, full of playful delight and wishing for her union with him, circumambulated the blazing fire and entered it while the people looked on.
m.3.26.43: Seeing his fate, that courtesan Mahānandā, a young woman, was utterly astonished and fell into remorse, O best of sages.
m.3.26.44: Then that grieving courtesan, remembering the spotless dharma, looked at all her kinsfolk and spoke piteous words.
m.3.26.45: Mahānandā said: When I took the jewelled bracelet, I made a true promise: for three days I am the acknowledged wife of this vaiśya.
m.3.26.46: Because of a deed done by me, this vaiśya, a keeper of Śiva's vow, has died. Therefore I will enter the fire together with him.
m.3.26.47: Truth-speaking teachers have said: She is one who follows her own dharma. When I do this out of love, let truth not perish in me.
m.3.26.48: The highest dharma rests on truth; by truth comes the supreme goal; by truth come heaven and liberation; on truth everything is established.
m.3.26.49: Nandīśvara said: Thus firmly resolved, though her kinsmen tried to stop her, the woman, fearing the breaking of truth, set her mind on giving up her life.
m.3.26.50: Having given all her possessions to eminent brāhmaṇas and meditated on Sadāśiva, she circled that fire three times and turned to enter it.
m.3.26.51: As she was falling into the blazing fire, her mind offered at his feet, Śiva, the Self of the universe, appeared and stopped her.
m.3.26.52: Beholding him, the God of all gods, three-eyed, crowned with the crescent moon, shining like millions of moons, suns and fires, she stood just as she was, as if stunned, as if afraid.
m.3.26.53: She was overwhelmed, terrified, trembling, stupefied, with tears streaming; comforting her and taking her hands, he spoke these words.
m.3.26.54: Śiva said: To test your truthfulness, your dharma, your steadfastness and your unwavering devotion to me, I came to you having become a vaiśya.
m.3.26.55: By my māyā I kindled the fire and your dancing hall was burnt; having made the jewelled liṅga burn, I entered the fire.
m.3.26.56: You, remembering truth, entered the fire along with me; therefore I shall grant you enjoyments hard even for the gods to attain.
m.3.26.57: Whatever you desire, O fair-hipped one, that indeed I give you. I am pleased by your devotion; there is nothing that cannot be given to you.
m.3.26.58: Nandīśvara said: When Śaṅkara, Gaurī's lord, loving to his devotees, had spoken thus, that courtesan Mahānandā replied to Śaṅkara.
m.3.26.59: The courtesan said: I have no desire for enjoyments on earth, in heaven or in the netherworld. I wish for nothing other than the touch of your lotus feet.
m.3.26.60: My servants and maidservants, and all my other kinsfolk, are all intent on seeing you and have entrusted their lives to you.
m.3.26.61: Lead all of them together with me to your own supreme abode and free us from the dreadful fear of rebirth. Salutations to you.
m.3.26.62: Nandīśvara said: Then Maheśvara, welcoming her words, led all of them together with her to his own supreme abode.
m.3.26.63: I have described to you the supreme Vaiśyanātha incarnation, which brought happiness to Mahānandā and ever grants bliss to devotees.
m.3.26.64: This story of Śiva's incarnation as the lord of the vaiśyas is supreme, purifying, divine and wonderful; it quickly bestows everything on the good, and brought great happiness to Mahānandā.
m.3.26.65: Whoever listens to this with devotion, or attentively recites it to others, does not fall from his own dharma and attains the supreme goal in the next world.
m.3.26.iti: Thus ends the twenty-sixth adhyāya, named The incarnation of Śiva called Vaiśyanātha, in the third saṃhitā, the Śatarudra-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.3.27.1: Nandīśvara said: Listen, dear one: I shall describe the Dvijeśvara incarnation of Śiva, the Supreme Self, an incarnation accompanied by Śivā, which gives happiness to the good.
m.3.27.2: Bhadrāyu, the best of kings, who was described earlier, dear one, on whom Śiva bestowed grace in the form of Ṛṣabha —
m.3.27.3: to test his righteousness, he manifested again in the form of Dvijeśvara; that very story I now tell.
m.3.27.4: By the power of Ṛṣabha, the mighty Bhadrāyu, having conquered his enemies in battle, obtained the throne, dear one.
m.3.27.5: The daughter of Candrāṅgada, the fair child born of Sīmantinī, the very chaste Kīrtimālinī, became his wife, O brahmin.
m.3.27.6: Once, O sage, in springtime, that Bhadrāyu entered a dense forest with his beloved for recreation.
m.3.27.7: Then in that lovely forest the king sported together with his beloved, who protected those who came for refuge.
m.3.27.8: Then the Supreme Lord Śaṅkara, wishing to see the firmness of his righteousness, performed a sport right there together with Śivā.
m.3.27.9: Śivā and Śiva both, becoming a brahmin couple in that forest and creating an illusory tiger, appeared by their own play.
m.3.27.10: Then, not far from him, the two were running, overcome with fear, pursued by the tiger, weeping.
m.3.27.11: Then, dear one, King Bhadrāyu, the bull among kṣatriyas and refuge of all, saw the two stricken ones crying out.
m.3.27.12: Then, O tiger among sages, that brahmin couple of his own māyā, overcome with fear, spoke to the great king Bhadrāyu.
m.3.27.13: The brahmin couple said: Protect, protect us both, O great king, best of knowers of dharma. This tiger is coming to devour us, O great lord.
m.3.27.14: This savage beast, like Death itself, terrifying to all living beings — before it reaches and eats us, protect us, O knower of dharma.
m.3.27.15: Nandīśvara said: Hearing their cry thus, the lord of kings, the great hero, very quickly took up his bow —
m.3.27.16: at that moment the tiger, full of illusion, rushing up, seized the wife of that excellent brahmin in their midst.
m.3.27.17: As she wailed loudly—O lord, lord, O beloved, alas Śambhu! Alas, Guru of the world!—the dreadful tiger seized her in its jaws.
m.3.27.18: Meanwhile the king struck the tiger with sharp arrows, but it was not pained by them in the least, like a great mountain by rains.
m.3.27.19: That mighty tiger, only lightly hurt by the king, forcibly dragged the woman and swiftly went away.
m.3.27.20: Seeing his wife carried off by the tiger, the brahmin, greatly astonished, following the way of the world, wept bitterly again and again.
m.3.27.21: Having wept for a long time, that brahmin — the Lord disguised by māyā, the remover of pride — spoke to King Bhadrāyu.
m.3.27.22: The great brahmin said: O king, where are your great weapons? Where is your great protecting bow? Where is your strength equal to twelve thousand great elephants?
m.3.27.23: What use is your sword, your conch? What use your knowledge of mantra-weapons? What use the power of great weapons, what use your abundant might?
m.3.27.24: All that, and whatever else resides in you, has become fruitless, since you are unable to prevent the killing of forest-dwellers.
m.3.27.25: This is the highest duty of a kṣatriya: protection from injury. When that duty befitting your lineage is lost, what use is your life?
m.3.27.26: Kings who know dharma protect the afflicted who come for refuge, with their lives and wealth; without that they are like the dead.
m.3.27.27: For those who fail to protect the afflicted, death is better than life; for the wealthy who do not give, mendicancy is better than householder life.
m.3.27.28: The wise consider eating poison better, entering fire better, than failing to protect the wretched, the helpless and the distressed.
m.3.27.29: Nandīśvara said: Hearing his lament thus and the censure of his own valour, the king, out of grief, reflected within himself thus:
m.3.27.30: Alas! Today my manliness is lost through reversal of fate; today my fame too is lost, and a grievous sin has befallen me.
m.3.27.31: The duty befitting my lineage is lost for me, unfortunate and foolish; surely my prosperity, kingdom and life will come to ruin.
m.3.27.32: Today I shall free this brahmin, who has lost his wife and is tormented by grief, from his sorrow, even by giving up my dearest life.
m.3.27.33: Having thus resolved in his mind, Bhadrāyu, the best of kings, fell at his feet and spoke, consoling him.
m.3.27.34: Bhadrāyu said: Showing mercy to me, a mere kṣatriya bereft of vigour, O brahmin, abandon your grief, O most wise one; today I shall give you whatever you desire.
m.3.27.35: This kingdom, this queen, and this body of mine — all this is at your disposal. What boon do you desire?
m.3.27.36: The brahmin said: What use is a mirror to a blind man, or houses to one who lives on alms? What use is a book to a fool, what use wealth to one without a wife?
m.3.27.37: Therefore I, whose wife is taken away and who have never enjoyed pleasures, desire this chief queen of yours: let her be given to me.
m.3.27.38: Bhadrāyu said: I am a giver of wealth to the ends of the earth, of the kingdom, of elephants and horses, of my own body, of anything at all — but never of a wife.
m.3.27.39: The sin incurred by enjoying another's wife cannot be washed away even by hundreds of expiations.
m.3.27.40: The brahmin said: Let alone the dreadful slaying of a brahmin, or even drinking liquor — I shall destroy such sins by austerity; how much more the sin of adultery.
m.3.27.41: Therefore give me this wife of yours; I have no other desire. By failing to protect those stricken with fear, you will surely go to hell.
m.3.27.42: Nandīśvara said: Frightened by the brahmin's words, the king reflected: Failing to protect a suppliant is a great sin; giving away my wife is better than that.
m.3.27.43: So, having given my wife to this foremost brahmin and being freed from sin, I shall at once enter the fire, and my fame will become known.
m.3.27.44: Having resolved thus in his mind, he kindled a blazing fire, summoned that brahmin, and made the gift of his wife with the pouring of water.
m.3.27.45: Having bathed himself and become pure, bowing to the lords of the gods, he circumambulated that fire three times and, with concentrated mind, meditated on Śiva.
m.3.27.46: Then, as he was about to fall into the fire, his mind fixed on the Lord's feet, the Lord of the universe, who had appeared as the lord of brahmins, stopped him.
m.3.27.47: That Lord, five-faced, three-eyed, bearer of the Pināka bow, with the crescent moon as his crest-ornament, with a mass of long, tawny, radiant matted locks, with the splendour of ten million midday suns—
m.3.27.48: White as a lotus stalk, clad in an elephant hide, the crown of his head sprinkled by the waves of the Gaṅgā, his neck adorned with garlands of serpent-kings, resplendent with crown, girdle, armlets and bracelets—
m.3.27.49: —holding in his hands trident, sword, skull-staff, axe, shield, deer, the gesture of fearlessness, and the Pināka bow, mounted on the bull, adorned with a dark-blue throat—that Lord manifested before him, the king beheld.
m.3.27.50: Then showers of heavenly flowers quickly fell from the sky; divine instruments sounded, and goddesses danced and sang.
m.3.27.51: There came, being praised, Hari and Brahmā, and likewise the gods, Indra and the others, the sages headed by Nārada, and others too.
m.3.27.52: Then a great festival took place there, increasing devotion, while the king looked on, his joined palms bowed in devotion.
m.3.27.53: His heart expanding with the bliss of that vision, his body bathed in streaming tears, his hair standing on end, with faltering syllables and folded palms, he praised the Lord with words.
m.3.27.54: Then the blessed Supreme Lord, the treasure of compassion, thus praised by the king, being pleased, spoke to him, together with Pārvatī.
m.3.27.55: O king, I am fully pleased with your devotion, and even more by your righteousness. Ask a boon, for yourself together with your wife; I shall grant it, no doubt.
m.3.27.56: To test your disposition I came, having become a brahmin. She who was seized by the tiger is indeed the Goddess Śivā herself.
m.3.27.57: The tiger whose body was unharmed by your arrows was illusory. Wishing to see your steadfastness, I asked for your wife.
m.3.27.58: Nandīśvara said: Having heard these words of the Lord, King Bhadrāyu, bowing again and praising the Master, humbly spoke.
m.3.27.59: Bhadrāyu said: This alone is the boon, O Lord: that you, the Supreme Lord, have become visible to me, scorched as I am by the heat of worldly existence.
m.3.27.60: Yet since you grant a boon by your own grace, O Lord, O Master, I choose from you, the best of boon-givers, a supreme boon.
m.3.27.61: My father Vajrabāhu with his wife, O Maheśvara, and I with my wife, O Lord, may we be ever servants of your feet.
m.3.27.62: The merchant named Padmākara and his son called Sunaya—all these, O Maheśāna, make them always your attendants by your side.
m.3.27.63: Nandīśvara said: Then the queen, his wife Kīrtimālinī, enraptured, having propitiated Giriśa with devotion, asked for an excellent boon.
m.3.27.64: The queen said: Candrāṅgada is my father and Sīmantinī my mother; for the two of them, O Mahādeva, I joyfully ask nearness to you by your side.
m.3.27.65: Nandīśvara said: Saying, so be it, the Lord of Gaurī, pleased and loving to his devotees, granted the two of them the boons they desired and vanished in an instant.
m.3.27.66: Bhadrāyu too, having received the grace of the Trident-bearer with great joy, enjoyed many pleasures together with Kīrtimālinī.
m.3.27.67: Having ruled the kingdom for ten thousand years with unimpeded valour, he handed the kingdom over to his son and went to Śiva's presence.
m.3.27.68: Candrāṅgada too, the great king, and that queen Sīmantinī, having worshipped Giriśa with devotion, went to the abode of Śambhu.
m.3.27.69: Thus I have described to you, O lord, the supreme Dvijeśvara incarnation of Maheśvara, which bestowed supreme bliss on Bhadrāyu.
m.3.27.70: This supreme, purifying and most wondrous account of Śiva's incarnation named Dvijeśa, of pure fame—one who hears or recites it attains Śambhu's abode.
m.3.27.71: Whoever, with concentrated mind, listens to this daily or causes it to be heard does not fall from his own dharma, and attains the highest goal in the next world.
m.3.27.iti: Thus ends the twenty-seventh adhyāya, named The incarnation of Śiva called Dvijeśa, in the third saṃhitā, the Śatarudra-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.3.28.1: Nandīśvara said: Listen, O wise one; I shall describe the incarnation of Śiva, the Supreme Self, which is supreme bliss and is called Yatinātha, O sage.
m.3.28.2: On the mountain called Arbudācala, near it, there lived Āhuka, born of the Bhilla race, O lord of sages.
m.3.28.3: His wife, named Āhukā, was indeed firm in her vows. Both of them were great Śaivas, worshippers of Śiva.
m.3.28.4: Once the Bhilla, ever devoted to Śiva, went very far away to get food for himself and his wife, O sage.
m.3.28.5: Meanwhile Śaṅkara, assuming the body of an ascetic, came in the evening to the Bhilla's house there in order to test him.
m.3.28.6: At that moment the master of the house came there, and the wise man worshipped the lord of ascetics with love.
m.3.28.7: To test his disposition, that Śaṅkara in ascetic form, the performer of great sport, as if afraid, spoke affectionately in a plaintive voice.
m.3.28.8: The lord of ascetics said: Give me a place to stay today; at dawn I shall certainly go, O Bhilla. May there be welfare for you always.
m.3.28.9: The Bhilla said: What you have said is right, master; but listen to my word to you. My place is very small; how can there be lodging for you?
m.3.28.10: Nandīśvara said: Thus addressed by him, the ascetic made up his mind to leave. Just then the Bhilla woman, having reflected, spoke these words to her husband.
m.3.28.11: The Bhilla woman said: Husband, give the ascetic a place; do not turn the guest away. Consider the duty of a householder; otherwise there will be ruin of dharma.
m.3.28.12: You stay comfortably inside the house with the ascetic; I shall stay outside, with the large weapons too.
m.3.28.13: Nandīśvara said: Hearing those auspicious, righteous words of his wife, the Bhilla woman, the Bhilla reflected in his mind:
m.3.28.14: Having put my wife outside, how can I stay in the house? Yet the ascetic's going elsewhere would bring unrighteousness upon me.
m.3.28.15: Neither of the two is at all proper for a householder. Whatever is to be will surely be; I must stay outside the house.
m.3.28.16: Then, having insisted thus and gladly placed the two inside the house, and having arranged his weapons, the Bhilla stayed outside the house.
m.3.28.17: In the night cruel, violent beasts attacked him, and he too made a great effort then, as far as his strength allowed.
m.3.28.18: Though striving thus and though strong, the Bhilla was forcibly devoured by the beasts, impelled by his past karma (prārabdha).
m.3.28.19: Rising at dawn, the ascetic, seeing that forest-dwelling Bhilla devoured by the beasts, became exceedingly grieved.
m.3.28.20: Seeing the ascetic grieved, the Bhilla woman, though grieving herself, suppressed her own sorrow through fortitude and spoke these words.
m.3.28.21: The Bhilla woman said: Why do you grieve? Good has now come about, O ascetic. He is blessed and has fulfilled his purpose, since such a death has befallen him.
m.3.28.22: And I shall follow him, becoming ashes in the fire, O ascetic. Have a pyre built gladly; this is the eternal dharma of women.
m.3.28.23: Hearing her words and thinking them beneficial, the ascetic himself built the pyre, and she entered it in accordance with her own dharma.
m.3.28.24: At that moment Śiva manifested in person before her. Hara, praising her lovingly, said: Blessed one, blessed one!
m.3.28.25: Hara said: Ask for a boon; I am pleased with your conduct, O sinless one. There is nothing that cannot be given to you; I am especially subject to you.
m.3.28.26: Nandīśvara said: Hearing Śambhu's words, which bestow supreme bliss, she attained great joy and lost all awareness of anything else.
m.3.28.27: Observing her state, Hara became very pleased, and the lord Śambhu again said to her: Ask for a boon.
m.3.28.28: Śiva said: This ascetic, who is my own form, will become a swan; in your next birth he will lovingly bring about the union of you two.
