m.5.5.33: Forsaking father and mother, false witness, lying to brahmins, meat -eating by Śiva's devotees, and eating what is forbidden;
m.5.5.34: and killing innocent creatures in the forest; and when what a good man would set aside for brahmins one does not apply to a righteous purpose;
m.5.5.35: and the deed of those who set fire on the paths of cows, in forests, or in villages — these are terrible sins, equal to killing a brahmin.
m.5.5.36: Seizing all that a poor man owns; the sale of men, women, elephants, horses, cows, land, silver, garments, medicinal herbs, and juices,
m.5.5.37: of sandal, aloe-wood, camphor, musk, and silk garments — the sale of these made knowingly by twice-born men when not in distress,
m.5.5.38: and misappropriating a deposit placed in one's hands — these are held equal to stealing gold. Not giving marriageable daughters to a suitable bridegroom,
m.5.5.39: going to the wives of one's son or friend, and to sisters; the terrible violation of a maiden; consorting with the wife of a drunkard;
m.5.5.40: and going to a woman of one's own class — these are held equal to violating the guru's wife. The great sins have been told; now hear about the minor sins.
m.5.5.iti: Thus ends the fifth adhyāya, named The description of the great sins, in the fifth saṃhitā, the Umā-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.5.6.1: Sanatkumāra said: Stealing the property of brahmins, and also violating the rules of inheritance, excessive pride and excessive anger, hypocrisy, ingratitude,
m.5.6.2: excessive attachment to sense-objects, miserliness, envy of the good, going to others' wives, defiling the daughters of good people,
m.5.6.3: the elder brother who stays unmarried while his younger brother marries (parivitti), the younger who marries first (parivettā), and the girl by whom he is so married; giving a girl in marriage to those two, and officiating at sacrifices for those very two,
m.5.6.4: destroying the trees of Śiva's hermitages and flower-gardens; and he who inflicts even slight pain on those dwelling in hermitages,
m.5.6.5: harming one with his servants and household, his cattle, grain and wealth; theft of base metals, grain and cattle, and likewise polluting waters,
m.5.6.6: selling sacrifices, gardens and ponds, or one's wife and children; selling the merit of pilgrimages and fasts, of vows and the rites of upanayana,
m.5.6.7: those who, utterly conquered by women, live on women's wealth; failing to protect women, and enjoying women by deceit,
m.5.6.8: not giving what has fallen due in time, living on interest from grain, accepting wealth from a censured person, living by fraud in merchandise,
m.5.6.9: the use of poisons and killing-spells, constantly yoking bulls, rites of expulsion (uccāṭana) and black magic (abhicāra), taking grain, and practising medicine,
m.5.6.10: he whose undertaking of good deeds is for the enjoyment of palate and lust; one who always teaches for a fee, and whatever Vedic knowledge and the like is sold,
m.5.6.11: abandoning the vows of brahmacarya and the like, following the conduct of others, studying false scriptures, relying on dry logic,
m.5.6.12: the reviling of gods, fire, gurus and holy men, and of a brahmin, whether to their face or behind their back, and also of kings and regional rulers,
m.5.6.13: those who have abandoned worship of ancestors and gods, who forsake their own duties, the ill-behaved, unbelievers, sinners, and those who always speak untruth,
m.5.6.14: he who has intercourse on a festival day (parvan), by day, or in water, in an unnatural orifice, with animals, or with a menstruating woman,
m.5.6.15: those who cut off the hopes of wife, son or friend when they approach, speakers of unpleasant things to people, the cruel, and breakers of agreements,
m.5.6.16: one who breaches ponds and wells, sellers of liquids, and he who makes distinction in the food served to those seated in the same row,
m.5.6.17: Women and men guilty of these sins are declared to be committers of minor sins (upapātaka). Others too are tainted with these; listen, I shall tell you of them.
m.5.6.18: Those men who ruin the affairs of cows, brahmins and maidens, of masters, friends and ascetics, are declared destined for hell.
m.5.6.19: Those who burn with longing for another's wife, who point out others' wealth to thieves, who constantly steal others' wealth, and who follow false weights,
m.5.6.20: those who cause suffering to brahmins, who raise a blow against them, twice-born men who consort with a śūdra woman, and those who prepare liquor at will,
m.5.6.21: cruel men devoted to sin, men fond of violence, and those who perform acts like giving and sacrifice for the sake of a livelihood,
m.5.6.22: those who discharge excrement and the like in cowpens, fire, water and streets, in the shade of trees and on hills, and in gardens and temples,
m.5.6.23: those addicted to drinking liquor in places of modesty, hermitages and temples, lechers given to dalliance, and those intent on seeking out others' weak points,
m.5.6.24: those who obstruct the road with bamboo, bricks, stones, wood, horns and stakes, and those who seize another's boundary,
m.5.6.25: makers of forged edicts, those devoted to fraudulent deeds, those who deal fraudulently in cooked food, grain and cloth,
m.5.6.26: he who makes bows, weapons and arrows and buys and sells them, he who is extremely merciless toward servants, and he who harshly tames animals,
m.5.6.27: he who quietly listens to the words of one speaking falsely, the betrayer of master, friend and guru, the deceitful, the fickle, the rogue,
m.5.6.28: those who eat while neglecting their hungry wife, sons and friends, children, the old, the weak and the sick, servants, guests and relatives,
m.5.6.29: He who himself eats sweet food and does not give to brahmins should be known as a futile cook, censured among the expounders of the Veda.
m.5.6.30: those of uncontrolled senses who, having themselves taken up observances, abandon them; those who falsely wear the garb of renunciation; and those who deface the image of Hara,
m.5.6.31: those cruel ones who beat a cow and subdue it again and again, who do not nourish weak ones and constantly abandon them,
m.5.6.32: who torment them with excessive loads and make one that cannot bear it carry them, who yoke them when they have not eaten and do not release them when tied,
m.5.6.33: Those who do not carefully tend cows and bulls afflicted by loads, wounds and disease, or tormented by hunger, are cow-killers, declared destined for hell.
m.5.6.34: Those most sinful ones who castrate bulls, and who make a barren cow carry loads, are men destined for great hell.
m.5.6.35: Those who have arrived with hope, emaciated by hunger, thirst and toil — guests, the helpless, and independent wanderers who have come to the house —
m.5.6.36: those longing for food, or the wretched, children, the old, the weak and the sick — the fools who show them no compassion go to the ocean of hell.
m.5.6.37: Wealth turns back at the house, relatives at the cremation ground; only good and evil deeds follow the one who departs.
m.5.6.38: A base brahmin who lives by goats and sheep, by buffaloes, by sea-trade, who is husband of a śūdra woman, or who lives like a śūdra or by a kṣatriya's livelihood, becomes hell-bound.
m.5.6.39: Craftsmen, artisans, physicians, goldsmiths, royal standard-bearers and hired servants — all of them, when given to fraud, are declared hell-bound.
m.5.6.40: He who, transgressing what is proper, levies tax merely at his own whim, is roasted in hell; so too the man who delights in punishment.
m.5.6.41: The king whose subjects in his kingdom are oppressed by bribe-takers, by officials bought at will, and by thieves, is cooked in the hells.
m.5.6.42: Those brahmins who accept gifts from a king who acts unjustly go to terrible hells; there is no doubt.
m.5.6.43: He who, having unjustly taken wealth from the subjects, gives it to brahmins, he too is cooked in the hells, just like the king.
m.5.6.44: The sin that belongs to adulterers, thieves and violent men, and also to one attached to others' wives, always accrues to the king who does not restrain them.
m.5.6.45: A king who, without investigation, regards a non-thief as a thief or a thief as a non-thief, and therefore has him killed, goes to hell.
m.5.6.46: Ghee, oil, food and drinks, honey, meat, liquor and spirits, jaggery, sugarcane, vegetables and milk, curd, roots and fruits,
m.5.6.47: grass, wood, leaves and flowers, medicine and one's own food, sandals, umbrella, cart, seat and water-pot,
m.5.6.48: copper, lead and tin, weapons, conch and other water-born things, musical instruments, bamboo articles and other household goods,
m.5.6.49: and garments, coarse and fine, made of wool, cotton, silk and fine thread — those who out of greed steal these,
m.5.6.50: — having stolen these and other various goods, even small ones, they surely go to the hells.
m.5.6.51: Having stolen another's property, whatever it may be, even as little as a mustard seed, men go to hell; there is no doubt about this.
m.5.6.52: Through such sins, a man, immediately after departing from life, obtains a body of complete form for the sake of bodily torment.
m.5.6.53: By Yama's command these go with that body to Yama's world, being led by Yama's very terrible messengers, sorely afflicted.
m.5.6.54: For gods, animals and humans whose minds are devoted to unrighteousness, Dharmarāja is known as the chastiser, with very terrible and various punishments.
m.5.6.55: For those who observe rules and right conduct but have slipped through carelessness, the guru is the chastiser, through expiations; Yama is not accepted as their punisher by the wise.
m.5.6.56: For adulterers, thieves and those who deal unjustly, the king is declared the chastiser; for those whose sins are hidden, it is Dharmarāja.
m.5.6.57: Therefore one should perform expiation for a sin committed; otherwise there is no destruction of a sin not experienced in its fruit, even in hundreds of crores of kalpas.
m.5.6.58: He who himself does a deed, causes it to be done, or approves of it, by body, mind or speech — for him the fruit is the course leading to sin's consequences.
m.5.6.iti: Thus ends the sixth adhyāya, named The description of the kinds of sin, in the fifth saṃhitā, the Umā-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.5.7.1: Sanatkumāra said: Now, because of sins of four kinds, men go to the world of Yama, which is dreadful and causes terror; all embodied beings go there helplessly.
m.5.7.2: It must be understood to apply to all creatures: to beings in the womb, to those being born, to children, to the young and the middle-aged, and to women, men and neuters.
m.5.7.3: And here the fruit of the good and evil deeds of embodied beings is examined by Citragupta and all the others, and likewise by those headed by Vasiṣṭha.
m.5.7.4: There are no living beings who do not go to the abode of Yama. For a deed that has been done must surely be experienced; let this be pondered.
m.5.7.5: Of these, the men whose deeds are good, whose minds are gentle and who are full of compassion go to Yama's dwelling by the pleasant eastern path.
m.5.7.6: But those who do sinful deeds, the wicked who are devoid of giving, go to Yama's abode by the dreadful southern path.
m.5.7.7: Having passed beyond eighty-six thousand yojanas, that city of Vaivasvata Yama is to be known, situated there in manifold forms.
m.5.7.8: To men of meritorious deeds it appears as though near at hand; to sinners, who go by the terrible path, it is very far away.
m.5.7.9: They go by a path beset with sharp thorns, strewn with gravel, and laid with sharp stones like razor edges;
m.5.7.10: in places by a path with deep mud and swarming with leeches, in places furnished with darbha grass like iron needles;
m.5.7.11: by mountains mostly of steep precipices, very rugged and thick with trees, and by a road covered with glowing coals, they go in misery.
m.5.7.12: In places with uneven pits, in places with clods very hard to cross, with burning-hot sand and likewise with sharp stakes;
m.5.7.13: in places overrun with bamboo thickets spreading with many branches; somewhere by a painful path in darkness without any support;
m.5.7.14: in places with sharp iron caltrops, again with forest fire, in places with heated rocks, and in places covered with snow;
m.5.7.15: in places covered with sand into which one sinks up to the throat, in places with foul water, and in places with dung-fire;
m.5.7.16: in places with lions, wolves, tigers and very fierce mosquitoes, in places with huge leeches, and in places likewise with pythons;
m.5.7.17: with fierce flies, in places with serpents of virulent poison, and with herds of rutting elephants, mad with strength and crushing;
m.5.7.18: with sharp-tusked boars furrowing the path, with sharp-horned buffaloes, and with beasts of prey of every kind;
m.5.7.19: tormented by fierce ḍākinīs, by hideous rākṣasas and by most dreadful diseases, they indeed proceed.
m.5.7.20: Struck by a very violent wind mixed with thick dust and by a shower of huge stones, they go without refuge.
m.5.7.21: In places they go on being burnt by falling lightning, and pierced on all sides by a great shower of arrows.
m.5.7.22: They are indeed burnt by falling thunderbolts, by dreadful falls of meteors, and by a shower of blazing coals.
m.5.7.23: Filled up by a great shower of dust they weep, and again and again they are terrified by the dreadful roars of great clouds.
m.5.7.24: Cut on all sides by a shower of sharp weapons and drenched by torrents of very caustic water, they go on.
m.5.7.25: Afflicted on every side by an extremely cold, dry and harsh wind, they wither and shrivel up.
m.5.7.26: Thus, by a terrible road, without provisions for the journey, without support, hard to pass, waterless all around,
m.5.7.27: very rugged and long, without people or shelter, of the form of darkness, painful, and the haunt of every evil thing,
m.5.7.28: all embodied beings who are deluded and do sinful deeds are led by force by the most dreadful messengers of Yama, who carry out his command.
m.5.7.29: Alone, in the power of others, deprived of friends and kin, lamenting their own deeds and weeping again and again,
m.5.7.30: having become pretas, naked, with throats, lips and palates parched, ghastly, stricken with fear, burning and tormented by hunger,
m.5.7.31: some men, bound with chains, lying on their backs and held by the feet, are dragged; and as they are dragged they are beaten by Yama's messengers of fierce strength.
m.5.7.32: Others, face down, scraped along on their chests, in great misery, are dragged with a rope tied to their tufts of hair.
m.5.7.33: Other embodied beings, pierced in the forehead with a goad, suffer; some are dragged on their backs along a thorny path, in places along a road of burning coals.
m.5.7.34: With arms bound behind them, squeezed at the belly, loaded with chains and with their hands firmly nailed,
m.5.7.35: some are dragged by a noose on the neck; others go on in great misery; they are dragged by a rope with a hook driven into the tongue.
m.5.7.36: Likewise others are dragged by a rope through a pierced nose; others, pierced in the cheeks and likewise in the lips, are dragged by a rope.
m.5.7.37: With the tips of their feet and hands cut off, with ears, lips and noses cut off, with penis and testicles severed, their limbs and joints cut and split,
m.5.7.38: being pierced through with lances and pierced with arrows, running hither and thither, crying out, without refuge,
m.5.7.39: struck again and again with mallets and iron rods, and with various dreadful thorns shining like fire and the sun,
m.5.7.40: they are pierced with bhindipāla darts, streaming pus and blood; smeared with excrement and worms, the helpless men are led on.
m.5.7.41: Begging for water, or for food when hungry, pleading for shade, and again for fire when afflicted by cold,
m.5.7.42: thus men devoid of charity go along, longing for comfort. Those who have taken gifts given in life as their provisions for the journey go happily to Yama's abode.
m.5.7.43: When, in this manner and with hardship, they have reached the city of the departed, they are announced by the messengers and then placed before Yama.
m.5.7.44: There, those who have done good deeds Yama honours with words of welcome, the offering of a seat, water for the feet and arghya, and kind speech.
m.5.7.45: Blessed are you, great souls, doers of what the Vedas enjoin, by whom merit has been performed for the sake of heavenly happiness.
m.5.7.46: Mounting a celestial chariot adorned with celestial women and enjoyments, go to spotless heaven, furnished with all desires.
m.5.7.47: Having enjoyed great pleasures there, at the end, upon the exhaustion of your merit, whatever small evil remains, that you will again experience here.
m.5.7.48: Righteous men, who are like friends to themselves, behold a gentle face and the King of Dharma himself.
m.5.7.49: But those of cruel deeds see him terrifying, his face dreadful with fangs, his eyes crooked with knitted brows,
m.5.7.50: with hair standing up, a great beard, lips quivering upward, eighteen-armed, angry, resembling a heap of blue collyrium,
m.5.7.51: his hands raising all weapons, threatening with the rod of all punishment, mounted on a great buffalo, with eyes like blazing fire,
m.5.7.52: wearing red garlands and garments, towering like great Meru, roaring like the clouds of dissolution, as if drinking up the great ocean,
m.5.7.53: as if swallowing the king of mountains, as if vomiting fire. And Death stands near, with a radiance like the fire of time's end;
m.5.7.54: and Kāla, resembling collyrium, and terrifying Kṛtānta, Mārī, the fierce Mahāmārī, and dreadful Kālarātri;
m.5.7.55: various diseases, leprosies, of many forms, fearsome, bearing spears, tridents and goads, with nooses, discuses and swords in their hands,
m.5.7.56: bearing thunderbolt-like beaks, fierce, carrying razors, quivers and bows, all bearing various weapons, great heroes, terrifying;
m.5.7.57: countless great heroes, with a radiance like black collyrium, their hands raised with all weapons—the terrifying messengers of Yama.
m.5.7.58: The most sinful behold that Yama, terrible to look upon, surrounded by this retinue, and the fearsome Citragupta.
m.5.7.59: Yama severely rebukes those evil-doers, and the venerable Citragupta instructs them with words of dharma.
m.5.7.iti: Thus ends the seventh adhyāya, named The description of the road to the world of hell and of the form of Yama's messengers, in the fifth saṃhitā, the Umā-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.5.8.1: Citragupta said: O you whose deeds are wicked, stealers of others' wealth, proud of your beauty and strength, violators of others' wives.
m.5.8.2: The deed that one does oneself is the very thing one experiences as its result in turn. Why then did you commit evil, only to bring about your own ruin?
m.5.8.3: Why do you lament now, tormented by your own deeds? Let your own deeds be experienced; the fault indeed lies with no one else.
m.5.8.4: Sanatkumāra said: In the same way those kings, arrogant with the power of their misdeeds, arrived before him on account of their own terrible deeds.
m.5.8.5: Them too Citragupta, the great lord, knower of dharma, filled with anger, admonishes according to the instruction of King Yama.
m.5.8.6: Citragupta said: O kings of wicked conduct, destroyers of your subjects, why did you commit evil for the sake of a kingdom that lasts but a short time?
m.5.8.7: Since, out of delusion from the enjoyment of kingship, you punished your subjects by force and unjustly, let the fruit of that be experienced now, O kings.
m.5.8.8: Where now is that kingdom and wife for whose sake evil was done? Abandoning all that, you stand here alone.
m.5.8.9: I see that the strength by which the subjects were crushed is gone. Now, as you are being dealt with by Yama's messengers, what will your state be like?
m.5.8.10: Sanatkumāra said: Thus reproached by Yama with many kinds of words, those kings grieve over their own deeds and stand in silence.
m.5.8.11: Having thus pointed out the deeds of the kings, Yama, the king of dharma, speaks these words to his messengers for cleansing the mire of their sins.
m.5.8.12: Yama said: O Caṇḍa, O Mahācaṇḍa, seize these kings by force and purify them in due order, according to rule, in the fires of hell.
m.5.8.13: Sanatkumāra said: Then, quickly taking hold of the kings, seizing them by the feet, whirling them around with force, tossing them up and catching them again,
m.5.8.14: with all their great might they dash them violently on an exceedingly heated rock surface, like great trees struck by a thunderbolt.
m.5.8.15: Then, shattered, he streams blood from his ears; that embodied being then becomes senseless and motionless.
m.5.8.16: Then, touched by the wind, he is revived again by them; and then, for the purification of his sins, they cast him into the ocean of hell.
m.5.8.17: Beneath the earth are the divisions (koṭi) of hell, seven groups, twenty-eight in number, situated at the end of the seventh nether level in dreadful darkness.
m.5.8.18: The first division is called Ghorā; Sughorā lies below it; then Atighorā, Mahāghorā, and the fifth, Ghorarūpā;
m.5.8.19: the sixth is called Talātalā, the seventh Bhayānakā, the eighth Kālarātri, and the ninth Bhayotkaṭā;
m.5.8.20: the tenth, below that, is Caṇḍā; further below is Mahācaṇḍā; then another, Caṇḍakolāhalā; Pracaṇḍā; Caṇḍanāyikā;
m.5.8.21: Padmā, Padmāvatī, Bhītā, Bhīmā, Bhīṣaṇanāyikā, Karālā, Vikarālā, and Vajrā, which is known as the twentieth;
m.5.8.22: Trikoṇā, Pañcakoṇā, Sudīrghā, Akhilārtidā, Samā, Bhīmabalā, Abhogrā, and Dīptaprāyā, which is the twenty-eighth.
m.5.8.23: Thus these dreadful divisions of hell have been told to you by name; they are exactly twenty-eight, consisting of torments for sinners.
m.5.8.24: For each of these divisions, in order, five chief hells are to be known; learn them by name.
m.5.8.25: The first of them is Raurava, where embodied beings weep; and through the torments of Mahāraurava even the great weep.
m.5.8.26: Then Śīta and also Uṣṇa: these five are known as the first chief hells. Sughora, Sumahātīkṣṇa, and likewise Sañjīvana are known next.
m.5.8.27: Mahātama, Viloma, Vilopa, and also Kaṇṭaka, Tīvravega, Karāla, Vikarāla, Prakampana,
m.5.8.28: Mahāvakra, Kāla, Kālasūtra, Pragarjana, Sūcīmukha, Suneti, Khādaka, Suprapīḍana,
m.5.8.29: Kumbhīpāka and Supāka, the extremely cruel Krakaca, Aṅgārarāśibhavana, and then Medo'sṛkprahita,
m.5.8.30: Tīkṣṇatuṇḍa, Śakuni, Mahāsaṃvartaka, Kratu, Taptajantu, Paṅkalepa, Pratimāṃsa, Trapūdbhava,
m.5.8.31: Ucchvāsa, Sunirucchvāsa, Sudīrgha, Kūṭaśālmali, Duriṣṭa, Sumahāvāda, Pravāha, Supratāpana,
m.5.8.32: then Megha, Vṛṣa, Śālma; those with the faces of lions, tigers, and elephants; those with the faces of dogs, boars, goats, buffaloes, owls, ruddy geese, and wolves;
m.5.8.33: those named Grāha, Kumbhīna, and Nakra; Sarpa, Kūrma, and Vāyasa; those named Gṛdhra, Ulūka, and Halauka; Śārdūla, Kratha, and Karkaṭa;
m.5.8.34: Maṇḍūka, the Pūtivaktras, Raktākṣa, the Pūtimṛttikās, Kaṇadhūmra, likewise Agni, and likewise Kṛmigandhivapus,
m.5.8.35: Agnīdhra, Apratiṣṭha, Rudhirābha, Śvabhojana, Lālābhakṣa and Antrabhakṣa, and the very cruel Sarvabhakṣa,
m.5.8.36: Kaṇṭaka, Suviśāla, Vikaṭa, Kaṭapūtana, Ambarīṣa, Kaṭāha, and the painful river Vaitaraṇī,
m.5.8.37: Sutaptalohaśayana (the bed of red-hot iron), Ekapāda, Prapūraṇa, the dreadful Asitālavana (forest of sword-palms), Asthibhaṅga, Supūraṇa,
m.5.8.38: Vilātasa, also Asuyantra, Kūṭapāśa, Pramardana, Mahācūrṇa, also Asucūrṇa, and likewise the mountain made of heated iron,
m.5.8.39: the Mountain, Kṣuradhārā (razor's edge), likewise Yamalaparvata (twin mountains), the well of urine, excrement, and tears, and the cold well of caustic brine,
m.5.8.40: the device of pestle and mortar, the stone-cart and plough, the thicket of palm-leaf swords, and the pavilion of the great cart.
m.5.8.41: Then come Sammoha, Asthibhaṅga, Tapta, Cala, Ayoguḍa, Bahuduḥkha, Mahākleśa, Kaśmala, Samala and Mala.
m.5.8.42: Hālāhala, Virūpa, Svarūpa, Yamānuga, Ekapāda, Tripāda, Tīvra, Acīvara and Tamas.
m.5.8.43: These, in order, are the twenty-eight hells; they are arranged in groups of five by five, and in due sequence there are five by five crores of hells under them, with their chiefs.
m.5.8.44: They are made known as belonging to Raurava; the hells are traditionally counted as a hundred and forty — this is declared to be the great circle of hells.
m.5.8.45: Thus, O Vyāsa, I have fully described to you the arrangement of hell; from such enumeration arises dispassion. Now hear also that course of sinners.
m.5.8.iti: Thus ends the eighth adhyāya, named The description of the world of hell, in the fifth saṃhitā, the Umā-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.5.9.1: Sanatkumāra said: In these hells the sinners are cooked and parched in the fires of hell, intensely, by various torments, until their own karma is exhausted.
m.5.9.2: Just as metals are smelted in fire through the removal of their own impurities, so there sinful men are purified through the destruction of sin, in accordance with their deeds.
m.5.9.3: Then, having bound them very tightly by the hands with a chain, Yama's servants hang the men from the topmost branches of great trees.
m.5.9.4: Then, flung with all force by the servants, they swing; and swinging with tremendous speed, they lose consciousness and are carried a yojana away.
m.5.9.5: And again, to the feet of those hanging in mid-air, a hundred loads of iron are tied by Yama's mighty messengers.
m.5.9.6: Severely afflicted by that great weight, the men brood on their own deeds and remain silent and motionless.
m.5.9.7: Then the evil-doers are struck on all sides by the terrible servants with fire-coloured goads and dreadful iron rods.
m.5.9.8: Then they are smeared all over, again and again, with burning, fierce caustic, more scorching even than fire.
m.5.9.9: Thoroughly smeared with the molten substance, their limbs cut, they are battered to pieces; and again, their limbs being torn open in order, beginning from the head,
m.5.9.10: they are cooked like eggplants in heated iron cauldrons; likewise they are thrown into a well full of excrement, and again into a mass of worms,
m.5.9.11: and again they are thrown into a pond full of fat, blood and pus; they are devoured by sharp-toothed worms and by iron-beaked crows,
m.5.9.12: by dogs, gadflies, wolves, tigers and fierce beasts with hideous faces; and they are also roasted like fish on heaps of blazing coals.
m.5.9.13: Pierced by very sharp spikes on account of their sinful deeds, men, trampled in oil-presses because of their own terrible actions,
m.5.9.14: are crushed like sesame seeds in the hell called Cakra, reduced to lumps of human flesh; and they are fried in many ways in the heat, in heated iron vessels.
m.5.9.15: In well-heated cauldrons full of oil, again and again, in many ways; and the tongue is cooked after the body is pressed down at the chest and feet.
m.5.9.16: Here great torments are inflicted on the body, exceedingly and on every side; in this way men pass in succession through all the hells.
m.5.9.17: In all the hells, O Vyāsa, various torments of Yama, causing intense pain, are inflicted on every limb by Yama's attendants.
m.5.9.18: Taking a burning coal and filling his mouth with it, the sinner is beaten; then again and again the mouth is filled with burning caustic and molten copper,
m.5.9.19: and then with extremely hot ghee and oil; his mouth being pried open this way and that and forcibly filled, he is beaten.
m.5.9.20: Being filled here and there with excrement and worms, they are made to embrace the very fierce, blazing iron śālmali tree.
m.5.9.21: And they are struck on the back again with blazing great hammers, and cut with a powerful, toothed and very blunt saw.
m.5.9.22: Beginning from the head they are tormented because of the terrible deeds born of themselves; they are made to eat their own flesh, and their own blood is drunk.
m.5.9.23: Those who, always nourishing only themselves, never gave food or drink are crushed like sugarcane after being battered with clubs.
m.5.9.24: Then in the terrible Asitāla forest they are cut to pieces; with all their limbs pierced by needles, impaled on the points of heated stakes,
m.5.9.25: shaken about many times, they suffer yet do not die; for their bodies are such as to endure pleasure and pain.
m.5.9.26: Their flesh is torn from the body, and they are smashed with clubs by Yama's terrible messengers of jagged-toothed form and overpowering strength.
m.5.9.27: In the hell Nirucchvāsa they remain breathless for a long time; likewise in Ucchvāsa, the abode of sand, men are beaten and tossed up.
m.5.9.28: In Raurava, weeping, they are tormented with various kinds of blows; and through the torments of Mahāraurava even the mighty weep.
m.5.9.29: On the feet, mouth, anus, head, eyes and crown they are struck with hammers and with sharp, red-hot iron spikes.
m.5.9.30: They are placed again and again on scorching sand; thrown into a fiercely heated mire of creatures, they wail discordantly.
m.5.9.31: O sage, sinners of cruel deeds are cooked again in the Kumbhīpāka hells, in heated oils, utterly unbearable.
m.5.9.32: Those sinners are cast into the painful Lālābhakṣa hells, and likewise into hells in various places, again and again.
m.5.9.33: A sinful man devoid of merit is cast into the hell Sūcīmukha of great affliction and is beaten by Yama's servants.
m.5.9.34: Thrown into an iron pot, breathing ever more faintly, men are cooked by a great fire because of their own sins alone.
m.5.9.35: Bound tightly with ropes and the like, they are crushed on rocks, thrown into blind wells, and stung severely by bees.
m.5.9.36: With all their limbs pierced by worms and shattered a hundredfold, they are thereafter thrown into wells of very sharp caustic.
m.5.9.37: Here in the hell Mahājvāla the sinners cry out in misery; burned by its flames they run hither and thither.
m.5.9.38: Bringing their limbs round to the back, with the two ends joined and fastened at the shoulders, and drawing them tightly through the middle by the back of the arms,
m.5.9.39: all are bound very tightly to one another with noose-ropes; bound into bundles, they are seen undergoing torments in Mahājvāla.
m.5.9.40: Wrapped in ropes and smeared with mud, they are cooked in a fire of dung and chaff, yet they do not die.
m.5.9.41: Those sinners of very cruel conduct, having been dashed hundreds of times against rough rocks, are then cooked like grass.
m.5.9.42: Men are fiercely devoured by numerous sharp-mouthed worms that have entered inside their bodies, until their own bodies are wasted away.
m.5.9.43: Thrown into a mass of worms, into heaps of pus, flesh and bones, they remain with terrified hearts, crushed between two mountains.
m.5.9.44: The body is smeared with heated adamantine plaster, and, head down and feet up, they are scorched again and again by fire.
m.5.9.45: Helpless under another's control, they chew a red-hot iron club thrust inside their mouths, and they are beaten by them with hammers.
m.5.9.46: Thus, O Vyāsa, evil-doers are indeed tormented in the hells. Now I shall describe, for the sake of truth, the wretched disfigurement of those doers.
m.5.9.iti: Thus ends the ninth adhyāya, named The general description of the passage to hell, in the fifth saṃhitā, the Umā-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.5.10.1: Sanatkumāra said: One who engages in false teaching goes to the hell called Dvijihva; there he is tormented by sharp ploughs half a krośa wide drawn across his tongue.
m.5.10.2: The cruel one who reviles his mother, father or teacher is beaten, his mouth filled with excrement mixed with worms.
m.5.10.3: Those men who damage Śiva's temples, gardens, step-wells, wells and ponds, and the dwelling of brahmins, and who amuse themselves there,
m.5.10.4: and, intoxicated with pride, practise there for pleasure rubbing with unguents, oil-massage, bathing, drinking water, eating, sport, sexual intercourse and gambling,
m.5.10.5: they are tormented by various terrible crushings, such as in sugarcane presses, and are cooked in the fires of hell until the dissolution of beings.
m.5.10.6: Adulterers are beaten in that very form in which they sinned; they are made to tightly embrace a red-hot woman made of iron.
m.5.10.7: And men in the shape of her former lovers, blazing on all sides, tightly embrace the unchaste woman, and they weep.
m.5.10.8: Those who listen to slander of the good have their ears stuffed with fire-coloured, heated iron nails, and ones made of copper and the like,
m.5.10.9: with molten tin, lead and brass, with boiling milk again and again, with very hot pungent oil, or again with adamantine cement.
m.5.10.10: Having filled the ears in succession, these torments take place in all the hells, one after another, on every side.
m.5.10.11: In the same way, for all the senses, terrible torments come in turn for each, according to the sin, and for what was done with the body.
m.5.10.12: Those deluded ones who, through the fault of touch, touch another man's wife have their hands violently filled with fire-coloured dust.
m.5.10.13: Their body is smeared all over with caustics and the like, and in all the hells there are torments of great pain.
m.5.10.14: Men who frown at their parents and make angry gestures with hands and eyes have their faces, inside and out, firmly studded with spikes.
m.5.10.15: With whatever senses men misbehave towards another's wife, those very senses of theirs are likewise mutilated by Yama's servants.
m.5.10.16: The lustful who stare at others' wives with fixed gaze have their eyes filled with fire-coloured needles,
m.5.10.17: and then with caustics and the like; all these torments of Yama take place right here in succession, O tiger among sages — truly, truly, without doubt.
m.5.10.18: Those who eat without first offering to the gods, fire, teachers and brahmins have their tongue and mouth filled with hundreds of heated iron nails.
m.5.10.19: Men who out of greed pluck by hand the flowers of the gods' gardens, smell them, and moreover wear them on their heads,
m.5.10.20: have their heads filled with heated iron spikes, and then their noses intensely with very abundant caustics and the like.
m.5.10.21: Those who revile the great-souled reciter, the teacher of dharma, devotees of the gods, fire and teachers, and the eternal dharma-śāstra —
m.5.10.22: in their chest and throat, tongue, the joints of the teeth, palate and lip, nose, head, and all the joints of the limbs,
m.5.10.23: fire-coloured, heated, three-pronged iron spikes are driven in many times with hammers at these places.
m.5.10.24: Then the body is filled all over with burning caustic, and great torments indeed befall the body on every side.
m.5.10.25: They pass again in succession through all the hells. Those who seize others' property and touch a brahmin with their feet,
m.5.10.26: or touch with the feet the implements of Śiva's worship, a cow, or whatever is written containing knowledge and the like — their hands, feet and so on are filled with torments all over.
m.5.10.27: And in all the hells there arise many strange and very painful torments, again and again, arising in the hands and feet.
m.5.10.28: Sinners who discharge excrement and urine within the precincts of Śiva's temple or anywhere in the gods' gardens —
m.5.10.29: their penis with the testicles is crushed with iron hammers, and likewise filled again with fire-coloured needles.
m.5.10.30: Then the embodied being's anus and penis are tightly filled again and again with a great quantity of sharp molten caustic.
m.5.10.31: Next, the sin from which suffering arises for the mind and all the senses: those who, out of craving, do not give gifts even though they have wealth,
m.5.10.32: and who disregard a guest arriving at the proper time while in the householder's stage — having incurred sin from that, they go to an impure hell.
m.5.10.33: Those who eat without giving food to dogs together with crows have their mouths forced open, pinned by a pair of pegs,
m.5.10.34: and they are tormented within by worms, fierce creatures, iron-beaked crows, and many kinds of fierce afflictions.
m.5.10.35: The offering formula: Śyāma and Śabala, the two who guard the path of Yama — to them I give this; may those two accept this offering.
m.5.10.36: And the crows of the west, north-west, south and south-west — crows of meritorious deeds — may they accept my offering.
m.5.10.37: Those who carefully worship Śivā, offer oblations into the fire according to rule, and give the bali-offering with Śaiva mantras do not see Yama;
m.5.10.38: they do not see him; they go to heaven. Therefore one should give the offering day after day. Having made a square maṇḍala scented with perfumes and the like,
m.5.10.39: one should place an offering for Dhanvantari in the north-east, for Indra in the east, for Yama in the south, for Varuṇa in the west, and for Soma on the right side.
m.5.10.40: Having placed an offering for the Pitṛs, one should then place one for Aryaman in the east, and for Dhātṛ and Vidhātṛ at the doorway.
m.5.10.41: He should scatter food on the ground for dogs, for dog-keepers and for birds. By gods, ancestors and humans, by pretas and bhūtas together with guhyakas,
m.5.10.42: by birds, worms and insects — the householder is relied upon for sustenance. The svāhā-call, the svadhā-call, the vaṣaṭ-call as the third,
m.5.10.43: and likewise the hanta-call as the other — these are the four teats of the cow. The gods drink from the svāhā teat, and likewise the ancestors from the svadhā,
m.5.10.44: likewise other gods and the lords of beings drink from the vaṣaṭ teat, and humans constantly drink from the hanta teat.
m.5.10.45: The man who, with faith and in proper order, constantly tends this cow at the right time, becomes fit for the status of one who keeps the sacred fire.
m.5.10.46: But he who abandons it, or is negligent, sinks into Tāmisra hell. Therefore, having offered the bali to them, he should wait a moment standing at the door, reflecting.
m.5.10.47: A guest afflicted by hunger, even one living in the same village, he should duly feed with good food, according to his means, from his own meal.
m.5.10.48: He whose guest turns back from his house with hopes broken — that guest goes away, giving him his own sins and taking his merit.
m.5.10.49: Then the man who eats only the food he likes without sharing is again bound in chains; pierced here through the urge of his tongue, he remains for a long time.
m.5.10.50: For his flesh is cut out in pieces the size of a sesame seed and given to them to eat, and having pierced him, his blood too.
m.5.10.51: He is tormented again and again, thoroughly, with whips in succession, suffering great pain from hunger and likewise from extreme thirst.
m.5.10.52: Such and other extremely dreadful torments belong to those who do sinful deeds. What is attained at the end, hear that in brief.
m.5.10.53: He who commits a great sin and practises only a little dharma, or one whose dharma is weightier — hear the condition of these two.
m.5.10.54: The fruit of good deeds is not spoken of, owing to the force of the heavy sin; there, though endowed with many enjoyments, he does not obtain happiness.
m.5.10.55: So, anxious and greatly tormented, he finds no pleasure in foods, because of the lack of anything further before him, every morning, day after day.
m.5.10.56: The man of weighty dharma, even when fasting, like a wealthy householder, firm in his observances, does not feel distress.
m.5.10.57: There are those terrible sins by which a man on earth is split a hundredfold, like a mountain struck by a thunderbolt.
m.5.10.iti: Thus ends the tenth adhyāya, named The description of the passage to hell and of what is undergone there, in the fifth saṃhitā, the Umā-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.5.11.1: Vyāsa said: Men who have committed sins travel the road of Yama burdened with great suffering. O lord, tell me the righteous deeds (dharmas) by which men travel that road in comfort.
m.5.11.2: Sanatkumāra said: A deed once done, good or bad, must certainly be experienced; there is no question about it. Now I shall tell you those righteous deeds that bring happiness.
m.5.11.3: Those men who here in this world do good deeds, who are gentle-minded and compassionate, travel happily along Yama's fearsome road.
m.5.11.4: The man who gives shoes and wooden sandals to eminent brahmins goes comfortably to Yama's abode on a great horse.
m.5.11.5: By giving an umbrella, embodied beings go along that road as if sheltered by an umbrella; by giving a palanquin one travels comfortably in such a vehicle.
m.5.11.6: By giving a bed and a seat one goes comfortably, well rested. Those who create shady groves or plant trees along the road go to Yama's world free of fatigue even in the scorching heat.
m.5.11.7: Men who lay out flower gardens travel in a Puṣpaka chariot; and those who build temples of the gods sport within a mansion.
m.5.11.8: Likewise those who build hermitages for ascetics and shelters for the destitute also sport within a mansion.
m.5.11.9: Men who worship the gods, the fire, the guru, brahmins, and their mother and father go on that road honoured, at their ease, in a vehicle that moves at will.
m.5.11.10: Those who give lamps go illuminating all the directions; by giving shelter to others men go happily, free from affliction.
m.5.11.11: Men who serve their guru go on that road resting along the way; those who give musical instruments to brahmins go happily, as if in their own home.
m.5.11.12: Givers of cows go as if provided with the fulfilment of every desire. Whatever food and drink a man has given here, he obtains on that road.
m.5.11.13: By providing water for washing the feet one travels on a road supplied with water; and he who massages others' feet with oil goes on horseback.
m.5.11.14: O Vyāsa, Yama does not approach the one who always gives foot-washing water, oil-massage, lamps, food and shelter.
m.5.11.15: By giving gold and gems one goes on, crossing over difficult places; by giving silver and oxen he reaches Yama's world with ease.
m.5.11.16: Through such gifts as these men go happily to Yama's abode, and in heaven they constantly obtain various enjoyments.
m.5.11.17: Of all gifts the gift of food is declared the highest: it gives immediate satisfaction, is pleasing to the heart, and increases strength and intelligence.
m.5.11.18: O best of sages, there is no gift equal to the gift of food. Living beings arise from food, and without it they die.
m.5.11.19: Blood, flesh, fat and semen develop from food in succession; from semen living beings are born. Therefore the world consists of food.
m.5.11.20: Even if they obtain gold, gems, horses, lordly elephants, women, garlands, sandal paste and all such things, the hungry take no delight in them.
m.5.11.21: Those in the womb, those being born, children, the old and the middle-aged, gods, Dānavas and Rākṣasas, all crave food.
m.5.11.22: Hunger is declared the foremost disease among all diseases, and here it is destroyed by the ointment of the medicine called food; there is no doubt.
m.5.11.23: There is no suffering equal to hunger, no disease equal to hunger, no happiness equal to health, and no enemy equal to anger.
m.5.11.24: Hence great merit is proclaimed in the gift of food, for all embodied beings, scorched by the fire of hunger, die.
m.5.11.25: The giver of food is called the giver of life, and the giver of life is the giver of everything. Therefore by giving food one obtains the fruit of all gifts.
m.5.11.26: When someone whose body has been nourished by another's food and drink accumulates merit, half of it belongs to that giver of food and half to the doer; there is no doubt.
m.5.11.27: Whatever jewels, enjoyments, women and vehicles exist in the three worlds, the giver of food obtains all that, both here and hereafter.
m.5.11.28: The body is the supreme means for dharma, wealth, desire and liberation. Therefore one should sustain one's body with food and drink.
m.5.11.29: They praise food alone; everything is founded on food. There has never been, nor will there ever be, a gift equal to food.
m.5.11.30: O sage, this entire universe is sustained by food. Food gives vigour in the world, for the life-breaths are founded on food.
m.5.11.31: One who desires his own prosperity should give food to a mendicant and to a high-souled brahmin, even at the cost of hardship to his family.
m.5.11.32: He who gives food to a supplicant, a distressed brahmin, lays up for himself the finest treasure for the next world.
m.5.11.33: A householder seeking prosperity should honour a brahmin who arrives at mealtime, weary from the road, coming to his house for sustenance.
m.5.11.34: O Vyāsa, the giver of food, good-natured and free of envy, should honour the guest, casting off any anger that has arisen; he gains great happiness in heaven and here.
m.5.11.35: One should not revile the one who has come, nor drive him away in any way. Even given to an outcaste (śvapāka) or a dog, the gift of food is never lost.
m.5.11.36: He who ungrudgingly gives food to a weary stranger, never seen before, who is on the road, attains prosperity.
m.5.11.37: O great sage, the man who gratifies the ancestors, the gods, brahmins and guests with food gains great fruit of merit.
m.5.11.38: The gift of food and drink is excellent whether to a śūdra or to a brahmin. One should not ask about the recipient's gotra, Vedic school, Vedic study or homeland.
m.5.11.39: The man who, when asked for alms by a brahmin here, gives him food goes to the highest heaven and stays there until the dissolution of beings.
m.5.11.40: For the giver of food, trees bearing the fruits of all desires come into being in heaven, just as the brahmins here are filled with joy by him.
m.5.11.41: O sage, the worlds that have been fashioned in heaven through the gift of food for the giver of food are exceedingly divine; listen to the description of them, O great sage.
m.5.11.42: In heaven the mansions of those great souls shine forth, of many shapes and forms and endowed with all kinds of desired things.
m.5.11.43: There are also trees standing beside the mansions that bear the fruit of every desire, golden ponds, auspicious wells, and long lakes everywhere.
m.5.11.44: And thousands of auspicious drinks proclaim themselves; there are mountains made of foods to be chewed and eaten, as well as garments and ornaments.
m.5.11.45: There are rivers flowing with milk, and likewise mountains of ghee, palaces of pale white radiance, and couches gleaming with gold.
m.5.11.46: Givers of food go to those worlds; therefore one should be a giver of food, if one desires one's own welfare in this world and the next.
m.5.11.47: These greatly radiant worlds belong to the meritorious givers of food; therefore food should certainly be given by humans, above all else.
m.5.11.48: Food is Prajāpati manifest; food is Viṣṇu, and Hara himself. Therefore there has never been, nor will there be, a gift equal to food.
m.5.11.49: Even having committed a very great sin, one who afterwards becomes a giver of food is freed from all sins and goes to the world of heaven.
m.5.11.50: Food, drink, horses, cows, garments, beds, umbrellas and seats—these eight gifts are especially commended for the world of the departed.
m.5.11.51: Since by such special gifts a man travels to the city of Dharmarāja in an aerial chariot, therefore one should practise giving.
m.5.11.52: Whoever reads this sinless account of the power of the gift of food, or causes others to read it, becomes prosperous.
m.5.11.53: O great sage, whoever listens to it, or recites it to Brāhmaṇas at a śrāddha, for him the gift of food reaches the ancestors as imperishable.
m.5.11.iti: Thus ends the eleventh adhyāya, named The description of the greatness of the gift of food, in the fifth saṃhitā, the Umā-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.5.12.1: Sanatkumāra said: The gift of water is supreme, always the best of gifts; it is held to be the refreshment and the life of all the multitudes of living beings.
m.5.12.2: Therefore one should, with great affection, provide a water-shed (prapā) open to all without restriction. Building a reservoir of water brings great joy.
m.5.12.3: It brings joy in this world or the next — truly, truly, there is no doubt. Therefore a man should have step-wells, wells and tanks constructed.
m.5.12.4: A well whose water flows removes half the sin of a man of wrong deeds, if it is kept constantly well-functioning.
m.5.12.5: He saves his whole lineage in whose dug reservoir cows, brāhmaṇas and good men always drink.
m.5.12.6: He whose water remains freely available in the hot season never meets with anything very difficult, perilous or distressing.
m.5.12.7: I shall also tell the merits that are declared for tanks that have been built. One who possesses a tank is honoured everywhere in the three worlds.
m.5.12.8: Or else, like friendship in a friend's house, free from the distress of friends — the establishing of tanks is excellent and produces fame.
m.5.12.9: The wise call it the fruit of dharma, artha and kāma. He by whom a tank is well made has endless merit.
m.5.12.10: A tank is the supreme refuge of the four kinds of beings; tanks and the like all bestow the highest prosperity.
m.5.12.11: Gods, humans, gandharvas, ancestors, nāgas and rākṣasas, and stationary beings too, take refuge in a reservoir.
m.5.12.12: He in whose tank water remains during the rainy season obtains the fruit of the agnihotra — so said the Self-born Brahmā.
m.5.12.13: He in whose tank water remains in autumn gains the fruit of giving a thousand cows; there is no doubt here.
m.5.12.14: He whose water remains in early winter and late winter obtains the fruit of a sacrifice with abundant gold.
m.5.12.15: For him whose water remains in spring and likewise in summer, the wise declare the fruit of the atirātra and aśvamedha sacrifices.
m.5.12.16: O sage Vyāsa, the fruit of reservoirs, the supreme delighting of living beings, has been told; now hear the merits of planting trees.
m.5.12.17: One who plants trees in a wilderness delivers all the generations of his ancestral line, past and future; therefore one should plant trees.
m.5.12.18: These trees become his sons there, no doubt about it; and he, having gone to the other world, attains imperishable worlds.
m.5.12.19: Trees worship all the hosts of gods with their flowers, the ancestors with their fruits, and all guests with their shade.
m.5.12.20: Kinnaras, serpents, rākṣasas, gods, gandharvas and humans, and likewise the hosts of sages, take shelter in trees.
m.5.12.21: Flowering and fruit-bearing, they satisfy people here; in this world and the next they are regarded, by dharma, as sons.
m.5.12.22: The maker of tanks, the planter of trees, the twice-born who has performed sacrifices, and others who speak the truth — these do not fall from heaven.
m.5.12.23: Truth alone is the supreme Brahman, truth alone the supreme austerity, truth alone the supreme sacrifice, truth alone the supreme scripture.
m.5.12.24: Truth stays awake among those who sleep; truth is the supreme state. By truth the earth is upheld; in truth everything is established.
m.5.12.25: Austerity, sacrifice and merit, in the worship of gods, sages and ancestors, water and knowledge — all of these, everything, rests on truth.
m.5.12.26: Truth is sacrifice, austerity, charity, the mantras and the goddess Sarasvatī; truth likewise is celibacy, and truth indeed is the syllable Om.
m.5.12.27: By truth the wind blows, by truth the sun gives heat, by truth fire burns, by truth heaven endures.
m.5.12.28: The preservation of all the Vedas and bathing in all the holy places — one who conducts himself by truth in the world obtains all this without doubt.
m.5.12.29: A thousand aśvamedhas and truth were weighed in the balance — even with hundreds of thousands of rites, truth alone outweighs.
m.5.12.30: By truth gods, ancestors, humans, serpents and rākṣasas are pleased; through truth all the worlds with moving and unmoving beings are pleased.
m.5.12.31: They call truth the supreme dharma, they call truth the supreme state, they call truth the supreme Brahman; therefore one should always speak the truth.
m.5.12.32: Sages devoted to truth, having performed very arduous austerity, devoted to the dharma of truth, became perfected, and thereupon went to heaven.
m.5.12.33: They went in aerial chariots filled with hosts of apsarases, with attendants all around. One should always speak the truth; nothing is higher than truth.
m.5.12.34: One should bathe, with a concentrated mind, in the fathomless, vast, perfected holy ford of truth, the pure lake; that place is regarded as supreme.
m.5.12.35: Those people who do not speak falsehood, whether for their own sake, for another's, or even for a son's sake — those men go to heaven.
m.5.12.36: The Vedas, sacrifices and mantras always abide in brāhmaṇas, but they do not shine in the untruthful; therefore one should practise truth.
m.5.12.37: Vyāsa said: O one rich in austerity, tell me again, in particular, the fruit of austerity for all the classes and for brāhmaṇas.
m.5.12.38: Sanatkumāra said: I shall expound the chapter on austerity, which accomplishes all desires and aims, and which is very hard for the twice-born to practise; hear it as I relate it.
m.5.12.39: Austerity is declared to be supreme; by austerity the fruit is attained. Those who are ever devoted to austerity rejoice together with the gods.
m.5.12.40: By austerity heaven is attained, by austerity fame is attained, by austerity one's desire is attained; austerity is the means to every aim.
m.5.12.41: By austerity one attains liberation; by austerity one obtains what is great: a wealth of knowledge and realised wisdom, good fortune, and beauty as well.
m.5.12.42: A man obtains things of many kinds through austerity; through austerity he obtains everything, whatever he desires in his mind.
m.5.12.43: Those who have not performed austerity never go to the world of Brahmā; Śaṅkara, the Supreme Lord, is not attainable by those who have not performed austerity.
m.5.12.44: Whatever purpose a person resolves upon when he performs austerity, all that the man attains, both in the next world and here.
m.5.12.45: The drinker of liquor, the adulterer with another's wife, the slayer of a brāhmaṇa, the violator of the teacher's bed — through austerity such a one crosses over everything and is freed on every side.
m.5.12.46: Even Sthāṇu, the lord of all, and the eternal Viṣṇu, Brahmā, Agni, Śakra, and others too are endowed with austerity.
m.5.12.47: Eighty-eight thousand sages of upward-drawn seed (celibates) rejoice in heaven through austerity, united with the gods.
m.5.12.48: Through austerity sovereignty is obtained; and that Śakra, lord of the gods, the slayer of Vṛtra, protected everything day after day through austerity.
m.5.12.49: The two gods Sun and Moon, devoted to the welfare of all worlds, shine through austerity alone; so also the stars and the planets.
m.5.12.50: Indeed there is no happiness in the world that comes without austerity; all happiness comes through austerity alone — so the knowers of the Veda know.
m.5.12.51: Knowledge, realised wisdom, health, and likewise beauty and good fortune — and happiness at all times — are obtained through austerity.
m.5.12.52: By austerity the universe is created — Brahmā creates the universe without toil; Viṣṇu protects it, Hara too devours it, and Śeṣa bears the entire earth.
m.5.12.53: O great sage, Viśvāmitra, son of Gādhi, a kṣatriya, then became a brāhmaṇa through austerity alone; this is renowned in the three worlds.
m.5.12.54: Thus, O greatly wise one, the supreme greatness of austerity has been told to you; now hear the greatness of Vedic study, which is superior to and higher than austerity.
m.5.12.iti: Thus ends the twelfth adhyāya, named The description of the greatness of austerity, in the fifth saṃhitā, the Umā-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.5.13.1: Sanatkumāra said: Whoever practises austerity in the forest, living on wild roots and fruits, and whoever studies even a single Ṛc verse — the fruit of the latter would be equal to that, O sage.
m.5.13.2: Whatever merit the best of the twice-born obtains from studying the Veda, he enjoys double that fruit from teaching it.
m.5.13.3: Just as the world becomes lightless without moon and sun, so is it without the Purāṇa; therefore, O sage, it should always be studied.
m.5.13.4: He who, by means of the scripture, awakens the world that is constantly tormented in hell through ignorance — therefore the one versed in the Purāṇa is worthy of honour.
m.5.13.5: Among all worthy recipients, the knower of the Purāṇa is the best; because he protects (trāyate) from falling (patana), he is therefore called a pātra (worthy recipient).
m.5.13.6: One should never regard a knower of the Purāṇa as a mere mortal; the knower of the Purāṇa is all-knowing — he is Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Hara, the guru.
m.5.13.7: Wealth, grain, gold and various garments should be given to the knower of the Purāṇa, for welfare here and hereafter.
m.5.13.8: The good man who with great affection gives auspicious things to the knower of the Purāṇa, a worthy recipient, attains the supreme state.
m.5.13.9: Hear the meritorious fruit of one who gives to a worthy recipient land, a cow, chariots, and fine elephants and horses.
m.5.13.10: That man obtains imperishable fulfilment of all desires, both in this birth and hereafter, and also the fruit of the Aśvamedha sacrifice.
m.5.13.11: He who gives him land that is ploughed, fruitful and good, indeed delivers ten generations of his line before and ten after.
m.5.13.12: Having enjoyed all desires here, at the end, possessing a divine body, he goes to Śivaloka in a divine aerial car.
m.5.13.13: The gods are not so pleased by sacrifices, nor by sprinklings, offerings or flower-worship, as by the reading of the sacred book.
m.5.13.14: Whoever causes a religious book to be read in a temple of Śambhu, or of Viṣṇu, the Sun, or any god — hear the fruit of that too.
m.5.13.15: That man obtains the fruit of the Rājasūya and Aśvamedha sacrifices, and swiftly piercing through the world of the Sun, he goes to Brahmaloka.
m.5.13.16: Having stayed there for hundreds of kalpas, he becomes a king on earth and enjoys pleasures free of hindrance; there is no need for doubt about this.
m.5.13.17: Whatever fruit is declared for a thousand Aśvamedhas, that fruit he obtains who performs japa before the deity.
m.5.13.18: Apart from the Itihāsa and Purāṇa recited in the auspicious temple of Śambhu, nothing else is so pleasing to Śambhu and likewise to the other gods.
m.5.13.19: Therefore the reading of the book should be done with every effort; likewise, hearing it with love grants the fruit of all desires.
m.5.13.20: By hearing the Purāṇa of Śambhu a man becomes sinless; having enjoyed abundant pleasures, he would attain Śivaloka.
m.5.13.21: Whatever merit comes from the Rājasūya and from a hundred Agniṣṭomas, that merit one obtains merely by hearing the story of Śambhu.
m.5.13.22: The fruit of bathing in all sacred waters and of giving a crore of cows — that fruit one obtains by hearing the story of Śambhu, O sage.
m.5.13.23: Those who always listen to the story of Śambhu, which purifies the worlds, should not be regarded as humans; they are Rudras indeed, without doubt.
m.5.13.24: The sages know the very dust of the lotus-feet of the good who listen to Śiva's noble glory and who proclaim it to be sacred places (tīrthas).
m.5.13.25: Embodied beings who long to reach the state of the highest good should always listen with devotion to the Purāṇic story of Śiva.
m.5.13.26: If one is unable to hear the Purāṇic story constantly, then, self-restrained, he should hear it daily, even for a short while (a muhūrta).
m.5.13.27: If a man is unable to hear it daily, O sage, he should hear the story of Śaṅkara in the holy months and other sacred times.
m.5.13.28: O lord of sages, a man who listens to the story of Śiva crosses over saṃsāra, having burnt the great forest of karma.
m.5.13.29: Men who with devotion listen to the story of Śiva for a muhūrta, or half of that, or even a moment, will meet no evil fate.
m.5.13.30: Whatever merit there is in all gifts or in all sacrifices, O sage, that fruit becomes steadfast through hearing the Purāṇa of Śambhu.
m.5.13.31: Especially in the Kali age, O Vyāsa, no higher dharma for men, devoted to meditation on liberation, is taught than hearing the Purāṇa.
m.5.13.32: Hearing the Purāṇa of Śambhu and likewise chanting his name are, for men, the delightful fruit of the wish-fulfilling tree, without doubt.
m.5.13.33: In the Kali age, for the welfare of dull-witted men whose minds have abandoned dharma and right conduct, Śambhu created the nectar-essence called the Purāṇa.
m.5.13.34: A man who drinks nectar becomes free from age and death alone; but by drinking the nectar of Śambhu's story, his whole family becomes free from age and death.
m.5.13.35: The state that belongs to the virtuous, to sacrificers and to ascetics — that state, dear one, is quickly attained indeed by hearing the Purāṇa.
m.5.13.36: When the attainment of knowledge does not come, the treatises on yoga should be studied with effort, and the Purāṇic scripture should indeed be heard.
m.5.13.37: Through hearing the Purāṇa, sin constantly diminishes and dharma grows; the man of knowledge does not fall into saṃsāra.
m.5.13.38: Therefore the Purāṇas should be heard with effort, for gaining dharma, wealth and desire, and likewise for attaining the path to liberation.
m.5.13.39: Whatever fruit comes from sacrifices, gifts, austerities and from resorting to sacred places — that fruit a man obtains by hearing the Purāṇa.
m.5.13.40: If the Purāṇas, which are the eyes for seeing the path of dharma, did not exist, then who here — even one keeping vows — would abide by or know the account of the world beyond?
m.5.13.41: Whoever, endowed with devotion, listens to or reads even one among the twenty-six Purāṇas is liberated; there is no doubt about this.
m.5.13.42: No other path bestowing happiness is seen; the path of the Purāṇas is indeed always the best. Without scripture all this does not shine, like the worlds of living beings deprived of the sun.
m.5.13.iti: Thus ends the thirteenth adhyāya, named The description of the greatness of the Purāṇa, in the fifth saṃhitā, the Umā-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.5.14.1: Sanatkumāra said: The formidable gifts and the great gifts are praised. They should always be given to worthy recipients, and they deliver one's own self, the donor.
m.5.14.2: O best of the twice-born, the gift of gold, the gift of a cow and the gift of land: those who receive these purifying gifts deliver both themselves and him the giver.
m.5.14.3: The gift of gold, the gift of a cow, and the gift of land: having made these excellent gifts, one is freed from sins.
m.5.14.4: Gifts of equal worth are praised: cows, land and Sarasvatī knowledge. Two are praised as equal in power, but Sarasvatī is superior.
m.5.14.5: Oxen, cows, an umbrella, clothing, a pair of sandals, as well as drink and food, should always be given to those who ask.
m.5.14.6: Whatever wealth, designated by a formal resolve, is given to brahmins and to supplicants in distress—by that one becomes noble-minded.
m.5.14.7: Gold, sesame, elephants, a maiden, a female servant, a house, a chariot, gems, and tawny cows: these indeed are the ten great gifts.
m.5.14.8: A brahmin who knows true knowledge, on accepting all these, at once delivers the generous donors and himself as well; there is no doubt.
m.5.14.9: Men who give gold with a pure mind—the deities bestow blessings upon such a one from all sides; so I have heard.
m.5.14.10: Agni indeed is all the deities, and gold is Agni (the fire). Therefore, by giving gold, all the deities are in effect given.
m.5.14.11: The gift of land is supremely excellent, bestowing the fruit of all desires—especially the gift of a golden earth, which was performed by Pṛthu of old.
m.5.14.12: Those who witness the earth being given along with gold are freed from all sins and go to the supreme state.
m.5.14.13: Now I shall describe another gift, the best of all, O sage, by which people do not see Yama's wilderness, which brings much suffering.
m.5.14.14: With a pure mind one should perform the wilderness gift according to rule, with wealth earned justly, free from miserliness with money.
m.5.14.15: Having made a cow out of a prastha of sesame, endowed with all good qualities, and a calf for the cow of gold, very splendid, bearing all auspicious marks,
m.5.14.16: and having made an eight-petalled lotus with auspicious unbroken rice-grains smeared with saffron, one should worship there all the gods beginning with Rudra with deep devotion.
m.5.14.17: Having thus worshipped, one should give that cow, with gems and gold and adorned with all ornaments, to a brahmin according to one's means.
m.5.14.18: Then one should eat only at night and give lamps in abundance. This should be carefully performed on the full-moon day of Kārttika.
m.5.14.19: Whoever does this properly, according to the rite and to his means, does not see the dreadful fear of Yama's road, nor hell.
m.5.14.20: Even having committed sins without number, he, with his kinsmen and friends, sports in heaven, O Vyāsa, for as long as fourteen Indras reign.
m.5.14.21: The gift of a cow made according to rule is regarded here as the best of all; O Vyāsa, no higher gift equal to it has been declared.
m.5.14.22: Whoever gives a tawny cow with her calf, with gold-tipped horns, with a bronze milking vessel, with silver hooves, marked with all auspicious signs—
m.5.14.23: that cow, through those very qualities, becomes a wish-yielding cow and comes to that man, the giver, O Vyāsa, in the next world and in this life.
m.5.14.24: Whatever is most desired in the world and whatever is dear in one's home—that should be given to a virtuous person by one who wishes that very thing to be imperishable.
m.5.14.25: The gift of the Tulāpuruṣa (one's own weight on the balance) is indeed the highest gift among gifts. If one desires one's own welfare, one should mount the balance.
m.5.14.26: By performing it one is freed from sins arising from killing and binding others. The balance-gift is of great merit and destroys all sins.
m.5.14.27: Whoever, having committed sins without number, performs the balance-gift is freed from all sins and goes to heaven without doubt.
m.5.14.28: Whatever sin was committed by day or at night, at the two twilights, at midday or at the end of night, in the three times, by body, mind and speech—the Tulāpuruṣa indeed removes it.
m.5.14.29: Whatever sin was committed by me as a child, as an old man, as a youth, knowingly, or even while devoted to knowledge—may the Tulāpuruṣa, the foe of Smara (Śiva), swiftly take away all that sin of mine.
m.5.14.30: The wealth bestowed by me today on a worthy recipient, full in measure, placed on the balance—together with it may whatever remaining merit of mine, done or not done, come to me.
m.5.14.31: Sanatkumāra said: Having uttered this, one, ever well-disposed, should give it to brahmins. It should not be given to a single one; otherwise there would be no deliverance from it.
m.5.14.32: Whoever, O Vyāsa, gives the excellent Tulāpuruṣa in this way, having destroyed his sin, would abide in a divine state for as long as fourteen Indras reign.
m.5.14.iti: Thus ends the fourteenth adhyāya, named The description of gifts in general, in the fifth saṃhitā, the Umā-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.5.15.1: Vyāsa said: Tell me, for the welfare of human beings, that one gift which, when given alone, yields the fruit of all gifts.
m.5.15.2: Sanatkumāra said: Listen: from even a single gift given at the proper time, people obtain the fruit of all gifts. I shall tell you that.
m.5.15.3: The highest of all gifts is the gift of the Brahmāṇḍa (cosmic egg); it should be given by people who desire liberation, for crossing over saṃsāra.
m.5.15.4: Whatever fruit a man obtains when the whole Brahmāṇḍa is given, he obtains from that single gift; he becomes lord of the seven worlds.
m.5.15.5: As long as the moon and sun remain in the sky, or as long as the earth stands firm, so long does that man, the giver of the Brahmāṇḍa, together with his kinsmen, sport in the abode of the heaven-dwellers, in all the regions that follow his wishes; afterwards he goes, for joy, to the abode of Mādhava, which is very hard to attain even for the gods.
m.5.15.6: Vyāsa said: O Lord, tell me of the Brahmāṇḍa: of what measure it is, of what nature, on what it rests and how it came to be, so that I may have clear understanding.
m.5.15.7: Sanatkumāra said: O sage, listen; I shall declare in brief the height and extent of the Brahmāṇḍa; having heard it, one is freed from sin.
m.5.15.8: That which is the unmanifest cause, and also manifest, auspicious (Śiva) and free from ill — from that, having become twofold in the course of time, Brahmā is born.
m.5.15.9: Brahmā creates the Brahmāṇḍa consisting of fourteen worlds. I shall describe it in order, dear one, in brief; listen attentively.
m.5.15.10: There are seven Pātālas, and likewise seven worlds above; the height of that universe, which stands in the midst of the waters, is twofold.
m.5.15.11: Its support is the serpent, and he is declared to be Viṣṇu; on account of Brahmā's words he bears all this.
m.5.15.12: Neither gods nor dānavas are able to recount the virtues of this Śeṣa, who is called Ananta by the Siddhas and is worshipped by hosts of divine sages.
m.5.15.13: Possessing a thousand heads, he illumines all the directions with the thousand jewels of his hoods, adorned with spotless svastika marks.
m.5.15.14: His eyes rolling with intoxication, he shines like a white mountain with fire; garlanded and crowned, he always wears a single earring.
m.5.15.15: Clad in blue, overflowing with intoxication, he is like a white mountain adorned by the stream of the celestial Gaṅgā with its clouds — like a second Kailāsa mountain.
m.5.15.16: The tip of his hand resting on a plough, holding an excellent pestle, he is worshipped reverently by golden-hued serpent maidens.
m.5.15.17: He is Rudra in the form of Saṅkarṣaṇa, blazing with flames of poison-fire; at the end of the kalpa, flames of fire issue repeatedly from his mouths and, having burnt the three worlds, become quiet — so we have heard.
m.5.15.18: That Śeṣa, lord of beings, worshipped for his countless virtues, dwells at the root of Pātāla, bearing the circle of the earth on his back.
m.5.15.19: The power of his might cannot be described, nor his true form even be known, even by the eager gods.
m.5.15.20: Who can tell the might of him on whom this entire earth rests like a garland of flowers, reddened by the rays of his hood-jewels?
m.5.15.21: When Ananta yawns, his eyes rolling with intoxication, then this earth with its mountains, oceans and forests trembles.
m.5.15.22: Each Pātāla, O best of sages, is ten thousand yojanas in extent: Atala, Vitala, Sutala and Rasātala,
m.5.15.23: Tala, Talātala, and the foremost, Pātāla, held to be the seventh. These seven worlds below the earth should be known by the wise.
m.5.15.24: Their height is double; all of them have grounds of jewels; the palaces are jewelled and the grounds are made of gold.
m.5.15.25: In them dwell Dānavas and Daityas, likewise the races of Nāgas, great serpents, and Rākṣasas born of Daityas.
m.5.15.26: Nārada, having come from them to heaven, declared in the midst of the heavenly assembly: The Pātālas are far more delightful than the heaven-world.
m.5.15.27: Where there are ornaments of many kinds and radiant jewels, bright and gladdening — what can equal that Pātāla?
m.5.15.28: Who, even if liberated, would not feel delight in Pātāla, adorned here and there with Daitya and Dānava maidens?
m.5.15.29: Where there are no rays of the sun by day nor of the moon by night, where there is neither cold nor heat — here there is only the radiance of jewels.
m.5.15.30: Where foods to be chewed and eaten, rice and drinks are enjoyed abundantly by the joyful, and time, though passing, is not noticed, O best of sages.
m.5.15.31: Where there is the call of the male cuckoo, lotuses and lotus-ponds, rivers, delightful lakes and charming garments,
m.5.15.32: very bright ornaments and fragrant unguents, the sounds of lutes, flutes and drums, and songs, O brāhmaṇa.
m.5.15.33: And in Pātāla these pleasures are enjoyed by Daityas and serpents; they are attained through austerity by Dānavas, Siddhas and humans.
m.5.15.iti: Thus ends the fifteenth adhyāya, named The description of the Pātāla worlds, in the account of the universe, in the fifth saṃhitā, the Umā-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.5.16.1: Sanatkumāra said: And hear from me, O best of eminent sages, about those hells situated above their heads, where sinners are cooked.
m.5.16.2: Raurava, Śūkara, Rodha, Tāla, Vivasana, likewise Mahājvāla, Taptakumbha, Lavaṇa and also Vilohita;
m.5.16.3: Vaitaraṇī, Pūyavahā, Kṛmiśa, Kṛmibhojana, the dreadful Asipatravana, and the terrible Lālābhakṣa;
m.5.16.4: Likewise Pūyavaha, Prāya, Vahnijvāla, Adhaśśiras, Sandaṃśa, Kālasūtra, Tamas, Avīci and Rodhana;
m.5.16.5: Then Śvabhojana, Ruṣṭa, Mahāraurava and Śālmalī — these and many others are the hells there, which bring suffering.
m.5.16.6: In them are cooked those men who delight in sinful deeds. I shall tell of them in order, O Vyāsa; listen attentively.
m.5.16.7: He who gives false testimony, except for the sake of brahmins, gods and cows, and he who always speaks untruth — that man goes to Raurava.
m.5.16.8: The killer of an embryo, the stealer of gold, the confiner of cows, the betrayer of trust, the drinker of liquor, the slayer of a brahmin, the stealer of others' property —
m.5.16.9: and whoever associates with them — he, when dead, goes to hell, O Vyāsa, as also for killing a guru. Into Taptakumbha goes the seller of a sister, mother, cow or daughter,
m.5.16.10: and the seller of a chaste woman. The usurer and the seller of hair are cooked in Taptaloha, as is he who abandons a devotee.
m.5.16.11: The vilest of men who despises his elders and eats selfishly afterwards, the defiler of the gods, and he who sells images of the gods,
m.5.16.12: and he who goes to forbidden women — at the end goes to Saptabala, O twice-born. The thief, the cow-killer, the outcast, and likewise the violator of moral bounds,
m.5.16.13: the hater of gods, brahmins and ancestors, and he who spoils gems — he goes to Kṛmibhakṣa; the performer of evil sacrifices eats worms.
m.5.16.14: The vilest man who eats before offering to the ancestors, gods and deities — that fool goes to Lālābhakṣa, as does the man who falsifies the scriptures.
m.5.16.15: He who is attended by an outcaste, the twice-born who accepts from the wicked, the one who sacrifices for those unfit to sacrifice, and likewise the eater of forbidden food —
m.5.16.16: these fall into Rudhiraugha, as do those who sell Soma. The destroyer of honey -hives and the destroyer of villages goes to the cruel river Vaitaraṇī.
m.5.16.17: Those intoxicated by fresh youth and those who break moral bounds go to Kṛmya, as do the impure and those who live off unchaste women.
m.5.16.18: He who cuts trees needlessly goes to Asipatravana. Keepers of rams and hunters of deer fall into Vahnijvāla.
m.5.16.19: The brahmin, kṣatriya or vaiśya whose conduct is corrupt goes at the end to that very place, O twice-born, as does he who gives fire to Śvapākas.
m.5.16.20: Those who break vows and those who have fallen from their own āśrama fall into the exceedingly dreadful torment of Sandaṃśa.
m.5.16.21: Celibate students who spill semen in dreams, and those by whom sons are not taught, fall into Śvabhojana.
m.5.16.22: These and other hells, by hundreds and thousands, exist, in which evildoers, subjected to torments, are cooked.
m.5.16.23: Likewise there are these sins and others by thousands, whose fruits are endured by men dwelling in the various hells.
m.5.16.24: Men who perform acts contrary to the duties of varṇa and āśrama, by deed, mind or speech, fall into hell.
m.5.16.25: The denizens of hell are seen by the deities in heaven as having their heads downward; the denizens of hell see all the gods below them, faces turned downward.
m.5.16.26: Immobile beings, worms, water-born creatures, birds, beasts, men, the righteous, the gods, and likewise those seeking liberation — each more numerous than the next in due order.
m.5.16.27: As many creatures as are in heaven, so many are the dwellers in hell. The sinner who turns away from expiation goes to hell.
m.5.16.28: Grave expiations for grave sins and light ones for light sins — so declared Svāyambhuva Manu, O Kāleya.
m.5.16.29: Of all those deeds that have been declared as expiations for all of them, the supreme and complete expiation is the constant remembrance of Hara.
m.5.16.30: For the man in whom remorse arises after a sin is committed, the one supreme expiation is the remembrance of Śiva.
m.5.16.31: Remembering Śiva at midday and other times — at dawn, at night and at twilight — a man attains the Māheśvara state and becomes one whose sins are destroyed.
m.5.16.32: Merely by remembering Śiva, that Śambhu, lord of Umā, one attains liberation or heaven, the complete destruction of all afflictions.
m.5.16.33: O chief of brahmins, for him no obstacle from sin — nor hindrance to japa, homa, worship and the like — arises anywhere in the three worlds, O best of sages.
m.5.16.34: He whose mind is fixed on Maheśvara during japa, homa, worship and the like — whatever merit there is, that is accomplished by him, with its fruit such as the lordship of the gods.
m.5.16.35: The man who remembers Śiva with devotion day and night does not go to hell, O sage, for he has all his sins destroyed.
m.5.16.36: Sin and merit are what are called hell and heaven, O best of the twice-born; of these two, one leads to suffering and the other to happiness and prosperity.
m.5.16.37: That very thing, having been a source of delight, becomes again a source of suffering. Therefore nothing is by nature suffering, nor is anything by nature happiness.
m.5.16.38: This is a transformation of the mind, marked by happiness and suffering. Knowledge alone is the supreme Brahman; knowledge leads to the truth.
m.5.16.39: This whole universe, with its moving and unmoving beings, is of the nature of knowledge. Nothing exists beyond supreme knowledge, O sage.
m.5.16.40: Thus I have described this entire circle of hells. Hereafter I shall now describe the sphere of the earth.
m.5.16.iti: Thus ends the sixteenth adhyāya, named The description of deliverance from hell, in the description of the universe, in the fifth saṃhitā, the Umā-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.5.17.1: Sanatkumāra said: O son of Parāśara, listen as I describe, very briefly and properly, the sphere of the earth together with its seven continents and the rest.
m.5.17.2: Jambū, Plakṣa, Śālmali, Kuśa, Krauñca, Śāka, and Puṣkara as the seventh — all are surrounded by seven oceans.
m.5.17.3: The oceans are of salt water and sugarcane juice, ghee, curd, milk and fresh water. Jambūdvīpa stands in the middle of all these.
m.5.17.4: In its middle too, O Kāleya, is Meru, the golden mountain. It has entered sixteen thousand yojanas below the ground, and its height
