m.5.17.5: is eighty-four thousand by those measures; at the summit it is extended thirty-two thousand. This is the mountain standing on the surface of the earth; its extent all around
m.5.17.6: at the base is sixteen thousand; it stands in the shape of the pericarp of a lotus. Himavān, Hemakūṭa and Niṣadha lie to its south.
m.5.17.7: Nīla, Śveta and Śṛṅgī are the boundary mountains (varṣa-parvata) in the north. These are of ten thousand yojanas, full of jewels, and of reddish lustre.
m.5.17.8: They are a thousand yojanas high and just as wide. Bhārata is known as the first region (varṣa), and after it Kimpuruṣa.
m.5.17.9: After that is another, Harivarṣa — these lie to the south of Meru, O sage. Ramyaka is on the northern side, and in its portion is Hiraṇmaya.
m.5.17.10: And in the north are the Kurus, just as Bhārata is in the south. Each of these is nine thousand yojanas, O best of sages.
m.5.17.11: Ilāvṛta is in the middle of them, and in its middle Meru rises high. Ilāvṛta extends there nine thousand yojanas in the four directions around Meru,
m.5.17.12: O best of seers. And here are four mountains, made as buttresses (viṣkambha) of Meru, joined to it and rising up again.
m.5.17.13: In the east is the one named Mandara, in the south Gandhamādana; Vipula stands in the western part and Supārśva in the north.
m.5.17.14: The Kadamba, the Jambū tree, the Pippala and the Vaṭa — trees eleven hundred yojanas in extent — are the banners of these mountains.
m.5.17.15: Listen, O great sage, to the reason for the name Jambūdvīpa. Great trees shine there; I shall tell you their nature.
m.5.17.16: The fruits of that Jambū tree, as large as great elephants, fall on the ridge of the mountain and burst open on every side.
m.5.17.17: From their juice there flows there a river famed as the Jambū river; it runs all around there and is drunk by those who dwell there.
m.5.17.18: No sweat, no foul odour, no old age, no seizure of the senses — none of that arises for the people who live on its bank.
m.5.17.19: And its juice, reaching the clay of the bank dried by pleasant winds, becomes the gold called Jāmbūnada, the ornament of the Siddhas.
m.5.17.20: Bhadrāśva lies to the east of Meru and Ketumāla to the west — these are two regions, O best of sages; between them is Ilāvṛta.
m.5.17.21: In the east is the forest Caitraratha, in the south Gandhamādana, likewise Vibhrāja in the west, and in the north Nandana is renowned.
m.5.17.22: Aruṇoda, Mahābhadra, Śītoda and Mānasa are renowned — these four lakes are in every way to be enjoyed by the gods.
m.5.17.23: Śītāñjana, Kuruṅga, Kurara and Mālyavān — headed by these, one after another, are the filament-mountains (kesarācala) to the east of Meru.
m.5.17.24: Trikūṭa, Śiśira, Pataṅga, Rucaka, Niṣadha, Kapila and others are the filament-mountains in the south.
m.5.17.25: Sinīvāsa, Kusumbha, Kapila, Nārada and the mountains beginning with Nāga are the filament-mountains in the west.
m.5.17.26: Śaṅkhacūḍa, then Ṛṣabha, the mountain named Haṃsa, and likewise Kālañjara and others are the filament-mountains in the north.
m.5.17.27: On top of Meru, in the middle, is the golden city of Brahmā (Vidhi), fourteen thousand yojanas in measure.
m.5.17.28: Around it, in due order, eight cities of the eight guardians of the worlds are arranged, each according to its direction and its form.
m.5.17.29: And into that city of Brahmā falls the river Gaṅgā, issuing from the foot of Viṣṇu, after flooding the orb of the moon.
m.5.17.30: Having fallen there, she became fourfold in the directions, in order: Sītā, Alakanandā, Cakṣu and Bhadrā.
m.5.17.31: Sītā goes to the east of the mountain, Nandā to the south, Cakṣu to the west, and Bhadrā to the north.
m.5.17.32: Passing over all the mountains, that Gaṅgā who travels the three paths, having become purified, went in the four directions to the great ocean.
m.5.17.33: Nīla and Niṣadha, and Mālyavān and Gandhamādana — in the midst of these stands Meru, shaped like the pericarp of a lotus.
m.5.17.34: Bhārata, Ketumāla, Bhadrāśva and the Kurus are the petals of the world-lotus; the boundary mountains are their limits.
m.5.17.35: Jaṭhara and Devakūṭa extend north–south in length; Gandhamādana and Kailāsa run east and west.
m.5.17.36: East and west of Meru stand Niṣadha and the Nīla mountain, stretching south and north, situated within the pericarp.
m.5.17.37: Jaṭhara and the others stand around Meru, set in pairs; these, Śveta and the rest, are the very lovely filament-mountains.
m.5.17.38: Between the mountains are valleys frequented by Siddhas and Cāraṇas, and in them are very delightful groves and cities.
m.5.17.39: These belong to all the gods, Yakṣas, Gandharvas and Rākṣasas; gods and Daityas sport day and night in those mountainous regions.
m.5.17.40: These are the abodes of the righteous, proclaimed as earthly heavens; doers of sin never go to them, nor do they ever see them.
m.5.17.41: O great sage, in the eight regions (varṣas) beginning with Kimpuruṣa there is no sorrow, no misfortune, no anxiety, nor hunger, fear and the like.
m.5.17.42: The people are healthy, free from dread, devoid of all suffering, and of stable lifespan, living ten or twelve thousand years.
m.5.17.43: And as for the ages Kṛta, Tretā and the rest, there is no such reckoning in those places; the waters everywhere are from the earth, and the god of rain does not rain upon them.
m.5.17.44: In these seven regions there are rivers, beautiful and with golden sands, by the hundreds, and small ones too; in them virtuous people would sport.
m.5.17.iti: Thus ends the seventeenth adhyāya, named The description of the varṣas of Jambūdvīpa, in the account of the universe, in the fifth saṃhitā, the Umā-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.5.18.1: Sanatkumāra said: I shall describe the region (varṣa) Bhārata, which lies south of the Himālaya and north of the ocean, where the progeny of Bharata dwell.
m.5.18.2: Its extent, O great sage, is nine thousand yojanas. The wise regard it as the land of action for attaining heaven and final liberation.
m.5.18.3: From here men attain heaven and also hell. I now tell you the nine divisions of the region Bhārata.
m.5.18.4: Indradyumna, Kaseru, Tāmravarṇa, Gabhastimān, Nāgadvīpa, Saumya, Gandharva, and then Vāruṇa;
m.5.18.5: and this is the ninth of them, an island enclosed by the ocean. This island measures a thousand yojanas from south to north.
m.5.18.6: In its east live the Kirātas, in the south the Yavanas are settled, and likewise others are to be known in the west, while in the north are ascetics.
m.5.18.7: In the middle are Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas and Śūdras in large numbers, established in their livelihoods of sacrifice, warfare, trade and service.
m.5.18.8: Mahendra, Malaya, Sahya, Sudāmā, the Ṛkṣa mountain, Vindhya and Pāriyātra—these are the seven principal (kula) mountains here.
m.5.18.9: The rivers Vedasmṛti, Purāṇā and others arise from Pāriyātra, O sage; they are known to remove all sins by being seen and even by being touched.
m.5.18.10: Narmadā, Surasā and others—seven chief ones and thousands of others—are great rivers rising from the Vindhya, auspicious and removing all sins.
m.5.18.11: The rivers headed by Godāvarī, Bhīmarathī and Tāpī, issuing from the Ṛkṣa mountain, at once dispel sin and fear.
m.5.18.12: Likewise the rivers Kṛṣṇā, Veṇī and others rise from the foot of Sahya; those headed by Kṛtamālā and Tāmraparṇī rise from Malaya.
m.5.18.13: Triyāmā, Ṛṣikulyā and others are said to rise from Mahendra; Ṛṣikulyā, Kumārī and others arise from the foot of Śuktimat.
m.5.18.14: Various peoples dwell in those regions; they drink the water of these rivers and of various lakes.
m.5.18.15: In the region Bhārata, O great sage, there are the four ages, Kṛta and the rest; they do not prevail in the other continents.
m.5.18.16: Here gifts are given, and here virtuous sacrificers perform rites; ascetics practise austerity with devotion for the sake of the next world.
m.5.18.17: For this is the land of action in Jambūdvīpa, O great sage; and even here Bhārata is the best, whereas the other lands are lands of enjoyment.
m.5.18.18: Only rarely, O best of sages, does a mortal obtain human birth here, after thousands of births, through accumulations of merit.
m.5.18.19: The gods indeed sing songs: Blessed are they who live in the land of Bhārata, which is the path to the abode of heaven and liberation; even we gods become men there again.
m.5.18.20: Having surrendered all the fruits born of action unto Śambhu, whose form is the supreme Self, I shall attain oneness with his very being.
m.5.18.21: Blessed indeed are those men who will attain this, endowed with happiness and engaged in right action; those whose birth is in Bhārata gain both heaven and liberation.
m.5.18.22: I have described Jambūdvīpa, a hundred thousand yojanas in extent, perfectly circular, and well encircled by the salt ocean.
m.5.18.23: Encircling the salt ocean, which measures a hundred thousand yojanas, lies Plakṣadvīpa, said to be twice that in size, O Brahmin.
m.5.18.24: Gomanta, Candra, Nārada, Dardura, Somaka, the mountain Sumanas, and Vaibhrāja the excellent are its mountains.
m.5.18.25: On these lovely boundary mountains people live together constantly, and gods and Gandharvas always dwell in these regions.
m.5.18.26: There the people have no mental afflictions or diseases anywhere; men there live for ten thousand years.
m.5.18.27: Anutaptā, Śikhī, Pāpaghnī, Tridivā, Kṛpā, Amṛtā and Sukṛtā—these are the seven rivers here.
m.5.18.28: There are also thousands of small rivers and mountains there; the peoples, greatly delighted, drink from those rivers.
m.5.18.29: There too there is no succession of the ages; as in all the seven regions, time is always like the Tretā age, O great sage.
m.5.18.30: They are Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas and Śūdras, O best of sages. In its middle stands a very great tree, like the wish-fulfilling tree,
m.5.18.31: the Plakṣa; after its name the island is called Plakṣadvīpa, O best of the twice-born. There the Lord Śaṅkara, benefactor of the world, is worshipped,
m.5.18.32: as are Hari and Lord Brahmā, with yantras and Vedic mantras. Now hear from me, again in brief, about Śālmali.
m.5.18.33: There too are seven regions; hear their names from me: Śveta, Harita, Jīmūta, Rohita,
m.5.18.34: Vaikala, Mānasa, and Suprabha the seventh, O sage. Because of the Śālmala tree the island is called Śālmali.
m.5.18.35: It remains constantly surrounded by an ocean twice its size. The rivers mark out the regions; hear their names from me:
m.5.18.36: Śuklā, Raktā, Hiraṇyā, Candrā, Śubhrā, Vimocanā, and Nivṛtti the seventh of them—with holy, very cool waters.
m.5.18.37: Those seven regions are inhabited by the four classes, who ever worship the Lord Śambhu with various sacrifices.
m.5.18.38: In that most delightful land the gods are present. This island is surrounded by the ocean of wine (surā).
m.5.18.39: Beyond it on all sides lies Kuśadvīpa, twice as large. There dwell Daityas and Dānavas together with men,
m.5.18.40: and likewise gods, Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Kimpuruṣas and others; there too are the four classes, each devoted to its own duties.
m.5.18.41: And right there in Kuśadvīpa they worship Brahmā and Janārdana, and likewise Īśāna, the giver of the fruits of all desires.
m.5.18.42: Its mountains are Kuśeśaya, Hari, Dyutimān and likewise Puṣpavān, Maṇidruma, Hemaśaila, and the seventh, Mount Mandara.
m.5.18.43: And there are seven rivers; hear their names truly: Dhūtapāpā, Śivā, Pavitrā, and likewise Sammiti,
m.5.18.44: Vidyā, Dambhā, and another, Mahī; these remove all sins. There are others by the thousands, with pure waters and golden sands.
m.5.18.45: In Kuśadvīpa there is a clump of kuśa grass; the island is surrounded by the ocean of ghee. O fortunate one, let the next great one, Krauñcadvīpa, be heard.
m.5.18.46: It is surrounded by an ocean of whey (curd-cream), twice its size. O wise one, hear from me the names of its regional mountains.
m.5.18.47: Krauñca and Vāmana, the third Andhakāraka, Divāvṛti, Manas, Puṇḍarīka and Dundubhi.
m.5.18.48: On those regional mountains, all golden and delightful, the people dwell free from fear, together with friendly hosts of gods.
m.5.18.49: Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas and Śūdras are named there in due order. There are seven great rivers there, and others by the thousands:
m.5.18.50: Gaurī, Kumudvatī, Sandhyā, Rātri, Manojavā, Śānti and Puṇḍarīkā, whose pure water the people drink.
m.5.18.51: There the Lord is worshipped in the form of Yoga-Rudra. And the ocean of whey is in turn surrounded by Śākadvīpa,
m.5.18.52: which is twice its size. It has seven mountains; hear their names from me. In the east there is the Udaya mountain, and beyond it Jaladhāra,
m.5.18.53: and at the back (west) the Asta mountain, as well as Avikeśa and Kesarī. There stands the great Śāka tree, frequented by Siddhas and Gandharvas.
m.5.18.54: There are holy countries there, endowed with the four social classes, and here are very holy rivers that remove all sins and fears:
m.5.18.55: Sukumārī, Kumārī, Nalinī and Veṇukā, Ikṣu, Reṇukā, and likewise Gabhasti the seventh.
m.5.18.56: O great sage, there are thousands of other small rivers there, and likewise mountains by the hundreds and thousands.
m.5.18.57: There is no decline of dharma among them. Men, having come from heaven, roam the earth together in those regions.
m.5.18.58: In Śākadvīpa the Sun is always worshipped with love by the peoples, properly, through the prescribed rites, by those of controlled self.
m.5.18.59: That island too is surrounded on all sides by the ocean of milk, twice its size; and the milk ocean, O Vyāsa, is surrounded all round by the island called Puṣkara,
m.5.18.60: which is twice its size. There is the great regional mountain famed here as Mānasa, rising fifty thousand yojanas upward,
m.5.18.61: and as many in extent on all sides, ring-shaped, as though dividing the ring of Puṣkaradvīpa through the middle.
m.5.18.62: By that very mountain the island takes the form of ring-shaped regions. There men live for ten thousand years,
m.5.18.63: free from disease, without sorrow, devoid of passion and hatred. Adharma is not known among them, O sage, nor captor and slayer.
m.5.18.64: Truth and falsehood as opposites do not exist there; it is ever a peaceful dwelling. The people are alike in dress, of one form, golden in colour.
m.5.18.65: And this region, O Kāleya, is earthly yet comparable to heaven. Time there gives happiness to all and is free from old age and disease.
m.5.18.66: In Puṣkara, in its regions Dhātakīkhaṇḍa and Mahāvīta, O great sage, in Puṣkaradvīpa there is a banyan tree, the supreme abode of Brahmā.
m.5.18.67: In it dwells Brahmā, worshipped by gods and asuras. Puṣkara is encircled by the ocean of sweet water.
m.5.18.68: Thus the seven islands are surrounded by the seven oceans; and the islands and oceans are matched by successive ones, each twice as large.
m.5.18.69: Their rise and excess has been stated; in the oceans the waters always remain the same; they never become diminished.
m.5.18.70: Just as water in a pot, resting below, swells through contact with fire, O best of sages, so when the moon waxes the water surely rises upward.
m.5.18.71: At the rising and setting of the moon the waters swell and subside; hence they are less and more in the bright and dark fortnights.
m.5.18.72: The rise and fall of the waters of all the oceans are seen to be a hundred and ten measures; this has been told to you, O best of sages.
m.5.18.73: In Puṣkaradvīpa, O brāhmaṇa, all the people always take as their food the sweet substance (khaṇḍa) that presents itself there of its own accord.
m.5.18.74: Beyond the sweet-water ocean there is no settlement of beings; there is a golden land, twice as large, devoid of all creatures.
m.5.18.75: Beyond that is the mountain Lokāloka; that mountain is so many thousands of yojanas in height and ten thousand yojanas in breadth.
m.5.18.76: Beyond lies darkness, enclosed by the shell of the cosmic egg. This earth, O great sage, with its islands and mountains, is fifty crores of yojanas in extent.
m.5.18.77: Being the support of all, surpassing all beings in qualities, this Ilā (Earth), O Kāleya, is the nourisher of all the worlds.
m.5.18.iti: Thus ends the eighteenth adhyāya, named The description of the seven dvīpas, in the account of the universe, in the fifth saṃhitā, the Umā-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.5.19.1: Sanatkumāra said: As far as the rays of the sun and the moon illuminate, the earth is of that extent; it is called Bhūloka.
m.5.19.2: The orb of the sun is situated a hundred thousand yojanas from the earth; its measure is always reckoned in thousands of yojanas.
m.5.19.3: They likewise describe the measure of the moon of the world: the moon stands above the sun at a distance reckoned as a hundred thousand yojanas.
m.5.19.4: The entire sphere of the planets, together with the constellations, is situated above the moon, ten thousand yojanas higher all around.
m.5.19.5: Budha is above that, then Kāvya (Śukra); above him the sphere of Bhauma (Mars); above that Bṛhaspati, and above him Śanaiścara (Saturn).
m.5.19.6: The sphere of the Seven Sages is situated one hundred thousand yojanas beyond that; and a hundred thousand above the sages stands Dhruva.
m.5.19.7: That Dhruva is the pivot of the wheel of luminaries. The region above the earth and below Dhruva should be known as Bhūḥ, Bhuvaḥ and Svaḥ.
m.5.19.8: One crore of yojanas above Dhruva is Maharloka, where dwell those who live for a kalpa. These seven sons of Brahmā dwell there:
m.5.19.9: Sanaka, Sananda, the third Sanātana, Kapila, Āsuri, Voḍhu, and likewise Pañcaśikha.
m.5.19.10: Above that, Śukra is situated within two hundred thousand yojanas; two hundred thousand yojanas below him is said to be the son of Soma (Budha).
m.5.19.11: Two hundred thousand yojanas above him stands Bhauma, O sage; two hundred thousand yojanas above that stands Jīva, the Guru (Jupiter).
m.5.19.12: Two hundred thousand yojanas above Jīva is placed Sauri (Saturn). These are declared the seven planets, each stationed in its own zodiacal sign.
m.5.19.13: At eleven (Rudra) hundred-thousand yojanas above stand the Seven Sages; the position of Dhruva is declared to be at thirteen (Viśva) hundred-thousand yojanas.
m.5.19.14: Four times further above Janaloka, Tapas-loka is said to be, where the Vairāja gods dwell, free from burning.
m.5.19.15: Six times beyond Tapoloka is set Satyaloka; it is to be known as Brahmaloka, where those of stainless mind dwell,
m.5.19.16: devoted to truth and dharma, wise, and celibate — those who have gone there; and humans dwell in Bhūloka.
m.5.19.17: In Bhuvarloka dwell perfected sages of divine form; in Svargaloka the gods: the Ādityas, Maruts, Vasus, the two Aśvins,
m.5.19.18: the Viśvedevas, likewise the Rudras, Sādhyas, Nāgas, birds and others; then there are the nine planets and the sages free from sin.
m.5.19.19: These seven great worlds have been told to you, O Kāleya, and the seven Pātālas too, and the extent of the cosmic egg.
m.5.19.20: Like the fruit of the wood-apple tree, it is round above and likewise below; this is enclosed on all sides by the shell of the egg.
m.5.19.21: That is enveloped on all sides by water ten times its size, and also by fire, air, ether and darkness likewise,
m.5.19.22: and by Bhūtādi and by Mahat, each tenfold greater in succession; and enveloping Mahat is Pradhāna, beyond which stands Puruṣa.
m.5.19.23: Of that infinite Supreme Self there is no reckoning at all; hence he is known as Ananta, since there is no measure of him.
m.5.19.24: That supreme Prakṛti is the cause of all, O sage. Thousands of thousands and tens of thousands of eggs—
m.5.19.25: many such have come forth from that unmanifest source. As fire is in wood, oil in sesame, and ghee in milk,
m.5.19.26: so this Supreme Self, self-aware, pervades all. From the primal seed they are produced; then from them other egg-born beings,
m.5.19.27: from them sons, and likewise from them other seeds of others. From Mahat down to the specific elements, thus arise the gods and the rest.
m.5.19.28: Just as there is no diminution of a tree through a tree sprouting from its seed, and as fire is produced from the sun-stone by the sun,
m.5.19.29: so creation comes forth, yet Śiva does not desire anything in it. Through the union of Śiva and Śakti the gods and others come into being.
m.5.19.30: Likewise, by their own karma alone they attain growth. He who is Brahmā, Viṣṇu and the Rudras — he is extolled as Śiva.
m.5.19.31: He from whom all comes forth and into whom all will dissolve, the doer of all actions — he is extolled as Śiva.
m.5.19.32: Vyāsa said: O all-knowing Sanatkumāra, dispel my great doubt: are there worlds above the cosmic egg or not, O sage?
m.5.19.33: Sanatkumāra said: There are indeed worlds above the cosmic egg, O lord of sages. Listen to them in detail; having come here, I shall tell you.
m.5.19.34: Beyond Brahmā's world is the world renowned as Vaikuṇṭha; it shines with great splendour, and there Viṣṇu is established.
m.5.19.35: Above that is the most wondrous Kaumāra world, where the radiant general, the son of Śambhu, shines.
m.5.19.36: Beyond that shines the supremely divine world of Umā, where the one Śakti, Śivā, mother of the three gods, is resplendent.
m.5.19.37: She is Prakṛti, higher than the highest, consisting of rajas, sattva and tamas; yet the Goddess herself is beyond the guṇas, changeless, of the nature of Śiva.
m.5.19.38: Above that is to be known the eternal Śivaloka, imperishable, supremely divine, ever endowed with great beauty,
m.5.19.39: where the supreme Brahman, Śambhu Maheśvara, shines — father of the three gods, lord of all, beyond the three guṇas.
m.5.19.40: Above that there are no worlds; near it is Goloka, where dwell the mother-cows called Suśīlā, dear to Śiva.
m.5.19.41: Its guardian, named Kṛṣṇa, shines there by Śaṅkara's command, established by Śiva himself, who moves freely by his own will, together with his Śakti.
m.5.19.42: O Vyāsa, the world of Śiva is wondrous, without any support, enchanting, likewise indescribable, and resplendent with manifold things.
m.5.19.43: Śiva himself is its presiding lord, the crest-jewel of all gods, to be served by Viṣṇu, Brahmā and Hara, the Supreme Self, stainless.
m.5.19.44: Thus, dear son, the arrangement of the whole cosmic egg has been told to you, and the arrangement of the worlds above it. What else do you wish to hear?
m.5.19.iti: Thus ends the nineteenth adhyāya, named The description of the worlds, in the fifth saṃhitā, the Umā-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.5.20.1: Vyāsa said: O Sanatkumāra, all-knowing one, O best of the virtuous, tell me how that state is attained, having reached which men endowed with devotion to Śiva do not return.
m.5.20.2: Sanatkumāra said: O Vyāsa, son of Parāśara, listen with affection to the auspicious goal: the vow of the pure devotees, and likewise the pure austerity of ascetics.
m.5.20.3: Those of pure deeds, endowed with very pure austerity, who constantly worship Śiva — they are worthy of reverence in every way, day after day.
m.5.20.4: Those who have not practised austerity do not reach Śiva's world, free from affliction. Austerity alone, O great sage, is the true cause of Śiva's grace.
m.5.20.5: By austerity the hosts of gods rejoice manifestly in heaven, and so do the seers and sages; know my words here to be true.
m.5.20.6: Whatever is very hard to bear, hard to propitiate, very far off, hard to overcome — all that is achievable by austerity, for austerity itself is insurmountable.
m.5.20.7: Brahmā is ever firmly established in austerity, and so are Viṣṇu and Hara; all the gods and goddesses have attained through austerity a fruit hard to obtain.
m.5.20.8: With whatever disposition one abides and performs austerity, from that austerity the corresponding result is obtained by them in this world; there is no doubt.
m.5.20.9: Austerity is traditionally held to be threefold — sāttvika, rājasa and tāmasa; O Vyāsa, it should be understood as the means of all means.
m.5.20.10: The sāttvika belongs to the gods and to celibate ascetics whose seed flows upward; the rājasa to the Dānavas and likewise to humans; the tāmasa to the Rākṣasas and to men of cruel deeds.
m.5.20.11: Its fruit is declared threefold by sages who see the truth. Japa, meditation and auspicious worship of the gods with devotion —
m.5.20.12: — that is designated sāttvika, accomplishing every fruit, the means to what the mind desires both in this world and the next.
m.5.20.13: Austerity aimed at the fruits of desires is called rājasa. Having severely tormented one's own body with unbearable practices that dry up the body —
m.5.20.14: — such austerity is declared tāmasa, a means to what the mind desires.
m.5.20.15: One should know the sāttvika to be the highest, and with it an unwavering righteous mind; bathing, worship, japa, fire-offering, pure cleanliness, non-violence,
m.5.20.16: the observance of vows and fasts, silence, restraint of the senses, intelligence, learning, truthfulness, freedom from anger, giving, forbearance, self-control, compassion,
m.5.20.17: the construction of step-wells, wells, tanks and the like, and of temples; the Kṛcchra and Cāndrāyaṇa penances, sacrifice, holy places of pilgrimage, and hermitages too —
m.5.20.18: these are the stations of dharma that bestow happiness on the wise; this is the supreme true dharma, O Vyāsa, and the cause of devotion to Śiva.
m.5.20.19: Let the yogic union of saṅkrānti and viṣuvat (the shifting and balancing of the breath) be applied in the state freed from sound (nāda); meditation at the three junctures of the day, contemplation of light, and holding the state of unmanī —
m.5.20.20: exhalation, inhalation and retention — prāṇāyāma is held to be threefold; knowledge of the movement through the channels (nāḍī), and restraint through withdrawal of the senses (pratyāhāra) —
m.5.20.21: the fourth state (turīya), and below it the intellect, accompanied by the eight powers beginning with aṇimā — this is declared superior to the former, the means to supreme knowledge.
m.5.20.22: The wood-like state, the death-like state, or the green state — so they are proclaimed; these are various attainments that destroy all sins.
m.5.20.23: Woman, bed and drink, garments, incense and unguents, the chewing of betel — these are the five splendours of royal power;
m.5.20.24: loads of gold, and copper, houses, gems and cows, learning in the Vedas and śāstras, song, dance and ornaments,
m.5.20.25: conches, vīṇās and drums, a lordly elephant, a parasol and chowries — these are the forms of enjoyment; attached to them, one becomes infatuated.
m.5.20.26: Like a mirror dimmed, O sage, he is crushed by attachments (sneha, also oil) like sesame; and, deluded in understanding, he even dismisses it, saying, go away quickly.
m.5.20.27: Though knowing, he wanders here in saṃsāra like a water-wheel, afflicted with sorrow in all kinds of births, among both the immobile and the moving.
m.5.20.28: Thus, having passed through all births in his wandering, by the course of time he attains the human state, which is extremely rare.
m.5.20.29: Even out of sequence human birth may be obtained through the weight of merit; the courses of actions are declared to be manifold, according to their heaviness and lightness.
m.5.20.30: Having obtained the human state, the means to heaven and liberation, he who does not pursue his own good grieves for a long time after death.
m.5.20.31: For all gods and asuras the human state is very hard to obtain; having obtained it, one should act in such a way that one does not go to hell.
m.5.20.32: If, having obtained the rare human state, there is no effort toward gaining heaven and final release, that birth is declared futile.
m.5.20.33: The human state is declared the root of everything, of the four aims of life; having obtained it through dharma, O Vyāsa, one should carefully preserve it.
m.5.20.34: Having obtained the human state, rooted in dharma and accomplishing all aims, if there is to be effort for gain, then one should oneself guard the root.
m.5.20.35: Who, having obtained even among humans the status of a Brahmin, which is truly rare, does not pursue his own good — who else is more senseless than he?
m.5.20.36: Of all the continents, this alone is called the land of action; from here heaven and liberation, once earned, are attained.
m.5.20.37: Having obtained the impermanent human state in this land, Bhārata-varṣa, whoever does not work for his own good has truly cheated himself.
m.5.20.38: This is the land of action, O Brahmin; that heaven is known as the land of fruits. Whatever action is done here is enjoyed in heaven.
m.5.20.39: As long as the body is healthy, one should practise dharma; when unwell, even if urged by others, one is unable to do anything.
m.5.20.40: He who does not accomplish the permanent by means of the impermanent body — for him the permanent is lost, and the impermanent perishes as well.
m.5.20.41: Pieces upon pieces of one's lifespan fall away before his very eyes; why does he not awaken, though taught by the passing of day and night?
m.5.20.42: Since it is not known when death will come, and to whom, who can find steadiness in the face of sudden death?
m.5.20.43: Since he will surely depart alone, abandoning everything, why does he not at some time give this wealth in charity as provisions for the journey?
m.5.20.44: One who has taken charity as provisions for the journey goes happily to the abode of Yama; otherwise the creature suffers on a road devoid of provisions.
m.5.20.45: Those whose merits are complete in every respect at the destined time—for them, as they go to the region of heaven, there is gain at every step.
m.5.20.46: Knowing this, a man should perform merit and avoid sin. Through merit one attains divinity; the one without merit goes to hell.
m.5.20.47: Those who have taken refuge, even slightly, in Śiva, the lord of the gods, do not see the terrible Yama, nor hell either.
m.5.20.48: But, because of sins and great delusions, such men dwell there for a short time by Śiva's command, and then go to Śiva's abode.
m.5.20.49: Those, however, who have taken refuge in Maheśvara with their whole being are not stained by sin, as a lotus leaf is not wetted by water.
m.5.20.50: Those by whom the name Śiva has been uttered, and likewise Hara, Hara—they have no fear of hell, nor indeed of Yama, O best of sages.
m.5.20.51: The two syllables Śi-va are the provisions for the other world, the untroubled means to liberation, the sole abode of all accumulated merit.
m.5.20.52: The name of Śiva alone is the sole remedy for the great disease of worldly existence; I see no other cure for the disease of saṃsāra.
m.5.20.53: Long ago a Pulkasa, having committed thousands of brahmin-slayings, attained liberation by hearing the pure name Śiva.
m.5.20.54: Therefore the wise man should constantly increase his devotion to the Lord. Through devotion to Śiva, O greatly wise one, one obtains both enjoyment and liberation.
m.5.20.iti: Thus ends the twentieth adhyāya, named The particular account of Manu, in the fifth saṃhitā, the Umā-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.5.21.1: Vyāsa said: Brāhmaṇa-hood is indeed hard to attain; by nature one becomes a brāhmaṇa. From the mouth of the Lord arose the kṣatriya class, from the arms and from the thighs the vaiśyas,
m.5.21.2: and the śūdra was born from the feet — such is the revealed word from his mouth. How then do they attain a higher position from a lower station? Tell me this.
m.5.21.3: Sanatkumāra said: Through evil deeds, O Kāleya, humans fall from their station; therefore, having attained the best station, a wise man should guard it.
m.5.21.4: He who, abandoning brāhmaṇa-hood, is born in a kṣatriya womb, fallen from brāhmaṇa-status, takes up kṣatriya-hood.
m.5.21.5: Likewise the deluded one, through practising adharma, keeps revolving downward, for he enters darkness for thousands of births.
m.5.21.6: Therefore, having obtained the highest station, one should not be careless nor ruin it; a man should always guard his own station, even when he meets with misfortunes.
m.5.21.7: He who, having attained auspicious brāhmaṇa-hood, despises brāhmaṇa-status and does not know what may and may not be eaten — that man becomes a kṣatriya.
m.5.21.8: By what action an intelligent śūdra is born a vaiśya, and by which one becomes of the highest class — all that I shall tell you.
m.5.21.9: Being a śūdra, one should practise the śūdra's duties as prescribed, and properly render service to the three higher classes always.
m.5.21.10: Even a śūdra who does so, desiring advancement, attains vaiśya-hood. The vaiśya who employs his wealth rightly and offers oblations according to rule,
m.5.21.11: taking up the agnihotra and eating only the food left over after offerings — that vaiśya is born in a kṣatriya family; there is no doubt about this.
m.5.21.12: The kṣatriya is born anew through properly consecrated sacrifices with fees given; seeking heaven, he studies the Veda and always takes refuge in the three sacred fires.
m.5.21.13: With hands and feet ever moist from charity and ablutions, he should protect the earth by dharma; and, devoted to dharma, approach his own wife in her season,
m.5.21.14: saying, let hospitality be given to all, to the three classes and to all beings; and for the sake of cows, brāhmaṇas and himself he should be slain in battle.
m.5.21.15: Thereby, his self purified by fire and mantras, the kṣatriya becomes a brāhmaṇa; becoming a brāhmaṇa according to rule, he is born as a sacrificial priest.
m.5.21.16: Ever devoted to his own duties, truthful, with senses conquered, he attains a vast heaven and becomes dear even to the gods.
m.5.21.17: Brāhmaṇa-hood is indeed hard to obtain; men achieve it with difficulty. Through brāhmaṇa-status one obtains everything, and liberation as well, O lord of sages.
m.5.21.18: Therefore with every effort a brāhmaṇa devoted to dharma should guard the supreme brāhmaṇa-status, the means of attaining all aims.
m.5.21.19: Vyāsa said: You have mentioned here the greatness of battle, O best of sages; I wish to hear this. Tell it, O best of speakers.
m.5.21.20: Sanatkumāra said: Having worshipped with sacrifices such as the Agniṣṭoma with abundant fees, one does not obtain the fruit that one would obtain in battle.
m.5.21.21: So the knowers of truth and the knowers of sacrificial rites have always declared. Therefore I shall tell you the fruit that belongs to those who live by weapons.
m.5.21.22: Gain of merit, gain of wealth, and likewise gain of fame come to the hero who longs for battle, crushing the enemy's army.
m.5.21.23: His are dharma, wealth and desire, and the merit of sacrifice with fees. He who, facing the enemy, gives his life mounts that celestial vehicle;
m.5.21.24: he is born in the world of Viṣṇu. And he who is unvanquished in battle, if he does not die, obtains the merit of four horse-sacrifices.
m.5.21.25: But the hero who, not abandoning his weapon, dies at the front of the army, standing face to face with the foe, does not return from heaven.
m.5.21.26: Whether king, prince, or army commander, the hero who is slain by a kṣatriya in combat attains an imperishable world.
m.5.21.27: As many of his hairs as are pierced by missiles in the great battle, so many imperishable worlds, yielding every desire, does he obtain.
m.5.21.28: The hero's seat, the hero's bed, and a firm abiding in the hero's station are always his, O Vyāsa, in this world and the next.
m.5.21.29: Those who die for the sake of cows, of brāhmaṇas, and of their land and master go to happiness just as the virtuous do.
m.5.21.30: Whoever, having killed a brāhmaṇa, afterwards gives up his life there in battle for his master — he does not return from heaven.
m.5.21.31: For one killed by flesh-eating beasts or by elephants for the sake of brāhmaṇas, cows or master, the destiny is supreme, abundant and imperishable.
m.5.21.32: A capable man here may manage to sacrifice even with hundreds of rites, but giving up one's own body in battle is extremely hard to do.
m.5.21.33: Battle is most meritorious, leads to heaven, reveals one's true nature, and is universal in scope — for all classes, and for the kṣatriya in particular.
m.5.21.34: I shall now fully declare the eternal law of war: whom one should strike and whom one should spare.
m.5.21.35: An assailant who approaches intent on killing, even a twice-born versed in the Vedāntas — one may kill him; one does not thereby become a slayer of a brāhmaṇa.
m.5.21.36: Even one who deserves to be killed must not be killed if he begs for water. O Vyāsa, the man who kills the distressed in battle becomes a brāhmaṇa-slayer.
m.5.21.37: Having killed the sick, the weak, a child, a woman, an orphan, the pitiable, or one whose bow is broken or whose bowstring is cut, one certainly becomes a brāhmaṇa-slayer.
m.5.21.38: Reflecting thus, the truly wise man should gladly be devoted to battle; having obtained the fruit of his birth, he rejoices here and hereafter.
m.5.21.iti: Thus ends the twenty-first adhyāya, named The description of the fruit of battle, in the fifth saṃhitā, the Umā-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.5.22.1: Vyāsa said: O dear one, O lord of sages, now tell me in due order the process of the birth of the living being, and also its stay in the womb, for the sake of cultivating dispassion.
m.5.22.2: Sanatkumāra said: Listen, O Vyāsa: I shall tell you briefly yet completely the essence of the scriptures—the true dispassion of one seeking liberation, which severs the bondage of worldly existence.
m.5.22.3: Inside the cooking vessel of the stomach, food lies separately and water separately. The water is placed above the fire, and the food above the water.
m.5.22.4: Below the water is that fire; the vital air situated there slowly fans the fire. The fire, being fanned by the air, makes the water very hot.
m.5.22.5: That food is then cooked all over by the hot water. When cooked, it becomes twofold: the waste separately and the essence separately.
m.5.22.6: The waste, divided into twelve impurities, goes out of the body; but the essence flows within the body, and by it the body becomes nourished.
m.5.22.7: Ears, eyes, nose, tongue, teeth, penis, anus, nails—the seats of impurity—and phlegm, sweat, feces and urine: these are known as the twelve.
m.5.22.8: All the channels, bound to the heart-lotus on every side, should be known as carriers of the essence. I shall tell their manner, O sage.
m.5.22.9: At their openings the vital breath places that subtle essence; with that essence the vital breath fills those channels again.
m.5.22.10: Then, filled, they spread throughout the body. Thereupon that essence, lying within the channels, by the body's own heat…
m.5.22.11: …is cooked, and from its being cooked there arises again a twofold product. First the skin is enveloped by it, and blood is produced.
m.5.22.12: From blood come body-hair and flesh; from flesh, head-hair and sinew; likewise from sinew, the bones; nails and marrow arise from bone.
m.5.22.13: From marrow as cause, by transformation, comes semen, whose nature is procreation. Thus the twelvefold transformation of food is proclaimed.
m.5.22.14: Semen is born of food, and from semen comes the origin of the divine body. When, at the proper season, faultless semen is lodged in the womb,
m.5.22.15: then, touched by air, it becomes one with the woman's blood. At the time of the discharge of semen, the living being, joined with its causal subtle factors,
m.5.22.16: enveloped, enters the womb, impelled by its own deeds. That semen and blood, united in one place, becomes the embryonic fluid (kalala) in one day.
m.5.22.17: In five nights the kalala takes the form of a bubble; in seven nights the bubble becomes a lump of flesh.
m.5.22.18: The neck, head, shoulders, spine, belly, hands and feet, the sides, the waist, and the body likewise—
m.5.22.19: arise here gradually within just two months. In three months all the sprouting joints are formed.
m.5.22.20: In four months the fingers arise in due order; and in five months the mouth, nose and ears.
m.5.22.21: The row of teeth, the private part and the nails arise; and within six months the openings of the ears form.
m.5.22.22: The anus, urinary passage, genitals and navel come into being; and the joints in the limbs arise in seven months.
m.5.22.23: Complete with limbs and minor parts, fully matured, it remains in the mother's belly, covered by the caul, O best of sages.
m.5.22.24: By the six-flavoured essence stolen from the mother's food, conveyed through the attached umbilical cord, it grows day by day.
m.5.22.25: Then, when this little body is complete, the living being regains memory; it knows pleasure and pain, sleep and dream, and what was done before.
m.5.22.26: I died and was born again; born, I died again. Thousands of various wombs have been seen by me in being born.
m.5.22.27: Now, as soon as I am born and have gained right impressions, I shall pursue that good by which there will be no further birth in a womb.
m.5.22.28: Thinking thus while in the womb: When I have come out of the womb, I shall seek the knowledge of Śiva, which ends worldly existence.
m.5.22.29: Thus the living being, greatly tormented by the suffering of the womb, remains there under the sway of karma, pondering the means to liberation.
m.5.22.30: Just as someone crushed under a great mountain remains in pain, so the embodied one, wrapped in the caul, remains in pain.
m.5.22.31: As one who has fallen into the ocean remains in pain, utterly distraught, so then it is, its limbs soaked in the womb-fluid, constantly agitated.
m.5.22.32: Just as someone placed in an iron pot is cooked by fire, so, cast into the pot of the womb, it is cooked by the digestive fire.
m.5.22.33: Whatever pain arises for one ceaselessly pierced by red-hot needles, greater than that is the pain of one dwelling there.
m.5.22.34: For embodied beings there is nowhere any pain or hardship greater than dwelling in the womb—full of suffering, most dreadful, extremely oppressive.
m.5.22.35: This exceedingly great suffering is declared to befall sinners; for those of righteous mind, birth always takes place in seven months.
m.5.22.36: Pain even harder to bear than that of the womb arises from the squeezing in the vaginal passage—for sinful souls, O Vyāsa, not for those endowed with dharma.
m.5.22.37: Such is the pain of one squeezed all over like sugarcane in a press, and struck on the head with the mallet of sin.
m.5.22.38: Just as sesame seeds pressed in a mill become pithless in a moment, so the body becomes pithless from the squeezing of the vaginal passage.
m.5.22.39: This body has bones for its legs, beams and pillars, is held together by the binding of sinews, is plastered with the clay of blood and flesh, and is a vessel for the stuff of feces and urine;
m.5.22.40: covered with head-hair, body-hair and nails; an abode of disease, afflicted; with the mouth as its one great door, and adorned with eight windows.
m.5.22.41: The body has the two lips as its door-panels and is likewise furnished with the tongue as its bolt. It is tormented by thirst for enjoyments, deluded, and it follows the sway of attachment and aversion.
m.5.22.42: With its limbs and lesser limbs folded together, enveloped in the membrane of the womb, it comes out through the narrow, confined passage of the womb.
m.5.22.43: Its limbs are smeared with feces, urine and blood; it emerges from its sheath; it is known as a cage of bones — such is the body to be understood in this world.
m.5.22.44: It has three hundred and sixty bones and five hundred muscles, and is covered all around by three and a half crores of hairs.
m.5.22.45: The body is pervaded all around by as many crores of channels (nāḍīs), gross and subtle; they are declared to be both visible and invisible.
m.5.22.46: Through these channels what lies within flows outward as sweat and fluids. Thirty-two teeth are declared, and twenty nails are recorded.
m.5.22.47: Of bile there is to be known a kuḍava; of phlegm an āḍhaka is stated; of fat (vasā) twenty palas, and half that of kapila.
m.5.22.48: Two and a half tulās are to be known; ten palas of fatty tissue (medas); three palas of the vital blood, and four times that of marrow.
m.5.22.49: Semen is to be known as half a kuḍava; that seed is the strength of embodied beings. Of flesh, in a single mass, a thousand palas is stated.
m.5.22.50: Blood is to be known as a hundred palas; feces and urine, in measure, are four and four añjalis respectively, O best of sages.
m.5.22.51: Thus this body is the non-eternal house of the eternal Self, impure house of the pure Self, fashioned out of the bondage of karma.
m.5.22.iti: Thus ends the twenty-second adhyāya, named The description of the origin of the body, in the fifth saṃhitā, the Umā-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.5.23.1: Sanatkumāra said: Listen, O Vyāsa of great intellect, O sage: I shall briefly tell you of the impurity of the body and of the power of its nature.
m.5.23.2: Since the body arises from the union of semen and blood, and is always filled with faeces and urine, it is therefore considered impure.
m.5.23.3: Just as a pot filled inside with excrement is not clean though washed outside, so this body, even while being cleansed, remains impure for that reason.
m.5.23.4: Even the most purifying things—the five products of the cow and sacrificial oblations—become impure in an instant on reaching it; what else then is impure, if not this?
m.5.23.5: Even delightful and fragrant foods and drinks quickly become impure on reaching it; what else then is impure?
m.5.23.6: O people, why do you not see the putrid filth that comes out of one's own body day after day? How can its container be pure?
m.5.23.7: Even when cleansed with the five cow-products, kuśa grass and water, the body does not become spotless, like a piece of charcoal being rubbed.
m.5.23.8: How can that body be purified whose streams constantly flow, like those of a mountain, with phlegm, urine, faeces and the like?
m.5.23.9: In the body, the receptacle of all impurities, there is not even a single pure spot, as in a leather bag of faeces and urine.
m.5.23.10: Having touched the outlets of one's own body, the hand is cleansed with earth and water; yet why does the hand of this vessel of impurity not fall off?
m.5.23.11: The body, though carefully refined with fragrant incense and the like, does not abandon its nature, like a dog's tail that has been bent straight.
m.5.23.12: Just as a thing black by its very nature cannot become white by any means, so the body, though thoroughly cleansed, would not become spotless.
m.5.23.13: Though smelling its own foul odour, though seeing its own filth, though pinching its nose, this world does not become dispassionate.
m.5.23.14: Ah, the might of delusion, by which this world is veiled! Though plainly seeing the body's own defect, one does not become detached.
m.5.23.15: For the man who does not become detached by the foul smell of his own body, what other cause of detachment can be taught?
m.5.23.16: In the whole world, the body alone is impure; by contact with its filthy parts even something pure becomes impure.
m.5.23.17: Cleansing of the body is declared to be for removing smell and smear; by the removal of both there is purity, and it is purified by contact with what is pure.
m.5.23.18: One may perform cleansing till death with all the water of the Gaṅgā and with loads of earth like mountains, yet one corrupt in disposition is not purified.
m.5.23.19: An evil-souled person is never purified by baths at holy places or by austerities. Does a dog's skin bag, washed at a holy place, attain purity?
m.5.23.20: For one corrupt in inner disposition, even entering the fire yields neither heaven nor liberation—only the burning of the body.
m.5.23.21: Even with all the water of the Gaṅgā and a mountain of earth, a man corrupt in disposition, devoted to bathing from birth, is not purified—thus indeed we declare.
m.5.23.22: Even if he kindles a great fire sprinkled with ghee and oil, its flames turning to the right, and enters it and is burnt, one corrupt in disposition gains neither merit nor any other fruit.
m.5.23.23: Fish dwell always in the Gaṅgā and other holy waters, and flocks of birds in temples; devoid of pious disposition, they gain no fruit from immersion in holy waters, nor likewise from gifts.
m.5.23.24: Purity of disposition is the supreme purity and the standard in all acts: a wife is embraced with one feeling, a daughter with another.
m.5.23.25: The mind's attitude differs even toward things that are not different: a woman thinks of her son in one way and of her husband in another.
m.5.23.26: Behold fully the great power of this disposition: even when embraced by a woman, one without amorous feeling does not desire.
m.5.23.27: One would not eat the various foods and fragrant delicacies if one's mind is fixed in thought on the three—desire and the rest.
m.5.23.28: By disposition a man is bound; by disposition he is released. Through disposition, pure and pure-souled, he attains heaven and liberation.
m.5.23.29: One whose self is purified by single-minded disposition—whether burning offerings, making oblations, or praising—when he dies, quickly attains, through the gaining of knowledge, the worlds of those who have performed very many sacrifices.
m.5.23.30: For men, cleansing of the smear and stench of the faeces and urine of ignorance and passion is done with the spotless water of knowledge and, further, with the earth of true dispassion.
m.5.23.31: Thus this body is regarded as impure by nature; its substance is mere skin, it is pithless, like the hollow core of a plantain.
m.5.23.32: The wise one who, knowing the body thus to be full of defects, becomes loosened from the feeling arising from bodily enjoyment, calm in mind and serene in intellect—
m.5.23.33: —he crosses beyond saṃsāra and becomes liberated while living; but one who firmly clings to saṃsāra, hollow as the core of a plantain, remains bound.
m.5.23.34: Thus has been described this greatly painful suffering of birth, which befalls men through the fault of ignorance and under the sway of various actions.
m.5.23.35: In half a verse I shall state what has been said in crores of texts: mine is supreme sorrow, not mine is supreme happiness.
m.5.23.36: Many kings have gone from here to the other world; those endowed with freedom from possessiveness were freed, while others were bound by hundreds of thousands.
m.5.23.37: The memory that he had while in the womb is lost to him, through the stupefying pain of being pressed in the mechanism of the birth canal.
m.5.23.38: And merely by the touch of the dreadful outer air, bringing delusion, a fever arises in this embodied being.
m.5.23.39: From that great fever stupor arises, and in the stupefied one loss of memory quickly occurs again.
m.5.23.40: Then, through loss of memory, he has no memory of his former deeds, and attachment swiftly arises in the creature for that very birth.
m.5.23.41: This world, attached and deluded, does not engage in what ought to be done; it knows neither the self, nor the Supreme, nor the deity.
m.5.23.42: O good sage, though he has ears, he does not hear the highest good; though he has eyes capable of it, he does not see the highest good.
m.5.23.43: Walking slowly on a level path, he stumbles, as it were, at every step; though possessing intellect, he does not understand, even when being instructed by the wise.
m.5.23.44: Therefore a man suffers in saṃsāra, following the sway of craving that leads back to the womb, his understanding lost through sin, though the misery of the womb was once remembered.
m.5.23.45: Thus this great, supreme, divine scripture was spoken by Śiva for the purpose of expounding austerity, the means of attaining heaven and liberation.
m.5.23.46: That those who, while this auspicious knowledge exists — the means to all desires and goals — do not work for their own good: that indeed is a great wonder.
m.5.23.47: Again, in childhood there is great suffering, because the functions of the senses are undeveloped; even wishing, the child cannot speak or do anything to remedy it.
m.5.23.48: At teething there is great pain, and likewise from minor illness; and there is affliction from various childhood diseases and also from the child-seizing spirits.
m.5.23.49: Sometimes his body is overcome by hunger and thirst, sometimes he stays crying loudly; and out of delusion the child may do things like eating faeces and urine.
m.5.23.50: In boyhood, with the piercing of the ears, the disciplinary measures of mother and father, and the learning of letters and the like, various sufferings arise.
m.5.23.51: Even having just passed through the suffering of childhood and seeing it, the deluded-minded one does not do what is good for himself — that is the great wonder here.
m.5.23.52: Because the functions of the senses are fully active, from the torment of the disease of lust, and constantly when that object is not obtained — whence can there be happiness in youth?
m.5.23.53: And there is great suffering from jealousy for him who is infatuated through delusion, as for an inflamed eye; and renunciation of the beloved leads only to sorrow.
m.5.23.54: Tormented by the fire of lust, he finds no sleep at night; and even by day, whence happiness, with anxiety about earning wealth?
m.5.23.55: The drops of semen of a man whose mind is fixed on women are not considered a source of happiness; they are just like drops of sweat.
m.5.23.56: Whatever relief there is for a leper or a monkey tormented by worms from the burning of scratching — that, the knowers say, is the pleasure in women.
m.5.23.57: Such pleasure as one feels from pus discharging from a boil, such should be considered the pleasure in women; nothing more is found in them.
m.5.23.58: Such pleasure as arises from the evacuation of faeces and urine, such should be known the pleasure in women; the deluded imagine it otherwise.
m.5.23.59: In women, who are without substance and the abode of all faults, there is not even an atom of happiness — so it was declared by Pañcacūḍā.
m.5.23.60: Through honour and dishonour, through separation after union with the beloved, and youth seized by old age — where is happiness free of trouble?
m.5.23.61: In old age the body is slackened by wrinkles, grey hair and baldness, incapable in all activities, worn out by old age.
m.5.23.62: The youth of woman and man, charming and formerly dear to each other — that very youth, seized by old age, is no longer dear even to the two of them.
m.5.23.63: He who, even seeing his own self transformed by old age as if into something never seen before, still remains attached — who else is more senseless than he?
m.5.23.64: A man overcome by old age, because of his incapacity, is treated with contempt by kinsmen such as daughters and sons, and by servants who are hard to control.
m.5.23.65: One greatly afflicted by old age is unable to accomplish dharma, wealth, desire, or liberation; therefore one should practise dharma while young.
m.5.23.iti: Thus ends the twenty-third adhyāya, named The description of the impurity of the body and of the sorrows of childhood and the other stages, in the treatment of saṃsāra, in the fifth saṃhitā, the Umā-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.5.24.1: Vyāsa said: That censure concerning women which was declared by Pañcacūḍā, tell it to me briefly, O sage, if you are pleased with me.
m.5.24.2: Sanatkumāra said: I shall describe the nature of women exactly as it is; listen, O brahmin. By merely hearing it, supreme dispassion would arise.
m.5.24.3: Women indeed are the root of faults, ever light-minded, O sage. Therefore attachment to them should not be formed by vigilant seekers of liberation.
m.5.24.4: Here too they cite this ancient story: the dialogue of Nārada with the courtesan Pañcacūḍā.
m.5.24.5: Long ago the wise divine sage Nārada, roaming the worlds, saw the young, peerless apsaras Pañcacūḍā.
m.5.24.6: Nārada, best of sages, asked the fair-browed apsaras: There is a certain doubt in my heart; resolve it for me, O slender-waisted one.
m.5.24.7: Thus addressed, that excellent apsaras replied to the brahmin: If it is within my scope, I shall speak—if you consider me capable.
m.5.24.8: Nārada said: I shall by no means engage you in what is beyond your scope, gentle lady. I wish to hear from you about the nature of women, O slender-waisted one.
m.5.24.9: Sanatkumāra said: Hearing these words of the divine sage, the best of apsarases replied to that lord of sages, the divine sage, best of munis.
m.5.24.10: Pañcacūḍā said: Listen, O sage: a woman cannot be censured by one who is herself a woman. You know what women are and what they are like by nature.
m.5.24.11: You ought not to set me such a question, O divine sage. Having said this, Pañcacūḍā, best of apsarases, fell silent.
m.5.24.12: Then the foremost divine sage, having heard her excellent words, spoke to her again, out of desire for the welfare of the worlds.
m.5.24.13: Nārada said: There would be fault in speaking falsely; in truth no fault exists. Know this, and therefore speak that truth, O slender-waisted one.
m.5.24.14: Sanatkumāra said: Thus addressed, the sweetly smiling one, having made up her mind, eagerly began to speak of the perennial, true faults of women.
m.5.24.15: Pañcacūḍā said: Even women of good family, who have protectors and are beautiful, do not stay within bounds; that is the fault in women, O Nārada.
m.5.24.16: There is indeed nothing else more sinful than women. Women are truly the root of sins—so you too know.
m.5.24.17: Even having renowned, wealthy, handsome husbands as they desire, women, on finding an opportunity, cannot wait faithfully for them.
m.5.24.18: This wicked way belongs to us women, O lord: that, abandoning shame, we resort even to very sinful men.
m.5.24.19: Whoever courts a woman, comes near her, and renders her a little service—him alone do women desire.
m.5.24.20: It is because men do not solicit them, and from fear of the husband's people, that women, who know no bounds, keep within bounds with their husbands.
m.5.24.21: There is no one they reject; they have no fixed rule about age. Handsome or ugly, they enjoy a man.
m.5.24.22: Not from fear, nor from reproach, nor in any way for the sake of wealth, nor from ties of kin and family, do women remain with their husbands.
m.5.24.23: Women of good family envy women who are in their youth, wear the ornaments and garments they like, and live as they please.
m.5.24.24: Even those beloved women who are always highly honoured and guarded become attached to the hunchbacked, the blind, the dull-witted, and the dwarfish,
m.5.24.25: and even to the lame, O divine sage, and to other despicable men. In the worlds there is no one whom women will not approach, O great sage.
m.5.24.26: If somehow access to men is not available, O brahmin, they turn even to one another, and do not remain faithful to their husbands.
m.5.24.27: Only through not obtaining men, fear of attendants, and fear of death and bondage are those women thwarted in their hopes.
m.5.24.28: Fickle by nature, of wicked conduct, and hard to fathom in their intentions even for a wise man here, as they are driven by the pursuit of sexual pleasure.
m.5.24.29: Fire is never satisfied with fuel, nor the great ocean with rivers, nor Death with all beings, nor fair-eyed women with men.
m.5.24.30: And this is another secret of all women, O divine sage: on merely seeing a man, a woman's private part at once becomes moist.
m.5.24.31: On seeing a man well bathed, fragrant and free of dirt, women's private parts become moist, like water from a leather-bag vessel.
m.5.24.32: Women do not tolerate even an excellent husband who provides even for their bodily needs, who shows them honour and conciliation, and who protects them.
m.5.24.33: Neither from the highest enjoyment of pleasures nor from an accumulation of ornaments and wealth do they consider good to come, so much as from sexual union.
m.5.24.34: The Ender, Yama, Death, the netherworld, the submarine mare-fire, a razor's edge, poison, a serpent and fire—all these on one side, and women on the other.
m.5.24.35: Ever since the five great elements arose, since the world was ordained by the Creator, since men and women were fashioned—ever has fault resided in women, O Nārada.
m.5.24.36: Sanatkumāra said: Having heard her words, Nārada, pleased at heart, deemed them true, and thereupon became indifferent to women.
m.5.24.37: Thus I have respectfully told you the nature of women as declared by Pañcacūḍā, a cause of dispassion, O Vyāsa. What else do you wish to hear?
m.5.24.iti: Thus ends the twenty-fourth adhyāya, named The description of the nature of women, in the fifth saṃhitā, the Umā-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.5.25.1: Vyāsa said: O Sanatkumāra, all-knowing sage, I have listened with delight to the account of the nature of women from you. Now tell me the knowledge of time (of death).
m.5.25.2: Sanatkumāra said: This very question Pārvatī once asked the Supreme Lord, after hearing many divine stories, pleased, and having bowed deeply to him.
m.5.25.3: Pārvatī said: O Lord, by your grace I have understood the whole doctrine: how you are to be worshipped, O god, and with which mantras, according to rule.
m.5.25.4: Yet even now one doubt remains, O Lord, concerning the wheel of time: what the signs of death are, O god, and what the measure of one's lifespan is.
m.5.25.5: Tell me everything, O Lord, if I am dear to you. Thus questioned by the goddess, Maheśvara replied.
m.5.25.6: Īśvara said: Truly I shall tell you, beloved, the most excellent teaching, by which, O queen of the gods, men come to know the time of death.
m.5.25.7: It is known to within a day, a fortnight, a month, a season, a half-year or a year, through signs gross and subtle, external and internal.
m.5.25.8: That I shall now explain to you; listen truly, O beautiful one, O Umā, for the benefit of the worlds and for the sake of detachment.
m.5.25.9: If the body suddenly turns pale all over, with redness in its upper part, then one should know death will come within six months, beloved.
m.5.25.10: When the mouth, ears, eyes and tongue become stiff, then one should know death will come within six months, beloved.
m.5.25.11: If, O gentle one, one does not readily hear the roaring sound within, those who know time should recognise death within six months.
m.5.25.12: When one does not see the brightness coming from sun, moon and fire, and everything appears wholly black, then life lasts six months.
m.5.25.13: When, O goddess, beloved, the left hand throbs for a week, then his life lasts one month; there is no doubt.
m.5.25.14: When the limbs loosen and the palate dries up, then his life lasts one month; there is no doubt.
m.5.25.15: He whose nose runs while all three humours are disturbed lives a fortnight; one whose mouth and throat dry up has his life end at the close of six months.
m.5.25.16: He whose tongue becomes swollen and whose teeth grow moist, O lovely lady, meets death after six months; one should recognise it by these signs.
m.5.25.17: When, O fair-complexioned one, one does not see oneself reflected in water, oil, ghee or a mirror, or sees it distorted, as mere flesh,
m.5.25.18: he should be known by one who understands the wheel of time as having six months of life. Hear another sign, O queen of the gods, by which death is recognised.
m.5.25.19: When one sees one's own shadow headless, or finds oneself without a shadow, one does not live a month.
m.5.25.20: I have told the bodily signs of death, O Pārvatī. Now hear, gentle one, the external signs I now describe.
m.5.25.21: When, O goddess, the disc of the moon or sun appears rayless and of a pale-red hue, one perishes within half a month.
m.5.25.22: He who cannot see Arundhatī, the great path of the sky, the moon with its mark — seeing it without its mark — and the stars, lives one month.
m.5.25.23: If on seeing a planet there is confusion of directions, death surely comes in six months; likewise if one cannot see Utathya, the pole star, or the sun's disc.
m.5.25.24: When one sees a rainbow at night and a falling meteor at midday, and is surrounded by vultures and crows, one has six months of life; no doubt.
m.5.25.25: If the Seers (the Great Bear) and the path to heaven are not seen in the sky, men who know time should recognise six months of life.
m.5.25.26: If one suddenly sees the sun or the moon seized by Rāhu, or sees the circle of directions as if whirling, one clearly dies within six months.
m.5.25.27: If a man is suddenly swarmed by blue flies, his life should truly be known as one month.
m.5.25.28: If a vulture, crow or pigeon alights and stays on one's head, that creature dies quickly, within one month; no doubt.
m.5.25.29: Thus the varieties of external ill omens have been described. For the welfare of men I now speak briefly.
m.5.25.30: I tell how, O goddess, people know the time of death from both hands; between the left and right it is said to be directly perceptible.
m.5.25.31: Thus, in brief, the two fortnights are placed on the two hands, O beautiful goddess. Becoming pure, well bathed, with senses restrained, remembering the Lord,
m.5.25.32: having washed the hands with milk, one should rub them with red lac; having adorned the hands with perfumes and flowers, one should examine what is auspicious and inauspicious.
m.5.25.33: Starting from the little finger up to the thumb, beloved, in order of the three joints, on both hands,
m.5.25.34: having placed the lunar days beginning with the first (pratipad) on the joints, with hands held in a cupped form, seated facing east,
m.5.25.35: one should recite mentally the nine-syllabled mantra a hundred and eight times, and then carefully examine the hands at each joint.
m.5.25.36: On whichever joint a line appears black like a bee, on that lunar day death should be known to come, in the dark or bright fortnight accordingly, beloved.
m.5.25.37: Now I shall briefly describe the sign of time arising from the inner sound (nāda). Having known the going and coming of breath, one should act; listen, beloved.
m.5.25.38: Having carefully understood self-knowledge and the movement of the breath, O fair-hipped one — time runs as kṣaṇa, truṭi, lava, nimeṣa, kāṣṭhā and kalā,
m.5.25.39: muhūrta, day and night, fortnight, month, season, year, the cycle of years, yuga, kalpa and mahākalpa likewise —
m.5.25.40: thus Time, who is Sadāśiva, carries all away in due succession. Left, right and middle — these are remembered as the three paths of the breath.
m.5.25.41: Beginning from five days and going up to a limit of twenty-five days, when the breath moves in the left course, the sound (nāda) is the measure; this has been told to you.
m.5.25.42: The elements, the openings, the directions and the banner, O fair-complexioned one: in the left course the sound is the measure for one who knows time.
m.5.25.43: And the qualities that are modifications of the seasons, there itself, O spirited lady, are declared as the measure for the right course; this should be known by those who understand the breath.
m.5.25.44: When Iḍā and the other channels carry the breaths for a number of days equal to the elements (five), his life lasts within a year; there is no doubt.
m.5.25.45: With a flow of ten days he lives the measure of a year; with a flow of fifteen days, his life is ended in one year.
m.5.25.46: With a flow of twenty days one should then mark six months. When the left channel flows for a measure of twenty-five days,
m.5.25.47: then the life of that man whose life is ending is three months. With a measure of twenty-six days, two months are declared.
m.5.25.48: If it flows without any rest for a measure of twenty-seven days, one month of life is declared in the left range.
m.5.25.49: This measure should be understood according to the measure of the left breath. For the one other than the left (the right), the days are arranged in four groups in due order.
m.5.25.50: Placed in four positions, O Goddess, these sixteen are proclaimed. Now I shall tell their measure accurately.
m.5.25.51: Taking six days as the beginning of the count, according to rule, what falls within this in the left opening is set forth.
m.5.25.52: When it has prevailed for six days, he lives two years; one should also know eight months and eight days besides.
m.5.25.53: And when the breaths flow at the seventeenth, know it to be a year, no doubt; one should know seven months with six days, no doubt.
m.5.25.54: With the eight-day division he lives two years; four months are to be understood, with a limit of twenty-four days.
m.5.25.55: When the breaths flow for nine days, the span is three months; two months and another two months, and twelve days are declared.
m.5.25.56: For those that were stated before, their time is as given earlier; as for the intermediate days, their span is reckoned by that month.
m.5.25.57: With an eleven-day flow he lives one year; likewise nine months are declared, and days numbering eight as well.
m.5.25.58: With a twelve-day flow he lives one year; one should know seven months and also state six days.
m.5.25.59: And when the channel flows up to a limit of thirteen days, he will have a year, and four months are declared besides,
m.5.25.60: and the remaining life is twenty-four days; there is no doubt. When the flows of breath in the left last fourteen days,
m.5.25.61: he will have a year, and six months are declared, and twenty-four days of life as well; there is no doubt.
m.5.25.62: With a fifteen-day flow he lives nine months and twenty-four days; so it is stated by the knowers of time.
m.5.25.63: With a sixteen-day flow he lives ten months, with an excess of twenty-four days; so it is stated by the knowers of time.
m.5.25.64: With a seventeen-day flow one's life ends in nine months, with eighteen days here added; so it is stated, O mistress of adepts.
m.5.25.65: When, O Goddess, the left course lasts up to a limit of eighteen days, life is eight months, and twelve days are declared besides.
m.5.25.66: Ascertain here with certainty twenty-four days. When, O Goddess, the flow of breath lasts up to a limit of twenty-three days,
m.5.25.67: four months are declared, and likewise six days in addition. With a twenty-four-day flow he lives three months,
m.5.25.68: with eighteen days here; they draw life to a close through their movement. Whatever pertains to the intermediate days, those have been declared in brief.
m.5.25.69: The left course has been described; now hear about the right. With a twenty-eight-day flow he lives for the measure of a lunar fortnight.
m.5.25.70: With the flow remaining fixed in that next stage, he perishes in ten days; with a flow of thirty days, he perishes in five days.
m.5.25.71: When, O Goddess, it flows without interruption for thirty-one days, then his life is three days; there is no doubt.
m.5.25.72: And when the sun (the right channel) flows for a breath-count of thirty-two days, then his life is two days; there is no doubt.
m.5.25.73: The right breath has been described; I shall tell you of the middle one. When the flow of air goes into one part in the region of the face,
m.5.25.74: with a rushing flow, he lives one day. This wheel of the dying man has been declared by those who know the ancient lore.
m.5.25.75: This wheel of time concerning one whose life is ending has been told to you, O Goddess, for the welfare of the worlds. What else do you wish to hear?
m.5.25.iti: Thus ends the twenty-fifth adhyāya, named The description of the knowledge of time, in the fifth saṃhitā, the Umā-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.5.26.1: The Goddess said: O god, you have described to me the knowledge of the signs of time truly. Now tell me about the cheating of Time (death), how yogins accomplish it in truth.
m.5.26.2: Time indeed abides close at hand in all creatures; and how one for whom there is no death cheats Time when it has arrived—
m.5.26.3: Tell me that, O god, showing your affection toward me; and speak for the benefit of yogins, O giver of all happiness.
m.5.26.4: Śaṅkara said: Listen, O goddess; I shall explain briefly what you have asked me, O Śivā, for the benefit of all human beings.
m.5.26.5: Earth, water, likewise fire, wind and space: the combination of these is the body made of the five elements.
m.5.26.6: Space, then, is pervasive, abiding as all-reaching in all of them. In space they dissolve, and from it they arise again.
m.5.26.7: At separation, the elements of anyone always return to their own abode; there is no permanence of that combination, O beautiful one.
m.5.26.8: Likewise the wise there, through the power of austerity and mantras as well—they all know all this well; there is no doubt.
m.5.26.9: The Goddess said: Kāla, of dreadful form and terrifying, by whom all perishes into space, was burnt by you, O sole lord of heaven; then you, pleased again, being praised with hymns—he regained his own nature.
m.5.26.10: And he was told by you: With your form unseen, you will move among people known only by report. There your great power was seen, and by the boon of you, the Lord, he rose up again.
m.5.26.11: So now, sir, is there anything here by which Kāla is slain? Tell me that. You are the best of yogins, the Lord, self-dependent, who took on a body for the good of others, O Maheśa.
m.5.26.12: Śaṅkara said: He is not slain by the best of gods, nor by daityas, nor by yakṣas, rākṣasas, serpents and humans. But those yogins who, intent on meditation, remain in the body, slay Kāla with ease.
m.5.26.13: Sanatkumāra said: Having heard this from the guru of the three worlds, Gaurī laughed and said: Tell me truly how, and by what, this Kāla is slain. Śambhu at once said to her: O moon-faced one, hear how sinless yogins, single-minded, cast away the whole serpent of Time.
m.5.26.14: Śaṅkara said: The body, composed of the five elements, always endowed with their qualities, is produced, O fair-hipped one; and the earthly body dissolves into them.
m.5.26.15: From space wind is born, and from wind fire is born; from fire water is declared to arise, and from that earth comes into being.
m.5.26.16: The elements beginning with earth go successively into the higher one. Earth is said to have five qualities, and water four.
m.5.26.17: Fire likewise has three qualities, and wind two; space has sound as its single quality—so it is declared regarding earth and the rest.
m.5.26.18: Sound, touch, form, taste, and smell the fifth: when an element gives up its own respective quality, then that element perishes.
m.5.26.19: When it takes up its quality, it is said to be manifested. Know the five elements thus in truth, O queen of the gods.
m.5.26.20: Therefore, O goddess, the yogin desiring to conquer Time should constantly and diligently contemplate the qualities arising from the elements' portions, each at its own time.
m.5.26.21: The Goddess said: How is Time thoroughly conquered by yogins, O Lord, knower of yoga? Whether by meditation or by mantra—tell me all that.
m.5.26.22: Śaṅkara said: Listen, O goddess; I shall explain, out of a wish for the welfare of yogins. This exposition of supreme knowledge should not be given to just anyone.
m.5.26.23: It should be given to one who has faith, who is devoted and wise, not an unbeliever, pure, and ever devoted to dharma, O lovely lady.
m.5.26.24: The knower of yoga should practise yoga with steady breath on a good seat; in darkness, without a lamp, when people are asleep, he should hold concentration.
m.5.26.25: Closing the ears with the index fingers and pressing them for a short while, a piercing sound is then heard, arising from the inner fire.
m.5.26.26: Thus practising from twilight, food eaten is digested even in a moment; it quickly destroys all diseases and the many afflictions such as fever.
m.5.26.27: He who daily observes this form of sound for two ghaṭikās, having conquered death and desire, may roam here at his own will.
m.5.26.28: He becomes all-knowing and all-seeing and attains every siddhi. As a cloud thunders in the sky, well laden with the waters of the rainy season, so is that sound.
m.5.26.29: Hearing it, the yogin is at once freed from the bondage of saṃsāra. Then for yogins it constantly becomes subtler than the subtle.
m.5.26.30: Thus, O goddess, I have told you the method and sequence of śabdabrahman. As one seeking grain discards the straw, one should abandon bondage entirely.
m.5.26.31: Those who, having obtained this śabdabrahman, still long for something else, strike the sky with their fist and crave hunger and thirst.
m.5.26.32: One should know this supreme brahman—giver of happiness, cause of liberation, not external, imperishable, and free of all limiting adjuncts.
m.5.26.33: Deluded by the noose of Time, fallen under the sway of death's noose, those sinful, evil-minded ones do not know śabdabrahman.
m.5.26.34: They wander in saṃsāra as long as one does not find the abode; but when the supreme reality is known, one is freed from the bondage of birth.
m.5.26.35: Having diligently conquered that enemy, sleep and sloth, the great obstacle, sitting always in a comfortable posture, practising śabdabrahman thus—
m.5.26.36: Even a man a hundred years old, having obtained this, should practise it as long as he lives: it brings conquest of death, firmness of body, health, and increase of vital breath.
m.5.26.37: Its proof is seen in an old man; how much more in a young person. It is not Oṃkāra, nor a mantra, nor a seed-syllable, nor a letter.
m.5.26.38: The unstruck, unutterable śabdabrahman, auspicious and supreme—on that the wise constantly and diligently meditate, O goddess, my dear.
m.5.26.39: Therefore nine sounds are declared, discerned by knowers of prāṇa. I shall carefully describe them—the attainment of nāda—in due order.
m.5.26.40: The roar (ghoṣa), the ring of bell-metal, the horn, the bell, those born of the vīṇā, flute and the like, the kettledrum, the sound of the conch, and ninth, the thunder of clouds.
m.5.26.41: Having set aside the nine sounds, one should practise the tuṅkāra. Meditating in this way at all times, the yogin is not stained by merits or by sins.
m.5.26.42: O Devī, when one who listens through the practice of yoga no longer hears the sound, he dies; therefore the yogin should remain practising day and night.
m.5.26.43: From that practice the sound arises, and within seven days one conquers death. That sound, O Devī, is ninefold; I shall describe it as it truly is.
m.5.26.44: First it sounds as ghoṣa, supreme, purifying the self; this sound removes all diseases and is excellent for subjugation and attraction.
m.5.26.45: Second it sounds like bronze; with it one can halt the movement of living beings, and can bind poison and all spirits and planetary seizers—there is no doubt of this.
m.5.26.46: Third it sounds like a horn; one should employ it in sorcery, and apply it for causing enmity, for driving away, and for killing an enemy.
m.5.26.47: The fourth, the Supreme Lord declares, is the sound of a bell; it attracts all the gods—how much more men on earth.
m.5.26.48: And the maidens of the Yakṣas and Gandharvas, drawn by it, grant the yogin great siddhi as he desires, or even at his will.
m.5.26.49: The fifth sound is the vīṇā, always heard by yogins; from it, O Devī, arises the power of seeing from afar.
m.5.26.50: For one meditating on the sound of the flute, knowledge of all principles arises; and one meditating on the kettledrum becomes free from old age and death.
