m.5.38.32: Then King Bāhu, his kingdom taken, went to the forest; followed by his wife and grief-stricken, he gave up his life.
m.5.38.33: His wife, a Yādava princess, who was pregnant, had followed behind him; and poison had been given to her by her co-wife out of jealousy over her bearing the first son.
m.5.38.34: She, having prepared her husband's pyre, was ascending the fire; but Aurva the Bhārgava, O king, out of compassion restrained her.
m.5.38.35: Dwelling in his hermitage for the protection of the embryo, the queen served that best of sages, remembering Śaṅkara in her heart.
m.5.38.36: One day her embryo indeed came forth together with the poison, at an auspicious hour and under an auspicious ascendant, joined with five exalted planets.
m.5.38.37: And with that ascendant strong in every way, O best of sages, the mighty-armed king named Sagara was born.
m.5.38.38: Aurva performed the birth ceremony and other rites for that great soul, taught him the Vedas and śāstras, and then bestowed the missile on him.
m.5.38.39: That fiery missile, hard to withstand even for the immortals, the greatly fortunate Sagara, best of kings, received with joy according to due rite.
m.5.38.40: Endowed with the power of that missile and with his own strength, he, enraged, swiftly slew the Haihayas by the might of the missile.
m.5.38.41: And that Sagara, the foremost of the famous, won fame throughout the worlds and established dharma on the surface of the earth.
m.5.38.42: Then the Śakas, together with the Yavanas, the Kāmbojas and likewise the Pāhlavas, being slain at that time, went to Vasiṣṭha for refuge.
m.5.38.43: The greatly radiant Vasiṣṭha, having made a stratagem by means of an agreement and having given them assurance of safety, restrained King Sagara.
m.5.38.44: Sagara, mindful of his own vow and having heard his preceptor's word, destroyed their dharma and made them alter the style of their hair.
m.5.38.45: Having shaved half the head of the Śakas, he let them go; he shaved the whole head of the Yavanas, and likewise of the Kāmbojas.
m.5.38.46: The Pāradas were made shaven-haired and the Pāhnavas bearers of beards; all of them were made by that great-souled one devoid of Vedic recitation and the vaṣaṭ-call.
m.5.38.47: And the whole earth was conquered righteously by that king; all those kṣatriyas, dear one, were thus made devoid of dharma in former times.
m.5.38.48: That king, victorious through dharma, having conquered this earth, the ruler had a horse consecrated for the horse-sacrifice.
m.5.38.49: While he was letting it roam, that horse went to the south-eastern ocean, accompanied by his sixty thousand sons, O sage.
m.5.38.50: That horse was stolen near the seashore by Śakra, king of the gods, who was pursuing his own interest, and was made to enter the earth.
m.5.38.51: Then the great king Sagara, to search for that horse, had that region dug up on all sides by his sons.
m.5.38.52: Then, as the great ocean was being dug there, they came upon that primeval Person, the god Kapila, whose form is the universe.
m.5.38.53: By the fire that arose from his eyes as he awoke, the sixty thousand were burnt; only four were left.
m.5.38.54: Harṣaketu, Suketu, likewise another, Dharmaratha, and the valiant Pañcajana — these were the kings who continued his lineage.
m.5.38.55: And the blessed Hari himself gave him five boons: lineage, intelligence, fame, the ocean as a son, and wealth.
m.5.38.56: And through that deed of his, the ocean obtained the status of Sāgara; and he recovered that sacrificial horse from the ocean.
m.5.38.57: That greatly renowned one performed a hundred horse-sacrifices; and there he worshipped the manifestations of Śambhu and the deities, he and the priests being of good vows.
m.5.38.iti: Thus ends the thirty-eighth adhyāya, named The description of the lineage from Satyavrata to Sagara, in the fifth saṃhitā, the Umā-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.5.39.1: Śaunaka said: How were the sons of Sagara born, heroic, mighty, valourous, sixty thousand in number? Or by what means? Tell me.
m.5.39.2: Sūta said: Sagara had two wives whose sins had been burnt away by austerity. Aurva, the best of sages, being pleased, granted the two of them a boon.
m.5.39.3: One chose sixty thousand sons of great vigour; the other, endowed with the boon, chose as she wished a single son to perpetuate the line.
m.5.39.4: Having come there, and having then obtained those many brave sons, she gave birth to a gourd full of seeds, which was divided apart.
m.5.39.5: All those boys, increasers of delight, grew up in due order in pots filled with ghee, tended by their own nurses.
m.5.39.6: Of those great-souled ones, who were burnt there by the fire of Kapila, one son named Pañcajana became king.
m.5.39.7: Then Pañcajana had a son named Aṃśumān, full of valour. His son was Dilīpa, whose son was Bhagīratha,
m.5.39.8: the lord who brought down Gaṅgā, the best of rivers, led her to the ocean, and regarded her as his daughter.
m.5.39.9: Bhagīratha's son was the king known as Śrutasena; his son was Nābhāga, a son supremely righteous.
m.5.39.10: Ambarīṣa was the son of Nābhāga; from him came Sindhudvīpa. The valourous Ayutājit was the heir of Sindhudvīpa.
m.5.39.11: Ayutājit's son was Ṛtuparṇa of great fame. He knew the secret of divine dice, and that king became the friend of Nala.
m.5.39.12: Ṛtuparṇa's son was Anuparṇa of great splendour; his son was Kalmāṣapāda, also called by name Mitrasaha.
m.5.39.13: Kalmāṣapāda's son was renowned as Sarvakarman; and the renowned Anaraṇya was the son of Sarvaśarman.
m.5.39.14: Anaraṇya's son was the learned king Muṇḍidruha; his son was Niṣadha, and then Rati, also called Khaṭvāṅga,
m.5.39.15: by whom, having come here from heaven and obtained life for only a muhūrta, all three worlds were won through wisdom and truth, O sinless one.
m.5.39.16: His son was Dīrghabāhu; Raghu was his son. Aja was his son, and from him came Daśaratha.
m.5.39.17: From Daśaratha was born Rāma, righteous-souled and of great fame — he, a portion of Viṣṇu and a great devotee of Śiva, by whom the descendant of Pulastya Rāvaṇa was slain.
m.5.39.18: His story has been described in many ways in the Purāṇas and is well known in the Rāmāyaṇa; therefore it is not told here in detail.
m.5.39.19: To Rāma was born a son, renowned as Kuśa. From Kuśa was born Atithi, and his son was Niṣadha.
m.5.39.20: Niṣadha's son was Nala, and Nala's son was Nabha. From Nabha came Puṇḍarīka, and after him Kṣemadhanvā is remembered.
m.5.39.21: Kṣemadhanvā's son was the powerful Devānīka; Devānīka's son was the lord named Ahīnagu.
m.5.39.22: Ahīnagu's heir was the valourous one named Sahasvān; his son was Vīrasena, who was born in the Ikṣvāku lineage.
m.5.39.23: Vīrasena's heir was Pāriyātra; then came a son named Bala, and from him was born a son, Sthala.
m.5.39.24: From him came a son, the powerful Yakṣa, born of a portion of the Sun. His son was Aguṇa, and from him came a son, Vidhṛti.
m.5.39.25: His son Hiraṇyanābha became a teacher of yoga; he was a disciple of the sage Jaimini, skilled in the knowledge of the Self.
m.5.39.26: From that best of kings Kauśalya Yājñavalkya then learned the yoga called adhyātma, which cleaves the knot of the heart.
m.5.39.27: His son was named Puṣya; his son was called Dhruva; his son was Agnivarṇa, and after him a son named Śīghra.
m.5.39.28: His son, named Maru, became perfected in yoga; that lord dwells even today in the place called Kalāpa village.
m.5.39.29: At the end of the Kali age, together with the sages dwelling there, he himself will restore the vanished Solar dynasty in particular.
m.5.39.30: His son was Pṛthuśruta; his son is remembered as Sandhi; his son was Amarṣaṇa, and his son was Marutvān.
m.5.39.31: His son was Viśvasāhva; his son was Prasenajit; his son was Takṣaka, and his son was Bṛhadbala.
m.5.39.32: These past kings of the Ikṣvāku dynasty have been fully recounted. Now hear of the future kings of that line, most knowing in dharma.
m.5.39.33: Bṛhadbala's son will be Bṛhadraṇa; the son of Bṛhadraṇa will be Urukriya.
m.5.39.34: His son will be Vatsavṛddha; after him the son Prativyomā; his son will be Bhānu, then Divāka, a commander of armies.
m.5.39.35: His son will be Sahadeva, a great hero; his son Bṛhadaśva; and his son the mighty Bhānumān.
m.5.39.36: Bhānumān's son will be the valourous Pratīkāśva; his son will be Supratīka, the best of kings.
m.5.39.37: His son will be Marudeva; then Sunakṣatra will be; his son Puṣkara; and his son Antarikṣa, O brāhmaṇas.
m.5.39.38: His son will be the heroic Sutapas; and after him the son of Mitracitta, Bṛhadbhāja; and his son is named Barhi.
m.5.39.39: His son will be Kṛtañjaya, and his son Raṇañjaya; then Sañjaya, and his son Maya; and his son Śākya.
m.5.39.40: His son will be Śuddhoda; his son Lāṅgala; his son Prasenajit; and his son the one called Śūdraka.
m.5.39.41: Ruṇaka will be his son; Suratha is remembered as his son. Sumitra will be his son, who is indeed the very end of the lineage's continuance.
m.5.39.42: This lineage of the Ikṣvākus — of kings of wondrous valour, most righteous and of good deeds — will indeed end with Sumitra.
m.5.39.43: Having reached Sumitra as its king, that auspicious lineage will come to its end in the Kali age; then, in the Kṛta age of the brāhma order, it will flourish again.
m.5.39.44: Thus, in the Vaivasvata lineage, the kings born of the Ikṣvāku line, givers of abundant sacrificial gifts, have been proclaimed according to their prominence.
m.5.39.45: This supremely meritorious creation line is that of Āditya Vivasvat and of the god Śrāddhadeva, the bestower of prosperity on creatures.
m.5.39.46: A man who reads or hears this creation line of Āditya, blessed with offspring and having enjoyed supreme happiness here, attains union (sāyujya) with the deity.
m.5.39.iti: Thus ends the thirty-ninth adhyāya, named The description of the kings born in the lineage of Vaivasvata, in the fifth saṃhitā, the Umā-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.5.40.1: Vyāsa said: Having heard thus the unsurpassed account of the lineage of the Sun, Śrāddhadeva, Śaunaka, the best of sages, respectfully questioned Sūta.
m.5.40.2: Śaunaka said: O Sūta, O Sūta, may you live long, disciple of Vyāsa; salutation to you. You have made us hear a supreme, divine and supremely purifying story.
m.5.40.3: You have spoken of the Sun as Śrāddhadeva, the increaser of the noble lineage. A doubt has arisen in me about that; I state it before you.
m.5.40.4: From what cause indeed does Vivasvat, the Āditya, have the status of Śrāddhadeva? I wish to hear that with delight; cut away this doubt of mine.
m.5.40.5: And tell me also, O lord, the greatness of the śrāddha and its fruit, by which the ancestors, being pleased, join him the performer with welfare.
m.5.40.6: And I wish to hear this too: the excellent creation of the Pitṛs. Narrate it in detail; show compassion, O greatly wise one.
m.5.40.7: Sūta said: I shall gladly tell you all of it, the creation of the Pitṛs, O Śaunaka, as it was narrated by Mārkaṇḍeya to Bhīṣma when he inquired.
m.5.40.8: It was sung by Sanatkumāra to the wise Mārkaṇḍeya; I shall declare it to you, a teaching that bestows the fruit of all desires.
m.5.40.9: Questioned by Yudhiṣṭhira, Bhīṣma, the best of upholders of dharma, lying on the bed of arrows, spoke; hear that, I tell it to you.
m.5.40.10: Yudhiṣṭhira said: How indeed is prosperity obtained among men by one who desires prosperity? I wish to hear this: doing what does one not come to grief?
m.5.40.11: Sūta said: Having heard the question put by Yudhiṣṭhira, Bhīṣma, the knower of dharma, spoke these words with great delight while all were listening.
m.5.40.12: Bhīṣma said: O Yudhiṣṭhira, those men who perform śrāddhas with devotion — through the śrāddhas each gratifies all of that, by the grace of the Pitṛs.
m.5.40.13: Men desiring fruits always perform śrāddhas, intending them for the father and likewise for the father's father,
m.5.40.14: and the father's grandfather, always in the three piṇḍas. The Pitṛs grant dharma to one desiring dharma, and progeny to one desiring progeny,
m.5.40.15: and prosperity to one desiring prosperity they grant, O Yudhiṣṭhira.
m.5.40.16: Yudhiṣṭhira said: The ancestors of some dwell in heaven, of others again in hell; and the fruit born of action is said to be fixed for living beings.
m.5.40.17: How do those śrāddhas, once offered, reach the ancestors? And how are those who dwell in hell able to obtain that fruit?
m.5.40.18: I have heard that even the gods in heaven worship the Pitṛs. I wish to hear this; tell me in detail.
m.5.40.19: Bhīṣma said: Here I shall recount to you, as I heard it, O subduer of foes, what was sung long ago by my father after he had gone to the other world.
m.5.40.20: At the time of my father's śrāddha, I held up the piṇḍa; my father, breaking through the ground, asked to receive it from my hand.
m.5.40.21: But I, concluding, this is not the rule seen in the ritual code, then gave the piṇḍa on the kuśa grass itself, without wavering.
m.5.40.22: Then my father, satisfied and pleased with me, spoke in a sweet voice, O best of the Bharatas, O sinless one:
m.5.40.23: Through you, a wise knower of dharma, I truly have an heir; I have been saved. The test was made by me, O best of men.
m.5.40.24: Whatever standard a king sets by his righteous conduct, the subjects always follow that, the conduct set as a standard.
m.5.40.25: Hear, O best of the Bharatas, the eternal Vedic duties. The standard of Vedic dharma has been upheld by you, my son.
m.5.40.26: Therefore, greatly pleased with you, I lovingly give you an unsurpassed boon, hard to obtain in the three worlds; accept it.
m.5.40.27: Death shall have no power over you as long as you wish to live; only after receiving permission from you will death prevail.
m.5.40.28: Or what other excellent boon that you desire shall I give you further? Tell me, O best of the Bharatas, what is in your mind.
m.5.40.29: When he had spoken thus, I saluted him with joined palms and said: I am fulfilled, since you are pleased, O giver of honour. I ask a certain question; let it be answered by you yourself.
m.5.40.30: He said to me: Speak it; if you wish, I shall tell you. Thus addressed, I asked him there, and the king, being asked, explained it.
m.5.40.31: Śantanu said: Hear, dear son; I shall answer your question truly, and tell the whole Pitṛkalpa, which I heard from Mārkaṇḍeya.
m.5.40.32: What you ask me, dear one, that very thing I asked the great sage Mārkaṇḍeya, and he, the knower of dharma, told me.
m.5.40.33: Mārkaṇḍeya said: Hear, O king: once, as I was gazing at the sky, I saw a great aerial chariot coming then near the mountain.
m.5.40.34: In that aerial chariot I saw a couch with the lustre of blazing embers, of great radiance, glowing, uniform and charming.
m.5.40.35: And there I saw, lying, a person of blazing splendour, the size of a thumb, like fire placed within fire.
m.5.40.36: I, having offered salutation to him and bowed my head to the lord, asked him: How may we know you, O mighty one?
m.5.40.37: That righteous one said to me: You do not possess that austerity by which you could know me, O sage, the son of Brahmā.
m.5.40.38: Know me as Sanatkumāra; what shall I do for you? The other sons of Brahmā are younger than I,
m.5.40.39: seven invincible brothers whose lineages are established. But we follow the ascetic's dharma, having restrained the self within the self.
m.5.40.40: As I was born, so I have remained; I am known as Kumāra. Therefore this name of mine, Sanatkumāra, has been declared, O sage.
m.5.40.41: Because, with devotion, you have performed austerities out of a longing to see me, here I am, seen by you. May good befall you. What wish of yours shall I fulfil?
m.5.40.42: To him who had spoken thus I said: Listen, O Lord, and narrate to me exactly as it happened the original creation of the Pitṛs.
m.5.40.43: Thus addressed, he said to me: Listen to all of it as it truly is. I shall tell you faithfully, dear child, the auspicious creation of the Pitṛs.
m.5.40.44: Sanatkumāra said: Long ago Brahmā created the gods and said to them: Worship me. But, setting him aside, they, eager for rewards, worshipped their own selves.
m.5.40.45: They were cursed by Brahmā: Fools, you shall become bereft of understanding. Therefore, knowing nothing and deprived of understanding, they approached the Grandfather;
m.5.40.46: bowing down, they all said to him: Please grant us your favour. Thus addressed, he spoke this to them, solely for the sake of expiation:
m.5.40.47: Ask your own sons; then you will regain knowledge. Thus told, they, bereft of understanding, earnestly questioned their sons.
m.5.40.48: Solely for the sake of expiation, the heaven-dwellers regained their understanding. Go, little sons — thus were they addressed by their sons, O sinless one.
m.5.40.49: Then those gods, under the curse, having been told by their sons, go, little sons, went and questioned the Creator about the meaning of being called sons.
m.5.40.50: Then the god Brahmā said to those doubting gods: Listen, all you immortals: you are not knowers of Brahman.
m.5.40.51: Therefore, what was told to you by those sons of yours, the best of the wise, should be accepted, casting aside doubt, just so and not otherwise.
m.5.40.52: You gods and you Pitṛs, dwellers of heaven, worship one another with great love, granting the fruits of all desires.
m.5.40.53: Sanatkumāra said: Then, by Brahmā's word, their doubts dispelled, they became loving towards one another and bestowers of happiness, O tiger among sages.
m.5.40.54: Then the gods said to them: Since we were called little sons by you, therefore you shall be our fathers — there is no doubt.
m.5.40.55: Whoever performs the rite in the śrāddha for the ancestors — no doubt — will be blessed; Soma, nourished by śrāddhas, will nourish the worlds:
m.5.40.56: the ocean, the mountains and forests, filled with moving and unmoving beings. And those men who, desiring prosperity, perform śrāddhas —
m.5.40.57: to them the ancestors, ever pleased, will grant prosperity. And those who in the śrāddha offer three rice-balls (piṇḍa), with name and lineage (gotra) —
m.5.40.58: the fathers and great-grandfathers, present everywhere and satisfied by the offerings of śrāddha, will continually prosper them.
m.5.40.59: So let that statement be true, O heaven-dwellers: we are all sons and fathers of one another.
m.5.40.60: Thus those Pitṛs and the gods, in accordance with dharma, became sons of each other; they are renowned on the face of the earth as fathers of one another.
m.5.40.iti: Thus ends the fortieth adhyāya, named The description of the power of the Pitṛs, in the section on śrāddha, in the fifth saṃhitā, the Umā-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.5.41.1: Sanatkumāra said: O best of ascetics, seven groups of Pitṛs (ancestors) are declared to dwell in heaven: four are embodied, and three are without form.
m.5.41.2: The hosts of gods worship them, and likewise the foremost classes, the brahmins and the rest. They, in turn, first nourish Soma by the power of yoga.
m.5.41.3: Therefore śrāddha offerings should be given, and especially to yogins. For all, the vessel should be of silver, or else adorned with silver.
m.5.41.4: A śrāddha given with the svadhā call placed first truly pleases the Pitṛs — having first made the nourishing offering to Fire, to Soma and to Yama,
m.5.41.5: and making the offering facing north into the fire, or, if there is no fire, into water. Whoever pleases the Pitṛs with devotion, the Pitṛs please him in return.
m.5.41.6: The Pitṛs bestow nourishment and abundant offspring, heaven, increase of health, and whatever else is desired.
m.5.41.7: O sage, the rite for the Pitṛs surpasses even the rite for the gods. You are devoted to the Pitṛs, O brahmin seer; through that you are free from old age and death.
m.5.41.8: The state that belongs to one devoted to the Pitṛs, O sage, is not reached through yoga. Therefore devotion to the Pitṛs should be practised especially, O great sage.
m.5.41.9: Mārkaṇḍeya said: Having spoken thus, the lord of the gods, after quickly granting him an eye endowed with discernment, hard to obtain even for the gods, went to his yogic state.
m.5.41.10: Listen further, O Bhīṣma: long ago the brahmin sons of Bhāradvāja, having attained the discipline of yoga, fell from it through misconduct.
m.5.41.11: Vāgduṣṭa, Krodhana, Hiṃsra, Piśuna, Kavi, Khasṛṣa and Pitṛvartī — so they were by names and likewise by deeds.
m.5.41.12: They were sons of Kauśika, dear one, and became disciples of Garga. When their father died, they all were then living away from home.
m.5.41.13: At the command of their teacher they were tending a milch cow, a tawny one with a calf of like colour; and then they all went astray.
m.5.41.14: On the way, as they were tormented by hunger, through childishness and delusion, O Bhārata, a cruel thought arose in them then to kill that cow.
m.5.41.15: Kavi and Khasṛpa pleaded for her, but the intent did not go away then; nor were those two able then to restrain their own brothers.
m.5.41.16: But Pitṛvartī, the brahmin among them who daily performed śrāddha as his regular rite, endowed with devotion to the Pitṛs, spoke to them all in anger:
m.5.41.17: If it must be done, let it be carried out as an offering to the Pitṛs, all of you performing the śrāddha with collected minds.
m.5.41.18: In this way this cow too will attain merit, there is no doubt; having worshipped the Pitṛs according to dharma, no unrighteousness will befall us.
m.5.41.19: Thus addressed, they all then sprinkled the cow, dedicated her to the Pitṛs, and consumed her, O Bhārata.
m.5.41.20: Having consumed the cow, they all reported to their teacher: The cow was killed by a tiger; please take the calf.
m.5.41.21: Out of guilelessness that brahmin accepted the calf. But through their false conduct the sin of cow-killing fell upon them.
m.5.41.22: Then, after some time, those seven brothers, dear one, met death when their lifespan came to an end.
m.5.41.23: Because of their cruelty, their violence, and their ignoble conduct toward the teacher, the seven brothers were born as those who delighted in fierce violence.
m.5.41.24: Thus the seven were born as hunters among the Daśārṇas, sons of a hunter, strong and high-minded, yet discerning in dharma.
m.5.41.25: Next they were all deer on the lovely mountain Kālañjara, devoted to their own duty, free from delusion, yet trembling with anxiety.
m.5.41.26: Reflecting on that very matter, which arose from remembrance of their former birth, they lived as forest-dwellers, patient, free from the pairs of opposites, and without possessions.
m.5.41.27: All those forest-dwellers were of good deeds and true dharma, free from unrighteous conduct, having attained the memory of their past births.
m.5.41.28: The dharma they had heard in former births in the houses of their teachers — just so their minds remained fixed, even within saṃsāra, upon turning back from the world.
m.5.41.29: Those ascetics, living on whatever food they obtained, gave up their lives in the midst of the mountain; and the places where they fell, O Bhārata,
m.5.41.30: are seen just so even today on the mountain Kālañjara, O king. Through that deed they were born as ones who had left behind both good and evil.
m.5.41.31: From an auspicious birth they passed to a more auspicious one, becoming cakravāka birds; in the auspicious land of Śaradvīpa the seven lived as water-dwellers.
m.5.41.32: Renouncing the life of mates, these sages upholding dharma were named Niḥsaṅga, Nirmama, Śānta, Nirdvandva, Niṣparigraha,
m.5.41.33: Nivṛtti and Nirvṛta — so were the birds known by name. All those birds were celibate and lived according to dharma.
m.5.41.34: Remembering their births, well matured, the seven celibates dwelt together, of true dharma, ever free from change.
m.5.41.35: Because of the false conduct toward their teacher committed through delusion in their brahmin birth, they received birth in animal wombs; and through the śrāddha they obtained knowledge.
m.5.41.36: Likewise, because the śrāddha was performed by them, steadfast, for the sake of the rite of the Pitṛs, knowledge and birth were then obtained in succession, each higher in quality.
m.5.41.37: The sacred knowledge (brahman) heard in former births in the houses of teachers remained established just so; therefore one should diligently cultivate knowledge.
m.5.41.38: Sumanas, Suvāk, Śuddha, the fifth Chidradarśaka, Svatantra and Suyajña — these are known by name as the Kulīṅgas.
m.5.41.39: While those birds wandered there, following dharma, a noteworthy event took place; hear of it, O great sage.
m.5.41.40: The king, lord of the Nīpas, endowed with majesty, glorious, surrounded by his women of the inner palace, entered that forest there.
m.5.41.41: That cakravāka bird named Svatantra, having seen that king going along, endowed with happiness and furnished with royal splendour, longed to be like him.
m.5.41.42: If there is any merit of mine, or austerity, or even religious observance — I am worn out by fasting and by unwavering austerity —
m.5.41.43: then by the full fruit of all that I have done, may I become such a king, a vessel of every good fortune.
m.5.41.44: Then the two cakravākas, his companions, said: Let us two be your ministers, wishing for what is dear and beneficial to you.
m.5.41.45: Saying, so be it, the boon was granted; then that was the destiny of him whose self was in yoga. And thus those two cakravākas spoke their own words in reply.
m.5.41.46: Sumanas said: Since you, speaking for worldly action even after attaining that discipline of yoga, ask for such a boon, therefore hear my words.
m.5.41.47: You will be a king, dear one, in Kāmpilya, the best of cities; and these two will be your ministers, overcome by their deviation from yoga.
m.5.41.48: The other three did not speak of kingship to those four companions. Again he showed favour: among them Sumanas spoke.
m.5.41.49: The curse will have an end; you will attain yoga again. And this Svatantra will know the cries of all creatures.
m.5.41.50: Through the grace of the ancestors, merit has been obtained by you, since, having sprinkled the cow according to dharma, its parts were offered to the ancestors.
m.5.41.51: Union with knowledge is, for all of us, the means to yoga. And this earnest statement, a single verse that has been uttered —
m.5.41.52: having heard it conveyed through another person, you will then attain yoga. Having said this, that bird, the wise Sumanas, fell silent.
m.5.41.53: Mārkaṇḍeya said: For the welfare of the worlds, dear one, O eminent son of Śantanu, I have thus told their story. What more do you wish to hear?
m.5.41.iti: Thus ends the forty-first adhyāya, named The description of the creation of the Pitṛs and of the destiny of the seven hunters, in the fifth saṃhitā, the Umā-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.5.42.1: Bhīṣma said: O Mārkaṇḍeya, greatly wise one, best among those who bear devotion to the Pitṛs, kindly tell me what happened after that, O best of sages.
m.5.42.2: Mārkaṇḍeya said: Those seven, who moved about the Mānasa lake, intent on the dharma of yoga, living on air and water, continually wasted away their bodies.
m.5.42.3: That king, surrounded by the women of his inner palace like Maghavan (Indra) in Nandana, having sported there for a very long time, went with his wife to his own city.
m.5.42.4: He had a son named Anūha, supremely righteous. Having installed that son in the kingdom, Vibhrāja went to the forest.
m.5.42.5: He began to perform austerities where those companions dwelt; there he, of great austerity, was without food, living on air.
m.5.42.6: Then, because it was illumined by him, that forest became well known by the name Vaibhrāja, bestowing success in yoga.
m.5.42.7: There indeed those birds—four steadfast in the dharma of yoga and three fallen from yoga—gave up their bodies.
m.5.42.8: In the city of Kāmpilya those seven great souls, headed by Brahmadatta, were born, all free from taint.
m.5.42.9: Here four retained memory of their former births, while three were deluded. Brahmadatta, independent and of great vigour, was born of Aṇuha.
m.5.42.10: Chidradarśin and Sunetra, masters of the Vedas and Vedāṅgas, who had dwelt together in their former birth, were born as heirs of a learned Vedic brahmin (śrotriya).
m.5.42.11: Pañcāla was a Bahvṛca (Ṛgvedin) and held the office of teacher; Puṇḍarīka, knower of two Vedas, was a Chandoga (Sāmavedin) and also an Adhvaryu.
m.5.42.12: Then the king, seeing his son Brahmadatta free of taint, consecrated him in his own kingdom and attained the supreme state.
m.5.42.13: Pañcāla and Puṇḍarīka, having established their sons in the house, entered the forest, and there they reached the highest state.
m.5.42.14: Brahmadatta's wife was named Sannati, O Bhārata; united with him in single-minded devotion, she delighted together with her husband.
m.5.42.15: The remaining companions, the cakravāka birds, were born in Kāmpilya as heirs of a śrotriya, in the family of a poor man, O king.
m.5.42.16: Dhṛtimān, Sumahātmā, Tattvadarśī and Nirutsuka—these four, accomplished in Vedic study, discerning the flaws of worldly life.
m.5.42.17: They, devoted to yoga and perfected, all set forth, having taken leave of one another and bowed to the lotus feet of Śambhu.
m.5.42.18: All those brahmins spoke again to their father: We shall make a provision for you by which you will maintain yourself.
m.5.42.19: Going to the taintless king Brahmadatta together with his ministers, you should make him hear this verse of great meaning.
m.5.42.20: Pleased at heart, he will give you villages and abundant enjoyments. Having said this much and having honoured that elder, they all attained the dharma of yoga and reached supreme bliss.
m.5.42.21: The father of those four great-souled brahmins, having learned the verse from his sons, felt as though he had accomplished his purpose.
m.5.42.22: He made the king and those two ministers hear that verse: Seven hunters in Daśārṇa, deer on Mount Kālañjara,
m.5.42.23: cakravākas on Śaradvīpa, swans on Lake Mānasa—they were born in Kurukṣetra as brahmins, masters of the Veda.
m.5.42.24: They have set out on the long road; why do you still languish? Hearing that, Brahmadatta, lord of men, fell into a swoon.
m.5.42.25: So too did his minister Pāñcāla and Puṇḍarīka, O Bhārata. Then, remembering that lake and regaining that yoga,
m.5.42.26: they endowed the brahmin with ample wealth and enjoyments. Having consecrated Viṣvaksena, subduer of foes, in his own kingdom,
m.5.42.27: Brahmadatta went to the forest with his wife; attaining yoga by sheer strength, he reached the state that is very hard to attain.
m.5.42.28: Puṇḍarīka too, righteous-souled, attained the unsurpassed Sāṅkhya-yoga; reaching the goal of yoga, he became perfected, purified by that deed.
m.5.42.29: Pāñcālya, of great austerity, having composed the Krama recitation of the Veda and produced the complete Śikṣā, attained the status of a teacher of yoga and foremost fame.
m.5.42.30: The valiant who, longing for freedom from rebirth, resort to this reach that supreme abode of Śambhu; may they destroy their sin today.
m.5.42.31: When a bodily, mental or verbal sin has been committed, O great sage, one should recite this properly with devotion, endowed with faith.
m.5.42.32: One is freed from all sins through repeatedly chanting Śiva's name. When this name of that God of gods is uttered,
m.5.42.33: sin dissolves like an unbaked pot in water. Therefore, when sin has been accumulated, immediately afterwards,
m.5.42.34: this should be recited for the allaying of sin, O great sage, and repeatedly by faithful men for obtaining the fruit of all desires.
m.5.42.35: Whoever reads this chapter or hears it for the sake of prosperity is freed from all sins and attains liberation; there is no doubt.
m.5.42.iti: Thus ends the forty-second adhyāya, named The description of the power of the ancestors, in the section on the ancestors, in the fifth saṃhitā, the Umā-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.5.43.1: Śaunaka said: O Sūta, O preceptor who is a disciple of Vyāsa, tell us now about the worship of the teacher, and also what is to be done at the end of hearing the text.
m.5.43.2: Sūta said: Having heard the supreme narrative, one should worship the teacher with devotion according to the rule; at the end of the text, with a gladdened mind, one should give gifts to the teacher according to the rule.
m.5.43.3: Then the wise man, having bowed to the speaker and having duly honoured him with ornaments for the hands and ears and with fine garments of soft cloth and the like,
m.5.43.4: and at the completion of the worship of Śiva, he should give a cow with her calf; having made a seat of gold weighing one pala, covered with cloth,
m.5.43.5: and having placed on it the auspicious text written in elegant letters, the wise man should give it to the teacher; thereby he becomes freed from the bonds of worldly existence.
m.5.43.6: A village, an elephant, a horse, and other things too according to one's capacity — all these, O sage, should be given to the great-souled reciter.
m.5.43.7: The Purāṇa heard properly, together with the prescribed procedure, is declared to be fruitful indeed; O sage Śaunaka, I have spoken only the truth.
m.5.43.8: Therefore, O sage, one should listen with devotion, in accordance with the prescribed procedure, to the Purāṇa, which is rich in the meaning of the Vedas, bestows merit, and is the heart of revelation (śruti).
m.5.43.iti: Thus ends the forty-third adhyāya, named The manner of worshipping Vyāsa, in the fifth saṃhitā, the Umā-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.5.44.1: The sages said: O greatly wise Sūta, treasury of compassion, tell us of the birth of Vyāsa. O master, O lord, by your supreme grace make us fulfilled.
m.5.44.2: The mother of Vyāsa is said to be the auspicious woman named Satyavatī; and that lady, it is said, was married by King Śantanu.
m.5.44.3: How was the great yogin Vyāsa born in her from Parāśara? A great doubt has arisen here; you should dispel it.
m.5.44.4: Sūta said: Once, while travelling on a pilgrimage, the yogin Parāśara by chance came to the lovely, auspicious bank of the Yamunā.
m.5.44.5: The righteous one then said to a Niṣāda fisherman who was having his meal: Take me quickly across the Yamunā by boat.
m.5.44.6: Thus addressed by that sage, the Niṣāda spoke to his own daughter Matsyagandhā: Girl, take him across quickly by boat.
m.5.44.7: O fortunate one, this ascetic, born from the womb of Adṛśyantī, an ocean of dharma, master of the four Vedas, wishes to cross.
m.5.44.8: Thus instructed by her father, Matsyagandhā ferried the great sage, radiant as the sun, seated in the boat.
m.5.44.9: Through the force of destiny, the great yogin—who had never been infatuated even on seeing the beauty of the Apsarases—became stricken with desire for her.
m.5.44.10: Wishing to take the charming fisherman's daughter, the sage touched her right hand with his right hand.
m.5.44.11: The large-eyed one said to him with a smile: What is this deed being done, condemned by those who restrain their speech (sages)?
m.5.44.12: You were born in the lovely lineage of Vasiṣṭha, O great-minded one, while I, O brāhmaṇa, am born of a Niṣāda; how could union between us two be fitting?
m.5.44.13: Human birth is hard to obtain, brāhmaṇhood especially; and even there, asceticism is hard to attain, O best of sages.
m.5.44.14: Endowed with learning, form, speech, lineage and character, you have fallen under the power of Kāma's arrows—this indeed is a great wonder.
m.5.44.15: Though he has set about an improper act, no one on earth is able to stop him from doing it, out of fear of this yogin's curse.
m.5.44.16: Having thus reflected in her heart, she said to the great sage: Have patience, master, until I have taken you across.
m.5.44.17: Sūta said: Hearing her words, Parāśara, king of yogins, swiftly let go of her hand, and then reached the other side of the river.
m.5.44.18: The sage, tormented by desire, again seized that girl; but the girl, trembling, said to that treasury of compassion:
m.5.44.19: O best of sages, I am foul-smelling, dark-complexioned, born of a Niṣāda; whereas you are of supremely noble thought, the best of yogins.
m.5.44.20: Union between us two is not fitting, like that of glass and gold; union between those alike in birth and form would bring happiness.
m.5.44.21: Being so addressed by her, he in a mere moment made the maiden Yojanagandhā ('fragrant for a league'), lovely in form and charming.
m.5.44.22: Again that sage, afflicted by desire, seized the girl; seeing him wishing to take her, Vāsavī spoke again:
m.5.44.23: Intercourse should be performed at night, not by day—so the scripture has declared. In union by day there is great fault, and also censure hard to bear.
m.5.44.24: Therefore wait until night comes. People are watching here, and my father is standing on the bank.
m.5.44.25: Hearing these words spoken by her, the bull among sages at once created a mist by the power of his merit.
m.5.44.26: When the mist had arisen, resembling night in its darkness, the girl, anxious about intercourse, again spoke to that sage:
m.5.44.27: O yogin, your seed is unfailing; if, having enjoyed me, you go away, I would be pregnant—then, master, what would become of me?
m.5.44.28: O greatly wise one, my vow of maidenhood will be destroyed; then people will laugh. What shall I say to my father?
m.5.44.29: Parāśara said: Delight with me freely, girl, in the pleasures born of love. Tell me your own wish; I will fulfil it now, beloved.
m.5.44.30: Because you make my command true, be Satyavatī by name, worthy of reverence by all yogins and even by the gods.
m.5.44.31: Satyavatī said: If neither my father nor my mother nor other people on earth come to know, and if my maidenhood is not destroyed, then accept me.
m.5.44.32: And, lord, may there be a son equal to you, possessed of wondrous power; may there be fragrance in my body always, and youth ever new.
m.5.44.33: Parāśara said: Listen, beloved: all you desire will be fulfilled. A son born of a portion of Viṣṇu, of great fame, will be yours.
m.5.44.34: Know that there is indeed some reason why I am afflicted by desire; for even on seeing the beauty of the Apsarases my mind was never deluded.
m.5.44.35: Having beheld you, fish-smelling one, I fell under the sway of delusion. Girl, what Brahmā has written on the forehead cannot turn out otherwise.
m.5.44.36: Your son, O fair-hipped one, will be the composer of the Purāṇas and the divider of the branches of the Veda, of renowned fame in the three worlds.
m.5.44.37: Having said this and enjoyed that lovely-limbed one, the master of yoga bathed in the water of the Yamunā and departed swiftly, O great sage.
m.5.44.38: She too quickly conceived an embryo radiant as the sun, and on an island of the Yamunā (daughter of the Sun) gave birth to a son like Kāmadeva.
m.5.44.39: Holding a water-pot in his left hand and an excellent staff in his right, adorned with tawny matted locks, he was a mass of splendour.
m.5.44.40: As soon as he was born, the radiant one said to his mother: Go, mother, as you wish; I too shall go hence.
m.5.44.41: Mother, whenever you have some task that your heart desires, I will come as soon as you remember me, in order to fulfil your wish.
m.5.44.42: Having said this and saluted his mother's feet, he who was a treasure of austerity went to a sacred ford that cleanses sin, to perform austerities.
m.5.44.43: She too, the virtuous one, went to her father's side, agitated by love for her son, recalling her son's deeds and describing her own good fortune.
m.5.44.44: Because the boy was born on an island (dvīpa), he became known as Dvaipāyana; and because he divided the branches of the Veda, he is celebrated as Vedavyāsa.
m.5.44.45: First he went to the king of tīrthas, Prayāga, which grants dharma, desire, wealth and liberation; then Naimiṣa, Kurukṣetra, Gaṅgādvāra, Avantikā,
m.5.44.46: Ayodhyā, Mathurā, Dvārakā, Amarāvatī, the Sarasvatī, the confluence of the Sindhu, and the meeting of the Gaṅgā with the ocean,
m.5.44.47: Kāñcī, Tryambaka, the bank of the Seven Godāvarīs, Kālañjara, Prabhāsa, and likewise the hermitage of Badarikā,
m.5.44.48: Mahālaya, likewise the Oṅkāra-kṣetra, Puruṣottama, Gokarṇa, Bhṛgukaccha, Bhṛgutuṅga and Puṣkara,
m.5.44.49: and the tīrthas beginning with Śrīparvata, and likewise Dhārātīrtha — having gone to these and bathed according to rule, he performed supreme austerity.
m.5.44.50: Thus, wandering through many tīrthas situated in various lands, the son of Kālikā Satyavatī reached the city of Vārāṇasī,
m.5.44.51: where Viśveśvara himself and the great goddess Annapūrṇā, the two treasures of compassion, shine forth to grant nectar to their devotees.
m.5.44.52: Having reached the tīrtha of Vārāṇasī and then seen Maṇikarṇikā, that lord of sages cast off the sin accumulated over ten million births.
m.5.44.53: Having seen all the liṅgas headed by Viśveśa, and bathed in all the pools, step-wells, wells and lakes,
m.5.44.54: having bowed to all the Vināyakas and saluted all the Gaurīs, and having worshipped Kālarāja Bhairava, the devourer of sin,
m.5.44.55: having diligently praised the gaṇas headed by Daṇḍanāyaka, and having pleased the Keśavas headed by Ādikeśava,
m.5.44.56: and having bowed again and again to the Suns headed by Lolārka, and tirelessly made offerings of piṇḍas at all the tīrthas,
m.5.44.57: the pure-souled one installed a liṅga named Vyāseśvara, by the sight of which, O brahmins, a man becomes a master of speech in the branches of learning.
m.5.44.58: Having worshipped with great devotion the liṅgas headed by Viśveśa, he pondered repeatedly: Which liṅga grants success quickly,
m.5.44.59: by worshipping which Mahādeva we may obtain all the branches of knowledge, and by whose grace I may gain the power to compose the Purāṇas?
m.5.44.60: Is it the glorious Oṅkāranātha, or perhaps Kṛttivāseśvara? Or Kedāreśa, Kāmeśa, Candreśa, or Trilocana?
m.5.44.61: Kāleśa, Vṛddhakāleśa, or Kalaśeśvara; Jyeṣṭheśa, Jambukeśa, or Jaigīṣavyeśvara?
m.5.44.62: Daśāśvamedha, Īśāna, or Drumacaṇḍeśa; Dṛkkeśa, Garuḍeśa, Gokarṇeśa, or Gaṇeśvara?
m.5.44.63: Or Prasannavadaneśa, Dharmeśa, Tārakeśvara, Nandikeśa, Nivāseśa, Patrīśa, or Prītikeśvara?
m.5.44.64: Parvateśa, Paśupati, or Hāṭakeśvara; or else Bṛhaspatīśvara, or Tilabhāṇḍeśa?
m.5.44.65: Is it Bhārabhūteśvara, or Mahālakṣmīśvara? Or Maruteśa, Mokṣeśa, Gaṅgeśa, or Narmadeśvara?
m.5.44.66: Kṛṣṇeśa, Parameśāna, or else Ratneśvara; Yāmuneśa, Lāṅgalīśa, or the all-pervading glorious Viśveśvara?
m.5.44.67: Or else Avimukteśvara, or Viśālākṣīśa; Vyāghreśvara, Varāheśa, or Vidyeśvara?
m.5.44.68: Varuṇeśa, Vidhīśa, or Harikeśeśvara; Bhavānīśa, Kapardīśa, Kandukeśa, or Ajeśvara?
m.5.44.69: Or else Viśvakarmeśvara, or Vīreśvara; Nādeśa, Kapileśa, or Bhuvaneśvara?
m.5.44.70: Vāṣkulīśa, Mahādeva, or else Siddhīśvara; Viśvedeveśvara, Vīrabhadreśa, or Bhairaveśvara?
m.5.44.71: Amṛteśa, Satīśa, or Pārvatīśvara; Siddheśvara, Mataṅgeśa, or else Bhūtīśvara?
m.5.44.72: Āṣāḍhīśa, Prakāśeśa, likewise Koṭirudreśvara, and Madālaseśvara — or perhaps Tilaparṇeśvara?
m.5.44.73: Or is it Hiraṇyagarbheśa, or the glorious Madhyameśvara? Among these and ten million other liṅgas, in which shall I take refuge?
m.5.44.74: Thus troubled by anxious thought, Vyāsa, whose self delighted in devotion to Śiva, reflected for a moment with a mind made steady by meditation.
m.5.44.75: Ah, I know. It had slipped my mind until now; my wish is accomplished: the liṅga worshipped by the Siddhas, which grants dharma, desire, wealth and liberation,
m.5.44.76: by the sight and touch of which the mind attains purity, and where indeed the door of heaven always stands open —
m.5.44.77: that supreme place in the great field of Avimukta, the field of the Siddhas, where abides the supreme liṅga called Madhyameśvara.
m.5.44.78: Indeed there is no other liṅga in Kāśī equal to Madhyameśvara, to see which the gods come at every festival day.
m.5.44.79: Therefore Mahādeva named Madhyameśvara is to be served; through worship of him many brahmins have attained perfection.
m.5.44.80: Since Śaṅkara, as the chief deity, stands in the middle of Kāśī for the happiness of the people of his own city, he is therefore called Madhyameśvara.
m.5.44.81: The Gandharva named Tumburu, and likewise the divine sage Nārada, by worshipping this Liṅga became masters of the science of music.
m.5.44.82: By worshipping this very one, Viṣṇu became the bestower of liberation; and so Brahmā, Viṣṇu and Rudra became the creator, preserver and destroyer.
m.5.44.83: Kubera too became the lord of wealth, and Vāmadeva indeed the king among Śaivas; the king named Khaṭvāṅga, who was childless, came to have offspring.
m.5.44.84: The Apsaras named Candrabhāmā, sweet-voiced as a cuckoo, dancing out of her own devotion, merged bodily into the midst of the Liṅga.
m.5.44.85: Śrīkara, the son of a cowherd woman, by serving Madhyameśvara obtained the rank of a gaṇa-leader of the compassionate Śiva.
m.5.44.86: Bhārgava and Gīṣpati, both gods worshipped by the Daityas and the Suras respectively, became masters of learning through the grace of the Lord Madhyameśa.
m.5.44.87: I too, worshipping here the Lord Madhyameśvara, shall surely and swiftly obtain the power to compose the Purāṇas.
m.5.44.88: Having thus made up his mind, the steadfast Vyāsa, son of Satyavatī, bathed in the waters of the Bhāgīrathī and, as a votary, took up a course of observance.
m.5.44.89: At times he lived on leaves, at times on fruits and vegetables; somewhere he lived on air, on water, and at times kept a vow of total fasting.
m.5.44.90: With such observances the righteous yogin worshipped Madhyameśvara at the three times of day with fruits from various trees.
m.5.44.91: When much time had thus passed, as the son of Kālikā, having bathed in the waters of the Tripathagā, was coming at dawn —
m.5.44.92: — just then the pure-souled one saw Maheśvara in the midst of the Liṅga: Madhyameśvara, the Lord, granter of the boons desired by devotees,
m.5.44.93: his left side adorned by Umā, with a tiger skin as upper garment, his form beautiful with the waves of the Gaṅgā moving in his mass of matted hair,
m.5.44.94: his locks moonlit by the radiance of the shining young autumn moon, all his limbs smeared with ash, his form white as camphor,
m.5.44.95: with eyes long, reaching to the ears, and lips red as coral, a boy with the form of a five-year-old, wearing ornaments fit for a child,
m.5.44.96: bearing a bodily radiance that humbles the pride of millions of Kandarpas, naked, his lotus-face smiling, playfully singing the Sāman,
m.5.44.97: an ocean of boundless compassion, bearing the name Bhaktavatsala (loving to devotees), quickly pleased, beloved of Umā, his face gracious with favour — Hara.
m.5.44.98: Having beheld him, with a voice choked with love he composed a hymn to him who is unreachable even by yogins, the friend of the afflicted, whose nature is consciousness.
m.5.44.99: Vedavyāsa said: O God of gods, O greatly blessed one, loving to those who seek refuge, hard to attain by speech, mind and action, beyond the range even of yogins.
m.5.44.100: The Vedas did not know your greatness, O Lord of Umā. You alone are the creator, sustainer and likewise destroyer of the world.
m.5.44.101: You are the first of all the gods, the Lord who is being, consciousness and bliss. You have neither name nor lineage; you are omniscient, O Sadāśiva.
m.5.44.102: You alone are the supreme Brahman, the remover of the noose of Māyā; you are not stained by the three guṇas, as a lotus leaf is not wetted by water.
m.5.44.103: You have no birth, no conduct, no country and no family; yet though such, you as Lord fulfil the desires of the three worlds.
m.5.44.104: Neither Brahmā, nor the Lord of Lakṣmī, nor the gods with Indra, nor the chief yogins know your true nature — you, such as you are, we worship.
m.5.44.105: From you is everything, and you indeed are everything; you are the Lord of Gaurī, the destroyer of the three cities; you are the child, the youth, the old man — you I fix in my heart.
m.5.44.106: Salutation to that Maheśa, meditated upon by devotees, to Śambhu, truly the Primeval Person, to Śaṅkara, the Supreme Self.
m.5.44.107: Having praised thus, as soon as he fell prostrate on the ground like a staff, that boy, delighted, spoke to Vedavyāsa.
m.5.44.108: Choose a boon, O yogin, whatever is in your mind; there is nothing that cannot be given, since I am subject to my devotees.
m.5.44.109: Then, rising up, delighted, the sage Vyāsa of great austerity replied: What is unknown to you who are omniscient, O Lord?
m.5.44.110: You are the inner Self of all, the blessed Śarva, the giver of everything; why does the Lord set me to begging, which brings abasement?
m.5.44.111: Hearing these words of Vyāsa of spotless mind, Mahādeva, bearing the form of a boy, smiled purely and said:
m.5.44.112: The boy said: O best of the knowers of Brahman, the wish you have formed in your heart will come true in a very short time, without doubt.
m.5.44.113: Abiding in your throat, O Brahmin, I, the Lord, the Inner Controller, shall properly bring forth the Purāṇas together with the Itihāsas.
m.5.44.114: This holy hymn uttered by you, the Abhilāṣāṣṭaka, grants desires when recited three times daily for a year in a shrine of Śambhu.
m.5.44.115: Recitation of this hymn is declared to increase learning and intelligence, to bring all prosperity, and to grant dharma and liberation to men.
m.5.44.116: Rising at dawn, well bathed, worshipping Śaṅkara's Liṅga and reciting this hymn for a year, even a fool would become a Bṛhaspati.
m.5.44.117: Whether by a woman or by a man, this hymn, recited with discipline for a year near the Liṅga, would increase intelligence and learning.
m.5.44.118: Having said this, that Mahādeva in the form of a boy merged into the Liṅga; and Vyāsa, shedding tears, was overwhelmed with love for Śiva.
m.5.44.119: Thus having obtained the boon from the great Lord Madhyameśvara, Vyāsa composed the eighteen Purāṇas with ease of his own.
m.5.44.120: The Brāhma, the Pādma, the Vaiṣṇava, the Śaiva, and likewise the Bhāgavata; the Bhaviṣya and the Nāradīya, and after that the Mārkaṇḍeya;
m.5.44.121: Then the Āgneya, the Brahmavaivarta, the Laiṅga and the Vārāha; then the one called Vāmana, the Kaurma, the Mātsya and the Gāruḍa;
m.5.44.122: likewise the Skānda, and the Purāṇa called Brahmāṇḍa, are proclaimed. They are bringers of fame and merit to the men who hear them, and their theme is the glory of Śaṅkara.
m.5.44.123: Sūta said: You earlier stated the names of the eighteen Purāṇas. Now, O best of Veda-knowers, give the explanation of those names.
m.5.44.124: Vyāsa said: This very question was put by Taṇḍi, born of Brahmā, addressing Nandikeśvara; what he said, I now tell.
m.5.44.125: Nandīśvara said: O Taṇḍi, since the speaker in it is the four-faced Brahmā himself, in person, that first Purāṇa is called the Brāhma, O sage.
m.5.44.126: That collection in which the greatness of the Padma Kalpa is related is therefore called the Pādma, the second Purāṇa.
m.5.44.127: The Purāṇa composed by Parāśara, which makes Viṣṇu known, is itself regarded as narrated by Vyāsa, because of the non-difference between son and father.
m.5.44.128: That in which, in the earlier and later sections, the deeds of Śiva are narrated abundantly — this is the Śaiva Purāṇa, as the knowers of the Purāṇas declare.
m.5.44.129: That in which the story of the Goddess Durgā is found is called the Bhāgavata — indeed, the Devī Purāṇa.
m.5.44.130: The Purāṇa spoken by Nārada they call the Nāradīya. That in which, O Taṇḍi, the great sage Mārkaṇḍeya was the speaker —
m.5.44.131: that is called the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa, the seventh. From its connection with Agni it is the Āgneya; from its telling of the future, the Bhaviṣya.
m.5.44.132: From the transformation (vivartana) of Brahman it is called the Brahmavaivarta; because it tells the story of the Liṅga, the Purāṇa is called the Liṅga.
m.5.44.133: The Purāṇa of the Boar is the Vārāha, the twelfth, O sage. That in which Skanda himself is the listener and Maheśvara in person the speaker —
m.5.44.134: that is called the Skānda. The story of Vāmana is the Vāmana; the Kaurma is the story of the Tortoise; the Mātsya is that proclaimed by the Fish.
m.5.44.135: That of which Garuḍa himself is the speaker is named the Gāruḍa; because it tells the story of the cosmic egg, it is proclaimed the Brahmāṇḍa.
m.5.44.136: Sūta said: This very question was put by me to the wise Vyāsa; then I heard from him the explanation of all the Purāṇas.
m.5.44.137: Thus Vyāsa was born from Parāśara in Satyavatī. He composed the Purāṇa collections and the excellent Mahābhārata.
m.5.44.138: Regarding Satyavatī's union with Parāśara and then again with Śantanu, O brahmin, you should not entertain doubt here.
m.5.44.139: This wondrous birth, which had its proper cause, has been narrated. In the conduct of the great, the discerning should take up only the virtues.
m.5.44.140: Whoever hears or even recites this supreme secret is freed from all sins and is honoured in the world of the sages.
m.5.44.iti: Thus ends the forty-fourth adhyāya, named The description of the birth of Vyāsa, in the fifth saṃhitā, the Umā-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.5.45.1: The sages said: We have heard the delightful story of Śambhu, filled with various narratives and joined with various incarnations, which grants enjoyment and liberation to men.
m.5.45.2: Now, O best of the knowers of Brahman, we wish to hear from you the charming story of the Mother of the world, the Blessed Goddess.
m.5.45.3: She who is the primordial, eternal Śakti of Maheśa, the Supreme Brahman, renowned as Umā, the supreme mother of the three worlds —
m.5.45.4: Two of her incarnations, Satī and Haimavatī, we have heard. O Sūta of great intellect, tell us of her other incarnations.
m.5.45.5: What intelligent person would grow weary of the act of hearing the virtues of the Holy Mother, which the wise never abandon?
m.5.45.6: Sūta said: Blessed are you, great souls; you are ever fulfilled, since you ask about the great story of Umā, the Supreme Mother.
m.5.45.7: The sages know that the dust of the lotus-feet of those who hear, ask about, and recite it is itself as sacred as the holy places.
m.5.45.8: Blessed and fulfilled are they, and blessed are their mother and family, whose mind is absorbed in the Holy Goddess, the supreme consciousness.
m.5.45.9: Those who do not praise the Queen of the gods, the cause of all causes, are deluded by the qualities of Māyā and are unfortunate; there is no doubt.
m.5.45.10: Those who do not worship the Great Goddess, an ocean of the essence of compassion, fall into the terrible blind well that is saṃsāra.
m.5.45.11: Just as one might abandon the Gaṅgā and go to desert water to quench one's thirst, so does one who abandons the Goddess go to another god distinct from her.
m.5.45.12: By the mere remembrance of her one effortlessly obtains the four aims of human life; what excellent man would abandon her?
m.5.45.13: Long ago the sage Medhas was asked this by the great-souled Suratha. What Medhas then said, listen to it; I shall tell you.
m.5.45.14: Formerly, in the Svārociṣa Manvantara, there was a king named Viratha. Suratha was his son, of great strength and valour.
m.5.45.15: He was generous in giving, truthful, skilled in his own dharma, accomplished, a devotee of the Goddess, an ocean of compassion, and protector of his subjects.
m.5.45.16: While he, with splendour like Indra's, was ruling the earth, there arose nine kings intent on seizing the land.
m.5.45.17: They besieged that king's capital named Kolā, and a tumultuous, dreadful battle took place with them.
m.5.45.18: In the battle that king was defeated by those powerful hosts of enemies, and, his kingdom wholly seized, he was driven out of Kolā.
m.5.45.19: That king came to his own city and ruled with his ministers; but there too he was defeated by powerful adversaries.
m.5.45.20: By fate, his own groups led by his ministers turned hostile, and they appropriated all the wealth that lay in the treasury.
m.5.45.21: Then the king left the city under the pretext of hunting; alone, mounting a horse, he went into a dense forest.
m.5.45.22: Wandering here and there, the king saw there the hermitage of an eminent sage, resplendent on every side with flower gardens,
m.5.45.23: filled with the sound of the Vedas, inhabited by peaceful creatures, surrounded on all sides by disciples, their disciples, and their disciples' disciples.
m.5.45.24: O wise ones, in that hermitage tigers and other mighty beasts did not harm the weak, owing to the power of that best of brahmins.
m.5.45.25: There the wise and very compassionate king dwelt, honoured by the lord of sages with kind words, food, and a seat.
m.5.45.26: One day that great king fell into an inescapable anxiety: Alas, for me, unfortunate, foolish, and bereft of power!
m.5.45.27: My kingdom has been taken entirely by hosts of enemies puffed up with pride. The kingdom protected by my forefathers is now enjoyed by enemies.
m.5.45.28: In this Caitra lineage there was no king like me. What shall I do? Where shall I go? How indeed may I regain the kingdom?
m.5.45.29: My long-standing officials and ministers — I do not know which king they have now approached and serve.
m.5.45.30: Having ruined the kingdom, I do not know what state they have now reached — those who were full of zeal on the battlefield and cutters-down of hosts of foes.
m.5.45.31: My great heroes serve another king. My mountain-like elephants and horses that ran swift as the wind —
m.5.45.32: and the treasury amassed by my forefathers — are they now being cared for by them or not? Thus the supremely righteous king fell under the sway of delusion.
m.5.45.33: Meanwhile a certain vaiśya arrived there. The king asked: Who are you, sir, and why have you come here?
m.5.45.34: Why do you appear dejected? Tell me this now. Hearing these pleasant words spoken by the king,
m.5.45.35: Samādhi, the best of vaiśyas, shedding tears from his eyes, replied to the king in words bowed with affection.
m.5.45.36: The merchant said: I am a vaiśya named Samādhi, born in a wealthy family. O lord of the earth, I was cast out by my sons, wife, and others out of greed for wealth.
m.5.45.37: O king, grieved by my own karma, I have come to the forest. I do not know the welfare of my sons, grandsons, and wives,
m.5.45.38: of my brothers, nephews, other kin, and friends; I do not rightly know their welfare, O lord, ocean of compassion.
m.5.45.39: The king said: Why do you, like a foolish creature, cherish love for those wicked sons and others, greedy for wealth, by whom you were driven out?
m.5.45.40: The merchant said: O king, you have spoken rightly, words rich in essential meaning; yet my mind is greatly deluded by the noose of affection.
m.5.45.41: Thus, O best of sages, the merchant and the king, both troubled by delusion, then went into the presence of Medhas, the foremost of sages.
m.5.45.42: That valiant king of men, very steadfast, accompanied by the chief of merchants, bowed with his head to the best of yogins.
m.5.45.43: Joining his palms, the king spoke these words to the sage: O blessed one, you should now cut away the delusion of us two.
m.5.45.44: I, abandoned by royal fortune, have taken refuge in a dense forest; yet, though my kingdom has been taken away, contentment does not arise in me at all.
m.5.45.45: And this merchant has been driven out of his home by his own people, his wife and others; yet his attachment does not come to an end.
m.5.45.46: Tell us what the cause is here: though we both have knowledge, our mind has become agitated by delusion. This is indeed a great foolishness.
m.5.45.47: The sage said: Mahāmāyā, the sustainer of the world, eternal, whose form is Power — she, drawing away the minds of all, deludes them.
m.5.45.48: O lord, all the gods beginning with Brahmā, deluded by her māyā, do not know the supreme reality — what then to speak of humans?
m.5.45.49: She creates the whole universe, she alone protects it, and she alone withdraws it in time — the supreme Goddess possessing the three guṇas.
m.5.45.50: He alone with whom she, the boon-giver who takes forms at will, is pleased passes beyond delusion — not otherwise, O best of kings.
m.5.45.51: The king said: Who is that goddess Mahāmāyā who deludes all? And how was that goddess born? Kindly tell me, O sage.
m.5.45.52: The sage said: When the world had become a single ocean and Keśava, king of yogins, spreading Śeṣa as his bed, resorted to yogic sleep and slept,
m.5.45.53: then two asuras were born from the ear-wax of Viṣṇu, named Madhu and Kaiṭabha, renowned on the face of the earth.
m.5.45.54: Radiant like the sun at the dissolution, terrible, huge-bodied, with great jaws, their faces dreadful with fangs, as if devouring the worlds,
m.5.45.55: seeing the lotus-seated Brahmā on the lotus of the Lord's navel, they became ready to kill him, saying, Hey, who are you?
m.5.45.56: Seeing those two daityas, and Janārdana lying asleep in the ocean of milk, the eldest of the gods praised the supreme Goddess.
m.5.45.57: Brahmā said: Protect, protect me, O Mahāmāyā, loving to those who seek refuge, O Mother of the world, from these two terrible-looking daityas.
m.5.45.58: I bow to Mahāmāyā, Yoganidrā, Umā, Satī, Kālarātri, Mahārātri, Moharātri, higher than the highest;
m.5.45.59: mother of the three gods, eternal, granting the desired fruits to devotees, protectress of all the gods, an ocean of compassion.
m.5.45.60: Through your power I, Brahmā, Mādhava, and the Lord of Girijā create, protect, and in due time destroy the world.
m.5.45.61: You are Svāhā, you are Svadhā, you are modesty (hrī); you are considered pure intelligence. You alone, O Mother, are contentment, nourishment, peace, forbearance, hunger, and compassion.
m.5.45.62: You alone, O Mother, are Viṣṇumāyā; you alone are regarded as consciousness. You are declared the supreme Power; you too are shame and thirst.
m.5.45.63: You are error; you are in the form of memory; you abide in the form of the mother. You are Lakṣmī in the homes of men who practise virtuous conduct.
m.5.45.64: You are birth (jāti); you are considered livelihood; you alone are in the form of pervasion. You alone, in the form of consciousness, pervade all and stand established.
m.5.45.65: Such as you are, O Ambikā, delude these two invincible asuras; O source of the world, awaken Nārāyaṇa, the unborn, all-pervading Lord.
m.5.45.66: The sage said: Entreated by Brahmā for the destruction of Madhu and Kaiṭabha, she — Mahāvidyā, sustainer of the world, presiding deity of all knowledge —
m.5.45.67: appeared, O king, on the bright twelfth day of Phālguna, the Power renowned as Mahākālī, enchantress of the three worlds.
m.5.45.68: Then a voice arose from the sky: Do not fear, O lotus-seated one. Today, having slain Madhu and Kaiṭabha in battle, I shall destroy this thorn.
m.5.45.69: Having said this, Mahāmāyā came forth from the eyes, mouth and other parts of Hari and stood in view of Brahmā, whose birth is from the Unmanifest.
m.5.45.70: And Hṛṣīkeśa, Janārdana, god of gods, arose. He saw before him the two daityas named Madhu and Kaiṭabha.
m.5.45.71: A fight began between them and Viṣṇu of incomparable splendour; then for five thousand years there was a hand-to-hand combat.
m.5.45.72: Deluded by the power of Mahāmāyā, the two foremost dānavas said to Ramā's beloved: Choose the boon you desire.
m.5.45.73: Nārāyaṇa said: If you two are pleased with me, let this boon be given to me: may you both be slain by me. I ask no other boon of you.
m.5.45.74: The sage said: Seeing the earth become one ocean, they said to Keśava: Slay us where this earth is not flooded with water.
m.5.45.75: Saying, so be it, the Lord raised his brilliantly blazing discus and, placing their heads on his own thigh, cut them off.
m.5.45.76: Thus, O king, the origin of Kālikā has been told to you. Now hear likewise the birth of Mahālakṣmī, O wise one.
m.5.45.77: Though changeless, she takes form; though formless, the goddess Umā manifests age after age to destroy the suffering of the gods.
m.5.45.78: All this is the splendour of her will; her assuming a body is said to be in play, for the sake of her devotees' describing her qualities.
m.5.45.iti: Thus ends the forty-fifth adhyāya, named The description of the incarnation of Mahākālikā, in the section on the slaying of Madhu and Kaiṭabha, in the fifth saṃhitā, the Umā-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.5.46.1: The sage said: There was an asura named Rambhāsura, the crest-jewel of the Daitya race. From him was born a Dānava of great might named Mahiṣa.
m.5.46.2: That lord of the Danujas, having conquered all the gods in battle, ruled the kingdom in heaven, seated on great Indra's throne.
m.5.46.3: Then the defeated gods went to Brahmā for refuge. Brahmā too, taking them along, went to where Viṣṇu and Śiva (Vṛṣākapī) were.
m.5.46.4: Having gone there, all the gods bowed to Śaṅkara and Keśava and narrated their own story accurately and in due order.
m.5.46.5: O two Lords, all of us have been driven out of heaven by the wicked Mahiṣa, having been defeated on the battlefield.
m.5.46.6: We wander in this mortal world and find peace nowhere. To what misery after misery have the gods led by Indra not been brought?
m.5.46.7: The Sun and Moon, the noose-bearer Varuṇa, Kubera and Yama, Indra, Agni, Vāyu, the Gandharvas, Vidyādharas and noble Cāraṇas —
m.5.46.8: — the duties proper to these and to others, that sinful asura, who makes the Daitya side fearless, performs himself.
m.5.46.9: Therefore you ought to protect us gods who have come for refuge; and may you two lords quickly devise a means of slaying him.
m.5.46.10: Hearing these words of the gods, Dāmodara and the Lord of Satī became extremely angry, their eyes rolling with rage.
m.5.46.11: Then from the mouths of Viṣṇu and Śambhu, filled with intense anger, and likewise from the bodies of the other gods, a radiance came forth.
m.5.46.12: All the gods, intent on meditating on Durgā, saw a mass of exceedingly great radiance blazing in the ten directions.
m.5.46.13: That most terrifying splendour, arisen from the bodies of all the gods, coalesced and became a woman — Mahiṣamardinī herself.
m.5.46.14: Her brilliant face arose from Śambhu's splendour; from Yama's came her hair, and from Viṣṇu's her arms.
m.5.46.15: From the Moon's splendour her pair of breasts was born; from Indra's her waist; from Varuṇa's her shanks and thighs.
m.5.46.16: From the Earth's splendour came her hips; from Brahmā's her two feet; from the Sun's her toes, and from the Vasus' her fingers.
m.5.46.17: From Kubera's splendour her nose, from Prajāpati's her teeth, from Agni's her three eyes, and from the Twilight's her two eyebrows.
m.5.46.18: From Vāyu's her two ears; and likewise from the splendour of the other heaven-dwellers arose that Supreme Goddess, the lotus-dweller Lakṣmī.
m.5.46.19: Then, beholding her who had arisen from the mass of splendour of all the gods, all the gods attained supreme joy.
m.5.46.20: Seeing her without weapons, the gods, lords of heaven headed by Brahmā, resolved to make that auspicious one armed.
m.5.46.21: Then Maheśa presented a trident to the Great Goddess; Lord Kṛṣṇa a discus; and the noose-bearer Varuṇa a conch and a noose.
m.5.46.22: Agni gave a spear, and Vāyu a bow and two quivers full of arrows; the Lord of Śacī gave the thunderbolt and a bell.
m.5.46.23: Yama gave the staff of Death, Prajāpati a rosary; Brahmā gave a water-pot, and the Sun placed his rays in her hair-pores.
m.5.46.24: Kāla gave her a sword and a gleaming shield; the Ocean of Milk a lovely necklace and likewise a pair of unaging garments.
m.5.46.25: It also gave a crest-jewel, a pair of earrings, and bracelets as well, a half-moon ornament, armlets, and a pair of charming anklets,
m.5.46.26: a neck ornament, and rings for all her fingers. And Viśvakarman gave her a beautiful axe,
m.5.46.27: many missiles, and likewise impenetrable armour. The Ocean gave a lovely fresh garland and a lotus.
m.5.46.28: Himavat gave a lion and various gems; Kubera presented her with a cup filled with wine.
m.5.46.29: And Śeṣa, leader of the serpents, gave her a serpent-necklace adorned with wondrous workmanship and strung with many fine gems.
m.5.46.30: Honoured by these and other gods with ornaments and weapons, the Goddess roared aloud again and again with peals of laughter.
m.5.46.31: The expanse of the sky was filled with her terrifying roar; there was a great echo, and the three worlds shook.
m.5.46.32: The four oceans surged and the earth trembled. Then the gods, afflicted by Mahiṣa, raised the cry of Victory!
m.5.46.33: Then all those gods praised Ambikā, the supreme Śakti in the form of Mahālakṣmī, with voices choked with devotion.
m.5.46.34: Seeing the world in turmoil, those enemies of the gods, with their soldiers in armour, rose up with weapons raised.
m.5.46.35: Mahiṣa too, filled with rage, rushed toward that sound. Then he saw the Goddess, who pervaded the three worlds with her radiance.
m.5.46.36: Meanwhile, the great heroes protected by Mahiṣāsura arrived there by the crore, bearing weapons.
m.5.46.37: Cikṣura, Cāmara and Udagra, Karāla, Uddhata and Bāṣkala, Tāmra, Ugrāsya and Ugravīrya, Biḍāla and Andhaka,
m.5.46.38: Durdhara and Durmukha, Trinetra and Mahāhanu — these and many other heroes skilled in war,
m.5.46.39: masters of weapons and missiles, fought in battle with the Goddess. Thus passed a terrible time as the two sides fought.
m.5.46.40: The masses of various weapons and missiles hurled by the hands of the enemy host became fruitless in an instant through the power of Mahāmāyā.
m.5.46.41: Then that Goddess struck down the enemies headed by Cikṣura, together with their troops, with her mace, arrows, trident, spear and axe.
m.5.46.42: When his own armies had thus been slain, Mahiṣāsura turned his attention to those troops born from the Goddess's breath.
m.5.46.43: He struck some with his hooves and some with his two horns, and again and again he tore others apart with his tail and his snout.
m.5.46.44: Having thus slain the Goddess's troops, that lord of the asuras rushed forward to kill the Goddess's lion; then she became enraged.
m.5.46.45: He too, of great might, in anger pounding the ground with his hooves, uprooted a mountain with his two horns, hurled it, and roared.
m.5.46.46: Heavy mountains, flung by him as he whirled about swiftly in every direction, fell from the sky onto the earth, O best of kings.
m.5.46.47: Clouds pierced by his horns broke apart into pieces, and the ocean, lashed by his tail, surged over its shores on every side.
m.5.46.48: Seeing Mahiṣāsura thus enraged, Ambikā, who grants fearlessness to the gods, devised the means of slaying him.
m.5.46.49: Then the Sovereign Goddess raised her noose, cast it over him and bound the buffalo; he too abandoned his buffalo form.
m.5.46.50: Then the deceiver quickly became a lion; just as Ambikā was about to cleave its head, he became a man with sword in hand.
m.5.46.51: The Goddess struck him, shield and sword in hand, with arrows; then, taking the body of an elephant, he tore at the lion with his trunk.
m.5.46.52: Then the Goddess cut off his trunk with her great sword, and the demon once again assumed his own form.
m.5.46.53: At that very moment he shook the three worlds with all their moving and unmoving beings. Then Caṇḍikā, the Great Māyā, of proud valour, became enraged.
m.5.46.54: She drank the drink again and again and laughed, her eyes rolling; and that asura too roared, puffed up with the intoxication of his strength and might.
m.5.46.55: That asura uprooted mountains and hurled them at her, and she swiftly pulverised them with the blows of volleys of arrows.
m.5.46.56: The Supreme Sovereign Goddess, her senses stirred, her face flushed from the intoxication of the wine, spoke in a voice deep as thunder-clouds.
m.5.46.57: The Goddess said: Ho, fool, ho, witless one, why do you persist in vain obstinacy? No asuras whatsoever in the three worlds can stand before me.
m.5.46.58: The sage said: Having spoken thus, the Goddess who embodies all the arts leapt up, pressed down the asura with her foot, and pierced him in the throat with her fierce trident.
m.5.46.59: Then, pinned under her foot, he came only half-way out of his own mouth, held fast by the Goddess's power.
m.5.46.60: That great wretch, still fighting though only half emerged, had his head cut off by her great sword and was felled to the ground.
m.5.46.61: Then his troops, crying out Alas! Alas! with faces downcast, fled from the battlefield in terror, calling, Save us, save us.
m.5.46.62: Then all the gods headed by Indra praised the Goddess; the gandharvas sang loudly and the troupes of dancers danced.
m.5.46.63: Thus, O king, the manifestation of Mahālakṣmī has been told to you; now hear, with a composed mind, the origin of Sarasvatī.
m.5.46.iti: Thus ends the forty-sixth adhyāya, named The description of the incarnation of Mahālakṣmī, in the account of the slaying of Mahiṣāsura, in the fifth saṃhitā, the Umā-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.5.47.1: The sage said: There was a demon, the Daitya Śumbha, and his brother the mighty Niśumbha. By these two brothers the three worlds, with all that moves and does not move, were overrun through their power.
m.5.47.2: Sorely oppressed by those two, the gods went to the Himālaya and bowed to the Mother of all beings, the giver of desires.
m.5.47.3: The gods said: Victory to you, O Durgā, O Great Ruler! Victory, O you who love your own people! Salutations again and again to you, Śivā, who protect the three worlds.
m.5.47.4: Salutation to the giver of liberation; salutations again and again to the Supreme Mother. Salutation to you who bring about the origin, maintenance and end of the whole of worldly existence.
m.5.47.5: Salutation to you who take the form of Kālikā; salutation to you of the form of Tārā. Salutation be to you, who have the nature of Chinnamastā, to Śrīvidyā.
m.5.47.6: O Bhuvaneśī, salutation to you; salutation to you of the form of Bhairavī. Salutation be to Bagalāmukhī; salutations again and again to Dhūmāvatī.
m.5.47.7: Salutation to Tripurasundarī; salutations again and again to you, Mātaṅgī. Salutation to you, the Unconquered; salutations again and again to Vijayā.
m.5.47.8: Salutations again and again to you, Jayā, Maṅgalā, Vilāsinī. Salutation to you whose form is the milch-cow granting all; salutation be to you of terrible form.
m.5.47.9: Salutation to you of invincible form; salutations again and again to you of eternal form. Salutations again and again to you, Rudrāṇī, protector of those who come for refuge.
m.5.47.10: Salutation to her who is known through Vedānta; salutation to you, the Supreme Self. Salutations again and again to the sovereign of endless crores of cosmic eggs.
m.5.47.11: Thus praised by the gods, Gaurī, the auspicious Śivā, pleased and granting boons, said to all the gods: Who is being praised here by you?
m.5.47.12: Then from Gaurī's body a maiden appeared, and while they looked on she spoke with great reverence to Śiva's Śakti:
m.5.47.13: O Mother, this hymn to me is being offered by all the dwellers of heaven, who are oppressed by the mighty Daityas Niśumbha and Śumbha.
m.5.47.14: Because she came forth from the sheath (kośa) of her body, she is therefore celebrated by the name Kauśikī—she who is in person the slayer of the demon Śumbha.
m.5.47.15: She is also called Ugratārikā and Mahogratārikā; and because she manifested thus, she is called Mātaṅgī on earth.
m.5.47.16: She said to all the gods: Remain free of fear. I shall accomplish your task—I am independent and need no support.
m.5.47.17: Having said this, the Goddess quickly vanished. But Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa, the two servants of those demon brothers, saw that Goddess.
m.5.47.18: Seeing her enchanting form, a delight to the eyes, the two fell to the ground, senseless and infatuated.
m.5.47.19: Going back, they told the king the whole story from the beginning: O king, I have seen a captivating woman such as never was before.
m.5.47.20: She is seated on a lovely peak of the Himālaya, riding a lion, attended on all sides by divine maidens with folded hands.
m.5.47.21: One massages her feet, another dresses her hair; one massages her hands, another has applied collyrium to her eyes.
m.5.47.22: One, taking a mirror in her hand, shows her her face; another offers betel leaf mixed with cloves, cardamom and the like.
m.5.47.23: One companion stands before her holding a spittoon in her hand; another adorns all her limbs with ornaments, garments and the like.
m.5.47.24: Her shanks and thighs are like plantain stems, her nose like a parrot's, her creeper-like arms like serpents; her feet bear tinkling anklets, and she wears a lovely girdle.
m.5.47.25: Her breasts sway with a pearl necklace fragrant with gleaming musk; her neck shines with a collar; she is graceful and adorned with garlands.
m.5.47.26: The goddess bears the half-moon and wears jewelled earrings; she has a lovely braid, large eyes, and is adorned with three eyes.
m.5.47.27: She holds a rosary of letters; bracelets shine on her wrists; her fingers bear golden rings, and her hands gleam with bright armlets.
m.5.47.28: Fair Gaurī is clad in white garments, resplendent in the lotus posture, with a tilaka dot of saffron and her head adorned with the moon.
m.5.47.29: She has the radiance of lightning; her breasts rise high under a bodice of priceless cloth; with eight lofty arms she holds excellent weapons.
m.5.47.30: No Asura woman, no Nāga woman, no Gandharva woman, no Dānava woman exists in the three worlds such as that charming one is.
m.5.47.31: Therefore her fitness for enjoyment befits you alone, for she is the jewel among women and you, lord, are the jewel among men.
m.5.47.32: Hearing what Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa said, that great demon sent a messenger named Sugrīva to her.
m.5.47.33: Go, messenger, to the snowy mountain; some beautiful woman dwells there. Tell her my words and bring her with all effort.
m.5.47.34: Thus instructed by him, Sugrīva, foremost of Dānavas, went to the Himālaya and spoke to Maheśvarī, the Mother of the world.
m.5.47.35: The messenger said: O Goddess, the demon Śumbha is a Daitya, and Niśumbha is his younger brother; he is famed in the three worlds, of great strength and valour.
m.5.47.36: I am a messenger sent by him; I have come into your presence. O Sovereign of the gods, hear now what he has said.
m.5.47.37: Having conquered Indra and the others in battle, I carried off their jewels. I myself enjoy the gods' share given in sacrifice by the gods and others.
m.5.47.38: I regard you as the jewel among women, standing above all jewels. Let you, such as you are, enjoy me or my younger brother with the delights born of love.
m.5.47.39: Hearing these words spoken by Śumbha and conveyed by the messenger, she, the Great Māyā, beloved as life to the Lord of beings, replied:
m.5.47.40: The Goddess said: You speak the truth, O messenger; nothing false is being said. But I made a certain vow long ago—learn it from me.
m.5.47.41: He who shakes off my pride, he who conquers me in battle, him alone am I willing to make my husband, and no other; this is certain.
m.5.47.42: So you tell Śumbha and Niśumbha my words; let him then do here whatever is fitting.
m.5.47.43: Having heard these words of the Goddess, the dānava named Sugrīva went there and reported them to the king in full detail.
