m.5.47.44: Then, having heard what the messenger said, Śumbha of terrible command, full of anger, spoke to Dhūmrākṣa, his general, the foremost of the mighty.
m.5.47.45: O Dhūmrākṣa, on the snowy mountain there is a certain beautiful woman. Go quickly and bring her, so that she will indeed come here.
m.5.47.46: In bringing her you need have no fear, O best of asuras; if she wishes to fight, battle must be waged with effort.
m.5.47.47: Thus instructed, the daitya called Dhūmralocana went to the Himālaya and spoke to the Ruler of the worlds, born of a portion of Umā.
m.5.47.48: Go to my master's presence; otherwise I, accompanied by a force of thousands of asuras, will kill you, O fair-hipped one.
m.5.47.49: The Goddess said: You have been sent by the king of the daityas, O hero; if you kill me, what can I do to you? But I consider going with you impossible without a battle.
m.5.47.50: Addressed thus, the dānava Dhūmralocana ran at her; with the mere utterance of huṃ Maheśvarī burned him up.
m.5.47.51: From then on that Goddess is called Dhūmāvatī on earth; when worshipped, she cuts down the host of enemies of her devotees.
m.5.47.52: When Dhūmrākṣa had been slain by the Goddess, his troops were chewed up by her furious mount; those who remained all fled.
m.5.47.53: Hearing that the daitya had thus been slain by the Goddess, the mighty Śumbha became greatly enraged, biting both his lips.
m.5.47.54: He dispatched in succession the asuras Caṇḍa, Muṇḍa and Raktabīja; and those daityas, so commanded, went to where Ambikā stood.
m.5.47.55: Seeing the Blessed Goddess mounted on the lion, attended by the powers Aṇimā and the rest, illuminating the directions with her radiance, the chief dānavas spoke.
m.5.47.56: O Goddess, go quickly into the presence of Śumbha and Niśumbha; otherwise we shall kill you together with your attendants and your mount.
m.5.47.57: Choose as husband him who is praised by the world-guardians and others, O lovely one; you will attain great bliss, hard to obtain even for the gods.
m.5.47.58: Having heard what was said, the Mother, the Supreme Goddess, smiled, and that Goddess uttered true and gracious words.
m.5.47.59: The Goddess said: Maheśāna is without a second, the supreme Brahman, Sadāśiva, whose true nature even the Vedas do not know; what then to speak of Viṣṇu and the others?
m.5.47.60: I am his subtle Prakṛti; how could I choose another husband? A lioness, even when tormented by desire, never chooses a jackal.
m.5.47.61: Nor does a she-elephant choose a donkey, nor a leopardess a hare. You speak falsely, O daityas, bound by the serpent of death.
m.5.47.62: Go to Pātāla, or fight, if you have the power. Hearing these anger-provoking words, they said to one another:
m.5.47.63: Considering you in our minds a weak woman, we do not kill you. But if there is desire for battle in your mind, then come, firm upon your lion.
m.5.47.64: As they quarreled thus, the strife grew; sharp arrows rained down in the battle from both sides.
m.5.47.65: Having thus fought with them in sport, the Supreme Goddess slew the great asura Raktabīja together with Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa.
m.5.47.66: Even though they had harboured hostile minds, these enemies of the gods in the end attained the supreme world, the world to which her own people go.
m.5.47.iti: Thus ends the forty-seventh adhyāya, named The slaying of Dhūmralocana, Caṇḍa, Muṇḍa and Raktabīja, in the fifth saṃhitā, the Umā-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.5.48.1: The king said: O lord, having heard that Dhūmrākṣa, Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa, and likewise the demon Raktabīja had been slain by the Goddess, Śumbha, the tormentor of the gods,
m.5.48.2: what did he do then, O brahmin? Tell me this now, to me who am eager to hear the sin-destroying story of the Source of the world.
m.5.48.3: The sage said: O king, having heard that these foremost Daityas were slain, the great demon of formidable valour commanded his own hosts, hard to withstand, in whom delight arose at the mere utterance of the word battle.
m.5.48.4: Let those born of the Kālaka lineage, endowed with strength, assembled at my command in hope of victory, together with the Kālakeya, Maurya and Daurhṛda asuras, and others too, quickly march forth.
m.5.48.5: Having instructed those Daityas, Niśumbha and Śumbha, mounted on chariots, went forth. The armies following those two mighty ones rose up from the earth like moths bound for destruction.
m.5.48.6: The army had the mṛdaṅga and mardala drums sounded, together with bherī, ḍiṇḍima, jharjhara and ānaka drums. On the battlefield the lovers of battle rejoiced, while those who loved their lives fled from the fight.
m.5.48.7: Then those warriors, clad in battle-garments, of flawless bodies, reached the battlefield, bearing masses of weapons and missiles, fiercely contending with one another out of desire for victory.
m.5.48.8: Some asuras mounted on elephants, some riding horses, and others mounted on chariots, not distinguishing their own people from the enemy, joyfully threw themselves into the battle in the company of the lord of the asuras.
m.5.48.9: The roar produced by the śataghnīs arose again and again, and by it the gods were shaken. A great darkness spread across the sky; the disc of the sun's chariot could not be seen.
m.5.48.10: Foot-soldiers marched forth by crores, full of pride and eager for victory; and other asuras, riding chariots, horses and elephants, went out joyfully — how many crores of them.
m.5.48.11: Rutting elephants, like dark mountains, spread their trumpeting cries over the battle; and camels too, resembling small hills, sent forth gurgling sounds from their throats.
m.5.48.12: And the horses neighed — bred in lofty lands, wearing large neck-ornaments, skilled in their paces; planting their hooves on the heads of elephants, they flew along the path of the sky like birds.
m.5.48.13: Seeing the enemy's army thus rushing upon her, Ambikā then strung her bow; she rang the bell that brings dismay to foes, and the lion too roared, shaking its mane.
m.5.48.14: Then Niśumbha, seeing Śivā standing on the snowy mountain with lovely ornaments and weapons, spoke words full of sentiment, like one well versed in the moods of amorous women.
m.5.48.15: For ladies like you, even a jasmine petal strewn upon your lovely body surely causes pain. How then, O great Goddess, will you wage a terrible battle with that very charming body?
m.5.48.16: Having uttered these words the great demon fell silent. Caṇḍikā said to him: Why do you prattle in vain, foolish asura? Give battle — or else go to the abode of the Nāgas.
m.5.48.17: Then the great chariot-warrior, exceedingly enraged, poured a wondrous rain of volleys of arrows in battle, as dense clouds rain water — as if the rainy season had then come to the battlefield.
m.5.48.18: He fought with sharp arrows, with tridents and axes, with bhindipālas, iron bars and bows, with the weapons called bhuśuṇḍī, prāsa and kṣurapra, and with great swords, alongside warriors arrogant with pride.
m.5.48.19: In that battle great elephants, like dark mountains, with their frontal globes split, staggered about; and the standards of Śumbha and Niśumbha, white as moving cranes, were left without flags and without supports.
m.5.48.20: Daityas with bodies split open like fish, and terrifying horses with severed necks, were made lifeless by Kālikā in battle; other asuras were turned into flesh for food by the lion.
m.5.48.21: Meanwhile streams carrying blood flowed forth; the river there overflowed with heaps of the slain. The warriors' hair was like water-moss, and their upper garments resembled white foam.
m.5.48.22: Horseman fell upon horseman, elephant-riders upon those on elephants, chariot-warrior upon chariot-lord, foot-soldier upon foot-soldiers: a great fight between evenly matched opponents took place.
m.5.48.23: Then Niśumbha reflected in his heart: This terrible time has now arrived. Through adverse time even a poor man may become very rich, and a very rich man poor.
m.5.48.24: A dullard may become of broad intellect, and a great intellect a dullard; a cruel man laden with faults may be praised. The very mighty meet defeat in battle, and the weak win at the front of combat.
m.5.48.25: Victory or defeat comes to embodied beings effortlessly, by the will of the Supreme Lord alone. Not even Maheśvara, the Lotus-born or the Lord of Ramā could live by overstepping Time.
m.5.48.26: Having come to the front of battle, heroes do not in their hearts regard flight as right. But how can there be victory in battle against her, by whom my entire army has been destroyed?
m.5.48.27: Surely she has come to accomplish the gods' purpose and to crush the Daitya army — she is the primeval form, the supreme Prakṛti, Śivā; she is by no means an ordinary worldly woman.
m.5.48.28: Even death dealt by a woman is proclaimed dishonourable by those eager to taste the relish of battle. Yet, without fighting, how shall we show our face in the presence of the asura king?
m.5.48.29: Having reflected thus, the great warrior mounted a mighty chariot urged on by its charioteer and went swiftly to where the consort of Maheśvara stood, whose blossoming youth is coveted by celestial women.
m.5.48.30: He said to her: O great Goddess, what is gained by slaying these warriors who live on wages? If you wish to fight, then let there be battle with us two, clad in fine battle-garments.
m.5.48.31: Then Kauśikī said to Kālī: Behold the obstinacy of these two. When calamity approaches, Time, the impeller of good and evil, gives the mind a perverse turn.
m.5.48.32: Then Niśumbha struck Caṇḍikā with thousands of arrows, and Kālikā likewise. Śivā shattered the arrows shot by the asura into a thousand pieces with volleys of her own arrows.
m.5.48.33: Then, raising a gleaming sword along with a shield, he struck the lion on the head. Ambikā split that sword with her great sword, as woodcutters split a tree with an axe.
m.5.48.34: His sword broken, he drove an arrow into the breast of the supreme Ambikā; that too was cut down. Again he hurled a trident at her heart; that too she pulverized with a blow of her fist.
m.5.48.35: Taking up a mace, the great warrior asura, facing death, again rushed at Ambā. She crushed that too with the edge of her trident; and again the trident he raised was split by another stroke.
m.5.48.36: Then Ambikā, with her own sharp arrows, like terrible serpents, fit for sucking the blood of the gods' enemies and smeared with poison, struck Niśumbha down and brought him to the ground.
m.5.48.37: When his younger brother of immeasurable strength had been felled, the lord of the asuras, filled with fury, standing in his chariot and equipped with eight arms, went to where the beloved of Maheśa was.
m.5.48.38: Then the Goddess blew her foe-subduing conch and made the unbearable twang of her bow; the lion too roared, shaking its mane, and the sky resounded with the three sounds.
m.5.48.39: Then the Mother of the world let out a loud laugh, and by it all the enemies of the gods were terrified. The gods then cried out Victory! when Ambikā said: Stand firm in battle.
m.5.48.40: That Daitya king hurled a great spear with blazing flames, and it was struck down by her meteor-like missile. Śivā split the arrows sent by Śumbha, and he too split a thousandfold the arrows shot by Śivā.
m.5.48.41: Caṇḍikā raised her trident and struck that great asura; he fell unconscious, like a mountain whose wings have been severed by Hari (Indra), shaking the sky and the earth together with the ocean.
m.5.48.42: Then, having endured the pain caused by the trident, the mighty one, creating ten thousand arms, struck Kālikā, the great Goddess mounted on her lion, with discuses that bring destruction to the immortals.
m.5.48.43: Then, playfully shattering his discuses, Śivā raised her trident and struck him; and the two brothers, having met death from the world-purifying lotus-hand of Śivā, attained the supreme state.
m.5.48.44: When that greatly valiant Niśumbha of terrible prowess, and Śumbha, were slain, all the daityas entered the abode of Bali (the netherworld).
m.5.48.45: Others among the enemies of the gods were devoured by Kālī, the lion and the rest; and still others fled in the ten directions, stricken with fear.
m.5.48.46: The rivers flowed along their courses with clear water; pleasant-touching breezes blew; the sky became spotless.
m.5.48.47: The sacrifice was begun again by the gods and the brahmarṣis, and all the dwellers of heaven, headed by the great Indra, became happy.
m.5.48.48: O lord, whoever with faith repeatedly studies this supremely pure and meritorious account of Umā, containing the slaying of the daitya kings—
m.5.48.49: he, having enjoyed here all pleasures, hard to obtain even for the gods, would go hereafter to Umā's abode through the grace of Mahāmāyā.
m.5.48.50: The sage said: Thus arose the Goddess, slayer of the asura Śumbha; she is called Sarasvatī, manifested directly from a portion of Umā, O king.
m.5.48.iti: Thus ends the forty-eighth adhyāya, named The description of the appearance of Sarasvatī, in the account of the slaying of Niśumbha and Śumbha, in the fifth saṃhitā, the Umā-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.5.49.1: The sages said: O Sūta, best knower of all matters, narrate the incarnation of Umā, the sovereign of the worlds, from whom Sarasvatī was born,
m.5.49.2: she who is celebrated as the supreme Brahman, the root Prakṛti, the sovereign Goddess; formless yet possessing form, eternal, full of bliss, the true one.
m.5.49.3: Sūta said: O ascetics, listen with love to this supreme and great account, by merely understanding which a man attains the highest goal.
m.5.49.4: Once there was a war between the gods and the demons against each other; through the power of Mahāmāyā, victory came to the immortals.
m.5.49.5: Then the immortals, puffed up with pride, spread their own praise: We are blessed, we are blessed! What can the demons do to us?
m.5.49.6: They, having seen our utterly unbearable might, went in fear to the abode of the Nāgas, crying, Flee, flee.
m.5.49.7: Ah, what strength! Ah, what splendour, destroying the race of the Daityas! Ah, the good fortune of the gods! Thus they all extolled themselves.
m.5.49.8: Then, at that very moment, a radiance appeared in the form of a towering mass; seeing that never-before-seen thing, the gods were astonished.
m.5.49.9: With choked throats they said, What is this? What is this? — not knowing the supreme power of Śyāmā, the breaker of pride.
m.5.49.10: Then the overlord of the gods commanded the gods: Go, you, and examine truly what this is.
m.5.49.11: Urged by the lord of the gods, Vāyu went near the radiance; and that radiance, addressing him, said to him, Who are you, sir?
m.5.49.12: Thus questioned then by that exceedingly mighty radiance, Vāyu, full of pride, said this: I am Vāyu, the life-breath of the world.
m.5.49.13: This whole world, moving and unmoving, is woven warp and woof in me alone, the support of all; I set the entire world in motion.
m.5.49.14: Then the great radiance said: If you are capable of moving things, O Vāyu, move this blade of grass placed here, by your own will.
m.5.49.15: Then the ever-moving one (Vāyu) strove with all his effort; when it did not move from its place, he became ashamed.
m.5.49.16: Falling silent, Vāyu then went to Indra's assembly and related what had happened, including his own defeat:
m.5.49.17: We all falsely imagine lordship over everything in ourselves; we are unable to do anything even to a trifling object.
m.5.49.18: Then Indra (Marutvān) sent all the gods; when they could not know it, Indra himself went.
m.5.49.19: Then, seeing Maghavan (Indra) approaching, the utterly unbearable radiance at once vanished, and Vāsava was astonished.
m.5.49.20: I take refuge in him alone whose deeds are such: thus the thousand-eyed Indra reflected again and again.
m.5.49.21: Meanwhile, there, Śiva's consort, whose very body is guileless compassion, in order to bestow grace on them and to take away their pride,
m.5.49.22: on the ninth day of the bright half of Caitra, when the sun stood at midday, the goddess Umā, whose form is being-consciousness-bliss, manifested.
m.5.49.23: Shining in the midst of the radiance, illuminating the directions with her lustre, clearly making all the gods understand: I alone am Brahman.
m.5.49.24: Holding in her four hands the gesture of granting boons, the noose, the goad and the gesture of fearlessness, served by the Vedas, lovely, proud in fresh youth;
m.5.49.25: clad in red garments, with red garlands and unguents, resembling ten million Kandarpas, with radiance equal to ten million moons,
m.5.49.26: Mahāmāyā, the inner controller of all, the witness of all beings, whose own nature is the supreme Brahman, spoke:
m.5.49.27: Umā said: Neither Brahmā, nor the foe of Mura (Viṣṇu), nor the Lord, the foe of the Cities (Śiva), can be proud in the least before me — what then to speak of the other gods?
m.5.49.28: I am the supreme Brahman, the supreme light, having the form of the twofold praṇava; I alone am everything; there is no one other than me.
m.5.49.29: Though formless, I have form; I am the essence of all principles, of unfathomable qualities, eternal, the form of both effect and cause.
m.5.49.30: Sometimes in the form of a beloved woman, sometimes in male form, sometimes in the form of both — I, the sovereign, am of all forms.
m.5.49.31: I am Viriñci (Brahmā), the creator; I am Acyuta, the protector of the world; I am Rudra, the destroyer; I am the enchantress of the whole universe.
m.5.49.32: All the powers headed by Kālikā, Kamalā and Vāṇī are indeed born from a portion of me alone, and so are all these digits.
m.5.49.33: By my power you conquered all the sons of Diti; not knowing me as such, you vainly consider yourselves lords of all.
m.5.49.34: Just as a conjurer makes a wooden doll dance, so I, the sovereign, make all beings dance.
m.5.49.35: From fear of me the wind blows, the oblation-eater (Agni) burns everything, and the guardians of the worlds ceaselessly perform their respective duties.
m.5.49.36: Sometimes for the hosts of gods, sometimes for the sons of Diti, I, independent, bring about victory fully, by my own play.
m.5.49.37: The imperishable supreme abode, beyond Māyā, higher than the highest, which the Vedas describe — that form is mine alone.
m.5.49.38: My form is held to be twofold, with qualities and without qualities: the one is mingled with Māyā, the second is not dependent on it.
m.5.49.39: Knowing me thus, O gods, abandon each your own pride and, filled with love, worship me, the eternal Prakṛti.
m.5.49.40: Hearing these words of the Goddess, pregnant with compassion, the gods, their necks bowed in devotion, praised the supreme Goddess:
m.5.49.41: Forgive us, O Mistress of the world; be gracious, O supreme Goddess. May such pride never again be ours, O Mother; show us mercy.
m.5.49.42: From then on, those gods, having abandoned their pride and with collected minds, worshipped Umā as before, according to the prescribed rites.
m.5.49.43: Thus, O brahmins, I have narrated to you the manifestation of Umā, by merely hearing which one attains the supreme state.
m.5.49.iti: Thus ends the forty-ninth adhyāya, named The description of the appearance of Umā, in the fifth saṃhitā, the Umā-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.5.50.1: The sages said: We all wish to hear the deeds of Durgā day after day. O most wise one, describe to us yet another wonderful truth about her.
m.5.50.2: As we listen to the many nectar-like stories from your lotus mouth, our mind is not satisfied, O Sūta, best of the knowers of all matters.
m.5.50.3: Sūta said: The mighty son of Ruru, known by the name Durgama, obtained the four Vedas through a boon granted by Brahmā.
m.5.50.4: Having also obtained a strength unconquerable by the gods, he wrought many calamities on the surface of the earth, and in heaven the gods trembled.
m.5.50.5: When the Vedas were lost, all rites were indeed lost; and the brāhmaṇas, along with the gods, then became of evil conduct.
m.5.50.6: There was no giving of gifts, no fierce austerity, no sacrifice, no oblation at all. Then a drought lasting a hundred years arose on the earth.
m.5.50.7: There was a great cry of distress in the three worlds; all people became miserable, sorely afflicted by hunger and thirst.
m.5.50.8: Rivers and oceans, step-wells, wells and lakes all became waterless; trees and creepers withered completely.
m.5.50.9: Then, seeing the great suffering of the dejected creatures, the gods went for refuge to Yogamāyā, the great Goddess.
m.5.50.10: The gods said: Protect, protect all your own creatures, O Mahāmāyā. Surely withdraw your anger, otherwise the worlds will perish.
m.5.50.11: Just as the demon Śumbha was slain, and mighty Niśumbha, Dhūmrākṣa, Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa, and the mighty Raktabīja,
m.5.50.12: the demon Kaiṭabha together with Madhu, and Mahiṣāsura too—in the same way, O ocean of compassion, friend of the afflicted, slay this one quickly.
m.5.50.13: Children commit faults at every step; who in the world bears with them except the mother alone?
m.5.50.14: Whenever suffering has come upon the gods and likewise the brāhmaṇas, then you swiftly descend and make the people happy.
m.5.50.15: Hearing their lament thus, the compassionate one then revealed a form made of endless eyes.
m.5.50.16: She held in her four hands a bow and arrow, a lotus, and various roots and fruits, her lotus face serene.
m.5.50.17: Then, seeing the creatures tormented, her eyes filled with compassion, she wept, deeply moved, for nine days and nine nights.
m.5.50.18: From her eyes she released streams of water by the thousands; by them the worlds and all the plants were refreshed.
m.5.50.19: The rivers and the oceans too became full of fathomless water; and vegetables, roots and fruits sprang up on the surface of the earth.
m.5.50.20: She distributed the fruits held in her hands to the gods, lovely grasses to the cows, and likewise to others according to what befitted them.
m.5.50.21: All became content—gods, twice-born and humans. Then the Goddess said: What else shall I do for you?
m.5.50.22: Then the gods, gathering together, said: The people have been gladdened by you. Show compassion and give back the Vedas that were seized by Durgama.
m.5.50.23: Saying, so be it, she said: Go, go to your own abodes; I shall give you back the Vedas before long.
m.5.50.24: Then the delighted gods, having bowed deeply to the source of the world whose eyes were like full-blown blue lotuses, went each to his own abode.
m.5.50.25: Then a tumult arose in heaven, on earth and in the sky. Hearing it, Raurava (the son of Ruru) at once besieged the city on all sides.
m.5.50.26: Then Śivā, having set up a fiery circle all around for the protection of the gods, herself went out from it.
m.5.50.27: Then a battle took place between the two, the Goddess and the demon; in the fight they rained sharp arrows that pierced armour.
m.5.50.28: Meanwhile, from her body there came forth beautiful forms: Kālī, Tārā, Chinnamastā, Śrīvidyā, Bhuvaneśvarī,
m.5.50.29: Bhairavī, Bagalā, Dhūmrā, the glorious Tripurasundarī, and Mātaṅgī—these ten Mahāvidyās came forth bearing weapons.
m.5.50.30: Then countless Mothers of divine form arose, all bearing the crescent moon, all with a radiance like lightning.
m.5.50.31: Then a terrifying battle began with the hosts of Mothers; by them the army of Raurava, a hundred akṣauhiṇīs, was slain.
m.5.50.32: Then she struck the demon Durgama with the edge of her trident; he fell upon the earth like a tree whose roots have been dug out.
m.5.50.33: Having thus slain the demon named Durgāsura, the Goddess took the four Vedas and gave them to the gods.
m.5.50.34: The gods said: For our sake you assumed a form made of endless eyes; therefore, O Ambikā, the sages will celebrate you as Śatākṣī ('Hundred-eyed').
m.5.50.35: Since the worlds were sustained by vegetables born from your own body, your name will be renowned as Śākambharī.
m.5.50.36: Since the great demon named Durgama was slain by you, O Śivā, people will therefore call you Durgā, the blessed and auspicious one.
m.5.50.37: O Yoganidrā, salutation to you; salutation be to you, O mighty one; salutation to you, giver of knowledge; to the Mother of the universe, salutation again and again.
m.5.50.38: To the Supreme Goddess who is made known through sayings such as Tat tvam asi (That thou art), the sovereign of endless crores of cosmic eggs, salutation again and again.
m.5.50.39: O Mother, we who are ignorant of your power are unable to praise you, who are hard to reach by speech, mind and body, and whose eyes are the sun, moon and fire.
m.5.50.40: Seeing gods such as us, who would show such compassion, apart from the sovereign of the gods, Mother Śatākṣī?
m.5.50.41: Act so that the three worlds are not continually overwhelmed by afflictions. In this way you should make an effort toward the destruction of our enemies.
m.5.50.42: The Goddess said: Just as cows, on seeing their calves, run eagerly and swiftly to them, so too I, on seeing you, run to you, being deeply stirred.
m.5.50.43: For me, who regard you as my children and would give even my life for you, a single moment of not seeing you passes like an age.
m.5.50.44: You who are rich in devotion should have no anxiety at all, while I remain present for you, removing your calamities.
m.5.50.45: Just as the Daityas were slain before, so shall I slay the Asuras. No doubt should be entertained about this; I speak the truth, the truth.
m.5.50.46: When Śumbha and Niśumbha, two other Daityas, come into being, then I, full of glory, shall be born of Yaśodā, the wife of Nanda,
m.5.50.47: assuming a womb-born form, I shall be born in the cowherds' settlement (Gokula). I shall slay those two Asuras; therefore they will call me Nandajā (born of Nanda).
m.5.50.48: Since I shall slay Aruṇa having assumed the form of a bee, people in the world will celebrate me as Bhrāmarī.
m.5.50.49: When, again taking on a terrible form, I devour the Rākṣasas, then my name will become renowned as Bhīmā Devī.
m.5.50.50: Whenever affliction arising from the Asuras thus occurs on earth, then each time I shall descend and bring about welfare, without doubt.
m.5.50.51: The goddess who is remembered as Śatākṣī is likewise regarded as Śākambharī; she alone is proclaimed as Durgā. The person is one and the same in all three.
m.5.50.52: There is no deity on earth as compassionate as Śatākṣī — the Great Goddess who, seeing the creatures in distress, wept for nine days.
m.5.50.iti: Thus ends the fiftieth adhyāya, named The description of the incarnations of Śatākṣī and others, in the fifth saṃhitā, the Umā-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.5.51.1: The sages said: O disciple of Vyāsa, O greatly fortunate Sūta, best of the Purāṇa-reciters, we wish to hear some further narrative concerning the Ruler (īśitṛ),
m.5.51.2: namely the unsurpassed kriyāyoga of Umā, the Mother of the world, which was told by Sanatkumāra to the great-souled Vyāsa.
m.5.51.3: Sūta said: Blessed are you, great souls, firm in your vow of devotion to the Goddess. Hear with reverence the supreme, hidden secret of the Parāśakti.
m.5.51.4: Vyāsa said: O Sanatkumāra, all-knowing son of Brahmā, of great intellect, I wish to hear the most wondrous kriyāyoga of Umā.
m.5.51.5: What is its characteristic, and what fruit arises when it is performed? And what is dear to the Supreme Mother—tell me all of that completely.
m.5.51.6: Sanatkumāra said: O Dvaipāyana, this secret about which you inquire—hear it all, O greatly wise one, from me as I describe it.
m.5.51.7: Jñānayoga, kriyāyoga and likewise bhaktiyoga—these three paths of the revered Mother are declared, granting worldly enjoyment and liberation.
m.5.51.8: Jñānayoga is the union of the mind with the Self; but the union with external objects is called kriyāyoga.
m.5.51.9: Bhaktiyoga is held to be the contemplation of the oneness of the Goddess and oneself. Among all three yogas, that foundational one is called kriyāyoga.
m.5.51.10: From action devotion arises; from devotion knowledge arises; from knowledge liberation arises—this is the settled conclusion in the scriptures.
m.5.51.11: Yoga is the principal cause of liberation, O best of sages; and kriyāyoga is the supreme means of attaining the object of yogic meditation.
m.5.51.12: One should know Māyā to be Prakṛti and the possessor of Māyā to be the eternal Brahman; knowing their form as non-different, one is released from the bondage of worldly existence.
m.5.51.13: Whoever builds a temple of the Goddess, of stone or likewise of wood, or of clay, O son of Kālī, hear the meritorious fruit of that. The great fruit accruing to one who worships with yoga day after day—
m.5.51.14: —that fruit he obtains who has a temple of the Goddess built. A thousand generations of his family yet to come and a thousand past—that righteous one saves, causing an abode of the revered Mother to be built.
m.5.51.15: Sin committed over ten million births, whether small or great, perishes from the very moment of beginning a temple of the revered Mother.
m.5.51.16: As the Gaṅgā is foremost among rivers and the Śoṇa among all male rivers, as the earth in forbearance and as the ocean in depth,
m.5.51.17: and as the sun excels among all the planets, so the revered Supreme Mother excels among all the gods.
m.5.51.18: She is the chief among all deities; he who has a house built for her attains eminence birth after birth.
m.5.51.19: In Vārāṇasī, in Kurukṣetra, in Prayāga and likewise Puṣkara, on the shore where the Gaṅgā meets the sea, in Naimiṣa, at Amarakaṇṭaka,
m.5.51.20: on the most holy Śrīparvata, at Gokarṇa, on Jñānaparvata, in Mathurā, in Ayodhyā and likewise in Dvārāvatī—
m.5.51.21: in these and other holy regions, or in any place whatsoever, one who has a dwelling of the Mother built is freed from bondage.
m.5.51.22: For as many years as the arrangement of bricks endures, for so many thousands of years he is honoured in Maṇidvīpa.
m.5.51.23: Whoever has images made, marked with all the proper characteristics, surely goes without fear to the supreme world of Umā.
m.5.51.24: Having installed an image of the Goddess at an auspicious season, planetary position and asterism, a mortal becomes fulfilled through the grace of Yogamāyā.
m.5.51.25: Those men of the family who will be and who have passed, up to the end of the kalpa—all of them he carries across, having installed a beautiful image of the Goddess.
m.5.51.26: Whatever merit would come from establishing the three worlds, O bull among sages, ten million times that merit comes from installing the revered Goddess.
m.5.51.27: Whoever, having installed the Goddess in the centre, installs the pañcāyatana deities in the four directions—his merit cannot be counted.
m.5.51.28: The fruit gained from ten million repetitions of Viṣṇu's names during an eclipse of the moon or sun—a hundred million times greater than that
m.5.51.29: comes from merely repeating Śiva's name; ten million times greater than that from repeating the name of the revered Goddess; and ten million times greater than that
m.5.51.30: is the merit obtained from building a temple of the Goddess. He by whom that Goddess, Mother of the world, embodiment of the three Vedas, has been installed—
m.5.51.31: for him nothing is hard to obtain, by the compassion of the revered Mother. Sons, grandsons and the rest flourish, and all impurity perishes.
m.5.51.32: Those who even in mind wish to perform the excellent installation of an image, they too go to Umā's supreme world, hard for sages to attain.
m.5.51.33: Whoever, seeing a temple being built, reflects in his mind, I will have one built when wealth comes to me—
m.5.51.34: —thus his family goes at once to heaven, there is no doubt. By the power of Mahāmāyā, what is hard to obtain in the three worlds?
m.5.51.35: Those who have taken refuge solely in the revered Supreme Mother, source of the world, should not be considered human beings; they are verily the Goddess's own attendants.
m.5.51.36: Those who, walking, sleeping or standing, day and night utter the two-syllabled name Umā—they are attendants of Śivā.
m.5.51.37: Those who, in regular and occasional rites, worship the Goddess, the supreme Śivā, with flowers, incense and lamps, will go to the abode of Umā.
m.5.51.38: Those who daily smear the Goddess's pavilion with cow dung or clay and sweep it will go to the abode of Umā.
m.5.51.39: Those by whom a charming, unsurpassed temple of the Goddess has been built—to the people of their family the Mother grants blessings.
m.5.51.40: May my own, the objects of my love, live a hundred years; may no paths of calamity befall them—thus the revered Mother speaks day and night.
m.5.51.41: He by whom an auspicious image of the great goddess Umā is caused to be made: ten thousand men born in his family are honoured in Maṇidvīpa.
m.5.51.42: Having installed an image of Mahāmāyā and worshipped it properly, whatever desire the practitioner prays for, that he obtains.
m.5.51.43: Who could count the fruit of one who bathes the excellent installed image of the holy Mother with ghee mixed with honey?
m.5.51.44: One should bathe the Supreme Goddess with waters containing sandal, aguru, camphor, spikenard, musta-grass and the like, and with the milk of cows of a single colour.
m.5.51.45: One should offer an excellent oblation with incense of eighteen ingredients, and perform the waving of lights (nīrājana) for the Goddess with wicks of camphor and ghee.
m.5.51.46: On the eighth of the dark fortnight, on the ninth, or on the new-moon day, or on the fifteenth lunar day, one should worship the Nurse of the worlds, especially with fragrances and flowers.
m.5.51.47: Reciting the Jananī-sūkta, or reciting the Śrī-sūkta, or else the Devī-sūkta, or even the root mantra.
m.5.51.48: Excepting viṣṇukrāntā and tulasī, every flower should be known as pleasing to the Goddess, and the lotus especially.
m.5.51.49: He who offers a golden flower, or even a silver one, to the Goddess goes to the supreme abode, attended by crores of siddhas.
m.5.51.50: At the end of worship, the servants of the Goddess must always ask pardon for faults: Be gracious, O Supreme Ruler, giver of joy to the world.
m.5.51.51: Praising her with such words, the mantra-practitioner, wholly devoted to the Goddess, should meditate on her as mounted on a lion, her hands showing the boon-giving and fear-dispelling gestures.
m.5.51.52: Having thus meditated on Maheśānī, who grants devotees the fruits they desire, one should arrange various ripe fruits as the food-offering.
m.5.51.53: But whoever eats the food-offering of Śambhu's Śakti, the Supreme Self, that man shakes off all impurity and becomes pure.
m.5.51.54: He who performs the Bhavānī vow on the third day of the bright half of Caitra, freed from the bonds of worldly existence, attains the supreme state.
m.5.51.55: On this very third day the wise one should hold the swing festival and worship Umā, the Nurse of the worlds, together with Śaṅkara,
m.5.51.56: with flowers, saffron, garments, camphor, aguru and sandal, incense, lamps, food-offerings, garlands, perfumes and other things too.
m.5.51.57: Then he should swing the Goddess Mahāmāyā, Maheśvarī, the holy Gaurī united with Śiva, who brings about all welfare.
m.5.51.58: He who every year on this day performs the vow and likewise the swinging, with discipline—to him Śivā grants everything he wishes.
m.5.51.59: The third day in the bright half of Mādhava (Vaiśākha) is called Akṣayā. Whoever on it diligently performs the vow of the World-Mother,
m.5.51.60: and worships Gaurī together with Śaṅkara with flowers of mallikā, mālatī, campā, japā, bandhūka and lotus,
m.5.51.61: shaking off the sin committed over a crore of births, arising from mind, speech and body, he enjoys here the four imperishable goals of life.
m.5.51.62: He who on the bright third of Jyeṣṭha performs the vow and worships Maheśvarī with supreme love—for him nothing is unattainable.
m.5.51.63: On the third day of the bright half of Āṣāḍha one should hold the chariot festival, most dear to the Goddess, according to one's means.
m.5.51.64: One should regard the chariot as the earth, its wheels as the moon and sun, the horses as the Vedas, and the charioteer as the lotus-born Brahmā.
m.5.51.65: Having fashioned the chariot thus, studded with clusters of various gems and resplendent with flower garlands, he should install Śivā in it.
m.5.51.66: The wise man should contemplate: The Supreme Mother is seated in the chariot to protect the world and to behold the world.
m.5.51.67: As the chariot moves slowly, one should raise the cry of victory: Protect us people who have taken refuge in you, O Goddess, loving to the afflicted.
m.5.51.68: With such words and the sounds of various instruments he should please her; and having taken the chariot to the boundary, he should worship her there in the chariot.
m.5.51.69: Then, having praised her with various hymns, he should bring her back to his own house and, making a hundred prostrations, pray to the World-Mother.
m.5.51.70: The learned one who thus performs the worship, vow and chariot festival, having enjoyed all pleasures here, goes in the end to the Goddess's abode.
m.5.51.71: Likewise, he who on the bright third of Śrāvaṇa and Bhādrapada performs the vow and worship of the Mother according to rule
m.5.51.72: rejoices constantly here with sons, grandsons and the like, and with wealth and the like; in the end he goes to Umā's world, which lies above all worlds.
m.5.51.73: In the bright half of Āśvina one should perform the Navarātra vow, by doing which all desires are fulfilled—there is no doubt.
m.5.51.74: Neither the four-faced Brahmā, nor the five-faced Śiva, nor the six-faced Skanda, nor anyone else is able to describe the power of this Navarātra vow.
m.5.51.75: O best of sages, by performing the Navarātra vow, King Suratha, son of Viratha, regained his own kingdom that had been taken away.
m.5.51.76: The wise King Sudarśana, son of Dhruvasandhi and lord of Ayodhyā, recovered his seized kingdom by its power.
m.5.51.77: Having performed this king of vows and worshipped Maheśvarī, Samādhi was freed from the bondage of saṃsāra and became a partaker of liberation.
m.5.51.78: The man who worships the Goddess on the third, fifth, seventh, eighth, ninth or fourteenth lunar day,
m.5.51.79: having performed the vow according to rule in the bright half of Āśvina—Śivā ceaselessly fulfils all his heart's desires.
m.5.51.80: He who performs the vow on the third day of the bright half of Kārttika, Mārgaśīrṣa, Pauṣa, Tapas (Māgha) and likewise Tapasya (Phālguna),
m.5.51.81: One who worships the goddess Maṅgalā with red flowers such as karavīra (oleander) and with fragrant incense obtains every auspicious thing.
m.5.51.82: Women should always perform this great vow for marital good fortune; men too should undertake it to obtain learning, wealth and sons.
m.5.51.83: Likewise, the Umā-Maheśvara vow and whatever other vows are dear to the Goddess should be performed with one's own devotion by those seeking liberation.
m.5.51.84: This Saṃhitā is supremely meritorious, increasing devotion to Śiva, filled with many narratives, auspicious, and bestowing both enjoyment and liberation.
m.5.51.85: Whoever listens to it with devotion, or attentively causes it to be heard, or reads it, or has it read, attains the supreme goal.
m.5.51.86: He in whose house this Saṃhitā rests, written in elegant letters and duly worshipped according to rule, would obtain all his desires.
m.5.51.87: He never has fear from evil beings such as bhūtas, pretas and piśācas; he surely obtains the wealth of sons, grandsons and the like—there is no doubt.
m.5.51.88: Therefore this delightful, supremely meritorious Umā Saṃhitā should always be heard and recited by those who desire devotion to Śiva.
m.5.51.iti: Thus ends the fifty-first adhyāya, named The exposition of kriyāyoga, in the fifth saṃhitā, the Umā-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.6.1.1: Salutation to Śiva, who is together with Ambā, with his gaṇas and with his sons; to the lord of Pradhāna and Puruṣa, the cause of creation, sustenance and dissolution.
m.6.1.2: The sages said: We have heard the delightful Umā Saṃhitā, filled with many narratives. Now tell us the Kailāsa Saṃhitā, which increases understanding of the principle of Śiva.
m.6.1.3: Vyāsa said: Listen with delight, O children, to the Saṃhitā called Kailāsa. Out of affection I shall tell you this supreme, divine text, devoted to the principle of Śiva.
m.6.1.4: Formerly, sages of great vigour, performing austerities on a peak of the Himālaya, desiring to go to Vārāṇasī, came to a common resolve.
m.6.1.5: Setting out from that mountain and reaching Kāśī, composed in mind, thinking, We must bathe, they then beheld Maṇikarṇikā.
m.6.1.6: Having bathed there and duly satisfied the gods and others with libations, then having seen the Jāhnavī and bathed in it, those lords of sages went to Viśveśa, lord of the thirty gods,
m.6.1.7: bowed and then worshipped him, filled with supreme devotion; and having praised him with hymns such as the Śatarudriya, those masters of the Vedas
m.6.1.8: all regarded themselves thus: We have attained our goal. Through Śiva's favour their aims were fully accomplished, and they were ever devoted to Śiva-bhakti.
m.6.1.9: At that time, seeing Sūta, who had gone out wishing to see the Pañcakrośa region and had come back, they joyfully saluted him.
m.6.1.10: He too, having bowed to Viśveśvara, the god of gods himself, the lord of Umā, then entered the Mukti-maṇḍapa together with them.
m.6.1.11: Then all the sages honoured the great-souled Sūta, the best of Purāṇa-reciters, seated there, with arghya and other offerings.
m.6.1.12: Then Sūta, pleased at heart, looking at the sages of good vows, asked about their welfare; and they too told of their own welfare.
m.6.1.13: Those lords of sages, knowing him to be delighted at heart, spoke introductory words in order to understand the meaning of the Praṇava.
m.6.1.14: The sages said: O disciple of Vyāsa, most fortunate Sūta, best of Purāṇa-reciters, you are blessed, for you are a devotee of Śiva and an ocean of all knowledge.
m.6.1.15: The blessed Vyāsa, teacher of the whole world, consecrated you alone and appointed you to the teachership of the Purāṇas.
m.6.1.16: Therefore the Purāṇic lore abides in your heart; and all the Purāṇas indeed proclaim the meaning of the Veda.
m.6.1.17: The Vedas arose from the Praṇava; the meaning of the Praṇava is Maheśvara. Hence the abode of Maheśvara, his seat, is established in you.
m.6.1.18: Having drunk the nectar of the meaning of the Praṇava, charming with the honey flowing from your lotus-mouth, we shall become free of affliction.
m.6.1.19: Above all, you alone are our teacher, no other, O great-minded one. Out of supreme compassion, tell us the supreme nature of Maheśa.
m.6.1.20: Hearing these words of theirs, the wise Sūta, dear to Vyāsa, bowing to Gaṇeśa, to the six-faced one, to Maheśāna himself, to Maheśvarī,
m.6.1.21: to the god Nandīśa, son of Śilāda, husband of Suyaśā, to Sanatkumāra and to Vyāsa, having bowed, spoke this.
m.6.1.22: Sūta said: Excellent, excellent, O most fortunate sages whose sins are destroyed! A very firm resolve has arisen in you, one that is hard to attain for evildoers.
m.6.1.23: What was taught by the teacher Pārāśarya to the sages dwelling in the Naimiṣa forest, that I shall tell, O bulls among sages.
m.6.1.24: By merely hearing it, devotion to Śiva arises in men. Be attentive today and listen with supreme joy.
m.6.1.25: Formerly, in the Svārociṣa Manvantara, sages of firm vows were performing austerities in the Naimiṣa forest, frequented by all the Siddhas,
m.6.1.26: conducting a long sacrificial session, propitiating Rudra, the lord of sacrifice, and wishing to know his supreme nature and sovereignty.
m.6.1.27: They all dwelt there, longing for the sight of Vyāsa, ever devoted to Śiva-bhakti, wearing ash and rudrākṣa.
m.6.1.28: Perceiving their disposition, the blessed Bādarāyaṇa, the Self of all, the fruit of Parāśara's austerity, appeared.
m.6.1.29: Seeing him, all the sages, with delighted faces and eyes, served him with every courtesy, beginning with rising to receive him.
m.6.1.30: Having honoured him, they offered him an auspicious golden seat. Then, comfortably seated on that golden seat, the great sage Pārāśarya spoke in a deep voice.
m.6.1.31: Vyāsa said: Is all well with you? Tell me. In this great sacrifice, has the lord of the sacrifice been properly worshipped by you?
m.6.1.32: For what purpose has the Supreme Lord, Sāmba, who releases from saṃsāra, been well worshipped here by you in this sacrifice with devotion?
m.6.1.33: Your undertaking appears to me to be prompted by a desire to hear about the supreme nature of Maheśa, of Śiva, for the sake of liberation.
m.6.1.34: Thus addressed by Vyāsa, the lord of sages of immeasurable splendour, the sages dwelling in the Naimiṣa forest, of supreme vigour,
m.6.1.35: bowed to the great-souled great sage Pārāśarya, whose mind was delighted with love for Śiva, and spoke to him.
m.6.1.36: The sages said: O blessed one, tiger among sages, born of a portion of Nārāyaṇa himself, treasury of compassion, greatly wise, master of all knowledge, O lord.
m.6.1.37: For you yourself are the treasury of the graces of this Mahādeva, the sustainer of the whole world, the creator, who is with Ambā and his gaṇas.
m.6.1.38: With minds behaving like bees that taste the nectar of your lotus feet, we have become fulfilled this very day through the sight of your lotus feet.
m.6.1.39: The sight of your lotus feet, surely hard for sinners to obtain, has been obtained by us; therefore we are men of merit.
m.6.1.40: O greatly fortunate one, in this region called Naimiṣāraṇya, all of us, engaged in a long sacrificial session, are expounders of the meaning of the Praṇava (Om).
m.6.1.41: Having firmly resolved that the Supreme Lord is to be heard about, and reflecting among ourselves on the supreme nature of the great Lord,
m.6.1.42: we have not understood it at all. Therefore, O lord, you ought to cut away all those doubts of us, who are of little understanding.
m.6.1.43: For in the three worlds there is none other than you who can cut away this doubt. Therefore, us who are sinking in the shoreless, deep ocean of delusion,
m.6.1.44: rescue us by the boat of the knowledge of Śiva, O treasury of compassion. We are eager in faith to know the true meaning of genuine devotion to Śiva.
m.6.1.45: Thus entreated there by the sages who had mastered the Vedas, the great sage, father of Śuka, foremost among the knowers of the meaning of all the Vedas, meditated on the Praṇava, the entire essence of Vedānta, the Supreme Lord,
m.6.1.46: having meditated, in the centre of the lotus-pericarp of his heart, on Śiva together with Ambā, the liberator from saṃsāra, the great sage, his mind delighted, spoke.
m.6.1.iti: Thus ends the first adhyāya, named The dialogue of Vyāsa, Śaunaka and others, in the sixth saṃhitā, the Kailāsa-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.6.2.1: Vyāsa said: Well asked is this, O brahmins, by you, the most fortunate ones; for the knowledge of Śiva, which reveals the meaning of the Praṇava, is hard to obtain.
m.6.2.2: Only for those with whom the Lord, who bears the excellent trident as his weapon, is directly pleased, does the knowledge of Śiva that reveals the meaning of the Praṇava…
m.6.2.3: …arise—there is no doubt; not for others, those devoid of devotion to Śiva—so declares the Veda; this is the settled conclusion regarding the truth.
m.6.2.4: Through your long sacrificial session the Lord, husband of Ambikā, has been worshipped by you—this I have seen today and know for certain.
m.6.2.5: Therefore I shall tell you, O believers, an ancient and wonderful narrative in the form of a dialogue between Umā and Maheśa.
m.6.2.6: Long ago Satī, daughter of Dakṣa and mother of the whole world, having abandoned her body at her father's sacrifice on account of the reviling of Śiva…
m.6.2.7: …then by her own power that goddess became the daughter of the Himavat mountain; and on Nārada's instruction she performed austerities for the sake of Śiva.
m.6.2.8: On that best of mountains, when the Lord of gods had married her according to the rite of self-choice, Pārvatī attained happiness.
m.6.2.9: Then on one occasion the great goddess Gaurī, comfortably seated with her husband on the great mountain, spoke to the god.
m.6.2.10: Mahādevī said: O Lord, supreme ruler, performer of the five cosmic functions, all-knowing one, easily reached through devotion, whose form is the supreme nectar.
m.6.2.11: Having abandoned the body of Dākṣāyaṇī because of the reviling of you, I have now become, O Maheśāna, the daughter of the mountain Himavat.
m.6.2.12: Out of compassion, O supreme Lord, by the rite of mantra initiation make me permanently established in the truth of the pure Self, O Maheśvara.
m.6.2.13: Thus entreated by the goddess, the god adorned with the cool-rayed moon then replied to the goddess with a delighted heart.
m.6.2.14: Mahādeva said: Blessed are you, O sovereign of the god of gods, since such a resolve has arisen in you. Having gone to the peak of Kailāsa, I shall make you such as you desire.
m.6.2.15: Then, going from Himavat to Kailāsa, lord of mountains, he imparted in due order, by the rite of initiation, the mantras beginning with the Praṇava.
m.6.2.16: Having uttered those mantras and established the goddess in the pure Self, Mahādeva went together with the goddess to the garden of the gods.
m.6.2.17: Then, with those full-blown flowers born of the wish-fulfilling trees, gathered by the goddess's dear companions headed by Sumālinī,…
m.6.2.18: …Śaṅkara adorned the great goddess, set her on his lap, and remained with a joyful face, gazing at her countenance.
m.6.2.19: Then there arose loving conversations between Pārvatī and the supreme Lord, for the welfare of all worlds, directly in accord with the meaning of the Veda.
m.6.2.20: Then the mother of all the world, resting on her husband's lap and gazing at his face, said this, O ascetics.
m.6.2.21: Śrī Devī said: O god, the mantras you taught are held to be accompanied by the Praṇava. Among these, I wish first to hear the definitive meaning of the Praṇava.
m.6.2.22: How did the Praṇava arise? Why is it called Praṇava? How many measures (mātrās) are declared in it? Why is it called the beginning of the Veda?
m.6.2.23: How many deities are declared in it? How is the contemplation of the gods and the rest to be done? Of how many kinds are the actions declared? How is its pervaded-and-pervader relationship?
m.6.2.24: How do the five Brahmans reside in this mantra in their order? How many kalās are declared? How is it that it constitutes the manifest universe?
m.6.2.25: And how, O Śiva, are the seats of the relation between the denoted and the denoting? Who is to be known as the qualified aspirant here? What is declared to be the subject?
m.6.2.26: What relation is to be understood here? What is said to be the purpose? What is the nature of the worshipper? And what is the place and the mode of worship?
m.6.2.27: What is the nature of the object to be worshipped, and what is the fruit for the worshipper? What is the procedure of practice, and what is the place of worship, O Lord?
m.6.2.28: What is the maṇḍala in the worship, and what are the seer and the rest, O Hara? What is the procedure of nyāsa and japa, and what is the sequence of the rite of worship?
m.6.2.29: All this, O Maheśāna, explain in detail. I wish to hear it truly, if you have compassion for me.
m.6.2.30: Thus questioned by the goddess, the Lord adorned with the moon praised Maheśānī and began to speak.
m.6.2.iti: Thus ends the second adhyāya, named The description of the questions asked by the Goddess, in the dialogue of the Goddess and the God, in the sixth saṃhitā, the Kailāsa-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.6.3.1: Īśvara said: Listen, O Goddess, I shall explain what you are asking me. By merely hearing it, the individual soul would become Śiva himself.
m.6.3.2: Full knowledge of the meaning of the praṇava alone is the knowledge whose nature is me. That mantra called praṇava is the seed of all branches of knowledge.
m.6.3.3: It should be known as extremely subtle yet of vast meaning, like the seed of a banyan tree; it is the beginning of the Vedas, the essence of the Vedas, and especially my own form.
m.6.3.4: I, the God beyond the three guṇas, omniscient, maker of all, the Lord, the all-pervading Śiva, abide in the one-syllabled mantra Om.
m.6.3.5: Whatever thing exists, all of it—by the predominance of the guṇas, whether taken collectively or separately—they declare to be the meaning of the praṇava.
m.6.3.6: Therefore this single syllable, which is Brahman, accomplishes all aims. By it—uttering Om—Śiva first brings forth the entire world.
m.6.3.7: Śiva indeed is this praṇava, or the praṇava is held to be Śiva, since there is no absolute difference between the denoted and that which denotes it.
m.6.3.8: Therefore the wise brahmarṣis, regarding the denoted and the denoter as one, know me, the God, as the single syllable.
m.6.3.9: Hence the seeker of liberation, free from agitation, should know that very praṇava, the cause of all, as me, the attributeless Supreme Lord.
m.6.3.10: This very mantra, O Queen of the gods, the crest-jewel of all mantras, I shall bestow in Kāśī for the liberation of living beings.
m.6.3.11: In this matter, O Ambikā, I shall first explain the extraction of the praṇava, by merely knowing which supreme accomplishment arises.
m.6.3.12: One should first extract Nivṛtti, the letter A, and after that Indhana, U; afterwards one should extract Kāla, M, then Daṇḍa and Īśvara, the bindu and nāda.
m.6.3.13: Thus extracted, this praṇava has the form of five elements, consisting of the three mātrās, bindu and nāda; it ever grants liberation to those who repeat it.
m.6.3.14: Of all living beings, from Brahmā down to the immobile, this praṇava is truly the life-breath (prāṇa); therefore it is called praṇava.
m.6.3.15: One should place the first letter A, then U to the north, and M in the middle, and its end in nāda — thus Om.
m.6.3.16: In the Oṃkāra, O best of sages, place the first letter, which is like water, in the south, and likewise U in the north, and M, which is like fire, in the middle.
m.6.3.17: A, U and M — this triad in order — are called the three mātrās; beyond them is the half-mātrā.
m.6.3.18: The half-mātrā, O Maheśānī, has the nature of bindu and nāda; it truly cannot be described, and it is to be known directly only by the knowers.
m.6.3.19: The Vedas truly declare, O beloved, that the primal śrutis such as Īśānaḥ sarvavidyānām (the Lord of all knowledges) arise from me alone.
m.6.3.20: Therefore I alone am the beginning of the Vedas, and the praṇava is my denoter; because it denotes me, it too is called the beginning of the Vedas.
m.6.3.21: A is the great seed, rajas, the four-faced creator Brahmā; U is Prakṛti, the womb, sattva, the preserver Hari.
m.6.3.22: M is Puruṣa, the seed-bearer, tamas, the destroyer Hara; the bindu is declared to be the god Maheśvara, the power of concealment.
m.6.3.23: Nāda is said to be Sadāśiva, the bestower of grace on all; at the summit of nāda one should contemplate Śiva, higher than the highest.
m.6.3.24: He is omniscient, the doer of all, lord of all, stainless, imperishable, indescribable, the Supreme Brahman itself, beyond both being and non-being.
m.6.3.25: Among the letters beginning with A, each succeeding one is the pervader and the lower one is the pervaded; thus one should contemplate throughout.
m.6.3.26: The five Brahmans, from Sadyojāta up to Īśāna, abiding in the five elements beginning with A, are in order my forms.
m.6.3.27: O Śivā, eight kalās born of Sadyojāta are declared to be in A; in U, thirteen kalās having the form of Vāmadeva are described.
m.6.3.28: Eight kalās having the form of Aghora abide in M; in the bindu four kalās have arisen, belonging to Tatpuruṣa.
m.6.3.29: In nāda five kalās arising from Īśāna are declared. Through contemplating the sixfold oneness, the praṇava is said to have the nature of the manifest universe.
m.6.3.30: Mantra, yantra, deity, the manifest universe, the guru, and the disciple—hear, O beloved, the meaning of these six categories.
m.6.3.31: The mantra, as stated before, is the aggregate of the five letters. That same mantra becomes the yantra; I shall describe the arrangement of its maṇḍala.
m.6.3.32: The yantra is the form of the deity; the deity has the form of the universe; the guru is said to have the form of the universe; the disciple is held to be the body of the guru.
m.6.3.33: According to the śruti, which says that Om is all this and that all is Brahman, this very meaning is declared to be the relation of denoted and denoter.
m.6.3.34: The Ādhāra, the Maṇipūra, then after that the heart, then Viśuddhi and Ājñā, then Śakti and Śānti, in order—
m.6.3.35: —these are the stations, O Queen of the gods; beyond Śānti is that which is higher than the highest. He in whom firm dispassion arises becomes the qualified aspirant.
m.6.3.36: I am the subject-matter, O Goddess, through contemplation of the oneness of the individual soul and Brahman. The subject-matter has been properly stated; now hear the relation, O Queen of the gods.
m.6.3.37: Here the relation is declared to be that of denoted and denoter, between the oneness of the individual self with me and the praṇava.
m.6.3.38: The aspirant should be devoted to vows and the like, tranquil, austere, with senses subdued, endowed with purity and good conduct, a brahmin firmly grounded in the Veda,
m.6.3.39: being detached from sense-objects both of this world and the next, a true devotee of the gods and brahmins, and observing vows to Śiva,
m.6.3.40: having approached a preceptor, an ascetic who knows the true meaning of all scriptures, who has crossed to the far shore of Vedānta knowledge, the best among the wise,
m.6.3.41: The wise, excellent disciple, endowed with qualities such as tranquillity and possessed of good conduct, should diligently please the guru with full-length prostrations and the like.
m.6.3.42: He who is the guru is declared to be Śiva; he who is Śiva is held to be the guru — having firmly settled this in his mind, he should make known his own intention to the guru.
m.6.3.43: Having obtained permission from the guru, he should live for twelve days observing a vow of subsisting on milk, on the seashore, by a river, on a mountain, or in a temple of Śiva.
m.6.3.44: On the fifth day of the bright fortnight, or else on the eleventh, the wise one, having bathed in the morning, pure in self and having performed his daily rites,
m.6.3.45: having invited the guru according to rule and performed the Nāndī-śrāddha, and then having had a shave done, excluding the armpits and the private parts,
m.6.3.46: the shaving of hair, beard and nails, and having bathed with a restrained mind, then having eaten barley-meal, in the evening, having bathed and worshipped at the twilight (sandhyā),
m.6.3.47: having performed the evening Aupāsana fire-offering, the twice-born, accompanied by the guru, having given the fee prescribed in the scriptures to Śiva in the form of the guru,
m.6.3.48: having gathered the materials for the oblation according to the procedure stated in his own Sūtra, and having duly installed the fire according to its distinctions such as the ordinary (laukika) and others,
m.6.3.49: But one who has already established the sacred fires should properly perform the Prājāpatya iṣṭi in the established Śrauta Vaiśvānara fire, with all his possessions as the sacrificial fee.
m.6.3.50: Then, having placed the fire within himself, the Brāhmaṇa should go forth from home. Having cooked the caru oblation in that fire, with the distinctions of fuel-sticks, food and ghee,
m.6.3.51: the self-controlled one, having offered oblations with each verse of the Puruṣa Sūkta, and having offered the Sviṣṭakṛt oblation according to the procedure stated in his own Sūtra,
m.6.3.52: and having offered the concluding rites (uparitantra), the wise one should then sit on a seat, to the north of the fire, covered with cloth, deer-skin and kuśa grass, and, silent and firm of mind, should recite the Gāyatrī until the Brāhma-muhūrta.
m.6.3.53: Then, having bathed as before and then cooked the caru, the wise one should offer oblations beginning with the Puruṣa Sūkta and ending with the Virajā mantras.
m.6.3.54: This may be done according to the view of Vāmadeva, or according to the view of Śaunaka and others; of these, the Vāmadeva method is foremost, since that sage was endowed with knowledge even in the womb.
m.6.3.55: Then, having completed the remainder of the homa, he should offer the morning Aupāsana; then, having placed the fire within himself and worshipped at the morning twilight,
m.6.3.56: after the sun has risen, he should then in due order enter into the Sāvitrī; having renounced the three desires and uttering the Praiṣa, the formula of renunciation, in due order,
m.6.3.57: having abandoned the tuft and the sacred thread, and then having cast off the waist-string and the like, he should go forth facing east, or else facing the northern direction.
m.6.3.58: He should take the staff, loincloth and the like, as befits conduct in the world; but if he is dispassionate regarding considerations of worldly conduct, he need not take them.
m.6.3.59: Then, going near the guru, he should prostrate three times like a staff; then, rising, he should stand near the guru's feet.
m.6.3.60: Then the guru, taking the white ash produced from the Virajā fire, and having duly smeared that disciple with it,
m.6.3.61: should then have him bear the Tripuṇḍra, the three lines of ash, with the mantras beginning Agni; the disciple should meditate on me seated together with you in the lotus of the heart.
m.6.3.62: Placing his hand on the disciple's head, with a pleased mind, the guru should utter into his right ear, together with the seer and the other particulars,
m.6.3.63: the Praṇava three times; then that best of gurus should teach its meaning — the sixfold meaning, together with full understanding,
m.6.3.64: and in twelve forms. He the disciple, having bowed to the guru on the ground like a staff, should always remain dependent on him and should thoroughly study the Vedānta.
m.6.3.65: He should constantly meditate on me alone, the Supreme Self, within the pure and changeless self — the imperishable witness of Brahman.
m.6.3.66: The ascetic devoted to the disciplines such as tranquillity, who has crossed to the far shore of Vedāntic knowledge and is free from envy, is declared to be qualified for this.
m.6.3.67: He should contemplate the heart-lotus — stainless, sorrowless, clear and supreme, eight-petalled, rich with filaments, resplendent above its pericarp —
m.6.3.68: having contemplated it as the seat comprising all from the Ādhāra-śakti up to the end of the three tattvas, he should meditate on the subtle space (dahara) in its centre.
m.6.3.69: Uttering Om, the one-syllabled Brahman, he should, with mind ever intent, meditate on me together with you in the centre of that space.
m.6.3.70: For a worshipper of this kind there is attainment of my world, and, having obtained knowledge from me, the fruit of union (sāyujya) with me, O beloved.
m.6.3.iti: Thus ends the third adhyāya, named The description of the procedure of saṃnyāsa, in the sixth saṃhitā, the Kailāsa-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.6.4.1: Īśvara said: Next I shall explain the daily rites of the renunciant, O Mahādevī, out of affection for you and in accordance with the tradition.
m.6.4.2: Rising at the Brāhma muhūrta, the ascetic should meditate on the Guru seated in the head, on the white thousand-petalled lotus.
m.6.4.3: The Guru resembling pure crystal, two-eyed, holding the gestures of boon and fearlessness, charming, bearing within himself the very true nature of Śiva.
m.6.4.4: Having worshipped him in due order with mentally offered sandal-paste and other items, and joining the palms in añjali, he should then bow to the Guru.
m.6.4.5: Whatever I do from morning until the end of evening, and from evening until morning, O Mahādeva, may that be your worship.
m.6.4.6: Having thus declared this to the Guru and then obtained the Guru's permission, seated, with breath restrained, self-controlled and with senses subdued,
m.6.4.7: he should contemplate the six cakras, from the Mūlādhāra up to the Brahmarandhra, supreme, full of all radiance, shining like ten million lightnings.
m.6.4.8: In their midst he should meditate on me, whose form is being-consciousness-bliss, the attributeless supreme Brahman, Sadāśiva, free from affliction.
m.6.4.9: The wise one, experiencing oneness with me, thinking, I am he, should then go out and walk far off as is comfortable.
m.6.4.10: The wise one, covering his head together with the nose with a cloth and placing grass on the ground, should relieve the body in the prescribed manner.
m.6.4.11: Rising, holding the genital, he should then go to a body of water; drawing water in the proper way, he should perform the purification diligently.
m.6.4.12: Having cleansed hands and feet and sipped water twice, remembering Om, facing north and silent, he should clean his teeth.
m.6.4.13: He should always do it with grass and leaves, except on the new-moon day and Ekādaśī; then he should cleanse the mouth with twelve mouthfuls of water.
m.6.4.14: Having sipped twice and cleansed the loins with earth and water, he should bathe with earth at the time of dawn.
m.6.4.15: Remembering the Guru and me, he should perform bathing, Sandhyā and the rest; for fear of prolixity it is not stated here and should be looked up elsewhere.
m.6.4.16: Forming the conch gesture, he should pour water on the head with the Praṇava, twelve times, or half that, or half of that.
m.6.4.17: Coming to the bank, washing the loincloth and sipping water twice, he should sprinkle with the Praṇava the cloth used for wiping the body.
m.6.4.18: Wiping the face first, then beginning from the head, he should wipe the whole body with that same cloth, standing in the presence of the Guru.
m.6.4.19: He should tie on, from the left, a clean loincloth with its string; then he should apply ash — its procedure is now told, O daughter of the mountain.
m.6.4.20: Having sipped twice and taken the ash with the Sadyojāta and other mantras, consecrating it with the mantras beginning Agniḥ, he should touch the body.
m.6.4.21: Then consecrating water with Āpo vā, he should sprinkle the ash with it, uttering Om āpo jyotiḥ and the mantra Mā nas toke.
m.6.4.22: Kneading it, he should make two portions, and divide one fivefold for the head, face, heart, private parts and feet, O Supreme Goddess,
m.6.4.23: with the five mantras in order, beginning with Īśāna and ending with Sadyojāta. Having smeared that portion, he should afterwards sprinkle with the Praṇava
m.6.4.24: the whole body. Then, washing the hands, he should take the other portion, knead it as before, and with it apply the tripuṇḍra marks,
m.6.4.25: with the Tryāyuṣa and Tryambaka mantras, the Praṇava and the Śiva mantra, on the head, the forehead, the chest and the shoulders,
m.6.4.26: on the navel, the arms, the joints and the back, in due order. Then, washing the hands and sipping water twice as prescribed,
m.6.4.27: the wise one, reciting the pañcīkaraṇa, should contemplate his own Guru, and perform six breath-controls in the manner to be described.
m.6.4.28: Taking water in the right hand and covering it with the left hand, he should consecrate it twelve times with the Praṇava.
m.6.4.29: Having thus sprinkled it on the head three times, he should then drink thrice, meditating with a collected mind on the Lord who is Oṃkāra,
m.6.4.30: stationed in the middle of the solar disc, supreme, full of all radiance, eight-armed, four-faced, wondrous, half-woman (Ardhanārī),
m.6.4.31: endowed with all wondrous qualities, adorned with all ornaments. Having meditated thus, he should then duly offer three arghyas.
m.6.4.32: Having recited the Praṇava one hundred and eight times, he should offer libations twelve times; sipping water again, he should duly perform three breath-controls.
m.6.4.33: He should come to the place of worship remembering Śiva in his mind; reaching the door and washing his feet, he should, silent, sip water twice.
m.6.4.34: He should enter there in due manner, right foot first; and inside the pavilion the wise one should construct the maṇḍala step by step.
m.6.4.iti: Thus ends the fourth adhyāya, named The description of the conduct of saṃnyāsa, in the sixth saṃhitā, the Kailāsa-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.6.5.1: Īśvara said: Having duly examined the ground by its smell, colour, taste and so on, there, in a place pleasing to the mind, with a canopy spread overhead,
m.6.5.2: on the well-plastered surface of the ground, resembling the inside of a mirror, he should mark out a square measuring two cubits (aratni).
m.6.5.3: Taking a palm-leaf whose length and breadth equal that square, he should make on it thirteen equal divisions.
m.6.5.4: Placing that leaf there, standing facing west, and taking a very strong coloured cord at its eastern side,
m.6.5.5: he should stretch the cords east–west and south–north in all four directions, O Sovereign of the lord of gods; one hundred and sixty-nine
m.6.5.6: compartments then result. Its central compartment is the pericarp; the eight compartments outside it are here called the eight petals.
m.6.5.7: He should make all the petals white in colour, having made the pericarp yellow and the circle reddish.
m.6.5.8: Beginning from the right of the petal of Indra (the eastern petal), O Queen of the gods, he should colour the junctions of the petals red and black in sequence.
m.6.5.9: In the pericarp he should draw the yantra that reveals the meaning of the praṇava: having drawn the seat (pīṭha) below, and Śrīkaṇṭha above it,
m.6.5.10: above that Amareśa, and Mahākāla in the middle, and the staff (daṇḍa) placed on its head; then he should draw Īśvara.
m.6.5.11: He should colour the seat dark and Śrīkaṇṭha yellow; and those two, Amareśa and Mahākāla, red and black respectively.
m.6.5.12: The wise man should make the staff smoky grey and Īśvara white. Having thus drawn the yantra, he should encircle it in red with the Sadya mantra.
m.6.5.13: With the very nāda arising from it he should pierce Īśāna, O Īśvarī. Then he should take up the outer rows in order, beginning with the south-east.
m.6.5.14: These four compartments in the corner portions, O beautiful one, having filled with white, and the set of four next with red minerals,
m.6.5.15: having filled those four, he should fashion them as the doors. Then he should fill the pair on their two sides with yellow.
m.6.5.16: In the middle of the south-east compartment, within a yellowish square, he should draw an eight-petalled lotus, reddish, with a yellow pericarp.
m.6.5.17: With concentrated mind he should write in the middle the letter ha joined with bindu. Then in the south-west compartment of the lotus design he should draw a square,
m.6.5.18: and a red eight-petalled lotus with yellow filaments and pericarp. The third letter of the śa-group (sa), joined with the sixth vowel,
m.6.5.19: furnished with the fourteenth vowel and adorned with bindu and nāda — this excellent seed-syllable, O auspicious one, he should write in the middle of the lotus.
m.6.5.20: In the north-east compartment of the lotus design he should likewise draw a lotus; the third letter of the ka-group (ga), joined with the fifth vowel,
m.6.5.21: he should write in its middle, well adorned with bindu at its neck. In the three outer rows, all around in order beginning from the east,
m.6.5.22: he should take five compartments, O daughter of the king of mountains, O Śivā. In the middle he should make the pericarp yellow and the circle red.
m.6.5.23: The best knower of the rite should make the petals red in colour; outside the petals he should fill the gaps with black.
m.6.5.24: The four beginning with the south-east he should fill with white alone. In the east he should draw a black hexagon with six dots,
m.6.5.25: in the south a red triangle, then in the north a white half-moon, and in the west a yellow
m.6.5.26: square. In these, in order, he should write the four seed-syllables: having drawn in the east the bindu, white, and black in the south,
m.6.5.27: the letter u, red, in the north, then the letter ma in the west, and the letter a, yellow — having thus made the four letters,
m.6.5.28: and beginning in the row below the uppermost row, O beautiful one, he should colour the set of four: yellow, white, red and black;
m.6.5.29: below that the set of four: white, dark, yellow and red; and below, in the triangle, red, white and yellow, O fair-faced one.
m.6.5.30: Thus, beginning from the south, he should proceed up to the north (Soma's quarter), O Īśvarī. In the row outside it he should colour from the east up to the middle:
m.6.5.31: yellow, red, black, dark, white and yellow. Beginning with the south-east, O dear one: red, dark, white,
m.6.5.32: red, black and red — this group of six is declared. The sequence starting from the south is stated as extending up to the east, O Maheśānī;
m.6.5.33: that starting from the south-west is to be known as extending up to the south-east, O Īśvarī; and beginning from the west it is stated as extending up to the south;
m.6.5.34: that starting from the north-west is stated as extending up to the south-west, O Mahādevī; that starting from the north (Soma) is stated as extending up to the west, O Supreme Sovereign;
m.6.5.35: and that starting from the north-east is to be known as extending up to the north-west, O Ambikā. Thus the procedure of the maṇḍala has been told to you by me, O Pārvatī.
m.6.5.36: Having thus drawn the maṇḍala, the self-controlled ascetic should himself perform the worship of the Sun, for he is intent on that reality.
m.6.5.iti: Thus ends the fifth adhyāya, named The description of the rite of the maṇḍala for saṃnyāsa, in the sixth saṃhitā, the Kailāsa-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.6.6.1: Īśvara said: Then, to the south of the maṇḍala, having spread a fine tiger skin, one should sprinkle it with pure water using the astra mantra.
m.6.6.2: First uttering the praṇava, one should next utter ādhāra; after that śakti-kamala, put in the dative ending and closing with namaḥ.
m.6.6.3: Having thus pronounced the mantra and seated himself on it facing north, he should restrain the breaths according to rule, preceded by uttering the praṇava.
m.6.6.4: Then he should apply ash with the mantras beginning agniḥ; bowing to the revered guru on his head, he should again draw a maṇḍala:
m.6.6.5: a triangle and circle, and on the outside a square, in order. Having worshipped it with Om, placing the conch together with its stand, he should worship it.
m.6.6.6: Filling it with pure, fragrant water with the praṇava, and worshipping it with sandal, flowers and the like, and with the praṇava seven times—
m.6.6.7: having consecrated it, he should then show over it the cow-gesture (dhenu-mudrā) and the conch-gesture; and with that water he should sprinkle, using the astra mantra,
m.6.6.8: himself and the articles of worship such as sandal and flowers. Having done three breath-controls, he should then perform the assignment of the seer and the rest.
m.6.6.9: Of this sacred Solar mantra the seer is Devabhāga; the metre is declared to be Gāyatrī; the god Sūrya, the Great Lord,
m.6.6.10: is the deity. He should assign the six limbs with the syllables beginning hrāṃ. Then he should sprinkle the lotus with the astra mantra, the lotus beyond the reach of fire.
m.6.6.11: On it the wise one should worship Prabhūtā and Vimalā, and then propitiate Sārā, in order beginning from the east and onward.
m.6.6.12: Then Kālāgnirudra, the Śakti named Ādhāra, Ananta, the Earth, and likewise the Jewel-island,
m.6.6.13: having visualized the grove of trees and then the jewelled house, and having worshipped the red seat, he should worship on its feet, beginning from the east,
m.6.6.14: the group of four: Dharma, Knowledge, Dispassion and Sovereignty; and he should worship Adharma and the rest in the corners beginning with the south-east (Agni's corner).
m.6.6.15: Then Māyā as the lower covering, and after that Vidyā as the upper covering; and having worshipped Sattva, Rajas and Tamas in due order,
m.6.6.16: he should worship in the directions beginning with the east and in the centre: Dīptā, Sūkṣmā, Jayā, Bhadrā, Vibhūti, Vimalā, Amoghā and Vaidyutā,
m.6.6.17: and the one named Sarvatomukhī; likewise the bulb and stalk, then its hollow, and after that the thorns,
m.6.6.18: the root, the coverings, the filaments of that lotus whose whole nature is radiance; the pericarp with five knots, and after that the petals,
m.6.6.19: the stamens, Brahmā and Viṣṇu, Rudra and the Self, the Inner Self too, and the Knowledge-Self and the Supreme Self—
m.6.6.20: having worshipped these, he should afterwards worship the yoga-seat called Saura. On the seat, the knower of the root mantra should visualize the deity's form with the root mantra.
m.6.6.21: Seated with breath restrained, by the root mantra alone raising the Śakti from his own root centre, by its power bringing it along the Piṅgalā path,
m.6.6.22: and having let it go out into the handful of flowers—then, in the heart-lotus of the shining one dwelling in the orb, whose body is red as vermilion, whose beloved forms his left half,
m.6.6.23: who holds a rosary, noose, khaṭvāṅga staff, skull, goad, lotus, conch and discus, who is four-faced, and adorned with eyes—
m.6.6.24: shining with twelve eyes—within his heart-lotus he should invoke him: first uttering the praṇava, then hrāṃ hrīṃ saḥ,
m.6.6.25: and after that, Mārtaṇḍa together with the Śakti of Radiance, I invoke, namaḥ—having thus invoked him, with the mudrā called Āvāhana,
m.6.6.26: mudrā, he should then display the mudrās of installation and the rest. Then, having assigned the limbs with the mantra ending in hrāṃ hrīṃ hrūṃ,
m.6.6.27: and having arranged the five offerings, he should worship three times with the root mantra. And on the filaments of the lotus, O Maheśvarī, the six limbs—
m.6.6.28: the wise one should worship around, in order, in the quarters of Agni, Īśa, Rakṣas and Vāyu. In the second enclosure the four forms are to be worshipped in order,
m.6.6.29: from the east up to the north, at the bases of the petals, O Pārvatī: Āditya, Bhāskara, Bhānu and Ravi, in succession.
m.6.6.30: Again, O beloved, Arka, Brahmā, Rudra and Viṣṇu are to be worshipped in the corners beginning with Īśāna, in the third enclosure.
m.6.6.31: He should worship these all around, in the middle of the petals beginning with the east: the Moon, Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, Saturn, and the two Darknesses (Rāhu and Ketu).
m.6.6.32: Or else he should worship the twelve Ādityas in the second enclosure, and in the third enclosure he should worship the twelve zodiac signs.
m.6.6.33: And outside it, all around, the seven oceans and the Gaṅgās; the sages, gods, Gandharvas, serpents and the hosts of Apsarases,
m.6.6.34: the Grāmaṇīs, likewise the Yakṣas, the Yātudhānas, the horses made of the seven metres, and the Bālakhilyas—these he should worship.
m.6.6.35: Having thus worshipped the god Divākara with his three enclosures, he should afterwards, with collected mind, draw a square maṇḍala,
