m.7.1.21.iti: Thus ends the twenty-first adhyāya, named The punishment of the gods, in the Pūrva-khaṇḍa of the seventh saṃhitā, the Vāyavīya-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.7.1.22.1: Vāyu said: At that moment a chariot appeared in the sky, shining like a thousand suns, with a bull-banner of beautiful cloth.
m.7.1.22.2: It was magnificent with a pair of jewel-like horses, had four chariot-wheels, and was adorned with many stored divine missiles, weapons and gems.
m.7.1.22.3: The charioteer of that excellent chariot, too, was the very one who had formerly stood on Śarva's chariot in the battle against Tripura.
m.7.1.22.4: That Brahmā, at the very command of the trident-bearer, brought that excellent chariot near Hari on the battlefield and, with joined palms, spoke.
m.7.1.22.5: O lord Bhadra, of auspicious form, the blessed, moon-adorned, imperishable hero commands you to mount the chariot.
m.7.1.22.6: Tryambaka, staying near Raibhya's hermitage together with Ambikā, is watching your irresistible valour, O mighty-armed one.
m.7.1.22.7: Hearing those words of his, that hero, the elephant among the gaṇas, favouring the Grandsire, mounted the divine chariot.
m.7.1.22.8: When he was thus on that excellent chariot with Brahmā as charioteer, Bhadra's splendour grew, like that of Rudra, the enemy of the cities.
m.7.1.22.9: Then the mighty Bhānukampa, placing at his mouth an excellent blazing conch shining like the full moon, blew it.
m.7.1.22.10: Hearing that sound of the conch, like that of a bursting ocean, the fire in the bellies of the gods blazed up out of fear.
m.7.1.22.11: In an instant the directions, along with the hollows of the sky, became crowded with Yakṣas, Vidyādharas, serpent-lords and Siddhas eager to see the battle.
m.7.1.22.12: Then that Nārāyaṇa-cloud, with the Śārṅga loosing arrows from the curve of the bow as a cloud does from its rainbow, struck the bull among the gaṇas with a great shower of arrows.
m.7.1.22.13: Seeing Viṣṇu coming on, raining arrows a hundredfold, Bhadra, who could release a thousand arrows, took up his victorious bow.
m.7.1.22.14: Taking up that divine bow, terrible in battle, he slowly drew it, as the Lord drew Meru as his bow.
m.7.1.22.15: As that bow was being drawn there arose a mighty sound; with that great sound it made the earth tremble.
m.7.1.22.16: Then the glorious lord of the gaṇas, of fierce valour, himself seized an excellent, terrible, blazing arrow like a venomous serpent.
m.7.1.22.17: As he drew out the arrow, his arm, joined to the mouth of the quiver, looked like a serpent about to enter an anthill.
m.7.1.22.18: Drawn out into his hand, the arrow at that moment shone like a young snake caught in the jaws of a great serpent.
m.7.1.22.19: Enraged, Bhadra, of Rudra's valour, deeply pierced the imperishable Viṣṇu on the forehead with a dense, sharp arrow.
m.7.1.22.20: Struck on the forehead, and already humiliated before, Viṣṇu grew angry at the lord of the gaṇas, as a bull at a lion.
m.7.1.22.21: Then, with a great thunderbolt-like arrow with a cruel tip, he pierced the king of the gaṇas in his serpent-like arm.
m.7.1.22.22: The mighty Vīrabhadra in turn swiftly shot into his arm again an arrow bright as ten thousand suns.
m.7.1.22.23: Viṣṇu struck Bhadra again, and Bhadra likewise Viṣṇu again; he struck him and he struck him — so, O brahmins, the two kept striking each other with arrows.
m.7.1.22.24: As the two swiftly released arrows at each other, a tumultuous, hair-raising battle arose between them.
m.7.1.22.25: Seeing that tumultuous battle between the two, a great cry of alarm raised by the sky-dwellers arose in the heavens.
m.7.1.22.26: Then, with a fire-tipped arrow bright as the sun, Bhadra pierced him very firmly in Viṣṇu's broad chest.
m.7.1.22.27: Struck hard by that arrow of fierce impact, he felt great pain and fell down unconscious.
m.7.1.22.28: Then, rising again as if after a moment, Hari regained consciousness and hurled all his divine missiles back at him.
m.7.1.22.29: And he, the commander of Śarva's army, suddenly warded off with terrible counter-arrows all the arrows released from Viṣṇu's bow.
m.7.1.22.30: Then Viṣṇu, eyes red with anger, released at that lord of the gaṇas an arrow marked with his own name, never obstructed anywhere. That arrow, with his excellent arrow named Bhadra, Bhadra —
m.7.1.22.31: — the lord cut into a hundred pieces on its path before it reached him. Then with one arrow he cut the Śārṅga, and with two the wings of Garuḍa,
m.7.1.22.32: he cut in the twinkling of an eye; it was like a marvel. Then Viṣṇu, through the power of yoga, from his body very terrible gods —
m.7.1.22.33: bearing conch, discus and mace in their hands — he sent forth by thousands. All of them, in a mere instant, as Śaṅkara burned the Tripura-demons,
m.7.1.22.34: the mighty-armed one burned up with fire produced from his eye. Then Viṣṇu, more enraged, swiftly raising his discus,
m.7.1.22.35: was then ready to hurl it at that hero. Seeing him standing before him with discus raised,
m.7.1.22.36: the lord of the gaṇas, as if smiling, paralysed him without effort. With his limbs paralysed, that terrible discus, unmatched anywhere,
m.7.1.22.37: Viṣṇu, though wishing to hurl it, was not able. As if gasping, holding up one arm bearing the discus,
m.7.1.22.38: he stood, become inert, motionless as a stone — like a soul without a body, or a bull without horns,
m.7.1.22.39: or a lion without fangs — so Viṣṇu stood. Seeing Viṣṇu fallen into that sorry state, the gods led by Indra, roused against the lord of the gaṇas like bulls against a lion,
m.7.1.22.40: took up their weapons and, enraged, came forward to fight. Seeing them in battle, Bhadra, as a lion sees petty beasts,
m.7.1.22.41: The blameless hero, Rudra's very own body, surrounded by excellent heroic gaṇas, paralysed the gods with a terrible loud laugh.
m.7.1.22.42: Likewise the right hand of Indra, the god of a hundred sacrifices, holding the thunderbolt, as he was about to hurl it with the thunderbolt raised, became as if painted motionless.
m.7.1.22.43: The arms of all the others too, though full of vigour, likewise fell back, like the undertakings of the lazy.
m.7.1.22.44: Thus, because all their power had been struck down by that Lord, the immortals were unable to stand before him in battle.
m.7.1.22.45: Overwhelmed with fear, they fled with their stiffened limbs; and some made a stand in the battle, agitated by fear of the hero's splendour.
m.7.1.22.46: Mighty-armed Vīrabhadra pierced the fleeing heroic gods with sharp arrows, as a cloud pelts the mountains with rains.
m.7.1.22.47: The many arms of that hero, like iron bars, shone with blazing weapons, like serpents with flames of fire.
m.7.1.22.48: That hero, discharging many missiles and weapons, shone like the source of the universe Brahmā sending forth all beings in the beginning.
m.7.1.22.49: As the sun covers the earth with its rays, so the hero in an instant covered the directions with arrows.
m.7.1.22.50: In the vault of the sky, the gold-adorned arrows of the lord of gaṇas, flying upward, came to be compared with forms of lightning.
m.7.1.22.51: Those great arrows, like water-snakes seizing frogs, parted the hosts of gods from their lives and drank the wine of their blood.
m.7.1.22.52: Some immortals with arms cut off, some with their fine faces severed, some torn open at the side, fell to the ground.
m.7.1.22.53: With bodies mangled by arrows and many joints severed, some, eyes rolling, fell dead upon the earth, as though wishing to enter the ground, as though longing to go into the sky.
m.7.1.22.54: Of those who found no shelter for themselves, hiding among one another, some entered the earth, others the caves of mountains.
m.7.1.22.55: Others went into the sky, and others entered the water. Thus, with the gods cut up in every limb, that hero shone—
m.7.1.22.56: like the Lord Bhairava when the host of creatures has been devoured, like the Enemy of Tripura when the array of the three cities had been burnt.
m.7.1.22.57: Thus the whole army of the gods, wretched and hideous to behold, took on a pitiable form brought about by the lord of gaṇas.
m.7.1.22.58: Then a terrible river began to flow, carrying as its water the blood of the heroic gods, proclaiming fear to living beings.
m.7.1.22.59: Drenched with blood, the sacrificial ground then looked like the dark Kauśikī, her garment wet with blood, after slaying Śumbha.
m.7.1.22.60: When that great and exceedingly dreadful battle had taken place, the earth shook, as if trembling with fear.
m.7.1.22.61: The great ocean, full of huge waves and whirlpools, was agitated; meteors fell as great portents, and trees shed their branches.
m.7.1.22.62: All the directions were gloomy and an inauspicious wind blew. Alas, what a reversal of fate! This rite was a horse-sacrifice; the sacrificer was Dakṣa himself, the Prajāpati, son of Brahmā;
m.7.1.22.63: Dharma and others were the assessors, the Garuḍa-bannered Viṣṇu was the protector, and the gods, Indra and the rest, in person received the shares;
m.7.1.22.64: yet the immediate beheading of the sacrificer and of the sacrifice together with the priests—that is the fruit which duly came about.
m.7.1.22.65: Therefore one should never perform a rite that is not prescribed by the Veda, nor one that excludes the Lord, nor one undertaken by the wicked.
m.7.1.22.66: Even having done very great merit and having sacrificed with hundreds of sacrifices, one who lacks devotion to Maheśvara does not obtain its fruit.
m.7.1.22.67: Even having committed a very great sin, whoever worships Śiva with devotion is freed from all sins; there is no need for doubt here.
m.7.1.22.68: What need of saying much here? For one devoted to reviling Śiva, charity is futile, austerity is futile, sacrifice is futile, oblation is futile.
m.7.1.22.69: Then the hosts of gods in the battle, together with Nārāyaṇa, with the Rudras and with the world-guardians, pierced by arrows released from the bow of the lord of gaṇas, overcome by intense pain, fled.
m.7.1.22.70: Here some, with dishevelled hair, staggered; there some, with tall bodies, sank down; here some, with shattered faces, fell; there some heroic gods perished.
m.7.1.22.71: And some gods there, stricken, their garments, ornaments, missiles and weapons slipped away, fell down, a wretched aspect showing on them, having abandoned their pride, arrogance and strength.
m.7.1.22.72: That unassailable lord of gaṇas, having scattered with his unfailing weapons Dakṣa's sacrifice that had set out on a wrong path, shone standing amid the lords of gaṇas like a lion among bulls.
m.7.1.22.iti: Thus ends the twenty-second adhyāya, named The destruction of Dakṣa's sacrifice, in the Pūrva-khaṇḍa of the seventh saṃhitā, the Vāyavīya-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.7.1.23.1: Vāyu said: Thus the gods led by Viṣṇu, their limbs cut and broken, fell in a moment into a wretched state and trembled, only a few of them left.
m.7.1.23.2: Those terrified heroic gods, and others too, in the battle, the Pramatha gaṇas, extremely enraged and urged on by Vīrabhadra,
m.7.1.23.3: seized them according to their offence and bound them with strong iron fetters on their hands and feet, on their necks and on their bellies.
m.7.1.23.4: At that moment Brahmā, who had won Śiva's affection by serving as charioteer, bowing down and entreating, spoke to Bhadra, who was praised by the daughter of the king of mountains.
m.7.1.23.5: Enough of anger, O lord; these heaven-dwellers are ruined. Be gracious; let everything be forgiven, together with the deeds of the Romaja gaṇas, O you of good vows.
m.7.1.23.6: Thus addressed by that Brahmā, the Supreme One, the lord of the gaṇas, well pleased, became calm out of respect for him.
m.7.1.23.7: And the gods, having obtained the opportunity from the minister of the god of gods, holding their joined palms on their heads, praised him with various hymns.
m.7.1.23.8: The gods said: Salutation to the auspicious, the peaceful one, destroyer of the sacrifice, bearer of the trident; to Rudra's Bhadra, lord of the Rudras, the very might of Rudra;
m.7.1.23.9: to him whose form is Kālāgnirudra, who took away the bodies of Kāla and Kāma, who struck off the heads of the deities and of the wicked Dakṣa.
m.7.1.23.10: Because of association with this sinful Dakṣa of evil deeds, we, though blameless, have been punished by you in battle, O hero.
m.7.1.23.11: All of us here are burnt and afraid of you, O lord. You alone are our refuge; protect us who have come to you for shelter.
m.7.1.23.12: Vāyu said: Pleased at being praised thus, the lord released the gods from their fetters and brought the immortals here into the presence of the god of gods.
m.7.1.23.13: There too was the god, the blessed lord, standing in the sky with his gaṇas — the all-pervading Śarva, great lord of all worlds.
m.7.1.23.14: Seeing that supreme lord, the gods led by Viṣṇu, both delighted and afraid, bowed to Maheśvara.
m.7.1.23.15: Seeing those frightened immortals, Hara, the great god who removes the distress of those who bow to him, smiling and glancing at Pārvatī, said this:
m.7.1.23.16: Mahādeva said: Do not be afraid, all you gods; you are indeed my own children. The rod of punishment was taken up here by me, the compassionate one, only for the sake of grace.
m.7.1.23.17: Your transgression, O immortals, has been forgiven by us; for when we are angry, you have neither standing nor life.
m.7.1.23.18: Vāyu said: Thus addressed by Śarva of boundless splendour, all the gods, their doubts at once dispelled, danced with joy.
m.7.1.23.19: Becoming glad at heart, their minds overwhelmed with bliss, the heaven-dwellers began to offer praise to Śaṅkara.
m.7.1.23.20: The gods said: You alone, O god, are the creator of all worlds, their protector and destroyer; you are the supreme lord, O you who assume embodied forms bearing rajas, tamas and sattva through the distinctions of your own forms called Ka (Brahmā), Viṣṇu and Rudra.
m.7.1.23.21: O you of all forms, salutation to you, O creator of the universe, O purifier; O formless one who, for the sake of devotees, take on a shape, O giver of happiness.
m.7.1.23.22: By your grace, O lord of gods, O Śaṅkara, the Moon became free of disease; and one who died by immersion in the waters of Yamunā (Mihira's daughter) attained happiness.
m.7.1.23.23: Sīmantinī, whose husband was lost, through worshipping you, O lord, by the Monday vow obtained unequalled marital fortune and sons.
m.7.1.23.24: To Śrīkara the god granted his own supreme abode; you protected Sudarśana from fear of the circle of kings.
m.7.1.23.25: The treasury of compassion rescued Medura together with his wife; and you, by your action, made the widow Śāradā a wife with a living husband.
m.7.1.23.26: Cutting off Bhadrāyu's misfortune, you gave him happiness; and Sauminī, through serving you, became freed from the bondage of worldly existence.
m.7.1.23.27: Viṣṇu said: You, O Śambhu, as Ka (Brahmā), Hari and Īśa, through the guṇas rajas, sattva and tamas, are creator, protector and destroyer, out of the wish to favour beings.
m.7.1.23.28: You remove all pride, display all splendour, are hidden at the root of all knowledge, and bestow grace on all.
m.7.1.23.29: From you is everything, you are everything, in you is everything, O lord of the mountain. Protect, protect, protect again; show your compassion upon me.
m.7.1.23.30: Then, at this juncture, Brahmā, bowing down with joined palms and thus finding the opportunity, made his request to the trident-bearer.
m.7.1.23.31: Brahmā said: Victory, O god, O Mahādeva, destroyer of the distress of those who bow! Who other than you is gracious in the face of such offences?
m.7.1.23.32: Those who were slain earlier in battle will regain themselves; for whom would there not be restoration when the supreme lord is pleased?
m.7.1.23.33: This disfigurement inflicted on the chief gods who committed offences, I regard as an ornament, because of the honour of your acceptance of them.
m.7.1.23.34: Being thus entreated by Brahmā, the Supreme One, the god of gods, looking at the face of the Goddess and as if smiling,
m.7.1.23.35: the lord, out of affection for lotus-born Brahmā, who was like a son to him, restored to the gods and others their limbs as before.
m.7.1.23.36: And to the goddesses, the mothers of the gods, who had been punished by the Pramathas and others, Giriśa also gave back their limbs as before.
m.7.1.23.37: For Dakṣa, the blessed grandsire Brahmā himself made a face — the face of an old goat — befitting his sin.
m.7.1.23.38: He too, regaining consciousness then, and seeing himself alive, now wise, frightened and with joined palms, praised Śambhu, pouring out many words.
m.7.1.23.39: Dakṣa said: Victory, O god, lord of the world, bestower of grace on the worlds! Show compassion, O great lord, and forgive my offence.
m.7.1.23.40: You alone are creator, sustainer and destroyer, lord of the worlds; I have come to know especially that you are the lord of all, of Viṣṇu and the rest.
m.7.1.23.41: By you alone is all this spread out, pervaded, created and destroyed. There are no lords greater than you, not even those beginning with Acyuta.
m.7.1.23.42: Vāyu said: Seeing him thus agitated, frightened, lamenting and guilty of the offence, the treasure-house of compassion said, as if smiling, do not be afraid.
m.7.1.23.43: Having spoken thus, the Lord, wishing to please Brahmā, his father, gave to that Dakṣa the imperishable leadership of the gaṇas.
m.7.1.23.44: Then the gods, Brahmā and the others, bowing with joined palms, praised Śaṅkara, lord of Girijā, with humble words.
m.7.1.23.45: Brahmā and the others said: Victory, O Śaṅkara, lord of gods, protector of the wretched, great Lord! Show compassion, O Maheśāna, and forgive our offence.
m.7.1.23.46: O protector of sacrifice, lord of sacrifice, destroyer of sacrifice, show compassion, O Maheśāna, and forgive our offence.
m.7.1.23.47: O God of gods, supreme Lord, sustainer of the lives of devotees, dispenser of punishment to the wicked, O Master, show compassion; salutation to you.
m.7.1.23.48: You, O Lord, are indeed the destroyer of the pride of the wicked who do not know you, and above all the protector of the good whose minds are attached to you.
m.7.1.23.49: Your conduct is truly wondrous. Surely by your grace every offence is to be forgiven; the mighty are tender toward the humble.
m.7.1.23.50: Vāyu said: Thus praised by the immortals headed by Brahmā, Mahādeva, the Lord, the Master tender to his devotees, the ocean of compassion, was pleased.
m.7.1.23.51: Śaṅkara, kind to the humble, showed favour to those heaven-dwellers, Brahmā and the rest, and with great delight granted them boons.
m.7.1.23.52: Then the supreme Lord, supremely compassionate, having dispelled all their fear, addressed the gods who had come for refuge, in words accompanied by a smile.
m.7.1.23.53: Śiva said: Whatever offence was committed here by the gods, constrained as if by the force of destiny's decree — seeing that you have come to me for refuge, all of it is indeed forgotten by Us.
m.7.1.23.54: Therefore you too, not dwelling in your minds on the affliction that has occurred here, free from shame — you headed by Hari, Viriñci and the king of gods — go happily now to the city of the gods.
m.7.1.23.55: Having thus addressed the gods, the lord of gods, Hara — who had wrecked the sacrifice performed by Dakṣa, himself beyond sacrifice — accompanied by Girijā and with his retinue, vanished from the sky while seeming still to stand there.
m.7.1.23.56: Then those gods too, their distress gone, recounting the most auspicious exploits of Bhadra, went at once through the sky, happily and at their ease — the many gods headed by Maghavan.
m.7.1.23.iti: Thus ends the twenty-third adhyāya, named The appeasing of Giriśa, in the Pūrva-khaṇḍa of the seventh saṃhitā, the Vāyavīya-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.7.1.24.1: The sages said: Having vanished from sight together with the Goddess and his attendants, where did Hara go? Where was his dwelling? And what did he do before he came to rest?
m.7.1.24.2: Vāyu said: The splendid Mandara, best of mountains, with wondrous caves, dear to the God of gods, became his dwelling on account of its austerity.
m.7.1.24.3: Great austerity had been performed by it in order to bear Śiva and Śivā on its own head; after a long time it obtained the joy born of the touch of their lotus feet.
m.7.1.24.4: The beauty of that mountain cannot be described in full even with a thousand mouths, even in hundreds of crores of years.
m.7.1.24.5: Even if its beauty could be described, I do not venture to describe it, lest by being put in common terms it be reduced to the beauty of other mountains.
m.7.1.24.6: But this much can be said: in this beautiful mountain there is, through some special richness, a beauty that makes it fit to be the dwelling of the Lord.
m.7.1.24.7: For this very reason the God, wishing to please the Goddess, made this exceedingly lovely mountain into their inner palace.
m.7.1.24.8: Its slopes, with spotless stones and trees, through the constant presence of Śiva and Śivā, put the whole world to shame.
m.7.1.24.9: Having acquired the sanctity of merit through constant use for bathing and drinking by the Parents of the world, and by waters spreading here and there —
m.7.1.24.10: — by the crystal-clear waters of cascades, light and cool to the touch, this mountain is anointed to sovereignty over the mountains.
m.7.1.24.11: At night that mountain shines with the moon resting at the edge of its peak, as if with the parasol of sovereignty over the mountains.
m.7.1.24.12: That mountain is fanned by the fluttering tails of the female yaks, as if by the chowries of sovereignty over all mountains.
m.7.1.24.13: In the morning, when the sun has risen, the jewel-adorned mountain stands as if wishing to see the beauty of its body in a mirror.
m.7.1.24.14: By trees chattering with warbling birds, with creeper-arms raised by the wind, constantly shedding flowers, with soft hanging shoots,
m.7.1.24.15: by trees matted with spreading creepers like ascetics with matted locks, the king of mountains seems to be waited upon, as if having been worshipped with blessings of victory.
m.7.1.24.16: With peaks facing downward, upward and sideways, it seems as if falling into Pātāla, as if leaping up from the earth's surface,
m.7.1.24.17: spreading on all sides in every direction, as if roaming in the sky, as if gazing at the whole world, as if dancing without pause.
m.7.1.24.18: With its cave-mouths and vast hollows, the mountain, mouth agape every day, seems to yawn because its loveliness is undigested,
m.7.1.24.19: as if devouring the whole world, as if drinking the ocean, as if vomiting forth the darkness within, as if intoxicating the sky with clouds.
m.7.1.24.20: Its various dwelling places, with interiors like mirrors, sheltered from the heat, with trees giving soft shade that removes fatigue,
m.7.1.24.21: with breezes cooled by contact with rivers, lakes, ponds and the like — these were made fruitful by Śiva and Śivā, who sat here and there.
m.7.1.24.22: Remembering this mountain, best in every respect, the Three-eyed One with Ambā, near the hermitage of Raibhya, having vanished, went there.
m.7.1.24.23: Reaching the garden there, Maheśvara with the Goddess sported with her in the lovely grounds of the inner palace.
m.7.1.24.24: As time passed thus and creatures multiplied, two demon brothers named Śumbha and Niśumbha were born.
m.7.1.24.25: By the power of their austerity, Brahmā, the Supreme One, granted them invulnerability in this world against all males.
m.7.1.24.26: But the maiden who is not womb-born, arising from a portion of Ambikā, whose love has not known a man's touch, whose prowess cannot be overcome —
m.7.1.24.27: by her let our death in battle come, when we are overpowered by desire for her. Thus requested by them, Brahmā said, so be it.
m.7.1.24.28: From then on, having conquered in battle the gods headed by Śakra, they wrongfully made the world devoid of Vedic recitation and the vaṣaṭ call.
m.7.1.24.29: For their slaying Brahmā again entreated the Lord of gods: Having reproached Ambā in private and made her angry somehow or other,
m.7.1.24.30: you should grant the gods the Śakti born from the sheath of her complexion, free of desire, in the form of a maiden, the slayer of Niśumbha and Śumbha.
m.7.1.24.31: Thus entreated by the Creator, the blessed Nīlalohita, smiling, in private called her Kālī (Dark One), as if reproaching her.
m.7.1.24.32: Then the fair-complexioned Goddess, angered on account of the remark about her complexion, smiling, spoke to her husband in words not easily appeased.
m.7.1.24.33: The Goddess said: If you have no delight in this complexion of mine, such as it is, how has this aversion been held in check for so long a time?
m.7.1.24.34: And though living without delight, how do you sport with me? Indeed, nothing in this world is impossible for the Lord, the master of the world.
m.7.1.24.35: For you, who delight in your own Self, love is no means of happiness; for that reason Smara was forcibly reduced to ashes.
m.7.1.24.36: And a woman not delighted in by her husband, even if beautiful in every limb, is born in vain indeed, even with all other virtues.
m.7.1.24.37: For this very creation of women has as its sole remaining purpose the husband's enjoyment. That being so, of what use is a woman who has become otherwise?
m.7.1.24.38: Therefore, abandoning this complexion which you reproached in private, I shall take on another complexion — or else I myself shall not take on any.
m.7.1.24.39: Having said this, the Goddess rose from the bed and spoke in a faltering voice; firmly resolved, she asked her husband's permission for austerity.
m.7.1.24.40: Then the Lord of beings himself, alarmed at this breach of affection, bowing at her feet, replied to Bhavānī.
m.7.1.24.41: Īśvara said: Not understanding my playful words, O beloved, why are you angry with me? From where else could delight arise for me, if I had no delight in you?
m.7.1.24.42: You are the mother of this world, and I am its father and lord as well. How then could it be that I have no delight in you?
m.7.1.24.43: Is even our mutual longing caused by Kāma? No, since the origin of the world took place even before the arising of Kāma.
m.7.1.24.44: The embodiment of desire (Kāma) was fashioned by me for the pleasure of ordinary beings. How then am I reproached by you because of the burning of Kāma?
m.7.1.24.45: The Mind-born (Kāma), regarding me as just like any of the gods, showed me some slight disrespect, and so was reduced to ashes by me.
m.7.1.24.46: Our sport too is for the sake of protecting this world; therefore, for that purpose, I made a playful remark to you today.
m.7.1.24.47: And that purpose will soon become clear to you yourself. But she, keeping in her heart the words that had provoked her anger, said this:
m.7.1.24.48: The Goddess said: O Lord, I have heard your flattering speech before, by which even I, very steadfast as I am, was deceived earlier.
m.7.1.24.49: A woman of good family who, being disliked by her husband, does not give up even her life, though virtuous, is surely regarded by the good as contemptible.
m.7.1.24.50: Great is your displeasure that my body is not fair; otherwise how would the playful remark, Kālī, fit?
m.7.1.24.51: Therefore, without casting off by the practice of austerity this darkness, censured by the good and unacceptable to you, I cannot bear to remain here.
m.7.1.24.52: Śiva said: If you are so distressed, what need is there of austerity? Become of another complexion, by my will or by your own will.
m.7.1.24.53: The Goddess said: I do not wish you, or myself, to change my complexion. Having propitiated Brahmā by austerity, I shall quickly become fair (Gaurī).
m.7.1.24.54: Īśvara said: Long ago, by my grace, Brahmā attained his status as Brahmā. Simply summon him, O great goddess; what will you achieve by austerity?
m.7.1.24.55: The Goddess said: All the gods beginning with Brahmā have obtained their positions from you alone. Even so, by your command, I wish to propitiate Brahmā by austerity.
m.7.1.24.56: Formerly, it is said, I was born as Dakṣa's daughter named Satī, and likewise I obtained you, the very lord of the worlds, as my husband.
m.7.1.24.57: So now too, having pleased the twice-born Vidhi (Brahmā) by austerity, I wish to become fair (Gaurī). What fault is there in this? Tell me.
m.7.1.24.58: Thus addressed by the great goddess, Vāmadeva, as if smiling, did not press her further, wishing to accomplish the work of the gods.
m.7.1.24.iti: Thus ends the twenty-fourth adhyāya, named Śiva's dwelling on Mount Mandara and his playful remark, in the Pūrva-khaṇḍa of the seventh saṃhitā, the Vāyavīya-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.7.1.25.1: Vāyu said: Then the Mother, devoted to her husband, having circumambulated her husband and restrained the pain of separation, went to the Himavat mountain.
m.7.1.25.2: The very place where she had formerly performed austerity together with her companions, that same place she chose again for austerity, out of fondness.
m.7.1.25.3: Then, having seen her father and mother in their house, having bowed to them and informed them of what had happened, and being granted permission by them, the virtuous lady—
m.7.1.25.4: going again to the penance-grove, putting aside her ornaments, bathing, and assuming the supremely purifying garb of an ascetic,
m.7.1.25.5: and resolving upon an exceedingly intense austerity, supremely hard to perform, ever holding in her mind her husband's lotus feet,
m.7.1.25.6: meditating on him alone in a temporary liṅga according to the external rite, worshipping him at the three junctions of the day with forest flowers, fruits and the like,
m.7.1.25.7: and thinking, He himself, assuming the form of Brahmā, will grant me the fruit of my austerity — constantly holding this thought, she performed austerity.
m.7.1.25.8: When a long time had passed while she was thus practising austerity, a certain great tiger, having caught sight of her, approached her with wicked intent.
m.7.1.25.9: Even as that exceedingly wicked one approached thus, his body became rigid, as if painted in a picture, in her presence.
m.7.1.25.10: Even on seeing that tiger approaching thus with wicked intent, the Goddess, by her very nature, was not shaken like an ordinary person.
m.7.1.25.11: He, with all his limbs paralysed and tormented by hunger, thinking incessantly, She is my prey, nothing else,
m.7.1.25.12: gazing constantly at the Goddess alone, day and night, stood before her, as though performing worship.
m.7.1.25.13: And in the Goddess's heart compassion arose: This one is my own constant worshipper, and a protector against wicked creatures.
m.7.1.25.14: Through the touch of her compassion alone, the tiger was suddenly and at once freed from the three impurities, and then he came to know the Goddess.
m.7.1.25.15: His hunger ceased, likewise the paralysis of his limbs and his inborn wickedness, and contentment arose in him.
m.7.1.25.16: Then, realising with supreme devotion that he had attained his life's purpose, he, having at once become a worshipper, served the Supreme Goddess.
m.7.1.25.17: He himself roamed the penance-grove, becoming one who drove away wicked creatures and other evil-minded beings.
m.7.1.25.18: The Goddess's austerity grew intense, ever more intense. And the gods, oppressed by the demons, went to Brahmā for refuge.
m.7.1.25.19: The gods reported their own suffering caused by the enemies' oppression, and how Śumbha and Niśumbha, intoxicated by their boons, inflicted it.
m.7.1.25.20: Brahmā too, hearing of the gods' suffering and filled with compassion, became intent on the slaying of the demons, recalling the story concerning the cause of their death.
m.7.1.25.21: Entreated, Brahmā together with the gods went to the Goddess's penance-grove, reflecting in his mind on the release of the gods from suffering through his own effort.
m.7.1.25.22: And the best of gods saw Bhavānī, the Supreme Goddess, established in excellent austerity, like the very foundation of the universe.
m.7.1.25.23: He bowed to the noble daughter of the lord of mountains, the mother of this world, of himself, of Hari and of Rudra, the wife of his father Śiva.
m.7.1.25.24: Seeing Brahmā arrived with the hosts of gods, the Goddess offered him a fitting arghya and honoured him with words of welcome and the like.
m.7.1.25.25: The lotus-born, responding with words of courtesy and greeting her warmly, asked the reason for her austerity as if he did not know.
m.7.1.25.26: Brahmā said: What is being accomplished here by the Goddess through this intense austerity? For the attainments that are the fruits of all austerities depend on you.
m.7.1.25.27: Having obtained as your own husband that very Supreme Lord who is the sustainer of the worlds, the fruit of austerity has already been attained.
m.7.1.25.28: Or else all this is the play of your sport. But this is a wonder: how do you endure separation from the Lord?
m.7.1.25.29: The Goddess said: Since your birth from the Lord at the beginning of creation is well known, you, the first of creatures, are my first-born son.
m.7.1.25.30: And again, when Bhava arose from your forehead for the increase of creatures, then you became my elder by being my father-in-law.
m.7.1.25.31: When the lord of mountains, my own father, became your son, then you became my grandfather, O grandfather of the worlds.
m.7.1.25.32: So how could I recount to such a one as you, the ordainer of the course of the world, what passed between me and my husband in the inner apartments?
m.7.1.25.33: What need of many words here? Casting off this darkness that is on my body, by means of the quality of sattva, I desire to become fair (Gaurī).
m.7.1.25.34: Brahmā said: For so small a purpose, why, O Goddess, has intense austerity been performed? Was your own will not sufficient? Indeed, this sport of yours is of such a kind.
m.7.1.25.35: Yet even your sport, O Mother of the world, is surely for the welfare of the worlds. Therefore let some fruit desired by me be accomplished through it.
m.7.1.25.36: Two demons named Niśumbha and Śumbha, granted boons by me, have grown arrogant and are oppressing the gods; their death has been ordained to come from you.
m.7.1.25.37: Enough of delay in this; be steadfast in an instant. The Śakti released from you today will be their death.
m.7.1.25.38: Thus entreated by Brahmā, the Goddess, daughter of the best of mountains, suddenly cast off the sheath of her skin and became Gaurī (the fair one).
m.7.1.25.39: That which was cast off as the skin-sheath became a maiden named Kauśikī, Kālī, resembling a dark rain-cloud.
m.7.1.25.40: She is the Śakti whose nature is Māyā, the Yoganidrā of Viṣṇu, with eight mighty arms bearing weapons such as the conch, discus and trident.
m.7.1.25.41: She was gentle, fierce, and mixed in nature, three-eyed, bearing the moon on her head, one whose delight knew no touch of a man, unassailable, and exceedingly beautiful.
m.7.1.25.42: This eternal Śakti was given by the Goddess to Brahmā — she who would be the slayer of Niśumbha and Śumbha, the two lions among the Daityas.
m.7.1.25.43: Brahmā too, greatly delighted, gave to that supreme Śakti a mighty lion, which came to serve as her mount.
m.7.1.25.44: And he appointed her dwelling in the Vindhya, and, having arranged her worship with offerings beginning with liquor, and with meat, fish and cakes, he gave his instructions.
m.7.1.25.45: And that Śakti, honoured by Brahmā the creator of the universe, bowing in due order to her mother Gaurī and to Brahmā,
m.7.1.25.46: surrounded by many Śaktis equal to herself, born from her own self, went to the Vindhya, intent on slaying the two Daitya lords.
m.7.1.25.47: And there in battle the two foremost Daityas were slain by her, their limbs and minds cut and pierced by her arrows and by the arrows of Kāma.
m.7.1.25.48: The detailed account of that battle is not given here, since it is described elsewhere; it should be inferred from the other account. I shall narrate to you the topic at hand.
m.7.1.25.iti: Thus ends the twenty-fifth adhyāya, named The Devī attains a fair complexion, in the Pūrva-khaṇḍa of the seventh saṃhitā, the Vāyavīya-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.7.1.26.1: Vāyu said: Having brought forth Kauśikī and handed her over to Brahmā, Gaurī then spoke to the Grandfather, seeking a favour from him in return.
m.7.1.26.2: The Goddess said: Have you seen this tiger, who has taken refuge in me? By him my penance grove has been protected from wicked creatures.
m.7.1.26.3: With his mind given over to me, he worships me, thinking of no other. Nothing is dearer to me than protecting him.
m.7.1.26.4: Therefore he should become one who moves in my inner apartments; and Śaṅkara will gladly grant him the rank of a lord of the Gaṇas.
m.7.1.26.5: Making him go ahead of me, I wish to depart with my friends. Let permission be granted to me by you, the lord of creatures.
m.7.1.26.6: Thus addressed, Brahmā, laughing and smiling at the Goddess as if she were naive, described the tiger's wickedness through his grim past deeds.
m.7.1.26.7: Brahmā said: Among animals, O Goddess, wild beasts are cruel; and where is the place for your auspicious grace? Is nectar to be poured straight into the mouth of a venomous snake?
m.7.1.26.8: Though he is a tiger only in appearance, he is some wicked night-roamer. Cows have been devoured by him, and Brahmins rich in austerity.
m.7.1.26.9: Gratifying himself on them as he pleases, he roams about, taking any form at will. Surely the fruit of sinful deeds must be experienced.
m.7.1.26.10: So what is to be done out of compassion toward such evil-minded ones? What purpose of the Goddess can be served by him, whose nature is by origin impure?
m.7.1.26.11: The Goddess said: All that you have said may be true; let him be such. Even so, he has sought refuge in me; one who has taken shelter with me is not to be abandoned.
m.7.1.26.12: Brahmā said: Not knowing his devotion, I told you of his past conduct. If he has devotion, what do sins matter? Your devotee does not perish.
m.7.1.26.13: What can even a meritorious deed accomplish without regard to your command? You alone are the unborn, the primeval Wisdom, the supreme Mistress.
m.7.1.26.14: For the ordering of bondage and liberation for all depends on you. Without you, O supreme Power, whose success comes through action alone?
m.7.1.26.15: You alone are the manifold power of beings, or rather the doer yourself; for an agent incapable of performing action—what will he accomplish?
m.7.1.26.16: For Viṣṇu, for me, and for the others—gods, Dānavas and Rākṣasas—your command alone is the cause of attaining their respective sovereignties.
m.7.1.26.17: Countless indeed are the Brahmās, Haris and Bhavas who have passed, and countless those yet to come—all following your command.
m.7.1.26.18: Without worshipping you, O Mistress of the gods, the fourfold aims of human life cannot be obtained even by all of us, the foremost of the gods.
m.7.1.26.19: Even an instant reversal between the state of Brahmā and the state of an immobile thing could occur, since merit and demerit alike are established by you alone.
m.7.1.26.20: For you are the primordial, eternal Power, without beginning, middle or end, of Śiva the supreme Self, the sustainer of all worlds.
m.7.1.26.21: For the sake of the course of all the worlds, entering some form or other, you sport in various modes. Who knows you in truth?
m.7.1.26.22: Therefore, though his deeds have been evil, let this tiger attain the highest perfection through your grace. What obstacle is there in this?
m.7.1.26.23: Having thus been fittingly reminded of her own supreme nature and entreated by Brahmā, Gaurī withdrew even from her penance.
m.7.1.26.24: Then, when Brahmā, having taken leave of the Goddess, had vanished, the Goddess, seeing her mother Menā together with Himavat,
m.7.1.26.25: having bowed to and consoled in many ways her parents, who could not bear the separation, the Goddess—leaving the trees of the penance grove, fond of her penance,
m.7.1.26.26: which, as if from grief at the separation, shed tears of flowers before her, and with the cries uttered by the birds perched on their various branches,
m.7.1.26.27: seemed to make a lament, agitated and deeply piteous—speaking thus to her friends, eager to see her husband,
m.7.1.26.28: and placing that tiger in front, out of affection, like a son of her own body, illuminating the ten directions with the radiance of her body,
m.7.1.26.29: Gaurī went to Mandara, where her husband Maheśvara was—the ordainer of all worlds, their creator, protector and destroyer.
m.7.1.26.iti: Thus ends the twenty-sixth adhyāya, named The end attained by the tiger, in the Pūrva-khaṇḍa of the seventh saṃhitā, the Vāyavīya-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.7.1.27.1: The sages said: Having made her body fair and divine, how did the goddess, daughter of the best of mountains, the virtuous one, see her husband after she had entered the palace?
m.7.1.27.2: At the time of her entry, what was done by the lords of the gaṇas stationed at the palace gate? And what did the god do then, having seen her?
m.7.1.27.3: Vāyu said: Such supreme rapture cannot readily be described, by which, filled with love, the hearts of those capable of feeling were carried away.
m.7.1.27.4: Announced by the door-keepers, who were all in excitement—the god being eager for the goddess's arrival—she, hesitant, entered within and beheld him.
m.7.1.27.5: Greeted with words by the lords of the gaṇas dwelling inside the palace, with their various expressions of affection, she bowed to Tryambaka.
m.7.1.27.6: Even before she had risen from bowing, the Supreme Lord seized her with both arms and embraced her all around with supreme joy.
m.7.1.27.7: Though he set about holding her on his lap, she sat down on the couch; then he forcibly lifted the sweetly smiling goddess from the couch onto his lap,
m.7.1.27.8: and, smiling, as if drinking in her face with wide-open eyes, the Lord, in order to converse with her, spoke alluding to what had been said before.
m.7.1.27.9: The God of gods said: Has that state of yours passed, O you who are beautiful in every limb, in which, because of anger, no means of appeasing you at all could be found?
m.7.1.27.10: Not even of my own will did I mean that you are Kālī, or that you are of another complexion; my mind, captivated by your nature, O fair-browed one, is full of anxiety.
m.7.1.27.11: How was the supreme state forgotten through association with a body assumed at will? In that state, the causes of disturbance of mind do not arise.
m.7.1.27.12: If, as with ordinary people, there were between us two any cause of displeasure toward each other, this world of the moving and unmoving would not exist at all.
m.7.1.27.13: I am established at the head of Fire, you abide at the head of Soma; the universe, consisting of Agni and Soma, is presided over by us two.
m.7.1.27.14: For if we two—who move about for the welfare of the world, having assumed bodies at our own will—were separated, the world would be without support.
m.7.1.27.15: And there is another reason here, established by scripture and reasoning: this world, moving and unmoving, is like speech and its meaning.
m.7.1.27.16: For you are directly the nectar of speech, and I am the supreme nectar of meaning; how could both nectars properly be separated?
m.7.1.27.17: You are the knowledge that makes me known; I am the knowable through your cognition. How can there be separation between us two, whose very nature is knowledge and the knowable?
m.7.1.27.18: I do not create this world by action, nor do I withdraw it so; since everything is attained by command alone, you, the Command, are indeed the weightier.
m.7.1.27.19: Since sovereignty, whose mark is independence, has command as its sole essence, what sort of sovereignty would I have if separated from Command?
m.7.1.27.20: There can never be existence for us two when separated. With the gods' purpose in view, I made a playful remark.
m.7.1.27.21: Nothing is unknown to you either; how is it that you became angry? Therefore your anger, even toward me, was made for the protection of the three worlds.
m.7.1.27.22: That which leads to harm for beings surely does not exist in you. When the Lord, the Supreme Lord himself, spoke thus affectionately,
m.7.1.27.23: she, the natural birthplace of the essences of the erotic sentiment, considering what her husband had said to be charming and true, with a smile as her answer,
m.7.1.27.24: out of modesty said nothing at all, except for an account of Kauśikī. That very account I now relate; hear the goddess's description.
m.7.1.27.25: The Goddess said: Has the Lord not seen her, Kauśikī, who was created by me? Such a maiden has not been in the world, nor will be.
m.7.1.27.26: Her valour, her might, her abode in the Vindhya, and likewise her victory in battle in slaying those two, Śumbha and Niśumbha,
m.7.1.27.27: and her granting of visible fruits to the world that always worships her, and her constant protection of the worlds—Brahmā will report these to you.
m.7.1.27.28: While the goddess was speaking thus, then, at her own command, the tiger was brought by a female companion and placed before them.
m.7.1.27.29: Looking at him, the goddess spoke again: O god, see this tiger, brought here and come near; there is no worshipper of mine equal to him.
m.7.1.27.30: By him my penance-grove was protected from hordes of the wicked; he is exceedingly devoted to me and trustworthy because of his guarding.
m.7.1.27.31: Leaving his own land, he has come for my grace. If you have become pleased with me, grant me this supreme favour:
m.7.1.27.32: let him remain always at the gate of the inner apartments, by appointment of Nandin himself, together with the guards and bearing their insignia, O Lord.
m.7.1.27.33: Vāyu said: Having heard the goddess's sweet, auspicious words, whose outcome was love, the god said to him, I am pleased, and at that very moment he was seen transformed:
m.7.1.27.34: bearing a golden cane-staff, a jacket studded with jewels, and a dagger resembling a serpent—a lord of the gaṇas wearing the garb of a guard.
m.7.1.27.35: Because Mahādeva together with Umā (Soma) and Nandin were delighted by him, he became famous by the name Somanandin.
m.7.1.27.36: Having thus done what was dear to the goddess, the god whose ornament is the half-moon adorned him with divine ornaments set with jewels.
m.7.1.27.37: Then Hara, the Lord of the mountain, adorned with the moon, placed Gaurī, the daughter of the king of mountains, dignified and captivating to all, on the couch and adorned her with ornaments for her lovely limbs.
m.7.1.27.iti: Thus ends the twenty-seventh adhyāya, named The reunion of the Devī and Śiva, in the Pūrva-khaṇḍa of the seventh saṃhitā, the Vāyavīya-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.7.1.28.1: The sages said: What was it that the God declared while reassuring the Goddess: that the universe consists of Agni and Soma, and also that it consists of speech and meaning?
m.7.1.28.2: And it was stated that sovereignty has command as its sole essence, and spoke of the state of commanding. We wish to hear this properly and in due order.
m.7.1.28.3: Vāyu said: That fiery, terrible body which belongs to Rudra is called Agni; Soma is the body belonging to Śakti, made of nectar, the pacifying body of Śakti.
m.7.1.28.4: That which is nectar is the kalā Pratiṣṭhā; fire is itself the kalā Vidyā. In all the subtle elements these very two exist as fluid essence (rasa) and fire (tejas).
m.7.1.28.5: The activity of fire is twofold: of the nature of the sun and of the nature of terrestrial fire. Likewise the activity of fluid essence: of the nature of the moon and of the nature of water.
m.7.1.28.6: Fire consists of lightning and the like; fluid essence consists of sweetness and the other tastes. By the distinctions of fire and fluid essence this moving and unmoving world is upheld.
m.7.1.28.7: From fire nectar is produced; by nectar fire is fed. Therefore the Agni–Soma pair, beneficial to the world, prevails.
m.7.1.28.8: Abundance of crops is for the oblation; rain is for the growth of crops; from rain alone comes the oblation. Therefore the world is upheld by Agni and Soma.
m.7.1.28.9: This fire blazes upward as far as the supreme lunar nectar; and the lunar nectar flows downward as far as the seat of fire.
m.7.1.28.10: Therefore Kālāgni is below and Śakti above; and there is burning upward as far as it reaches, and flooding downward.
m.7.1.28.11: Upheld by the supporting power (Ādhāra-śakti) alone, this Kālāgni moves upward; likewise Soma, resting in the abode of Śiva and Śakti, flows downward.
m.7.1.28.12: Śiva is above and Śakti below; Śakti is above and Śiva below. Thus there is nothing here not pervaded by Śiva and Śakti.
m.7.1.28.13: Since the world, burnt again and again by fire, is reduced to ash, they call this the potency of fire; therefore ash is that potency.
m.7.1.28.14: Whoever, knowing thus the true nature of ash, bathes with ash using the mantras beginning agnir iti—though bound, he is released from the fetter.
m.7.1.28.15: The ash, which is the potency of fire, when again flooded by Soma through a non-yogic method, becomes fit for the dominion of Prakṛti.
m.7.1.28.16: But that ash, flooded all around by the nectar-rain of Śakti through the yogic method, would turn one back from Prakṛti's dominion.
m.7.1.28.17: Hence, for conquering death, there should always be this flooding with nectar. For one who has obtained it in the touch of the nectar of Śiva and Śakti, whence can there be death?
m.7.1.28.18: He who knows the secret burning and flooding as described, having left the state of Agni and Soma, is not born again.
m.7.1.28.19: He who, having burnt the body with the fire of Śiva, floods it by the path of yoga with the lunar nectar of Śakti, becomes fit for immortality.
m.7.1.28.20: Keeping this meaning in mind, the God fittingly declared that the universe, the world, consists of Agni and Soma.
m.7.1.28.iti: Thus ends the twenty-eighth adhyāya, named The truth of the sacred ash, in the Pūrva-khaṇḍa of the seventh saṃhitā, the Vāyavīya-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.7.1.29.1: Vāyu said: I shall explain how the world's nature as word-and-meaning came about, and give a proper understanding of the six paths, briefly and not at length.
m.7.1.29.2: There is no object without a word, nor any word without meaning. Therefore, by convention, every word is able to convey every meaning.
m.7.1.29.3: This twofold manifestation as word and meaning is a transformation of Prakṛti; they call it the prakṛtic form of the two Śivas (Śiva and Śivā), the supreme selves.
m.7.1.29.4: The manifestation that consists of word is said by the wise to be threefold: gross, subtle and supreme. The gross is that which lies within the range of hearing.
m.7.1.29.5: The subtle is said to consist of thought; the supreme is free from thought. That power is the supreme Śakti, resting upon the Śiva-principle.
m.7.1.29.6: Through union with the power of knowledge she likewise strengthens the will; she is the aggregate of all powers, known by the name Śakti-tattva.
m.7.1.29.7: She has become the root-Prakṛti of the whole mass of effects; she herself is Kuṇḍalinī, Māyā, being the highest source of the pure path.
m.7.1.29.8: That very power, in divided form, unfolds as the six paths. Among them three paths are declared to be of word and three of meaning.
m.7.1.29.9: For all souls, according to their own purity, there are states of dissolution, enjoyment and authority, according to the division of all the principles.
m.7.1.29.10: Those principles are indeed pervaded by the kalās, as is fitting, because of the fivefold transformation of the supreme Prakṛti in the beginning.
m.7.1.29.11: And those kalās, beginning with Nivṛtti, are all-pervading: this is settled. The path of mantras, the path of words and the path of letters are the paths on the side of word;
m.7.1.29.12: and the path of worlds, the path of principles and the path of kalās are, in order, on the side of meaning. Here the mutual relation of pervaded and pervader among all of them is described.
m.7.1.29.13: All mantras are pervaded by words, since they are sentences; and words by letters, for the learned call a word a group of letters.
m.7.1.29.14: Letters are pervaded by the worlds, since they are perceived in them; the worlds too are pervaded by the multitude of principles, according to the order of origination from inner to outer,
m.7.1.29.15: they are pervaded by the causal principles, since they are produced by them in many ways. Some worlds here have arisen from within;
m.7.1.29.16: others are Purāṇic, and others are to be known from the Śaiva Āgama. Some principles too are well known in Sāṃkhya and Yoga,
m.7.1.29.17: and others besides, in their entirety, are well known in the Śaiva scriptures. Those principles are indeed pervaded by the kalās, as is fitting,
m.7.1.29.18: because of the fivefold transformation of the supreme Prakṛti in the beginning; and those five kalās, beginning with Nivṛtti, are pervaded successively, each by the next.
m.7.1.29.19: Hence the supreme Śakti, undivided, is the pervader of the six paths, since the state of supreme Prakṛti belongs to her, deriving from the Śiva-principle.
m.7.1.29.20: And everything from Śakti down to earth, arising from the Śiva-principle, is pervaded by that one alone, as pots and the like are by clay.
m.7.1.29.21: That is the supreme Śaiva abode, which is to be reached through the six paths. The Śakti, both pervading and non-pervading, is reached through purification of the five principles.
m.7.1.29.22: By Nivṛtti the extent of the cosmic egg up to Rudra is purified; by Pratiṣṭhā, what lies above that, up to the domain of the Unmanifest;
m.7.1.29.23: above that, by Vidyā, the middle region up to the limit of Viśveśvara; by Śānti what is above that; and at the end of the path, purification by Śāntyatītā,
m.7.1.29.24: which they call the supreme space, owing to its union with the supreme Prakṛti. These are the five principles by which the entire world is pervaded.
m.7.1.29.25: In this alone all of this should be seen by practitioners. Whoever, without knowing the pervasion of the paths, wishes to perform purification —
m.7.1.29.26: he is a deceiver, unable to bring about the fruit of purification; his labour is in vain and leads only to hell.
m.7.1.29.27: Without union with the descent of Śakti, the principles as they truly are, their pervasion and their unfolding cannot be known in this way.
m.7.1.29.28: Śakti is the supreme command of Śiva, of the nature of consciousness, the supreme Goddess, through whom, as cause, Śiva presides over everything.
m.7.1.29.29: On reflection, she belongs neither to the individual soul, nor is she Māyā, nor a modification; she is neither bondage nor liberation, yet she brings about bondage and liberation.
m.7.1.29.30: She is the utmost limit of all sovereignty, ever faithful to Śiva, sharing his nature, especially in those various states.
m.7.1.29.31: Through her alone he is a householder, and through him alone she is always the housewife. Their offspring, the effect, is the world born of the supreme Prakṛti.
m.7.1.29.32: He is the agent, she the instrumental cause: thus the distinction between them is established. Yet Śiva alone is truly one, and he abides in twofold form.
m.7.1.29.33: Some say their distinction is by way of the female and male states. Others hold that the supreme Śakti is inherent in Śiva,
m.7.1.29.34: of the nature of consciousness like the light of the sun, and yet distinct — so it is settled. Therefore Śiva is the supreme cause, and his command is the supreme Goddess.
m.7.1.29.35: Impelled by her alone, the imperishable Śaiva root-Prakṛti is called Mahāmāyā, Māyā, and Prakṛti of the three guṇas.
m.7.1.29.36: Threefold through the distinction of its effects, she gives birth to the six paths. That sixfold path, consisting of word and meaning, is the whole world.
m.7.1.29.37: They declare the entire body of scriptures, without remainder, to be nothing but the elaboration of this.
m.7.1.29.iti: Thus ends the twenty-ninth adhyāya, named The principle that is word and meaning, in the Pūrva-khaṇḍa of the seventh saṃhitā, the Vāyavīya-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.7.1.30.1: The sages said: Śiva's deeds are wondrous, secret and profound, hard to understand even for the gods; they bewilder our minds.
m.7.1.30.2: In the true nature (tattva) of Śiva and Śivā no fault is found; yet from their deeds an ordinary, worldly condition is seen in them as well.
m.7.1.30.3: Even Brahmā and the others, the causes of the creation, maintenance and dissolution of the worlds, having received his punishment and grace, are subject to Śiva's control.
m.7.1.30.4: Śiva, however, is the object of no one's punishment or grace; hence it is settled that independent sovereignty belongs to him alone.
m.7.1.30.5: If his sovereignty is thus marked by independence and established by his very nature, how could it be the ground for his having a form?
m.7.1.30.6: Nor does a form befit the independent one with respect to a root cause; for since a form too is an effect, its coming about would then be without a cause.
m.7.1.30.7: Everywhere one state is called supreme and another non-supreme; how can the two states, supreme and non-supreme, be united in one being?
m.7.1.30.8: For the supreme nature of this Supreme Self is partless (niṣkala); why then is that same one with parts (sakala)? For one's nature does not admit of reversal.
m.7.1.30.9: If his nature can be reversed, if he is independent by his own will, why does the Lord not reverse eternal and non-eternal?
m.7.1.30.10: To say that some embodied being with parts is one, and the partless Śiva another, and that the former is presided over by Śiva — this is said superficially everywhere.
m.7.1.30.11: Then the embodied self itself would be the form of this Śiva; and in that form the dependence of both embodied ones is certain.
m.7.1.30.12: Otherwise, how would a form be assumed by one who needs nothing? Therefore the assumption of a form implies a desire for some result to be achieved through that form.
m.7.1.30.13: Having a body at will does not prove independence, since such free will of beings follows karma.
m.7.1.30.14: Beings from Brahmā down to the piśācas are indeed able to take on and abandon a body at will; are they therefore beyond karma?
m.7.1.30.15: They regard the making of a body by will as like a magic show, since it does not go beyond the control conferred by powers such as aṇimā (minuteness).
m.7.1.30.16: Viṣṇu, when he assumed the universal form, was reproached by the great sage Dadhīca, who fought him and himself assumed that same form.
m.7.1.30.17: Even for Śiva, the Supreme Self who is above all, through his having a body a likeness to other souls appears to us.
m.7.1.30.18: They call Śiva, the supreme cause, the bestower of grace on all; how then does he who favours all punish some of the gods?
m.7.1.30.19: The god forcibly cut off the fifth head of evil-minded Brahmā, who was reviling Śiva, calling him son.
m.7.1.30.20: In the form of the Śarabha he violently, pinning him down with his feet, tore open with sharp claws the heart even of Viṣṇu as Nṛsiṃha.
m.7.1.30.21: Among the goddesses and gods, on account of Dakṣa's sacrifice, none was left unpunished by the hero Vīrabhadra.
m.7.1.30.22: And the three cities, with their women, their daityas and their children, were made fuel for the fire of his eye by the god in a single moment.
m.7.1.30.23: And Kāma himself, Rati's lord, the cause of delight for creatures, was offered into the fire of his eye even as the gods cried out.
m.7.1.30.24: And certain sky-going cows that poured a stream of milk on his head were, at that very moment, reduced to ashes by the god glancing at them in anger.
m.7.1.30.25: The demon Jalandhara, who had bound Viṣṇu with Ananta and hurled him a hundred yojanas, was split apart by Śiva, who turned water into a disc with his foot.
m.7.1.30.26: He who fashioned the disc from water struck him down with that very weapon; Hari, having obtained that disc through austerity, was ever endowed with prowess.
m.7.1.30.27: slays the race of the gods' enemies, merciless-minded and bent on killing; and Andhaka's chest was scorched by the trident as if by fire.
m.7.1.30.28: Having created from his throat the dark woman (Kālī), he felled Dāruka too; and having produced Kauśikī, who emerged from the sheath of Gaurī's skin,
m.7.1.30.29: Śumbha together with Niśumbha was brought to death in battle. And we have heard the great tale in the Skānda concerning Skanda:
m.7.1.30.30: For the slaying of the daitya-lord named Tāraka, the enemy of Indra, the god, entreated by Brahmā, went to the inner apartments on Mandara.
m.7.1.30.31: Having sported with the goddess for a very long time, then, through excess of love-play, causing it to be said that the earth had been as if pushed down to Rasātala,
m.7.1.30.32: and deceiving the goddess, not releasing in her his seed, so very hard to bear, but releasing it into Agni like a purified oblation, like nectar,
m.7.1.30.33: and having, through Fire, deposited portions of it in the Gaṅgā and other places, then gathering it gradually, little by little, from here and there,
m.7.1.30.34: it was placed somewhere in a reed-forest on Meru by Svāhā, who, in the form of the Kṛttikās, was making love with her own husband and had become golden;
m.7.1.30.35: it, in time, having lit up the ten directions with its radiance and coloured all the mountains, turning them golden along with Meru,
m.7.1.30.36: then, after a long time, when from that radiance there was born the Boy (Kumāra), of tender limbs, the very model of boys,
m.7.1.30.37: and when the worlds, with gods and asuras, having seen his charming childhood and form, were amazed and enchanted,
m.7.1.30.38: the god himself came with the goddess, eager to see his son; and having placed him on his lap, then gazing at his smiling face,
m.7.1.30.39: as though drinking nectar, with his inner self overcome by affection, while the gods and even dispassionate ascetics looked on,
m.7.1.30.40: having freely made the little boy dance upon his own chest, and having enjoyed his play, and honouring one another,
m.7.1.30.41: Having ordered the Devī's breast-milk for him and made him drink it, which was like nectar, and having instructed him, your incarnation is for the welfare of the worlds,
m.7.1.30.42: the god and the goddess themselves did not reach satiety in their love for him. Then, having made an alliance with Śakra, who was afraid of the asura Tāraka,
m.7.1.30.43: and having had him consecrated to the generalship of the heaven-dwellers, the god, enemy of Tripura, placing the son within, entering into him,
m.7.1.30.44: he himself remaining hidden — through Skanda, protected by Indra and the others, by his spear that split Mount Krauñca, resembling the fire of dissolution in battle,
m.7.1.30.45: the head of Tāraka was cut off, together with Śakra's fear. The gods headed by Hari and Brahmā offered praise in a special way.
m.7.1.30.46: Likewise the lord of the rākṣasas, Rāvaṇa himself, proud of his strength, lifting with his own long arms Kailāsa, the mountain of Śiva himself,
m.7.1.30.47: was crushed and sank into the earth by a mere movement of the big toe of the trident-bearing God of gods, who did not tolerate that offence.
m.7.1.30.48: For the sake of a boy who had taken refuge in him and whose life-span had run out, the god came swiftly and sent Death (Antaka) to the tip of his foot, kicking him away.
m.7.1.30.49: The submarine fire, not recognising the lord of bulls, his vehicle, attacked him and was dragged off seized by the throat; hence the world exists still as one expanse of water.
m.7.1.30.50: By those various dances, unknown to the world and beautiful with bliss, this world has been shaken again and again through the sequence of his dance-movements (aṅgahāra).
m.7.1.30.51: If Śiva, ever tranquil, favours all, he should surely fulfil the needs of all; how then could he, though able, fail to release everyone?
m.7.1.30.52: Even the diversity of beginningless karma is not the determining factor here, for karma too, as a cause, would itself be brought about by the Lord.
m.7.1.30.53: What need is there to say more here? Unbelief is what gives rise to these doubts; explain in such a way that it may quickly cease, O Māruta.
m.7.1.30.iti: Thus ends the thirtieth adhyāya, named The question on the truth of Śiva, in the Pūrva-khaṇḍa of the seventh saṃhitā, the Vāyavīya-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.7.1.31.1: Vāyu said: It is fitting, O brahmins, that you, prompted by reasoning, have raised this doubt; for in those of sound understanding, inquiry does not lead to disbelief.
m.7.1.31.2: I shall state here the proof, which removes the delusion of the good; but for the wicked, without the grace of the Lord, there remains a contrary disposition.
m.7.1.31.3: For Śiva, who is entirely full, there is nothing whatever to be done except grace toward others — this is firmly settled.
m.7.1.31.4: His own nature alone suffices for the work of grace toward others; otherwise, by one lacking such a nature, no one at all is graced.
m.7.1.31.5: All else — the world consisting of bound souls and bonds (paśu-pāśa) — is what is to be graced; and for the sake of grace to the other, there is the connection with the Lord's command.
m.7.1.31.6: The Lord, the giver of commands, always graces all. In accepting a purpose for that sake, how is Śiva dependent?
m.7.1.31.7: For there is no grace whatever that is independent of the one to be graced; hence the meaning of the word independence is characterised by non-dependence on anything for his own sake.
m.7.1.31.8: This world, however, which is to be graced, is held to be dependent, since without his grace it has no access to enjoyment and liberation.
m.7.1.31.9: Even the embodied souls (mūrtyātman) are to be graced, through Śiva's removal of their ignorance; nothing belonging to Śambhu here is governed by ignorance.
m.7.1.31.10: That through which, though itself with parts, the partless Śiva is apprehended by us — that embodied soul is figuratively called Śiva, the Śaiva form.
m.7.1.31.11: For that partless Śiva himself, the supreme cause, is not apprehended by any manifestation possessing form.
m.7.1.31.12: His being merely knowable through valid means establishes his nature; but on that account alone one should not think of disregarding the form, for without an indicating mark he is not approached.
m.7.1.31.13: For, like some directly visible image, prominent as a likeness of himself, the embodied soul is Śiva's form — the supreme indicator of him.
m.7.1.31.14: Just as fire is not perceived unless it has taken hold in wood, so too Śiva is not perceived unless he is seated in an embodied soul — this is the settled position.
m.7.1.31.15: Just as, when one is told to bring fire, fire by itself is not brought without burning wood, so Śiva is to be worshipped through the embodied soul.
m.7.1.31.16: For this very reason, in worship and the like, the embodied soul is conceived as Śiva, since what is done to the embodied soul is done directly to Śiva himself.
m.7.1.31.17: This is to be done in the liṅga and the like as well, and especially in the image; Śiva is worshipped by us as being each respective embodied soul.
m.7.1.31.18: Just as that embodied soul too is graced by the Supreme One, so are we, the bound souls, graced by Śiva abiding in the embodied soul.
m.7.1.31.19: Solely for the sake of gracing the worlds, all the embodied souls beginning with Sadāśiva are presided over by Śiva, the Supreme.
m.7.1.31.20: For the enjoyment and, especially, the liberation of souls, Śiva is connected with the embodied souls, whose nature is of the principles (tattva) and beyond the principles (atattva).
m.7.1.31.21: Enjoyment is held to be the ripening of karma, consisting of pleasure and pain; and there is no karma in Śiva — so of what nature could his enjoyment be?
m.7.1.31.22: Śiva graces all and punishes none, since the faults that belong to those who punish cannot exist in Śiva.
m.7.1.31.23: And whatever punishments are shown inflicted on Brahmā and others, those too were done solely for the welfare of the world by Śiva in the form of Śrīkaṇṭha.
m.7.1.31.24: Lordship over the cosmic egg belongs to Śrīkaṇṭha, without doubt; Śiva presides over the sporting form named Śrīkaṇṭha.
m.7.1.31.25: As has been told, only the gods and others who had faults were punished; thereby they too became free of sin, and the creatures were relieved of distress.
m.7.1.31.26: Punishment in itself is not despised by the wise; for this very reason the punishment by kings of those deserving punishment is praised.
m.7.1.31.27: He through whose lordship the whole range of effects is accomplished — if he did not exercise lordship, how would he be the Lord of the world?
m.7.1.31.28: The Lord's will is ordainership; the ordinance is the supreme command; command is the injunction to which all is subject: do this, do not do that.
m.7.1.31.29: Following his injunction is the mark of goodness; the opposite would be the mark of the wicked; but not everyone is seen to follow it.
m.7.1.31.30: If the good is to be protected, whatever is bad must be turned back; and it is turned back by conciliation and the other means — at the end, punishment is indeed the means.
m.7.1.31.31: This discipline, culminating in punishment, is characterized by a beneficial aim; therefore what is contrary to it they call harmful.
m.7.1.31.32: This is the Lord's example for those ever established in welfare; how could he be faulted by the good, when he punishes only the wicked?
m.7.1.31.33: In the world, the discernment of one who acts improperly is blameworthy; what distresses the world, that they call improper.
m.7.1.31.34: Not every punishment in the world is preceded by hatred; a father who would restrain his son and discipline him does not hate him.
m.7.1.31.35: Even one who, with impartiality, punishes those deserving punishment according to the proper way — some degree of harshness necessarily attends him too.
m.7.1.31.36: Otherwise he would not harm others at all, even those at fault; yet this one too, practising supreme impartiality, harms even the ignorant.
m.7.1.31.37: Therefore some insist that whoever inflicts harm, which is of the nature of pain, is cruel; others say there is no such rule.
m.7.1.31.38: In a physician who knows the cause of disease and applies painful treatment to the sick there is no cruelty at all; compassion alone is the motive here.
m.7.1.31.39: Compassion, too, is not a virtue toward violent adversaries; one who out of delusion is compassionate toward such is in fact cruel, his cruelty concealed by compassion.
m.7.1.31.40: Here too, neglect leads to fault when those who should be protected face adversaries; when one has the power, through neglect the one to be protected perishes at once.
m.7.1.31.41: But whoever sees one who should be protected caught in a serpent's mouth and ignores him, after imagining apparent faults in him, is in effect merciless as well.
m.7.1.31.42: Therefore it is not accepted that compassion is in every way only for good. What is accepted is Śiva's state of having all desires fulfilled; everything else is not accepted.
m.7.1.31.43: Even in the embodied souls (mūrtyātman), faults such as passion do in fact exist; yet these belong to them alone and in no way to Śiva.
m.7.1.31.44: Copper, even when penetrated by fire, still keeps its tarnish; yet that fire is not defiled on account of contact with the copper.
m.7.1.31.45: Fire does not incur impurity through contact with the impure; rather, the impure gains purity through union with fire.
m.7.1.31.46: In the same way, Śiva does not become impure through contact with souls that need purifying; rather, it is the soul to be purified that becomes pure through contact with Śiva.
m.7.1.31.47: When iron is penetrated by fire, the burning belongs to the fire alone, not to the iron. Likewise, in the embodied soul the lordship belongs to the Lord alone, not to the souls.
m.7.1.31.48: For it is not the wood that blazes upward; it is the fire that blazes. The state of becoming charcoal belongs to the wood, not to the fire; let the same be applied here too. For this very reason, in this world, even in wood, stone and clay,
m.7.1.31.49: Śiva-hood is attributed figuratively, solely by virtue of Śiva's pervading presence. Qualities such as friendliness are secondary; therefore they operate in differing ways, and for those coloured by those qualities they lead both to fault and to merit.
m.7.1.31.50: But for Śiva, who favours all that is secondary and not secondary, the operations of qualities lead neither to merit nor to fault.
m.7.1.31.51: The wise do not call the meaning of the word grace (anugraha) secondary; rather, it is release from saṃsāra, the good consisting in Śiva's command.
m.7.1.31.52: The good is doing his command; what is good, that is grace. Directing everything towards the good, he is the bestower of grace on all.
m.7.1.31.53: What is the meaning of the word help (upakāra), that too they call grace; since that too has the form of the good, Śiva is the helper of all.
m.7.1.31.54: Though everything, conscious and non-conscious, is always directed to the good, being obstructed by its own nature, it does not obtain the good equally.
m.7.1.31.55: Just as the sun does make the lotuses bloom with its rays, yet they do not bloom equally, in accordance with their own natures.
m.7.1.31.56: For the nature of things too is the cause of an outcome that is to be; nature does not accomplish for agents an outcome that is ceasing to be.
m.7.1.31.57: Contact with fire melts only gold, not charcoal; likewise Śiva releases only those whose impurity has ripened, not others.
m.7.1.31.58: Whatever is fit to become in a certain way does not become so by itself without the bringing-about of an agent; hence the agent would be independent and everlasting.
m.7.1.31.59: Just as Śiva, the bestower of grace on all, is stainless by nature, so the souls called jīvas are impure by nature.
m.7.1.31.60: Otherwise, how is it that these necessarily transmigrate, but not Śiva? The wise declare saṃsāra to be the bondage of karma and māyā for this soul.
m.7.1.31.61: That this bondage belongs to the soul alone and not to Śiva has a cause; that cause is the impurity of the souls themselves, innate and not adventitious.
m.7.1.31.62: If it were adventitious, it would have to come to someone through some cause; and whatever that cause, it would be one, of uniform nature, and could not explain the diversity of souls.
m.7.1.31.63: For, though soulhood is the same, some are bound and others liberated; and among the bound again some, by reason of laya, bhoga and adhikāra,
m.7.1.31.64: experience inequality in knowledge, lordship and the like, being higher and lower. Some attain the state of embodied souls (mūrtyātman); some are within the near range.
m.7.1.31.65: Among the embodied souls, some are Śivas, situated at the summits of the paths (adhvan); in the middle are the Maheśvaras; and the Rudras are situated at the lower level.
m.7.1.31.66: In the near range too, beyond māyā, there is a triad from the supreme cause: there the Ātman is situated below, and the Antarātman in the middle,
m.7.1.31.67: and above, the Paramātman — these are Brahmā, Viṣṇu and Maheśvara. Some Vasus abide, resorting to the level of the Paramātman,
m.7.1.31.68: some at the level of the Antarātman, and some likewise at the level of the Ātman. The Śaivas are at the Śāntyatīta level, then the Māheśvaras at the Śānta level;
m.7.1.31.69: in Vidyā likewise the Raudras, in Pratiṣṭhā the Vaiṣṇavas, and in Nivṛtti the souls — Brahmā and those born from Brahmā's limbs.
m.7.1.31.70: The eight divine births are the highest, the human birth is middling, and the five beginning with birds are the lowest; these are the fourteen births.
m.7.1.31.71: The state of being higher or lower should also be understood as due to the impurity of the transmigrating soul; just as for the one now liberated there was first unripeness and afterwards ripeness of impurity.
m.7.1.31.72: Impurity, both unripe and ripe, is the cause of saṃsāra; when it is unripe, men are lower, and when it is ripe, they are higher, in due order.
m.7.1.31.73: The bound souls (paśu) are divided threefold, having one, two or three impurities respectively. Among them, those with one impurity are considered highest, those with two middling, and those with three should be known as lowest; they are governed by those successively higher.
m.7.1.31.74: Those with two impurities and those with one govern, in order, those with three and two. Thus the conditioned (aupādhika) differentiation of the universe is conceived.
m.7.1.31.75: Śiva alone governs all those with one, two or three impurities. Just as this world, though not of the nature of Śiva, is governed by Śiva,
m.7.1.31.76: so the world, though not of the nature of Rudra, is governed by the Rudras. The great earth, extending up to the cosmic egg, is governed by the Śatarudras and others;
m.7.1.31.77: and the intermediate region, extending up to māyā, is pervaded all around continuously, in order, by Amareśa and others, down to the one of thumb-size.
m.7.1.31.78: Heaven, ending in Mahāmāyā, is governed by the lords of the worlds beginning with Vāyu and ending with Anāśrita, who dwell within the paths.
m.7.1.31.79: For they are directly the dwellers in heaven, likewise the dwellers in the intermediate region, and those stationed on earth; thus are the gods praised by those devoted to the gods.
m.7.1.31.80: Thus, through the three impurities, unripe and ripe, each separately acting as root causes, the disease of saṃsāra proceeds for souls.
m.7.1.31.81: The remedy for this disease is knowledge alone, and nothing else. The physician who prescribes it is Śambhu; Śiva is the supreme cause.
m.7.1.31.82: Śiva is able to release the bound souls even without suffering; as to why he causes suffering, no inquiry should be made here.
m.7.1.31.83: For it is certain that the whole of saṃsāra is suffering itself. How could suffering be non-suffering? For a thing's nature does not turn into its opposite.
m.7.1.31.84: A sick man does not become sick-free because of the physician's medicine (as the cause of disease); rather, the physician, by medicines, easily lifts the one afflicted by disease out of the disease.
m.7.1.31.85: Likewise, Śiva releases from suffering the bound souls, impure by nature and suffering by nature, through the application of the medicine of his own command.
m.7.1.31.86: The physician is not the cause of the disease, whereas Śiva is the cause of saṃsāra — even this disparity does not amount to a fault in him.
m.7.1.31.87: When suffering is established by nature, how is Śiva its cause? The impurity of souls is innate; it is that which makes them transmigrate.
m.7.1.31.88: But the impurity that causes saṃsāra — māyā and the rest, being insentient — does not operate by itself without Śiva's proximity.
m.7.1.31.89: Just as the magnet-stone, by mere proximity, aids the moving iron, so too is Śiva to this impurity — so say the wise.
m.7.1.31.90: His proximity, being eternal and uncaused, cannot be removed; hence Śiva, unknown, is ever the presiding controller of the world.
m.7.1.31.91: Nothing here is found to operate without Śiva. All this is impelled by him, yet he is not deluded.
