m.7.1.31.92: His Śakti, whose nature is command, is the controller, facing in all directions; by her all this is perpetually pervaded, yet he is not tainted.
m.7.1.31.93: Everything, from the very first, what is not-this and what is this, is to be ruled; he is the Lord. From his ruling comes his command; yet he is not tainted.
m.7.1.31.94: The evil-minded one who, out of delusion, thinks otherwise perishes — and that too solely through the majesty of his power; yet he is not tainted.
m.7.1.31.95: Meanwhile a bodiless voice was heard from the sky: True, Om, immortal, gentle — thus it clearly manifested.
m.7.1.31.96: Then all the sages, greatly delighted, all their doubts destroyed, filled with wonder, bowed to the lord Vāyu.
m.7.1.31.97: Though he had thus freed the sages of doubt, Vāyu, thinking that their knowledge was not yet firmly established, spoke thus.
m.7.1.31.98: Vāyu said: Knowledge is held to be twofold: indirect and direct. They call the indirect unstable, but the direct very stable.
m.7.1.31.99: That which is attained through reasoning and instruction is called indirect; the direct, however, will arise from excellent practice.
m.7.1.31.100: Having firmly resolved that there is no liberation without direct knowledge, strive tirelessly to perfect the excellent practice.
m.7.1.31.iti: Thus ends the thirty-first adhyāya, named The teaching of knowledge, in the Pūrva-khaṇḍa of the seventh saṃhitā, the Vāyavīya-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.7.1.32.1: The sages said: What is that best practice by which liberation is directly realised? And, O Māruta, you should now tell us its means as well.
m.7.1.32.2: Vāyu said: The Śaiva dharma is indeed the supreme dharma, designated the best practice, in which Śiva, who directly grants liberation, may be perceived immediately.
m.7.1.32.3: It should be known as fivefold, through five stages in sequence, consisting of ritual action, austerity, japa, meditation and knowledge, each unsurpassed.
m.7.1.32.4: The dharma accomplished by these very stages, each with its higher stage, is held to be supreme, in which there is knowledge, both indirect and direct, that grants liberation.
m.7.1.32.5: Both dharmas, the supreme and the non-supreme, are enjoined by the Veda; for the matter denoted by the word dharma, the Veda alone is our authority.
m.7.1.32.6: The supreme dharma, culminating in yoga, is found in the head of the Veda, the Upaniṣads; the non-supreme dharma likewise arises below, from the face of the Veda, its earlier portion.
m.7.1.32.7: The dharma for which those whose selves are no longer bound souls (paśu) are eligible is held to be supreme; the other is common, since all are eligible for it.
m.7.1.32.8: And this excellent dharma is the means to the higher dharma; it is properly elaborated, together with its subsidiaries, by the Dharmaśāstras and the like.
m.7.1.32.9: The Śaiva dharma is indeed the supreme dharma, designated the best practice; it has been elaborated to some extent by the Itihāsas and Purāṇas.
m.7.1.32.10: But it is fully set forth by the Śaiva Āgamas, with the full expanse of its limbs and sub-limbs, and is properly elaborated together with its sacraments and rules of eligibility.
m.7.1.32.11: The Śaiva Āgama, as composed, is twofold: Vedic (śrauta) and non-Vedic; the Vedic consists of the essence of the Veda, the other is held to be independent.
m.7.1.32.12: The independent Āgama was first tenfold and then again eighteenfold; established under names beginning with Kāmika, it is designated the Siddhānta.
m.7.1.32.13: That which consists of the essence of the Veda has an extent of a hundred crores of verses, and in it the supreme Pāśupata vow and knowledge are taught.
m.7.1.32.14: In the cycles of the yugas it is taught by one in the form of a yoga-teacher; it is set in motion by Śiva himself, descending here and there.
m.7.1.32.15: Having condensed it, its expounders are four great sages: Ruru, Dadhīca, Agastya, and the illustrious Upamanyu.
m.7.1.32.16: They are to be known as Pāśupatas, promulgators of the Saṃhitās; and the gurus of their lineage number in hundreds and thousands.
m.7.1.32.17: The supreme dharma taught there is fourfold, consisting of conduct (caryā) and the rest; among these, the Pāśupata yoga makes Śiva firmly perceptible.
m.7.1.32.18: Therefore the Pāśupata yoga is held to be the best practice; and within it, the fitting means taught by Brahmā is now described.
m.7.1.32.19: A yoga consisting of the eight names was devised by Śiva; through that yoga Śaiva wisdom arises swiftly.
m.7.1.32.20: Through wisdom one soon gains supreme, steady knowledge; Śiva is gracious to him in whom knowledge is firmly established.
m.7.1.32.21: From his grace comes the supreme yoga that makes Śiva directly perceived; through the direct perception of Śiva one is freed from the cause of saṃsāra.
m.7.1.32.22: Then he becomes free of saṃsāra; liberated, he becomes equal to Śiva. This is the means taught by Brahmā; that very means is now explained separately.
m.7.1.32.23: Śiva, Maheśvara, Rudra, Viṣṇu, Pitāmaha, Saṃsāravaidya (physician of worldly existence), Sarvajña (the omniscient) and Paramātman — these are the principal ones.
m.7.1.32.24: This principal group of eight names designates Śiva; the first five should be understood as corresponding in order to Śāntyatītā and the rest.
m.7.1.32.25: These are the names of Sadāśiva and the others, owing to their assumption of the five limiting adjuncts; but when the adjuncts cease, each name ceases accordingly.
m.7.1.32.26: For the position (pada) itself is eternal, while the holders of positions are regarded as non-eternal, since when the positions change, the holders are released.
m.7.1.32.27: In another cycle, the attainment of that position by others is spoken of again; thus the first group of five names would denote other selves.
m.7.1.32.28: But the other three names, through their connection with the material cause and the rest, and because they express threefold adjuncts, continue to apply to Śiva alone.
m.7.1.32.29: Because contact with beginningless impurity is by nature absent in him from the very outset, he is the utterly pure Self; hence he is called Śiva.
m.7.1.32.30: Or else, the Lord, sole treasure of all auspicious qualities, is called Śiva by the wise who expound the meaning of the Śiva-principle.
m.7.1.32.31: Prakṛti is held to be beyond the twenty-three tattvas; and beyond Prakṛti they declare the Puruṣa, the twenty-fifth.
m.7.1.32.32: He whom they call the syllable (svara, Om) at the beginning of the Veda, through the relation of denoted and denoter; and since his true nature is knowable through the Veda alone, he is established in the Vedānta.
m.7.1.32.33: He who is beyond that Puruṣa merged in Prakṛti is Maheśvara, because the activity of both Prakṛti and Puruṣa depends on him.
m.7.1.32.34: Or else, this imperishable principle of three guṇas is to be accepted as Prakṛti; one should know Māyā as Prakṛti, and Maheśvara as the wielder of Māyā.
m.7.1.32.35: The agitator of Māyā, the infinite one, through his union with Maheśvara, is proclaimed as the Self of Time, the supreme Self and so on, both gross and subtle.
m.7.1.32.36: Rud means sorrow or the cause of sorrow; because the Lord drives that away from us, Śiva, the supreme cause, is called Rudra by the wise.
m.7.1.32.37: Unwearied, Śiva pervades and presides over everything from the tattvas down to the elements, in bodies and the rest; therefore he is Rudra, present everywhere.
m.7.1.32.38: Since Śiva is the father even of those embodied beings who are the fathers of the world, he is declared Pitāmaha (grandfather) because of his fatherhood toward all.
m.7.1.32.39: Just as a physician who knows the root cause removes a disease by remedies and medicines, so likewise, through dissolution, enjoyment and office (laya, bhoga, adhikāra),
m.7.1.32.40: the Lord is always the remover of saṃsāra together with its root; hence he is called Saṃsāravaidya by those who know the meaning of all the tattvas.
m.7.1.32.41: Even though these senses exist for the purpose of attaining knowledge of the ten objects, bound souls do not know completely the things that occur in the three times, both gross and subtle.
m.7.1.32.42: The bound souls, covered with impurity (mala) by māyā itself, do not know them. But even when all the means of knowing every object are absent,
m.7.1.32.43: Sadāśiva knows effortlessly each thing exactly as it stands; therefore he is called omniscient.
m.7.1.32.44: Because of his eternal union with these supreme qualities he is the Self of all; and since there is no supreme self apart from himself, Śiva himself is the Supreme Self.
m.7.1.32.45: Having received this octad of names through the grace of the preceptor, one should cut the knot of the kalās beginning with Nivṛtti by means of the five names beginning with Śiva,
m.7.1.32.46: cutting them each in its proper way and in due order, and purifying them according to their qualities, with names/breaths repeated together with upward impulse (udghāta), or else with restrained breath;
m.7.1.32.47: having pierced the path furnished with the heart, throat, palate, the point between the brows and the brahmarandhra, and leading one's own self, in the form of the puryaṣṭaka, through the suṣumnā
m.7.1.32.48: having led it above the moon located at the dvādaśānta, into the radiance of Śiva, and having withdrawn the face of outward activity, then, through dissolution, according to the proper purification,
m.7.1.32.49: and when the body has again been drenched by the shower of nectar of Śakti, bringing one's own self, having the form of a nectar-self, down into the heart,
m.7.1.32.50: and meditating on Mahādeva Śaṅkara, loving towards his devotees, seated on a white lotus beyond the moon located at the dvādaśānta,
m.7.1.32.51: the god as Ardhanārīśvara, stainless, of charming form, resembling pure crystal, gracious, of cool radiance —
m.7.1.32.52: having meditated on the god in the mind, the man, with a composed mind, should then worship him with flowers of devotion, using the octad of Śiva's names alone.
m.7.1.32.53: At the end of the worship, the man, again restraining his breaths and concentrating his mind properly, should recite the octad of names of Śarva.
m.7.1.32.54: Having offered eight oblations in the navel, then concluding with the full oblation and a salutation, and having performed the final worship by offering eight flowers,
m.7.1.32.55: he should offer his own self by means of a palmful of water. Having done so, very soon he obtains the auspicious Pāśupata knowledge,
m.7.1.32.56: he obtains it, and firm establishment in it, and likewise unsurpassed conduct; and having attained the supreme yoga, he is liberated — of this there is no doubt.
m.7.1.32.iti: Thus ends the thirty-second adhyāya, named The best practice, in the Pūrva-khaṇḍa of the seventh saṃhitā, the Vāyavīya-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.7.1.33.1: The sages said: O lord, we wish to hear about the supreme Pāśupata vow, by performing which even Brahmā and the others are all known as Pāśupatas.
m.7.1.33.2: Vāyu said: I shall declare to you the secret Pāśupata vow, which cuts away all sins, a Vedic rite heard in the Atharvaśiras.
m.7.1.33.3: The time is the full-moon day of Caitra; the place is one that belongs to Śiva, or a holy field, a garden and the like, or a forest—any place that is commendable and of auspicious marks.
m.7.1.33.4: There, first, on the thirteenth lunar day, having bathed well and duly performed the daily rites, having taken leave of his own teacher, worshipped him and bowed to him,
m.7.1.33.5: having performed a special worship, himself wearing white garments, with a white sacred thread, and with white garlands and unguents,
m.7.1.33.6: seated on a seat of darbha grass, holding a handful of darbha, having done three breath-controls, facing east or north, and having meditated on the God and the Goddess by way of informing them of his intent,
m.7.1.33.7: he should become consecrated, resolving, I undertake this vow—either until the fall of the body, or for twelve years,
m.7.1.33.8: or half of that, or half of that again, or for twelve months, or half of that, or half of that again, or for a single month,
m.7.1.33.9: or for twelve days, or for six days, or half of that, or a single day—as the limit of the vow's resolution.
m.7.1.33.10: Having duly installed the fire for the purpose of the Virajā oblation, and having offered with ghee, with fuel-sticks and with caru in due order,
m.7.1.33.11: and having filled up that full oblation, he should again offer with the root mantra, using those same fuel-sticks and other materials, intending the purification of the principles (tattvas),
m.7.1.33.12: recollecting, may these principles in my body be purified: the five elements, the subtle elements, and the five organs of action,
m.7.1.33.13: the senses divided as those of knowledge and of action, by the division of five functions; the seven bodily constituents beginning with skin; the five vital airs beginning with prāṇa;
m.7.1.33.14: mind, intellect, ego-sense, the guṇas, Prakṛti and Puruṣa, Rāga, Vidyā and Kalā, Niyati and Kāla,
m.7.1.33.15: Māyā and Śuddhavidyā, Maheśvara and Sadāśiva, Śakti and the Śiva-principle—these, in order, they know as the principles.
m.7.1.33.16: Having offered with the Virajā mantras, this offerer becomes free of impurity (virajā); obtaining Śiva's grace, he indeed becomes possessed of knowledge.
m.7.1.33.17: Then, taking cow-dung, forming it into a ball, consecrating it with mantras, placing it in the fire and sprinkling it, on that day he should eat only sacrificial food.
m.7.1.33.18: At dawn on the fourteenth day, having done all that was described before, he should remain fasting that day and pass the remaining time.
m.7.1.33.19: In the morning on the festival (full-moon) day, having done likewise up to the end of the oblation, he should withdraw the Rudra-fire and carefully collect the ash.
m.7.1.33.20: Then, becoming one with matted hair, or shaven-headed, or with a single matted lock as a tuft, he should bathe; then, if he is free of shame, he may be sky-clad (naked).
m.7.1.33.21: Or he may wear ochre cloth, or garments of hide or rags, or a single cloth, or bark; and he should carry a staff and wear a girdle.
m.7.1.33.22: Afterwards, having washed his feet and sipped water twice, he should gather that ash produced from the Virajā fire for his own body,
m.7.1.33.23: and with the six Atharvan mantras beginning agniḥ, in order, having wiped the limbs from the head down to the feet, he should touch them with that ash.
m.7.1.33.24: Then, in the same order, taking up the ash, he should smear all his limbs with it, using the praṇava or the Śiva mantra.
m.7.1.33.25: Then he should make the tripuṇḍra, called tryāyuṣa; having attained the state of Śiva, he should then practise Śiva-yoga.
m.7.1.33.26: He should perform this Pāśupata vow in this way at the three junctures of the day; it grants enjoyment and liberation and removes the state of being a bound soul (paśutva).
m.7.1.33.27: Having cast off that paśu-state by performing the Pāśupata vow, the eternal Mahādeva in the form of the liṅga is to be worshipped.
m.7.1.33.28: He should arrange as a seat a golden eight-petalled lotus adorned with the nine gems, furnished with pericarp and filaments,
m.7.1.33.29: this if he has wealth; in its absence, a red or white lotus; and in the absence of that too, one made purely of mental conception.
m.7.1.33.30: Placing in the middle of that lotus's pericarp a small crystal liṅga with a pedestal, he should worship it duly and in order.
m.7.1.33.31: Having installed that purified liṅga according to rule, and having conceived the seat and the form in the manner of the five-faced Śiva,
m.7.1.33.32: he should bathe it with full golden pitchers filled with the five cow-products and other things, gathered according to his means.
m.7.1.33.33: Having anointed the liṅga together with its altar with fragrant substances, with camphor, sandal and the like, and saffron, and having adorned it with ornaments,
m.7.1.33.34: with bilva leaves, with lotuses, with red and white water-lilies, with blue lilies, and with various other fragrant flowers,
m.7.1.33.35: with holy, excellent and variegated leaves, with dūrvā grass, unbroken rice and the like—having worshipped as available, according to the procedure of the great worship,
m.7.1.33.36: he should present incense, lamp and food-offering; and having offered them, if he has means, he should also perform the auspicious festive rite.
m.7.1.33.37: All substances that are desired, excellent and justly earned should be offered, especially in this vow.
m.7.1.33.38: The number of bilva leaves, water-lilies and lotuses is held to be a thousand each; the alternative number, O twice-born, is one hundred and eight.
m.7.1.33.39: Even there, he should especially not omit the bilva leaf. They say one golden lotus is superior to a thousand lotuses.
m.7.1.33.40: For blue lilies and the rest too, this rule is the same as for bilva leaves. For other flowers there is no fixed rule; he should offer as available.
m.7.1.33.41: The eightfold arghya is the finest offering; incense and unguent are offered specifically to each face: sandal-paste on the face called Vāmadeva, and yellow orpiment on Tatpuruṣa,
m.7.1.33.42: and ashes on Īśāna. Some regard such things as unguent and not as incense, since a separate incense is prescribed. White aloe-wood is offered on the face called Aghora, and black aloe-wood further,
m.7.1.33.43: guggulu on Tatpuruṣa, saugandhika on Sadyojāta, the gentle face, and on Īśāna uśīra and the like — one should offer incense in this specific way.
m.7.1.33.44: Incense mixed with sugar, honey, camphor and ghee of a tawny cow, made of sandal, aloe-wood and other woods, is called the general incense.
m.7.1.33.45: Then a row of lamps with camphor wicks, rich in ghee, should be offered; after that arghya and sipping-water should be offered to each face.
m.7.1.33.46: In the first enclosure Heramba and Ṣaṇmukha are to be worshipped in order; and then, in the first enclosure, the Brahma-limbs are worshipped.
m.7.1.33.47: In the second enclosure the Vighneśas, the Cakravartins, are to be worshipped; in the third enclosure the eight forms beginning with Bhava are to be worshipped.
m.7.1.33.48: There also are worshipped the eleven forms beginning with Mahādeva; in the fourth enclosure all the lords of the gaṇas are to be worshipped.
m.7.1.33.49: Outside the lotus, in the fifth enclosure, in order, the regents of the ten directions are to be worshipped, together with their weapons and their attendants;
m.7.1.33.50: the mind-born sons of Brahmā, all the hosts of luminaries, all the goddesses and gods, and all, all the sky-goers,
m.7.1.33.51: and others dwelling in Pātāla, all the hosts of sages too, the yogins, all the sacrifices, the birds, and likewise the Mothers,
m.7.1.33.52: and the Kṣetrapālas with their hosts — all this moving and unmoving world is to be worshipped out of love for Śiva, regarding it as endowed with Śambhu's glory.
m.7.1.33.53: Then, at the end of the enclosure-worship, having worshipped the Supreme Lord, one should offer with devotion a delightful oblation-food with ghee, together with a fan.
m.7.1.33.54: Having given mouth-fresheners and the like, and betel with its accompaniments, and having adorned the Lord again with ornaments of various flowers,
m.7.1.33.55: at the end of the waving of lights, one should elaborate and complete the rest of the worship, and offer a cup with its accessories and a bed.
m.7.1.33.56: One should offer a moon-like necklace and a couch — all that is excellent, fit for a king and delightful, according to one's means.
m.7.1.33.57: Having done this and had it done, having made the fire-offering and the counter-worship, and having recited the Vyomeśa hymn, one should recite the five-syllable vidyā.
m.7.1.33.58: Having made circumambulation and prostration, one should surrender oneself; then, in front of the deity, one should worship the guru and a brahmin.
m.7.1.33.59: Having given arghya and eight flowers, having dismissed the deity from the liṅga, and having withdrawn the fire into one's own fire and dismissed it as well,
m.7.1.33.60: a person should perform daily the service described above in this way. Then that liṅga with its lotus, together with all the accessories,
m.7.1.33.61: one should offer to one's own guru or install in a Śiva temple. And having worshipped the gurus, the brahmins, and especially the vow-observers,
m.7.1.33.62: if able, one should gratify devotees, the twice-born, and the poor and helpless. He himself, if able, should keep a fast, or eat fruits and roots,
m.7.1.33.63: or live on milk, or eat alms, or eat once a day; eating at night, always taking moderate food, keeping to sleeping on the ground, pure,
m.7.1.33.64: sleeping on ashes or on grass, or wearing bark-cloth and deerskin, ever under the vow of celibacy — so one should observe this vow.
m.7.1.33.65: On Sunday, on the day of Ārdrā, on the fifteenth day of both fortnights, and on the eighth and fourteenth, one who is able should also fast.
m.7.1.33.66: With every effort one should avoid, in mind, deed and speech, heretics, the fallen, menstruating women, those in birth-impurity, outcastes and the like.
m.7.1.33.67: One should always be given to forbearance, generosity, compassion, truth and non-violence, content and tranquil, and devoted to japa and meditation.
m.7.1.33.68: One should bathe at the three junctures of the day, or else take an ash-bath, and perform the special worship with mind, words and speech.
m.7.1.33.69: What need to say more here? The vow-observer should do nothing inauspicious. But if through carelessness he acts so, he should weigh its gravity or lightness,
m.7.1.33.70: and perform suitable expiation through worship, fire-offering, japa and the like. Thus he should conduct himself until the completion of the vow, not carelessly.
m.7.1.33.71: He should make a gift of a cow, release a bull, and perform worship with all his wealth — a devotee, for the pleasure of Śiva, free of all desires.
m.7.1.33.72: This general procedure of this vow has been told in brief; I shall now declare the special rules for each month, as I have heard.
m.7.1.33.73: In Vaiśākha the liṅga is to be of diamond; in Jyeṣṭha an auspicious one of emerald; in Āṣāḍha one should know it to be of pearl; in Śrāvaṇa made of sapphire;
m.7.1.33.74: and in the month of Bhādrapada an excellent one made of ruby; in the month of Āśvina one should know the liṅga to be a fine one of gomedaka (hessonite).
m.7.1.33.75: In Kārttika a liṅga of coral; in Mārgaśīrṣa of cat's-eye; in Pauṣa made of topaz; and in Māgha of sun-stone;
m.7.1.33.76: in Phālguna one made of moonstone; in Caitra the interchange of these, or else; in all months, if gems are not obtainable, one of gold;
m.7.1.33.77: in the absence of gold, one of silver, or of copper, or likewise of stone, or of clay as available, or of lac, or of some other material,
m.7.1.33.78: or one may make a liṅga composed of all fragrant substances, as one likes. At the time of the vow's conclusion, having performed the daily rites,
m.7.1.33.79: having performed the special worship and made the fire-offering just as before, and having likewise worshipped the teacher and especially the vow-observers,
m.7.1.33.80: permitted also by the preceptor, facing east or north, seated on darbha grass with darbha in hand, and restraining the prāṇa and apāna breaths,
m.7.1.33.81: Having repeated the root mantra according to his capacity, having meditated on the three-eyed One together with Ambā, having taken leave as before and bowed with joined palms,
m.7.1.33.82: saying, O Lord, by your command I relinquish this vow, he should then cast away to the north the darbha grass placed at the base of the liṅga.
m.7.1.33.83: Then he should also give up the staff, matted hair, bark garment and girdle. Having again sipped water according to rule, he should utter the five-syllabled mantra.
m.7.1.33.84: He who, having taken the lifelong initiation, undisturbed, performs this vow until the end of his body, is indeed known as a naiṣṭhika lifelong observer.
m.7.1.33.85: He should be known as one beyond the stages of life (atyāśramī) and likewise as a great Pāśupata; he alone is the best of ascetics, and he alone is a great vow-keeper.
m.7.1.33.86: Among seekers of liberation there is none equal to him, who has fulfilled his duty. The ascetic who has become a naiṣṭhika they call the foremost of naiṣṭhikas.
m.7.1.33.87: He who performs this vow daily, or for twelve days, he too becomes equal to a naiṣṭhika, owing to his connection with an intense vow.
m.7.1.33.88: He who, devoted to vows and anointed with ghee, performs this vow even for two, three or one day, he too is a naiṣṭhika of a kind.
m.7.1.33.89: He who, free from desire, performs this supreme vow simply as a duty, with his self ever offered to Śiva — none anywhere is equal to him.
m.7.1.33.90: A learned twice-born covered with ash is at once freed from the most terrible sins arising from great crimes; there is no doubt of this.
m.7.1.33.91: The supreme potency of Rudra's fire is proclaimed to be ash. Therefore one endowed with ash is at all times potent.
m.7.1.33.92: The faults of one devoted to ash perish through contact with the fire of ash. One whose self is purified by ash-bathing is known as bhasmaniṣṭha, devoted to ash.
m.7.1.33.93: A man whose whole body is smeared with ash, who shines with ash and bears the tripuṇḍra, and who bathes in ash, is known as bhasmaniṣṭha.
m.7.1.33.94: Ghosts, spirits, piśācas and exceedingly unbearable diseases flee from the presence of one devoted to ash; there is no doubt.
m.7.1.33.95: It is called bhasita from its shining (bhāsana), bhasma from its devouring (bhakṣaṇa) of impurity; bhūti because it brings prosperity (bhūti), and rakṣā because it gives supreme protection (rakṣā).
m.7.1.33.96: What more need be said here as the reason for the greatness of ash? The god Maheśvara himself, as a vow-keeper, bathed in ash.
m.7.1.33.97: This ash belonging to the Supreme Lord is the supreme weapon of the Śaivas, by which the calamities in the austerity of Dhaumya's elder brother were warded off.
m.7.1.33.98: Therefore, having performed the Pāśupata vow with every effort, and gathering ash as one would wealth, one should be devoted to bathing in ash.
m.7.1.33.iti: Thus ends the thirty-third adhyāya, named The procedure of the vow of Paśupati, in the Pūrva-khaṇḍa of the seventh saṃhitā, the Vāyavīya-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.7.1.34.1: The sages said: The child, Dhaumya's elder brother, performed austerity for the sake of milk, and for that reason the god who bears the trident gave him the ocean of milk.
m.7.1.34.2: How did that little child come to be an expounder of the Śiva scriptures? And how did he come to know Śiva's true nature and become steadfast in austerity?
m.7.1.34.3: And how, having gained knowledge during his practice of austerity, did he obtain the ash, the supreme potency of Rudra's fire, as his own protection?
m.7.1.34.4: Vāyu said: This child who performed austerity was no ordinary one; he was the son of the wise Vyāghrapāda, the foremost of sages.
m.7.1.34.5: He had become perfected in a former birth; fallen from his own station for some reason, he had by good fortune been born as a sage's son.
m.7.1.34.6: His austerity, which sprang from a longing for milk, became the doorway to the grace of Mahādeva that was destined to come to him through good fortune.
m.7.1.34.7: Therefore Śaṅkara himself granted him lordship over all the gaṇas and eternal youth, together with the ocean of milk.
m.7.1.34.8: His acquisition of knowledge too came solely from Śaṅkara's grace; for the wise know the supreme Kaumāra knowledge to be directly full of śakti.
m.7.1.34.9: His being an expounder of the Śiva scriptures was also brought about by that grace, like Nandin, who obtained an ocean of knowledge from the mouths of Kumāra and Umā.
m.7.1.34.10: But the visible cause of his attaining knowledge of Śiva was, directly, his own mother's words, born of grief, on account of milk.
m.7.1.34.11: Once he drank a very little milk at his maternal uncle's hermitage; then with envy, seeing his uncle's son satisfied with excellent milk,
m.7.1.34.12: having seen his uncle's son standing there after drinking as much as he wanted, Upamanyu, son of Vyāghrapāda, spoke affectionately to his mother.
m.7.1.34.13: Upamanyu said: Mother, mother, O fortunate ascetic lady, give me cow's milk, very sweet and warm, and not a little; I will drink it.
m.7.1.34.14: Vāyu said: Hearing her son's words, his mother, the ascetic queen of Vyāghrapāda, was then grieved.
m.7.1.34.15: Fondling him with great love and embracing her son tenderly, she, sorrowful, then wept, remembering her own poverty.
m.7.1.34.16: Remembering the milk again and again, the radiant boy Upamanyu kept crying and said to her, give, give.
m.7.1.34.17: Recognising his stubbornness, the ascetic wife of the brāhmaṇa then devised a good means to calm that obstinacy.
m.7.1.34.18: Then, looking over the grains she herself had gathered by gleaning, the sweet-voiced woman mixed grain-flour with water,
m.7.1.34.19: and saying gently, come, come, my son, she, stricken with sorrow, embraced her son, took him up, and gave him the artificial milk.
m.7.1.34.20: Having drunk the artificial milk given by his mother, the boy, greatly distressed, said to his mother, this is not milk.
m.7.1.34.21: Then, grieved, she looked at him, kissed him on the head, wiped her son's lotus-like eyes with her hands, and said:
m.7.1.34.22: The mother said: Those rivers full of jewels, ranging through heaven and the netherworld, are not seen by the unfortunate, nor by those who lack devotion to Śiva.
m.7.1.34.23: Kingdom, heaven, liberation, food made from milk—these cherished things they do not obtain when Śiva is not pleased with them.
m.7.1.34.24: Everything is born of Bhava's grace, not of any other god's grace. Those devoted to other gods wander about, afflicted with sorrow.
m.7.1.34.25: So where would milk come from for us, who always live in the forest? Where are the means of getting milk, child, and where are we forest-dwellers?
m.7.1.34.26: Because of utter want and poverty, I, unfortunate as I am, gave you this false milk, made by mixing flour with water.
m.7.1.34.27: You drank a little sweet boiled milk at your uncle's house, and knowing the sweetness of what you drank, you keep remembering milk of that kind,
m.7.1.34.28: and by crying, this given to me is not milk, you grieve me. Without Śambhu's grace there is no milk for you.
m.7.1.34.29: Whatever is offered with devotion at the lotus feet of him, accompanied by Ambā and by his gaṇas, that is the cause of all prosperity.
m.7.1.34.30: Until now we have not worshipped Mahādeva, the giver of wealth, who grants to those with desires the fruits they desire, as declared.
m.7.1.34.31: Before this, we did not worship Śiva with wealth as our aim; therefore we have become poor, and therefore there is no milk for you.
m.7.1.34.32: Whatever was given in a former birth with Śiva as its object, O son, that alone is received—not otherwise, not what was given with Viṣṇu or another lord as its object.
m.7.1.34.33: Vāyu said: Hearing these truthful words of his mother, which betrayed her grief and more, the boy, though young, felt inward remorse and spoke these bold words.
m.7.1.34.34: Upamanyu said: Enough of grief from now on, mother. If Śaṅkara with Ambā exists, give up your grief, O fortunate one; all will be well.
m.7.1.34.35: Hear my words today, mother: if Mahādeva exists anywhere, then sooner or later I will obtain the ocean of milk.
m.7.1.34.36: Vāyu said: Hearing these words of the high-minded boy, his wise mother, greatly pleased, then replied.
m.7.1.34.37: The mother said: my dear, you have resolved well, and it increases my joy. Do not delay; worship Sadāśiva together with Ambā.
m.7.1.34.38: Śiva indeed is greater than all, the supreme cause. The whole world is made by him; Brahmā and the others are his servants.
m.7.1.34.39: Our sovereignty is wrought by his grace; we are servants of that lord. Apart from him we know no other—Śaṅkara, who brings welfare to the world.
m.7.1.34.40: Abandoning other gods in deed, mind and speech, worship him alone, together with Ambā and his gaṇas, with heartfelt devotion.
m.7.1.34.41: Of that God of gods, Śiva, the giver of boons, this mantra, namaḥ śivāya, is held to be the direct expressive name.
m.7.1.34.42: The seventy million great mantras, all the supreme ones together with the praṇava, dissolve into this very mantra and again come forth from it.
m.7.1.34.43: Those mantras become gracious and effective according to one's own eligibility and the like; but this one mantra alone, by the Lord's command, is open to all who are eligible.
m.7.1.34.44: Just as Śiva is able to protect all his own devotees, the lowly as well as the exalted, so too this mantra is able at all times.
m.7.1.34.45: And this mantra is indeed more powerful even than any other mantra; it alone is capable of protecting all, and no other is held to be so.
m.7.1.34.46: Therefore, giving up other mantras, be wholly devoted to the five-syllable mantra; when it rests on the tip of one's tongue, nothing here is difficult to attain.
m.7.1.34.47: And the Aghora weapon-mantra is the unsurpassed means of protection for Śaivas; considering that it too has arisen from that five-syllable mantra, be devoted to it, not otherwise.
m.7.1.34.48: This excellent ash was obtained by me from your father himself; it is perfected in the Virajā fire and wards off great calamities.
m.7.1.34.49: And take the mantra given to you by me, with my permission; by this alone, when repeated, protection will quickly be yours.
m.7.1.34.50: Vāyu said: Having thus instructed him and having said, may there be auspiciousness, the mother dismissed the young sage, who then placed her words on his head.
m.7.1.34.51: Having bowed to her and spoken thus, he set out to perform austerity; and then his mother said to him, may the gods bring you good fortune.
m.7.1.34.52: Permitted by her, he went to the Himālaya mountain and there, living on air and with concentrated mind, performed austerity hard to practise.
m.7.1.34.53: Having made a shrine with eight bricks and a liṅga of clay, and having invoked there Mahādeva, the imperishable, together with Ambā and his attendants,
m.7.1.34.54: and having worshipped him for a long time with devotion, with the five-syllable mantra alone, with leaves and flowers grown in the forest, he practised supreme austerity.
m.7.1.34.55: Then, as that boy Upamanyu, the best of brahmins, was practising austerity alone, emaciated, his mind attached to Śiva,
m.7.1.34.56: certain sages who had formerly been cursed by Marīci to become piśācas, tormenting him with demonic behaviour, created obstacles to his austerity.
m.7.1.34.57: And he, though being tormented by them, somehow continuing his austerity, kept crying out namaḥ śivāya like one in distress.
m.7.1.34.58: Merely on hearing that cry, those sages who had been obstructing his austerity let the boy go and attended upon him respectfully.
m.7.1.34.59: O sages, by the austerity of that great-souled brahmin Upamanyu, the whole world, moving and unmoving, became ablaze.
m.7.1.34.iti: Thus ends the thirty-fourth adhyāya, named The austerity of Upamanyu, in the Pūrva-khaṇḍa of the seventh saṃhitā, the Vāyavīya-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.7.1.35.1: Vāyu said: Then all those best of gods, their bodies blazing with the heat, quickly went to Vaikuṇṭha, and having bowed, they told Hari all of that.
m.7.1.35.2: Hearing their words then, the blessed Puruṣottama reflected, what is this, and he came to know its cause.
m.7.1.35.3: He went swiftly to Mandara, wishing to see Maheśvara. Seeing the god and bowing, he spoke thus with joined palms.
m.7.1.35.4: Viṣṇu said: O Lord, a certain brāhmaṇa known as Upamanyu has burned everything by his austerity for the sake of milk; restrain that.
m.7.1.35.5: Hearing these words of Viṣṇu, the god Maheśvara said: I shall restrain the child; so you go to your own abode.
m.7.1.35.6: Hearing Śambhu's words, that Viṣṇu, beloved of the gods, reassured all the immortals and the others and went to his own world.
m.7.1.35.7: Meanwhile the god, the Pināka-bearing supreme lord, assuming the form of Śakra, then resolved to go.
m.7.1.35.8: Then Sadāśiva, having himself assumed the body of the king of the immortals, went to the sage's penance-grove on a fine white elephant, together with gods, asuras, siddhas and great serpents.
m.7.1.35.9: That elephant then, gracefully fanning the lord with a divine yak-tail fan, held a white parasol with its left hand (trunk) over the king of the gods accompanied by Śacī.
m.7.1.35.10: The blessed Sadāśiva, accompanied by Umā, in the form of Śakra, shone with that parasol as Mount Mandara shines with the orb of the moon.
m.7.1.35.11: Having thus assumed the very form of Śakra, the supreme lord went to Upamanyu's hermitage to bestow grace.
m.7.1.35.12: Seeing that supreme lord Śiva bearing the form of Śakra, the best of great sages bowed with his head and himself spoke.
m.7.1.35.13: Upamanyu said: This hermitage of mine has been purified, O lord of gods, since you yourself have come, O lord of the world, blessed one, best of gods.
m.7.1.35.14: Vāyu said: Seeing the twice-born standing after speaking thus with hollowed palms joined, Hara, bearing the form of Śakra, spoke in a deep voice.
m.7.1.35.15: Śakra said: I am pleased with you by this austerity, O you of good vows; ask a boon. I will grant all you desire, O elder brother of Dhaumya, great sage.
m.7.1.35.16: Vāyu said: Addressed thus then by that Śakra, the foremost of sages, with joined palms, said: I choose devotion to Śiva.
m.7.1.35.17: Hearing that, Hari (Indra) said: Do you not know me, the protector of the gods, Śakra, sovereign of the three worlds, saluted by all the gods?
m.7.1.35.18: Be my devotee, O brahmin sage; worship me alone always. I will give you every good thing; and abandon Rudra, who is without qualities.
m.7.1.35.19: What purpose will you have with Rudra, who is without qualities, who is excluded from the row of gods and has become a piśāca?
m.7.1.35.20: Vāyu said: Hearing that, the sage, repeating the five-syllable mantra, and considering that he had come to create an obstacle to dharma, spoke to him.
m.7.1.35.21: Upamanyu said: All this has been said by you, intent on reviling Bhava; yet in passing you have indeed declared the great god's transcendence of the guṇas.
m.7.1.35.22: You indeed do not know Rudra, the lord of the lords of all gods, the progenitor of Brahmā, Viṣṇu and Maheśa, beyond Prakṛti.
m.7.1.35.23: Him whom the expounders of Brahman call being and non-being, manifest and unmanifest, eternal, one and many — from him therefore I choose a boon.
m.7.1.35.24: Him, the supreme, free from dialectical reasoning, granting the goal of Sāṅkhya and Yoga, whom the knowers of reality worship — from him therefore I choose a boon.
m.7.1.35.25: There is no reality higher than Śambhu, the cause of all causes, the creator of the gods Brahmā, Viṣṇu and the rest, the all-pervading one beyond the guṇas.
m.7.1.35.26: What use is saying much here? I infer today that a great sin was committed by me in another birth, since I have heard the reviling of Bhava.
m.7.1.35.27: Having heard the reviling of Bhava, one should at that very moment give up one's own body; having swiftly slain that reviler, he goes to Śiva's world.
m.7.1.35.28: Let this desire of mine for milk stand aside for now, O vilest of gods; having slain you with Śiva's weapon, I shall abandon this body.
m.7.1.35.29: Vāyu said: Having said this to him, Upamanyu, resolved himself to die, abandoning even his longing for milk, prepared to slay Śakra.
m.7.1.35.30: Then, taking dreadful ash consecrated with the Aghora weapon-mantra and hurling it at Śakra, the sage roared aloud.
m.7.1.35.31: Remembering Śambhu's pair of feet, Upamanyu, ready to burn his own body, stood holding the fiery concentration (āgneyī dhāraṇā).
m.7.1.35.32: When the brahmin had thus resolved, the blessed destroyer of Bhaga's eyes checked that yogin's concentration by a gentle counter-concentration.
m.7.1.35.33: That Aghora weapon he had released and hurled, Nandin, dear to Śaṅkara, caught in mid-course at the command of the Lord of Nandin.
m.7.1.35.34: The blessed supreme lord, assuming his own form, showed the brahmin his form crested with the crescent moon.
m.7.1.35.35: A thousand oceans of milk, and an ocean of nectar, and oceans of curd and the like, and an ocean of ghee,
m.7.1.35.36: an ocean of fruits, likewise an ocean of foods to chew and to eat, and a mountain of cakes — these the lord showed to the boy.
m.7.1.35.37: Thus the god was seen with the Goddess upon the bull, surrounded by the lords of the gaṇas and by divine weapons such as the trident.
m.7.1.35.38: Drums resounded in the sky and a shower of flowers fell; the ten directions were filled with gods headed by Viṣṇu, Brahmā and Indra.
m.7.1.35.39: Then Upamanyu, engulfed by the waves of an ocean of bliss, fell to the ground like a staff, with a mind bowed in devotion.
m.7.1.35.40: At that moment there, the blessed Bhava, smiling, called him, come, come, and, smelling (kissing) his head, granted him boons.
m.7.1.35.41: Śiva said: Enjoy with your kinsmen, always and as much as you wish, foods to be chewed and foods to be eaten. Be ever happy, free from sorrow, and devoted to me.
m.7.1.35.42: O Upamanyu, most fortunate one, this Pārvatī is indeed your mother. I have made you my son today, and the ocean of milk has been given to you.
m.7.1.35.43: And an ocean of honey, an ocean of curd and rice, an ocean of ghee and cooked rice, and an ocean of fruits and the like —
m.7.1.35.44: and mountains of cakes, and likewise an ocean of foods to be chewed and eaten — these have been given to you by me; accept them, O great sage.
m.7.1.35.45: Your father is Mahādeva and your mother is indeed Jagadambikā, the Mother of the world. Immortality has been granted by me, and the eternal leadership of the gaṇas.
m.7.1.35.46: Choose, with great joy, other excellent boons desired by your mind; being pleased, I shall grant them — there need be no hesitation about this.
m.7.1.35.47: Vāyu said: Having spoken thus, Mahādeva took him up with both hands, smelled (kissed) his head, and presented him to the Goddess, saying, this is your son.
m.7.1.35.48: And the Goddess, with affection as for Guha, placed her lotus-hand on his head and bestowed on him the imperishable status of Kumāra.
m.7.1.35.49: The Ocean of Milk too, taking bodily form and holding sweet milk in his hand, approached and gave him imperishable milk solidified into a mass.
m.7.1.35.50: With a fully satisfied mind, Śiva gave him yogic sovereignty, constant contentment, imperishable knowledge of Brahman, and supreme prosperity.
m.7.1.35.51: Then Śambhu, pleased at heart, seeing the splendour of his austerity, again gave a divine boon to the sage Upamanyu.
m.7.1.35.52: He gave him the Pāśupata vow, knowledge, and the discipline of the vow in its true essence, as well as supreme and lasting skill in exposition.
m.7.1.35.53: He too, having obtained divine boons and perpetual youthfulness from that Śiva and from that Śivā, became joyful.
m.7.1.35.54: Then, with a delighted heart, bowing low with joined palms, that brahmin begged a boon from Maheśvara, the God of gods.
m.7.1.35.55: Upamanyu said: Be gracious, O Lord of the god of gods; be gracious, O Supreme Lord. Grant me supreme, divine, unwavering devotion to you.
m.7.1.35.56: O Mahādeva, grant me always faith in those connected with you, and servitude to you, supreme love, and your presence at all times.
m.7.1.35.57: Having thus spoken, Upamanyu, the best of brahmins, pleased at heart, praised Mahādeva in a voice choked with joy.
m.7.1.35.58: O God of gods, O Mahādeva, loving to those who take refuge in you, be gracious always, O ocean of compassion, O Śaṅkara together with Ambā.
m.7.1.35.59: Vāyu said: Thus addressed, Mahādeva, the giver of boons to all, pleased at heart, replied to Upamanyu, the best of sages.
m.7.1.35.60: Śiva said: Dear Upamanyu, I am pleased; everything has been granted to you by me. You are a firm devotee, O brahmin sage; you were only being tested by me.
m.7.1.35.61: Be free from old age and death, free from sorrow, renowned, endowed with radiance, and possessed of divine knowledge.
m.7.1.35.62: Your kinsmen, family and lineage shall always be imperishable, O best of brahmins, and your devotion to me eternal.
m.7.1.35.63: And I shall always be present in your hermitage, O best of brahmins; you shall indeed roam joyfully near me.
m.7.1.35.64: Having spoken thus and granted the boons, the blessed Lord Īśāna, Hara, whose radiance equals ten million suns, vanished right there.
m.7.1.35.65: Upamanyu, pleased at heart, having obtained the boons from that boon-giver, went to his mother's dwelling and attained surpassing happiness.
m.7.1.35.iti: Thus ends the thirty-fifth adhyāya, named The life of Upamanyu, in the Pūrva-khaṇḍa of the seventh saṃhitā, the Vāyavīya-saṃhitā, contained in the saṃhitā of twenty-four thousand verses composed by Vyāsa, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.7.2.1.1: Om, salutation to him who is the cause of the turning of the wheel of all worldly existence, whose chest is marked with saffron from the pair of Gaurī's breasts.
m.7.2.1.2: Sūta said: Having told of the grace that Upamanyu obtained from the Lord, Vāyu rose from his observance when the sun had reached the middle of the sky.
m.7.2.1.3: And all those sages dwelling in the Naimiṣa forest, having made the resolve that now this matter should be asked,
m.7.2.1.4: having performed their own duties daily as before, they, seeing the venerable one approaching, sat down around him.
m.7.2.1.5: Then, at the end of his observance, that lord born of the sky took the excellent seat prepared in the middle of the assembly of sages.
m.7.2.1.6: Seated comfortably, Vāyu, revered by the worlds, holding in his heart the glorious manifest power of the Lord, spoke this:
m.7.2.1.7: I take refuge in that Mahādeva, the all-knowing, the unconquered, whose manifestation is this entire world of moving and unmoving beings.
m.7.2.1.8: Hearing this auspicious speech, the sages, whose sins were destroyed, spoke these excellent words in order to hear the full account of Śiva's glory.
m.7.2.1.9: The sages said: The account of the great-souled Upamanyu has been told by you, lord — what he obtained from the Supreme Lord through austerity, even undertaken for the sake of milk.
m.7.2.1.10: He, the elder brother of Dhaumya, was seen by Vāsudeva Kṛṣṇa of unwearied deeds; then by him (Kṛṣṇa), having performed the Pāśupata vow,
m.7.2.1.11: the supreme knowledge was obtained — this we have heard already. How did Kṛṣṇa obtain the supreme Pāśupata knowledge?
m.7.2.1.12: Vāyu said: Although the eternal Vāsudeva had descended of his own will, he, as if censuring the human condition, performed purification of the body.
m.7.2.1.13: For, to perform austerity for the sake of a son, he went to the hermitage of that great sage, frequented by sages, and there he saw the sage,
m.7.2.1.14: his whole body white with ash, his forehead marked with the tripuṇḍra, wearing a rudrākṣa garland as ornament, adorned with a crown of matted locks,
m.7.2.1.15: surrounded by sages who were his disciples, as the Veda is by the śāstras — Upamanyu, of great splendour, tranquil, devoted to meditation on Śiva.
m.7.2.1.16: Seeing him, Kṛṣṇa, with the hair of his whole body thrilled, bowed; with great reverence, having circumambulated him three times, he offered praise with deep delight, shoulders bent, palms joined.
m.7.2.1.17: Merely by the sage's glance, all of wise Kṛṣṇa's impurity was destroyed — that born of māyā and that born of karma as well.
m.7.2.1.18: Then Upamanyu, according to rule, having smeared that Kṛṣṇa, whose impurity was destroyed, with ash, with the mantras beginning agni in due order,
m.7.2.1.19: then, having made him perform the actual Pāśupata vow lasting twelve months, the sage bestowed on him the highest knowledge.
m.7.2.1.20: From that time on, sages of praiseworthy vows, all divine Pāśupatas, surrounded Kṛṣṇa and attended upon him.
m.7.2.1.21: Then, at the guru's command, Kṛṣṇa of supreme power performed austerity for the sake of a son, directing it to Śaṅkara together with Ambā.
m.7.2.1.22: By that austerity, at the end of a year, the Supreme Lord was seen — Śiva, endowed with supreme splendour, with Ambā and with his gaṇas.
m.7.2.1.23: Bowing to Hara of lovely form, who had appeared to grant a boon, Kṛṣṇa offered praise properly, with joined palms.
m.7.2.1.24: He obtained a son of his own, given to Viṣṇu by Śiva — accompanied by Ambā and the gaṇas — whose mind was pleased by the austerity.
m.7.2.1.25: Because Mahādeva, with Ambā (sa-amba), gave him his son, therefore he named Jāmbavatī's son Sāmba.
m.7.2.1.26: Thus all this has been told: how Kṛṣṇa of immeasurable deeds gained knowledge from the great sage and gained a son from Śaṅkara.
m.7.2.1.27: Whoever constantly recites this, hears it, or causes it to be heard, attains the knowledge gained by Viṣṇu and rejoices together with him.
m.7.2.1.iti: Thus ends the first adhyāya, named Kṛṣṇa obtains a son, in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the seventh saṃhitā, the Vāyavīya-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.7.2.2.1: The sages said: What is that Pāśupata knowledge? How is Śiva the Lord of creatures (Paśupati)? And how was Dhaumya's elder brother questioned by Kṛṣṇa, whose deeds are effortless?
m.7.2.2.2: Relate all this fully, O Vāyu, embodiment of Śaṅkara; for in the three worlds there is no other speaker equal to you, O lord.
m.7.2.2.3: Sūta said: Hearing these words of the great sages, Prabhañjana (Vāyu), having remembered Śiva the Lord, began to speak.
m.7.2.2.4: Vāyu said: Long ago, on Mount Mandara, the supreme Pāśupata knowledge was told to the Goddess by Maheśa himself, the god called Śrīkaṇṭha.
m.7.2.2.5: That very knowledge was asked about by Kṛṣṇa, who is Viṣṇu, source of the universe: the bound-creature-hood of the gods and others, and the lordship of Śiva.
m.7.2.2.6: As it was taught to Kṛṣṇa by the sage Upamanyu, so I shall tell it in brief; listen to it attentively.
m.7.2.2.7: Once, Viṣṇu, bearing the form of Kṛṣṇa, bowed duly to Upamanyu as he sat, and spoke these words.
m.7.2.2.8: Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: O revered one, I wish to hear the divine Pāśupata knowledge spoken by the God to the Goddess, and also his glory, in full.
m.7.2.2.9: How is the God the Lord of creatures? Who are declared to be the creatures (paśus)? By what fetters are they bound, and how are they released?
m.7.2.2.10: Thus urged by the great-souled one, the glorious Upamanyu bowed to the God and the Goddess and spoke just as he had been asked.
m.7.2.2.11: Upamanyu said: All beings from Brahmā down to the immobile plants, subject to the sway of saṃsāra, are declared to be the paśus of the trident-bearing God of gods.
m.7.2.2.12: Because he is their lord, Śiva, Lord of the gods, is called Paśupati. That Lord binds the paśus with fetters such as mala and māyā.
m.7.2.2.13: He alone is their liberator when properly worshipped with devotion. These twenty-four principles, māyā, karma and the guṇas—
m.7.2.2.14: —these are called the objects (viṣayas), the fetters that bind souls. Having bound the paśus, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass,
m.7.2.2.15: with these fetters the Lord God makes them carry out his own work. By the command of that Maheśa, Prakṛti brings forth intellect suited to the soul;
m.7.2.2.16: she gives birth to intellect; intellect produces ego; ego produces the eleven senses and likewise the five subtle elements,
m.7.2.2.17: by the command of Śiva, God of gods, giver of welfare. The subtle elements too, by his mighty command,
m.7.2.2.18: bring forth all the gross elements in due order; and they in turn produce the bodily union of embodied beings from Brahmā down to grass.
m.7.2.2.19: All the gross elements generate this by Śiva's command. Intellect determines; ego claims as mine;
m.7.2.2.20: the citta perceives, and the mind forms intentions; the ear and other senses grasp their objects, sound and the rest, separately—
m.7.2.2.21: only their own, not others, through the divine power of the God's command. And those which are speech and the rest, the organs of action,
m.7.2.2.22: perform each its own function and nothing else, by Śiva's command. Sound and the rest are grasped, and speech and the rest are performed,
m.7.2.2.23: for Śambhu's weighty command cannot be transgressed by anyone. Space grants room to all beings,
m.7.2.2.24: the all-pervading ether, solely by the command of the Supreme Lord. And likewise, under different names such as prāṇa, the world inside and outside—
m.7.2.2.25: all of it the Wind sustains by the command of Śarva. Fire carries the oblation of the gods and the offering (kavya) of the ancestors who partake of it,
m.7.2.2.26: and Fire performs cooking and the like by the Supreme Lord's command. By his command the waters give life and so on to all.
m.7.2.2.27: The Earth constantly upholds the world by the command of the Lord of the universe. Indra protects the gods, slays the asuras and guards the three worlds,
m.7.2.2.28: the king of the gods doing so by his command, which no god can transgress. Varuṇa ever exercises lordship over the waters,
m.7.2.2.29: and binds with his nooses those deserving punishment, by his command alone. The lord of the yakṣas, the lord of wealth, constantly gives wealth
m.7.2.2.30: to beings according to their merit, by the instruction of the Supreme Person. Īśāna perpetually bestows prosperity, and knowledge on the wise,
m.7.2.2.31: and restraint of the wicked—Īśāna does this by Śiva's command. Śeṣa bears the earth on his head by Śiva's appointment—
m.7.2.2.32: he whom they call the tāmasic, fierce (Raudra), end-bringing form of Hari. The four-faced Brahmā creates everything by the Lord's command,
m.7.2.2.33: and with other forms of his own he protects and at the end destroys. Viṣṇu protects the universe by the command of the Death of Death (Śiva),
m.7.2.2.34: and also creates and devours it with his own three bodies. Hara withdraws the whole world at the end, by his command alone,
m.7.2.2.35: and that Soul of the universe, divided threefold, also creates and protects. Time makes everything; Time destroys creatures;
m.7.2.2.36: Time preserves the universe—by the command of the Death of Death. Sustaining the world with his three portions and directing rain with his rays,
m.7.2.2.37: that Sun rains from the sky by the command of the God of gods. The Moon nourishes all kinds of plants and gladdens beings,
m.7.2.2.38: and the Moon is drunk by the gods, by the command of him whose ornament is the moon. The Ādityas, Vasus, Rudras, the two Aśvins and likewise the Maruts,
m.7.2.2.39: sky-goers, sages, Siddhas, serpents, humans, wild animals, cattle, birds, insects and the like, and immobile beings,
m.7.2.2.40: rivers, oceans, mountains, forests and lakes, the Vedas with their limbs, the śāstras, mantras, hymns of praise, sacrifices and the rest—
m.7.2.2.41: The worlds from Kālāgni up to Śiva, together with their lords, and the countless cosmic eggs (brahmāṇḍa) and their enveloping sheaths,
m.7.2.2.42: present, past and future, in their entirety; the directions and the intermediate directions, and the divisions of time beginning with the kalā,
m.7.2.2.43: and whatever is seen or heard in this world — all that is governed by the power of Śaṅkara's command.
m.7.2.2.44: By the power of his command the earth stands here, as do the mountains, the clouds, the oceans, the hosts of luminaries, the gods headed by Śakra — whatever exists, stable or enduring, sentient or insentient.
m.7.2.2.45: Upamanyu said: O Kṛṣṇa, hear this exceedingly wonderful deed wrought by the command of Śambhu of immeasurable acts, which I heard from the mouth of the Veda (śruti).
m.7.2.2.46: Long ago, it is said, the gods together with Indra, having conquered the asuras in battle, were quarrelling with one another, each saying, I am the victor, I.
m.7.2.2.47: Then Maheśvara himself, assuming a splendid guise, his body devoid of his own distinguishing marks, appeared in their midst as a yakṣa.
m.7.2.2.48: Taking up a single blade of grass on the ground, he said to those gods: Whoever is able to alter this, he indeed is the conqueror of the daityas.
m.7.2.2.49: Hearing the yakṣa's words, Śacī's lord, the wielder of the thunderbolt, somewhat angered, laughed at him and set about taking up the grass.
m.7.2.2.50: That grass could not be taken up even in thought; nevertheless, the bearer of the thunderbolt somehow hurled his thunderbolt to cut it.
m.7.2.2.51: That thunderbolt, struck by that grass as if it met on all sides with an adamant of its own, fell with its point turned aside.
m.7.2.2.52: Then the other guardians of the worlds, mighty and greatly enraged, hurled their own weapons by the thousands at the grass.
m.7.2.2.53: A great fire blazed up, a fierce wind blew, and the lord of the waters swelled, as when the dissolution (pralaya) has arrived.
m.7.2.2.54: Thus what the gods undertook with effort against the grass proved futile, ah Kṛṣṇa, through the yakṣa's own power.
m.7.2.2.55: Then the lord of the gods, indignant, said to the yakṣa: Who are you? Thereupon he vanished even as they looked on.
m.7.2.2.56: Meanwhile the Goddess Haimavatī, adorned with divine ornaments, radiant and sweetly smiling, appeared on the stage of the sky.
m.7.2.2.57: Seeing her, the gods headed by Śakra, filled with wonder, bowed and asked about the yakṣa: Who is that extraordinary yakṣa?
m.7.2.2.58: The Goddess said with a smile: He is beyond your perception. By him this wheel called saṃsāra, comprising the moving and the unmoving, is made to revolve.
m.7.2.2.59: By him the universe is made in the beginning, by him it is withdrawn again. There is none who could control him; by him everything is controlled.
m.7.2.2.60: Having said this, the great Goddess vanished right there; and all the gods, amazed, bowed to her and went to heaven.
m.7.2.2.iti: Thus ends the second adhyāya, named The greatness of Śiva, in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the seventh saṃhitā, the Vāyavīya-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.7.2.3.1: Upamanyu said: Listen, O Kṛṣṇa: this entire world, moving and unmoving, is pervaded by the forms that are the very self of Maheśa Śiva, the Supreme Self.
m.7.2.3.2: That Śiva, whose self is immeasurable, presides over all this through his own forms; thus is all this handed down in tradition.
m.7.2.3.3: Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Maheśāna and Sadāśiva are to be known as his forms, by which this universe is pervaded.
m.7.2.3.4: There are also five other bodies, called the Brahmans; there exists nothing here that is not pervaded by those bodies.
m.7.2.3.5: Īśāna, Tatpuruṣa, Aghora, Vāmadeva and Sadyojāta: these Brahmans are the five renowned forms of the god.
m.7.2.3.6: His form called Īśāna, the first and most venerable, directly presides over the knower of the field (kṣetrajña), the enjoyer of Prakṛti.
m.7.2.3.7: The form called Tatpuruṣa of Sthāṇu, the lord possessing form, presides over the unmanifest, the object of enjoyment, which is the substrate of the guṇas.
m.7.2.3.8: The highly worshipped form of Pinākin called Aghora presides over the principle of intellect (buddhi-tattva), endowed with the eight limbs beginning with dharma.
m.7.2.3.9: Those versed in the Āgamas call the form named Vāmadeva of Mahādeva, the ordainer, the presiding deity of ego (ahaṅkāra).
m.7.2.3.10: The wise declare the form named Sadyojāta of Śambhu of boundless splendour to be the presiding deity of the mind.
m.7.2.3.11: The wise know this form of the Lord named Īśāna as the ruler of the ear, of speech, of sound, and likewise of all-pervading ether.
m.7.2.3.12: All who are expert in the meaning of the Purāṇas know the lordly form called Tatpuruṣa as the ruler of skin, hand, touch and air.
m.7.2.3.13: The sages declare the form named Aghora to be the presiding deity of the eye, of the feet, of visible form, and likewise of fire.
m.7.2.3.14: They know the form named Vāmadeva, devoted to them, as the ruler of the tongue, of the anus, of taste, and likewise of water.
m.7.2.3.15: They declare the form named Sadyojāta as the ruler of the nose, of the generative organ, of smell, and of the earth.
m.7.2.3.16: These five forms of the god, the sole causes of all welfare, should be constantly worshipped with effort by men who seek welfare.
m.7.2.3.17: The world consists of the eight forms of that God of gods; the universe abides in him, he pervading it, like clusters of gems on a thread.
m.7.2.3.18: Śarva, Bhava, Rudra, Ugra, Bhīma, Paśupati, Īśāna and Mahādeva are the eight renowned forms.
m.7.2.3.19: Earth, water, fire, wind, ether, the knower of the field, the sun and the moon are presided over by the eight forms of Maheśa beginning with Śarva.
m.7.2.3.20: The form named Śarva, called Śārvī, whose nature is the all-bearing earth, supports the universe of moving and unmoving beings: such is the conclusion of scripture.
m.7.2.3.21: The form of Bhava, the Supreme Self, consisting of water, which gives life to the whole world, is celebrated as Bhāvī.
m.7.2.3.22: The form of Rudra called Raudrī, fiery, auspicious, of terrible appearance, abides pervading the universe, present outside and within.
m.7.2.3.23: Having the nature of wind, it sets this world in motion, sustains it, and itself moves; the good call this form of Ugra, the ordainer, Augrī.
m.7.2.3.24: Giving room to all, all-pervading, of the nature of space, the form of Bhīma called Bhīmā divides the multitude of beings.
m.7.2.3.25: Presiding over all souls, dwelling in all bodies, the form of Paśupati should be known as the cutter of the bonds of the bound souls.
m.7.2.3.26: Illuminating the whole world, the form of Maheśa called Īśāna, known as the Sun, moves through the sky.
m.7.2.3.27: The nectar-rayed moon, who nourishes the universe, is that form of Mahādeva named Mahādeva.
m.7.2.3.28: The self is the eighth form of that Śiva, the Supreme Self, pervading the other forms; therefore the universe has Śiva as its essence.
m.7.2.3.29: Just as the branches of a tree flourish by watering its root, so by the worship of Śiva the world, which is his body, flourishes.
m.7.2.3.30: They know the worship of Śiva to be the granting of fearlessness to all, the favouring of all, and the doing of good to all.
m.7.2.3.31: Just as here a father is pleased by the happiness of his sons, grandsons and others, so Śaṅkara is pleased by the happiness of all.
m.7.2.3.32: If harm is done to any embodied being whatsoever, that is surely a wrong done to the Eight-formed One; there is no doubt.
m.7.2.3.33: Worship with your whole being Rudra, the supreme cause, Śiva, who abides presiding over the universe in the form of his eight forms.
m.7.2.3.iti: Thus ends the third adhyāya, named Upamanyu's teaching to Kṛṣṇa, in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the seventh saṃhitā, the Vāyavīya-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.7.2.4.1: Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: O Lord, I have heard how this entire universe is pervaded by the forms of Śarva, the Supreme Lord of immeasurable splendour.
m.7.2.4.2: Now I wish to know the true nature of the two Supreme Rulers, and how this universe, which consists of female and male nature, is presided over by the two of them.
m.7.2.4.3: Upamanyu said: I shall tell you briefly the glorious manifestation of Śiva and Śivā and their true nature; to tell it in full is not possible even for Bhava himself.
m.7.2.4.4: The Great Goddess is Śakti herself, and Mahādeva is the possessor of Śakti; all this, moving and unmoving, is but a fraction of their glory.
m.7.2.4.5: Some reality is of insentient form, some reality is of the nature of consciousness; this pair is respectively pure and impure, higher and lower.
m.7.2.4.6: The circle of conscious beings that transmigrates, joined with the circle of insentient things, is the impure and lower; the other is the higher and auspicious.
m.7.2.4.7: Both the lower and the higher, this pair of conscious and insentient nature — lordship over it belongs by nature to Śiva and Śivā.
m.7.2.4.8: The universe is under the control of Śiva and Śivā; they are not under the control of the universe. Since this universe is what is to be ruled, therefore Śiva and Śivā are the Lords of the universe.
m.7.2.4.9: As Śiva is, so is the Goddess; as the Goddess is, so is Śiva. One should know no difference between these two, as between the moon and moonlight.
m.7.2.4.10: Just as this moon does not shine without moonlight, so Śiva, though existing, does not shine without Śakti.
m.7.2.4.11: For just as this sun does not exist without its radiance, so radiance does not exist without that sun, being wholly dependent on it.
m.7.2.4.12: Thus mutual dependence exists between Śakti and the possessor of Śakti: there is no Śakti without Śiva, and no Śiva without Śakti.
m.7.2.4.13: She through whom Śiva is ever potent in granting enjoyment and liberation to embodied beings — she is the primordial, sole, supreme Śakti, made of consciousness, resting in Śiva.
m.7.2.4.14: Whom they declare, by virtue of those various corresponding qualities, to be of the same nature as Śiva, the Lord of all, the Supreme Self.
m.7.2.4.15: That one supreme Śakti, whose form is consciousness and whose nature is to bring forth, divides the universe in many ways and arranges it by Śiva's will.
m.7.2.4.16: She is remembered as threefold: the root Prakṛti, Māyā, and the one with three guṇas; by her, Śivā, this world has been spread out and variously transformed.
m.7.2.4.17: The Śaktis are indeed distinguished as one, as two, as hundreds of thousands — in many ways, according to their function.
m.7.2.4.18: By Śiva's will the supreme Śakti, having become one with the Śiva-principle, then springs forth at the beginning of creation, like oil from sesame.
m.7.2.4.19: Then, when that Śakti was stirred by the power called Kriyā arising from the possessor of power, Nāda first appeared.
m.7.2.4.20: From Nāda issued Bindu; from Bindu the god Sadāśiva; from him Maheśvara was born, and from Maheśvara Śuddhavidyā.
m.7.2.4.21: She is the Trident-bearer's power, sovereign of speech, called Vāgīśā, who unfolds in the form of letters as Mātṛkā.
m.7.2.4.22: Then, through the entering of Ananta, Māyā emitted Kāla, Niyati, Kalā and Vidyā; from Kalā came Rāga and Puruṣa.
m.7.2.4.23: From Māyā again arose the Unmanifest, consisting of the three guṇas; and from that triple Unmanifest the three guṇas became separated.
m.7.2.4.24: They are sattva, rajas and tamas, by which the whole world is pervaded. From the guṇas, as they were agitated, arose the three forms called the Lords of the guṇas,
m.7.2.4.25: and the principles beginning with Mahat came into being in due order. From them, by Śiva's command, arose countless cosmic eggs and bodies, presided over by the Vidyeśas beginning with Ananta, the sovereigns.
m.7.2.4.26: The divisions of Śakti are proclaimed according to the differences of various bodies; they are to be known as of many forms through the distinction of gross and subtle.
m.7.2.4.27: That Śakti of Rudra is Raudrī; of Viṣṇu she is held to be Vaiṣṇavī; of Brahmā she is called Brahmāṇī; and of Indra she is named Aindrī.
m.7.2.4.28: What need of saying more here? Whatever is called the universe is pervaded by Śakti as its very self, as the body is by the inner Self.
m.7.2.4.29: Therefore the whole world, unmoving and moving, is made of Śakti. That which is called Kalā is the supreme Śakti of the Supreme Self.
m.7.2.4.30: Thus this supreme Śakti, following the will of the Lord, creates whatever universe there is, stationary and moving — this is the settled conclusion.
m.7.2.4.31: Through his own three powers — knowledge, action and will (the desire to act) — the Lord, the possessor of power, eternally pervades the universe and presides over it.
m.7.2.4.32: This should be thus, this should not be thus — of such a nature is the eternal will-power of Maheśa, which regulates effects.
m.7.2.4.33: The power of knowledge, in the form of intellect, determines truly the effect, the instrument, the cause and the purpose.
m.7.2.4.34: The power of action, whose form is resolve, fashions in an instant the whole world and every effect, as desired and as determined.
m.7.2.4.35: In accordance with these powers, she whose nature is to bring forth from Śakti, impelled by the supreme Śakti, gives birth to the whole world, the arising of the triad.
m.7.2.4.36: Thus, through union with Śakti, Śiva is called the possessor of Śakti; and this world, arising from Śakti and the possessor of Śakti, is both Śākta and Śaiva.
m.7.2.4.37: Just as a son is not born without a father and a mother, so this moving and unmoving world does not exist without Bhava and Bhavānī.
m.7.2.4.38: The universe originates from the female and the male, consists of female and male, is the glory of the female and the male, and is presided over by the female and the male.
m.7.2.4.39: Śiva is called the Supreme Self, and she is proclaimed Śivā; Śiva is called Sadāśiva, and Śivā is Manonmanī; Śiva is to be known as Maheśvara, and Śivā is called Māyā.
m.7.2.4.40: Puruṣa is the Supreme Lord (Parameśāna), Prakṛti is the Supreme Goddess (Parameśvarī); Rudra is Maheśvara himself, and Rudrāṇī is Rudra's beloved.
m.7.2.4.41: Viṣṇu is the god Viśveśvara Śiva, and Lakṣmī is Viśveśvara's beloved Pārvatī. When Śiva is the creator, he is Brahmā, and Brahmāṇī, Brahmā's beloved, is she.
m.7.2.4.42: The blessed Śambhu is the Sun, and the blessed Śivā is its radiance. The enemy of Manmatha is great Indra, and the daughter of the lord of mountains is Śacī.
m.7.2.4.43: Mahādeva is Fire (Jātavedas), and she who has half of Śarva's body is Svāhā. The god Tryambaka is Yama, and his beloved is the mountain's daughter.
m.7.2.4.44: The blessed Lord is Nirṛti, and the delight of the mountain is Nairṛtī. The blessed Rudra is Varuṇa, and the daughter of the earth-bearer Himālaya is Vāruṇī.
m.7.2.4.45: He whose crest is the young moon is Vāyu, and Śivā, who charms Śiva's mind, is his consort. The beheader of the sacrifice is the Yakṣa Kubera, and the daughter of the lord of the Himālaya is Ṛddhi.
m.7.2.4.46: He whose crest is the half-moon is the Moon, and Rudra's beloved is Rohiṇī. The supreme Lord is Īśāna, and his noble consort is the Supreme Goddess.
m.7.2.4.47: He who wears Ananta the serpent as a bracelet is Ananta, and the beloved of Ananta Śiva is Anantā. The enemy of Time is Kālāgnirudra, and the beloved of the ender of Time is Kālī.
m.7.2.4.48: Śambhu is the Manu called Puruṣa Svāyambhuva, and Śiva's beloved is Śatarūpā. Dakṣa is Mahādeva himself, and Prasūti is the Supreme Goddess.
m.7.2.4.49: Bhava is Ruci, and Bhavānī is called Ākūti by the wise. The god who destroyed Bhaga's eyes is Bhṛgu, and the beloved of the three-eyed one is Khyāti.
m.7.2.4.50: The blessed Rudra is Marīci, and Śarva's beloved is Sambhūti. The bearer of the Gaṅgā should be known as Aṅgiras, and Umā herself is regarded as Smṛti.
m.7.2.4.51: He who wears the moon on his head is Pulastya, and the beloved of the Pināka-bearer is Prīti. The destroyer of Tripura is Pulaha, and his beloved is Śiva's beloved.
m.7.2.4.52: The destroyer of the sacrifice is declared to be Kratu, and the Lord's beloved is Sannati. The three-eyed one is Atri, and Umā herself is regarded by the wise as Anasūyā.
m.7.2.4.53: The god who slew Kāla is Kaśyapa, and Maheśvarī is the mother of the gods Aditi. The enemy of Manmatha is Vasiṣṭha, and the Goddess herself is Arundhatī.
m.7.2.4.54: All males are Śaṅkara; all females are Maheśvarī. Therefore all women and men are the manifestations of those two alone.
m.7.2.4.55: The blessed Lord is the experiencer of objects; the Supreme Goddess is the object. All that is to be heard is Umā's form; the hearer is he whose excellent weapon is the trident.
m.7.2.4.56: Śaṅkara's beloved bears the whole range of things to be asked about; the asker is he alone, the soul of the universe, who has the young moon as his ornament.
m.7.2.4.57: Bhava's beloved bears the form of things to be seen; the seer is the god Viśveśvara, whose crest-jewel is the crescent moon.
m.7.2.4.58: All tastes are the Great Goddess; the taster is the god Śiva. All objects of love are Girijā, and the lover is the poison-eater.
m.7.2.4.59: The goddess Maheśvarī always bears the state of being the object of thought; the thinker is he alone, the soul of the universe, Mahādeva, Maheśvara.
m.7.2.4.60: Bhava's beloved bears the form of things to be known; the knower is that same blessed god whose crest is the lovely moon.
m.7.2.4.61: The blessed Lord, the Pināka-bearer, is the life-breath of all living beings; and Ambikā, in the form of water, is the sustenance of the life of all.
m.7.2.4.62: The Goddess, beloved of the destroyer of Tripura, bears the state of the field (kṣetra); then the blessed destroyer of Death bears the state of the knower of the field (kṣetrajña).
m.7.2.4.63: The god armed with the trident is the day; the beloved of the trident-bearer is the night. The god Śaṅkara is the sky; Śaṅkara's beloved is the earth.
m.7.2.4.64: The blessed Lord is the ocean; the daughter of the lord of mountains is the shore. The god with the bull-banner is the tree; the beloved of Viśveśvara is the creeper.
m.7.2.4.65: The blessed chastiser of the three cities bears everything masculine, and the Goddess who delights the god bears everything feminine.
m.7.2.4.66: The beloved of all bears the entire network of words, and he whose crest is the lovely moon bears the whole nature of meaning.
m.7.2.4.67: Whatever power is declared of whatever thing, each such power is the goddess Viśveśvarī, and each possessor of power is wholly Maheśvara.
m.7.2.4.68: Whatever is supreme, whatever is pure, whatever is meritorious and whatever is auspicious — each of these, the illustrious ones declare, is the unfolding of the splendour of those two.
m.7.2.4.69: Just as the flame of a lit lamp illumines a house, so this splendour of those two pervades and illumines the world.
m.7.2.4.70: The graded excellence of the universe, from a blade of grass up to the form of Śiva, follows the degree of nearness to those two — so says the supreme scripture.
m.7.2.4.71: These two, whose nature comprises all forms and who bestow every good, are always to be worshipped, bowed to and meditated upon.
m.7.2.4.72: O Kṛṣṇa, I have told you today this true nature of the two Supreme Lords according to my understanding, but not in its full extent.
m.7.2.4.73: For how can the true nature of the two Supreme Lords be told, which lies beyond even the minds of all the great ones?
m.7.2.4.74: It lies within the reach of those devoted to none else, whose minds are offered to the Lord; for others it does not rise into the intellect, while for them it rises exactly as it is.
m.7.2.4.75: This manifestation that has been described is the material one, and is regarded as the lower; the knowers of secrets know another, supreme, non-material and secret one.
m.7.2.4.76: That from which words turn back together with the mind and the senses — this is the supreme, non-material manifestation of the Supreme Lord.
m.7.2.4.77: That alone is here the supreme abode, that alone is here the supreme goal, that alone is here the ultimate limit — the manifestation of the Supreme One.
m.7.2.4.78: To attain it, those who have mastered their breath and conquered their senses strive here, so that the door of the prison-house of the womb is shut without a gap.
m.7.2.4.79: One who knows the manifestation of Śiva and Śivā — the reviving herb for those slain by the bite of the serpent of saṃsāra — fears nothing from anywhere.
m.7.2.4.80: He who truly knows both the supreme and the lower manifestation transcends the lower glory and attains the supreme glory.
m.7.2.4.81: O Kṛṣṇa, I have thus told you the true nature of the two Supreme Selves, Śiva and Śivā. Though it is a secret, you are worthy of it, since you are a devotee of Bharga (Śiva).
m.7.2.4.82: One should never declare the glory of the two Lords to those who are not disciples, nor to non-Śaivas, nor to non-devotees — this is the injunction of the Veda.
m.7.2.4.83: Therefore, O most auspicious one, you should certainly not tell it to outsiders; tell it to those who are like you and fit, and not otherwise.
m.7.2.4.84: Whoever imparts this glory of Śiva and Śivā to worthy persons is freed from the ocean of saṃsāra and attains union (sāyujya) with Śiva.
m.7.2.4.85: By reciting it, crores of great sins are destroyed; by repeating it three or four times, even more than those are destroyed.
m.7.2.4.86: Hostile enemies perish and friends likewise increase; Śaiva knowledge grows, and the mind turns toward truth.
m.7.2.4.87: There arises supreme devotion to Śiva together with Ambā, with his attendants and his retinue; and whatever else is most desired, that he attains without doubt.
m.7.2.4.88: If a devotee of Śiva, pure within, recites it with confidence, and if the fruit is obstructed by powerful past karmas, he should repeat it again and again; for him nothing here is hard to attain.
m.7.2.4.iti: Thus ends the fourth adhyāya, named The yoga of the glories of Gaurī and Śaṅkara, in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the seventh saṃhitā, the Vāyavīya-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.7.2.5.1: Upamanyu said: This whole universe, moving and unmoving, is the body of the God of gods; yet the bound souls (paśu) do not know it to be so, because of the heaviness of their bonds.
m.7.2.5.2: O delight of the Yadus, the great sages, not knowing his supreme, undifferentiated nature, speak of that One in many ways.
m.7.2.5.3: Some call Mahādeva, the Supreme without beginning or end, both the lower form of Brahman and likewise the higher, which is Brahman itself.
m.7.2.5.4: The lower Brahman is declared to consist of the elements, the senses, the inner organ, primordial matter and the sense-objects; the higher Brahman is of the nature of consciousness.
m.7.2.5.5: It is called Brahman because of its vastness or because of its power to expand. Both of these are forms of Brahman, belonging to the Lord who is master of Brahman. By some the Lord is said to have the nature of knowledge and nescience.
m.7.2.5.6: They call knowledge the conscious and nescience the unconscious; and the universe, consisting of knowledge and nescience, belongs to the all-pervading teacher of the universe,
m.7.2.5.7: it is indeed his form, without doubt, since the universe is under his control. Error, knowledge and the Supreme — thus they know the highest form of Śarva.
m.7.2.5.8: Mistaken cognition of objects, in its many kinds, is called error; awareness of things in their true form is proclaimed knowledge.
m.7.2.5.9: The reality free from conceptual distinctions is called the Supreme; its opposite is termed asat (non-being) by the expounders of the Veda.
m.7.2.5.10: Because he is lord of both, Śiva is called the lord of being and non-being. Some call him of the nature of the perishable and imperishable; others, beyond the perishable and imperishable.
m.7.2.5.11: The perishable is all beings; the unchanging is called the imperishable. Both are forms of the supreme Lord, since they are under his control.
m.7.2.5.12: Beyond these two is Śiva, the tranquil, remembered as transcending the perishable and imperishable. Him who is of the form of the aggregate and the individual, and the cause of the aggregate and the individual —
