m.7.2.5.13: some sages call Śiva, the supreme cause. They call the aggregate the unmanifest, and likewise the individual the manifest.
m.7.2.5.14: These two are forms of the supreme Lord, since they proceed from his will. Because he is the cause of both, Śiva is the supreme cause —
m.7.2.5.15: so say those who know the meaning of causation: the cause of the aggregate and the individual. By some the Lord is said to have the nature of genus and individual.
m.7.2.5.16: That which persists throughout every body is called the genus; the individual is of the nature of distinction, resting upon that collection of bodies.
m.7.2.5.17: Since genera and individuals are sustained by his command, therefore Mahādeva is regarded as having genus and individual for his body.
m.7.2.5.18: Śiva is said to be the self of primordial matter, spirit, the manifest and time. They call pradhāna Prakṛti, and likewise the knower of the field Puruṣa.
m.7.2.5.19: The wise call the twenty-three principles the manifest; time is the sole cause of the transformation of the world of effects.
m.7.2.5.20: Of these the Lord is the ruler, the sustainer, the one who sets them in motion and withdraws them, the sole cause of their appearance and disappearance, self-ruling and unborn.
m.7.2.5.21: Therefore Maheśvara, having the form of pradhāna, puruṣa, the manifest and time, is declared their cause, guide, ruler and sustainer.
m.7.2.5.22: By some the Lord is said to be Virāj and Hiraṇyagarbha: Hiraṇyagarbha is the cause of the worlds, and Virāj is the universe as a whole.
m.7.2.5.23: By the seers Śiva is called the Inner Controller and the Supreme; others declare him to be Prājña, Taijasa and Viśva.
m.7.2.5.24: Some call him terrible, others know him as wholly gentle; still others call him the knower, the means of knowing, the known and cognition.
m.7.2.5.25: Others call him the agent, the action, the effect, the instrument and the cause; others declare him the self of waking, dream and deep sleep.
m.7.2.5.26: Some call him the Fourth (turīya), others that beyond the Fourth; some call him without qualities, others know him as possessing qualities.
m.7.2.5.27: Some call him subject to transmigration, others free from it; some call him independent, others know him as dependent.
m.7.2.5.28: Some call him terrible, others know him as wholly gentle; some call him full of passion, and likewise others free from passion.
m.7.2.5.29: Some call him actionless, and other people active; some call him without senses, and likewise others possessed of senses.
m.7.2.5.30: Some call him permanent, others impermanent; some indeed call him formless, others know him as having form.
m.7.2.5.31: Some call him invisible, others know him as visible; some call him expressible, others inexpressible; some call him of the nature of sound, and others beyond sound.
m.7.2.5.32: Some call him made of thought, others devoid of thought; some call him of the nature of knowledge, and others discerning knowledge (vijñāna).
m.7.2.5.33: Some call him knowable, some unknowable; some call him the highest, and likewise others the lower.
m.7.2.5.34: The true nature of the Supreme Being, being thus variously conceived, the sages do not ascertain, on account of their manifold notions.
m.7.2.5.35: But those who have taken refuge in the supreme Lord with their whole being, they indeed know Śiva, the supreme cause, without effort.
m.7.2.5.36: As long as the bound soul does not see the ancient Seer, who has no lord over him, the ruler of the world, so long does he, fettered, remain in sorrow in this saṃsāra, turning like the rim of a wheel.
m.7.2.5.37: When the seer beholds the gold-hued Maker, the Lord, the Person, the source of Brahmā, then the knower, shaking off merit and demerit, stainless, attains supreme equality with him.
m.7.2.5.iti: Thus ends the fifth adhyāya, named The yoga of knowing the state of Paśupati, in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the seventh saṃhitā, the Vāyavīya-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.7.2.6.1: Upamanyu said: Śiva has no bondage of the āṇava impurity, nor of kārya karma, nor that arising from māyā; nor that of prakṛti, nor that of the intellect, nor likewise that consisting of ego (ahaṅkāra).
m.7.2.6.2: He has no bondage of the mind, nor of thought, nor of the senses; nor bondage of the subtle elements (tanmātras), nor any bondage of the gross elements.
m.7.2.6.3: For Śambhu of boundless splendour there is no time (kāla), no kalā, no nescience (avidyā), likewise no niyati; no attachment and no aversion.
m.7.2.6.4: Nor does he have clinging to life (abhiniveśa), nor good and bad deeds, nor their ripening, nor pleasure and pain which are their fruit.
m.7.2.6.5: Nor has he any connection with latent dispositions (āśaya), nor with the impressions of actions, nor with enjoyments and the impressions of enjoyments ranging over the three times.
m.7.2.6.6: He has no cause, no maker, no beginning, no end, nor any middle; no action, no instrument, nothing not to be done, nor anything to be done.
m.7.2.6.7: He has no kinsman or non-kinsman, no controller or impeller; no master, no guru, no protector, none superior and likewise none equal.
m.7.2.6.8: He has no birth and death, nothing desired or undesired; no injunction and no prohibition, no liberation and no bondage.
m.7.2.6.9: Whatever is inauspicious, none of it is ever his; and all that is auspicious is his, since Śiva is the Supreme Self.
m.7.2.6.10: That Śiva, presiding over all this by his own powers, remains unfallen from his own nature; therefore he is known as Sthāṇu (the Steadfast).
m.7.2.6.11: Since the world of moving and unmoving beings is presided over by Śiva, Śarva is known as having all forms; knowing him thus, one is not deluded.
m.7.2.6.12: Śarva, Rudra—salutation to him—the great Person, higher than being, golden-armed, the Blessed One, lord of gold, the Lord;
m.7.2.6.13: the lord of Ambikā, Īśāna, bearer of the Pināka bow, who rides the bull; the one Rudra, the supreme Brahman, the Person dark and tawny;
m.7.2.6.14: the size of a hair-tip, to be meditated upon in the middle of the heart, within the small inner space (dahara); golden-haired, lotus-eyed, ruddy and coppery;
m.7.2.6.15: that god who moves down among beings, blue-necked, golden; gentle, non-terrible, and likewise mixed; imperishable, immortal, undecaying.
m.7.2.6.16: He is the supreme distinct Person, the Blessed One, the ender of Death (Antaka), free from the sentient and insentient, and higher than the highest, beyond the manifest world.
m.7.2.6.17: When knowledge and lordship are seen in Śiva in their pre-eminence, the wise declare him to be established as surpassing even the lords of the worlds.
m.7.2.6.18: He alone, in the beginning, is the teacher of the full extent of the scriptures to the Brahmās born in each successive creation, who exist within the limits of time.
m.7.2.6.19: He is the guru even of the gurus who are bound by the limits of time; the lord of all, he is free from the limits of time.
m.7.2.6.20: His power is pure, innate, and surpassing all; his knowledge is incomparable and eternal; his body is utterly stainless;
m.7.2.6.21: his lordship is without rival, his bliss absolute; so too are his strength, the might of his splendour, valour, forbearance and compassion.
m.7.2.6.22: Being entirely full, he has no purpose of his own in creation and the rest; the fruit of all his activity is solely grace for others.
m.7.2.6.23: The praṇava (Om) is the word that denotes that Śiva, the Supreme Self; among words such as Śiva, Rudra and so on, the praṇava is held to be the highest.
m.7.2.6.24: Through meditation on Śambhu, who is denoted by the praṇava, and also through its repetition, whatever supreme attainment there is becomes attainable—of this there is no doubt.
m.7.2.6.25: Therefore the wise who have mastered the Āgamas, regarding the denoted and the denoting as one, call the god the One Syllable.
m.7.2.6.26: Its measures (mātrās) are declared at the summit of the Veda to be four: akāra, ukāra, makāra, and the nāda (resonance).
m.7.2.6.27: They call akāra the Ṛgveda; ukāra is said to be the Yajus; makāra the Sāman; and its nāda is held to be the Atharvan scripture.
m.7.2.6.28: Akāra is the great seed, rajas, the four-faced creator Brahmā; ukāra is prakṛti, the womb, sattva, the preserver Hari.
m.7.2.6.29: Makāra is puruṣa, the seed, tamas, Hara the destroyer; the nāda is the supreme Person, the Lord, attributeless and actionless—Śiva.
m.7.2.6.30: Having expressed this entire universe threefold by the three measures, the praṇava makes known the Self that is Śiva by the half-measure.
m.7.2.6.31: Than whom there is nothing higher or other, than whom there is nothing subtler nor greater; who, the One, stands motionless like a tree in heaven—by that Person this whole universe is filled.
m.7.2.6.iti: Thus ends the sixth adhyāya, named The truth of Śiva, in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the seventh saṃhitā, the Vāyavīya-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.7.2.7.1: His natural power (śakti) is knowledge (vidyā), distinct from the universe. It shines in the form of the One and of the many, like the radiance of the sun.
m.7.2.7.2: From her arose infinite powers, such as will, knowledge and action, and also Māyā and the rest, just as sparks arise from fire.
m.7.2.7.3: From her indeed arose Sadāśiva, Īśvara and the others, Vidyā, the Vidyeśvaras and the rest, the puruṣas, and Prakṛti, higher than the high.
m.7.2.7.4: The principles from Mahat down to the particular elements (viśeṣa), the forms beginning with Aja (Brahmā), and whatever else exists—all that is her effect; there is no doubt.
m.7.2.7.5: That Śakti is all-pervading, subtle, of the nature of awakened consciousness and bliss. The god Śiva, adorned with the moon, is called the possessor of Śakti.
m.7.2.7.6: Śiva is what is to be known; Śivā is knowledge, wisdom, śruti and smṛti. She is steadfastness, stability, firm abiding, and the powers of knowledge, will and action.
m.7.2.7.7: She is the command, the supreme Brahman, the two knowledges, higher and lower, pure knowledge and pure kalā—since everything is made by Śakti.
m.7.2.7.8: Māyā, Prakṛti, the individual soul, modification and transformation, the non-existent and the existent—whatever there is, all this is pervaded by her.
m.7.2.7.9: That goddess, by her Māyā, deludes the whole cosmic egg with its moving and unmoving beings without effort, and also releases it in play.
m.7.2.7.10: Together with her, who is of twenty-seven kinds, the Lord of all abides pervading the universe; therefore liberation here proceeds from him.
m.7.2.7.11: Long ago some sages, expounders of Brahman seeking liberation, their minds possessed by doubt, reflected on the truth as it is.
m.7.2.7.12: What is the cause? From where were we born? By what do we live? Where is our foundation? By whom are we governed?
m.7.2.7.13: By whom are we constantly kept in pleasures and in their opposites, ceaselessly? By whom was the inviolable order of the universe established?
m.7.2.7.14: Time, inherent nature, destiny, chance—these do not fit here; nor the elements, the womb, or the person; or is it a combination of these, or something beyond them?
m.7.2.7.15: Since time and the rest are insentient, and though the self is sentient, it experiences pleasures and pains because it is a created being and not a master—so it was pondered.
m.7.2.7.16: Following the yoga of meditation on that, they saw directly the Lord's power, which cuts the bonds, deeply hidden by its own qualities.
m.7.2.7.17: Their bonds cut by her, they beheld with divine sight Mahādeva, the possessor of Śakti, the cause of all causes.
m.7.2.7.18: He is the one who, immeasurable, by this power presides over all causes together with time and the self—who presides over everything.
m.7.2.7.19: Then, through grace, through the supreme yoga, and through the yoga of devotion they had perceived, they attained the divine goal.
m.7.2.7.20: Therefore, those who behold Śiva in the heart together with that Śakti have eternal peace, not others—so says the Śruti.
m.7.2.7.21: There is never any separation of the possessor of Śakti from Śakti. Therefore, because of the identity of Śakti and the possessor of Śakti, bliss comes from the two together.
m.7.2.7.22: Surely a sequence of knowledge and action is intended for liberation; yet when there is grace, that liberation rests in the palm of one's hand.
m.7.2.7.23: Whether a god or a demon, a beast or a bird, a parrot or even a worm—one is liberated by his grace.
m.7.2.7.24: Whether in the womb or being born, a child or a youth, old or dying, dwelling in heaven or in hell,
m.7.2.7.25: fallen or righteous, learned or foolish—when there is grace one is liberated that very instant; there is no doubt of this.
m.7.2.7.26: Out of compassion the Supreme Lord becomes gracious even to unworthy devotees, having removed their various impurities; there is no doubt.
m.7.2.7.27: That devotion arises from grace alone, and grace arises from devotion; discerning the difference of stages, the wise man is not confused about this.
m.7.2.7.28: This devotion, preceded by grace and bestowing enjoyment and liberation, cannot be attained by men in a single birth.
m.7.2.7.29: Maheśvara becomes gracious to those perfected over many births, who follow the Vedic and Smṛti rules, who are dispassionate and awakened.
m.7.2.7.30: When the Lord of gods is gracious, there arises in that bound soul a slight devotion, led by understanding: I have a Lord.
m.7.2.7.31: Then the man becomes engaged in austerity and various Śaiva duties; in performing them comes repeated practice of them, and from that supreme devotion arises.
m.7.2.7.32: By that supreme devotion supreme grace is obtained; from grace comes liberation from all bonds, and for the liberated one, bliss.
m.7.2.7.33: Even a mortal of slight devotion, after three births, will not be subject to the torment of the womb-machine; of this there is no doubt.
m.7.2.7.34: Service, whether with its auxiliary parts or without, is called devotion. It is further divided threefold according to its means: mind, speech and body.
m.7.2.7.35: Contemplation of Śiva's form and the like is known as mental service; japa and the like is verbal service; ritual worship and the like is bodily.
m.7.2.7.36: This service with three means is also called Śiva-dharma; and it has been declared fivefold by Śiva, the Supreme Self.
m.7.2.7.37: In brief: austerity, ritual action, japa, meditation and knowledge. Action is worship of the liṅga and the like; austerity is the Cāndrāyaṇa vow and the like.
m.7.2.7.38: Japa is the threefold repetition of the mantra of Śiva; meditation is contemplation of Śiva; and the knowledge taught in the Śaiva Āgamas is what is here called knowledge.
m.7.2.7.39: The Śivāgama was spoken by Śrīkaṇṭha Śiva to Śivā out of compassion for those who take refuge in Śiva; it is the sole means to the highest goods.
m.7.2.7.40: Therefore a wise man seeking the highest good should increase his devotion to Śiva, the supreme cause, and give up attachment to sense-objects.
m.7.2.7.iti: Thus ends the seventh adhyāya, named The account of the truth of Śiva, in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the seventh saṃhitā, the Vāyavīya-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.7.2.8.1: Kṛṣṇa said: O blessed one, I wish to hear the knowledge of Śiva, the essence of the Vedas, which Śiva himself expounded for the liberation of those who take refuge in him.
m.7.2.8.2: That knowledge is beyond the reach of non-devotees, the unintelligent and the undisciplined; it is endowed with five topics, is secret, and is reviled by the unwise.
m.7.2.8.3: In places it is contrary to the dharmas established for the varṇas and āśramas, in places in accord with them; it was drawn out in its entirety from the Veda with its six limbs, and from Sāṅkhya and Yoga.
m.7.2.8.4: It was spoken by the Supreme Lord, vast in extent, measuring a hundred crore verses by count of text. In it, how is the worship of the Lord to be performed?
m.7.2.8.5: Who is entitled to worship and the rest? How are the yoga of knowledge and the like practised? O you of good vows, please tell all that in full detail.
m.7.2.8.6: Upamanyu said: Condensing it, I shall tell the Śaiva doctrine, declared in the Veda and expounded by Śiva, free of praise, blame and the like, producing immediate conviction,
m.7.2.8.7: born of the guru's grace, divine, granting liberation without effort. I shall tell it briefly; its full extent cannot be told.
m.7.2.8.8: Long ago, with the desire to create, Śiva, the immovable Great Lord, the Master, endowed with real effect and cause, manifested himself from the Unmanifest.
m.7.2.8.9: And then the Lord, the seer surpassing the universe, generated Brahmā, the first god among the gods, the lord of sacred speech (brahmaṇaspati).
m.7.2.8.10: Brahmā, as he was being born, beheld the god, his father; and the progenitor god looked upon him being born, by his command.
m.7.2.8.11: Looked upon by Rudra, that god, the lord, created the universe, and he established the order of varṇas and āśramas, each separately.
m.7.2.8.12: He created Soma for the sake of sacrifice; from Soma were born heaven, earth, fire, the sun, sacrifice, Viṣṇu and the lord of Śacī (Indra).
m.7.2.8.13: They and other gods praised Rudra with the Rudrādhyāya; the Lord stood before the gods with a gracious face.
m.7.2.8.14: For the sake of his own play, the Great Lord took away their knowledge; then the gods, bewildered, asked him: Who are you?
m.7.2.8.15: The blessed Rudra said: I alone am the ancient one. I was in the very beginning, and I exist now, O best of gods,
m.7.2.8.16: and I shall be. There is no other apart from me. I alone satisfy the whole world with my own radiance.
m.7.2.8.17: There is none greater than or equal to me; he who knows me is liberated. Having said this, the blessed Rudra vanished right there.
m.7.2.8.18: Not seeing that Lord, praising him with Sāman chants, and performing the Pāśupata vow set forth in the Atharvaśiras,
m.7.2.8.19: the immortals then had all their limbs covered with ash. Then, to grant them grace, the Lord of creatures (paśupati), the Master,
m.7.2.8.20: the Lord, together with his attendants and with Umā, made himself present. Him whom yogins, sleepless, with breath mastered and sins burnt away,
m.7.2.8.21: see in the heart, that god the foremost of gods beheld. Her whom they call the supreme Power, following the Lord's will,
m.7.2.8.22: her, the lovely-eyed one, they saw at the left side of the Great Lord. Those who have shaken off saṃsāra and attained the supreme Śaiva state,
m.7.2.8.23: and those others who are eternally perfected—those lords of the gaṇas too were seen. Then the gods praised the Great Lord together with the Goddess
m.7.2.8.24: with divine hymns to Maheśvara, Vedic and also Purāṇic. The god with the bull-banner, looking at the gods with compassion,
m.7.2.8.25: well pleased, said in a voice naturally sweet, I am satisfied. Then the gods, bowing to the bull-bannered one whose mind was well pleased, reverently asked him this most worthy question:
m.7.2.8.26: The gods said: O blessed one, by what path are you to be worshipped on earth? Who is entitled to worship? Please tell us truly.
m.7.2.8.27: Then Hara, best of gods, glancing at the Goddess with a smile, revealed his own supreme, awesome form in the nature of the sun,
m.7.2.8.28: endowed with all sovereign qualities, supreme, consisting of all radiance, surrounded by powers, forms, limbs, planets and gods,
m.7.2.8.29: eight-armed, four-faced, wondrous, half-woman. Seeing this wondrous form, the gods led by Viṣṇu,
m.7.2.8.30: understood the god to be the sun and the Goddess the moon, and the rest as the five elements, and the moving and unmoving world as composed of that.
m.7.2.8.31: Having spoken thus, they offered him arghya and bowed to him:
m.7.2.8.32: To you, vermilion-hued, of beautiful disc, adorned with gold-coloured ornaments, lotus-eyed, holding a lotus, the cause of Brahmā, Indra and Nārāyaṇa—
m.7.2.8.33: accepting this excellent arghya offered to you, filled with fine gems, with golden water, rich with fine saffron and the like, with kuśa grass and flowers, together with a golden vessel—O Lord, be gracious.
m.7.2.8.34: Obeisance to you, Śiva, the peaceful, with your gaṇas, the first cause; to you who are Rudra, Viṣṇu and Brahmā, whose form is the sun.
m.7.2.8.35: Whoever, concentrated, worships Śiva in the solar disc and offers the excellent arghya at dawn, midday and evening,
m.7.2.8.36: or bows, or recites these verses that are the very mouth of the Veda—nothing is hard for him to obtain; if he is a devotee, he is surely liberated.
m.7.2.8.37: Therefore one should always worship Śiva in the form of the sun, with mind, deed and speech, for the sake of dharma, desire, wealth and liberation.
m.7.2.8.38: Then the Great Lord Hara, abiding in the disc, looking at the gods, gave them the scripture surpassing all Āgamas and vanished.
m.7.2.8.39: Knowing that in it the entitlement to worship belongs to brāhmaṇas, kṣatriyas and vaiśyas, the gods bowed to the lord of gods and went back as they had come.
m.7.2.8.40: Then, after a long time, when that scripture had disappeared, Maheśvarī, seated on his lap, questioned her husband.
m.7.2.8.41: Urged by her, the Goddess, the God adorned with the moon raised his hand and spoke the scripture that surpasses all the Āgamas.
m.7.2.8.42: And at the command of Parameṣṭhin Brahmā it was propagated in the world by me, by the teacher Agastya, and by the great sage Dadhīca.
m.7.2.8.43: The trident-bearer himself, too, descending onto the earth in the successive cycles of the yugas, establishes a lineage of knowledge for the liberation of those who take refuge in him.
m.7.2.8.44: Ṛbhu, Satya, Bhārgava, Aṅgiras, Savitṛ, O twice-born ones; Mṛtyu, the wise Śatakratu, Vasiṣṭha the foremost of sages;
m.7.2.8.45: Sārasvata, Tridhāman, Trivṛta the foremost of sages, Śatatejas, and Dharma himself, known as Nārāyaṇa;
m.7.2.8.46: Svarakṣa, the wise Āruṇi, and likewise Kṛtañjaya; Māmateya, Bharadvāja, Gautama, the excellent seer;
m.7.2.8.47: Vācaḥsravas, a sage in person, likewise the pure Sūkṣmāyaṇi, the sage Tṛṇabindu, Kṛṣṇa, Śakti, and next Śākteya;
m.7.2.8.48: Jātūkarṇya, and Hari himself as the sage Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana. Let you hear in order of these incarnations of Vyāsa, lords of yoga in the kalpa.
m.7.2.8.49: In the Liṅga Purāṇa, O you of good vows, are described the incarnations of Vyāsa at the ends of the Dvāpara ages, as well as the incarnations of the trident-bearer as yoga-teachers, and likewise among his disciples.
m.7.2.8.50: In each of these incarnations the Lord has four disciples of great vigour; and their disciples and their disciples' disciples number in hundreds and thousands.
m.7.2.8.51: By honouring them in the world, by carrying out the Śaiva injunctions and so on, the fortunate are liberated, as are those wholly imbued with devotion.
m.7.2.8.iti: Thus ends the eighth adhyāya, named The incarnations of Vyāsa, in the knowledge of the truth of Śiva, in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the seventh saṃhitā, the Vāyavīya-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.7.2.9.1: Kṛṣṇa said: O Lord, tell me of the incarnations of Śarva who, in all the cycles of the yugas, appeared in the guise of teachers of yoga, and also of his disciples.
m.7.2.9.2: Upamanyu said: Śveta, Sutāra, Madana, Suhotra and Kaṅka; Laugākṣi, Mahāmāya and likewise Jaigīṣavya;
m.7.2.9.3: Dadhivāha, Ṛṣabha, the sage Ugra, and Atri; Supālaka, Gautama, and likewise the sage Vedaśiras;
m.7.2.9.4: Gokarṇa, Guhāvāsin, and Śikhaṇḍin, who is remembered as another; Jaṭāmālin, Aṭṭahāsa, Dāruka and likewise Lāṅgulin;
m.7.2.9.5: Mahākāla, Śūlin, Daṇḍin and Muṇḍīśa; Sahiṣṇu, Somaśarman, and Lakulīśvara.
m.7.2.9.6: These, in this Vārāha kalpa, in the period of the seventh Manu, are the teachers of yoga, twenty-eight in number, appearing in the succession of the yugas.
m.7.2.9.7: Each of these has four disciples of tranquil mind, beginning with Śveta and ending with Ruṣya; I shall name them in order.
m.7.2.9.8: Śveta, Śvetaśikha, Śvetāśva and Śvetalohita; Dundubhi, Śatarūpa, Ṛcīka and likewise Ketumān;
m.7.2.9.9: Vikośa, Vikeśa, Vipāśa and Pāśanāśana; Sumukha, Durmukha, Durgama and Duratikrama;
m.7.2.9.10: Sanatkumāra, Sanaka, Sananda and Sanātana; Sudhāman, Virajas, Śaṅkha and Aṇḍaja;
m.7.2.9.11: Sārasvata, Megha, Meghavāha and Suvāhaka; Kapila, Āsuri, Pañcaśikha and Bāṣkala;
m.7.2.9.12: Parāśara, Garga, Bhārgava and likewise Aṅgiras; Balabandhu, Nirāmitra, Ketuśṛṅga and Tapodhana;
m.7.2.9.13: Lambodara, Lamba, Lambātman and Lambakeśaka; Sarvajña, Samabuddhi and likewise Sādhyasiddhi;
m.7.2.9.14: Sudhāman, Kaśyapa, Vasiṣṭha and likewise Virajas; Atri, Ugra, Guruśreṣṭha, then Śravana and Śraviṣṭaka;
m.7.2.9.15: Kuṇi, Kuṇibāhu, Kuśarīra and Kunetraka; Kāśyapa, Uśanas, Cyavana and Bṛhaspati;
m.7.2.9.16: Utathya, Vāmadeva, Mahākāla and Mahānila; Vācaḥśravas, Suvīra, Śyāvaka and Yatīśvara;
m.7.2.9.17: Hiraṇyanābha, Kauśalya, Lokākṣi and likewise Kuthumi; Sumantu, Jaimini, Kubandha and Kuśakandhara;
m.7.2.9.18: Plakṣa, Dārbhāyaṇi, Ketumān and likewise Gautama; Bhallavin, Madhupiṅga and likewise Śvetaketu;
m.7.2.9.19: Uśija, Bṛhadaśva, Devala and Kavi; Śālihotra, Suveṣa, Yuvanāśva and Śaradvasu;
m.7.2.9.20: Akṣapāda, Kaṇāda, Ulūka and Vatsa; Kulika, Garga, Mitraka and Ruṣya.
m.7.2.9.21: These are the disciples of Maheśa who appeared in the form of yoga-teachers; their number is one hundred together with twelve.
m.7.2.9.22: All are Pāśupatas, perfected ones, their bodies smeared with ash, knowers of the true meaning of all scriptures, masters of the Vedas and Vedāṅgas.
m.7.2.9.23: All delight in the Śaiva way of life and are devoted to the knowledge of Śiva; all are free from attachment, their minds attached to Śiva alone.
m.7.2.9.24: They are steadfast, enduring all pairs of opposites, delighting in the welfare of all beings; upright, gentle, self-possessed, having conquered anger and having conquered the senses.
m.7.2.9.25: Adorned with garlands of rudrākṣa, their foreheads marked with the tripuṇḍra; some with a tuft of matted hair, some wholly matted-haired, some without matted hair, some with shaven heads.
m.7.2.9.26: Living mostly on fruits and roots, devoted to breath-control (prāṇāyāma), filled with the sense of identity with Śiva, solely intent on meditation on Śiva;
m.7.2.9.27: they have utterly crushed the sprouting shoots of the poison-tree of saṃsāra, and are fully ready to depart for the supreme city of Śiva.
m.7.2.9.28: Whoever, regarding these as true preceptors, constantly worships Śiva, attains union (sāyujya) with Śiva; there need be no doubt about this.
m.7.2.9.iti: Thus ends the ninth adhyāya, named The yoga incarnations of Śiva, in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the seventh saṃhitā, the Vāyavīya-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.7.2.10.1: Kṛṣṇa said: O venerable one, chief of all yogins, lord of the gaṇas, lord of sages, equal in splendour to the six-faced Skanda, treasury of all knowledge, O teacher,
m.7.2.10.2: Most likely you, having descended upon the earth to cut asunder the bonds of men, abide here having assumed the body of a great sage, O supreme lord.
m.7.2.10.3: For otherwise, in this world, who other than you—be he a god or even a demon—could know the supreme state whose nature is Śiva?
m.7.2.10.4: Therefore, having drunk the nectar of Śiva-knowledge poured forth from your mouth, as if directly from the Pināka-bearer himself, my mind has not become satisfied.
m.7.2.10.5: O venerable one, what did the Supreme Goddess, seated on the lap of her husband, the very maker of all the worlds, ask her husband?
m.7.2.10.6: Upamanyu said: Fittingly have you asked, O Kṛṣṇa; I shall tell it exactly as it was to you, a devotee of Bhava, disciplined and of auspicious mind.
m.7.2.10.7: On the divine Mandara, the best of mountains, with its lovely caves, the divine Mahādeva, together with the Goddess, became absorbed in meditation.
m.7.2.10.8: Then the Goddess's dear friend Śubhāvatī, with a smiling face, brought blossoming, exceedingly lovely flowers.
m.7.2.10.9: Then Hara, the best of gods, having placed the Goddess on his own lap and adorned her with those flowers, sat there himself greatly delighted.
m.7.2.10.10: Then the goddesses who moved in the inner apartments, wearing divine ornaments, and the intimate chiefs of the gaṇas, served the Great Mistress of all worlds—
m.7.2.10.11: —and her husband, the all-complete Great Lord of all worlds; with fly-whisks in their hands they attended upon the Goddess and the God.
m.7.2.10.12: Then pleasing conversations took place, for the delight of the Great Lord and Lady and for the protection of those people in the world who have taken refuge in Śiva.
m.7.2.10.13: Then, seeing the opportunity, the Great Mistress of all worlds questioned her husband, the Great Lord of all worlds.
m.7.2.10.14: The Goddess said: By what means is Mahādeva brought under the control of mortals of dull mind, souls who are incapable of grasping the truth of the Self and the like, and whose selves are undisciplined?
m.7.2.10.15: Īśvara said: Not by ritual action, not by austerity, not by recitations, not by postures and the like, not by knowledge, nor by anything else am I brought under control without faith.
m.7.2.10.16: If people have faith in me, from whatever cause, I become controllable, touchable, visible, worshipable, and one who may be conversed with.
m.7.2.10.17: Therefore faith in me must be cultivated by one who wishes to bring me under control. The cause of faith here is the guarding of one's own dharma by those belonging to the varṇas.
m.7.2.10.18: Only the man who abides in the dharma of his own varṇa and āśrama comes to have faith in me, not anyone else.
m.7.2.10.19: The entire dharma of those in the āśramas here, established by the Veda, was formerly declared by Brahmā, preceded by my very command.
m.7.2.10.20: But that dharma of the Grandsire involves rites requiring much wealth; it is not abundant in ultimate fruit and is accompanied by hardship and toil. Through that great dharma, having obtained faith, which is very hard to gain—
m.7.2.10.21: —those of the varṇas who take refuge in me, with no other refuge, attain dharma, desire, wealth and liberation by an easy path.
m.7.2.10.22: The conduct of varṇa and āśrama has been arranged anew by me. In it, only my devotees among those of the varṇas—
m.7.2.10.23: —have eligibility, not others: this is my firm command. By the path thus commanded, those of the varṇas who take refuge in me—
m.7.2.10.24: —freed by my grace from the bonds of mala, māyā and the rest, having reached my supreme abode, from which return is hard, and having attained supreme likeness to me, have gone to bliss.
m.7.2.10.25: Therefore, whether one has obtained it or not, if he is my devotee, resorting to the varṇa-dharma declared by me, he should lift up himself by himself.
m.7.2.10.26: This is indeed a gain of what was not gained, greater by crores upon crores of times. Therefore one should practise the varṇa-dharma received from my own mouth.
m.7.2.10.27: For, O auspicious one, my incarnations exist in all the Manvantaras in the guise of yoga-teachers, O noble lady, and their lineages by the thousands.
m.7.2.10.28: For the undisciplined, the unintelligent and the undevoted, O Queen of gods, knowledge of this lineage is hard to obtain; therefore one should resort to it with effort.
m.7.2.10.29: That is loss, that is a great flaw, that is delusion, that is blindness and dumbness—that one, excluded from the path of liberation, should labour elsewhere.
m.7.2.10.30: Knowledge, ritual action, conduct and yoga—thus, O Queen of gods, my eternal dharma is declared to have four quarters.
m.7.2.10.31: Knowledge of paśu (the bound soul), pāśa (the bond) and pati (the Lord) is called jñāna. The purification of the six paths according to rule, dependent on the guru, is called kriyā.
m.7.2.10.32: The practice of the dharma of my worship and the like, enjoined according to varṇa and āśrama and prescribed by me alone, is called caryā.
m.7.2.10.33: The cessation of other mental activities in one whose mind is fixed on me, by the very path taught by me, is called yoga.
m.7.2.10.34: O Goddess, this purification of the mind is superior to a multitude of horse-sacrifices and also grants liberation; yet it is hard to attain for those who crave sense-objects.
m.7.2.10.35: Yoga, which removes former sins, is said to belong only to the dispassionate one who has conquered the group of senses through yama and niyama.
m.7.2.10.36: From dispassion knowledge arises; from knowledge yoga proceeds.
m.7.2.10.37: One who knows yoga, even if fallen, is liberated; there is no doubt about this. Compassion should be practised constantly, and non-violence, the gathering of knowledge,
m.7.2.10.38: truthfulness, non-stealing, belief in the scriptures, faith and control of the senses; teaching and study, sacrificing and officiating at sacrifices likewise;
m.7.2.10.39: meditation, contemplation of the Lord, and constant devotion to knowledge. The brāhmaṇa who conducts himself thus for the attainment of the yoga of knowledge—
m.7.2.10.40: —very soon, having gained realised knowledge, he attains yoga as well. O beloved, the knower, having burned this body in an instant with the fire of knowledge, the knower of yoga will cast off the bondage of karma through my grace.
m.7.2.10.41: Action that consists of merit and demerit is an obstacle to liberation. Therefore the yogin should, as a rule, give up both merit and demerit.
m.7.2.10.42: One is bound by performing action with desire for its fruit, not by the mere performance of action. Therefore one should give up the fruit of action.
m.7.2.10.43: O beloved, first, having fully worshipped me outwardly through the sacrifice of action, and having become devoted to the yoga of knowledge, one should afterwards practise yoga thoroughly.
m.7.2.10.44: Once my true nature is known, embodied beings who are yoked in yoga, to whom a clod, a stone and gold are alike, do not worship me through the sacrifice of action.
m.7.2.10.45: The excellent sage who is ever yoked, my devotee and composed, the yogin devoted to the yoga of knowledge, would attain union (sāyujya) with me.
m.7.2.10.46: But those members of the classes (varṇin) who have taken refuge in me yet whose minds are not free of attachment are entitled only to knowledge, conduct and ritual, being fit for these.
m.7.2.10.47: My worship should be known as twofold: external and internal. And by the distinction of speech, mind and body, they know my worship to be threefold.
m.7.2.10.48: Austerity, ritual action, repetition of mantra, meditation and knowledge, in that order: thus that same worship is again declared by the wise to be fivefold.
m.7.2.10.49: Worship of me and the like that is known to others is external; that same, when known only to oneself, is called internal.
m.7.2.10.50: The mind inclined towards me is called mind, not mere mind; speech devoted to my name is indeed regarded as speech, not any other.
m.7.2.10.51: The body marked with the signs prescribed by my teaching, such as the tripuṇḍra, and devoted to service of me, is truly a body, and no other.
m.7.2.10.52: Worship of me is to be known as action (karma); among external things, sacrifice and the like is not so called. Wasting the body for my sake is austerity; the kṛcchra penances and the like are not considered so.
m.7.2.10.53: Japa is the repeated practice of the five-syllabled mantra, and of the praṇava, and recitation of the Rudrādhyāya and the like, not the study of the Vedas and the like.
m.7.2.10.54: Meditation is contemplation of my form and the like, not absorptions on objects such as the self. Knowledge is understanding the meaning of my Āgamas, not knowing other subjects.
m.7.2.10.55: Whether in the external or the internal, wherever the mind finds delight owing to previous impressions, O Devī, one should practise steadfastness in that principle.
m.7.2.10.56: The internal is better than the external, a hundred times superior, because it is free from admixture and because faults, even visible ones, cannot arise in it.
m.7.2.10.57: One should know purity as internal; external cleanliness is not called purity, since one whose self is devoid of inner purity is impure even when outwardly pure.
m.7.2.10.58: Worship, both external and internal, must be preceded by heartfelt feeling (bhāva); O Devī, worship without feeling is solely a cause of deception.
m.7.2.10.59: What can men do for me, who have accomplished all and am pure? Whether external or internal, it is the feeling that is accepted by me.
m.7.2.10.60: O Devī, action whose sole essence is feeling, done by mind, deed and speech without ever expecting a fruit, is my eternal dharma.
m.7.2.10.61: O Ruler of the gods, refuge in me taken with a fruit in view is slight, since one who seeks fruit is capable of abandoning me when it is absent.
m.7.2.10.62: Yet even for a seeker of fruit whose mind is firmly set on me, I am the giver of fruit according to his feeling, O blameless one.
m.7.2.10.63: Those whose mind is inclined toward me without regard for fruit, even if they later pray for a fruit, they too are devotees dear to me.
m.7.2.10.64: Those who, solely by the force of former impressions, having considered fruit and no-fruit, helplessly take refuge in me, are held to be dearest to me.
m.7.2.10.65: For them there is truly no gain higher than gaining me; and for me too, O Supreme Goddess, there is no gain other than gaining them.
m.7.2.10.66: Through my grace, their feeling, offered to me, bestows the fruit, supreme nirvāṇa, as if by force.
m.7.2.10.67: They declare eightfold the marks of those great souls, devoted to none other, whose minds are surrendered to me, and who are qualified for my dharma.
m.7.2.10.68: Affection for my devotees, rejoicing in my worship, worshipping me oneself, and bodily exertion for my sake;
m.7.2.10.69: devotion in hearing my stories, changes in voice, eyes and limbs from emotion, constant remembrance of me, and being one who lives depending on me;
m.7.2.10.70: In whomever this eightfold sign is found, even in a mleccha, he is the foremost of brāhmaṇas, a sage, glorious; he is an ascetic, and he is a learned man.
m.7.2.10.71: A knower of the four Vedas is not thereby dear to me; but one who is my devotee, even a dog-eater, to him one should give, from him one may receive, and he is to be honoured just as I am.
m.7.2.10.72: Whoever offers me with devotion a leaf, a flower, a fruit or water, I am not lost to him, and he is not lost to me.
m.7.2.10.iti: Thus ends the tenth adhyāya, named Devotion to Śiva, in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the seventh saṃhitā, the Vāyavīya-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.7.2.11.1: Īśvara said: Now, O Ruler of the gods, I shall tell in brief the duties of the classes (varṇa-dharma) for the devotees who are qualified, learned, and foremost among the twice-born.
m.7.2.11.2: Bathing three times a day, the fire-rite, worship of the liṅga in due order, giving, an attitude of devotion towards the Lord, compassion everywhere and at all times,
m.7.2.11.3: truthfulness, contentment, faith in the scriptures, non-violence towards all creatures, modesty, reverent trust, study, yoga, and constant teaching,
m.7.2.11.4: exposition, celibacy, listening to scripture, austerity, forbearance, purity, the tuft of hair and sacred thread, the turban and the upper garment,
m.7.2.11.5: not resorting to what is forbidden, wearing ashes and rudrākṣa beads, worship on the festival days, O Goddess, especially on the fourteenth lunar day,
m.7.2.11.6: drinking the brahmakūrca every month according to rule, and especially worshipping me after bathing me with that very mixture, O beloved,
m.7.2.11.7: complete renunciation of food from all sorts of rites, avoidance of food from ancestral offerings (śrāddha), likewise of stale food, and especially of barley-gruel,
m.7.2.11.8: and avoidance of liquor, of what smells of liquor, and of food-offerings — this is common to all classes, and especially binding on brāhmaṇas.
m.7.2.11.9: Forbearance, tranquillity, contentment, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, knowledge of me, dispassion, the use of ashes,
m.7.2.11.10: and withdrawal from all attachment — these ten are especially the marks of yogins; further, eating alms-food by day.
m.7.2.11.11: This is held to be the same for those in the forest-dweller stage. No food is to be eaten at night by any of the celibate students.
m.7.2.11.12: Teaching and officiating at sacrifices are not prescribed by me here for the kṣatriya, and especially not for the vaiśya; for them there is non-acceptance of gifts.
m.7.2.11.13: Protection of all classes, slaying of enemies in battle, and the destruction of harmful birds and beasts and of wicked men,
m.7.2.11.14: distrust everywhere but trust in my yogins, union with women at the proper times, and the guarding of the army,
m.7.2.11.15: knowing the affairs of the world through spies constantly sent about, always bearing weapons, and wearing ashes as armour —
m.7.2.11.16: this is the summary of duty for kings who abide in my way of life. Tending cattle, trade and agriculture are declared the duties of the vaiśya.
m.7.2.11.17: Service to the other classes is declared the duty of the śūdra, as well as making gardens and resorting to my sacred places.
m.7.2.11.18: For the householder, going only to his lawful wife is prescribed; celibacy for forest-dwellers, ascetics and students.
m.7.2.11.19: For women, service to the husband is the eternal duty, no other; and, O auspicious one, worship of me too, if there is the husband's permission.
m.7.2.11.20: The woman who abandons service to her husband and is intent on vows — that woman goes to hell; there need be no doubt about this.
m.7.2.11.21: Now I shall tell the eternal duty of a woman bereft of her husband: vows, giving, austerity, purity, sleeping on the ground, eating only at night,
m.7.2.11.22: celibacy, constant bathing with ashes or with water, tranquillity, silence, forbearance, and regular sharing of food according to rule,
m.7.2.11.23: fasting according to rule on the eighth and fourteenth days, especially on the full-moon day, and on the eleventh, and worship of me.
m.7.2.11.24: Thus, O Goddess, has been told by me in brief the duty of those who follow the stages of life — of brāhmaṇas, kṣatriyas and vaiśyas, of ascetics and of students,
m.7.2.11.25: likewise of forest-dwellers and householders, O beautiful one, and of śūdras and women: this is the eternal dharma.
m.7.2.11.26: I am to be meditated upon by you, O Ruler of the gods; the six-syllable mantra is always to be repeated; and the entire dharma taught in the Veda is to be observed — this is the summary of the meaning of dharma.
m.7.2.11.27: Now, those men in the world who have taken a body by their own will, who are endowed with intense devotion and joined with impressions from former lives —
m.7.2.11.28: whether detached from or attached even to the objects of sense such as women, they are not stained by sins, as a lotus leaf is not wetted by water.
m.7.2.11.29: For those pure, discerning ones who possess knowledge of me as the Self and are purified by my grace, the maintaining of the āśrama rules is merely a burden.
m.7.2.11.30: For them, as for me, there is nothing to be done or not done, no samādhi or ultimate resort, no injunction and no prohibition.
m.7.2.11.31: Just as here for me, who am wholly complete, nothing remains to be achieved, so too for them who have accomplished their purpose — there is no doubt.
m.7.2.11.32: They are Rudras who, having come down from Rudra's world, have assumed human state for the benefit of my devotees; there is no doubt of this.
m.7.2.11.33: Just as my command sets Brahmā and the others in motion, so their direction sets other men in motion.
m.7.2.11.34: Because they are the bearers of my command, and through the excess of their true devotion, by merely beholding me in them the destruction of all sins comes about.
m.7.2.11.35: And for men devoted to me there arise signs indicating excellent fruit, which reveal matters not seen before.
m.7.2.11.36: Trembling and sweating, shedding of tears, faltering of the voice in the throat, and the experience of bliss and the like may occur suddenly and repeatedly.
m.7.2.11.37: By these unfailing signs, singly or all together, and by states of feeling mild, middling or intense, those best of men are to be recognised.
m.7.2.11.38: Just as iron, through being pervaded by fire, is no longer mere iron, so through my presence they are not mere humans.
m.7.2.11.39: A wise man should not despise these Rudras bearing mortal bodies, thinking them to be ordinary men because of their likeness in hands, feet and so on.
m.7.2.11.40: Contempt shown towards them by men of deluded mind takes away life, fortune, family and good character, and brings hell.
m.7.2.11.41: For the great souls who have been lifted up and who depend on nothing other than me, even the position of Brahmā, Viṣṇu and the Lord of the gods Indra becomes as light and worthless as cotton.
m.7.2.11.42: The lordship belonging to the lords of the guṇas — whether pertaining to buddhi, to prakṛti, or likewise to puruṣa — is impure; therefore it is to be abandoned by those who seek the state beyond the guṇas.
m.7.2.11.43: Now, what is the use of saying much? The sole means for attaining the highest good is the attachment of the mind to me, by whatever cause it may arise.
m.7.2.11.44: Upamanyu said: Thus, by Śiva, the lord Śrīkaṇṭha, the Supreme Self, this compendium of the essential meaning of knowledge was spoken for the welfare of the worlds.
m.7.2.11.45: The Vedas and śāstras in their entirety, together with the itihāsas and purāṇas, and all the sciences, are an elaborate exposition of this compendium of knowledge.
m.7.2.11.46: Knowledge, the knowable, what is to be practised, eligibility, the means, and the goal — because it is a compendium of these six topics, this is called the Compendium.
m.7.2.11.47: Knowledge is that which is imparted under the authority of the guru; the knowable is the bond (pāśa), the bound soul (paśu) and the Lord (pati); what is to be practised is the worship of the liṅga and the like; and the eligible one is whoever is a devotee.
m.7.2.11.48: The means is Śiva's mantra and the like; the goal is equality with Śiva. From knowing this compendium of six topics, omniscience is said to arise.
m.7.2.11.49: First, having worshipped Śiva externally with devotion through ritual sacrifice and the like, according to one's means, one should afterwards become devoted to internal worship.
m.7.2.11.50: He whose delight, owing to the weight of his merit, is in the inner worship and not in the outer — for that great soul no external rite need be performed.
m.7.2.11.51: For one who is satisfied with the nectar of knowledge, a Śaiva whose self has become Śiva through devotion, there is never, O Kṛṣṇa, any duty, either inward or outward.
m.7.2.11.52: Therefore, having gradually given up the external and likewise the internal, and having beheld the knowable through knowledge, one should give up knowledge as well.
m.7.2.11.53: If the mind is not one-pointed on Śiva, what is gained by action, even when performed? If the mind is indeed one-pointed, what need is there of action, even when performed?
m.7.2.11.54: Therefore, whether without performing rites or performing them in sequence, internal and external, by whatever means, one should fix the mind on Śiva.
m.7.2.11.55: For the good whose minds are fixed on Śiva and whose intellects are firmly established, there is supreme bliss here and hereafter — everywhere.
m.7.2.11.56: Here, through this mantra Om namaḥ Śivāya, come the accomplishments; therefore it should be mastered for prosperity both higher and lower.
m.7.2.11.iti: Thus ends the eleventh adhyāya, named The knowledge of Śiva, in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the seventh saṃhitā, the Vāyavīya-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.7.2.12.1: Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: O best of great sages, O all-knowing one, O great ocean of all knowledge, I wish to hear, as it truly is, the greatness of the five-syllabled mantra.
m.7.2.12.2: Upamanyu said: The greatness of the five-syllabled mantra cannot be told in full even in hundreds of crores of years; therefore hear it in brief.
m.7.2.12.3: In the Veda and in the Śiva-Āgama, in both, this six-syllabled mantra is the accomplisher of every aim for all devotees of Śiva.
m.7.2.12.4: That utterance, consisting of Śiva, has few syllables yet is rich in meaning; it is the essence of the Veda, the giver of liberation, established by Śiva's command, and free from doubt.
m.7.2.12.5: That utterance of the Supreme Lord is endowed with manifold powers (siddhi), divine, delighting the minds of people, of well-ascertained meaning, and profound.
m.7.2.12.6: For the accomplishment of every aim of all embodied beings, the Omniscient One proclaimed the mantra oṃ namaḥ śivāya, easy for the mouth to pronounce.
m.7.2.12.7: That primordial six-syllabled mantra is the seed of all knowledge; it should be understood as extremely subtle yet of great meaning, like the seed of the banyan tree.
m.7.2.12.8: The God beyond the three guṇas, omniscient, maker of all, the Lord, the all-pervading Śiva, abides in the one-syllabled mantra Om.
m.7.2.12.9: The subtle one-syllabled Brahmans, Īśāna and the rest, are established in due order in the mantra namaḥ śivāya. In the subtle six-syllabled mantra Śiva has the five Brahmans as his body.
m.7.2.12.10: He abides in it directly and by his own nature through the relation of the denoted and the denoting. Śiva, being immeasurable, is the denoted; the mantra is held to be that which denotes him.
m.7.2.12.11: This relation of denoted and denoter between the two is beginningless, just as this terrible ocean of saṃsāra has been proceeding without beginning.
m.7.2.12.12: So too Śiva, beginningless, stands as the liberator from saṃsāra. Just as medicine is by its nature the counteragent of diseases,
m.7.2.12.13: so Śiva is held to be the counteragent of the ills of saṃsāra. If this Lord of the world did not exist, this universe would be mere darkness,
m.7.2.12.14: because Prakṛti is insentient and the soul (puruṣa) is ignorant. Whatever is insentient—Pradhāna, atoms and the like—
m.7.2.12.15: is not seen to be an agent by itself without an intelligent cause. And the teaching of dharma and adharma, bondage and liberation, as established by reflection,
m.7.2.12.16: and the first creation of souls do not come about without an omniscient one—just as the sick, joyless, suffer without a physician.
m.7.2.12.17: Therefore there exists a beginningless, omniscient, all-complete Sadāśiva, the Lord, the rescuer of souls from the ocean of saṃsāra.
m.7.2.12.18: Free from beginning, middle and end, naturally pure, the Lord, omniscient and all-complete—thus is Śiva to be known in the Śiva-Āgama.
m.7.2.12.19: This mantra is his name, and he is held to be what it names. Because of this relation of name and named, the mantra is established as the supreme Śiva himself.
m.7.2.12.20: This much indeed is the knowledge of Śiva, this much the supreme state: the six-syllabled utterance of Śiva, oṃ namaḥ śivāya.
m.7.2.12.21: This Śaiva utterance, of the nature of Śiva, is an injunction, not mere eulogy (arthavāda). Śiva, who is omniscient, entirely complete and naturally pure,
m.7.2.12.22: and the bestower of grace on the worlds—how could he speak of what is false? A thing as it really stands, with its merits and faults by its nature,
m.7.2.12.23: and its fruit in full, as far as it extends—so the Omniscient One would declare it. Only one who is seized by faults such as passion and ignorance would speak falsehood.
m.7.2.12.24: Those two faults do not exist in the Lord; how then could he speak otherwise? The stainless utterance composed by the omniscient Śiva, who knows no fault whatsoever, is authoritative—there is no doubt.
m.7.2.12.25: Therefore the words of the Lord are to be trusted by the wise regarding the true nature of merit and sin; one who lacks faith in them goes downward.
m.7.2.12.26: Whatever most excellent words are spoken by tranquil great sages for the attainment of heaven and liberation should be known as well-spoken (subhāṣita).
m.7.2.12.27: Speech that follows passion, hatred, falsehood, anger, lust and craving is called ill-spoken, because it is a cause of hell.
m.7.2.12.28: What use is speech, even if refined (saṃskṛta), soft or charming, if it is born of ignorance and passion and causes the afflictions of saṃsāra?
m.7.2.12.29: Speech by hearing which good arises and passion and the rest are destroyed should be known as beautiful, even if it is ill-formed.
m.7.2.12.30: Though mantras are many, nowhere is there any equal to the stainless mantra composed by the omniscient Śiva.
m.7.2.12.31: The Vedas and śāstras together with their auxiliaries are contained in the six-syllabled mantra; therefore there is no other mantra anywhere equal to it.
m.7.2.12.32: The six-syllabled mantra is diversified in many ways into seven crore great mantras and subsidiary mantras, as a sūtra is unfolded in the form of its commentary (vṛtti).
m.7.2.12.33: All the teachings on Śiva and all the fields of knowledge are, in brief, a commentary (bhāṣya) on the six-syllabled sūtra.
m.7.2.12.34: What need has he of many mantras or of very extensive scriptures, in whose heart this mantra oṃ namaḥ śivāya is established?
m.7.2.12.35: He who has made firm the practice of the mantra oṃ namaḥ śivāya has studied, has heard, has done everything and performed every rite.
m.7.2.12.36: He on the tip of whose tongue the three syllables śivāya, joined with namaḥ and the rest, abide—his life is fruitful.
m.7.2.12.37: Whether an outcaste or a base person, a fool or a learned man, one who is devoted to japa of the five-syllabled mantra is freed from the cage of sin.
m.7.2.12.38: Thus it was spoken by the Supreme Lord, the trident-bearer, when asked by the Goddess, for the welfare of all mortals, and especially of the twice-born.
m.7.2.12.iti: Thus ends the twelfth adhyāya, named The greatness of the five-syllabled mantra, in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the seventh saṃhitā, the Vāyavīya-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.7.2.13.1: The Goddess said: In the Kali age, when time is defiled, hard to conquer and hard to overcome, when the world is shrouded in the darkness of unrighteousness and has turned its face away from dharma,
m.7.2.13.2: when the conduct of the varṇas and āśramas has dwindled, when calamity has arrived, when all eligibility for rites is doubtful, or when its reversal is certain,
m.7.2.13.3: then, when instruction is obstructed and the succession of teacher and disciple has vanished — by what means are your devotees liberated, O Maheśvara?
m.7.2.13.4: Īśvara said: Taking refuge in my supreme, heart-pleasing five-syllabled vidyā, and with their minds purified by devotion, the men born in Kali are liberated.
m.7.2.13.5: Even for those tainted by faults of mind, speech and body beyond telling or remembering, for the ungrateful, the slanderers, the deceitful,
m.7.2.13.6: the greedy and the crooked-minded — if their hearts incline toward me, my five-syllabled vidyā carries them across the fear of saṃsāra.
m.7.2.13.7: Thus, O Devī, I have vowed again and again on earth: even a fallen devotee of mine would be liberated by this vidyā.
m.7.2.13.8: The Goddess said: If a mortal has fallen entirely, he becomes unfit for rites; and a rite performed by one unfit leads indeed to hell. How then would a fallen one be liberated by this vidyā?
m.7.2.13.9: Īśvara said: What you have said is true; yet listen, O beautiful one, to that which I formerly kept hidden, regarding it as a secret.
m.7.2.13.10: If a fallen man, deluded, worships me with mantras other than my five-syllabled mantra, he would undoubtedly go to hell.
m.7.2.13.11: Those who live on water, those who live on air, and others emaciated by vows — by these vows they do not attain union with my world.
m.7.2.13.12: But whoever worships me even once with devotion through the five-syllabled mantra alone, he too would reach my abode, solely by the greatness of this mantra.
m.7.2.13.13: Therefore austerities, sacrifices, vows and observances — these are not equal even to a ten-millionth part of worship with the five-syllabled mantra.
m.7.2.13.14: Whether bound or freed from the noose, whoever worships me with the five-syllabled mantra would be liberated; there is no need for deliberation here.
m.7.2.13.15: Whether without Rudra-initiation or with it, fallen or foolish, the man who worships me even once with the five-syllabled mantra is liberated.
m.7.2.13.16: O Devī, if one worships me with devotion with the six-syllabled or likewise the five-syllabled mantra, together with the brahma- and aṅga-mantras, he is liberated.
m.7.2.13.17: Fallen or not fallen, my devotee who has conquered anger should worship me with this mantra, whether he has received it from a guru or not.
m.7.2.13.18: Yet here, one who has received it is countless millions of times superior to one who has not. Therefore, O Devī, having received it, one should worship me with this mantra.
m.7.2.13.19: But he who, having received it, worships me fully with devotion, endowed with friendliness and other virtues and devoted to celibacy, would attain likeness to me.
m.7.2.13.20: What need to say more here? All devotees are eligible for my five-syllabled mantra; therefore it is indeed the most excellent.
m.7.2.13.21: By the power of the five-syllabled mantra the worlds, the Vedas, the great sages, the eternal dharmas, the gods and this entire universe endure.
m.7.2.13.22: When dissolution arrives and all moving and unmoving beings perish, everything, having entered into Prakṛti, will dissolve there.
m.7.2.13.23: I alone remain, O Devī; there is no second anywhere. Then the Vedas and all the śāstras abide in the five-syllabled mantra.
m.7.2.13.24: They do not perish at all, being protected by my power. Then creation arose from me through the differentiation of Prakṛti and the selves,
m.7.2.13.25: and of those whose selves are the embodiments of the guṇas; then came an intermediate dissolution. At that time the god Nārāyaṇa sleeps, having assumed a body made of māyā,
m.7.2.13.26: resting on the serpent-couch amid the waters. From the lotus of his navel was born the five-faced Grandfather Brahmā.
m.7.2.13.27: Desiring to create the three worlds but unable, being without helpers, he first created ten mind-born sages of immeasurable vigour.
m.7.2.13.28: For the increase of their accomplishment, the Grandfather said to me: O Mahādeva, O Maheśvara, grant power to my sons.
m.7.2.13.29: Thus entreated by him, I, bearing five faces, uttered the five syllables in order to the lotus-born Brahmā.
m.7.2.13.30: Receiving them with his five mouths, that Grandfather of the worlds came to know me, Maheśvara, through the relation of the signified and the signifier.
m.7.2.13.31: Having learned its application according to rule, Prajāpati, the mantra now perfected in him, gave the mantra and its true meaning to his sons.
m.7.2.13.32: And they, having received that jewel of mantras directly from the Grandfather of the worlds, desiring to worship me by the path he had enjoined,
m.7.2.13.33: — on a lovely peak of Meru is a mountain named Muñjavān, splendid, ever dear to me, always guarded by my devotees —
m.7.2.13.34: near it, eager to create the world, they performed intense austerity for a thousand divine years, living on air.
m.7.2.13.35: Seeing their devotion, I at once became visible to them; the ṛṣi, metre, kīlaka, bīja, śakti and deity of the mantra,
m.7.2.13.36: the nyāsa, the six limbs, the binding of the directions and the application — all of it I declared to those noble ones for the growth of the world's creation.
m.7.2.13.37: Then those sages, strengthened by austerity through the greatness of the mantra, duly spread out creation, with gods, asuras and humans.
m.7.2.13.38: Now the form of this supreme vidyā is told: first namaḥ should be uttered, and after that śivāya.
m.7.2.13.39: This is that five-syllabled vidyā, abiding at the crown of all the Śrutis, the eternal seed of everything that is born.
m.7.2.13.40: First issued from my mouth, she is the very expression denoting me; in form she shines like heated gold, with full, high breasts.
m.7.2.13.41: She is four-armed and three-eyed, with the young moon as her crest. She holds a lotus and a blue water-lily in her hands. She is gentle, and her hands show the gestures of granting boons and dispelling fear.
m.7.2.13.42: She is endowed with all auspicious marks and adorned with every ornament. She is seated on a white lotus seat, and her hair is dark and curly.
m.7.2.13.43: Her five syllables are of five kinds of colour, each with a radiating circle of rays: yellow, black, smoky, golden, and red.
m.7.2.13.44: If these are to be used separately, they are adorned with bindu and nāda. The bindu resembles a half-moon, and the nāda has the shape of a lamp-flame.
m.7.2.13.45: O fair-faced one, the second syllable is the bīja among the seeds of this mantra. One should declare the fifth, together with the fourth preceded by a long vowel, to be the śakti.
m.7.2.13.46: Vāmadeva is said to be the seer, and paṅkti the metre. The deity of this mantra, O fair-faced one, is I, Śiva, myself.
m.7.2.13.47: O lovely-hipped one, Gautama, Atri, Viśvāmitra, Aṅgiras, and Bharadvāja are held to be the seers of the syllables, in order.
m.7.2.13.48: Gāyatrī, anuṣṭubh, triṣṭubh, bṛhatī, and virāṭ are the metres, and Indra, Rudra, Hari, Brahmā, and Skanda are their deities.
m.7.2.13.49: O fair-faced one, they declare my five faces to be their places, from the eastern face up to the upper one, beginning with na, in due order.
m.7.2.13.50: The first syllable and the fourth are udātta; the second and the fifth are svarita; and the third is held to be nihita (low-pitched).
m.7.2.13.51: One should know its names as Mūlavidyā, Śiva, Śaiva, Sūtra, and Pañcākṣara. It is my great Śaiva heart.
m.7.2.13.52: The syllable na is called the head, ma is called the crest-lock, śi likewise the armour, and va is called the eye.
m.7.2.13.53: The syllable ya is the weapon. When namaḥ, svāhā, vaṣaṭ, huṃ, vauṣaṭ, and also phaṭ are added at the end of the syllables, then they become limbs (aṅga).
m.7.2.13.54: Even there, this is the root mantra, through combination with a slight difference; and there too the fifth syllable is adorned with the twelve vowels.
m.7.2.13.55: Therefore, with this mantra, by way of mind, speech, and body, one should perform the worship of us two, and likewise japa, homa, and the rest.
m.7.2.13.56: According to one's understanding, according to the time, according to scripture, according to one's mind, according to one's capacity, according to one's means, according to propriety, and according to one's delight —
m.7.2.13.57: — whenever it is done with devotion, wherever it is done, and by whomever it is done, O Devī, worship will lead to liberation.
m.7.2.13.58: Whatever is done with a mind attached to me, O beautiful one, is dear to me and auspicious, whether done in proper order or out of order.
m.7.2.13.59: Even so, for those devotees of mine who are not utterly helpless, I myself have laid down the rules in all the scriptures.
m.7.2.13.60: There, first, I shall explain the auspicious receiving of the mantra, without which japa is fruitless, and by which it becomes fruitful.
m.7.2.13.iti: Thus ends the thirteenth adhyāya, named The greatness of the five-syllabled mantra, in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the seventh saṃhitā, the Vāyavīya-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.7.2.14.1: Īśvara said: O fair-faced one, mantra-repetition that lacks the guru's sanction, lacks the prescribed rites, lacks faith, and lacks the fee offered for the sanction is fruitless, even if it is repeated constantly.
m.7.2.14.2: A mantra perfected through sanction, perfected through rites, perfected through faith, is of my very nature; if it is thus accompanied by the fee as well, there is success in the mantra, bearing great fruit.
m.7.2.14.3: Having approached a guru—a brāhmaṇa preceptor who knows the truth, who practises japa, is endowed with good qualities, and is devoted to meditation and yoga—
m.7.2.14.4: one should, endowed with purity of disposition, strive to please him by speech, by mind, by body, and by wealth.
m.7.2.14.5: The brāhmaṇa should always worship the preceptor with the utmost effort. Elephants, horses, chariots, jewels, fields and houses,
m.7.2.14.6: ornaments, garments, grains and riches—these one should give to the guru with devotion, when one has the means.
m.7.2.14.7: If one desires success for oneself, one should not be miserly with wealth. Afterwards, having offered one's own self to the guru together with one's belongings,
m.7.2.14.8: having thus worshipped him properly according to one's capacity, without deceiving, one should receive from the guru the mantra and also knowledge, in due order.
m.7.2.14.9: The guru, thus pleased, taking the disciple—who is a worshipper, has dwelt with him for a year, is eager to serve, free of ego, bathed, pure and fasting—
m.7.2.14.10: having bathed him for purification with ghee from a full pot, and with water purified by mantras and mixed with sacred substances,
m.7.2.14.11: having adorned the well-dressed disciple with fragrances, garlands, garments and ornaments, having had the auspicious-day blessing (puṇyāha) recited, and having honoured the brāhmaṇas,
m.7.2.14.12: on a seashore, by a river, in a cow-pen, or in a temple, or in a clean place or a house, at a time conducive to success, on a suitable lunar day,
m.7.2.14.13: under a constellation and an auspicious yoga free from all defects—then, bestowing grace, he should impart my knowledge according to rule.
m.7.2.14.14: In a secluded place, with a very serene mind, he should pronounce it correctly with proper intonation; having uttered it and made the disciple utter that supreme mantra of us two,
m.7.2.14.15: saying, may it be propitious, may it be auspicious, may it be splendid, may it be dear—thus the guru should give the mantra, and after that the sanction too.
m.7.2.14.16: Having thus received the mantra and the sanction from the guru, the disciple, composed, having made the formal resolve, should repeat it daily, beginning with the preliminary observance (puraścaraṇa).
m.7.2.14.17: As long as he lives he should repeat it daily one thousand and eight times; becoming single-minded and devoted to it, he attains the supreme state.
m.7.2.14.18: One who, eating only at night and self-restrained, reverently repeats the mantra a lakh times for each syllable, multiplied by four, is known as a performer of puraścaraṇa.
m.7.2.14.19: He who, having performed the puraścaraṇa, then becomes a daily reciter—there is none equal to him in the world; he becomes perfected and a bestower of perfection.
m.7.2.14.20: Having bathed, having fixed a pleasing seat in a clean place, having contemplated me together with you in the heart, and then having contemplated one's own guru,
m.7.2.14.21: facing north or east, silent and with one-pointed mind, having purified the five elements by burning, flooding and the like,
m.7.2.14.22: having performed the mantra-placements (nyāsa) and so on, his body made fruitful thereby, meditating on the forms of us two and restraining the prāṇa and apāna breaths,
m.7.2.14.23: remembering the seat of the mantra, its own form, its seer, metre, presiding deity, seed-syllable, power, and also its sentence, one should repeat the five-syllabled mantra.
m.7.2.14.24: Those versed in the meaning of the Āgamas declare mental repetition to be the highest, whispered repetition the middling, and verbal audible repetition the lowest.
m.7.2.14.25: In order, they say, the highest has Rudra as its deity, the middling has Viṣṇu as its deity, and the lowest has Brahmā as its deity.
m.7.2.14.26: When one utters the mantra with the voice, with high, low and circumflex accents, its words and syllables distinct or indistinct, this is known as verbal japa.
m.7.2.14.27: That which is uttered slightly by mere movement of the tongue, unheard by others or heard only a little, is called whispered (upāṃśu).
m.7.2.14.28: The repeated contemplation by the intellect of sound and meaning along the series of syllables, from letter to letter and word to word, is called mental japa.
m.7.2.14.29: Verbal japa counts as only one; whispered is said to be worth a hundred; mental is declared worth a thousand; and the sagarbha japa is a hundred times more.
m.7.2.14.30: Japa joined with breath-control is called sagarbha. Even breath-control without japa (agarbha) is praised at the beginning and end.
m.7.2.14.31: Restraining the breaths, the wise one who knows the mantra's meaning should recollect the mantra forty times; one unable to do so should repeat it according to capacity.
m.7.2.14.32: One should perform breath-control five times, three times, or once, either agarbha or sagarbha; of these, the sagarbha is commended.
m.7.2.14.33: Japa accompanied by meditation is said to be a thousand times greater even than the sagarbha. Of these five kinds, one japa should be performed according to one's capacity.
m.7.2.14.34: Counting japa on the fingers is thus declared to yield a single measure; one should know counting by the lines of the fingers to be eightfold, and with putrajīva seeds tenfold more.
m.7.2.14.35: With conch-shell beads it is a hundredfold, with coral a thousandfold, with crystal ten-thousandfold, and with pearls it is said to be a hundred-thousandfold.
m.7.2.14.36: With lotus-seeds it is a millionfold, and with gold beads it is said to be ten millionfold; with a knot of kuśa grass and with rudrākṣa beads it becomes infinitely multiplied.
m.7.2.14.37: In the practice of japa, a rosary made of thirty beads gives wealth; one of twenty-seven beads bestows nourishment.
m.7.2.14.38: One made of twenty-five beads grants liberation; with fifteen beads it yields the fruits of hostile magic (abhicāra).
m.7.2.14.39: One should know the thumb as granting liberation, the index finger as destroying enemies, the middle finger as giving wealth; and this ring finger brings peace.
m.7.2.14.40: Among these, a rosary of one hundred and eight beads is the very best; a rosary numbering one hundred is excellent, and one of fifty is middling.
m.7.2.14.41: A rosary of fifty-four beads is declared to be excellent and dear to the heart. With such a rosary one should perform japa, and should not show it to anyone.
m.7.2.14.42: The little finger is said to be kṣariṇī, causing the merit to leak away; the others are auspicious in the act of japa. One should count the japa with the thumb together with the other fingers.
m.7.2.14.43: For japa done without the thumb is fruitless. Japa at home one should know as of ordinary value; in a cowshed they know it to be a hundredfold.
m.7.2.14.44: In a sacred forest and likewise in a garden it is said to be a thousandfold; on a holy mountain ten thousandfold; at a river it is declared to be a hundred thousandfold.
m.7.2.14.45: In a temple they declare it ten-millionfold, and in my presence infinite. In the presence of the sun, fire, the guru, the moon, a lamp and water,
m.7.2.14.46: and of brahmins and cows, japa is commended. Japa facing east brings control over others, and facing south is for hostile rites (abhicāra).
m.7.2.14.47: One should know facing west as bestowing wealth, and facing north gives peace. In the presence of the sun, fire, brahmins, gods and gurus,
m.7.2.14.48: and of other venerable beings who are present, one should not repeat the mantra with face turned away. Wearing a turban, wearing a jacket, naked, with hair untied, with the neck covered,
m.7.2.14.49: with impure hands, unclean, or while lamenting, one should never do japa. Anger, intoxication, sneezing—these three—spitting and yawning,
m.7.2.14.50: and the sight of dogs and lowly persons one should avoid during japa. If these occur, one should sip water, or remember me together with you,
m.7.2.14.51: or gaze at the heavenly lights, or perform breath-control. Without a seat, or lying down, walking, or standing up,
m.7.2.14.52: on a street, in an inauspicious place, or in darkness one should not do japa. One should not do japa with legs stretched out, nor in the cock posture,
m.7.2.14.53: or mounted on a vehicle or a bed, or distraught with worry. If one is able, one should observe all this; if unable, one should do japa according to one's capacity.
m.7.2.14.54: What is the use of saying much here? Hear my word in brief: one of good conduct who does japa purely and meditates attains welfare.
m.7.2.14.55: Right conduct is the highest dharma; right conduct is the highest wealth; right conduct is the highest knowledge; right conduct is the highest goal.
m.7.2.14.56: A man devoid of right conduct is censured in the world, and he will not be happy in the hereafter either; therefore one should be possessed of right conduct.
m.7.2.14.57: Whatever action is enjoined for a person in the Veda and in the śāstra by Vedic authorities, his proper practice of that is good conduct, and nothing else.
m.7.2.14.58: And because it is practised by the good (sat), it is called sadācāra. They say that the root cause of that good conduct is faith (āstikya).
m.7.2.14.59: If a man is a believer (āstika), even if he slips from good conduct through negligence and the like, he is never corrupted; therefore one should adopt faith.
m.7.2.14.60: Just as here there is happiness and sorrow through good and evil deeds, so also it exists in the hereafter—this conviction is called āstikya.
m.7.2.14.61: I shall tell you another secret; this must be guarded, beloved. It should not be told to just anyone, to an unbeliever, or to a paśu (one in bondage).
m.7.2.14.62: For one devoid of good conduct, for the fallen and for the outcaste, there is no protection higher than the Pañcākṣara in the Kali age.
m.7.2.14.63: Whether one is walking or standing, acting as one pleases, impure or pure, this mantra is never fruitless.
m.7.2.14.64: For men without proper conduct, whose six paths (ṣaḍadhvan) have not been purified, even if not imparted by a guru, this mantra is never fruitless.
m.7.2.14.65: Even for an outcaste, a fool, a deluded person, one who is fallen, one without restraint, a lowly person—this mantra is never fruitless.
m.7.2.14.66: For one who, though in any condition whatever, has supreme devotion to me, it surely succeeds, without doubt—but not for anyone else.
m.7.2.14.67: For this mantra, beloved, the ascendant, lunar day, asterism, weekday, yoga and the like need not be considered at all; it is never asleep, but always awake.
m.7.2.14.68: This great mantra is never at any time hostile to anyone; it will be either well-accomplished, accomplished, or to be accomplished.
m.7.2.14.69: Imparted by a guru who has attained perfection, it is called well-accomplished (susiddha); but if given by one not perfected, it is merely accomplished-to-be-accomplished (siddha-sādhya).
m.7.2.14.70: Whether practised to perfection or not, it surely succeeds, no doubt, for one endowed with exceeding faith in me, in the mantra and likewise in the guru.
m.7.2.14.71: Therefore, abandoning other mantras, which are fraught with danger on account of the requirements of eligibility, the wise man should resort directly to the supreme vidyā, the Pañcākṣarī.
m.7.2.14.72: When other mantras are accomplished, this mantra is not thereby accomplished; but when this great mantra is accomplished, those too become accomplished.
m.7.2.14.73: Just as, O Maheśvarī, even when the gods are attained I am not attained, but when I am attained they are attained—the same rule holds for these mantras.
m.7.2.14.74: The defects that belong to all other mantras do not arise in this one at all, since this mantra operates without regard to caste and the like.
m.7.2.14.75: Even so, one should not rashly employ it for petty ends or against adversaries, for this mantra is of great power.
m.7.2.14.76: Upamanyu said: Thus the procedure of the Pañcākṣara, just as it is, was told directly to Mahādevī by Mahādeva, the trident-bearer, for the welfare of the worlds.
m.7.2.14.77: Whoever recites this with devotion, or listens to it attentively, is freed from all sins and attains the supreme goal.
m.7.2.14.iti: Thus ends the fourteenth adhyāya, named The glory of the five-syllabled mantra, in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the seventh saṃhitā, the Vāyavīya-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.7.2.15.1: Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: O Blessed One, O Lord, you have told me the greatness of the mantra and the procedure for its application, just as if it were the Veda itself.
m.7.2.15.2: Now I wish to hear about the supreme Śaiva rite of consecration; in the account of receiving the mantra it was only hinted at a little, not explained in detail.
m.7.2.15.3: Upamanyu said: Well then, I shall tell you of the consecration, supreme and holy, which purifies all sins, as expounded by Śiva.
m.7.2.15.4: Because through it a man becomes properly qualified for worship and the rest, it is called saṃskāra; it is the purification of the six paths.
m.7.2.15.5: Since by it knowledge is given (dīyate) and the bondage of fetters is destroyed (kṣīyate), this very saṃskāra is also called dīkṣā.
m.7.2.15.6: In the Śaiva scripture, initiation is taught by Śiva, the Supreme Self, as threefold: Śāmbhavī, Śāktī and Māntrī.
m.7.2.15.7: By the mere glance of the guru, by his touch, or even by his speech, there instantly arises in a creature an awareness that brings about the destruction of the fetters.
m.7.2.15.8: That initiation is called Śāmbhavī; it is again divided in two—intense and more intense—according to the difference in the destruction of the fetters.
m.7.2.15.9: That by which liberation comes at once is held to be the more intense; the intense one completely purifies the sins of a man while he is still living.
m.7.2.15.10: The Śāktī initiation, consisting of knowledge, is performed by the guru entering the disciple's body by the path of yoga, with the eye of knowledge.
m.7.2.15.11: The Māntrī initiation, consisting of ritual action, preceded by the fire-pit and the maṇḍala, is to be performed externally by the guru, for those disciples of slow and slower receptivity.
m.7.2.15.12: The disciple deserves grace in accordance with the descent of divine power, because, in brief, following Śaiva dharma has that as its root.
m.7.2.15.13: Where the power has not descended, there no purification arises—neither knowledge, nor Śaiva conduct, nor liberation, nor attainments.
m.7.2.15.14: Therefore, having carefully observed the signs of an abundant descent of power, the guru should purify the disciple either by knowledge or by ritual.
m.7.2.15.15: He who out of delusion acts otherwise, that foolish one perishes. Therefore the guru should examine the disciple in every way.
m.7.2.15.16: The mark of the descent of power is the arising of awakening and bliss, because that supreme Power has the form of awakening and bliss.
m.7.2.15.17: The sign of bliss and awakening is transformations of the inner faculty, such as appear as trembling, horripilation, and changes in the voice, eyes and limbs.
m.7.2.15.18: The disciple too should examine the guru by these signs, as seen in those in contact with him, those associated with him in Śiva-worship and the like, or those devoted to him.
m.7.2.15.19: Since the disciple is the one to be taught, he has reason for reverence toward the guru; therefore with every effort he should show reverence to the guru.
m.7.2.15.20: He who is the guru is declared to be Śiva; he who is Śiva is known as the guru. Or rather, the guru is Śiva himself, abiding in the form of knowledge.
