m.7.2.31.109: Next Brahmā, a form of the God of gods, lord of the earth-sphere, possessing lordship of sixty-four qualities, established in the principle of intellect (buddhi-tattva),
m.7.2.31.110: without qualities, mixed with qualities, and likewise pure quality alone; the god of changeless nature, thereafter, first, common in action,
m.7.2.31.111: and of uncommon actions in the sequence of creation, maintenance and dissolution; thus divided threefold, fourfold and again fivefold,
m.7.2.31.112: worshipped together with his followers in the fourth enclosure of Śambhu, dear to Śiva, attached to Śiva, delighting in the worship of Śiva's feet —
m.7.2.31.113: honouring the command of Śiva and Śivā, may he bestow auspiciousness on me. Hiraṇyagarbha, the lord of the world, Virāṭ, Kāla and Puruṣa,
m.7.2.31.114: Sanatkumāra, Sanaka, Sananda and Sanātana, and the lords of creatures, Dakṣa and the others, sons of Brahmā,
m.7.2.31.115: the eleven with their wives, and Dharma and Saṅkalpa too — these, delighting in Śiva's worship, wholly devoted to Śiva,
m.7.2.31.116: all subject to Śiva's command — may they bestow auspiciousness on me. Likewise the four Vedas together with the Itihāsas and Purāṇas,
m.7.2.31.117: the Dharmaśāstras, accompanied by the Vedic sciences, mutually non-contradictory in meaning, expounding the nature of Śiva —
m.7.2.31.118: honouring the command of Śiva and Śivā, may they bestow auspiciousness on me. Next Rudra, Mahādeva, the weightier form of Śambhu,
m.7.2.31.119: lord of the sphere of fire, the master possessing the sovereignty of Puruṣa, endowed with the self-identity of Śiva, without qualities yet of the nature of the three qualities,
m.7.2.31.120: purely sāttvika, and also rājasa and tāmasa; at first delighting in changelessness, but thereafter of uniform modification,
m.7.2.31.121: He is of unique deeds, distinct from the others in carrying out creation and the rest; the one who cut off even Brahmā's head, who is both his father and his son.
m.7.2.31.122: Father and also son, controller even of Viṣṇu, the constant enlightener of both of them, the gracious Lord.
m.7.2.31.123: Rudra, who abides within and outside the cosmic egg, lord of both worlds, dear to Śiva, devoted to Śiva, delighting in the worship of Śiva's feet —
m.7.2.31.124: — placing Śiva's command foremost, may he grant me auspiciousness. His Brahman mantras and six limbs, and likewise the group of eight Vidyeśas,
m.7.2.31.125: and the four distinct forms headed by Śiva, worshippers of Śiva — Śiva, Bhava, Hara, and also Mṛḍa as the other — placing Śiva's command foremost, may they grant me auspiciousness.
m.7.2.31.126: Next, Viṣṇu, the supreme body of Maheśa Śiva himself, directly the lord of the water principle, established in the state of the Unmanifest,
m.7.2.31.127: beyond the guṇas, yet abounding in sattva, and likewise consisting of guṇa alone; identifying himself with the unchanging, whose transformation is shared by the three,
m.7.2.31.128: of unique deeds, distinct in carrying out creation and the rest, vying even with Svayambhū Brahmā born from Śiva's right side,
m.7.2.31.129: directly created by the primal Brahmā and yet also his creator; abiding within and outside the cosmic egg, Viṣṇu, lord of the two worlds,
m.7.2.31.130: slayer of the asuras, bearer of the discus, and likewise the younger brother of Śakra, who appeared here in ten forms on the pretext of Bhṛgu's curse,
m.7.2.31.131: who of his own will descended upon the earth to check the burden of the earth; of immeasurable strength, master of māyā, deluding the world by māyā,
m.7.2.31.132: taking the form of Mahāviṣṇu or else of Sadāviṣṇu, ever worshipped by the Vaiṣṇavas on a seat made of the three forms,
m.7.2.31.133: dear to Śiva, devoted to Śiva, delighting in the worship of Śiva's feet — placing Śiva's command foremost, may he grant me auspiciousness.
m.7.2.31.134: Vāsudeva, Aniruddha, Pradyumna, and after them Saṅkarṣaṇa are declared to be the four forms of Hari.
m.7.2.31.135: Matsya, Kūrma, Varāha, Nārasiṃha, then Vāmana, the three Rāmas, likewise Kṛṣṇa, and Viṣṇu with the horse's face,
m.7.2.31.136: the discus, weapon of Nārāyaṇa, the conch Pāñcajanya and the bow Śārṅga — honouring the command of Śiva and Śivā, may they grant me auspiciousness.
m.7.2.31.137: Prabhā, Sarasvatī, Gaurī and Lakṣmī, imbued with devotion to Śiva — at the bidding of Śiva and Śivā, may these grant me auspiciousness.
m.7.2.31.138: Indra, Agni, Yama, Nirṛti, Varuṇa, Vāyu, Soma, Kubera, and likewise Īśāna bearing the trident —
m.7.2.31.139: all devoted to Śiva's worship, imbued with true devotion to Śiva — honouring the command of Śiva and Śivā, may they grant me auspiciousness.
m.7.2.31.140: The trident, the thunderbolt, likewise the axe and the arrow, the sword, noose and goad, and the Pināka, the best of weapons —
m.7.2.31.141: these divine weapons of the God and the Goddess — honouring the command of Śiva and Śivā, may they always protect me.
m.7.2.31.142: The god bearing the form of a bull, son of Surabhi, of great might, rivalling the fire called Vaḍavā, surrounded by the five mother-cows,
m.7.2.31.143: who through austerity attained the status of vehicle of the two supreme lords — placing their command foremost, may he grant my desire.
m.7.2.31.144: Nandā, Sunandā, Surabhi, Suśīlā and Sumanā — these five mother-cows dwell in Śiva's world,
m.7.2.31.145: ever intent on devotion to Śiva, wholly given to Śiva's worship — by the command of Śiva and Śivā alone, may they grant what I desire.
m.7.2.31.146: The Kṣetrapāla, of great splendour, resembling a dark rain-cloud, his face fearsome with fangs, radiant with quivering red lips,
m.7.2.31.147: with red, upstanding hair, glorious, eyes crooked with frowning brows, three round red eyes, adorned with the moon and serpents,
m.7.2.31.148: naked, his hands raised holding trident, noose, sword and skull; Bhairava, surrounded by Bhairavas, Siddhas and Yoginīs,
m.7.2.31.149: who, seated in every sacred field, stands as protector of the good, supremely intent on bowing to Śiva, imbued with true devotion to Śiva,
m.7.2.31.150: especially protecting those who take refuge in Śiva like his own sons — honouring the command of Śiva and Śivā, may he grant me auspiciousness.
m.7.2.31.151: Tālajaṅgha and the others, the four worshipped in his first enclosure — honouring the command of Śiva and Śivā, may they protect me.
m.7.2.31.152: And Bhairava and the others who surround him on all sides — may they too favour me, out of reverence for Śiva's command.
m.7.2.31.153: The sages headed by Nārada, divine and worshipped even by the gods; the Sādhyas, the Nāgas, and the gods who dwell in Janaloka;
m.7.2.31.154: those whose offices have ceased, dwelling in Maharloka; the seven sages, and others too, together with the hosts of the celestial-car dwellers —
m.7.2.31.155: all devoted to Śiva's worship, obedient to Śiva's command — by the command of Śiva and Śivā, may they grant me what I long for.
m.7.2.31.156: The four classes of divine beings from the Gandharvas down to the Piśācas; the Siddhas, Vidyādharas and the others, and whatever other sky-rangers there are;
m.7.2.31.157: the Asuras and Rākṣasas dwelling in the nether regions, the serpent-lords headed by Ananta, the birds headed by Vainateya (Garuḍa);
m.7.2.31.158: the Kūṣmāṇḍas, Pretas and Vetālas, the Grahas and other hosts of Bhūtas, the Ḍākinīs, Yoginīs, and Śākinīs of like kind;
m.7.2.31.159: sacred fields, gardens, houses and the like, holy fords and shrines, islands, oceans, rivers, other great streams, and lakes;
m.7.2.31.160: the mountains headed by Sumeru, the forests all around, animals, birds, trees, worms, insects and the like, and wild beasts —
m.7.2.31.161: All the worlds as well, the lords of the worlds, the cosmic eggs together with their coverings, the quarters, and the ten elephants of the directions,
m.7.2.31.162: the letters, the words, the mantras, and the tattvas together with their presiding lords, the Rudras who uphold the cosmic egg, and the other Rudras along with their Śaktis,
m.7.2.31.163: and whatever in this world is seen, inferred or heard — may all of them grant my desire, by the command of Śiva and Śivā alone.
m.7.2.31.164: Then the supreme Śaiva knowledge, which releases the bound souls from their fetters, divine, called Pañcārtha, which lies beyond the knowledge of the bound,
m.7.2.31.165: and the scripture called Śivadharma, and its sequel called Śivadharmottara, the Purāṇa known as Śaiva and as Śivadharma, equal in authority to the Veda,
m.7.2.31.166: and the Śaiva Āgamas, and the others of four kinds beginning with the Kāmika — honoured and worshipped here without distinction from Śiva and Śivā,
m.7.2.31.167: commanded by those two alone for the fulfilment of my intended aim — may they approve this rite as fruitful and well performed.
m.7.2.31.168: The teachers from Śveta down to Nakulīśa together with their disciples, the gurus of their lineage, and especially my own gurus,
m.7.2.31.169: the Śaivas and the Māheśvaras devoted to knowledge and ritual action — may they approve this rite as fruitful and well performed.
m.7.2.31.170: All the worldly Brāhmaṇas, the Kṣatriyas and the Vaiśyas in due order, knowers of the truth of the Vedas and Vedāṅgas, experts in all the śāstras,
m.7.2.31.171: the Sāṅkhyas, the Vaiśeṣikas, the Yogins and the Naiyāyika men, the Sauras, the Brāhmas, the Raudras, the Vaiṣṇavas and other men,
m.7.2.31.172: all the cultured and the distinguished, restrained by Śiva's command — may they approve this rite which accomplishes my intended aim.
m.7.2.31.173: The Śaivas who stand on the Siddhānta path, the Śaiva Pāśupatas likewise, the Śaivas who bear the Great Vow, and other Śaivas, the Kāpālikas —
m.7.2.31.174: keepers of Śiva's command, worthy of worship even by me by Śiva's ordinance — may they all favour me and proclaim the rite fruitful.
m.7.2.31.175: Those established in the Dakṣiṇa knowledge and those who follow the Dakṣiṇa and Uttara paths — may they act without opposition to the mantra of me who seek the highest good.
m.7.2.31.176: Unbelievers, the deceitful, the ungrateful, the tāmasic, heretics and the exceedingly sinful — may they keep far away from me.
m.7.2.31.177: What need is there here of praising many? Whoever at all are believers — may they all favour me, and may the good proclaim auspiciousness.
m.7.2.31.178: Salutation to you, Śiva, together with Ambā and with your sons, the primal cause, enveloped by the manifest universe in the form of the five coverings.
m.7.2.31.179: Having said this and prostrated on the ground like a staff before Śiva and Śivā, one should recite the five-syllabled mantra no fewer than one hundred and eight times.
m.7.2.31.180: Likewise, having recited the Śakti mantra and made the offering of it, and having begged pardon of the Lord, one should complete the remainder of the worship.
m.7.2.31.181: This most meritorious hymn is dear to the hearts of Śiva and Śivā; it grants all desires and is directly the sole means to enjoyment and liberation.
m.7.2.31.182: Whoever recites this daily, or listens to it with a concentrated mind, quickly shakes off his sins and attains union with Śiva.
m.7.2.31.183: The slayer of a cow, the ungrateful, the killer of a hero or of an embryo, one who kills a refugee, one who betrays a friend's trust,
m.7.2.31.184: one of wicked and sinful conduct, the slayer of a mother or of a father — by reciting this hymn he is freed from each such sin.
m.7.2.31.185: In fears that portend great calamity, such as bad dreams, if one recites this, one will not suffer calamity from them.
m.7.2.31.186: Long life, health, prosperity and whatever else is desired — a man who persists in reciting this hymn obtains all that.
m.7.2.31.187: The fruit described is that of reciting the Śiva hymn without worship; the fruit of reciting it after worship cannot be told.
m.7.2.31.188: Let this gaining of fruits be set aside: when this is recited, the God together with Ambikā, merely on hearing it, stands present in the sky.
m.7.2.31.189: Therefore, having worshipped the God of gods together with Umā in the sky, one should stand with joined palms and recite this hymn.
m.7.2.31.iti: Thus ends the thirty-first adhyāya, named The great hymn to Śiva, in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the seventh saṃhitā, the Vāyavīya-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.7.2.32.1: Upamanyu said: O Kṛṣṇa, I have told you this supreme rite, which grants success here and in the next world and consists of a combination of ritual action, austerity, japa and meditation.
m.7.2.32.2: Now I shall describe the great rite for Śaiva men which yields fruit in this very world, consisting of worship, fire-oblation, japa, meditation, austerity and gifts.
m.7.2.32.3: In this, the best knower of the meaning of mantras should first perfect the mantra, because a rite producing visible success does not otherwise yield fruit.
m.7.2.32.4: Even one who has perfected the mantra, if he is wise, should not rashly perform a rite whose fruit is obstructed by some powerful unseen force.
m.7.2.32.5: For that obstruction, however, an expiation can be made here. Having examined it through omens and the like, he should first perform the expiation.
m.7.2.32.6: The man who, out of delusion, performs a rite meant for worldly fruit in any other way will not obtain its fruit by it, and will become an object of ridicule.
m.7.2.32.7: One lacking confidence should never perform a rite of visible fruit; such a person is indeed without faith, and one without faith does not attain the fruit.
m.7.2.32.8: Even if the rite is fruitless, the fault is not the god's, since for men who act as prescribed the fruit is seen in this very world.
m.7.2.32.9: The practitioner who has perfected the mantra, removed the obstruction, and is confident and faithful obtains that fruit by performing the rite.
m.7.2.32.10: Moreover, to obtain that fruit he should be devoted to celibacy, and at night he should eat sacrificial food, or milk-rice, or fruits.
m.7.2.32.11: Whatever is forbidden, such as violence, he should not do even in thought. He should always be pure, his limbs smeared with ash and well attired.
m.7.2.32.12: Having thus become observant of conduct, on an auspicious day favourable to himself, in a place with the characteristics described earlier, adorned with garlands of flowers and the like,
m.7.2.32.13: having duly smeared the ground with cow-dung over an area of at least one hasta, he should draw an auspicious lotus, shining with its own radiance,
m.7.2.32.14: made of refined gold, eight-petalled, with filaments, furnished with a pericarp in the middle, adorned with all gems,
m.7.2.32.15: and furnished with a stalk matching its own form. On a bulb likewise made of gold, properly according to rule,
m.7.2.32.16: and there again conceiving mentally all the powers beginning with aṇimā, having installed according to rule a liṅga with a pedestal, bearing the proper marks, made of gems, or of gold, or of crystal,
m.7.2.32.17: having invoked the imperishable god there, together with Ambā and his attendants, he should worship him. There the Maheśvara form of the Lord who possesses form is to be visualised:
m.7.2.32.18: four-armed, four-faced, decorated with all ornaments, clothed in a tiger skin, with a slightly smiling face,
m.7.2.32.19: with hands showing the boon-giving and fear-dispelling gestures, and likewise holding a deer and an axe. Or else it may be visualised as eight-armed, according to the meditator's preference.
m.7.2.32.20: Then it holds the trident, battle-axe, sword and thunderbolt on the right, and likewise on the left the noose and goad, a shield and a serpent.
m.7.2.32.21: Its radiance resembles the rising sun, and each face has three eyes. Its eastern face is gentle, with a lustre matching its own form;
m.7.2.32.22: the southern resembles a dark rain-cloud and is terrible to behold; the northern is coral-coloured, adorned with dark locks;
m.7.2.32.23: the western shines like the full moon, gentle, bearing the crescent of the moon. Seated on its lap is the supreme Śakti of Maheśvara,
m.7.2.32.24: known as Mahālakṣmī, dark-complexioned and enchanting to all. Having made the image of such a form and having duly performed the sakalīkaraṇa in order,
m.7.2.32.25: then, having invoked the embodied supreme Cause, he should worship him. For his bath he should prepare there the pañcagavya of a tawny cow,
m.7.2.32.26: the pañcāmṛta, and especially whole seeds. Having made a maṇḍala in front, adorned with gem-powders and the like,
m.7.2.32.27: he should place the Īśāna pot on the pericarp, and afterwards arrange the Sadya and other pots around it.
m.7.2.32.28: Then he should place the eight pots of the Vidyeśas in order, beginning from the east; having filled them with water from sacred fords and wound thread round them as before,
m.7.2.32.29: having put in sacred substances with mantras and according to procedure, and having covered them all around with fine silk or other cloth,
m.7.2.32.30: and having placed the mantra on each, preceded by the respective mantras — when the time of bathing has come, amid the sounds of all auspicious instruments,
m.7.2.32.31: he should bathe the Supreme Lord with the pañcagavya and the rest. Then the kuśa-water and the others, and also the gold- and gem-waters,
m.7.2.32.32: prepared with fragrances, flowers and the like and consecrated with mantras — taking them up one after another with the mantra, he should bathe Maheśvara with each of them in order,
m.7.2.32.33: and he should perform the worship with fragrances, flowers and so on, and lamps. The unguent should be at least one pala and at most eleven palas.
m.7.2.32.34: One should offer flowers of gold and gems, auspicious and fragrant ones, blue lotuses and other water-lilies, and bilva leaves in great number,
m.7.2.32.35: and red and white lotuses for Śambhu. The incense is made from black aloe-wood, with camphor, ghee and guggulu;
m.7.2.32.36: the lamps are prepared with ghee from a tawny cow, with wicks of camphor. The five Brahma-mantras, the six limbs, and the enclosure deities are to be worshipped.
m.7.2.32.37: The food-offering is a great caru cooked in milk, with jaggery and ghee; and the drinking water is scented with pāṭala flowers, water-lilies, lotuses and the like;
m.7.2.32.38: well-prepared betel with the five fragrant spices; and especially ornaments made of gold and gems,
m.7.2.32.39: and garments that are colourful, fine, new and beautiful to look at are to be offered, together with singing, instrumental music and the like.
m.7.2.32.40: The japa of the root mantra is one lakh as the highest count; and the worship here is at least once and at most three times, according to the fruit desired.
m.7.2.32.41: The oblation should number at least ten, and at most a hundred, for each substance. In rites of killing, driving away and the like, Śiva is to be meditated upon in his terrible form.
m.7.2.32.42: In a rite for pacification or for prosperity, Śambhu is to be meditated upon in a gentle form, in the Śiva-liṅga, in the Śiva-fire, and in other images as well.
m.7.2.32.43: In rites of killing and the like, the ladle and spoon should be made of iron; elsewhere, in all rites of pacification and the rest, they should be of gold.
m.7.2.32.44: With dūrvā grass mixed with ghee and cow's milk, likewise with honey, with caru together with ghee, or with milk alone —
m.7.2.32.45: — one should offer oblations for conquering death; with sesame for the alleviation of disease; and with ghee and milk, or with lotuses alone,
m.7.2.32.46: one desiring prosperity should offer oblations for the removal of great poverty. One seeking to bring others under control should offer jāti flowers together with ghee.
m.7.2.32.47: With ghee and karavīra flowers a twice-born should perform the rite of attraction; with oil one should perform driving away, and again with honey, immobilisation.
m.7.2.32.48: Immobilization is done also with mustard, but felling with garlic; striking is done with the blood of both the donkey and the camel.
m.7.2.32.49: For killing and driving away one should use rohi seeds mixed with sesame; and one should perform the rite of causing enmity with the oil of the lāṅgalaka plant.
m.7.2.32.50: Binding, and also immobilizing an army, is done with rohi seed, and with oblation-substances mixed throughout with red mustard.
m.7.2.32.51: In a hostile (ābhicārika) rite one should offer oils pressed by a hand-mill, together with kaṭukī husks and cotton seeds.
m.7.2.32.52: In a hostile rite one should offer mustard seeds mixed with oil. Milk grants relief from fever and likewise yields the fruit of good fortune.
m.7.2.32.53: An oblation with honey, ghee and curd combined brings every accomplishment; so too with milk and rice grains, or with caru alone.
m.7.2.32.54: Pacification or prosperity is achieved, and especially subjugation and attraction, through an oblation with the seven substances beginning with the fuel-sticks.
m.7.2.32.55: Oblation with bilva leaves especially brings subjugation, attraction and prosperity, and likewise grants victory over an enemy.
m.7.2.32.56: In pacification rites the fuel-sticks are of palāśa, khadira and the like; in cruel rites, those from karavīra and arka; and thorny ones in rites of conflict.
m.7.2.32.57: One who is tranquil should perform the pacification rite, and especially the prosperity rite; but one who is pitiless and angry in mind would perform the hostile rite.
m.7.2.32.58: In an extremely dire situation, if there is no other remedy, one may perform the hostile rite directed at an assailant (ātatāyin).
m.7.2.32.59: One should not perform a hostile rite directed at the ruler of one's own realm, nor at anyone who is a believer, highly righteous, or worthy of honour,
m.7.2.32.60: — one should not perform it directed at him even if he is an assailant; nor at anyone at all who has taken refuge in Śiva in mind, deed or speech.
m.7.2.32.61: Having performed a hostile rite directed at the ruler of one's own realm, or at one who has taken refuge in Śiva, a man falls to ruin at once.
m.7.2.32.62: Therefore, if one desires one's own happiness, one should not harm the protector of one's own realm, or any devotee of Śiva, by hostile rites and the like.
m.7.2.32.63: And having performed killing and the like directed at anyone else, one should, filled with remorse, perform expiation.
m.7.2.32.64: Poor or rich, one may perform this even on a Bāṇa-liṅga, or on a self-manifested liṅga, or on one established by sages, or a Vedic one.
m.7.2.32.65: In the absence of gold and gems, and when unable to acquire them, one should perform this mentally, or with substitute substances.
m.7.2.32.66: One who is capable in some part but incapable in another part — he too, if he performs according to his capacity, attains the fruit.
m.7.2.32.67: Where, even when this rite has been performed, the fruit is not seen, one should repeat it twice or thrice; then the fruit is certainly seen.
m.7.2.32.68: Whatever excellent material was used in the worship — gold, gems and the like — all of it one should give to the guru, and the fee (dakṣiṇā) separately from that.
m.7.2.32.69: If he does not want it, one should offer all of it to Śiva, or to Śiva's devotees; it is not to be given to others.
m.7.2.32.70: One who accomplishes the rite himself by his own ability, without relying on a guru or others, should also act in this way here; he should not take the materials back for himself.
m.7.2.32.71: The fool who out of greed takes for himself the excellent materials that formed part of the worship will not obtain what he desires; there is no doubt about this.
m.7.2.32.72: As for the liṅga that was worshipped, one may take it oneself or not; if one takes it, then it should be worshipped daily, either by oneself or by another.
m.7.2.32.73: For one who performs this rite exactly as prescribed, without lapse, the fruit never fails; so what further inducement is needed?
m.7.2.32.74: Nevertheless I shall describe in brief the supreme accomplishment of the rite. Even one assailed by enemies or by diseases in many ways,
m.7.2.32.75: or even one gone into the mouth of death, is released without harm. The utterly wretched becomes honoured; the destitute becomes like Vaiśravaṇa (Kubera).
m.7.2.32.76: Even the ugly becomes like Kāma; even the old becomes youthful; an enemy at once becomes a friend; an opponent becomes a servant.
m.7.2.32.77: What was nectar becomes poison for his foes, and even poison becomes nectar; even the ocean becomes dry land, and dry land becomes the sea.
m.7.2.32.78: A chasm becomes a mountain, and that mountain becomes a chasm; fire becomes a lotus-pond, and a lake becomes fire.
m.7.2.32.79: What was a garden becomes a forest, and that forest becomes a garden; a petty deer becomes a lion, and a lion becomes a pet deer.
m.7.2.32.80: Women come to him like eager lovers; Lakṣmī (fortune) becomes faithful; speech becomes like a willing servant; and fame roams everywhere like a courtesan.
m.7.2.32.81: For the one who has accomplished this rite, the intellect becomes like one who moves at his own will; the mind becomes like a diamond needle; his power becomes like a mighty wind; his strength becomes like a rutting elephant.
m.7.2.32.82: Any undertaking set up on the enemies' side becomes paralysed despite their great efforts; all of the enemies' own friends turn into the enemy's camp against them.
m.7.2.32.83: The enemies, together with their kinsmen, become like corpses even while alive; and he himself, even if fallen into calamity, is freed from misfortune and indeed becomes like nectar (immortal).
m.7.2.32.84: Even unwholesome food constantly consumed becomes like an elixir; and love-delight, though enjoyed incessantly, ever feels new.
m.7.2.32.85: Everything, the future and so on, becomes as clear as an āmalaka fruit held in the hand; even the powers beginning with aṇimā (minuteness) come as spontaneous fruits.
m.7.2.32.86: What is the use of saying much here? When this rite has been accomplished, there is nothing unattainable in the fulfilment of all desires and aims.
m.7.2.32.iti: Thus ends the thirty-second adhyāya, named Rites for attainments in this world, in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the seventh saṃhitā, the Vāyavīya-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.7.2.33.1: Upamanyu said: Next I shall explain the rite that is purely for the next world. There is no act equal to it in the three worlds.
m.7.2.33.2: It is endowed with surpassing merit and has been performed by all the gods—by Brahmā, by Viṣṇu, and especially by Rudra;
m.7.2.33.3: by Indra and the other guardians of the worlds, by the nine planets beginning with the Sun, by the great sages who know Brahman, such as Viśvāmitra and Vasiṣṭha;
m.7.2.33.4: by Śveta, Agastya, Dadhīca and others, and by us who have taken refuge in Śiva; by the lords of the gaṇas such as Nandīśvara, Mahākāla and Bhṛṅgīśa;
m.7.2.33.5: by the Daityas dwelling in Pātāla, by the great serpents such as Śeṣa, by Siddhas, Yakṣas and Gandharvas, by Rākṣasas, Bhūtas and Piśācas—
m.7.2.33.6: this rite was performed by all of them, and each attained his own position. By this rite all the gods attained their divinity.
m.7.2.33.7: Brahmā attained his Brahmā-hood, Viṣṇu attained his Viṣṇu-hood, Rudra attained his Rudra-hood, and Indra attained his Indra-hood.
m.7.2.33.8: And Gaṇeśa attained his lordship of the gaṇas by this rite. Having bathed the liṅga—Śiva and Śivā—with water mixed with white sandal, having worshipped it with white, fully blossomed lotuses and bowed down,
m.7.2.33.9: one should there make a beautiful lotus-seat possessing the proper marks—if one has the wealth, of gold and the like, or of jewels and the like, according to one's means.
m.7.2.33.10: In the middle of its cluster of filaments one should place a small liṅga, the size of a thumb, beautiful, auspicious, made of all fragrant substances.
m.7.2.33.11: Having placed it on the right (south), one should worship it with bilva leaves. On the southern side one should offer aguru, and on the west red arsenic;
m.7.2.33.12: on the north one should offer sandal, and on the east yellow orpiment. One should also worship with fragrant, lovely and variegated flowers.
m.7.2.33.13: One should offer incense of black aguru mixed with guggulu all around, and present very fine, unfolded garments.
m.7.2.33.14: One should have milk-rice mixed with ghee and ghee lamps offered. Having offered everything with the mantra, one should then circumambulate.
m.7.2.33.15: Having bowed with devotion to the Lord of the gods and praised him, at the end one should ask forgiveness. Then one should offer the liṅga together with all the offerings,
m.7.2.33.16: to Śiva with the Śiva-mantra, resorting to the southern form (Dakṣiṇāmūrti). Whoever thus daily worships the auspicious liṅga made of the five fragrant substances,
m.7.2.33.17: freed from all sins, is honoured in Śiva's world. This is the supreme secret vow, the great vow of the Śiva-liṅga.
m.7.2.33.18: It has been told to you, a devotee; it should not be given to just anyone. It should be given to devotees of Śiva—so it was declared by Śiva of old.
m.7.2.33.iti: Thus ends the thirty-third adhyāya, named The rules of rites for the world beyond, in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the seventh saṃhitā, the Vāyavīya-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.7.2.34.1: Upamanyu said: Whatever attainment has been proclaimed here as arising from the obligatory, the occasional and the optional rites, all of it is obtained at once through the installation of a liṅga or an image.
m.7.2.34.2: The whole world consists of the liṅga; everything is established in the liṅga. Therefore, when the liṅga is installed, everything becomes established.
m.7.2.34.3: Whether by Brahmā, by Viṣṇu, by Rudra or by anyone else — none secures the stability of his own position by setting aside the installation of the liṅga.
m.7.2.34.4: What else need be said here as the reason for installation, since even Śiva himself installed the liṅga of Viśveśvara?
m.7.2.34.5: Therefore, with every effort, for well-being here and hereafter, one should install a liṅga of the Supreme Lord, or else an image.
m.7.2.34.6: Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: What is this that is called the liṅga? How is Maheśvara the bearer of the liṅga? How does he have the nature of the liṅga, and why is Śiva worshipped in it?
m.7.2.34.7: Upamanyu said: The Unmanifest is called the liṅga — the origin and dissolution of the three guṇas, without beginning or end, which is the material cause of the universe.
m.7.2.34.8: That alone is primordial Nature (mūlaprakṛti) and Māyā, whose nature is like space. From that alone this world of moving and unmoving beings has arisen.
m.7.2.34.9: That world is threefold: impure, pure, and pure-impure. From it arise Śiva, Maheśa, Rudra, Viṣṇu and the Grandsire (Brahmā),
m.7.2.34.10: and the elements together with the senses, are born, and they dissolve into it by Śiva's command. For this very reason Śiva is called the liṅga-possessor, since he commands the liṅga.
m.7.2.34.11: For, unbidden by him, it cannot of itself become capable of any effect; and the universe born from it dissolves back into that very liṅga.
m.7.2.34.12: It is by this that it has the nature of the liṅga, and not by anything else. And the liṅga is the body of Śiva and Śivā, since it is presided over by the two of them.
m.7.2.34.13: Therefore one should always worship Śiva together with Ambā there. The pedestal of the liṅga is the Great Goddess; the liṅga is Maheśvara himself.
m.7.2.34.14: By worshipping these two alone, both he and she are worshipped. In ultimate truth, however, they do not have the liṅga as their body.
m.7.2.34.15: For those two are utterly pure; it is called their body only figuratively. That very liṅga is the supreme Śakti of Śiva, the Supreme Self.
m.7.2.34.16: When the Śakti receives his command, she brings forth the moving and unmoving world. His greatness cannot be told even in hundreds of years,
m.7.2.34.17: by which even Brahmā and Nārāyaṇa were bewildered in the beginning. Long ago, when the dissolution of these three worlds had come,
m.7.2.34.18: Viṣṇu, lying on his bed upon the waters, slept happily, undisturbed. By chance Brahmā, the Grandsire of the worlds, came there.
m.7.2.34.19: He saw the lotus-eyed one sleeping undisturbed. Deluded by Śambhu's Māyā, the Grandsire spoke to Viṣṇu.
m.7.2.34.20: Striking Mādhava in anger and rousing him, he said: Tell me, who are you? Struck by that sharp blow of the hand, he at once
m.7.2.34.21: awoke, rose from his bed and saw Parameṣṭhin (Brahmā). Inwardly enraged, yet outwardly as though unangered, Hari spoke to him:
m.7.2.34.22: Where have you come from, child? Why are you agitated? Tell me. Hearing these words of Viṣṇu, which suggested his own superiority,
m.7.2.34.23: Brahmā, bound in enmity by rajas, again spoke to him: Why do you call me child, as a teacher would his own pupil?
m.7.2.34.24: Do you not know me, the Lord, whose creation this manifold world is? Dividing myself threefold, I create this and then it is protected by me;
m.7.2.34.25: and I destroy it. No other creator than me exists in the world. When this was said, the imperishable Viṣṇu also spoke to Brahmā:
m.7.2.34.26: I alone am the first maker of this, its destroyer and its protector. You too descended long ago from my own imperishable body.
m.7.2.34.27: By my command you, making yourself threefold, create the three worlds, protect them, and at the end withdraw them and create them again.
m.7.2.34.28: You have forgotten Nārāyaṇa, the flawless Lord of the world; thus you disregard me, who am directly your own father.
m.7.2.34.29: There is no fault of yours in this; you are deluded by my Māyā. By my grace this delusion of yours will soon depart.
m.7.2.34.30: Hear the truth, O four-faced one: I indeed am the Lord of all gods — creator, sustainer and destroyer. There is no lord equal to me.
m.7.2.34.31: Thus a dispute arose between Brahmā and Viṣṇu, and there ensued a great, terrible, hair-raising battle,
m.7.2.34.32: as the two, bound in enmity by rajas, struck each other fiercely with their fists. To remove the pride of those two gods and to awaken them,
m.7.2.34.33: a wondrous liṅga of the Lord appeared between them, rich with thousands of garlands of flames, immeasurable and incomparable,
m.7.2.34.34: free from decrease and growth, devoid of beginning, middle and end. By its thousand flames Brahmā and Viṣṇu were bewildered.
m.7.2.34.35: Abandoning the fight, they then wondered, what is this? When its true nature did not become clear to them,
m.7.2.34.36: then they set out to examine its beginning and end.
m.7.2.34.37: There Brahmā, taking the form of a swan with wings on every side and becoming swift as mind and wind, went upward with great effort.
m.7.2.34.38: Nārāyaṇa too, the Self of the universe, assuming an immeasurable boar form like a mass of dark collyrium, went downward.
m.7.2.34.39: Thus for a thousand years Viṣṇu, the boar, hastened downward, yet did not see even a trace of the root of that liṅga.
m.7.2.34.40: For the same length of time the Grandsire went upward, wishing to know its end; utterly exhausted and not having seen the end, he fell down.
m.7.2.34.41: In the same way the blessed Viṣṇu, exhausted, his eyes full of agitation, quickly rose up from below with great hardship.
m.7.2.34.42: Then the two met each other, their glances wide with wonder; deluded by Śambhu's māyā, they did not know what was to be done and what was not.
m.7.2.34.43: Both, standing behind it, beside it and in front of it, bowed down and then pondered, what is the nature of this?
m.7.2.34.iti: Thus ends the thirty-fourth adhyāya, named The delusion of Hari and Vidhi, in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the seventh saṃhitā, the Vāyavīya-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.7.2.35.1: Upamanyu said: Then there appeared there, with resonance, Brahman marked by sound: the one-syllabled Brahman Om, which makes Brahman known.
m.7.2.35.2: Even that was at first not understood by Brahmā and likewise by Viṣṇu, because the minds of the two were obscured by rajas and tamas.
m.7.2.35.3: Then that single syllable became divided fourfold: into the three morae a, u, m, and beyond them the half-mora.
m.7.2.35.4: There the letter a rested on the southern side of the blazing liṅga, the letter u likewise on the northern, and the letter m in its middle.
m.7.2.35.5: The nāda consisting of the half-mora was heard at the top of the liṅga. Even when that praṇava, the supreme syllable, had then been divided,
m.7.2.35.6: those two gods understood nothing of the meaning of the division. Then the unmanifest praṇava underwent transformation in the form of the Vedas.
m.7.2.35.7: There the letter a became the Ṛk, the letter u the imperishable Yajus, the letter m became the Sāman, and the nāda the Atharvan śruti.
m.7.2.35.8: This Ṛk set forth its own meaning in brief: among the guṇas, rajas; among the forms, Brahmā, the first; and among the activities —
m.7.2.35.9: creation; among the worlds, the earth; among the tattvas, the imperishable Ātman; in the path of the kalās, Nivṛtti; and among the five Brahmans, Sadyojāta;
m.7.2.35.10: among the parts of the liṅga, the lower part; among the three causes, the one called bīja (seed); and among the powers beginning with aṇimā, the lordship of sixty-four qualities that pertains to buddhi.
m.7.2.35.11: Thus the whole world is pervaded by the Ṛk through these ten meanings. Then the Yajus set forth its own tenfold meaning:
m.7.2.35.12: among the guṇas, sattva; among the forms, Viṣṇu, the first; among the activities, preservation; among the worlds, the mid-space; and among the three tattvas, Vidyā;
m.7.2.35.13: among the kalā-paths, Pratiṣṭhā; among the five Brahmans, Vāmadeva; among the parts of the liṅga, the middle; and among the three causes, the yoni (womb);
m.7.2.35.14: and likewise the prākṛta lordship — hence the universe consists of the Yajus. Then the Sāman set forth its own meaning tenfold:
m.7.2.35.15: among the guṇas, tamas; among the forms, Rudra, the first; among the activities, dissolution in the three worlds; among the tattvas, Śiva, the highest;
m.7.2.35.16: among the kalās, Vidyā; and likewise among the five Brahmans, Aghora; among the parts of the liṅga, the part above the pedestal; among the three causes, the seed-bearer;
m.7.2.35.17: and likewise the pauruṣa lordship — thus the world is pervaded by the Sāman. Then the Atharvan declared its first meaning: being beyond the guṇas;
m.7.2.35.18: then, among the forms, Sadāśiva, Maheśvara himself; among the activities, of Śiva the supreme Self, though actionless,
m.7.2.35.19: the bestowal of grace on beings, by which creatures are liberated; among the worlds, that from which words turn back together with the mind —
m.7.2.35.20: above that, beyond the Unmanā world, the supramundane Soma-world, where the Lord Soma (he who is with Umā) ever dwells together with Umā;
m.7.2.35.21: above that, beyond the Unmanā world, reaching which one does not return; and among the kalās, Śānti, Śāntyatītā and Vyāpikā;
m.7.2.35.22: among the five Brahmans, Tatpuruṣa and likewise Īśāna; among the parts marked by nāda, the unsurpassed top of the liṅga,
m.7.2.35.23: where Śiva, alone and partless, is to be invoked and worshipped; then, among those tattvas, beyond bindu, beyond nāda, beyond śakti, and beyond the supreme beyond that,
m.7.2.35.24: the tattva beyond every tattva, in ultimate truth no tattva at all; among the causes, transcending the three — beyond the cause that agitates māyā,
m.7.2.35.25: beyond Ananta, beyond Śuddhavidyā, and beyond Maheśvara, the overlord of all the Vidyeśvaras, yet not beyond the supreme Sadāśiva,
m.7.2.35.26: beyond the god whose body is all mantras, endowed with the three śaktis, five-faced, ten-armed, himself both with and without parts;
m.7.2.35.27: beyond even him, beyond the supreme bindu, beyond the half-moon and the supreme beyond that; beyond the supreme Lord of the Night beyond that, and beyond the one called nāda and what is beyond it;
m.7.2.35.28: beyond the still higher Lord of Suṣumnā, beyond even the Lord of the Brahmarandhra, beyond what is higher than that, beyond Śakti, and beyond the Śiva-tattva —
m.7.2.35.29: it declared Śiva, the supreme cause itself, himself without cause, the ordainer of causes, the meditator and the object of meditation, imperishable,
m.7.2.35.30: abiding in the midst of the supreme ether, situated above the supreme Self, endowed with all lordship, lord of all, having no lord over him;
m.7.2.35.31: and beyond the lordship born of māyā, impure, human and the like, both lower and higher, to be abandoned, lying within the range of the impure path;
m.7.2.35.32: beyond that, beyond the higher-than-high lordship beginning with Śuddhavidyā and ending with Unmanā — the supreme lordship, primal beyond Unmanā, and beginningless,
m.7.2.35.33: boundless, dependent on no other, unsurpassable, steady. Thus, with meanings of ten kinds, this Atharvan śruti —
m.7.2.35.34: since it is the weightiest, therefore the universe is pervaded by the Atharvan. The Ṛgveda then said: This waking state is expressed by me,
m.7.2.35.35: by which I am ever the expresser of the ātma-tattva. The Yajurveda likewise said: The dream state is expressed by me,
m.7.2.35.36: since in me Vidyā, the knowable, is transformed into the form of what is to be enjoyed. And the Sāman said: What is called deep sleep — thus everything is expressed by me;
m.7.2.35.37: this is denoted by Śiva, the tāmasa one, who is my meaning. The Atharvan said: What is called the fourth (turīya), and also what is beyond the fourth,
m.7.2.35.38: is expressed by me; therefore I belong to the state beyond the paths. The triad constituted by the paths is designated Śiva, Vidyā and Ātman.
m.7.2.35.39: That triad of the three guṇas, attainable through the three Vedas, is to be purified by one who seeks the highest state. What lies beyond the paths, called turīya, is nirvāṇa, the supreme state;
m.7.2.35.40: and what is beyond that, because it is free of the guṇas, is the purifier of this path. The nāda that makes both known, and the nādānta, are of my nature.
m.7.2.35.41: Therefore, because I am independent as its meaning, the Supreme Lord is its principal sense. Whatever object exists, all of that is also its meaning, in a secondary or a principal way.
m.7.2.35.42: They declare all things, taken together and also separately, to be the meaning of the praṇava. Therefore this one syllable, which is Brahman, denotes all meanings.
m.7.2.35.43: By it, uttering Om, Śiva first makes the entire world. For Śiva is this praṇava, and the praṇava is declared to be Śiva.
m.7.2.35.44: For there is no absolute difference between what is denoted and what denotes it. Rudra is beyond thought, since words, together with the mind,
m.7.2.35.45: turn back without reaching him. Yet he is denoted by the single syllable. From the single part of the syllable called A, Brahmā, called Ātman, is designated.
m.7.2.35.46: From the single letter called U, Viṣṇu, called Vidyā, is declared. From the single letter called M, Rudra, called Śiva, is spoken of.
m.7.2.35.47: From the right side of Maheśa was born Brahmā, known as Ātman; from the left side arose Viṣṇu, who is therefore called Vidyā.
m.7.2.35.48: From Śiva's heart arose Nīlarudra, known as Śiva. Brahmā is the initiator of creation; Viṣṇu, the deluder, of preservation;
m.7.2.35.49: and likewise Rudra is the initiator of dissolution, and always the controller of those two.
m.7.2.35.50: Therefore those three are called the causes of the world; and Śiva, the source of the three causes, is the supreme cause.
m.7.2.35.51: Because you two, bound in enmity by rajas, did not understand this meaning, the liṅga appeared between you to awaken you.
m.7.2.35.52: Thus they call me Om, as has been stated here by Atharvan, and by the Ṛk verses, the Yajus formulas, the Sāman chants, and other branches by the thousand.
m.7.2.35.53: Even though the Vedas themselves thus plainly declare it with their own mouths, the two could not grasp it, as if it were something experienced in a dream.
m.7.2.35.54: So, to awaken them there and to remove their darkness, everything was imprinted on the liṅga too, just as the Vedas had declared it.
m.7.2.35.55: Having seen that imprinted on the liṅga, then, by the grace of the Lord of the liṅga, the two gods became calm in mind and awakened.
m.7.2.35.56: Knowing the origin and dissolution and the true nature of the six paths, and the abode higher than them, and the Person who possesses that abode,
m.7.2.35.57: the Brahman beyond which there is nothing higher, partless, Śiva the Lord, eternally the master of this universe made of bound souls (paśu) and bonds (pāśa),
m.7.2.35.58: fearing nothing from any quarter, utterly beyond, without growth or decay, imperishable, pervading outside and inside, yet free of outside and inside,
m.7.2.35.59: unsurpassed, eternal, distinct from all the worlds, without marks, indescribable, beyond the range of speech and mind,
m.7.2.35.60: whose sole essence is light, peaceful, gracious, ever-risen, the abode of all auspiciousness, accompanied by a Śakti of the same nature —
m.7.2.35.61: having come to know the god Virūpākṣa, Brahmā and Nārāyaṇa then, frightened, joined their palms above their heads and spoke these words.
m.7.2.35.62: Brahmā said: Ignorant or knowing, I was created by you in the beginning, O God. If I have fallen into such delusion, who is at fault in this?
m.7.2.35.63: Let this ignorance of mine be set aside. When you are present, O Lord, who could fearlessly speak of what must be done, whether by himself or by another?
m.7.2.35.64: Even the quarrel between us two has indeed been auspicious, since it has yielded the fruit of bowing at the feet of you, the Lord, the God of gods.
m.7.2.35.65: Viṣṇu said: O God, there is no speech equal to your greatness with which to praise you; yet before the Lord, silence on the part of servants is a transgression.
m.7.2.35.66: What would be fitting to do here? Only this is suited to the occasion. Though not knowing, having babbled something or other, I bow to you.
m.7.2.35.67: The status of cause given by you was forgotten through your māyā; deluded and full of ego, I have been corrected once again.
m.7.2.35.68: What use are many entreaties? I am deeply afraid, O Lord, because I set out to measure you, the immeasurable.
m.7.2.35.69: They call you Mahādeva, the destroyer of the distress of the frightened; therefore, O Śaṅkara, please forgive my transgression today.
m.7.2.35.70: Thus entreated by those two lords, Maheśvara, pleased, showed favour to the two gods and spoke with a smile.
m.7.2.35.71: Īśvara said: Dear child, dear child, O Vidhi (Brahmā), O Viṣṇu, deluded by my māyā, you two, priding yourselves on lordship and with enmity roused against each other,
m.7.2.35.72: carried your quarrel as far as battle and did not stop, it is said. Then the creation of beings was interrupted, since you two are the causes of the world,
m.7.2.35.73: because of the disagreement between you two born of ignorance and pride. To put an end to that, your pride and delusion, by me alone,
m.7.2.35.74: have thus been removed today through the play of the liṅga's manifestation. Therefore, giving up quarrel and shame completely,
m.7.2.35.75: may you two perform your respective tasks, free of jealousy. Formerly, by my command, together with the mantra, all the knowledge-compendia (jñāna-saṃhitā)
m.7.2.35.76: were given by me to you two, so that your status as causes might be established; and the supreme jewel among mantras, called the sūtra, consisting of five syllables,
m.7.2.35.77: was taught by me; all that has been forgotten by you two today. And I give it all again, as before, by my command,
m.7.2.35.78: since without it you two are not capable of creation and protection. Having spoken thus, Mahādeva, to Nārāyaṇa and Pitāmaha (Brahmā),
m.7.2.35.79: gave to those two the king of mantras together with the knowledge-compendium. Having received the great, divine, supreme command of Maheśvara,
m.7.2.35.80: and the mantra-jewel of great meaning, and likewise all the kalās, the two prostrated themselves like a staff at the feet of the God of gods.
m.7.2.35.81: Then the two stood there, freed from fear and motionless with bliss. Meanwhile, wondrously, like a magic show, the divine liṅga of the Lord—
m.7.2.35.82: —the liṅga vanished somewhere and could no longer be perceived by the two. Then, lamenting, alas, alas, at the sudden breaking of their affection,
m.7.2.35.83: and saying to each other, what a marvel is this that has happened, and reflecting on the inconceivable glory of Śambhu, they became free of distress.
m.7.2.35.84: Having entered into supreme friendship and embraced each other, the two foremost of gods departed to attend to the business of the world.
m.7.2.35.85: From then on, all the gods and asuras beginning with Śakra, the sages, men, Nāgas and women too, install the liṅga according to the prescribed rites and worship him in the liṅga.
m.7.2.35.iti: Thus ends the thirty-fifth adhyāya, named The removal of the delusion of Hari and Vidhi, in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the seventh saṃhitā, the Vāyavīya-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.7.2.36.1: Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: O Lord, I wish to hear the excellent rite of installation (pratiṣṭhā) of the liṅga and also of the image, as Śiva ordained it.
m.7.2.36.2: Upamanyu said: On a day not unfavourable to oneself, in the bright fortnight, one should make a liṅga of proper measurements, following the method taught in the Śaiva scriptures.
m.7.2.36.3: Then, having chosen an auspicious site and examined the ground, one should perform the ten preparatory rites, beginning with the marking out of the characteristic lines.
m.7.2.36.4: Before those ten rites, having worshipped Vināyaka and done the purification of the place and the rest, one should bring the liṅga to the bathing hall.
m.7.2.36.5: Then, with a golden stylus dipped in saffron and other liquids, one should inscribe the marked characteristic lines according to the Śilpa-śāstra.
m.7.2.36.6: With waters mixed with eight kinds of earth, or likewise with five kinds of earth, and with the five cow-products, one should purify the liṅga together with its pedestal.
m.7.2.36.7: Having worshipped it together with its pedestal and taken it to a body of water—a celestial one or another—one should there perform the adhivāsa of the liṅga together with its pedestal.
m.7.2.36.8: In a pure adhivāsa pavilion, endowed with every adornment, with arched gateways and an enclosure, encircled by garlands of darbha grass,
m.7.2.36.9: furnished with the eight elephants of the quarters, provided with eight pots for the guardians of the directions, equipped with the eight auspicious objects, and where worship of the directional guardians has been performed,
m.7.2.36.10: having made a broad seat-platform of metal or of wood, marked with a lotus seat, one should place it there in the middle.
m.7.2.36.11: Having worshipped the doorkeepers, the four beginning with Bhadra, in order—Subhadra, Vibhadra, Sunanda and Vinandaka—
m.7.2.36.12: having bathed and worshipped the liṅga together with its pedestal, and having wrapped it all round with two cloths along with kūrcas (bundles of darbha),
m.7.2.36.13: and having slowly brought it to the water, one should lay it upon the platform with its head to the east, the line (sūtra) below, and its pedestal to the west.
m.7.2.36.14: There one should keep the liṅga in adhivāsa, accompanied by all auspicious things, for five nights, three nights, or even one night.
m.7.2.36.15: Having dismissed what was worshipped there and purified it as before, having worshipped it in the manner of a festival procession, one should bring it to the hall of the couch.
m.7.2.36.16: There too one should make the place of the couch in the middle of a maṇḍala; having bathed the liṅga with pure waters, one should worship it in due order.
m.7.2.36.17: In the north-east, on ground that is clean and smeared, having drawn a lotus and purified the Śiva-pot, one should invoke Śiva there and worship him.
m.7.2.36.18: Having designed a white lotus in the middle of the altar according to rule, one should also draw the lotus of Caṇḍikā to its west.
m.7.2.36.19: Having prepared a couch with new cloths of linen and the like, or with flowers or darbha grass, one should place a golden flower upon it.
m.7.2.36.20: Having brought the liṅga there amid the sounds of every auspicious instrument, with a pair of red cloths together with a kūrca all round,
m.7.2.36.21: having wrapped it together with its pedestal, one should lay it down as before. Having drawn a lotus in front, on its petals in due order
m.7.2.36.22: one should set the pots of the Vidyeśas, and in the middle the Śaiva vardhanī pot. Around the three lotuses the best of the twice-born should offer oblations.
m.7.2.36.23: They are to be conceived as the eight forms of Śiva, stationed all round beginning from the east; or else four, in the cardinal directions, good Vedic reciters together with mantra-repeaters.
m.7.2.36.24: They should offer oblations; they are regarded as the four forms beginning with Viriñci. The preceptor, first among them, in the north-east or else in the west,
m.7.2.36.25: should perform the principal homa with the seven substances in due order; the other twice-born should offer a quarter or a half of what the ācārya offers.
m.7.2.36.26: Or the guru alone may offer the principal oblation here. First, having offered the full oblation, and a hundred and eight oblations with ghee,
m.7.2.36.27: one should place the Śiva-hand on the head of the liṅga with the root mantra. Offering a hundred, fifty, or half of that, in order, with the seven substances,
m.7.2.36.28: after each offering one should touch the liṅga and the pedestal again and again. Then, having offered the full oblation, one should give the fees in due order:
m.7.2.36.29: to the hotṛ priests and to the architect a quarter or a half of the ācārya's fee; half of that is to be given to the others and to the assembly members, according to one's means.
m.7.2.36.30: Then, having placed a golden bull or a kūrca in the pit, with earth-water, with the five cow-products, and again with pure water,
m.7.2.36.31: one should set in the pit the Brahma-stone, purified and smeared with sandal. Then, having performed kara-nyāsa with the nine names of the Śaktis,
m.7.2.36.32: one should deposit on the Brahma-stone orpiment and other minerals, together with seeds, fragrances and herbs, by the rule stated in the Śaiva scriptures.
m.7.2.36.33: Having set up a substitute liṅga made from a milky-sap tree, and having ascertained that it stands properly, removing it, one should set the liṅga upon the Brahma-stone,
m.7.2.36.34: one should install it slightly inclined toward the north-east with the root-vidyā; and then, joining the pedestal, recalling the Śākta root mantra,
m.7.2.36.35: having made the binding with binding substances and purified the place, and having offered arghya and flowers, they should again draw the curtain.
m.7.2.36.36: Then, for the sprinkling and other rites as appropriate, having brought the pots from the place of the couch, one should set them in order in front of the liṅga.
m.7.2.36.37: Then, beginning the great worship and having worshipped the ten pots, recalling the Śiva-mantra within the water of the Śiva-pot,
m.7.2.36.38: taking it up by joining thumb and ring finger, one should raise it; the knower of mantras should place it in the middle of the Īśāna portion of the liṅga.
m.7.2.36.39: Likewise one should place the Śakti, the Vidyā and the Vidyeśas in due order at the base of the liṅga; then one should sprinkle the liṅga with the Śiva-waters.
m.7.2.36.40: Having anointed the pedestal with the vardhanī and the liṅga again with the Vidyeśa pots, one should afterwards arrange the seat beginning with the ādhāra (support).
m.7.2.36.41: Having performed the placement (nyāsa) of the five kalās, one should contemplate the liṅga as blazing with radiance; then, with joined palms, facing north-east, one should invoke the two Śivas, Śiva and Śivā, as directly present,
m.7.2.36.42: contemplating the God coming down from the expanse of the sky together with the Goddess, mounted on the king of bulls or on a celestial car, adorned, rich in the splendour of every ornament, amid the sounds of all auspicious instruments,
m.7.2.36.43: surrounded by gods and dānavas headed by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśa, the Sun and Indra, all their limbs moist with bliss, with joined palms placed upon their heads,
m.7.2.36.44: surrounded on all sides by them praising, dancing and bowing. Then, having performed worship with the five offerings (upacāras), one should conclude it.
m.7.2.36.45: There is no rite higher than this, namely than the fivefold offering. One should perform the installation for images too in every respect as for the liṅga.
m.7.2.36.46: At the time of carving out the features, the opening of the eyes should be done. During the water-residence and on the bed, one should lay them the images face downward.
m.7.2.36.47: With mantras one should join the deity in the heart of that image laid on the water of the pot. They declare installation in a place where a temple has been built to be superior to that without a temple.
m.7.2.36.48: One who is capable should first build the temple and afterwards perform the installation rite. If one is incapable, having installed a liṅga or else an image,
m.7.2.36.49: he should afterwards build a temple of Śiva in accordance with his means. And next I shall describe the excellent rite of installation for domestic worship.
m.7.2.36.50: Having made a small image or a liṅga endowed with the proper marks, when the northern course of the sun has arrived, in the bright fortnight, on an auspicious day,
m.7.2.36.51: having made an altar in an auspicious place, one should draw a lotus there as before; having strewn leaves, flowers and so on, and having set a pot in the middle,
m.7.2.36.52: one should place four vessels around it in the four directions. The five Brahman mantras, with their five seed-syllables, in those five vessels—
m.7.2.36.53: having placed them, worshipped them, shown the mudrās and so on, and protected them; having purified the liṅga or image with earth, water and the like as before,
m.7.2.36.54: one should set it, covered with flowers, on an excellent seat placed to the north; placing a flower on its head, one should sprinkle it with the sprinkling-water.
m.7.2.36.55: Having again worshipped it with flowers, preceded by cries of victory and the like, one should bathe it with the root mantra, using the pots charged with the mantras ending with Īśāna.
m.7.2.36.56: Then, having performed the placement of the five kalās and the worship as before, one should daily worship there the three-eyed God together with the Goddess.
m.7.2.36.57: Or else, having placed a single pot, furnished with the mantra of the form (mūrti-mantra), within the lotus, one should perform all the rest as before.
m.7.2.36.58: A liṅga that has been severely defiled should be purified and installed again; one that is defiled should be re-consecrated by sprinkling; one slightly defiled should simply be worshipped.
m.7.2.36.59: Liṅgas called Bāṇa may or may not be installed, since they were already consecrated by Śiva himself beforehand.
m.7.2.36.60: The remaining ones are to be installed; but those seen to be like the Bāṇa liṅgas—in the case of a self-manifested liṅga, a divine one, and likewise one established by sages—
m.7.2.36.61: if it lacks a pedestal, one should fit a pedestal, perform the rite of sprinkling, and worship Śiva there; installation is not prescribed for them.
m.7.2.36.62: A liṅga that is burnt, loosened, or with damaged parts should be cast into a body of water; one fit for repair should be joined together and then the installation rite performed.
m.7.2.36.63: From a defective image or liṅga, after first worshipping the deity, one should withdraw the deity into the heart and then carry out repair or abandonment, as appropriate.
m.7.2.36.64: If worship is interrupted for one day, one should perform double worship; for two nights, a great worship; beyond that, re-consecration by sprinkling.
m.7.2.36.65: If worship is interrupted for many days, beyond a month, some prescribe fresh installation, others the procedure of re-consecration by sprinkling.
m.7.2.36.66: In the re-consecration of a liṅga and the like, having withdrawn the deity as before, having bathed it with earth and water in the order of eight and five,
m.7.2.36.67: and having bathed it with the products of the cow and purified it with darbha-water, one should sprinkle it with the sprinkling-water a hundred and eight times with the root mantra.
m.7.2.36.68: Placing his hand, holding flowers and kuśa grass, on the top of the liṅga, he should repeat the root mantra five times over a hundred and eight times.
m.7.2.36.69: Then with the root mantra he should also touch it from the top down to the pedestal, and, having invoked the deity as before, perform a great worship.
m.7.2.36.70: When an installed liṅga is not available, one should worship the Lord Śiva at a place sacred to Śiva, or in water, in fire, in the sun, or likewise in the sky.
m.7.2.36.iti: Thus ends the thirty-sixth adhyāya, named The rite of installation, in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the seventh saṃhitā, the Vāyavīya-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.7.2.37.1: Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: All that the Lord has taught in summary, drawing out the essence of knowledge, ritual action and conduct, I have heard, and it is equal to the Veda.
m.7.2.37.2: Now I wish to hear about yoga, which is supremely hard to attain, together with who is qualified for it, its limbs, its procedure and its purpose.
m.7.2.37.3: If death comes first, before yoga and the rest have been brought to completion, tell me the means by which the goal can be accomplished at once, so that a man does not become a destroyer of his own self.
m.7.2.37.4: Please explain truly that means, its cause, its proper time and instruments, and the gradation of its varieties.
m.7.2.37.5: Upamanyu said: Fittingly have you asked, O Kṛṣṇa, you who know the purport of every question. So I shall tell all of it in order; listen attentively.
m.7.2.37.6: The steady activity, fixed on Śiva, of a mind whose other activities have been restrained—that, in brief, is yoga; and it is indeed fivefold.
m.7.2.37.7: Mantra-yoga, sparśa-yoga, bhāva-yoga, and another, abhāva-yoga; and mahā-yoga is held to be the highest of all.
m.7.2.37.8: The undistracted activity of the mind, resting on the meaning signified by the mantra, arising solely through the power of repeated practice of the mantra, is called mantra-yoga.
m.7.2.37.9: That same mental activity, led by breath-control, is called sparśa-yoga; when it is free of both mantra and touch, it is declared bhāva-yoga.
m.7.2.37.10: That in which the universe is contemplated as a form whose parts have dissolved is called abhāva-yoga, because the existing object no longer appears.
m.7.2.37.11: The mental activity in which Śiva's own nature alone, without any limiting adjunct, is contemplated—that Śaiva state of mind is here called mahā-yoga.
m.7.2.37.12: He whose mind is detached from objects, both those seen in this world and those heard of in scripture—he alone is qualified for yoga, no one else.
m.7.2.37.13: The mind becomes detached simply by constantly seeing the faults of both kinds of objects and the virtues of the Lord.
m.7.2.37.14: All yoga, in brief, has either eight limbs or six limbs: yama, niyama, and posture beginning with svastika;
m.7.2.37.15: breath-control, withdrawal of the senses, concentration, meditation and absorption—these eight limbs of yoga are declared by the wise.
m.7.2.37.16: Posture, restraint of breath, withdrawal, then concentration, meditation and absorption—these, in brief, are the six limbs of yoga.
m.7.2.37.17: The distinct definitions of these are set forth in the Śiva-śāstra, and in the other Śiva-āgamas, especially the Kāmika and the rest,
m.7.2.37.18: and likewise in the Yoga-śāstras and in certain Purāṇas. Non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy and non-possession—this is called yama by the good, as it consists of five components.
m.7.2.37.19: Purity, contentment, austerity, recitation and devotion to the Lord—thus niyama is of five kinds according to the division of its parts.
m.7.2.37.20: Svastika, padma, the half-moon, vīra, yoga, prasādhita, paryaṅka and yatheṣṭa (as one pleases)—posture is declared to be eightfold.
m.7.2.37.21: Prāṇa is the air arising in one's own body; its āyāma is its restraint. It is said to be threefold: recaka, pūraka and kumbhaka.
m.7.2.37.22: Pressing one nostril with a finger, one should expel the air of the belly through the other; this is known as recaka.
m.7.2.37.23: One should fill the body with external air through the other nostril, like a leather bag; from this filling it is held to be pūraka.
m.7.2.37.24: When one neither releases nor takes in the air, which remains within and without, and stays motionless, full like a pot, that is kumbhaka.
m.7.2.37.25: This triad beginning with recaka should be neither hurried nor slow; the practitioner of yoga, self-controlled, should practise it by gradual progression.
m.7.2.37.26: The practice of recaka and the rest, preceded by purification of the channels and culminating in voluntary departure from the body, is taught in the instruction of yoga.
m.7.2.37.27: The restraint in breath-control, following the sequence beginning with kanyaka, is taught as fourfold according to the division of measure and quality.
m.7.2.37.28: Of the four, the kanyaka consists of twelve measures; the middle one has two udghātas and consists of twenty-four measures.
m.7.2.37.29: The highest has three udghātas and is of thirty-six measures; the prāṇāyāma beyond that produces sweating, trembling and the like.
m.7.2.37.30: For the yogin there then arise horripilation born of bliss, the shedding of tears from the eyes, babbling, whirling, fainting and the like.
m.7.2.37.31: Circling the knee with the hand, neither fast nor slow, one should snap the fingers; that duration is declared a mātrā.
m.7.2.37.32: The measures are to be understood in order according to the sequence of udghātas. One should practise breath-control preceded by purification of the channels.
m.7.2.37.33: Breath-control is known to be twofold: agarbha and sagarbha. Agarbha is without recitation and meditation; sagarbha is accompanied by them.
m.7.2.37.34: Breath-control joined with the seed is a hundred times greater than the seedless; therefore yogins practise breath-restraint with the seed.
m.7.2.37.35: By the very conquest of prāṇa the winds of the body are conquered: prāṇa, apāna, samāna, udāna and vyāna,
m.7.2.37.36: nāga, kūrma, kṛkala, devadatta and dhanañjaya. Because it makes the going-forth (prayāṇa), it is called prāṇa.
m.7.2.37.37: The one called apāna leads downward the food and other things that are eaten; vyāna pervades all the limbs, making them grow.
m.7.2.37.38: Because it stirs up the vital points, the wind is called udāna; because it carries nourishment evenly to all the limbs, it is called samāna.
m.7.2.37.39: Nāga is said to act in belching, kūrma resides in opening the eyes, kṛkala is to be known in sneezing, devadatta in yawning.
m.7.2.37.40: All-pervading dhanañjaya does not leave even the dead body. This breath-control, practised gradually, becomes effective.
m.7.2.37.41: Prāṇāyāma burns away every fault and protects the practitioner's body. When the breath has been properly mastered, one should look for its signs.
m.7.2.37.42: First, feces, urine and phlegm become scanty; there arises the capacity to eat much, and likewise breathing out only after a long interval.
m.7.2.37.43: Lightness, swiftness of movement, vigour, excellence of voice, the destruction of all diseases, strength, radiance, beauty of form,
m.7.2.37.44: steadfastness, intelligence, youthfulness, stability and serenity are its signs. Austerities, the destruction of sins, sacrifices, gifts, vows and the like —
m.7.2.37.45: these do not equal a sixteenth part of that prāṇāyāma. The senses here are attached each to its own objects;
m.7.2.37.46: that by which one forcibly withdraws and restrains them is called pratyāhāra. The senses, with the mind foremost, lead to heaven and to hell:
m.7.2.37.47: when restrained they lead to heaven, when let loose to hell. Therefore the wise person who seeks happiness, established in knowledge and dispassion,
m.7.2.37.48: should quickly rein in the horses of the senses and lift up the self by the self. Dhāraṇā, in brief, is the binding of the mind to a place.
m.7.2.37.49: And the place is Śiva alone, nothing else, since anything else is subject to the threefold fault. When the mind, fixed on that place for some set period of time,
m.7.2.37.50: does not slip from its target, that is dhāraṇā, and not otherwise. The first steadiness of the mind arises from dhāraṇā.
m.7.2.37.51: Therefore one should make the mind firm through the persistent practice of dhāraṇā. The root dhyai is taught in the sense of thinking; thinking of Śiva again and again
m.7.2.37.52: with an undistracted mind — that is called dhyāna. And that uniform awareness of a mind settled on the object of meditation,
m.7.2.37.53: a stream free of any other cognition, is called dhyāna. Abandoning everything else, Śiva alone, the bestower of welfare,
m.7.2.37.54: the supreme Lord over the lords of the gods, is to be meditated upon — so the Atharvan scripture concludes. Likewise the supreme Śivā is to be meditated upon; the two, Śiva and Śivā, pervade all beings.
m.7.2.37.55: Those two, known from śruti, smṛti and the śāstras, all-pervading, ever risen, omniscient, are to be meditated upon constantly in the distinctions of their many forms.
m.7.2.37.56: Liberation is the first result, and the other result is the powers such as aṇimā; thus the purpose of this meditation is to be known as twofold.
m.7.2.37.57: The meditator, meditation, the object of meditation, and the purpose of meditation — knowing this fourfold set, the knower of yoga should practise yoga.
m.7.2.37.58: Endowed with knowledge and dispassion, full of faith, possessed of patience, free from possessiveness and ever zealous — such a person is declared a fit meditator.
m.7.2.37.59: Tired of japa, one should meditate again; tired of meditation, one should do japa again. For one devoted to japa and meditation, yoga is quickly accomplished.
m.7.2.37.60: Dhāraṇā lasts twelve prāṇāyāmas; dhyāna lasts twelve dhāraṇās; the span of twelve dhyānas is called samādhi.
m.7.2.37.61: Samādhi is declared to be the final limb of yoga; and through samādhi the light of wisdom spreads everywhere.
m.7.2.37.62: That shining in which only the object appears, which stands still like a calm ocean, as though empty of its own form, is called samādhi.
m.7.2.37.63: Having merged the mind in the object of meditation, he should behold it very steadily. The yogin so absorbed, like a fire that has gone out, is said to be established in samādhi.
m.7.2.37.64: He does not hear, nor smell, nor speak, nor see; nor does he perceive touch, nor does his mind form intentions.
m.7.2.37.65: Nor does he identify with anything, nor is he bound; like a piece of wood — one whose self is thus dissolved in Śiva is here called established in samādhi.
m.7.2.37.66: Just as a lamp placed where there is no wind never flickers, so too is one fixed in samādhi; therefore the wise one should not waver from it.
m.7.2.37.67: For the yogin who thus diligently practises the supreme yoga, all the obstacles to it gradually perish, O wise ones.
m.7.2.37.iti: Thus ends the thirty-seventh adhyāya, named The course of yoga, in the Uttara-khaṇḍa, within the dialogue of Vāyu and the sages of Naimiṣa, of the seventh saṃhitā, the Vāyavīya-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.7.2.38.1: Upamanyu said: Sloth, severe diseases, negligence, doubt about the yogic stage, instability of mind, lack of faith, erroneous perception,
m.7.2.38.2: sorrows, dejection, and fickleness toward sense objects — these ten are declared to be the obstacles for men who practise yoga.
m.7.2.38.3: Sloth is the indolence of the body and mind of yogins; diseases are disorders born of imbalance of the bodily elements, arising from faults of karma.
m.7.2.38.4: Negligence means failure in the cultivation of the means of yoga. Knowledge seized by both alternatives — is it this, or that? — is doubt about the stage.
m.7.2.38.5: The lack of firm footing of the mind is called instability. Lack of faith is an attitude devoid of devotion toward the path of yoga.
m.7.2.38.6: The understanding that is inverted is called delusion. The sorrow of the mind in men, born of ignorance, they know as the ādhyātmika sorrow.
m.7.2.38.7: The sorrow that arises from the body because of deeds done formerly is ādhibhautika; that caused by thunderbolts, weapons, poison and the like is declared ādhidaivika.
m.7.2.38.8: Agitation born of the frustration of desire they call dejection. Wandering among varied sense objects is fickleness.
m.7.2.38.9: When these obstacles are pacified, for the yogin intent on yoga there arise divine disturbances (upasargas); they are indicators of attainment.
m.7.2.38.10: Intuition, hearing, understanding of speech, seeing, tasting and feeling — these six are the upasargas; they are attainments that lead to the loss of yoga.
m.7.2.38.11: Pratibhā is said to be the manifestation, exactly as it is, of an object that is subtle, concealed, past, remote or yet to come.
m.7.2.38.12: Śravaṇa is the hearing of all sounds without effort; vārttā is the understanding of the speech of all embodied beings.
m.7.2.38.13: Darśana is the seeing of divine things without effort; likewise āsvāda is said to be the tasting of divine flavours.
m.7.2.38.14: Likewise the one renowned as vedanā is the perception of touch and of divine smells and the rest. The lords of the worlds up to that of Brahmā —
m.7.2.38.15: stand before him and give many jewels; speech, sweet at will and of many kinds, flows forth.
m.7.2.38.16: All elixirs and likewise divine herbs become effective for him; celestial women, bowing to him, offer their gifts.
m.7.2.38.17: When even a single part of yogic attainment is seen, the mind should turn to liberation, thinking: Just as this has been seen by me, so too liberation will come.
m.7.2.38.18: Thinness, stoutness, childhood, old age and youth, assuming the forms of various species, bearing a body of four elements,
m.7.2.38.19: without the earthly portion, and constant possession of fragrant scent — thus they declare the eightfold paiśāca, earthly state.
m.7.2.38.20: Dwelling in water, and likewise emerging from the earth; if he wishes, he is able himself to drink even the ocean without distress;
m.7.2.38.21: wherever in this world he wishes, there water appears; holding a mass of water in the hand without a pot or the like;
m.7.2.38.22: whatever thing, even tasteless, he wishes to eat acquires flavour and other qualities at that very moment; and bearing a body of three elements;
m.7.2.38.23: freedom of the body from wounds, together with the earthly powers — this is the wondrous sixteenfold watery lordship.
m.7.2.38.24: Producing fire from the body, freedom from fear of its heat, the power to burn this world effortlessly if he should wish,
m.7.2.38.25: or placing fire in water, holding fire in the hand, restoring creation as before when it has been burnt, cooking food and the like in the mouth, forming a body from two elements, together with the watery lordship —
m.7.2.38.26: this they call the twenty-fourfold fiery lordship. Swiftness like the mind, entering into beings in an instant,
m.7.2.38.27: bearing great loads such as mountains without effort, heaviness and lightness, holding the wind in the hand,
m.7.2.38.28: shaking even the earth by the touch of a fingertip and the like, forming a body from one element, joined with the fiery enjoyments —
m.7.2.38.29: the sages know as the thirty-twofold airy lordship. Producing a body without shadow, invisibility of the senses,
m.7.2.38.30: moving through the sky at will, contact with the objects of the senses, crossing through space, and placing it within one's own body,
m.7.2.38.31: making space into a solid mass, and bodilessness, joined with the airy lordship — this great forty-fold
m.7.2.38.32: is declared the Aindra lordship; they call it the ethereal. Obtaining things at will and departing at will,
m.7.2.38.33: overpowering everything, seeing all secret matters, creating according to beings' actions, control, a pleasing appearance,
m.7.2.38.34: and seeing the course of saṃsāra, together with the Aindra enjoyments — this is the lunar lordship, mental, superior in qualities.
m.7.2.38.35: Cutting, striking, binding and likewise releasing, seizing all beings who are subject to saṃsāra,
m.7.2.38.36: and granting favour to all, and likewise conquest of death and time — this egoic lordship they call the Prājāpatya.
m.7.2.38.37: This, with the lunar enjoyments, is great and fifty-sixfold. Creation by mere resolve, protection and likewise destruction,
m.7.2.38.38: one's own authority over all, directing the minds of beings, being unequalled by anything, creating a world separately,
m.7.2.38.39: bringing about good and evil, joined with the Prājāpatya powers — this they call the sixty-fourfold Brāhma lordship.
m.7.2.38.40: Beyond this intellectual lordship they know the secondary, prakṛtic lordship; that is declared the Vaiṣṇava, and to it alone belongs the maintenance of the world. That entire state cannot be described by Brahmā or by others.
m.7.2.38.41: That is the station of Puruṣa, the station of the guṇas, the station of Gaṇeśa, and the station of the Lord (Aiśvara). That highest station cannot be known even slightly by Viṣṇu or by others.
m.7.2.38.42: And all the attainments of knowledge, too, are indeed obstacles; they must be held in check with effort, through supreme dispassion.
m.7.2.38.43: For one whose mind is attached to impure appearances and to the qualities of powers, the supreme lordship—fearless and fulfilling all desires—is not attained.
m.7.2.38.44: Therefore, he who abandons like straw the qualities and enjoyments of gods, asuras and kings—his is the supreme success in yoga.
m.7.2.38.45: Or else, wishing to bestow grace on the world, the sage may wander about; having enjoyed qualities and pleasures as he wishes, he will attain liberation.
m.7.2.38.46: Now I shall tell the practice of yoga; listen attentively. It should be done at an auspicious time, in an auspicious place such as a shrine of Śiva, solitary, free of creatures, silent, and free from disturbance;
m.7.2.38.47: on ground well smeared with cow-dung, pleasant, perfumed with scents, incense and the like, strewn with loose flowers, and adorned with canopies and so on;
m.7.2.38.48: furnished with kuśa grass, flowers, fuel-sticks, water, fruits and roots; not near fire, not near water, nor on a heap of dry leaves;
m.7.2.38.49: not in a place swarming with gnats and mosquitoes, crowded with snakes and beasts of prey, nor full of vicious animals, nor where there is fear, nor surrounded by wicked people;
m.7.2.38.50: not in a cremation ground, at a shrine or an anthill, in a ruined house, at a crossroads, on the bank of rivers, streams or the ocean, or in the middle of a street;
m.7.2.38.51: not in an old garden, a cowpen and the like, not in an undesirable or censured place; not when one has belching from indigestion or sour taste, nor in a place defiled by excrement and urine;
