m.7.2.38.52: nor when suffering vomiting, indigestion or diarrhoea, nor after overeating, nor when tired; nor should one be troubled by excessive worry, nor excessively hungry and thirsty;
m.7.2.38.53: nor should one practise yoga while engaged in duties for one's guru and the like. Moderate in food and recreation, moderate in effort in one's actions,
m.7.2.38.54: moderate in sleep and waking, free from all strain, he should take a seat that is soft, pleasing, broad, quite even and clean.
m.7.2.38.55: He should practise among the postures such as padmaka and svastika. Having bowed in due order to those worthy of salutation, ending with his own guru,
m.7.2.38.56: with neck, head and chest straight, he should not remain with eyes tightly shut; with head slightly raised, he should not let his teeth touch each other.
m.7.2.38.57: Placing the tongue motionless, resting at the tips of the teeth, guarding the testicles and also the genital with the heels,
m.7.2.38.58: placing the arms crosswise, without strain, upon the thighs, and setting the back of the right hand upon the left palm,
m.7.2.38.59: gently raising the back and pushing the chest forward, gazing at the tip of his own nose and not looking about in the directions,
m.7.2.38.60: with the movement of breath held in check, motionless like a stone, contemplating Śiva together with Ambā within the shrine of his own body,
m.7.2.38.61: he should worship them by the sacrifice of meditation in the middle of the pedestal of the heart-lotus. Or at the root, at the tip of the nose, at the navel, at the throat, or in the cavities of the palate,
m.7.2.38.62: between the brows, at the place of the aperture, at the forehead, or at the crown of the head, he should meditate, having duly imagined the supreme seat of Śiva and Śivā.
m.7.2.38.63: There, either with the surrounding retinue (āvaraṇa) or without it, he should meditate on Śiva according to rule in a two-petalled, sixteen-spoked or twelve-spoked lotus,
m.7.2.38.64: or in a ten-spoked, six-cornered or four-cornered one, he should meditate on Śiva. Between the brows is a two-petalled lotus, bright as lightning.
m.7.2.38.65: On the southern and northern petals of the lotus situated between the brows, in order, which are of the colour of lightning, are the letters at the end of the alphabet.
m.7.2.38.66: The petals of the sixteen-spoked lotus are the sixteen vowels, beginning from the east in order; this lotus lies from the root of the kanda.
m.7.2.38.67: The letters beginning with ka and ending with ṭha are, in order, the petals of the sun-coloured lotus; that is to be meditated upon within the heart.
m.7.2.38.68: The letters ḍa through pha, in order, are declared to be the petals of the lotus white as cow's milk, above the navel towards the back. And below, this lotus has six petals,
m.7.2.38.69: of the lotus coloured like smokeless embers, the letters beginning with ba and ending with la. Of the golden lotus of the mūlādhāra, the letters from va to sa are, in order, set as its petals.
m.7.2.38.70: Now, among these lotuses, wherever the mind delights, there alone he should contemplate the god and the goddess with a steady intellect.
m.7.2.38.71: He should meditate on him as thumb-sized, stainless, shining all around, shaped like the flame of a pure lamp, fully adorned with his own Śakti;
m.7.2.38.72: or shaped like the crescent of the moon, or in the form of a star, or like the awn of nīvāra rice, or resembling a lotus-stalk fibre;
m.7.2.38.73: shaped like a kadamba ball, or like a drop of dew. If the meditator desires mastery over the principles beginning with earth,
m.7.2.38.74: he should contemplate the gross form presiding over each respective principle. The eight forms beginning with Brahmā and ending with Sadāśiva, and those beginning with Bhava,
m.7.2.38.75: are the gross forms of Śiva, as determined in the Śaiva scriptures. These forms are terrible, mixed, and tranquil; by the lords among sages,
m.7.2.38.76: free from desire for fruits and skilled in contemplation, they are to be contemplated. If the terrible ones are contemplated, they bring about the destruction of sin and disease.
m.7.2.38.77: With the mixed forms the result comes after a long time; with the gentle, neither immediately nor after a long time. Through the gentle ones especially, liberation, peace and wisdom are attained.
m.7.2.38.78: And the attainments are accomplished here step by step; of this there is no doubt.
m.7.2.38.iti: Thus ends the thirty-eighth adhyāya, named The obstacles that arise in the course of yoga, in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the seventh saṃhitā, the Vāyavīya-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.7.2.39.1: Upamanyu said: Some yogins meditate on him alone, thinking that for those who remember Śrīkaṇṭha, the Lord, the accomplishment of all aims comes about at once.
m.7.2.39.2: Some practise gross meditation for the steadying of the mind. On the gross the mind becomes motionless, and then on the subtle it becomes firm.
m.7.2.39.3: When Śiva himself is contemplated directly, all the siddhis are accomplished. Even when other forms are meditated upon, one should contemplate in them the form of Śiva.
m.7.2.39.4: One should observe the steadiness of the mind and meditate on that object again and again. They have declared meditation to be at first with an object, and afterwards without an object.
m.7.2.39.5: Of these, the view of the wise is that meditation without any object does not strictly exist, for it is a certain continuous flow of the intellect that is called meditation.
m.7.2.39.6: Therefore, in objectless meditation, the intellect alone, without an object, functions here. Hence meditation with an object is that which rests on the image of the rays of the rising sun;
m.7.2.39.7: that resting on the subtle is objectless; in ultimate truth there is no other. Alternatively, meditation with an object is that which depends on a form,
m.7.2.39.8: and awareness of the formless Self is held to be objectless meditation. That same meditation is called seedless and with seed,
m.7.2.39.9: according as it rests on the formless or likewise on a form. Therefore, having first practised meditation with an object and with seed,
m.7.2.39.10: at the end one should practise the objectless, seedless meditation for complete accomplishment. Through prāṇāyāma the states of the Goddess, śānti and the rest, are attained in sequence:
m.7.2.39.11: śānti, praśānti, dīpti, and after that prasāda. The calming of all calamities is called śānti.
m.7.2.39.12: The destruction of darkness within and without is declared to be praśānti. The illumination that is outward and inward is called dīpti.
m.7.2.39.13: The healthy, settled state of the intellect is proclaimed to be prasāda. And all the instruments, external and internal,
m.7.2.39.14: quickly become clear through the clarity of the intellect. The meditator, meditation, the object of meditation, and the purpose of meditation — knowing this fourfold set, the meditator should practise meditation.
m.7.2.39.15: One endowed with knowledge and dispassion, ever of unagitated mind, full of faith, and serene in spirit, is declared by the wise to be a meditator.
m.7.2.39.16: The verbal root dhyai is known to be used in the sense of thinking; so thinking of Śiva again and again
m.7.2.39.17: — just as even a little practice of yoga would destroy sin — and the thought of one who meditates with faith on the Supreme Lord even for a moment,
m.7.2.39.18: with an undistracted mind, is called meditation.
m.7.2.39.19: The support of this meditation, which has the form of a flow of the intellect, is called by the wise the object of meditation; and that is Śiva himself together with Ambā.
m.7.2.39.20: The certainty of liberation and full lordly power, beginning with aṇimā, are declared to be the direct purpose of complete meditation on Śiva.
m.7.2.39.21: Since from meditation one obtains both happiness and liberation, a man should therefore abandon everything and devote himself to meditation.
m.7.2.39.22: There is no knowledge without meditation, and no meditation for one who is not a yogin. He who has both meditation and knowledge has crossed the ocean of worldly existence.
m.7.2.39.23: Knowledge that is clear, one-pointed, and free from all limiting adjuncts is attained only by the yogin who is engaged in the practice of yoga.
m.7.2.39.24: The mind of those whose sins are wholly destroyed turns to knowledge and meditation; for those whose intellect is struck by sin, even talk of it is very hard to come by.
m.7.2.39.25: Just as a greatly blazing fire burns up both the dry and the wet, so the fire of meditation burns good and bad karma in an instant.
m.7.2.39.26: Just as even a very small lamp dispels a vast darkness, so even a little practice of yoga destroys great sin.
m.7.2.39.27: For one who meditates with faith on the Supreme Lord even for a moment, the very great good that arises has no end at all.
m.7.2.39.28: There is no pilgrimage place equal to meditation, no austerity equal to meditation, no sacrifice equal to meditation; therefore one should practise meditation.
m.7.2.39.29: Yogins do not resort to sacred places full of water or to gods made of stone and clay, because of their conviction in their own Self.
m.7.2.39.30: For yogins the subtle divine body of the Lord becomes directly perceptible, just as for those not yoked in yoga it is the gross form fashioned of clay, wood and the like.
m.7.2.39.31: Just as here the king's inner attendants are dear to him, not the outer ones, so those devoted to inner meditation are dear to Śambhu, not the performers of rites.
m.7.2.39.32: Just as in the world the outer servants in a king's palace, though they see its riches, do not greatly enjoy its fruits, so too here the ritualists.
m.7.2.39.33: If such aspirants perish midway, one who has striven for jñānayoga will, by the mere effort at yoga, go to the world of Rudra.
m.7.2.39.34: Having enjoyed happiness there, he is born in a family of yogins; obtaining jñānayoga again, he passes beyond saṃsāra.
m.7.2.39.35: The state that a man attains even by merely desiring to know yoga, he does not attain even by all the great sacrifices.
m.7.2.39.36: The fruit gained by worshipping ten million twice-born men learned in the Vedas — that fruit is gained by giving merely alms to a Śiva-yogin.
m.7.2.39.37: Whatever fruit lies in sacrifices, the agnihotra, gifts, pilgrimages and fire-offerings — all that fruit one obtains by giving food to yogins.
m.7.2.39.38: Those deluded ones who slander Śiva-yogins fall, together with their listeners, into the hells until the destruction of the earth.
m.7.2.39.39: Only when there is a listener can there be a speaker of slander against yogins; therefore the listener is held by the very great to be the more sinful and deserving of punishment. But those who constantly honour Śiva-yogins with devotion
m.7.2.39.40: obtain great enjoyments and, at the end, the yoga of Śaṅkara. Therefore Śiva-yogins should be duly worshipped by men who desire enjoyments.
m.7.2.39.41: Yogins should be served with shelter, food, drink and the like, and with beds, coverings and so on. Because it is full of essence, the dharma of yoga cannot be broken by the mallets of sin.
m.7.2.39.42: It should be known to be like a diamond-grain. So too yogins are not stained by sin or by floods of sins, just as a lotus leaf is not wetted by water.
m.7.2.39.43: In whatever land a sage devoted to Śiva-yoga constantly dwells, even that land becomes purified; what then need be said of his being pure?
m.7.2.39.44: Therefore the wise man, abandoning every other duty, should diligently practise Śiva-yoga for the removal of all sorrows.
m.7.2.39.45: The yogin who has attained the fruit of yoga may, out of desire for the welfare of the worlds, enjoy pleasures as he wishes and roam about, or remain here.
m.7.2.39.46: Or else, regarding sensual pleasure as merely petty and renouncing it through the yoga of dispassion, let him at his own will be freed from action.
m.7.2.39.47: But the mortal who sees death approaching and ill omens in abundance should, intent on undertaking yoga, take refuge in a holy place of Śiva.
m.7.2.39.48: While dwelling there, if that man is steadfast of mind, he may of his own accord give up his life-breaths even without disease and the like,
m.7.2.39.49: having undertaken fasting, or having offered his body into Śiva's fire, or having cast his own body into Śiva's sacred waters by immersion —
m.7.2.39.50: whoever gives up his life according to the rule stated in the Śaiva scriptures is liberated at once; there is no need for deliberation on this.
m.7.2.39.51: Or if one who has taken refuge in a holy place of Śiva dies helplessly through disease and the like, he too is likewise liberated; there is no doubt of this.
m.7.2.39.52: For they declare death through fasting and the like to be the best, since it is undertaken with a mind made steadfast by trust in scripture.
m.7.2.39.53: Whoever, having killed one given to reviling Śiva, or being himself afflicted in the attempt, gives up his life-breaths so hard to give up, is not born again.
m.7.2.39.54: He who, unable to kill one given to reviling Śiva, dies by his own hand is liberated at once, together with twenty-one generations of his family.
m.7.2.39.55: Whoever gives up his life for Śiva's sake, or for the sake of a devotee of Śiva — no man standing on the path of liberation is equal to him.
m.7.2.39.56: Therefore his liberation from the circle of saṃsāra is swifter. Or, having somehow adopted any one of these means —
m.7.2.39.57: or if one who has duly received the purification of the six paths dies, one should not perform for him here the after-death rites as is done for bound souls (paśus).
m.7.2.39.58: Nor should his son and others in particular incur ritual impurity. For the sake of Śaiva practice or for the sake of Śaiva knowledge, one may either bury his body in the ground or burn it with pure fire,
m.7.2.39.59: or cast it into auspicious waters, or leave it like a piece of wood or a clod of earth. And if one wishes to perform a rite with reference to him,
m.7.2.39.60: one should perform only an auspicious rite and satisfy devotees according to one's ability. A Śaiva may take his wealth if his offspring are Śaiva; if there are none, one should give it to Śiva; offspring who are paśus (uninitiated) should not receive it.
m.7.2.39.iti: Thus ends the thirty-ninth adhyāya, named Śaiva yoga, in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the seventh saṃhitā, the Vāyavīya-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.7.2.40.1: Sūta said: Thus Vāyu related to the sages, who had bowed before him, the yoga of knowledge that the Yādava Kṛṣṇa had received from Upamanyu, the conqueror of anger. Then, his own form made manifest, he vanished at once into the sky in the evening.
m.7.2.40.2: Then at daybreak all the ascetics of Naimiṣa set out to perform the avabhṛtha concluding bath at the end of the sacrificial session.
m.7.2.40.3: Then, at Brahmā's command, the goddess Sarasvatī herself began to flow as an auspicious river, clear and with sweet waters.
m.7.2.40.4: Seeing the river Sarasvatī, the sages, delighted at heart, completed the sacrificial session they had begun and bathed there.
m.7.2.40.5: Then, having satisfied the gods and others with its auspicious waters, and recalling what had happened before, they went toward Vārāṇasī.
m.7.2.40.6: Then, seeing the Bhāgīrathī Gaṅgā descending from the foot of the Himālaya and flowing southward, they bathed there and went on along her bank.
m.7.2.40.7: Then, reaching Vārāṇasī, all of them rejoiced, and they bathed in the Gaṅgā where she flows northward,
m.7.2.40.8: and having seen the Avimukteśvara liṅga and worshipped it according to rule, as they were about to depart they saw there, in the sky, something shining—
m.7.2.40.9: a divine, most wondrous radiance, like ten million suns, which with the expanse of its own lustre pervaded the spaces of all the directions.
m.7.2.40.10: Then Pāśupata adepts, sages whose bodies were covered with ash, approached in hundreds and became merged in that radiance.
m.7.2.40.11: When those great-souled ascetics had thus dissolved into it, the radiance at once disappeared; it was like a marvel.
m.7.2.40.12: Seeing that great wonder, the great sages of Naimiṣa, not knowing what it was, went toward Brahmā's forest.
m.7.2.40.13: Even before their going, Vāyu, the purifier of the worlds, had reported his meeting with the Naimiṣa sages and the great-souled one's dialogue with them,
m.7.2.40.14: then their pure understanding directed to Śiva together with Ambā and his attendants, and also the completion of the long sacrificial session of those sacrificers—
m.7.2.40.15: having reported all this to Brahmā, the sustainer of the worlds and source of the Veda, and permitted by him, he had gone to his own city for his own business.
m.7.2.40.16: Now Brahmā, seated in his abode, was attending to Tumburu and Nārada, who were competing with each other and disputing about singing;
m.7.2.40.17: acting as arbiter, enjoying the rasas arising from the songs they produced, he sat at ease, attended by Gandharvas and Apsarases.
m.7.2.40.18: At that time, because it was not an opportune moment, the sages were stopped at the door by the doorkeepers and sat down to one side outside Brahmā's palace.
m.7.2.40.19: Then Nārada, having attained equality with Tumburu in singing, and permitted by Brahmā, the Supreme Lord, to keep company with him,
m.7.2.40.20: abandoning their mutual rivalry and reaching the highest friendship, together with him, and surrounded by Apsarases and Gandharvas,
m.7.2.40.21: came out of the Creator's palace, like the sun from a cloud, to sing with the vīṇā before the god Nakulīśvara, the Lord.
m.7.2.40.22: Seeing him, Nārada, the bull among sages, those sages of the six clans bowed and with great respect asked whether it was a suitable time to see the Lord.
m.7.2.40.23: Saying, this is indeed the right moment, go in from here, he went off, intent on other matters and in great haste.
m.7.2.40.24: Then those stationed at the door announced them to Brahmā, and thereupon they, forming a group, entered the dwelling of the Egg-born Brahmā.
m.7.2.40.25: Having entered, they bowed to the god from afar, prostrating on the ground like a staff; then, permitted by him, they gathered around and stood near him.
m.7.2.40.26: The Lotus-seated one, having asked about the welfare of those standing there, said: Your story is known to me, since Vāyu himself told us.
m.7.2.40.27: What did you do afterwards, when the Wind had vanished? When the Lord of gods had said this, the sages—about what happened after the avabhṛtha bath:
m.7.2.40.28: their going to the sacred ford of the Gaṅgā, the journey to Vārāṇasī, the seeing there of the liṅgas established by the lords of the gods,
m.7.2.40.29: the single worship of the Avimukteśvara liṅga as well, and the sight in the sky of that great mass of radiance,
m.7.2.40.30: the dissolution of the sages there, then the withdrawal of the radiance, and their wish for knowledge of its true nature, though they had pondered it themselves—
m.7.2.40.31: all this they told him in detail, bowing again and again. Having heard what the sages related, the four-faced Creator of all,
m.7.2.40.32: shook his head slightly and spoke in a deep voice: Supreme otherworldly perfection is drawing near to you.
m.7.2.40.33: The Lord, long worshipped by you through the long sacrificial session, has become inclined to grace—this is indicated by what has happened.
m.7.2.40.34: What you saw shining in the sky at Vārāṇasī was the supreme radiance of Maheśvara itself, known as the Liṅga.
m.7.2.40.35: And the sages who merged there, keepers of the Vedic Pāśupata vow, lifelong celibates whose sins were burnt away, became liberated and established in themselves.
m.7.2.40.36: That liberation is soon to be attained by you too through this Lord—this very meaning is indicated by the radiance you saw.
m.7.2.40.37: So this time has come to you of its own accord by destiny. Go to the southern peak of Meru, frequented by the gods,
m.7.2.40.38: where my son Sanatkumāra, the supreme sage, dwells, awaiting the coming in person of Nandin, lord of the bhūtas.
m.7.2.40.39: Long ago Sanatkumāra, even on seeing the Supreme Lord, out of ignorance thought himself the chief of all yogins and was spoiled in humility;
m.7.2.40.40: and, utterly fearless, he did not perform the proper courtesies such as rising to greet him. For that offence the angered Nandin turned him into a great camel.
m.7.2.40.41: Then, after a long time, I, grieving on his account, worshipped the God and the Goddess, and also propitiated Nandin,
m.7.2.40.42: and somehow, with effort, his wickedness was removed, and he was restored as before to the state of youth prefixed by Sanat, that is, to being Sanatkumāra.
m.7.2.40.43: Then Mahādeva, as if smiling, said to the lord of the gaṇas: Disregarding me myself, the sage became so arrogant.
m.7.2.40.44: Therefore you yourself, O sinless one, tell him my true nature—Brahmā's firstborn son, who regards me as though I were deluded.
m.7.2.40.45: By me alone he is given to you as a disciple, to be the promulgator of my knowledge; and he will perform your consecration as overseer of dharma.
m.7.2.40.46: Thus addressed again, the foremost of all the hosts of beings accepted the command, receiving it on his head, as he had before.
m.7.2.40.47: Likewise Sanatkumāra too, at my instruction, is performing on Meru austerity hard to perform, to win the grace of this gaṇa Nandin.
m.7.2.40.48: He should be seen by you before his meeting with the lord of the gaṇas; to bestow grace on him, Nandī will soon come there.
m.7.2.40.49: Thus quickly instructed and sent off by the universal yogin, the sages went to the Kumāra peak, south of Meru.
m.7.2.40.iti: Thus ends the fortieth adhyāya, named The journey of the sages of Naimiṣa, in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the seventh saṃhitā, the Vāyavīya-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
m.7.2.41.1: Sūta said: There was a lake named Skandasaras, like an ocean, whose water was sweet as nectar, cool, clear, deep and light.
m.7.2.41.2: It was enclosed all around by heaps of crystal stones, and all its quarters were covered with the blooming flowers of every season.
m.7.2.41.3: With its moss, blue lotuses, lotuses, and white water-lilies like stars, and its waves like clouds, it was like the sky come down to earth.
m.7.2.41.4: Its eight quarters shone with lovely stairways and landings made of blue stone, easy for going down and coming up.
m.7.2.41.5: It was frequented by young sages who had gone down into it and in great numbers come up out of it, bathed, wearing white sacred threads, white loincloths and bark garments,
m.7.2.41.6: some with matted locks and topknots, some shaven, adorned with the tripuṇḍra mark, their faces smiling and overcome by dispassion — young sons of sages,
m.7.2.41.7: with pots, cups of lotus leaves, auspicious jars, water-pots, and other such vessels like karakas,
m.7.2.41.8: its water was carried daily for themselves, for others, and especially for the deities, and flowers were gathered there.
m.7.2.41.9: It was frequented by sages of right conduct, standing on rocks in the water for fear of touching the lowly, their limbs grey with the ash they had applied,
m.7.2.41.10: by them diving here and there in the waters, cultured and dear ones seated on rocks, offering sesame, unbroken rice and flowers, having laid aside their darbha rings,
m.7.2.41.11: having completed the libations — first to the gods, in the middle to the sages, then to the ancestors — as one should, presenting offerings to the learned twice-born who had come for the daily bath,
m.7.2.41.12: with breezes laden with the scent of the many bali-offerings and flowers made at place after place, by those performing worship and the like on the altars, preceded by the arghya to the Sun.
m.7.2.41.13: In some places herd-leading elephants were diving, surfacing and wandering loose; in others does, deer and horses had come, driven by thirst;
m.7.2.41.14: in some places peacocks and fine elephants came out after drinking water; in others it was resplendent with bulls and rival bulls butting against the banks.
m.7.2.41.15: In places with the cries of kāraṇḍava ducks, in places with the calls of sārasa cranes, in places with the cries of cakravāka birds, in places with the songs of bees,
m.7.2.41.16: it seemed to be speaking again and again, with affection, to all those creatures who used it for bathing, drinking and the like and lived on the wealth of its trees.
m.7.2.41.17: With the calls of crowds of cuckoos nestled in the tops of the trees on its banks, it was inviting day and night all who were afflicted by the heat.
m.7.2.41.18: On the northern shore of that lake, beneath a wish-fulfilling tree, on an altar made of diamond-stone, on a soft deerskin,
m.7.2.41.19: they saw Sanatkumāra seated, ever bearing the body of a child, steady of mind, having just then come out of samādhi,
m.7.2.41.20: being attended by sages and worshipped even by the lords of yogins. Those Naimiṣa sages saw him, and bowing, approached him.
m.7.2.41.21: Just as they were telling him, who had asked, the reason for their coming, a tumultuous sound of drums was heard in the sky.
m.7.2.41.22: At that very moment a celestial car, radiant as the sun, was seen, surrounded on all sides by countless lords of the gaṇas,
m.7.2.41.23: crowded with troops of apsarases, surrounded by Rudra's maidens, resounding with mṛdaṅga and muraja drums, filled with the sound of flutes and vīṇās,
m.7.2.41.24: rich with canopies of many-coloured gems, shining with strings of pearls, and by sages, siddhas, gandharvas, yakṣas, cāraṇas and kinnaras
m.7.2.41.25: dancing, singing and playing instruments, it was surrounded; with a banner bearing the emblem of the heroic bull, on a staff of coral,
m.7.2.41.26: its gateway honoured by that banner, the sign of its dignity. In the middle of that celestial car, between a pair of chowries,
m.7.2.41.27: beneath a parasol with a jewelled handle, pure like the moon, seated on a divine lion-throne together with the goddess Suyaśā,
m.7.2.41.28: by his splendour, his form and his three eyes and other features making those who approached recognise in him the likeness of the Lord,
m.7.2.41.29: like the inviolable command of the Maker of the world come in person, like Śambhu's grace to all standing visibly before them,
m.7.2.41.30: — the son of Śilāda himself, bearing the glorious, excellent trident as his weapon, chief of the gaṇas of the Lord of the universe, like a second Viśveśvara,
m.7.2.41.31: able to restrain and to favour even the creators of the universe, four-armed, noble of limb, adorned with a crescent of the moon,
m.7.2.41.32: adorned with a serpent on his neck and the moon on his crown, like sovereignty embodied, like power in action,
m.7.2.41.33: like liberation fulfilled, like omniscience in company — seeing him, Brahmā's son, his face beaming with joy, together with the sages,
m.7.2.41.34: rose and stood with folded hands, as if offering himself to him. Then, meanwhile, when that celestial car had come down to earth,
m.7.2.41.35: having prostrated like a staff before the lord and praised him, he presented the sages: These sages of the six lineages, long engaged in a sacrificial session at Naimiṣa, have come, directed by Brahmā, out of a longing to see you from long before.
m.7.2.41.36: Hearing the words of Brahmā's son, Nandī at once cut their bonds with a glance, and having bestowed the Śaiva dharma and the lordly yoga of knowledge, went back to the side of the god.
m.7.2.41.37: All that was told by Sanatkumāra directly to Vyāsa, my teacher; and it was told to me by the revered Vyāsa; and by me it has been related to you in brief.
m.7.2.41.38: This jewel among Purāṇas, belonging to the Chastiser of the Cities, should not be told to those who do not know the Veda, nor to an undevoted disciple, nor to unbelievers; for if given out of delusion it brings hell.
m.7.2.41.39: Those by whom it is given, received, read or heard in the proper way, accompanied by service — to them it surely grants happiness, the triad of aims headed by dharma, and at the end liberation.
m.7.2.41.40: A mutual service has been rendered by you and by me through our joining on the path of the Purāṇas. Therefore I shall go, my desire fulfilled. May everything always be auspicious for us.
m.7.2.41.41: When Sūta had given his blessings and departed, and the sacrifice, that great undertaking, had come to its end, and when the age of Kali was growing polluted by attachment to sense-objects, the sages of good conduct took up their dwelling in the environs of Vārāṇasī.
m.7.2.41.42: Then those blameless ones, out of the desire to be freed from the bonds of the bound soul (paśu), performed the Pāśupata vow in its entirety, and, having mastered complete knowledge and meditative absorption, attained supreme bliss.
m.7.2.41.43: Vyāsa said: Thus this beneficial Śiva Purāṇa is complete. It should be read with care and reverence, and in the same way it should be heard.
m.7.2.41.44: It should not be recited to an unbeliever, to one without faith, or to a deceitful person, nor to one not devoted to Maheśa, nor likewise to a hypocrite who makes a show of dharma.
m.7.2.41.45: By hearing this even once, sin is reduced to ashes; one without devotion obtains devotion, and a devotee comes to share in an abundance of devotion.
m.7.2.41.46: When it is heard again, true devotion arises; and from hearing it yet again, liberation results. Therefore those who seek liberation should hear it again and again.
m.7.2.41.47: Five recitations of this Purāṇa should be performed with a pure mind; one who does so with the supreme fruit in view attains it, without doubt.
m.7.2.41.48: Kings of old, brāhmaṇas, and excellent vaiśyas, having recited it seven times, obtained the vision of Śiva.
m.7.2.41.49: Even now, whatever human being, intent on devotion, hears this shall enjoy all pleasures here and at the end attain liberation.
m.7.2.41.50: This Śiva Purāṇa is supremely dear to Śiva; it grants enjoyment and liberation, is equal to the Veda, and increases devotion.
m.7.2.41.51: May that Śaṅkara, together with his gaṇas, his sons, and Ambā, always bestow welfare upon the reciter and the listener of this Śiva Purāṇa.
m.7.2.41.iti: Thus ends the forty-first adhyāya, named Vyāsa's teaching and the greatness of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa, in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the seventh saṃhitā, the Vāyavīya-saṃhitā, of the Śrī Śivamahāpurāṇa.
